everyday.story: In a shared document, if one person edits, everyone else must wait. That is a lock. Now imagine the document keeps the old version for readers while one person edits a new version. Readers are never blocked. That is the idea behind MVCC. Two people editing the same line still have to sort it out.
maps: Readers see the old copy, the editor works on a new one
Two people editing the same line
words: A claim that stops others from changing or reading the same row for a while.
Keeping several versions of a row so readers see an old version while a writer makes a new one.
Two transactions each waiting for the other, so neither can move.
A frozen view of the data as it was at one moment.

title: Replication
tagline: Keep copies of your data on more machines, so more people can read it and one failure does not stop you.
explain: Replication means keeping copies of the same database on several machines. You do it for three reasons: availability (another copy takes over if one dies), read scaling (spread read queries across copies), and safety (a copy survives losing a machine or a data center). It does not make writes faster.
## The usual setup: primary and replicas

One machine, the primary, accepts all writes. It records every change in its write-ahead log (WAL) and streams that log to one or more replicas, which replay it. Replicas serve read-only queries. If the primary fails, you promote a replica to be the new primary. This is called failover.
## Synchronous vs asynchronous

- Asynchronous: the primary commits and replies to the client right away, and ships the change to replicas afterwards. Fast, but if the primary dies before a change reaches any replica, that committed change is lost after failover. This is the common default.
- Synchronous: the primary waits for at least one replica to confirm before replying. No lost commits, but every write pays the network round trip, and if the replica is down, writes stall unless you configure fallback.
- A middle path is to require confirmation from one of several replicas.
## Replication lag and the trouble it causes

With asynchronous replication, a replica is always slightly behind the primary. Usually milliseconds, but under heavy write load or a slow network it can reach seconds or minutes. The classic symptom is read-your-own-writes failure:

> A user changes their profile name. The write goes to the primary. The page reloads and the read goes to a replica that has not received the change yet, so the user sees the old name and thinks the save failed. Fixes: read from the primary for a short time after a user writes; route 'important' reads to the primary; or record the WAL position of the write and only read from a replica that has reached it.
## Failover: where it goes wrong

- Promoting a lagging replica loses the unreplicated changes.
- Split brain: the old primary comes back and believes it is still the primary, so two machines accept writes and the data diverges. Real systems use a consensus or fencing mechanism so only one primary exists at a time.
- Applications must reconnect to the new primary. A connection pool or proxy that tracks the primary helps.
## Other topologies

- Multi-primary (multi-master): several machines accept writes. It needs conflict resolution, because two people can change the same row in two places. Powerful but complicated.
- Logical replication: replicates row changes by table rather than the raw log, useful for upgrades and for feeding other systems.
- Cascading replicas: a replica feeds other replicas to reduce load on the primary.
## In Django

Declare more than one entry in DATABASES (for example default and replica) and add a database router with db_for_read and db_for_write so reads go to the replica and writes to the primary. Remember that inside a transaction you usually want the primary, and that anything that must see a just-written row should read from the primary.
Interview staples: sync vs async trade-off, what replication lag is and how it shows up, what failover and split brain are, and why replicas help reads but not writes.
keyPoints: Replication ≠ backup. PITR = base backup + archived WAL.
Async: faster, may lose last commits. Sync: safer, couples availability.
Route reads by consistency need, not by default.
Failover risks: split-brain, lag, promotion of a stale replica.

sql.title: Observing lag

django.title: Database router for read replicas
django.note: Real systems add "sticky primary for N seconds after a write" per session, or compare LSNs. Django does not do this for you.

exercise: Define RPO/RTO for a store. Decide which endpoints may use a replica, and how the API handles replication lag right after checkout.
pitfalls: Treating a replica as a backup.
Reading order status from a replica immediately after creating it.
Never testing a restore.

interview.q: Replication vs backup?
interview.a: Replication improves availability and read scale but copies deletes and corruption. Backups and WAL/PITR enable recovery to an earlier moment.

interview.q: Synchronous vs asynchronous replication?
interview.a: Sync waits for configured standby acknowledgement: less acknowledged-write loss, more latency and coupling. Async is faster but can lag and lose recent commits on failover.

interview.q: What are RPO and RTO?
interview.a: RPO = tolerable data-loss window; RTO = tolerable recovery time. Backup frequency, WAL archiving, replication mode and failover automation determine them.

interview.q: Recover from an accidental DELETE?
interview.a: Stop further damage, preserve evidence, restore a backup to a separate instance, replay WAL to just before the delete, validate, then extract/cut over.

basis: Mid priority at 0-5 yrs, core at 5+: read/write routers, failover and eventual consistency are senior Django topics.

scenes.title: Replication, step by step

learn.text: Why one primary is not enough
Reads on replicas, writes on the primary

steps.title: One database does everything
body: Every read and every write goes to one primary database. Reads far outnumber writes, and the primary is at 95% CPU. Numbers here are illustrative.
It is also one machine: if it dies, writes and reads stop.

steps.title: Add a replica for reads
body: A replica is a copy of the primary that applies every change it sends. It can answer read queries, so the primary only has to do the writes.
In Django, a database router sends reads to the replica and writes to the primary.

steps.title: Writes flow one way
body: Every write goes to the primary, which streams the change to each replica. A replica applies changes in the order they happened, so it always shows a state the primary once had.
Replicas are read-only copies; they never accept writes of their own.

callout.text: Replication spreads read load and gives you a spare copy. It does not spread write load.

steps.title: Replication lag
body: Copying takes time. With asynchronous replication the replica can be a little behind the primary: here 2 seconds.
A user saves their profile, the page reloads and reads from the replica, and they see the old data.

callout.text: Lag is normal, not a failure. Design for it: the same query can return different answers from the primary and a replica.

changes: ~ Replica lags the primary by 2 s

predict.question: A user saves a change, then reloads a page that reads from a replica 2 seconds behind. What do they see?
predict.why: The replica has not applied the write yet, so it still returns the old row. This is replication lag.

steps.title: Read your own writes
body: After a user writes, send that user's next reads to the primary for a short time (or until the replica has caught up). Other users keep using replicas.
In Django a router can check a flag you set on the request or session, or you can use .using('default') for the specific read.

card.title: Django
lines: # everything else reads from the replica

changes: + A short window of primary reads after a write

steps.title: The primary fails
body: The primary crashes. Writes fail until a replica is promoted to take its place; this is failover. Tools or a managed database can do it automatically.
The replica must be told it is now the primary, and the app must send its writes there.

steps.title: After promotion, and what may be lost
body: Replica 1 becomes the primary and a new replica joins. With asynchronous replication, changes that had not yet reached the replica when the old primary died are not on the new primary: here the last 2 seconds of writes.
Synchronous replication waits for the replica before confirming a write, which avoids that loss but makes every write slower.

callout.text: Asynchronous replication trades possible loss of the very latest writes for fast writes. Decide which you can accept.

changes: - The last 2 s of old-primary writes

steps.title: Recap: copies for reads and for survival
body: Replicas spread reads and give you a spare copy to promote. The costs are lag (stale reads), possible loss on failover with async replication, and more machines to run.
Remember: reads from replicas, writes to the primary, read-your-writes for the writer, and know what a failover can lose.

lines: 1 reads to replicas, writes to the primary
5 async is fast, sync is safer

everyday.plain: Replication keeps copies of your data on other machines, so reading is shared and one failure does not stop you.
everyday.story: A popular textbook has one copy in the library, and fifty students queue for it. The library buys four more copies and puts them on different floors. Now more students can read at once, and if one copy is lost, the others remain. But a correction made in one copy takes a moment to reach the others. And copies are not a backup: if someone writes a wrong line in all copies, they are all wrong.

All copies have the same mistake

Switching to a spare machine when the main one fails.

title: Sharding
tagline: Split one huge database into smaller parts on different machines. Try this last.
explain: Sharding splits one large dataset across several database servers, so each server holds only a part, called a shard. Replication copies the same data to many machines; sharding divides different data between machines. You shard when a single primary can no longer handle the write volume or the data size, even after you have optimized queries, added indexes, and added replicas.
## Try these first

Sharding adds permanent complexity. Before it: add indexes, fix slow queries, add caching, scale the machine up (vertical scaling), add read replicas, archive old data, and consider partitioning a big table inside one database. Many systems never need sharding.
## Partitioning vs sharding

Partitioning splits one table into pieces, but they live in the same database server. It helps queries and maintenance (drop an old month instantly). Sharding spreads the pieces across several servers, which is what actually raises the ceiling on writes and storage.
## The shard key
Every row is routed to a shard using a shard key, such as user_id. Choosing the key is the most important decision, and it is hard to change later.

- Range sharding: shard 1 holds ids 1 to 1 million, shard 2 the next million. Simple, and range queries are easy, but new data piles onto the newest shard, creating a hotspot.
- Hash sharding: shard = hash(key) mod N. Spreads load evenly, but range queries must ask every shard, and changing N moves most of the data.
- Directory (lookup) sharding: a table maps each key to its shard. Flexible, but the lookup becomes a dependency and a possible bottleneck.
- Consistent hashing: keys and servers sit on a ring, so adding a server moves only a small share of keys. Used in distributed caches and many datastores.

> Shard by user_id, so all of one user's rows live together. 'Show my orders' touches one shard. But 'total sales today across all users' must ask every shard and merge the results. Shard by country instead and a country with most of your users becomes a hotspot. A good key has high cardinality, spreads load evenly, and matches your most common query.
Hash-mod routing has a hidden cost: changing the number of servers reshuffles almost every key. Consistent hashing fixes that. Add a server and compare.
@viz:hashring
## What you give up

- Joins and transactions across shards are hard or impossible. Either keep related data on the same shard or accept eventual consistency and design around it.
- Unique constraints and auto-increment ids are only unique per shard. You need globally unique ids, such as UUIDs or snowflake-style ids.
- Resharding (changing the number of shards) is a heavy operation. Plan for it with many small logical shards mapped onto few physical servers.
- Operations multiply: backups, migrations, and monitoring per shard.
## In Django

Django can talk to several databases and route with a database router, so you can implement shard routing, but it gives you no built-in sharding and no cross-shard joins. Most teams use managed sharded databases or a tool such as Citus for PostgreSQL rather than hand-rolling it.

Interview staples: shard vs replica vs partition, how to choose a shard key, hotspots, and how to handle cross-shard queries. In system design answers, always say you would scale vertically, add replicas and caching first, and shard only when the numbers demand it.
keyPoints: Order of escalation: index → pool → vertical → partition → replicas → shard.
Shard key: high cardinality, even, aligned with queries.
Cross-shard queries/transactions are the cost you pay.
Plan rebalancing before day one.

interview.q: Partitioning vs sharding?
interview.a: Partitioning divides a table within one database/cluster. Sharding distributes data across independent database nodes and adds routing and coordination complexity.

interview.q: How do you choose a shard key?
interview.a: Query locality, cardinality, even distribution, tenant/customer boundaries, growth, hotspot risk and the cost of cross-shard operations.

interview.q: When should you shard?
interview.a: Only after measuring and exhausting indexing, query redesign, pooling, vertical scale, partitioning and replicas — and after quantifying the operational cost.

title: Consistency Models
tagline: How up to date must the data be for each feature? Decide that feature by feature.
explain: Consistency models describe what a reader is guaranteed to see when data is stored on more than one machine, or both in a database and in a cache. Strong guarantees are easier to reason about and cost latency and availability. Weak guarantees are fast and available and push complexity onto you.
## The main models

- Strong (linearizable) consistency: once a write completes, every later read, anywhere, sees it. Behaves like a single copy. Needs coordination between machines, so it is slower and can become unavailable during network failures.
- Eventual consistency: if no new writes arrive, all copies converge to the same value eventually. Reads in the meantime may return older data. Fast and highly available.
- Read-your-writes: you always see your own writes, even if others do not yet.
- Monotonic reads: you never see data go backwards in time between two reads.
- Causal consistency: if one event causes another (a reply to a post), everyone sees them in that order.
## The CAP theorem and PACELC

CAP says that during a network partition (some machines cannot talk to others), a distributed system must choose between consistency (refuse or delay some requests to stay correct) and availability (keep answering, possibly with stale data). It does not say you only get two of three in normal operation. PACELC extends it: even without a partition, there is a trade-off between latency and consistency. Strong consistency costs round trips.

> A bank balance must not be stale: choose consistency, accept that some requests fail during a partition. A video view counter or a social feed can be a few seconds stale: choose availability and eventual consistency.
## Consistency in everyday backends: the cache
The most common place you meet this is a cache in front of a database. The cache and the database are two copies, and you must keep them in step.

- Cache-aside: read from cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache. On a write, update the database and delete the cache entry. Deleting is safer than updating the cache.
- Write-through: write to the cache and the database together. Simple, but writes pay both costs.
- Write-behind: write to the cache and flush to the database later. Fast, but you can lose data on a crash.
- TTL (time to live): every entry expires after some time, which bounds how stale it can be. Always set one.
@viz:cache-aside
## The stale-cache race

Even cache-aside can go wrong. Reader A misses the cache and reads the old value from the database. Meanwhile writer B updates the database and deletes the cache entry. Then A writes its old value into the cache. The cache now holds stale data until the TTL expires. This is why TTLs matter, and why for critical data you read from the database. Another danger is a cache stampede: a popular key expires and hundreds of requests hit the database at once. Mitigate with a lock around the rebuild, jittered TTLs, or refreshing before expiry.
## In Django

Use the cache framework with Redis: cache.get, cache.set with a timeout, and cache.delete on writes. Delete cached entries in transaction.on_commit() so you never invalidate before the database change is visible. For data you can regenerate, a short TTL is often the simplest correct answer.
Interview staples: strong vs eventual consistency with an example of each, CAP stated correctly, cache-aside with its race condition, and stampede mitigation.
keyPoints: Per-feature consistency table: price, stock, order status, feed, counters.
Read-your-writes: after a write, route that user to the primary / bypass cache.
Monotonic reads: never show a user older data than they already saw.
Invalidate cache in transaction.on_commit.

-- primary, after commit
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();            -- 0/3000148

-- replica: has it replayed that point yet?
SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= '0/3000148'::pg_lsn AS caught_up;

django.title: Invalidate after commit
django.code:
def update_price(product_id, new_price):
    with transaction.atomic():
        Product.objects.filter(pk=product_id).update(price=new_price)
        # delete cache only once the new price is visible to other connections
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: cache.delete(f"product:{product_id}"))
django.note: Invalidating inside the transaction before commit lets another request re-cache the OLD value — a classic stale-cache bug.

interview.q: What is eventual consistency?
interview.a: Replicas or derived views converge after propagation; clients may briefly see stale data. Define the acceptable staleness and user-visible behavior.

interview.q: What is replication lag and why does it matter?
interview.a: A replica may not yet contain a recent commit. Read-after-write flows should use the primary or wait/route based on the consistency needed.

interview.q: How would you cache product data safely?
interview.a: Cache-aside with TTL, invalidate on write after commit, version keys or short TTL for correctness, stampede protection (lock / single-flight), and fall back to the DB if Redis is down.

body: In Django, run the invalidation in transaction.on_commit(), so it happens only after the data is visible to other readers.

steps.title: Read your own writes
body: With replicas, a user who just saved something may read from a replica that has not caught up and see the old value. After a write, send that user's next reads to the primary for a short time, or until the replica has caught up.

steps.title: Monotonic reads and a staleness bound

A bound can be tested and monitored.

body: When a popular key expires, thousands of requests can miss at once and all go to the database. Add jitter to TTLs, use a lock so one request refills it, or refresh before expiry.
Recap: choose per feature, invalidate on commit, read your own writes, give a staleness bound.

everyday.plain: Different features need different levels of 'everyone sees the same thing right now'.
everyday.story: When you post a photo, it is fine if a friend sees it a few seconds late. When you transfer money, it is not fine if the balance shows two different numbers. So the photo feature can use a relaxed rule, and the bank must use a strict one. Strict is safer but slower. You choose per feature.
maps: Photo shows up a bit late
words: Everyone always sees the latest write.
Copies may differ for a short while, but they will agree later.
After you change something, you always see your own change.

title: Django ORM in Depth
tagline: Use Python instead of SQL with Django, and avoid the slow mistakes it makes easy.
explain: The ORM lets you write database queries as Python. It is convenient, and it hides the SQL, which is where most Django performance bugs come from. The goal of this lesson is to always know what SQL your code produces and how many queries it runs.
## QuerySets are lazy

A QuerySet is lazy: building it runs no SQL. The query executes when you iterate it, call list(), len() or bool() on it, or call .get(), .count() or .exists(). The results are cached on that QuerySet object, so iterating it twice hits the database once. But chaining another .filter() creates a new QuerySet and a new query.

> orders = Order.objects.filter(status='paid')   # no query yet
for o in orders: ...                              # one query runs here
len(orders)                                       # uses the cache, no new query
orders.count()                                    # runs a new SELECT COUNT(*)
If you only need to know whether any row exists, use .exists(), which stops at the first match. len(qs) loads every row into memory just to count them.
## The N+1 problem

The classic production bug: one query fetches a list, then one extra query runs per row whenever you touch a related object in a loop. Templates and serializers do this silently. With 100 orders, printing order.customer.name in a loop runs 101 queries.

- select_related() follows foreign keys and one-to-one links with a SQL JOIN, in a single query. Use it for 'the one related object'.
- prefetch_related() runs one extra query per relation and joins in Python. Use it for reverse foreign keys and many-to-many, where a JOIN would multiply rows.
- Prefetch() lets you filter or order the prefetched rows, or store them under a custom attribute.

> Order.objects.select_related('customer').prefetch_related('items__product')
This is 3 queries in total (orders joined with customers, then items, then products), no matter how many orders there are.
## Push work into the database

- F() expressions: refer to a column inside the query. update(stock=F('stock') - 1) is one atomic UPDATE with no read-modify-write race.
- Q() objects: build OR and NOT conditions, as in Q(status='paid') | Q(total__gt=1000).
- annotate() with Count, Sum or Avg: a per-row aggregate, which is a GROUP BY. aggregate() returns a single summary dictionary for the whole set.
- values() and values_list(): fetch only the columns you need, as dictionaries or tuples, skipping model object creation.
- only() and defer(): load a model but skip heavy columns.
- update(), bulk_create() and bulk_update() are single statements, but they skip save() overrides and signals.
## Migrations

A migration is a Python file that records a schema change. makemigrations writes it from your model changes and migrate applies it. Treat migrations as production code. Never edit one that has already been applied anywhere. On a big table, adding a column with a default, or an index without CONCURRENTLY, can lock the table, so add the column as nullable, backfill in batches, then add the constraint. Use RunPython with a reverse function for data changes, and keep schema and data migrations separate.
## See under the hood

str(qs.query) shows the SQL, qs.explain() shows the plan, django-debug-toolbar shows the query count per page, and assertNumQueries in a test locks the count in so a regression fails the build. When the ORM cannot express a query, use raw() or a cursor with parameters (%s placeholders, never f-strings).
keyPoints: QuerySets are lazy and cached; .exists() and .count() beat len(qs) when you do not need the rows.
N+1 = 1 + N queries. select_related = JOIN (single-valued relations); prefetch_related = extra query (multi-valued).
F() updates atomically in the database; Q() builds OR/NOT; annotate() = GROUP BY per row; aggregate() = one result.
update() and bulk_*() skip save() and signals.
Measure, do not guess: qs.query, qs.explain(), assertNumQueries.

sql.title: N+1 versus JOIN versus prefetch
annotate() is a GROUP BY
sql.code:
-- Order.objects.annotate(n_items=Count("items"), total=Sum(F("items__quantity") * F("items__unit_price")))
-- produces roughly:
SELECT o.id, COUNT(i.product_id) AS n_items, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id;

sql.title: F() is one atomic UPDATE
sql.code:
-- Inventory.objects.filter(product_id=42, available_qty__gte=1).update(available_qty=F("available_qty") - 1)
UPDATE inventory
   SET available_qty = available_qty - 1
 WHERE product_id = 42 AND available_qty >= 1;     -- rows affected = 1 or 0, no read-modify-write race

django.title: Fix N+1, prove it, push work to the database, migrate safely
django.code:
from django.db import migrations, models
from django.db.models import F, Q, Count, Sum, Prefetch
from django.contrib.postgres.operations import AddIndexConcurrently

# 1) N+1 and the fix
for o in Order.objects.all()[:20]:
    print(o.customer.full_name)                 # 1 + 20 queries

orders = (Order.objects
          .select_related("customer")                                                      # JOIN
          .prefetch_related(Prefetch("items", queryset=OrderItem.objects.select_related("product")))
          [:20])                                                                           # 2 queries total

# 2) make N+1 a failing test, not a production incident
class OrderListTests(TestCase):
    def test_query_count_is_constant(self):
        with self.assertNumQueries(2):
            list(orders_for_list())

# 3) let the database do the work
Inventory.objects.filter(product_id=42, available_qty__gte=1).update(available_qty=F("available_qty") - 1)
Product.objects.filter(Q(active=True) & (Q(price__lt=500) | Q(name__icontains="sale")))
Order.objects.annotate(n_items=Count("items"), total=Sum(F("items__quantity") * F("items__unit_price")))

# 4) index a big table without blocking writes
class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    atomic = False                                # CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction
    operations = [AddIndexConcurrently("product", models.Index(fields=["category", "-created_at"], name="idx_prod_cat_created"))]
django.note: Put assertNumQueries on every list endpoint. It turns an N+1 into a failing test instead of a slow production page. Test against PostgreSQL where you can; SQLite hides locking and planner behavior.

exercise: Take a view that lists 20 orders with the customer name and each order's items. Count the queries (debug toolbar or assertNumQueries) before and after fixing it with select_related and prefetch_related, then write the test that locks the count in. Finally add a composite index with AddIndexConcurrently and show with qs.explain() that it is used.
pitfalls: Touching related objects in a loop, template or serializer without select_related/prefetch_related.
Calling .filter() on an already-prefetched relation: it ignores the prefetch cache and queries again. Use Prefetch(queryset=…) instead.
Using len(qs) or bool(qs) just to check for rows: use .exists() / .count().
Read-modify-write in Python (obj.qty -= 1; obj.save()) instead of F(): lost updates under concurrency.
Expecting update(), bulk_create() or bulk_update() to run save() overrides or signals.
Adding a column with a default, or backfilling millions of rows, in one migration on a live table.

interview.q: select_related vs prefetch_related?
interview.a: select_related does a SQL JOIN and loads the related row in the same query; it works for ForeignKey and OneToOne (single-valued). prefetch_related issues a separate query per relation and stitches the results together in Python; use it for reverse foreign keys and many-to-many, or when a JOIN would multiply rows. Prefetch() lets you filter or order the prefetched queryset.

interview.q: How do you find and fix an N+1 problem in Django?
interview.a: Detect it with django-debug-toolbar, query logging, or assertNumQueries in a test. Fix it by loading what you will touch up front: select_related for FK/one-to-one, prefetch_related for the rest. Then lock the query count in with assertNumQueries so it cannot regress.

interview.q: get() vs filter()?
interview.a: get() returns exactly one object and raises DoesNotExist if none or MultipleObjectsReturned if several. filter() returns a QuerySet that may be empty and is lazy. Use get_object_or_404 in views.

interview.q: Explain QuerySet laziness and caching.
interview.a: Creating or chaining a QuerySet runs no SQL; it executes on iteration, list(), len(), bool(), get(), count() or exists(). Once evaluated, results are cached on that object, so iterating again does not re-query, but a new .filter() builds a new QuerySet and queries again.

interview.q: update() vs save() on a model?
interview.a: update() on a QuerySet issues one UPDATE statement, returns the number of rows changed, and skips save() overrides and pre/post_save signals. save() works on one instance, runs the override and signals, and writes all fields unless you pass update_fields.

interview.q: What is an F() expression and why use it?
interview.a: F() refers to a column value inside the database, e.g. update(qty=F('qty') - 1). The calculation happens in one atomic UPDATE, so concurrent requests cannot overwrite each other the way a Python read-modify-write can.

interview.q: annotate() vs aggregate()?
interview.a: aggregate() collapses the whole queryset to one dict of values (e.g. total revenue). annotate() adds a computed value to each row, which with Count/Sum becomes a GROUP BY (e.g. item count per order).

interview.q: How do you add an index to a large table in production without blocking writes?
interview.a: Use AddIndexConcurrently from django.contrib.postgres.operations in a migration with atomic = False, which runs CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Backfill data in batches in a separate step.

basis: Core. select_related/prefetch_related, F and Q objects, aggregation and migrations are the standard mid-level Django ORM topics; N+1, indexing and zero-downtime migrations appear at senior level.

scenes.title: The N+1 query problem, step by step

steps.title: List 100 orders with their customers
body: A page lists 100 orders and prints each order's customer name. The code looks harmless: a loop over orders and order.customer.name.
Behind that attribute access the ORM may run a query.

steps.title: 1 query for the orders
body: Order.objects.all() runs one query that returns 100 orders. The customer is not loaded yet: each order only holds a customer_id.
So far: 1 query.

steps.title: Then 1 query per order
body: Touching order.customer for the first order makes a query for that customer. The next order makes another. After 100 orders that is 100 more queries.
1 query for the list plus N queries for the related rows: the N+1 problem.

callout.text: N+1 is invisible in the code and in small test data. It shows up as a page that gets slower with every row.

steps.title: select_related: join in one query
body: For a foreign key or one-to-one, ask the ORM to join: Order.objects.select_related('customer'). One SQL JOIN returns each order with its customer.
Queries drop from 101 to 1.

steps.title: prefetch_related: two queries for many-to-many
body: For many-to-many and reverse foreign keys a JOIN would repeat rows, so prefetch_related runs a second query for all the related rows and joins them in Python.
Two queries however many orders there are.

steps.title: Find it before users do
body: Count queries in tests with assertNumQueries, look at the SQL in the Django debug toolbar, or log queries in development. Test with realistic row counts.
A test that pins the query count catches a regression the day it is introduced.

steps.title: Recap: ask for related rows up front
body: N+1 means 1 query plus one per row for related data. Use select_related for single related objects, prefetch_related for collections, and pin the count in a test.
Fewer round trips is almost always the first thing to fix in a slow Django page.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 loop touching a relation? suspect N+1

everyday.plain: Django lets you work with the database using Python objects, but you must know what queries it quietly sends.
everyday.story: You ask an assistant: 'bring me 50 customers and their cities'. A careless assistant brings the customers, then walks back to the office 50 times to ask 'what is this one's city?'. A smart assistant gets customers and cities in one trip. Django can behave like either, depending on how you ask. The slow version is called the N+1 problem.
maps: A separate trip for each customer
Telling the assistant exactly what you need

A Django description of a database query that runs only when needed.
One query to get a list, then one more query for each item in it.

title: Django REST Framework & API Design
tagline: Build the menu that other programs use to talk to your app.
explain: Django REST Framework (DRF) turns Django models into HTTP APIs. It is built from a few layers, and knowing what each layer does lets you drop down a level when the magic gets in your way.
## Serializers

A serializer does two jobs: it validates incoming data (deserialization) and shapes outgoing data (serialization). ModelSerializer generates fields and validators from a model. Add field-level validation with validate_<field>() and cross-field rules with validate(). Keep business rules out of the serializer where possible and in a service function, so they work from the API, the admin and management commands alike.

> class OrderSerializer(ModelSerializer):
    class Meta: model = Order; fields = ['id', 'items', 'total']; read_only_fields = ['total']
Marking total read-only means a client can send any number and it is ignored. Never trust a client-sent price or status.
## Views: three layers

- APIView: you write get, post and so on yourself. Full control.
- Generic views (ListCreateAPIView and friends): mixins that provide the common list, create, retrieve, update and delete behavior.
- ViewSet plus a Router: full CRUD from one class and automatic URLs. Least code, most magic.
## Authentication and permissions

Authentication answers who you are (session, token, or JWT through a third-party package). Permissions answer whether you may do this. IsAuthenticated protects the view, but the bug that ships to production is the missing object-level check: any logged-in user can fetch /orders/123. Fix it by filtering get_queryset() by request.user, or by implementing has_object_permission. Throttling limits request rates per user, IP or scope.
## List endpoints

- Pagination: page-number and limit/offset pagination use SQL OFFSET and get slower on deep pages, because the database must skip all earlier rows. Cursor pagination uses a keyset (WHERE id < last_seen ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT n) so it stays fast and stable while rows are inserted.
- Filtering and ordering: allow only a list of named fields, never arbitrary columns.
- Query tuning: serializers are the most common place N+1 hides, so build the queryset in get_queryset() with select_related and prefetch_related.
## Write endpoints

- Validate in the serializer and keep business rules in a service function inside transaction.atomic().
- Return consistent status codes: 400 validation error, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 429 throttled.
- PUT replaces the whole resource, PATCH changes part of it.
- Make POSTs that create valuable things idempotent with an Idempotency-Key header, so a retry after a timeout cannot create a duplicate order.
- Version your API (a URL prefix such as /api/v1/) before clients depend on it.
keyPoints: Serializer = validation + representation; ModelSerializer generates both from the model.
APIView → generic views → ViewSet + Router: less code, more magic.
Authentication ≠ authorization. Object-level checks prevent IDOR.
Cursor pagination for big or fast-changing lists; allowlist ordering and filter fields.
N+1 hides in serializers: optimize get_queryset().
PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates; Idempotency-Key makes POST retry-safe.

sql.title: Offset versus cursor (keyset) pagination
sql.code:
-- Offset: the database reads and discards 100,000 rows to return 20
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

-- Cursor / keyset: start after the last row you returned; an index on (created_at, id) makes it cheap
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-11-01 10:00:00+00', 98765)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

sql.title: Idempotency keys
sql.code:
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key             TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  request_hash    TEXT NOT NULL,
  response_status INTEGER,
  response_body   JSONB,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING;  0 rows inserted -> a retry: return the stored response

django.title: A safe, fast list endpoint
django.code:
from rest_framework import serializers, viewsets, filters
from rest_framework.pagination import CursorPagination
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.throttling import ScopedRateThrottle

class OrderSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    items = OrderItemSerializer(many=True, read_only=True)
    class Meta:
        model = Order
        fields = ["id", "status", "total_amount", "created_at", "items"]   # explicit, never "__all__"
        read_only_fields = ["status", "total_amount"]                       # the client may not set these

class OrderPagination(CursorPagination):
    page_size = 20
    ordering = ("-created_at", "-id")                                       # stable, indexed ordering

class OrderViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = OrderSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]
    pagination_class = OrderPagination
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ["created_at", "total_amount"]                        # allowlist
    throttle_classes = [ScopedRateThrottle]
    throttle_scope = "orders"                                               # rate set in REST_FRAMEWORK["DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES"]

    def get_queryset(self):
        return (Order.objects
                .filter(customer__user=self.request.user)                   # object-level isolation: no IDOR
                .select_related("customer")
                .prefetch_related("items__product"))                        # no N+1 inside the serializer
django.note: For POST /orders, read the Idempotency-Key header, look it up in your idempotency table inside the same transaction, and return the stored response on a repeat. The serializer should never accept price, status or total from the client.

exercise: Build GET /orders with cursor pagination, an ordering allowlist and object-level isolation, and a test using assertNumQueries that proves the query count does not grow with the number of orders. Then build POST /orders with an Idempotency-Key and test that sending it twice returns the same order and creates only one.
pitfalls: fields = "__all__" leaking internal columns or allowing mass assignment.
Checking IsAuthenticated but never filtering objects by owner (IDOR).
Nested serializers or SerializerMethodField running a query per row.
Offset pagination on large tables; ordering by a non-unique field with cursor pagination.
Letting clients order or filter by any field.
Trusting the client for price, total or status; returning 200 with an error body.

interview.q: What does a DRF serializer do?
interview.a: It validates incoming data (deserialization) and converts model instances to primitive types for the response (serialization). ModelSerializer generates fields and validators from a model; validate_<field>() and validate() add custom rules.

interview.q: APIView vs generic views vs ViewSets?
interview.a: APIView gives you raw HTTP method handlers. Generic views add reusable mixins (list, create, retrieve…). ViewSets group related actions into one class and a Router generates the URLs. Moving up the stack means less code and less visibility; drop down when you need custom behavior.

interview.q: Authentication vs permissions in DRF?
interview.a: Authentication identifies the caller (session, token, JWT via a package). Permissions decide if that caller may perform the action (IsAuthenticated, custom classes, has_object_permission). Both run before the view body.

interview.q: How do you prevent one user reading another user's data (IDOR)?
interview.a: Authorize the object, not just the user: filter get_queryset() by the owner (e.g. customer__user=request.user) so other people's objects return 404, or implement has_object_permission, and test it with two users.

interview.q: Why prefer cursor pagination over offset?
interview.a: OFFSET makes the database scan and discard all earlier rows, so deep pages get slow, and inserts between requests cause skipped or duplicated items. Cursor (keyset) pagination filters from the last seen value using an index, so it stays fast and stable. It needs a stable, unique ordering.

interview.q: How do you avoid N+1 in DRF?
interview.a: Build the queryset in get_queryset() with select_related / prefetch_related for everything the serializer touches, and lock the count with assertNumQueries.

interview.q: PUT vs PATCH?
interview.a: PUT replaces the whole resource and expects all required fields; PATCH applies a partial update (serializer partial=True).

interview.q: How do you make POST /orders safe to retry?
interview.a: Require an Idempotency-Key header, store key + request hash + response in the same transaction as the order, and on a repeat return the stored response instead of creating another order. A unique constraint on the key protects against concurrent duplicates.

basis: Core for Django roles. Serializers, viewsets, routers, filtering and pagination are in the Middle (3-5 yrs) Django topic list; API design is the mid-level focus.

scenes.title: A DRF API, step by step

steps.title: A request through DRF
body: The client sends JSON. The view authenticates the caller, the serializer validates the input, the queryset talks to the database, and the serializer turns the result back into JSON.
A ModelSerializer generates the fields and validation from the model.

card.title: Pieces
lines: Router     maps URLs to a ViewSet

steps.title: Serializer validates before saving
body: Bad input is rejected with a 400 and field errors before it reaches the database. List the fields explicitly rather than fields = '__all__', which can expose internal columns or allow mass assignment.
Use read_only_fields for ids and owners.

steps.title: Authenticated is not authorized
body: Checking IsAuthenticated only proves who the caller is. If /orders/7/ returns any order to any logged-in user, one user can read another's data: an insecure direct object reference (IDOR).
Filter the queryset by owner.

predict.question: A logged-in user requests /orders/7/, which belongs to someone else. The view checks only IsAuthenticated. What happens?
predict.why: Authentication passed and nothing checked ownership, so the object is returned. Restrict the queryset (filter(owner=request.user)) or add an object-level permission.

steps.title: Fix: filter by owner
body: Override get_queryset so a user only ever sees their own rows. A request for someone else's id then returns 404.
Object-level permissions are an alternative when ownership is more complex.

steps.title: N+1 hides in serializers
body: A nested serializer or a SerializerMethodField that touches a related object runs one extra query per row. 100 orders can mean 101 queries. Use select_related for single links and prefetch_related for many, in get_queryset().
Numbers here are illustrative.

steps.title: Cursor pagination and safe filters
body: Offset pagination gets slower and can skip or repeat rows when data changes while paging. Cursor pagination follows a position and stays stable and fast for big or fast-changing lists.
Allowlist the ordering and filter fields clients may use.

steps.title: Retries and idempotency
body: PUT replaces a resource, PATCH changes part of it. A POST that is retried after a timeout can create a duplicate, so accept an Idempotency-Key header and store it with a UNIQUE constraint.
Recap: validate, scope by owner, avoid N+1, paginate by cursor, make writes retry-safe.

everyday.plain: An API is a menu that other programs order from, and Django REST Framework helps you build it neatly.
everyday.story: A restaurant has a menu. A customer does not walk into the kitchen. He orders by name, and the waiter brings the dish. If he orders something that is not on the menu, the waiter says no politely. An API is the menu for programs. The waiter is your view, the dish is the data, and the polite 'no' is a clear error message.
maps: A proper error and status code
words: A set of addresses other programs can call to get or change data.
Code that turns your data into JSON and checks incoming JSON.
A class that groups the actions for one kind of thing, like list, create and delete.
Returning a long list in pages instead of all at once.

title: Celery & Background Jobs
tagline: Do slow jobs in the background so the user is not kept waiting.
explain: Anything slow or unreliable, such as sending email, calling a payment API, generating a PDF or resizing an image, should not run inside the web request. The user waits, a slow third party ties up your web workers, and a failure becomes a failed page. Celery moves that work out of the request into a background worker.
## How it fits together

- Producer: your Django app calls task.delay(args). That publishes a message (the task name and its arguments) to a broker.
- Broker: a queue such as Redis or RabbitMQ that holds messages until a worker takes one.
- Worker: a separate process that consumes messages and runs your task function. Run more workers to process more at once.
- Result backend: optional storage for return values. You only need it if you read results back.
- Beat: a scheduler process that enqueues periodic tasks, such as nightly reports and cleanup.
Follow one message through the system, then see what happens when the worker dies.
@viz:celery-flow
## Delivery is at-least-once

By default a task is acknowledged just before it runs, so a worker crash mid-task can lose it. With acks_late the message is redelivered after a crash, and may then run twice. Either way you cannot assume exactly once, so write idempotent tasks: make the effect safe to repeat, with a unique constraint or a 'processed' marker. This is the same idea as an Idempotency-Key. Also pass IDs, not model instances, and re-load fresh data inside the task, because the object may have changed or been deleted by the time it runs.
## The race that bites everyone
If you call .delay() inside transaction.atomic(), the worker can pick the task up before your transaction commits, then fail with DoesNotExist because the row is not visible yet.

> with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(...)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(order.id))
The task is only queued after COMMIT succeeds, and not at all if the transaction rolls back. If even that is not enough (the process can crash between COMMIT and the enqueue), use the outbox pattern: write a to-do row in the same transaction, and let a separate publisher send it.
## Failure is a normal case

- Retries: autoretry_for with retry_backoff and jitter, and a max_retries cap so a poison task cannot loop forever.
- Time limits: soft and hard limits so a hung task does not hold a worker forever.
- Separate queues: keep slow, bulk work apart from urgent work such as password-reset emails.
- Monitoring: watch queue length and failure rate. A silently backed-up queue is an outage that nobody noticed.
keyPoints: Web app → broker (Redis/RabbitMQ) → worker. Result backend only if you need results.
At-least-once delivery means tasks must be idempotent.
Pass IDs and re-load inside the task; never pass model instances.
Enqueue with transaction.on_commit(); outbox pattern when you cannot lose the job.
Retries: backoff + jitter + max_retries; add time limits.
Monitor queue depth and failures.

sql.title: Idempotent effect: do it once even if the task runs twice
sql.code:
CREATE TABLE points_ledger (
  order_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES orders(id),   -- one row per order, enforced by the database
  points     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO points_ledger (order_id, points) VALUES (42, 10)
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO NOTHING;      -- a retry or duplicate delivery inserts 0 rows and changes nothing

sql.title: Outbox pattern
sql.code:
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id         BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  task       TEXT  NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
);
-- INSERT the row in the SAME transaction as the order. A publisher then claims unsent rows:
SELECT id, task, payload FROM outbox
WHERE sent_at IS NULL
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 50;

django.title: Idempotent task, enqueued after commit
django.code:
# orders/tasks.py
from celery import shared_task
from django.db import OperationalError, transaction

@shared_task(bind=True, autoretry_for=(OperationalError,), retry_backoff=True, retry_jitter=True,
             max_retries=5, soft_time_limit=30)
def award_points(self, order_id):                      # pass the ID, not the Order
    with transaction.atomic():
        PointsLedger.objects.get_or_create(order_id=order_id, defaults={"points": 10})   # unique(order_id)
    # a retry or duplicate delivery finds the row and does nothing

# orders/services.py
@transaction.atomic
def place_order(customer, cart):
    order = Order.objects.create(customer=customer, status="pending")
    ...
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: award_points.delay(order.id))   # enqueue only after COMMIT
django.note: For effects outside your database (an email, a payment call) a unique row cannot make the effect itself idempotent. Use the provider's idempotency key where it exists, or accept at-least-once delivery and design the message so a duplicate is harmless.

exercise: Add a Celery task that awards points once per order. Prove with a test that calling the task twice for the same order creates one ledger row. Then deliberately call .delay() inside atomic() with a worker running and watch the DoesNotExist race, and fix it with transaction.on_commit.
pitfalls: Calling .delay() inside transaction.atomic() (the worker runs before the COMMIT).
Passing model instances or non-serializable arguments instead of IDs.
Assuming exactly-once execution; non-idempotent tasks that double-charge or double-email.
Retrying forever with no backoff, no max_retries and no time limit.
No monitoring of queue length; running multiple Beat instances and double-scheduling.

interview.q: Why and how would you use Celery in a Django app?
interview.a: To move slow or unreliable work (email, payments, reports) out of the request cycle. Django publishes a message to a broker (Redis/RabbitMQ), workers consume and execute it; a result backend is optional. It improves response time and lets you retry and schedule work.

interview.q: Why use transaction.on_commit with Celery?
interview.a: If you enqueue inside atomic(), the worker may run before the transaction commits and not find the row (DoesNotExist). on_commit runs the callback only after a successful COMMIT, so the data is visible. If the process may crash between commit and enqueue, use an outbox table.

interview.q: What happens if a Celery task runs twice?
interview.a: It can: delivery is at-least-once, especially with acks_late or after a worker crash or retry. Make tasks idempotent, for example with a unique constraint or a processed marker, so a repeat is harmless.

interview.q: How do you configure retries with backoff?
interview.a: Use autoretry_for for the exception types, retry_backoff=True (optionally retry_jitter), and a max_retries cap; add soft_time_limit/time_limit so a stuck task cannot hang a worker.

interview.q: What should you pass as Celery task arguments?
interview.a: Small, JSON-serializable values such as IDs. Re-load the object inside the task so you act on current data and avoid serializing stale model instances.

interview.q: Celery Beat vs cron?
interview.a: Beat is Celery's scheduler: it enqueues periodic tasks that workers execute, with schedules defined in config or the database. Run exactly one Beat instance or tasks will be scheduled twice; cron is simpler for a single host with no queue.

interview.q: How do you make sure an event is not lost if the app crashes right after commit?
interview.a: The transactional outbox: insert an outbox row in the same transaction as the business change, and have a publisher read unsent rows (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) and enqueue them, marking them sent.

basis: Mid priority at 0-5 yrs, core at 5+. Celery setup, Beat and retries with backoff are Senior Django topics, junior roles ask only for basic awareness, and on_commit before enqueueing is a named senior topic.

body: A view creates an Order row and then calls a Celery task, send_receipt.delay(order.id), to email the customer in the background.
The queue and the worker run separately from the web request, and the worker reads the order from the database by id.

steps.title: The task is queued inside the transaction
body: The .delay() call happens before the transaction commits, so the task message reaches the queue immediately while the new order row is still invisible to other connections.
The web request is not finished with the transaction yet.

steps.title: The worker is faster than the commit
body: A worker picks up the task straight away and looks for order 42. The commit has not happened, so the row does not exist for it: DoesNotExist, and the task fails or retries.
It works in development and fails in production when the queue is fast and the database is busy.

callout.text: This is a race condition between the commit and the worker. It is intermittent, which makes it hard to reproduce.

steps.title: transaction.on_commit: queue after the commit
body: Register the .delay() call with transaction.on_commit. Django runs it only after the transaction has committed, so the row is visible by the time the worker looks.
If the transaction rolls back, the callback never runs and no task is queued for an order that does not exist.
changes: + The task is queued only after COMMIT

steps.title: Rollbacks queue nothing
body: If the transaction raises and rolls back, the on_commit callback is discarded. No task is queued for data that was never saved.
That removes the opposite problem: a worker acting on an order the customer never actually placed.

steps.title: Pass ids, not objects, and make the task safe to repeat
body: Pass the order's id: the worker fetches fresh data, and the message stays small. Make the task idempotent, since a queue may deliver a task more than once.
See the message queues lesson for acknowledgements and retries.

title: Web Security for Django APIs
tagline: The common ways websites get hacked, and how to stop them.
explain: Django is secure by default in several places, if you do not switch the protection off. Most real vulnerabilities come from stepping outside those defaults. Learn what is protected for you and what is not.
## What Django protects by default

- SQL injection: the ORM sends parameters separately from the SQL text, so queries built with filter() are not injectable.
- XSS (cross-site scripting): templates auto-escape variables, which blocks most XSS.
- CSRF (cross-site request forgery): CsrfViewMiddleware rejects state-changing requests from a browser that lack a valid token.
- Clickjacking: XFrameOptionsMiddleware sets X-Frame-Options so other sites cannot frame your pages.
- Passwords: stored as salted, slow hashes (PBKDF2 by default), never plaintext.
## How people break out of the defaults

- Raw SQL built with f-strings or % formatting. Always pass parameters: cursor.execute('... WHERE id = %s', [value]).
- mark_safe() or the |safe filter on user input, which switches auto-escaping off.
- @csrf_exempt on views that use cookie authentication.
- DEBUG=True in production, which leaks settings and stack traces, or a leaked SECRET_KEY, which lets an attacker forge sessions and signed data.
- An over-permissive ALLOWED_HOSTS, or CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS together with credentials.

> Bad: User.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE username = '{name}'")
Sending name = "x' OR '1'='1" returns every user. Good: User.objects.raw('SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE username = %s', [name]), where the value is sent separately and never parsed as SQL.
## Broken access control: the bug the framework cannot catch

IDOR (insecure direct object reference) means /orders/123 works for any logged-in user, not only its owner. Authentication proves who someone is. Every object access also needs an authorization check: filter the queryset by request.user, or verify ownership before returning or changing data. This is one of the most common API flaws, because it is easy to forget and every test as the owner still passes.
## CORS vs CSRF, and going to production

CSRF protects cookie-authenticated browsers from cross-site form posts. CORS decides which other origins may read your API's responses from JavaScript. They are different problems and one does not replace the other. For production:

- Serve over HTTPS and set SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE and HSTS.
- Keep secrets in environment variables, never in the repository.
- Set DEBUG=False and a strict ALLOWED_HOSTS.
- Rate-limit login and other abusable endpoints.
- Run python manage.py check --deploy, which lists missing hardening settings.
- Keep Django and dependencies updated, because security fixes ship as patch releases.
keyPoints: ORM parameters prevent SQL injection; raw SQL must use %s parameters, never f-strings.
Auto-escaping blocks XSS; mark_safe on user input defeats it.
CSRF token = proof the request came from your own page; CORS controls cross-origin reads.
Authentication ≠ authorization: check object ownership (IDOR).
Never ship DEBUG=True or a committed SECRET_KEY; run check --deploy.

sql.title: Parameters keep input out of the SQL text
sql.code:
-- Vulnerable: user input becomes part of the statement
--   SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1';     -- returns every customer

-- Safe: the value travels separately from the statement
PREPARE find_customer(text) AS
  SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = $1;
EXECUTE find_customer($$' OR '1'='1$$);                      -- treated as an ordinary string, matches nothing

sql.title: Least-privilege database role

django.title: Injection, IDOR and production settings
django.code:
# SQL injection: never format user input into SQL
Customer.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = '{email}'")     # VULNERABLE
Customer.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = %s", [email])    # safe: parameters
Customer.objects.filter(email=email)                                         # safest: the ORM

# IDOR: authorize the object, not just the user
def order_detail(request, pk):
    order = get_object_or_404(Order, pk=pk, customer__user=request.user)     # someone else's order -> 404
    return JsonResponse(serialize(order))

# settings for production
DEBUG = False
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["api.example.com"]
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000
# then run:  python manage.py check --deploy
django.note: Run check --deploy in CI so a risky setting fails the build. Returning 404 (not 403) for other people's objects avoids confirming that the object exists.

exercise: Write a test where user B requests user A's order and expects 404, watch it fail on a naive view, then fix the view. Run manage.py check --deploy against your settings and resolve every warning, noting which ones you consciously accept.
pitfalls: @csrf_exempt on views that use cookie/session authentication.
mark_safe() or |safe on anything a user can influence.
Authenticating the user but not authorizing the specific object (IDOR).
fields = "__all__" on serializers (mass assignment of is_staff, owner, status…).
DEBUG=True, hard-coded SECRET_KEY, or secrets committed to git.
Logging passwords, tokens or full request bodies.

interview.q: How does Django protect against SQL injection?
interview.a: The ORM builds queries with parameters sent separately from the SQL text, so user input is never interpreted as SQL. The risk returns with raw() / cursor.execute() when you format strings yourself; always pass parameters (%s with a list).

interview.q: How does CSRF protection work in Django?
interview.a: CsrfViewMiddleware gives each session a secret token and requires unsafe requests (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) to send it in the form or a header; a malicious site cannot read the token, so cross-site requests are rejected. It matters for cookie/session authentication; token-in-header APIs are not vulnerable the same way.

interview.q: How are XSS attacks prevented, and how can you break it?
interview.a: Django templates auto-escape variables so injected HTML/JS renders as text. You break it with mark_safe(), |safe or autoescape off on untrusted data, or by building HTML strings yourself.

interview.q: What is IDOR and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: Insecure direct object reference: an endpoint like /orders/123 returns the object to any authenticated user. Prevent it by authorizing each object, e.g. get_object_or_404(Order, pk=pk, customer__user=request.user), or has_object_permission in DRF, and by testing with two users.

interview.q: CORS vs CSRF?
interview.a: CSRF is an attack where another site makes a victim's browser send an authenticated request; the defense is a token. CORS is a browser policy controlling which origins may read cross-origin responses via JavaScript; it does not stop requests from being sent. Misconfigured wildcard CORS with credentials is a vulnerability.

interview.q: How does Django store passwords?
interview.a: As a salted, iterated hash (PBKDF2 with SHA256 by default), with the algorithm and parameters stored in the value so hashers can be upgraded; plaintext passwords are never stored.

interview.q: What does manage.py check --deploy do?
interview.a: It audits settings for production risks, such as DEBUG, missing HTTPS redirect, insecure cookies, missing HSTS or a weak SECRET_KEY, and reports warnings. Running it in CI keeps risky settings from shipping.

basis: Core. CSRF, SQL injection, XSS and password hashing are in the Middle Django topic list, and SQL-injection prevention is part of the junior backend bar.

scenes.title: Web security, step by step

steps.title: SQL injection: never build SQL with f-strings
body: If you paste user input into a SQL string, the input can contain SQL. A search for  x' OR '1'='1  can return every row.
The ORM sends values as parameters, so it is safe by default.

steps.title: Parameters keep data separate from SQL
body: With raw SQL, pass the values separately with %s placeholders. The driver sends them as data, never as part of the statement.
Prefer the ORM; use raw SQL only when needed.

steps.title: XSS: untrusted text becomes script
body: If an attacker's text is rendered as HTML, their script runs in other users' browsers with those users' sessions. Django templates escape output automatically.
mark_safe() or |safe on anything a user can influence turns that protection off.

predict.question: A comment containing <script> is shown with {{ comment|safe }}. What happens in other users' browsers?
predict.why: |safe disables auto-escaping, so the browser treats the text as HTML and runs the script. Keep escaping on for user content.

steps.title: CSRF: another site makes your browser send a request
body: A browser attaches your session cookie to requests to your site, even ones triggered by a page on another site. Without a check, that page can make a state-changing request as you.
Django's CSRF token proves the request came from a page of your own.

steps.title: CSRF token and CORS
body: Django's CsrfViewMiddleware rejects state-changing requests without the right token. Do not use @csrf_exempt on views that rely on cookie or session login.
CORS is a different control: it decides which other origins may read responses, not which may send requests.

callout.text: CORS does not stop CSRF. They protect different things.

steps.title: IDOR and secrets
body: Authentication is not authorization: check that this user may touch this object. Never run with DEBUG=True or a committed SECRET_KEY in production.
Django's manage.py check --deploy reports many such misconfigurations.

lines: SECRET_KEY from the environment, not the repo

steps.title: Recap
body: ORM or %s parameters for SQL. Auto-escaping on. CSRF token on session-cookie views. Check object ownership. No DEBUG or committed secrets in production.

everyday.plain: Most security problems come from trusting what users send, or from letting people see things that are not theirs.
everyday.story: A hotel gives each guest a key card for one room. It would be a serious mistake if the same card opened every room, or if the staff opened any door when someone just said 'I am the manager'. Web security is about checking who someone is, and checking each time whether they are allowed to open this particular door.

title: Database System Design Interviews
tagline: Plan a big product out loud in 45 minutes: first the numbers, then the tables, then how it grows.
explain: A design interview gives you a vague product ('design a URL shortener', 'design a chat app') and watches how you think. You are not being tested on a memorised answer. You are being tested on a method: ask questions, put numbers on the problem, design the data, find the bottleneck, and say what you gave up.
## What interviewers look at

Public prep guides describe the bar by seniority. At mid level the interviewer expects breadth with limited depth, and expects you to drive the requirements, the API and the schema yourself. At senior level you are expected to go deep in about two places and to point out the limits of your own design. So practice leading the conversation, not waiting to be asked.
## A six-step structure you can reuse

- Clarify requirements: what must it do, how many users, how fast, how reliable, and what is out of scope.
- Estimate the load: reads and writes per second, storage per year.
- Define the API and the data model: a handful of endpoints, a handful of tables, the keys and the indexes.
- Choose the storage and the hard part: relational, key-value or both, and how you generate ids or keep counts right.
- Find the bottleneck and scale only that: cache, replicas, partitioning, sharding, queues.
- State trade-offs and failure modes: what breaks, what is stale, what you would monitor.
Step through the structure on a real example. Notice that the scaling step comes fifth. The design is built from the numbers, not from a favourite architecture.
@viz:sd-framework
## Estimation: numbers worth remembering

Per-second numbers are almost always smaller than daily numbers suggest. There are 86,400 seconds in a day, so about 100 thousand events a day is 1 per second, 1 million a day is about 12 per second, and 1 billion a day is about 12 thousand per second. Real traffic is bursty, so a common rule of thumb is to plan for a peak of 2 to 3 times the average. Storage is rows times bytes per row times a factor for indexes and overhead.

> 10 million daily users, each sending 40 messages: 400 million writes a day, about 4,600 a second on average and about 14,000 at peak. That is beyond what one primary should be asked to take comfortably, so the design needs partitioning by conversation, queued writes, or a store built for that write rate. A blog with 20,000 daily users needs one database and no discussion at all.
Use the estimator above to feel how the numbers change the answer. Its limits are my rough rules of thumb, not a standard, so always say your assumption out loud and offer to benchmark.
## The scaling toolbox, in the order to reach for it

- Fix queries and add the right indexes (Making Queries Fast).
- Cache hot reads (Consistency Models).
- Add read replicas, and accept replication lag (Replication).
- Partition big tables, usually by time, and archive old data.
- Move slow or bursty work to a queue (Celery).
- Shard last, because it makes joins, transactions and unique ids hard (Sharding).
Interviewers notice candidates who jump straight to sharding or microservices. Saying 'the numbers do not need it yet' is a strong answer.
## Three sketches to practice

- Orders: orders and order_items tables, a price snapshot on each line, stock decremented with an atomic conditional UPDATE or SELECT FOR UPDATE, and an idempotency key so a retried payment cannot create a second order.
- Chat inbox: messages keyed by (conversation_id, created_at, id), one composite index, keyset pagination for history, and partitioning by time once the table is large.
- Likes and counters: a derived counter column updated with F() inside the same transaction, or batched through a queue if one post gets hot enough to become a lock bottleneck.
## Common mistakes

- Starting to draw boxes before asking a single question.
- Never putting a number on the problem.
- Choosing NoSQL or sharding with no reason tied to the access pattern.
- Ignoring consistency: money and stock need transactions, a view counter does not.
- No failure story: what happens when the primary dies, the cache is empty, or a worker crashes mid-task.
keyPoints: Method over memorisation: clarify, estimate, model the data, find the bottleneck, state trade-offs.
Per-second numbers: 1M events a day is about 12 a second. Plan for a 2-3x peak.
Scale in order: query fixes and indexes, cache, replicas, partitioning, queues, sharding last.
Mid level drives requirements and schema. Senior goes deep in a couple of places and names the limits of the design.
Always say the consistency requirement and the failure mode out loud.

exercise: Pick one product (ride-hailing, a booking site, a marketplace). On one page write: requirements, an estimate of writes and reads per second and storage per year, 4 to 6 tables with keys and indexes, the single biggest bottleneck, and the first scaling step you would take. Use the estimator to check your numbers. Then talk through it aloud in 10 minutes without notes, and note where you hesitated.
pitfalls: Quoting daily numbers and never converting them to per second.
Proposing sharding or a new database before showing that the numbers need it.
Treating every part of the system as needing the same consistency.
Designing only the happy path and having no answer for 'what if the primary dies?'.
Memorising one famous design instead of practicing the method on unfamiliar products.

interview.q: How do you approach an open-ended design question?
interview.a: I clarify requirements and what is out of scope, estimate reads, writes and storage per second and per year, sketch the API and schema, pick storage for the access pattern, identify the first bottleneck and scale only that, then state trade-offs and failure modes. I drive that order myself rather than waiting for prompts.

interview.q: A service has 1 million daily active users. How would you estimate its write load?
interview.a: Multiply users by writes per user and divide by 86,400 seconds. One write per user per day is about 12 writes a second, ten writes each is about 120. Then multiply by 2 to 3 for peak. The point is that the number is usually small enough for one primary, which I would say before considering anything fancier.

interview.q: When would you shard a database?
interview.a: After indexes, caching, replicas and partitioning are not enough, typically when peak write rate or total data size outgrows one primary. I would pick a shard key with high cardinality that matches the main query, accept that cross-shard joins and transactions get hard, and plan for resharding.

interview.q: SQL or NoSQL for a chat application's messages?
interview.a: Start from the access pattern: fetch recent messages for one conversation, in order, at high write volume. That is a key-and-range lookup, which fits a wide-column or partitioned store well. A relational database also works at moderate scale with a composite index and partitioning. I would keep users and billing relational either way.

interview.q: How do you make sure a payment is not charged twice when the client retries?
interview.a: Use an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key with the request, the server stores the key with the result under a unique constraint, and a repeat request returns the stored result instead of acting again. Combine it with a transaction so the order and the key are written together.

interview.q: One celebrity row or partition gets far more traffic than the rest. What do you do?
interview.a: That is a hot key. Options are caching it aggressively, splitting the counter across several rows and summing them, adding a local in-process cache, or choosing a shard key that spreads the load. I would measure first to confirm it is the actual bottleneck.

The sources describe system design as breadth and self-driven requirements, API and schema at mid level and depth in about two areas at senior level. The capacity thresholds in the estimator are my rough rules of thumb, not a published standard.
