title: Running Databases in Production
tagline: Keep a real database healthy: connections, safe changes, backups and warning signs.
explain: Writing a good schema is half the job. In production the database also has to survive deploys, traffic spikes and human mistakes. This lesson covers the four things that most often go wrong: running out of connections, changing the schema on a live system, losing data, and not noticing a problem until users do.
## Connection pooling

Every open connection to PostgreSQL is a separate server process that uses memory, so more connections does not mean more speed. The default limit is 100. With Django, each worker thread keeps its own connection, and the Django docs say the database must support at least as many connections as you have worker threads. Add app instances and you can quietly walk into 'too many clients'.

- CONN_MAX_AGE: the default is 0, which closes the connection at the end of every request. A positive number of seconds reuses connections and saves the cost of reconnecting. Pair it with CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS = True so a connection the server has closed is detected instead of causing an error.
- Django 5.1 and later can use a real pool with OPTIONS pool, which needs psycopg[pool] and is ignored with psycopg2. The docs also say that under ASGI, persistent connections should be disabled in favour of pooling.
- An external pooler such as PgBouncer sits between all your app instances and the database and shares a small number of real connections between many clients. PgBouncer has three modes: session pooling holds a server connection for as long as the client stays connected, transaction pooling assigns one only during a transaction, and statement pooling is the most aggressive and disallows multi-statement transactions. Its documentation says transaction pooling breaks a few session-based PostgreSQL features and can be used only when the application cooperates: its feature table marks SET/RESET, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors, PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, session-level advisory locks and the LOAD statement as never working in that mode.
@viz:pool
## Changing a live schema safely

During a rolling deploy, old and new code run at the same time. So every schema change must work with both versions. The pattern is expand, backfill, contract: add what the new code needs without breaking the old code, migrate the data, switch the code over, and only then remove what is no longer used, in a later release. Use the animation above to compare a one-step rename with the safe sequence.

- Adding a nullable column is cheap and compatible with old code. Dropping or renaming a column that running code still uses is what breaks deploys.
- CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds an index without blocking inserts, updates and deletes. The PostgreSQL docs say it takes significantly longer and does more work, cannot run inside a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an INVALID index behind that you should drop and retry.
- In Django, use AddIndexConcurrently from django.contrib.postgres.operations and set atomic = False on that migration.
- To add a CHECK constraint to a big table, add it NOT VALID first and validate it later. Django has AddConstraintNotValid and ValidateConstraint, and the docs say to run them in two separate migrations.
- Backfill data in batches, each in its own short transaction. The Django how-to shows batches of 1,000 with atomic = False. One huge UPDATE holds locks for a long time and bloats the table.
- Set a lock_timeout for migration sessions. A migration that waits for a lock also makes every later query wait behind it, so it is better for the migration to give up quickly and be retried.
- Give every RunPython a reverse function. Without one, migrating backwards raises an error. Use the historical models from apps.get_model, because they do not run your custom save() methods.
## Backups and recovery

There are two kinds. A logical backup (pg_dump) exports data as SQL or a custom format. It is simple and portable, and it is a snapshot of one moment. A physical backup is a copy of the data files plus a continuous archive of the write-ahead log (WAL). Replaying the WAL on top of that base backup lets you restore to any point after the backup was taken, which is called point-in-time recovery. That is how you undo a mistake such as an accidental DELETE: restore to one minute before it.

The PostgreSQL docs note some limits: continuous archiving restores a whole cluster and not a subset, it needs a lot of archive storage, configuration files are not included and need separate backups, and pg_dump output cannot be part of a continuous-archiving setup. Two numbers frame every backup plan. RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can afford to lose. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long you can afford to be down. Frequent WAL archiving lowers RPO, and a rehearsed restore lowers RTO. Test restores regularly, because a backup you have never restored is only a hope.
## What to watch

- Slow queries: the slow query log (log_min_duration_statement) and the pg_stat_statements extension.
- Connections used versus max_connections, to see pool exhaustion coming.
- Sessions stuck 'idle in transaction' and very old transactions. They hold locks and stop VACUUM from cleaning up (see Concurrency Control).
- Blocked queries: pg_stat_activity with pg_blocking_pids shows who is waiting for whom.
- Replication lag and free disk space.
## When the database is slow: a calm checklist

- Did something just change? A deploy, a migration, a new query, a traffic spike.
- Are connections near the limit?
- Is anything blocked, and by what? Is there a long transaction?
- Which statements are slowest now? EXPLAIN them.
- Fix the cause, not just the symptom, and write down what you saw. Terminating a stuck session is a last resort, and you should know what it was doing first.
keyPoints: Connections are expensive: pool them. Django: CONN_MAX_AGE plus CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS, a pool in 5.1+, or PgBouncer.
Old and new code run together during a deploy, so schema changes use expand, backfill, contract.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids write locks but is slower, cannot run in a transaction, and may leave an INVALID index.
Backfill in small batches. Give migrations a lock_timeout and a reverse function.
pg_dump is logical. PITR needs a base backup plus continuous WAL archiving. Know RPO and RTO, and test restores.

sql.title: Safe index and constraint changes
Connections, long transactions and blocked queries
sql.code:
-- how close to the limit are we?
SELECT count(*) AS connections, current_setting('max_connections') AS max
FROM pg_stat_activity;

-- sessions holding a transaction open while doing nothing
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS open_for, left(query, 80) AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start;

-- who is waiting for whom?
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, left(query, 80) AS waiting_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

django.title: Pooling settings and a non-blocking index migration
django.note: Keep schema changes and data backfills in separate migrations. If a concurrent build fails it can leave an INVALID index, so check for one and drop it before retrying.

exercise: On a local PostgreSQL, create a users table with 1 million rows. Write the expand, backfill, contract sequence to rename a column using three separate migrations, with the backfill in batches of 1,000. Time the backfill, then build an index with and without CONCURRENTLY while a second session keeps inserting, and compare what blocks. Finally take a pg_dump, restore it into a new database, and check the row counts match.
pitfalls: Renaming or dropping a column in the same release as the code that stops using it.
Running one giant UPDATE for a backfill and holding locks for minutes.
Raising max_connections instead of pooling, which spends more memory for the same work.
Leaving an INVALID index behind after a failed concurrent build.
Having backups but never testing a restore.

interview.q: Why do you need connection pooling, and how do you set it up with Django?
interview.a: Each connection is a server process with real memory cost, and Django keeps one per worker thread, so many instances can exhaust max_connections. I would set CONN_MAX_AGE with CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS, or on Django 5.1+ enable the psycopg pool through OPTIONS pool, or put PgBouncer in front for many instances. Under ASGI the docs recommend pooling over persistent connections.

interview.q: How do you rename a column on a live table with zero downtime?
interview.a: Expand, backfill, contract. Add the new nullable column, deploy code that writes both, backfill old rows in batches, deploy code that reads the new column, stop writing the old one, and drop it in a later release. Each step is compatible with the code running before and after it.

interview.q: What are the caveats of CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY?
interview.a: It does not block writes, but it takes longer and does more work, cannot run inside a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an INVALID index that must be dropped before you retry. In Django you use AddIndexConcurrently and set atomic = False on the migration.

interview.q: What is the difference between pg_dump and point-in-time recovery?
interview.a: pg_dump is a logical snapshot of the data at one moment. Point-in-time recovery uses a physical base backup plus a continuous archive of WAL files, so you can restore to any moment after the base backup, for example just before an accidental delete. pg_dump cannot be part of that setup.

interview.q: What are RPO and RTO?
interview.a: RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much recent data you can afford to lose, which WAL archiving frequency controls. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long you can afford to be down, which depends on how fast and how rehearsed your restore is.

interview.q: The database suddenly gets slow. What do you check?
interview.a: What changed recently, then connection count against the limit, then blocked queries and long or idle-in-transaction sessions, then the slowest statements and their plans. I fix the cause, and I would terminate a session only after seeing what it was doing.

body: After a safe period, remove the old column in a last migration, once no running code uses it. This step is the only one that cannot be undone by redeploying old code.

body: During a rolling deploy two versions of the code run at once, so a schema change must work for both. Split risky changes into expand, backfill, switch and contract.

title: Big-O and Choosing a Data Structure
tagline: Know how your code slows down as data grows, and pick the right container for your data.
explain: Big-O notation describes how the work a piece of code does grows as its input grows. It ignores machine speed and constant factors, because what matters is the shape of the growth. Interviewers ask 'what is the complexity?' after almost every coding problem, and the same thinking decides real design questions, such as why a database index (a tree search) beats scanning a whole table.
## How to read the complexity of code

- One loop over n items: O(n).
- A loop inside a loop, both over n items: O(n²). Over two different sizes it is O(n × m).
- Cutting the problem in half every step (binary search): O(log n).
- Sorting: O(n log n).
- A single lookup by index or by key: O(1).
- Drop constants and smaller terms. 3n + 10 is O(n), and n² + n is O(n²).
- If steps run one after another, add them. If one step runs inside another, multiply them.

Unless told otherwise, give the worst case, and say so. Two other words appear in interviews. Average case means the typical case. Amortized means the cost averaged over many operations: appending to a Python list is O(1) amortized because an occasional append has to resize the list and costs O(n), but those resizes are rare.
## The structures you need to know

- List (array): index in O(1), append O(1) amortized, 'x in list' O(n), insert or delete at the front O(n).
- Dict (hash map) and set: lookup, insert and delete O(1) on average. The Python docs note that if every key hashed to the same value each operation would degrade to O(n), so the O(1) is an average that relies on a good hash.
- Stack: last in, first out. A list with append and pop works.
- Queue: first in, first out. Use collections.deque, which the Python docs recommend when you need to add or remove at both ends. list.pop(0) is O(n) because every item shifts.
- Heap: gives the smallest item fast. Python's heapq pushes and pops in O(log n), which is the tool for 'top k' questions.
- Tree and graph: nodes connected by edges. Database indexes are trees, and many problems are graph searches.
## Space and the time-for-memory trade

Space complexity counts the extra memory you use. Most speed-ups spend memory: a set of seen values uses O(n) extra space and turns an O(n²) search into O(n). Say both numbers out loud in an interview.

> Two-sum: find two numbers in a list that add up to a target. Brute force checks every pair, so it is O(n²) time and O(1) space. Walking the list once while keeping a dict of numbers already seen, and asking 'have I seen target minus this number?', is O(n) time and O(n) space. For 100,000 numbers that is about 5 billion pair checks versus 100,000 lookups.
## How to answer in an interview

- State the brute-force idea and its complexity first. It shows you understand the problem.
- Name the bottleneck (here, checking every pair) and ask which structure removes it.
- State the new time and space complexity.
- Test edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives, very large input.
keyPoints: Big-O is the shape of growth, not seconds. Drop constants and lower-order terms.
Nested loops multiply, sequential steps add, halving gives log n, sorting is n log n.
dict and set are O(1) on average, 'x in list' is O(n), list.pop(0) is O(n), so use deque for queues.
Most speed-ups trade memory for time: a set or dict of seen values.
Always state time AND space, and say whether you mean worst, average or amortized.

sql.title: Two-sum: O(n²) then O(n)
Measure it yourself
sql.code:
import timeit

n = 20_000
items_list = list(range(n))
items_set = set(items_list)

# the last element is the worst case for a list scan
print('list:', timeit.timeit(lambda: (n - 1) in items_list, number=2000))
print('set: ', timeit.timeit(lambda: (n - 1) in items_set, number=2000))
# Double n and run again: the list time doubles, the set time barely moves.

exercise: Write two_sum_slow and two_sum_fast and time both with timeit for n = 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 (skip the slow one for the largest). Write down how the time grew each time n multiplied by 10, and match it to O(n²) and O(n). Then list five operations in code you have written at work and state their complexity, for example an `in` check on a list inside a loop in a view.
pitfalls: Saying O(n) for a loop that contains an 'x in list' check: that is O(n²).
Forgetting that string concatenation in a loop, slicing and sorted() copy data and cost time and space.
Using a list as a queue with pop(0) instead of collections.deque.
Giving only time complexity and never mentioning the extra space.
Treating average-case hash lookups as a guarantee without saying 'on average'.

interview.q: What is Big-O notation and why do we use it?
interview.a: It describes how the work an algorithm does grows with the size of its input, ignoring constants and machine speed. We use it to compare approaches and to predict whether code will still be fast when the data is 100 times bigger.

interview.q: What is the complexity of looking up a key in a Python dict, and when can it be worse?
interview.a: O(1) on average. In the worst case, when many keys hash to the same value, a lookup can degrade to O(n), so the O(1) is an average-case statement that depends on a well-distributed hash.

interview.q: Why is appending to a Python list O(1) if resizing is O(n)?
interview.a: It is amortized O(1). The list over-allocates, so resizes are rare and the occasional O(n) copy averages out over many appends.

interview.q: How would you implement a queue in Python and why not use a list?
interview.a: Use collections.deque with append and popleft, which are designed for adding and removing at both ends. list.pop(0) is O(n) because every remaining element shifts forward.

interview.q: You loop over list A of size n and, for each item, check membership in list B of size m. What is the complexity and how do you improve it?
interview.a: O(n × m), because 'in' on a list scans. Convert B to a set first, which costs O(m), and each membership check becomes O(1) on average, giving O(n + m) in total with O(m) extra space.

interview.q: What is the difference between time and space complexity, and how do they trade off?
interview.a: Time counts the steps and space counts the extra memory. Many optimizations spend memory to save time, such as caching results or keeping a set of seen values, so I state both.

title: Coding Patterns That Solve Most Interview Problems
tagline: A few ideas solve most coding questions. Learn to spot which one fits.
explain: Most coding questions are not new problems. They are one of a small number of patterns wearing a disguise. Learning to recognize the signal in the wording, then applying a template you can write from memory, is faster than inventing a solution under pressure. This lesson covers four patterns. Watch each one run in the animation, then write it yourself.
## A routine for any problem

- Restate the problem and ask about edge cases and input size. Size tells you the complexity you need: around 10^5 items means O(n log n) or better.
- Work one small example by hand.
- State the brute force and its complexity.
- Look for the signal that points to a pattern and name the bottleneck you are removing.
- Code it plainly, then test with your example and the edge cases: empty, one element, duplicates, all equal.
## Binary search: sorted data, or a yes/no question that flips once

Signal: the data is sorted, or you can ask 'is the answer at least x?' and the answer changes from no to yes exactly once. Each step looks at the middle and discards half, so it takes O(log n). A million items need about 20 looks. The bug to avoid is the off-by-one: use lo <= hi and move to mid + 1 or mid - 1, so the range always shrinks.
## Two pointers: sorted data, pairs, or in-place work

Signal: a sorted array and a pair or triple that must meet a condition, or removing duplicates in place. One pointer starts at each end (or one reads while one writes) and each only moves in one direction, so the whole pass is O(n) instead of the O(n²) of trying every pair. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right. If it is too big, move the right pointer left.
## Sliding window: contiguous subarrays and substrings

Signal: 'longest', 'shortest' or 'best' contiguous run, with a limit. Keep a window and update its total as it slides: add the new element on the right, drop the old one on the left. That is O(n), against O(n × k) if every window were added up again.
## BFS: shortest path with equal steps, and exploring a graph

Signal: a grid, a graph or a tree, and 'minimum number of steps' or 'level by level'. Breadth-first search uses a queue and a seen set. Because it visits everything one hop away, then two hops, the first time it reaches a node is by a shortest path. It costs O(V + E). The seen set is not optional: without it, a cycle makes the search loop forever.
## What to practice next

Depth-first search and recursion, hash-map counting, heaps for top-k problems, backtracking, and dynamic programming build on the same routine. Practise a few problems per pattern until you can write the template without looking, then mix them so you have to identify the pattern yourself.
keyPoints: Recognise the signal: sorted data, a pair, a contiguous run, or steps on a graph.
Binary search is O(log n): shrink with lo <= hi and mid +/- 1 to avoid off-by-one bugs.
Two pointers and sliding window turn O(n²) or O(n x k) into one O(n) pass.
BFS uses a queue plus a seen set and finds shortest paths when every step costs the same.
Brute force first, name the bottleneck, then apply the pattern, then test edge cases.

sql.title: Binary search
Two pointers
Sliding window
sql.code:
def best_window_sum(a, k):
    total = sum(a[:k])
    best = total
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        total += a[i] - a[i - k]    # add the new element, drop the old one
        best = max(best, total)
    return best

exercise: Pick one problem per pattern, for example: search in a sorted list, pair with a given sum in a sorted list, longest substring without repeating characters, and fewest moves between two cells of a grid. For each one write the brute force and its complexity first, then the pattern solution, then three edge-case tests. Time yourself: aim for 30 minutes per medium problem, including tests.
pitfalls: Binary search with lo < hi or mid = lo, which can loop forever or skip the last element.
Using two pointers on data that is not sorted, so moving a pointer proves nothing.
Recomputing the whole window sum inside the loop and losing the speed-up.
Forgetting the seen set in BFS or DFS and looping forever on a cycle.
Jumping to code before testing the idea on a small example by hand.

interview.q: When can you use binary search?
interview.a: When the data is sorted, or when a yes/no question about a candidate answer flips exactly once as the candidate grows. Each check halves the search space, so it is O(log n).

interview.q: How do two pointers reduce a pair-sum problem from O(n²) to O(n)?
interview.a: On a sorted array, start one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, only moving the left pointer right can increase it, and if it is too big only moving the right pointer left can decrease it. Each pointer moves one way, so there are at most n moves.

interview.q: Describe the sliding window technique.
interview.a: Keep a window over a contiguous range and update its aggregate incrementally as it moves: add the element entering, remove the one leaving. That makes each step O(1) and the pass O(n), instead of recomputing each window from scratch.

interview.q: Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
interview.a: It visits nodes in order of distance: everything one hop away before anything two hops away. So the first time it reaches a node, it has arrived by a path with the fewest edges.

interview.q: What is the time and space complexity of BFS?
interview.a: O(V + E) time, because each node and each edge is processed once, and O(V) space for the queue and the seen set.

interview.q: How do you approach a problem you have never seen?
interview.a: I restate it, ask about size and edge cases, work a small example by hand, state the brute force and its complexity, look for a pattern signal to remove the bottleneck, code it, then test edge cases out loud.

title: Behavioral Interviews and STAR Stories
tagline: Prepare five true stories from your work that can answer almost any 'tell me about a time' question.
explain: Behavioral questions ('tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate') test judgment and how you work, and nearly every interview loop includes them. The Amazon interview guide, for example, tells candidates to prepare for Leadership Principles questions and to use the STAR structure. The good news is that you do not need fifty answers. You need a handful of strong stories you can bend to fit the question.
## The STAR structure

- Situation: the context in one or two sentences. Where, when, what was at stake.
- Task: what you were responsible for. This is your part, not the team's.
- Action: what YOU did, step by step. This should be the longest part. Say 'I', not 'we', for the things you personally did.
- Result: what changed, with a number if you can, and what you learned or would do differently.
## Build a story bank

Write five stories from real work and tag each with the themes it can answer: a conflict, a failure or mistake, a tight deadline, taking ownership beyond your role, and working with unclear requirements. A good story usually fits three or four questions, so five stories cover most of what you will be asked.
## What makes an answer strong

- A specific moment, not a general habit. 'Last March the payment retries were double-charging customers' beats 'I usually care about quality'.
- Numbers in the Result: latency cut from 900 ms to 200 ms, 3 hours of manual work saved a week, 40 customers affected.
- Your decisions and the trade-offs you weighed, not just what happened.
- Honesty about mistakes. A failure story is strong when it shows what you changed afterwards.
- Two to three minutes. Practise out loud with a timer, because a story that reads well on paper often runs long.
## Common traps

Describing the team's work instead of yours, spending most of the time on the Situation, ending without a result, blaming others in a conflict story, and giving a rehearsed script that does not answer the question that was asked. Listen to the question, pick the story, then adapt the emphasis.

At 0 to 2 years the examples can come from coursework and small projects. At 2 to 5 years interviewers expect ownership and trade-offs. Past 5 years, expect questions about influencing others, mentoring and disagreeing with leadership.
keyPoints: STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Spend most of the time on Action and say 'I'.
Prepare five real stories tagged by theme: conflict, failure, deadline, ownership, ambiguity.
Put a number in the Result, and say what you learned.
Keep it to two or three minutes and practice out loud.
Answer the question asked: choose the story that fits, then adapt it.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.
interview.a: Pick a real disagreement about a technical decision. State the situation briefly, say what you wanted and why, how you listened to the other view, what evidence or experiment you proposed, and how it was resolved. Show respect for the other person and a result, even if it was a compromise.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you made a mistake.
interview.a: Choose a real, moderate mistake. Own it plainly, explain how you found it and limited the damage, then say what you changed so it cannot happen again, such as a test, a check or a process step.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you worked under a tight deadline.
interview.a: Describe what had to ship and by when, how you prioritized and what you chose to cut or defer, how you communicated the trade-off, and the outcome. Show that you protected quality where it mattered.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you took ownership of something outside your role.
interview.a: Describe a gap nobody was covering, why you decided to act, what you did and who you involved, and the result. Show initiative that was useful, not just extra work.

interview.q: What is the STAR method and why use it?
interview.a: Situation, Task, Action, Result: a way to tell a clear, specific story. It keeps the answer focused on what you personally did and what it achieved, and stops it from turning into a vague general statement.

title: Python Internals Interviewers Ask About
tagline: How Python really works: names and objects, the list trap, generators, decorators and the GIL.
explain: Python interviews rarely ask you to recite syntax. They probe whether you understand how the language behaves: why a default argument remembers old values, what the GIL does, and when to use a generator. Each of these produces a classic bug or a classic question, and the animation shows all three happening.
## Names point to objects

A Python variable is a name bound to an object, not a box holding a value. 'b = a' does not copy anything: both names point at the same object. For immutable objects (int, str, tuple) that is harmless because they cannot change. For mutable objects (list, dict, set) a change made through one name is visible through the other. Use 'is' to ask whether two names point at the same object and '==' to ask whether two objects are equal. For a copy, use list(a) or a.copy() for a shallow copy, and copy.deepcopy for nested data.
## The mutable default argument trap

The Python tutorial warns that a default value is evaluated only once, when the function is defined, and that this matters when the default is a mutable object such as a list. With 'def f(a, L=[])', every call that omits L shares the same list, so f(1), f(2), f(3) returns [1], then [1, 2], then [1, 2, 3]. The fix the docs show is to use None as the default and create the list inside the function. The same rule applies in Django: a JSONField default should be a callable such as list, not an instance such as [].
## Generators and lazy evaluation

A function containing yield is a generator function. Calling it gives a generator iterator that runs until the next yield, suspends while remembering its local variables, and resumes where it left off. The important effect is memory: a generator produces one item at a time, so you can process a ten-million-row file or queryset without holding it all in memory. A list comprehension builds the whole list first. A generator expression, written with parentheses, is the lazy version. In Django, queryset.iterator() applies the same idea to rows.
## Decorators and closures

A function can be passed around and returned like any value. A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a wrapped version, which is how @login_required, @transaction.atomic and @cache_page work. Use functools.wraps inside a decorator so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring.
## The GIL: what it does and does not do

The Python glossary defines the global interpreter lock as the mechanism CPython uses so that only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. It makes the object model, including built-ins such as dict, safe against concurrent access, at the expense of much of the parallelism of multi-core machines. Two details matter: the GIL is always released when doing I/O, and some extension modules release it for heavy work such as compression or hashing. So threads help I/O-bound work (waiting on the network or database) but not CPU-bound pure Python. For CPU-bound work use multiprocessing, which runs separate processes with their own interpreters, or move the work to a native library. asyncio handles many waiting tasks on one thread.

Python 3.13 added a free-threaded build where the GIL is disabled. The docs say single-threaded code runs somewhat slower on it and it uses more memory, and that some third-party extension modules may not be ready and will re-enable the GIL. Treat it as something to know about, and do not assume your production interpreter has it.
## Other topics that come up

- *args and **kwargs, and keyword-only arguments.
- Context managers (with) and how __enter__ and __exit__ guarantee cleanup, as in transaction.atomic().
- Dunder methods such as __str__, __repr__, __eq__ and __hash__. Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes if they are used as dict keys.
- Exceptions: raise, try/except/else/finally, and catching specific exceptions instead of a bare except.
keyPoints: Names bind to objects. Mutable objects change through every name that points at them.
Default arguments are evaluated once: use None and create the object inside.
Generators are lazy and keep memory flat. A list comprehension builds everything first.
The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time. It is released for I/O, so threads suit I/O-bound work, and processes suit CPU-bound work.
A decorator wraps a function. Use functools.wraps so the wrapper keeps the original's name.

sql.title: Mutable default, and the fix
sql.code:
def add_bad(item, bucket=[]):      # the list is created ONCE, at definition
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add_bad(1))   # [1]
print(add_bad(2))   # [1, 2]   <- surprise: shared with the first call

def add_good(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []                 # a fresh list on every call
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

def read_numbers(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            yield int(line)         # one value at a time

total = sum(read_numbers('huge.txt'))      # never holds the whole file

squares_list = [x * x for x in range(10_000_000)]   # builds all 10M values now
squares_gen = (x * x for x in range(10_000_000))    # builds each when asked

from django.db import models

class Settings(models.Model):
    # GOOD: a callable, so every row gets its own new list
    tags = models.JSONField(default=list)

interview.q: What is the mutable default argument problem and how do you fix it?
interview.a: A default value is evaluated once when the function is defined, so a mutable default such as a list is shared by every call that omits it. Use None as the default and create the list inside the function.

interview.q: What is the difference between 'is' and '=='?
interview.a: '==' tests whether two objects are equal in value, using __eq__. 'is' tests whether two names point to the very same object. Use 'is' for None and singletons, and '==' for values.

interview.q: What is the GIL and does it mean Python can't use multiple threads?
interview.a: The global interpreter lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in CPython. Threads still run, and the lock is released during I/O, so threads help I/O-bound work. For CPU-bound work you use multiprocessing or native extensions that release the lock.

interview.q: What is a generator and when would you use one?
interview.a: A function with yield that produces values one at a time and remembers its state between them. I use it to process large or streaming data without holding everything in memory, such as iterating a big file or queryset.

interview.q: What is a decorator?
interview.a: A function that takes a function and returns a new function that wraps it, adding behavior before or after the call. login_required and transaction.atomic are examples. I use functools.wraps so the wrapper keeps the original name and docstring.

interview.q: Shallow copy versus deep copy?
interview.a: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but its elements are still the same objects. A deep copy recursively copies nested objects too, so changes to the copy never affect the original.

interview.q: Threads, processes or asyncio for a service that calls many slow APIs?
interview.a: That work is I/O-bound, so threads or asyncio fit. asyncio handles very many concurrent waits on one thread but requires async-compatible libraries. Threads are simpler to add to existing blocking code. Processes are for CPU-bound work.

title: Python asyncio: Tasks, Cancellation and Blocking
tagline: Run many waits at once on one thread, and know exactly what happens when one of them fails, times out or blocks.
explain: asyncio lets one thread juggle many tasks that spend their time waiting. It is the engine under async web frameworks and many network clients. The syntax is small. The mistakes are in the details: forgetting to await, losing a task, and blocking the loop.
## Coroutines do nothing until you run them

Calling an async def function only creates a coroutine object. Nothing runs. asyncio.run(main()) starts the event loop and runs the top-level coroutine. Inside, await runs another coroutine to completion before continuing, so two awaited sleeps of one second take about two seconds in total.
## Tasks run at the same time

asyncio.create_task() schedules a coroutine to run on the loop and returns a Task at once. While your code awaits something else, the task makes progress. The same two one-second sleeps as tasks take about one second. One trap from the docs: the loop keeps only weak references to tasks, so keep your own reference, or the task may be garbage collected before it finishes.
## Task groups

asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11) is the safe way to run several tasks. Leaving the async with block waits for all of them. If one fails with an error that is not a cancellation, the group cancels the rest, then raises the errors together as an ExceptionGroup, which you catch with except*. Prefer it to loose create_task calls.
## gather, and its different failure rule

asyncio.gather(*aws) waits for several awaitables and returns their results in order. By default the first exception propagates immediately, but the other awaitables are not canceled and keep running. With return_exceptions=True, exceptions are returned as results instead. If gather itself is canceled, all of its awaitables are canceled. That difference from TaskGroup surprises people.
## Timeouts and cancellation

asyncio.timeout(delay) is an async context manager that cancels the work and raises TimeoutError, which you catch outside the block. asyncio.wait_for does a similar job for one awaitable and waits for the cancellation to finish. Cancelling a task raises CancelledError inside it at the next await, and CancelledError derives from BaseException. Clean up in try/finally and re-raise. Swallowing it hides the cancellation from the code that asked for it. asyncio.shield protects an inner task from cancellation, though the caller still receives CancelledError.
## Never block the loop

A blocking call such as time.sleep, a slow library or heavy computation inside a coroutine freezes every other task, because the loop is one thread. Move it to a thread with asyncio.to_thread, which is intended for I/O-bound work, or to an executor for heavier jobs. Python's debug mode, turned on with asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1, logs callbacks that run longer than 100 milliseconds and warns about coroutines that were never awaited.
## How to talk through it

Say that asyncio is for many waits, not for CPU work. Show create_task or TaskGroup for concurrency, explain the gather versus TaskGroup failure rule, cover timeouts and cancellation with cleanup, and finish with the rule never to block the loop.
keyPoints: A coroutine does nothing until awaited or scheduled; asyncio.run starts the loop.
create_task runs coroutines concurrently; keep a reference to each task.
TaskGroup cancels the rest if one task fails; gather by default does not.
timeout() and wait_for cancel; CancelledError is a BaseException, so clean up with finally and re-raise.
Never block the loop: use asyncio.to_thread for blocking calls.

sql.title: Awaiting one by one versus together
sql.code:
import asyncio, time

async def work(name, delay, log):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    log.append(name)
    return name

async def one_after_another():
    log = []
    await work("a", 0.1, log)
    await work("b", 0.1, log)
    return log

async def together():
    log = []
    t1 = asyncio.create_task(work("a", 0.1, log))      # scheduled now, runs while we wait
    t2 = asyncio.create_task(work("b", 0.1, log))
    await t1
    await t2
    return log

def timed(coro_fn):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    asyncio.run(coro_fn())
    return time.perf_counter() - start

assert timed(one_after_another) >= 0.19                # about 0.2 s: the waits add up
assert timed(together) < 0.17                          # about 0.1 s: the waits overlap

sql.title: TaskGroup, cleanup on cancellation, and timeout
sql.code:
import asyncio

async def boom():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    raise ValueError("bad")

async def slow(cleaned):
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
    finally:
        cleaned.append("cleanup")                       # runs when the task is cancelled

async def group():
    cleaned, errors = [], []
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:          # the first failure cancels the other tasks
            tg.create_task(slow(cleaned))
            tg.create_task(boom())
    except* ValueError as eg:                          # no return inside except*: collect, then return below
        errors = [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions]
    return cleaned, errors

cleaned, errors = asyncio.run(group())
assert cleaned == ["cleanup"] and errors == ["bad"]

async def with_timeout():
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.05):
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
    except TimeoutError:                                # caught outside the block
        return "timed out"

assert asyncio.run(with_timeout()) == "timed out"

sql.title: A blocking call freezes the loop
sql.code:
import asyncio, time

async def demo(block):
    ticks = []
    async def ticker():
        for _ in range(3):
            await asyncio.sleep(0.02)
            ticks.append(1)
    t = asyncio.create_task(ticker())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)                              # let the ticker start
    if block:
        time.sleep(0.1)                                 # blocks the whole event loop
    else:
        await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.1)        # the loop keeps running meanwhile
    seen = len(ticks)
    await t
    return seen

assert asyncio.run(demo(block=False)) == 3              # the ticker ran during the wait
assert asyncio.run(demo(block=True)) == 0               # a blocking call froze everything

exercise: Write a function that fetches ten pretend URLs (simulate each with asyncio.sleep of a random short time). Run it sequentially, then with create_task, then with TaskGroup, and print the three times. Make one of the ten fail and compare what gather and TaskGroup do to the other nine. Then add a time limit with asyncio.timeout and make sure each task cleans up in a finally block when canceled.
pitfalls: Calling a coroutine without await, so it never runs and only a warning appears.
Using time.sleep or a blocking library in a coroutine.
Not keeping a reference to a task created with create_task.
Catching CancelledError and not re-raising it.
Assuming gather cancels the other awaitables when one fails.

interview.q: What is the difference between a coroutine and a task?
interview.a: A coroutine is the object made by calling an async def function and does nothing until awaited. A task wraps a coroutine and schedules it on the event loop so it runs concurrently with other work.

interview.q: How do TaskGroup and gather differ when one task fails?
interview.a: TaskGroup cancels the remaining tasks and raises an ExceptionGroup. gather by default propagates the first exception but does not cancel the other awaitables, which keep running.

interview.q: How do you set a time limit on an async operation?
interview.a: Wrap it in asyncio.timeout(seconds), or use asyncio.wait_for. The work is canceled and TimeoutError is raised.

interview.q: What happens if you call time.sleep in a coroutine?
interview.a: It blocks the whole event loop thread, so no other task runs until it returns. Use await asyncio.sleep, or run blocking code with asyncio.to_thread.

interview.q: Why must you re-raise CancelledError?
interview.a: Cancellation is how the caller asks the task to stop. Swallowing it hides that from the caller. Clean up in finally and let it propagate.

basis: Why it is here: asyncio is the foundation for async Python services, and interviewers ask how it differs from threads and what can go wrong. That a coroutine does nothing until run, asyncio.run, the create_task weak-reference warning, TaskGroup and ExceptionGroup, gather's failure rule and return_exceptions, timeout and wait_for, CancelledError being a BaseException, shield, to_thread, debug mode, the 100 millisecond slow-callback log and never-awaited warnings are from the Python asyncio pages I read; the end of the tasks page came through a summary. The code samples run in the test suite's Python and the small delays in them are illustrative assumptions. The advice on what to say first is my own judgment. Hours and priority are my judgment; the roadmap treats this lesson as nice to have.

scenes.title: One loop, many tasks

steps.title: Calling a coroutine only creates it
body: fetch() returns a coroutine object and nothing runs. asyncio.run(main()) starts the loop and runs the top-level coroutine.
A coroutine that is never awaited gives a RuntimeWarning.

steps.title: Tasks run while you wait
body: create_task() schedules a coroutine and returns a Task at once. Two 1-second waits as tasks take about 1 second. Awaited one after the other they take about 2.
Keep a reference to each task.

hud.v: ~1 s as tasks, ~2 s in a row

predict.question: Two coroutines each await a 1 second sleep. About how long in total if you await them one after the other?
predict.why: Awaiting runs each to completion first, so the waits add up.

steps.title: TaskGroup: one failure cancels the rest
body: async with asyncio.TaskGroup() waits for all its tasks. If one raises an error, the group cancels the others and raises the errors as an ExceptionGroup, caught with except*.
Prefer it to loose create_task calls.

steps.title: gather has a different rule
body: By default gather propagates the first exception, but the other awaitables are not canceled and keep running. return_exceptions=True returns errors as results.
If gather itself is canceled, all its awaitables are canceled.

callout.text: TaskGroup and gather differ here: choose on purpose.

predict.question: With gather and default settings, one awaitable raises. What happens to the others?
predict.why: The first exception propagates, and the other awaitables are not canceled.

steps.title: Timeouts cancel the work
body: async with asyncio.timeout(5): ... cancels the work after 5 seconds and raises TimeoutError, which you catch outside the block.
CancelledError is a BaseException: clean up with finally and re-raise it.

steps.title: A blocking call freezes the whole loop
body: time.sleep(1) in a coroutine blocks the loop thread, and every task waits. Move blocking work to asyncio.to_thread, or an executor for heavy jobs.
Debug mode logs callbacks running longer than 100 ms.

callout.text: Use asyncio.to_thread for blocking I/O-bound code.

everyday.plain: Cook several dishes at once by switching between them whenever one is waiting, instead of standing and watching each pot.
everyday.story: A cook puts rice on, and while it simmers she chops vegetables, then stirs the dal. She never stands idle. But if she stares at the rice and refuses to move, every other dish stops. asyncio is a cook who switches whenever something is waiting.

title: The Django Request Cycle and Middleware
tagline: Follow one web request from the moment it arrives until the reply goes back.
explain: When you can draw what happens between a browser sending a request and Django returning a page, most Django questions become easy: where authentication happens, why middleware order matters, where an exception is handled, and why a view never ran. This lesson follows one request all the way through.
## The path of a request

A WSGI or ASGI server such as Gunicorn receives the HTTP request and hands Django an HttpRequest. Django then runs it through the middleware stack, finds the view through the URL configuration, calls the view, and sends the response back out through the middleware in the opposite direction.
## Middleware is an onion

The Django docs describe middleware as a framework of hooks into request and response processing, a light plugin system for globally altering input or output. Each middleware wraps the next. A middleware gets a get_response callable: it does its work before the request goes in, calls get_response(request), then does its work on the response coming back. During the request phase Django applies middleware top to bottom in the order of the MIDDLEWARE setting. The response then passes through the layers in reverse order.

- Order matters because middleware can depend on each other. The docs' example: AuthenticationMiddleware stores the authenticated user using sessions, so it must come after SessionMiddleware.
- A middleware can short-circuit by returning a response without calling get_response. Then no layer inside it, including the view, sees the request, and the response only travels back out through the layers the request passed through. This is how an auth or rate-limit check rejects a request early.
- Class-based middleware may also define process_view (just before the view), process_exception (when the view raises) and process_template_response. Returning None means 'carry on'. Returning a response means 'stop here'.
## URL routing

The docs list the steps. Django determines the root URLconf (normally the ROOT_URLCONF setting), loads it and reads urlpatterns, runs through each pattern in order and stops at the first match, then calls the view with the HttpRequest first and any captured values as arguments. If nothing matches, or an exception is raised, Django calls an error-handling view. Two consequences: put specific patterns before general ones, because the first match wins, and remember that the URLconf looks only at the path, not the query string or the HTTP method.
## The view and what it returns

A view is any callable that takes a request and returns a response. It can be a function or a class-based view. Inside it you usually talk to the ORM, which means a database query happens here, then you render a template or build a JSON response. In Django REST Framework the view layer adds authentication, permission and throttle checks before your handler runs.
## Where common things live

- request.user comes from AuthenticationMiddleware, which reads the session.
- CSRF checking is CsrfViewMiddleware, so it runs before your view.
- An unhandled exception in a view becomes a 500 response, and middleware such as process_exception can turn it into something else.
- Per-request transactions are the ATOMIC_REQUESTS setting, which wraps the view in a transaction.
## Testing a request

The Django test client (self.client.get, self.client.post) runs a request through the whole stack without a network, so a test exercises middleware, URL routing and the view together. Use assertNumQueries to lock in the query count.
keyPoints: Server → middleware (top to bottom) → URL resolver (first match wins) → view → response back through middleware (bottom to top).
Middleware order matters: AuthenticationMiddleware must come after SessionMiddleware.
A middleware that returns a response without calling get_response short-circuits: the view never runs.
process_view, process_exception and process_template_response are extra hooks for class-based middleware.
URL patterns are tried in order, only the path is matched, and no match leads to an error view such as 404.

sql.title: URL order: first match wins
sql.code:
# urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path('articles/2003/', views.special_case_2003),       # specific first
    path('articles/<int:year>/', views.year_archive),
    path('articles/<int:year>/<int:month>/', views.month_archive),
]
# /articles/2003/    -> special_case_2003 (matched first)
# /articles/2005/    -> year_archive(request, year=2005)
# /articles/2003     -> no match (the patterns need the trailing slash) -> 404

django.title: A function-based middleware that times every request
django.code:
import logging, time

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def timing_middleware(get_response):
    # one-time setup when the server starts
    def middleware(request):
        start = time.perf_counter()          # runs BEFORE the view (and inner middleware)
        response = get_response(request)     # everything inside the onion
        ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        logger.info('%s %s -> %s in %.0f ms', request.method, request.path, response.status_code, ms)
        return response                      # runs AFTER the view, on the way out
    return middleware

# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    'myapp.middleware.timing_middleware',
    # ...
]
django.note: This follows the function-based pattern in the Django docs. Placing it first would also time the other middleware, placing it later times less.

Response goes back out through A only

steps.title: Setup: three middleware, A, B, C
body: Order in MIDDLEWARE is A, B, C, and the view sits in the middle. B is an auth check that returns 401 when there is no token.

predict.question: MIDDLEWARE is [A, B, C]. B returns a response without calling get_response. Which layers handle the response on the way out?
predict.why: C was never reached, so it never sees the response. The response goes back out only through the layers the request passed in through: B, then A.

steps.title: Request goes in: A runs
body: A does its pre-work and calls get_response, which is B.

steps.title: B rejects the request
body: B finds no token, so it returns a 401 response and never calls get_response. C and the view never see the request.

steps.title: Response goes back out through A only
body: The response returns only through layers the request passed through. A does its post-work and the client gets the 401.
The docs: if a layer short-circuits, none of the layers inside it, including the view, see the request or the response.

exercise: Add the timing middleware from this lesson to a project and read its log lines. Then write a second middleware that returns a 401 JSON response when a header is missing, place it before and after SessionMiddleware, and observe the difference. Write a test with the test client that proves the view never ran when the header is missing (for example by asserting a counter on the view did not change).
pitfalls: Putting a middleware that needs request.user before AuthenticationMiddleware.
Doing slow work in a middleware, which adds latency to every request.
Putting a general URL pattern above a specific one so the specific view is never reached.
Forgetting that the URLconf matches only the path, not the HTTP method, so the view must check the method.
Reading request.POST in middleware before the view, which can prevent later changes to upload handling.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens when a request hits a Django app.
interview.a: The WSGI or ASGI server builds an HttpRequest. It passes through MIDDLEWARE top to bottom, the URL resolver picks the first matching pattern, the view runs and usually calls the ORM, and the response travels back out through the middleware bottom to top before the server sends it.

interview.q: What is middleware and why does its order matter?
interview.a: It is a layer of hooks around request and response processing. Order matters because layers can depend on each other: AuthenticationMiddleware uses the session, so it must come after SessionMiddleware.

interview.q: How can a middleware stop a request from reaching the view?
interview.a: By returning a response without calling get_response. Then the inner layers and the view never run, and the response goes back out only through the layers the request already passed.

interview.q: What do process_view and process_exception do?
interview.a: process_view runs just before the view and can return a response to skip it. process_exception runs when the view raises, and can return a response to handle the error. Returning None lets normal processing continue.

interview.q: How does Django match URLs?
interview.a: It reads urlpatterns from the root URLconf and tries each pattern in order, stopping at the first match, then calls that view with the request and captured values. If nothing matches it invokes an error view such as 404.

interview.q: Where does request.user come from?
interview.a: AuthenticationMiddleware attaches it to the request using the session, so it is available in views as long as that middleware is enabled and ordered after SessionMiddleware.

The onion model, short-circuiting, the hooks, the middleware ordering example and the five URL-routing steps are all taken from the Django docs pages I opened. Hours are my estimate.

title: Designing Django Models
tagline: Turn each business thing into one model class, then say exactly what is allowed in it and how it links to the others.
explain: A Django model is a Python class that describes one table. Each attribute is a column, and each instance is a row. The more exactly you describe the data here, the fewer bad rows ever reach the database.
## One class, one table

A model subclasses django.db.models.Model. If you do not declare a primary key, Django adds an automatic one (a BigAutoField by default). Every model has exactly one primary key, and changing it on a saved object and saving again creates a new row, not an update.
## null and blank are not the same

null is about the database: can the column hold NULL? blank is about validation: may a form leave it empty? Both default to False. They are separate on purpose. A text field is usually blank=True with no null=True, so an empty value is one thing (an empty string) and not two things (an empty string and NULL). That last rule is common practice, and it is my own judgment, not a sentence from the docs.
## Choices and defaults

choices takes pairs of stored value and label, and Django adds get_FOO_display() to show the label. default can be a plain value or a callable, and a callable runs for each new object. db_default sets the default inside the database itself. If both are set, default wins for objects created through the ORM.
## Relationships

ForeignKey(Other, on_delete=...) is many-to-one and always needs on_delete. ManyToManyField is many-to-many. OneToOneField is one-to-one. You can pass the related model as a string such as "shop.Product" when the class is defined later or in another app. When a many-to-many link needs its own data (the date a student joined a course), give it a through model, and add a UniqueConstraint on the two foreign keys so the same pair cannot be added twice.
## Meta: rules for the whole table

The inner class Meta holds options that are not fields. ordering sets the default sort, and the docs warn that ordering is not a free operation, because the database must sort. indexes takes a list of models.Index objects. constraints takes a list such as CheckConstraint(condition=Q(age__gte=18), name='age_gte_18') or UniqueConstraint. The older unique_together still works, but the docs say to use UniqueConstraint instead. db_table defaults to the app label, an underscore and the model name. managed = False tells Django not to create or change the table.
## Three kinds of inheritance

An abstract base class (Meta.abstract = True) makes no table. It only shares fields between children. Multi-table inheritance gives the parent and the child a table each, joined by an automatic one-to-one link. A proxy model (Meta.proxy = True) shares its parent's table and changes only Python behavior, such as a default ordering or an extra method. Pick abstract to share columns, and proxy to share a table.
## Methods and managers

Put logic about one row on the model as a method. Put logic about the whole table on a manager or a custom QuerySet. Always define __str__, because the admin and the shell show it. If you override save(), call super().save() or nothing is written. Managers are reachable only from the class (Book.objects), not from an instance.
## How to talk through it

Start from the questions the app asks of the data, then list entities and their links. Say what must be unique, what may be empty, and what happens to children when a parent is deleted. Then say which of those rules you enforce in the database (constraints) and which only in forms. Rules that matter should live in the database, because code paths other than your forms can write data too.
keyPoints: A model is one table; an instance is one row; a field is one column.
null is for the database, blank is for validation; text fields usually use blank=True without null=True.
Every ForeignKey needs on_delete. Use through models and a UniqueConstraint when a link carries its own data.
Put rules that must never break in Meta.constraints, not only in forms.
Abstract shares columns, multi-table splits across tables, proxy shares a table and changes behavior.

Abstract base class and proxy model

django.title: See what the migration will run
django.code:
python manage.py makemigrations shop
python manage.py sqlmigrate shop 0001   # prints the CREATE TABLE and constraint SQL
python manage.py migrate
django.note: Read the SQL before you migrate. It shows the real column types, the constraints and the indexes Django will create.

exercise: Model a small library: books, authors, members and loans. Decide which fields may be blank, which must be unique, and what happens to loans when a member is deleted. Put at least two rules in Meta.constraints. Then run makemigrations and read the SQL with sqlmigrate to see what Django will create. Finally write one custom QuerySet method (overdue loans) and say why it is not a model method.
pitfalls: Using null=True on text fields, so an empty value has two spellings: '' and NULL.
Choosing on_delete=CASCADE without thinking: deleting one parent silently deletes a lot of rows.
Enforcing a rule only in a ModelForm, then writing bad data from a script or the admin.
Using multi-table inheritance for sharing a few fields, which adds a join to every query.
Overriding save() without calling super().save().

interview.q: What is the difference between null=True and blank=True?
interview.a: null controls whether the database column may hold NULL. blank controls whether validation (forms, the admin, full_clean) accepts an empty value. They are independent. For text fields the usual choice is blank=True and no null, so empty means only an empty string.

interview.q: When would you give a many-to-many a through model?
interview.a: When the link has data of its own, such as a join date or a role, or when you want to control it with constraints. Add a UniqueConstraint on the two foreign keys so the same pair cannot appear twice.

interview.q: What are the three kinds of model inheritance in Django, and when do you use each?
interview.a: Abstract base class: share fields, no table of its own. Multi-table inheritance: parent and child each have a table joined by a one-to-one link, which costs a join. Proxy: same table, different Python behavior such as ordering or methods. Use abstract for shared columns and proxy for behavior.

interview.q: Why put a rule in Meta.constraints and not only in a form?
interview.a: Forms only guard the paths that use them. Scripts, the admin, other services and bulk operations can still write bad rows. A database constraint holds for every path.

interview.q: What does on_delete do, and how do you choose a value?
interview.a: It says what happens to child rows when the parent is deleted: CASCADE deletes them, PROTECT blocks the delete, SET_NULL clears the link. Choose from the business meaning: loans of a deleted member are history to keep (PROTECT or SET_NULL), not noise to delete.

interview.q: Where does logic about the whole table go, and where does logic about one row go?
interview.a: Whole-table logic goes on a manager or custom QuerySet (Book.objects.in_stock()). One-row logic goes on the model as a method (book.is_available()).

basis: Why it is here: every Django interview asks how you would model a domain, and the field options and Meta rules decide whether bad data can get in. The facts about fields, relationships, through models, Meta options, constraints and inheritance are from the Django docs pages on models and model Meta options that I read (the second half of the models page came through a summary). The advice that text fields use blank=True without null=True, and the choice of when to use each inheritance style, is my own judgment, not a published standard. The library example is my own worked example. Hours and priority are my judgment. The roadmap lowers this lesson for non-Django roles.

title: Class-Based Views and Forms
tagline: Handle a web page as a class with one method per HTTP verb, and let a form check the data before you use it.
explain: A class-based view (CBV) is a class whose methods are named after HTTP methods: get(), post(), and so on. It replaces the if request.method == 'POST' branch of a function view with one method per verb. Forms do the other half of the job: they turn raw submitted text into checked Python values.
## What as_view() really does

In urls.py you write MyView.as_view(). That call returns an ordinary function for the URL resolver. On every request Django creates a new instance of your class, calls setup() to attach request, args and kwargs, and then calls dispatch(). dispatch() looks at the HTTP method and calls the method with the same name. If you did not define one, the client gets a 405 response (HttpResponseNotAllowed).
## Configuring a view

Class attributes can be changed in a subclass, or passed to as_view() as keyword arguments, for example GreetingView.as_view(greeting='G'day'). The docs note that as_view() arguments are set once, when the URLs are imported, so do not put per-request data there. Generic views such as TemplateView use TemplateResponseMixin, which reads the template_name attribute and gives you render_to_response().
## Mixins

A mixin is a small class that adds one behavior, such as LoginRequiredMixin. A view may have only one parent that inherits from View, and every other parent should be a mixin. The docs warn that combining two full views, such as ProcessFormView and ListView, will not work as expected. List mixins first, so their methods run before the view's.
## Forms: from text to checked values

A form is a class with fields. Given data (request.POST) it is bound; with no data it is unbound. Calling is_valid() runs the checks on every field and fills cleaned_data with real Python values (a BooleanField gives a boolean, not the string 'on'). A ModelForm builds its fields from a model. The admin is built on ModelForm.
## The pattern every form view follows

On GET, build an unbound form and render it. On POST, build a bound form from request.POST and call is_valid(). If it is valid, do the work and redirect (HttpResponseRedirect), so a refresh does not submit twice. If it is not valid, render the same bound form again: it keeps what the user typed and shows the errors. A POST form needs {% csrf_token %} in the template, or CsrfViewMiddleware rejects it.
## Where the extra checks go

Field options such as max_length are checked first. For rules between fields, a form has a clean() method, and for one field a clean_<name>() method. The docs page on forms that I read points to a separate page for this order, and I did not open that page, so treat the order as general Django knowledge to confirm in the docs.
## Protecting a view

Wrap the view in the URLconf, login_required(MyView.as_view()), or decorate the class with method_decorator(login_required, name='dispatch'). The docs also point to LoginRequiredMixin as the class-based way. Decorators in method_decorator run in the order you list them.
## How to talk through it

Say that a CBV is a way to share behavior: use a function view for a one-off page and a generic view or mixin when many pages do the same thing. Then walk one request: as_view, setup, dispatch, handler, form, redirect. Name the two traps: mixing too many mixins until nobody knows which method runs, and trusting request.POST without a form.
keyPoints: as_view() makes a fresh instance per request, calls setup(), then dispatch(), which calls get() or post().
A missing method gives a 405 response, not an error page.
Forms: bound means it has data; is_valid() fills cleaned_data; always redirect after a good POST.
A form POST needs {% csrf_token %} in the template.
One parent from View; all other parents are mixins.
