A form with a check across two fields

django.title: Protect a class-based view
django.note: dispatch runs before get() or post(), so decorating it protects every method of the class.

exercise: Build a contact page as a class-based view with a form. Make it work for GET and POST, redirect after success, and show errors on failure. Then write three tests with the test client: GET shows the form, a bad POST shows errors and keeps the typed values, a good POST redirects. Finally protect the view so only logged-in users reach it, once with a mixin and once with method_decorator, and say which you prefer and why.
pitfalls: Returning a render() after a successful POST, so a refresh submits the form again.
Forgetting {% csrf_token %}, then wondering why every POST is rejected.
Using request.POST directly and skipping the form, so nothing is validated.
Stacking many mixins until it is unclear which method runs first.
Setting per-request data in as_view() arguments, which are fixed once at import time.

interview.q: What does as_view() do?
interview.a: It returns a function for the URL resolver. On each request that function creates a new instance of the view class, calls setup() and then dispatch(), which calls the method matching the HTTP verb, or returns 405 if there is none.

interview.q: When would you choose a class-based view over a function view?
interview.a: When many views share behavior (listing, detail, forms) and you can reuse a generic view or a mixin. A function view is simpler for a one-off page. It is a judgment call, not a rule.

interview.q: What is the difference between a bound and an unbound form?
interview.a: A bound form was given data, for example request.POST, so it can be validated and can show errors. An unbound form has no data and is used to show an empty form or defaults.

interview.q: Why redirect after a successful POST?
interview.a: So that refreshing the page does not send the form again. The redirect makes the browser load a fresh GET page.

interview.q: How do you restrict a class-based view to logged-in users?
interview.a: Wrap it in login_required in the URLconf, decorate dispatch with method_decorator(login_required), or add LoginRequiredMixin as the first parent.

references.title: Django docs: Introduction to class-based views

basis: Why it is here: class-based views and forms are the standard way Django handles pages, and interviewers ask how a request reaches get() or post() and what is_valid() does. The as_view, setup and dispatch steps, the 405 behavior, mixin rules, decorating a class, bound and unbound forms, cleaned_data, the GET and POST pattern and csrf_token are from the Django pages on class-based views and forms that I read. The order of clean_<field> and clean() is not on those pages, and I did not open the validation page, so that part is general knowledge to check in the docs. The advice on when to prefer a class-based view is my own judgment. Hours and priority are my judgment; the roadmap lowers this lesson for non-Django roles.

scenes.title: From URL to form to redirect

steps.title: as_view() builds a fresh instance for every request
body: MyView.as_view() returns a function for the URL resolver. On each request Django creates a new instance, calls setup() to attach the request, and then dispatch().
Because each request gets its own instance, instance attributes are safe from other users' requests.
changes: + A view instance for this request

steps.title: dispatch() picks the method named after the verb
body: A GET request calls get(), a POST calls post(). If the class has no method for the verb, the client gets 405 Method Not Allowed.
This replaces the if request.method == 'POST' branch of a function view.

predict.question: A view defines only get(). What happens when a browser sends POST?
predict.why: dispatch() finds no post() method and returns HttpResponseNotAllowed, status 405.

steps.title: GET builds an unbound form and renders it
body: With no data, the form is unbound. The view passes it to the template, which draws the boxes and the csrf token.
Nothing is checked yet because nothing was sent.

steps.title: A bad POST re-renders the bound form with errors
body: The view builds the form from request.POST and calls is_valid(). The checks fail, so the form is shown again, bound: it keeps what the user typed and lists the errors.
No data is saved.

callout.text: Return render() here, not a redirect, so the user sees their mistakes.

steps.title: A good POST saves and redirects
body: is_valid() is True, so cleaned_data holds real Python values. The view saves them and returns a redirect.
The redirect makes the browser load a new GET page, so a refresh does not post the form twice.

predict.question: After a successful POST, what should the view return?
predict.why: A redirect. Then a browser refresh repeats the harmless GET, not the POST.

steps.title: Protect the view with a decorator or a mixin
body: login_required(MyView.as_view()) wraps the view in the URLconf. method_decorator(login_required, name='dispatch') decorates the class. LoginRequiredMixin does it in class style.
All three put a check in front of every handler.
changes: + Login check in front of the view

callout.text: One parent from View; every other parent is a mixin.

everyday.plain: A view is a class with one method for each kind of request, and a form checks what the user sent.
everyday.story: At a bank counter the clerk handles a deposit slip one way and a withdrawal slip another way. Before doing anything, the clerk checks the slip is filled in correctly. If it is wrong, it goes back to you with notes. A class-based view and a form work the same way.
words: A view written as a class, with one method per HTTP verb.
The method that looks at the HTTP verb and calls the matching handler.
A small class that adds one behavior to a view.
A form that has been given data, so it can be checked.
A hidden value in a form that proves the post came from your own page.

title: Caching in Django
tagline: Keep the answer to an expensive question nearby, pick the right place to keep it, and know when to throw it away.
explain: Most pages answer the same questions again and again. A cache stores an answer so the next request skips the slow work. Django gives you four places to cache, from the whole site down to one value, and the browser can cache too.
## Pick a backend first

The CACHES setting names the backend. Memcached and Redis (RedisCache) are shared by all your server processes, which is what production needs. DatabaseCache stores values in a table you create with createcachetable. FileBasedCache uses files. LocMemCache is the default, and the docs say it is per-process, nice for development and probably not a good choice for production. DummyCache stores nothing, for tests. The default TIMEOUT is 300 seconds. KEY_PREFIX and VERSION let several sites or releases share one cache without clashing.
## Four levels

The per-site cache uses UpdateCacheMiddleware first and FetchFromCacheMiddleware last in MIDDLEWARE, and it caches GET and HEAD responses with status 200. The per-view cache is the @cache_page(60 * 15) decorator. The template fragment cache is {% cache 500 sidebar request.user.id %} around one slow block. The low-level API is cache.get(key) and cache.set(key, value, timeout). Go from the bottom up: cache the smallest thing that is slow and does not change per user.
## The cache-aside pattern

The usual code asks the cache first. On a cache hit it returns the stored value. On a miss it does the slow work, stores the result with a timeout, and returns it. Django has cache.get_or_set for this shape. This is the same pattern as the caching-at-scale lesson, now in Django code.
@viz:cache-aside
## Two traps with local memory

Each server process has its own LocMemCache, so with four workers you have four separate caches. One user can see old data on one request and new data on the next, and your hit rate falls. Use a shared backend when you run more than one process.
## The hard part: knowing when to delete

A cache is a copy, and a copy goes stale. A timeout is the simple answer: the data may be old for up to that many seconds. If it must be fresh at once, delete the key when you write the data. Do it with transaction.on_commit, so you never clear the cache for a change that rolls back. Version the key (VERSION or a number inside the key) when a whole format changes.
## Let the browser cache too

HTTP has its own cache. Cache-Control: max-age=604800 keeps a response fresh for a week. no-cache means reuse only after checking with the server. no-store means keep nothing. private allows only the user's own cache, and immutable is for files that never change. A server that sends an ETag can answer a later check with 304 Not Modified and no body. This is free speed for static files and some API responses. Never let a shared cache store per-user pages.
## How to talk through it

Say what is slow, what is safe to share between users, how old it may be, and how you delete it. Name the backend, the timeout and the invalidation. Mention that a cache hides load but does not fix a bad query, and that you measure the hit rate before and after.
keyPoints: CACHES names the backend; LocMemCache is per-process, so use Redis or Memcached when you run many workers.
Four levels: per-site middleware, @cache_page, the {% cache %} tag, and cache.get and cache.set.
Cache-aside: get; on a miss do the work, set with a timeout, return.
Delete or version keys when data changes, and clear after commit with on_commit.
Cache-Control and ETag let the browser cache; no-cache is not no-store.

sql.title: Cache-aside with a timeout and a clear on write
sql.code:
from django.core.cache import cache
from django.db import transaction

def top_products():
    key = 'top-products:v1'
    products = cache.get(key)
    if products is None:                       # miss: do the slow work once
        products = list(Product.objects.order_by('-sales')[:10].values('id', 'name'))
        cache.set(key, products, timeout=300)
    return products

def update_product(product, **fields):
    with transaction.atomic():
        for name, value in fields.items():
            setattr(product, name, value)
        product.save()
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: cache.delete('top-products:v1'))   # only after a real commit

sql.title: Per-view cache and settings

django.title: Cache a slow template block
django.note: The extra arguments after the name make a separate cached copy for each value, here one per user.

exercise: Find the slowest read-only page in a project, measure it, then cache it at the lowest level that works. Use cache-aside with a 5 minute timeout, then add clearing on write with on_commit. Run it with two worker processes and LocMemCache, show that users see different data, then switch to Redis and show it is fixed. Report the hit rate and the response time before and after.
pitfalls: Using LocMemCache with several workers and getting a different cache in each one.
Caching a page that shows the logged-in user's name or cart and serving it to someone else.
Clearing the cache inside a transaction that later rolls back, or clearing before the commit so a reader refills it with old data.
No timeout (None) on data that changes, so it is wrong until someone restarts the server.
Confusing no-cache with no-store: no-cache still stores, it just revalidates before reuse.

interview.q: Why is the default local-memory cache a poor choice in production?
interview.a: It is per-process. Each worker has its own copy, so users can see different data on different requests, and each cache warms up separately. Use Redis or Memcached so all processes share one cache.

interview.q: What are Django's levels of caching?
interview.a: The per-site cache middleware, the per-view @cache_page decorator, the template fragment tag {% cache %}, and the low-level API with cache.get and cache.set. Cache the smallest slow part that is the same for many users.

interview.q: How do you keep a cache from serving stale data?
interview.a: Use a timeout for data that can be a little old. For data that must be fresh, delete or version the key when the data changes, and do it in transaction.on_commit so you only clear after a real commit.

interview.q: What is the difference between Cache-Control no-cache and no-store?
interview.a: no-store means nothing may be stored. no-cache means it may be stored, but must be checked with the server before it is reused.

interview.q: What does an ETag do?
interview.a: It is a value that identifies a version of a response. The client sends it back in If-None-Match, and if nothing changed the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body.

basis: Why it is here: caching is the first thing asked about when a Django page is slow. The backends and their class names, the per-process warning about LocMemCache, the 300 second default timeout, KEY_PREFIX and VERSION, the per-site middleware order, cache_page, the template fragment tag, the set signature and createcachetable are from the Django cache page; the first part of that page was read verbatim and the later API details came through a summary. The Cache-Control, no-cache versus no-store, ETag and 304 facts are from the MDN HTTP caching page I read, also partly summarized. Clearing a cache in on_commit follows the Django transactions page. Which level to cache first, and the sample timeouts, are my own judgment and illustrative assumptions, not measurements. Hours and priority are my judgment.

scenes.title: A page gets faster, and then goes stale

steps.title: Every request pays for the slow query
body: The view runs the same expensive database query on every request, and the answer rarely changes.
At 200 requests a second, that is 200 identical queries a second (an illustrative number).

steps.title: Cache-aside: ask the cache first
body: The view calls cache.get(key). On a miss it runs the query, stores the result with cache.set(key, value, timeout=300), and returns it.
300 seconds is also Django's default timeout.
changes: + A shared cache beside the app

steps.title: The next requests are hits
body: The value is in the cache, so the database is not touched. Hit rate rises and latency falls.
The cost: for up to the timeout, users may see data that is a little old.

predict.question: What is the price of a 300 second timeout?
options: Users may see data up to 5 minutes old
predict.why: A timeout trades freshness for speed: a value can be old by up to its timeout.

steps.title: The default local-memory cache is per process
body: LocMemCache lives inside each worker process. With several workers, each has its own copy, so one user can see new data on one request and old data on the next.
The Django docs say it is nice for development and probably not a good choice for production.

callout.text: More than one worker? Use Redis or Memcached.

steps.title: Delete the key after the data changes
body: When the product is updated, delete the cached value so the next read fills it with fresh data. Do it inside transaction.on_commit so a rolled-back change never clears the cache.
A timeout is the fallback if a delete is ever missed.

callout.text: Clear after the commit, not before, or a reader can refill the cache with the old value.

steps.title: Let the browser cache with Cache-Control and ETag
body: Cache-Control: max-age=604800 keeps a file fresh in the browser for a week. With an ETag, the browser asks 'has this changed?' and the server may answer 304 Not Modified with no body.
no-cache means check before reuse. no-store means keep nothing.

predict.question: Which header value stops a response from being stored at all?
predict.why: no-store forbids storing. no-cache allows storing but needs a check before every reuse.

steps.title: Cache the smallest slow thing that is the same for everyone
body: Prefer a fragment or a value over a whole page when parts are personal. Never serve a cached page with one user's name or cart to another user.
Measure the hit rate. A cache nobody hits is only extra complexity.

callout.text: A cache hides a slow query. It does not fix it.

everyday.plain: Keep the answer to a slow question close by, so you do not work it out again for every visitor.
everyday.story: A tea stall sells the same cup of tea to hundreds of people. The owner keeps a flask of hot tea ready instead of brewing one cup each time. When the flask runs low or goes cold, a fresh pot is made. A cache is that flask.
words: A fast store that keeps the answer to an earlier request.
The answer was already in the cache, so the slow work was skipped.
How many seconds a cached value is kept before it expires.
Removing or replacing a cached value because the real data changed.
A label for one version of a response, used to ask if it changed.

title: Async Django and ASGI
tagline: Let one worker wait on many slow calls at once, and learn exactly where Django is still synchronous.
explain: Most of the time a web view is waiting: for the database, for another service, for a file. A WSGI server gives each waiting request its own thread. An ASGI server runs an event loop, so one worker can wait on many things at once. Django can run either way, and the difference only pays off in certain cases.
## What makes a view async

A view is async if calling it returns a coroutine. For a function view, declare it with async def. For a class-based view, make the handlers (get, post) async, not __init__ or as_view. Django checks this for you. An async view still runs under WSGI, but in a one-off event loop, without the benefit. For the full benefit you need an ASGI server such as Uvicorn, Daphne or Hypercorn, started with a path like myproject.asgi:application.
## The cost of mixing sync and async

Every switch between sync and async costs about a millisecond, says the Django page. Synchronous middleware sitting between an ASGI server and an async view forces Django to switch into sync code and back, and it holds a thread for each request. To get the full gain, run no synchronous middleware. Django logs 'Asynchronous handler adapted for middleware' at debug level when this happens.
## Calling sync code from async code

sync_to_async(func) runs a normal function in a thread and lets you await it. By default thread_sensitive=True, so all such calls share one thread, which keeps non-thread-safe code like database connections safe. async_to_sync does the reverse. Code that is not safe to run beside an event loop raises SynchronousOnlyOperation, and the DJANGO_ALLOW_ASYNC_UNSAFE setting that hides it is not for production.
## The ORM in async code

Most queryset methods that run a query have an a-prefixed twin: aget, afirst, acreate, asave. You can write async for on any queryset. Transactions do not yet work in async mode. The docs say to put transactional code in one sync function and call it with sync_to_async. Persistent connections (CONN_MAX_AGE) should be turned off in async mode.
## What helps and what does not

Async helps when a view spends its time waiting on several independent slow calls, such as three outside APIs, because asyncio.gather can wait for all three together. It does not speed up CPU-bound work, and one blocking call inside an async view, such as time.sleep or a slow library, stalls the whole event loop for everyone. That rule of thumb is my own judgment; the mechanics come from the Django and Python docs.
## Cancellation
If a client disconnects, the view sees asyncio.CancelledError. You can catch it for cleanup, and then you should re-raise it.
## How to talk through it

Say what the view waits on. If it is mostly one database query, async gains little, and plain sync code is simpler. If it fans out to several slow services or holds long connections, async is a good fit. Then name the traps: sync middleware, blocking calls, and transactions.
keyPoints: WSGI: one thread per request. ASGI: an event loop, so one worker can wait on many things.
A view is async if calling it returns a coroutine; the full benefit needs an ASGI server.
Each sync-to-async switch costs about a millisecond; sync middleware forces it for every request.
Use a-prefixed ORM methods; transactions are not async yet, so wrap them in one sync function.
One blocking call in an async view stalls the event loop for everyone.

sql.title: Waiting on three calls together (standard library only)
sql.code:
import asyncio, time

async def slow(name, seconds):
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
    return name

async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(slow('a', 0.2), slow('b', 0.2), slow('c', 0.2))
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    assert results == ['a', 'b', 'c']
    assert elapsed < 0.45          # about 0.2 s together, not 0.6 s one after another

asyncio.run(main())

sql.title: An async Django view with a sync transaction helper
sql.code:
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async
from django.db import transaction
from django.http import JsonResponse

@sync_to_async
def place_order(user_id, items):          # transactions are not async yet: keep them in one sync function
    with transaction.atomic():
        order = Order.objects.create(user_id=user_id)
        OrderLine.objects.bulk_create([OrderLine(order=order, **i) for i in items])
    return order.id

async def checkout(request):
    book = await Book.objects.aget(pk=request.GET['book'])      # async ORM method
    order_id = await place_order(request.user.id, [{'book': book, 'qty': 1}])
    return JsonResponse({'order': order_id})

pip install uvicorn
python -m uvicorn myproject.asgi:application

# production with process management
pip install uvicorn uvicorn-worker gunicorn
python -m gunicorn myproject.asgi:application -k uvicorn_worker.UvicornWorker

exercise: Write a view that calls three slow endpoints (simulate them with asyncio.sleep). Make a sync version and an async version with asyncio.gather and measure both. Then add one blocking time.sleep to the async view, run two requests together, and show the second one is delayed. Finally move the blocking call into sync_to_async or asyncio.to_thread and show the delay is gone.
pitfalls: Making a view async that only runs one database query, and gaining nothing.
Leaving a synchronous middleware in the stack and losing the benefit of ASGI.
Calling time.sleep or a blocking library inside an async view, which stalls everyone.
Using transaction.atomic directly in async code, where transactions do not work yet.
Setting DJANGO_ALLOW_ASYNC_UNSAFE in production to silence an error that is telling the truth.

interview.q: What is the difference between WSGI and ASGI?
interview.a: WSGI is the synchronous standard: one request occupies one thread until it finishes. ASGI supports async code and long-lived connections, so an event loop can wait on many requests at once. Django can run under either.

interview.q: When is an async view worth it?
interview.a: When the view mostly waits on several independent slow calls (other services, slow I/O) that can overlap, or when it holds many long connections. For a single database query or CPU-heavy work it gains little.

interview.q: What does sync_to_async do, and what is thread_sensitive?
interview.a: It lets async code await a normal function by running it in a thread. With thread_sensitive=True, the default, all such calls share one thread, which keeps code that is not thread-safe, like database access, safe.

interview.q: Why can sync middleware slow an async Django app?
interview.a: Django has to switch from async to sync and back around it, which costs about a millisecond each time, and it holds a thread for each request. Async middleware avoids the hop.

interview.q: Can you use transaction.atomic in an async view?
interview.a: Not directly. The docs say transactions do not yet work in async mode. Put the transactional code in a sync function and call it with sync_to_async.

basis: Why it is here: async views and ASGI come up whenever an interviewer asks how Django scales past one thread per request. The asyncio.gather, create_task and cancellation facts are from the Python asyncio pages I read; the end of the tasks page came through a summary. The timings in the example are illustrative assumptions, not measurements. When async is worth it, and the advice to avoid it for a single query, are my own judgment. Hours and priority are my judgment.

scenes.title: One worker, many waits

steps.title: Under WSGI each waiting request holds a thread
body: A synchronous server gives one thread to each request until it finishes. While the view waits on a slow service, that thread does nothing.
Many slow requests mean many idle threads (an illustrative picture).

steps.title: ASGI adds an event loop
body: An ASGI server runs an event loop. When a request awaits something, the loop switches to another task, so one worker can have many requests in flight.
Start it with a path such as myproject.asgi:application under Uvicorn, Daphne or Hypercorn.

steps.title: Overlap independent waits with gather
body: An async view can start calls to Service A and Service B together with asyncio.gather and wait for both. If each takes 200 ms, the view takes about 200 ms, not 400 ms (illustrative).
This is where async pays off.

predict.question: Two independent calls take 200 ms each. About how long does one async view take if it awaits them with gather?
predict.why: gather runs both waits together, so the view takes about as long as the slowest call.

steps.title: Sync middleware forces a thread hop
body: A synchronous middleware between the ASGI server and an async view makes Django switch into sync code and back for every request. Each switch costs about a millisecond, and a thread is held.
Django logs 'Asynchronous handler adapted for middleware' at debug level.
changes: + A sync middleware in the path

callout.text: For the full benefit, use no synchronous middleware.

steps.title: The ORM has async methods, but transactions do not
body: Use aget, afirst, acreate, asave, and async for on querysets. Transactions do not yet work in async mode, so put the transactional code in one sync function and call it with sync_to_async.
Turn off persistent connections (CONN_MAX_AGE) in async mode.

predict.question: Which can you NOT do directly in an async view?
predict.why: Transactions do not yet work in async mode. Wrap them in a sync function and call it with sync_to_async.

steps.title: One blocking call stalls the whole loop
body: A time.sleep or a slow synchronous library inside an async view blocks the event loop thread. Every other request on that worker waits.
Move blocking work to sync_to_async, asyncio.to_thread or an executor.

callout.text: Python's debug mode logs callbacks that run longer than 100 ms.

everyday.plain: Let one worker wait for many slow things at the same time, instead of waiting for them one by one.
everyday.story: A cook puts rice on the stove and, while it cooks, chops vegetables and heats the oil. She does not stand and stare at the rice. Doing other work while one thing waits is what async code does. But if she stops to watch the pot, everything else stops too.

A blocking call that stalls everything

The loop that switches between tasks whenever one is waiting.
A function defined with async def that can pause while it waits.
A call that makes the whole thread wait and do nothing else.
A path of execution inside a process; a sync server uses one for each request.

title: Signals, Transactions and on_commit
tagline: React to events in your app without tangling the code, and make sure side effects only happen after the data is really saved.
explain: Two Django features meet in one famous bug. Signals let one part of the app react when another part does something. Transactions decide when changes become real. If a signal sends an email before the transaction commits, and then the transaction rolls back, the user gets an email about something that never happened.
## Signals in one minute

A signal is a notice that something happened. A receiver is a function that runs when it does. You attach one with the @receiver decorator or Signal.connect(). A receiver must accept sender and **kwargs, because Django may add arguments later, and a receiver written as my_callback(sender) will break. Receivers are held by weak reference by default, so a local function can be garbage collected.
## Where to connect them

Put receivers in a signals submodule of your app and import it in AppConfig.ready(). Connecting them there means they exist once the app has loaded. ready() can run more than once in tests, so give each receiver a dispatch_uid so it only binds once. send() lets a receiver's exception rise to the caller. send_robust() catches it and returns it in a list instead. Async receivers are supported too.
## A warning from the docs

The Django page says signals can quickly lead to code that is hard to understand, and suggests a direct function call where one will do. In practice a signal is right when the sender should not know who listens, as in a reusable app. In your own code, a plain call is clearer and easier to test. That second sentence is my own judgment.
## Transactions: when changes become real

By default Django is in autocommit: each query commits at once. transaction.atomic() groups queries so they all commit or all roll back. Nested atomic blocks make savepoints. ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True wraps each view in a transaction, and a view that raises rolls everything back.
## The exception trap

Do not catch a database error inside an atomic block and carry on. After an IntegrityError the transaction is broken and further queries raise TransactionManagementError. Wrap the risky part in its own inner atomic block and put try/except outside it. Also remember that a rollback does not restore Python field values on your objects.
## on_commit: do it after the data is safe

transaction.on_commit(func) runs func after a successful commit. If the transaction rolls back, the callback is discarded. If there is no transaction, it runs at once. The callback takes no arguments, so use functools.partial or a lambda. This is the right place to start a Celery task, send an email, or clear a cache, because the data is now visible to other connections.
@viz:celery-flow
## How to talk through it

Explain the bug first: a task queued inside a transaction can run before the row exists for the worker, or run for a change that is later rolled back. Then give the fix, on_commit, and name the limit: it runs only if the commit succeeds, so a failing callback cannot undo the commit and needs its own retry.
keyPoints: A receiver must accept sender and **kwargs; connect it in AppConfig.ready() and use dispatch_uid.
The docs warn signals make code hard to follow; prefer a direct call when the sender may know the listener.
atomic groups queries; nested blocks are savepoints; do not catch DB errors inside the same atomic block.
on_commit runs after a successful commit and is discarded on rollback.
Start tasks, send emails and clear caches in on_commit, not in the middle of a transaction.

sql.title: Side effects after the commit
Handling a database error without breaking the transaction
sql.code:
from django.db import IntegrityError, transaction

def add_member(group, user):
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():              # inner block = savepoint
            Membership.objects.create(group=group, user=user)
    except IntegrityError:                      # caught outside the inner atomic block
        return False                            # the outer transaction is still usable
    return True

django.title: Test that a callback waits for the commit
django.note: A plain TestCase wraps each test in a transaction that never commits, so on_commit callbacks do not run unless you capture them.

exercise: Write a post_save receiver that queues a receipt email when an Order is created. First do it the naive way, inside the receiver, and write a test that rolls the transaction back and shows the email was still sent. Then fix it with transaction.on_commit and show with TestCase.captureOnCommitCallbacks that the callback runs only after the commit. Finally say when you would replace the signal with a plain function call.
pitfalls: Sending an email or queuing a task inside the transaction, so it runs for data that is rolled back or not yet visible.
Catching IntegrityError inside the same atomic block and continuing, which breaks the transaction.
Writing a receiver as def handler(sender): without **kwargs.
Connecting receivers at import time in random places, and ending up with duplicates when ready() runs twice.
Using signals for logic that one function call would make obvious.

interview.q: What is a Django signal and when would you use one?
interview.a: A way for one part of an app to announce that something happened, so other parts can react without the sender knowing them. It suits reusable apps. In your own code a direct call is often clearer, and the docs warn signals can make code hard to follow.

interview.q: Why must a signal receiver accept **kwargs?
interview.a: Django may add new arguments to a signal later. A receiver that accepts only sender would break on upgrade.

interview.q: What does transaction.on_commit do?
interview.a: It registers a function to run after the current transaction commits successfully. If the transaction rolls back, the function never runs. Outside a transaction it runs immediately.

interview.q: Why is sending a task from post_save risky?
interview.a: post_save fires inside the transaction. A worker may run the task before the commit, so the row is not visible yet, or the transaction may roll back, so the task acts on data that never existed. Use on_commit.

interview.q: What happens if you catch an IntegrityError inside an atomic block?
interview.a: The transaction is already broken, so the next query raises TransactionManagementError. Wrap the failing code in its own inner atomic block and catch the error outside that block.

basis: Why it is here: the post_save-then-task race is one of the best-known Django bugs, and interviewers ask how on_commit fixes it. The receiver rules (sender and **kwargs, weak references, AppConfig.ready, dispatch_uid, send versus send_robust, the warning about hard-to-follow code) are from the Django signals page I read. Autocommit, ATOMIC_REQUESTS, atomic and savepoints, the broken-transaction rule, field values not being reverted, and on_commit behavior are from the Django transactions page I read. When to prefer a plain function call is my own judgment. The test example with captureOnCommitCallbacks, and the remark that a plain TestCase never commits, are not on the pages I read; they are from my own knowledge of Django's test tools, so confirm them in the docs. Hours and priority are my judgment; the roadmap lowers this lesson for non-Django roles.

scenes.title: Tell the worker only after the data is safe

steps.title: Saving a model fires a signal
body: When the view saves an Order, Django sends post_save. A receiver connected with @receiver runs.
The receiver must accept sender and **kwargs.

steps.title: The naive receiver queues the task right away
body: The receiver puts a task on the queue straight away, inside the open transaction.
A worker may pick it up at once.
changes: + A task queued inside the transaction

steps.title: The worker looks for a row that is not visible yet
body: The worker runs before the commit. It asks the database for the order and finds nothing, because uncommitted rows are not visible to other connections.
The task fails or is retried for no good reason.

pill.text: Order matching query does not exist

changes: + A race between worker and commit

predict.question: Why can the worker not see the new order?
options: The transaction has not committed yet
The task has the wrong name
predict.why: Other connections cannot see uncommitted rows, so the worker may look too early.

steps.title: A rollback makes it worse
body: If the transaction rolls back after the task was queued, the task now refers to an order that never existed, or sends a receipt for a failed purchase.
The queue cannot take it back.
changes: + A task for data that does not exist

steps.title: on_commit runs the callback after the commit
body: The receiver calls transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(pk)). Django keeps the callback and runs it only after a successful commit. On rollback it is discarded.
Now the worker always finds the row.

callout.text: Starting tasks, sending emails and clearing caches all belong in on_commit.

steps.title: Do not catch database errors inside the same atomic block
body: After an IntegrityError the transaction is broken, and the next query raises TransactionManagementError. Wrap the risky call in its own inner atomic block (a savepoint) and catch the error outside it.
Field values on your Python objects are not restored by a rollback.

predict.question: You catch IntegrityError inside the same atomic block and run another query. What happens?
predict.why: The transaction is broken after a database error. Use an inner atomic block and catch outside it.

steps.title: Use a signal only when the sender should not know the listener
body: The docs warn that signals can quickly make code hard to understand. In your own code, a direct function call is easier to read and test.
Signals fit reusable apps, where the sender cannot know who listens (judgment).

callout.text: If you can call the function directly, do.

everyday.plain: Announce that something happened, but only do the follow-up work after the data is really saved.
everyday.story: You post a letter to say your parcel is on the way. If the shop cancels the order a minute later, the letter was wrong. A careful shop posts the letter only after the order is final. on_commit is that careful shop.
maps: Sending an email or a task
words: A notice that something happened, which other code can listen for.
A function that runs when a signal is sent.
A group of database changes that all succeed or all fail together.
A marked point inside a transaction that you can roll back to.
A hook that runs your function only after the transaction commits.

title: Production Settings and Deployment
tagline: Take a project from runserver to a safe, fast production server: the settings, the app server, HTTPS and static files.
explain: runserver is for you, on your laptop. Production needs a real app server, a web server in front, HTTPS, and a different set of settings. Django ships a checklist and a command that finds many mistakes for you.
## Run the check

python manage.py check --deploy inspects your settings against the deployment checklist. Run it against your production settings, and read every warning. It is not a full audit, but it catches the common ones.
## The settings that matter most

SECRET_KEY must be a large random value, kept secret and loaded from an environment variable or a file, never committed. DEBUG must be False, because True leaks source excerpts, local variables and settings. ALLOWED_HOSTS must list your domains, or with DEBUG off Django will not work at all. You can have the web server reject unknown hosts too. Read these from the environment so the same code runs in every place.
## HTTPS

Any site with a login should serve everything over HTTPS. Turn on SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT (or redirect in the web server), and set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE to True so cookies never travel over plain HTTP. Add HSTS with SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS so browsers insist on HTTPS next time. If a proxy ends TLS for you, SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER tells Django which header says the request was secure, and the docs warn that setting it wrongly can open CSRF holes, so only trust a header your own proxy sets.
## The app server

A WSGI app is run by Gunicorn. gunicorn myproject.wsgi starts one process with one thread on 127.0.0.1:8000, and you tune the worker count for your machine. For async you use an ASGI server such as Uvicorn, and Gunicorn can manage Uvicorn workers. Put nginx or another web server in front, acting as a reverse proxy: it terminates HTTPS, serves static files and passes the rest to the app server on localhost.
## Static files and media

Set STATIC_ROOT and run collectstatic so all static files land in one folder the web server can serve. Anything under MEDIA_ROOT is uploaded by users, so it is untrusted, and the web server must never execute it.
## Connections, caches and errors

CONN_MAX_AGE keeps database connections open between requests, which helps when connecting is a big part of request time (turn it off for async). The default cache is local memory, per process, which you probably do not want in production. Send errors somewhere you will see them: ADMINS get 500 emails and MANAGERS get 404 emails, but a monitoring service scales better than email. Add custom 404 and 500 templates.
## How to talk through it

Walk the request: browser to nginx over HTTPS, nginx to Gunicorn on localhost, Django, database. Then list what you changed from development: DEBUG off, a secret from the environment, allowed hosts, secure cookies, static files collected, a shared cache, logging. Finish with check --deploy.
keyPoints: Run python manage.py check --deploy against the production settings and read every warning.
DEBUG False, a random SECRET_KEY from the environment, and a correct ALLOWED_HOSTS.
HTTPS: redirect, secure cookies, HSTS, and trust a proxy header only if your own proxy sets it.
Gunicorn (or an ASGI server) behind nginx; collectstatic into STATIC_ROOT; never execute uploads.
Use a shared cache, set CONN_MAX_AGE thoughtfully, and send errors to a monitoring service.

sql.title: Settings read from the environment
sql.code:
import os

DEBUG = os.environ.get('DJANGO_DEBUG', '0') == '1'
SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']          # fails loudly if missing
ALLOWED_HOSTS = os.environ.get('DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS', '').split(',')

if not DEBUG:
    SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
    CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
    SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000        # start small (for example 3600) and raise it once HTTPS works everywhere
    STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'staticfiles'

sql.title: Run the app server and the check
sql.code:
python manage.py check --deploy
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
gunicorn myproject.wsgi --bind 127.0.0.1:8000 --workers 3
# nginx terminates HTTPS and proxies to 127.0.0.1:8000

django.title: A deployment check in CI
django.code:
DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings DJANGO_DEBUG=0 \
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=$CI_SECRET python manage.py check --deploy --fail-level WARNING
django.note: --fail-level makes the command exit with an error, so a warning stops the pipeline.

exercise: Take a small Django project and prepare it for production. Read every setting from the environment, run check --deploy, and fix each warning. Put Gunicorn behind nginx with HTTPS (a free certificate is fine), run collectstatic, and confirm DEBUG is off by triggering a 500 and checking that no code is shown. Write down which settings you changed and why.
pitfalls: Leaving DEBUG on in production, which exposes source, variables and settings in error pages.
Committing SECRET_KEY to the repository.
Setting SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER to a header that clients can forge.
Setting a long HSTS time before HTTPS works on every subdomain.
Serving user uploads from a place where the web server will execute them.

interview.q: What does python manage.py check --deploy do?
interview.a: It runs Django's checks against the deployment checklist, such as DEBUG, SECRET_KEY, secure cookies and HTTPS settings, and prints warnings for the ones it finds wrong. Run it with the production settings.

interview.q: Why must DEBUG be False in production?
interview.a: With DEBUG on, error pages show source excerpts, local variables and settings, which leaks secrets and helps an attacker.

interview.q: Why run Gunicorn behind nginx?
interview.a: nginx terminates HTTPS, serves static files and buffers slow clients, and passes dynamic requests to Gunicorn on localhost. The app server then does only application work.

interview.q: What do SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE do?
interview.a: They make the browser send those cookies only over HTTPS, so they are never sent in plain text by accident.

interview.q: What is the risk of SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER?
interview.a: It tells Django to trust a header to decide whether a request was secure. If a client can forge that header, security checks can be fooled, so set it only when your own proxy sets and overwrites the header.

references.title: Django docs: How to use Django with Gunicorn

basis: Why it is here: every backend interview asks what you change to take a Django app to production, and the project's own deploy files use Gunicorn behind nginx. check --deploy, SECRET_KEY, DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS, CACHES, STATIC_ROOT, MEDIA_ROOT being untrusted, secure cookies, CONN_MAX_AGE and error reporting are from the Django deployment checklist I read. SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER and its warning, the HSTS setting names, and the Host header rules are from the Django security page I read, which gives no numeric HSTS values. The Gunicorn command and its default of one process with one thread on 127.0.0.1:8000, and the Uvicorn commands, are from the Django deployment pages I read; those pages give no worker count. The --fail-level option in the CI example is not on the pages I read; it is from my own knowledge of manage.py check, so confirm it in the docs. The example HSTS value and worker count are illustrative assumptions, not recommendations. How to order the walk-through is my own judgment. Hours and priority are my judgment.

scenes.title: From runserver to production

steps.title: runserver is for development only
body: The development server is not built for load or safety. In production Django is run by an app server such as Gunicorn, and DEBUG must be off.
gunicorn myproject.wsgi starts one process with one thread on 127.0.0.1:8000 by default.

steps.title: Read secrets and switches from the environment
body: SECRET_KEY, DEBUG and ALLOWED_HOSTS come from environment variables. The same code runs everywhere, and secrets never enter the repository.
A missing SECRET_KEY should fail loudly at start-up.

steps.title: Serve everything over HTTPS
body: nginx terminates HTTPS and passes requests to Gunicorn on localhost. Django adds SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, secure session and CSRF cookies, and HSTS so browsers use HTTPS next time.
TLS gives encryption, integrity and authentication.

steps.title: Trust a proxy header only if your own proxy sets it
body: Behind a proxy, Django cannot see TLS itself. SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER names a header that says the request was secure. If a client can forge it, security checks can be fooled; the docs warn of CSRF problems.
Make sure your proxy overwrites that header on every request.

callout.text: A header you trust blindly is a header an attacker can send.

predict.question: When is it safe to use SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER?
options: Only when your own proxy sets and overwrites the header
predict.why: A client could send the header itself, so only trust it when your proxy always sets it.

steps.title: collectstatic puts static files in one place
body: Set STATIC_ROOT and run collectstatic. nginx serves that folder directly, so Django does not spend time on images and CSS.
Files in MEDIA_ROOT come from users: untrusted, and never to be executed.

steps.title: Tune workers, connections and caches
body: Choose a worker count for your machine. CONN_MAX_AGE keeps database connections open, which helps when connecting is slow. The default cache is per process, so use a shared one.
Send errors to a monitoring service, not only email.

steps.title: Let Django check your settings
body: python manage.py check --deploy compares your settings to the deployment checklist and prints warnings. Run it in your pipeline against the production settings.
Fix each warning or write down why you accept it.

callout.text: Make check --deploy part of every release.

everyday.plain: Move from your own practice setup to a safe, public one, with locks on the doors.
everyday.story: At home you cook with the kitchen door open and the recipe book out. A restaurant needs a licence, locked doors, a clean counter and a proper kitchen. Production settings are the restaurant rules for your Django app.
words: A setting that shows detailed errors; it must be off in production.
A private value Django uses to sign data such as sessions.
Web traffic that is encrypted so others cannot read or change it.
The command that gathers all static files into one folder to serve.
A server in front of your app that passes requests on and can handle HTTPS.

title: Authentication: Sessions, Tokens and JWT
tagline: How a website knows who you are, and remembers you on the next request.
explain: HTTP is stateless: each request arrives with no memory of the last one. Authentication is how a service decides who is making a request, and every scheme is a different answer to 'how do I recognize this client on the next request?'. The three you must be able to compare are server-side sessions, tokens and JWTs.
## Sessions: the server remembers

After login, Django stores session data on the server and sends the browser a cookie that holds only a session ID. The Django docs state that the cookies contain a session ID, not the data itself, unless you use the cookie-based backend. By default sessions are stored in the database, and there are cache, cached-database, file and signed-cookie backends. Because the server keeps the record, it can delete it at logout or on demand, which instantly ends that session.

- Set SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY (the docs recommend leaving it True) so JavaScript cannot read the cookie, and use secure cookies over HTTPS in production.
- Cookie-based authentication needs CSRF protection, because the browser attaches the cookie automatically to requests from other sites.
- The signed-cookie backend is signed but not encrypted, so the client can read the data, it can be replayed, and it is not invalidated at logout. The docs warn about each of these.
- Django does not remove expired sessions for you. Run clearsessions regularly.
## Tokens: the client carries a secret

With DRF's TokenAuthentication, the client sends an Authorization header of the form 'Token <key>'. The key is looked up in the database on each request. It suits native and mobile clients, which do not use browser cookies. The DRF docs say to serve token and basic authentication only over HTTPS in production, and describe the built-in version as fairly simple, pointing to third-party packages for expiry or several tokens per user.
## JWT: a signed token the server does not need to look up

A JSON Web Token carries its own claims (who the user is, when it expires) plus a signature made with a secret key. The DRF docs note that, unlike the built-in TokenAuthentication, JWT authentication does not need a database to validate a token. JWT is not built into DRF, and the docs point to third-party packages. The general design points are worth knowing:

- RFC 7519 defines a JWT as a set of claims carried in either a JWS (signed) or a JWE (encrypted). The common kind is the signed one. It gives integrity, not confidentiality: it cannot be altered, but anyone holding the token can read the claims. An encrypted JWE exists but is less common. Never put secrets in a signed token.
- Because the server does not look it up, you cannot simply delete it. A stolen token works until it expires, so use short lifetimes plus a refresh token, or keep a denylist, and accept the extra state that implies.
- Where the client stores it is a trade-off. A token in JavaScript-readable storage can be stolen by XSS. An HttpOnly cookie is hidden from scripts but brings CSRF back.
## Choosing

- A browser app on your own domain: Django sessions, the simplest and easiest to revoke.
- Mobile or third-party API clients: tokens over HTTPS.
- Many services that must verify users without calling a central store: short-lived JWTs.
Whatever you choose, authentication is not authorization: you still must check, for every object, that this user may touch it (IDOR, see Web Security).
## Passwords
Django stores passwords as salted, slow hashes (PBKDF2 by default), never plaintext. Do not invent your own scheme: use django.contrib.auth for login, and its password validators and change flows.
keyPoints: Sessions: the cookie holds an ID, the server holds the data and can revoke it instantly.
DRF TokenAuthentication: 'Authorization: Token <key>', looked up in the database, HTTPS only.
JWT: signed (tamper-proof) but readable, validated without a database lookup, hard to revoke before expiry.
Cookie auth needs CSRF protection and HttpOnly. Tokens in JS storage face XSS risk.
Authentication is not authorization: check object ownership on every access.

sql.code:
# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    # ...
    'rest_framework',
    'rest_framework.authtoken',      # required for TokenAuthentication; then run migrate
]

REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',   # browser, same site
        'rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication',     # mobile and API clients
    ],
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': ['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated'],
}

# client sends:   Authorization: Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b

sql.title: What a JWT looks like
sql.code:
# three base64url parts joined by dots: header.payload.signature
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9 . eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsImV4cCI6MTc2NDAwMDAwMH0 . <signature>

# decoded header  : {"alg": "HS256"}
# decoded payload : {"sub": "42", "exp": 1764000000}     <- readable by anyone
# signature       : HMAC of header+payload with the server's secret key
#                   -> any change to the payload invalidates it

body: The browser posts the credentials. Django checks the password hash.

learn.text: The client stores and sends it
The server verifies without a database

steps.title: The server signs a token
body: After login the server builds a payload with the user and an expiry, then signs it with a secret key.

predict.question: A user's JWT is stolen. They log out. Can the attacker still use the token?
options: Yes, until it expires, unless the server tracks revocation
Only if they also have the password
predict.why: The server never stored the token, so there is nothing to delete. This is the main trade-off of JWT, and the reason for short lifetimes, refresh tokens and denylists.

steps.title: The client stores and sends it
body: Typically in the Authorization header on each request.
A signed token (JWS) is encoded, not encrypted: anyone holding it can read the payload. RFC 7519 says a JWS provides integrity, and only a JWE encrypts the claims.

steps.title: The server verifies without a database
body: It recomputes the signature with its secret and checks the expiry. If both are fine, the claims are trusted. No lookup is needed, which is why JWT suits many services.

steps.title: The catch: revocation
body: The server keeps no record, so it cannot simply delete the token. A stolen token works until exp.

card.title: User clicks 'log out' after the token is stolen
lines: Scheme                        Attacker can still use it?
Server-side session           No, the record was deleted
Long-lived JWT                YES, until it expires
Short JWT (15 min) + refresh  only for a few minutes
JWT + denylist                No, but you now keep server state

exercise: Build a tiny Django project with session login and a DRF token endpoint. Prove with the test client that: a request without credentials gets 401 or 403, a session-authenticated request works, a token-authenticated request works, and after logout the old session cookie no longer works. Then decode a JWT by hand (split on the dots and base64url-decode the first two parts) and confirm you can read the payload without the secret.
pitfalls: Believing a JWT is encrypted. It is signed, and its payload is readable.
Issuing long-lived JWTs with no way to revoke them.
Using token or basic authentication over plain HTTP.
Relying on cookie auth for an API without handling CSRF.
Authenticating the user but never checking ownership of the object requested.

interview.q: How do Django sessions work?
interview.a: After login Django stores the session data on the server, by default in the database, and sends a cookie containing only the session ID. On each request SessionMiddleware reads the cookie, loads the data and AuthenticationMiddleware sets request.user. Deleting the server record ends the session.

interview.q: Session authentication versus JWT: when would you choose each?
interview.a: Sessions for a browser app on the same domain, because they are simple and revocable instantly. JWT when many services must verify identity without calling a central store, using short lifetimes and refresh tokens because a JWT cannot be revoked easily.

interview.q: Is a JWT encrypted?
interview.a: Not usually. RFC 7519 says a JWT is a claims set carried in a JWS (signed) or a JWE (encrypted). The common signed kind prevents tampering but the payload is only encoded, so anyone with the token can read it. Do not store secrets in it, or use an encrypted JWE if you must.

interview.q: How does DRF TokenAuthentication work, and what are its limits?
interview.a: The client sends 'Authorization: Token <key>' and DRF looks the key up in the database. It must only be used over HTTPS, and the built-in version has no expiry and one token per user, so third-party packages are used when you need more.

interview.q: Why does cookie-based authentication need CSRF protection?
interview.a: Browsers attach cookies automatically to requests, even ones triggered from another site. A CSRF token proves the request came from your own page.

interview.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
interview.a: Authentication establishes who the user is. Authorization decides what that user may do with a specific resource. A logged-in user must still be checked for ownership of the object, or you get IDOR bugs.

basis: Priority 2 is my judgment: authentication is asked in most backend interviews, but the depth expected grows with seniority. The session behavior, the signed-cookie warnings, the token header format, the HTTPS caveat and the note that JWT needs no database lookup come from the Django and DRF pages I opened. The definition of a JWT (signed JWS versus encrypted JWE, and that a signature gives integrity but not confidentiality) comes from RFC 7519, which I opened. The advice on token lifetimes, denylists and client-side storage is general industry practice, not taken from those pages.

everyday.plain: Authentication is proving who you are, and then the server remembering you for later requests.
everyday.story: At a cinema you show your ticket once at the door and get a wristband. After that, staff just look at the wristband. A session is like the cinema keeping a list of wristband numbers. A JWT is like a wristband that carries your seat details, printed and stamped, so staff can check it without calling the office.

Staff checking the list at the office
A stamped wristband that checks itself
words: Server-side memory that you are logged in, found using a cookie.
A string you send with each request to prove who you are.
A signed token that carries your details, so the server can check it without a lookup.
A small piece of data the browser stores and sends back to the same site.

title: Git Workflow: Branches, Merge vs Rebase and Undoing Mistakes
tagline: Work on branches, keep history clean, and know how to undo each kind of mistake.
explain: Git is the tool every team uses to share and track code, and interviews check that you can use it beyond add, commit and push. The skill that shows is knowing what each command does to history, because that tells you which undo is safe.
## Three places your changes live

- The working tree: the files on disk, where you edit.
- The staging area (the index): the changes you have chosen to include in the next commit, set with git add.
- The repository: the commits already recorded, made with git commit.
A commit is a snapshot with a message and a pointer to its parent commit. A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit, so creating one is cheap.
## A day-to-day workflow

- Branch off the main branch for each piece of work: git switch -c feature/order-export.
- Commit small, with messages that say why, not just what.
- Push the branch and open a pull request. Others review, CI runs, and the branch is merged.
- Keep branches short-lived. The longer a branch lives, the worse the conflicts.
## Merge versus rebase

Both bring the work from one branch into another. The Pro Git book describes the difference. A merge takes the two branch tips and their most recent common ancestor and creates a new merge commit, so the history keeps its parallel shape. A rebase takes the changes introduced by each commit on your branch and replays them on top of another branch, so the history becomes a straight line, as if the work had happened in series. The final content is the same. Only the history differs.

The book's rule for rebasing: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Rebasing abandons the existing commits and creates new, similar but different ones. If others already have the old commits, your histories diverge and merging them brings duplicate commits and a messy history. In practice: rebase your own local work before pushing, and never rebase what you have already pushed and shared.
## Resolving a conflict

A conflict means both sides changed the same lines. Git marks the file with conflict markers. Open the file, choose or combine the correct content, remove the markers, git add the file, and continue the merge or rebase. Run the tests afterwards, because a clean merge in text is not always a correct merge in behavior.
## Undoing things: pick by situation

- Edited a file and want it back: git restore <file>.
- Staged something by mistake: git restore --staged <file>.
- Last commit message wrong or a file forgotten, not pushed: git commit --amend.
- A commit that is already shared is wrong: git revert <commit> records a new commit that reverses the effect of the earlier one (that is what its documentation says it does), so history is not rewritten.
- Move your local branch back: git reset. Be careful with --hard, which discards changes, and avoid resetting commits you have pushed.
- Lost something: git reflog lists where your branch pointers have been, and often lets you recover.
- Need to switch tasks with unfinished work: git stash.
keyPoints: Working tree, staging area and repository are three separate places. A branch is a pointer to a commit.
Merge keeps parallel history with a merge commit. Rebase replays commits and gives a linear history.
Never rebase commits you have already pushed and that others may use.
Use git revert for shared commits and git reset only on local work.
git reflog is the safety net for lost commits.

sql.title: Everyday commands
sql.code:
git switch -c feature/order-export      # new branch from where you are
git status                              # what changed, what is staged
git add -p                              # stage chosen hunks, not whole files
git commit -m "Export orders as CSV: stream rows to avoid loading all in memory"
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main                  # replay MY local commits on the latest main (before pushing)
git push -u origin feature/order-export # then open a pull request

sql.title: Undo toolbox
sql.code:
git restore app/views.py                # discard unstaged edits to a file
git restore --staged app/views.py      # unstage, keep the edits
git commit --amend                     # fix the LAST commit (only if not pushed)
git revert abc1234                     # safe undo of a shared commit: adds a new commit
git stash        # park unfinished work ...
git stash pop    # ... and bring it back
git reflog                             # find a 'lost' commit and recover it
git switch -c rescue abc1234           # put a branch on it

scenes.title: Branch and merge

steps.title: One commit on main
body: Each commit points to its parent. 'main' is a pointer to the latest commit, and HEAD says which branch you are on.

steps.title: Create a branch and commit
body: git switch -c feature adds a pointer. Commits on it move only that pointer.

steps.title: Meanwhile main moves on
body: A teammate's work lands on main. The history now has two parallel lines.

steps.title: Merge feature into main
body: Git creates a merge commit M with two parents. Nothing is rewritten, and the parallel history is preserved.

scenes.title: Rebase instead of merge

learn.text: The rule: do not rebase shared commits

steps.title: The same starting point
body: feature has C2. main has moved on to C3.

predict.question: You pushed a branch and a teammate pulled it. You then rebase it and force-push. What happens?
options: Histories diverge and merging brings duplicate commits
Git refuses to ever do this
predict.why: Rebasing creates new commits and abandons the old ones, but your teammate still has the old ones. The Pro Git book's rule: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.

steps.title: git rebase main
body: Git takes the change made in C2 and replays it on top of C3. The new commit is C2', a similar commit with a new identity.

steps.title: Fast-forward main
body: Now main can simply move forward. The history is a straight line, as if the work happened in series.

steps.title: The rule: do not rebase shared commits
body: If you pushed C2 and a teammate built C4 on it, rebasing replaces C2 with C2'. Your histories no longer match, and merging them produces duplicate commits.
Rebase your own local commits before you push. Never rebase work other people have pulled.

card.title: Rebasing a pushed branch
lines: Teammate            C2 and C4 (built on C2)
After merge         C2, C2' and C4: duplicates

scenes.title: Which undo?

steps.title: Not committed yet
body: The change only exists in your working tree or staging area.

card.title: Pick the command
lines: Discard edits to a file  git restore <file>
Unstage but keep edits   git restore --staged <file>

steps.title: Committed, not pushed
body: Only you have it, so rewriting is safe.

card.title: Pick the command
lines: Fix the last commit                  git commit --amend
Drop the last commit, keep the work  git reset --soft HEAD~1
Tidy several local commits           git rebase -i

steps.title: Already pushed or shared
body: Others may have it, so do not rewrite history. Add a new commit instead.

card.title: Pick the command
lines: Undo a bad shared commit  git revert <commit>
Rewrite pushed history    avoid: it breaks teammates

steps.title: Lost something?
body: git reflog records where your branch pointers have been, so a 'deleted' commit can usually be found and recovered.

exercise: In a throwaway repository, create main with two commits, branch off, commit on both branches, then do the same history twice: once with merge and once with rebase, and run git log --graph --oneline each time to compare the shapes. Then cause a conflict on purpose and resolve it. Finally commit something wrong and fix it with each of amend, revert and reset, noting when each is safe.
pitfalls: Rebasing or force-pushing a branch other people have pulled.
Using git reset --hard without checking what it will discard.
Giant commits with messages such as 'fixes' that cannot be reviewed or reverted.
Long-lived branches that drift from main and produce painful conflicts.
Committing secrets or build output instead of ignoring them.

interview.q: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
interview.a: Merge combines two branch tips with a merge commit and keeps the parallel history. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch and gives a linear history. The final content is the same, only the history differs.

interview.q: When should you not rebase?
interview.a: Never rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that others may have based work on. Rebasing replaces commits with new ones, so shared histories diverge and merging them creates duplicates. Rebase local, unpushed work only.

interview.q: How do you undo a commit that has already been pushed?
interview.a: Use git revert, which adds a new commit that reverses the change, so shared history is not rewritten. Rewriting pushed history with reset and force-push would break teammates.

interview.q: What is the staging area?
interview.a: The index: the set of changes you have chosen with git add to include in the next commit. It lets you commit part of your working changes and build clean, focused commits.

interview.q: How do you recover a commit you think you lost?
interview.a: Use git reflog to see where HEAD and branches have pointed recently, find the commit hash, and create a branch on it.

interview.q: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
interview.a: Open the conflicted file, decide the correct content where the markers show both sides, remove the markers, git add the file and continue the merge or rebase, then run the tests.

basis: Priority 2 is my judgment: Git is used daily in every role and basic questions appear in interviews, but it is quick to learn compared with the other tracks, so I treat it as a beginner lesson that experience shortens. The description of merge and rebase and the rule about not rebasing shared commits come from the Pro Git page I opened. The description of git revert comes from the git-revert page, which I opened. The rest of the undo command guide reflects standard Git usage and is not taken from those pages.

At the end you combine your changes. Git does this for code. A branch is your private copy to try things in, and a merge brings the changes back together.

Going back to the last good draft

A separate line of work that does not disturb the main one.
Joining the changes from one branch into another.
Replaying your commits on top of another branch to keep history in a straight line.

title: Docker and Containers for Django
tagline: Pack your app and everything it needs into one box that runs the same everywhere.
explain: A container packages your application with its dependencies so it runs the same on your laptop, in CI and on a server. Docker is the tool most teams use to build and run containers, and 'how would you containerise this Django app?' is a standard backend interview question.
## Images, containers and layers

An image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile. A container is a running instance of an image. Containers share the host machine's operating-system kernel, so they start in seconds and are lighter than virtual machines, which each run a full operating system.

The Docker docs explain that each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer, and each layer adds content on top of the layers before it. Docker caches layers. If a layer's inputs change, that layer is rebuilt, and the docs add that all the layers after it are also affected and must run again, even if they would produce the same output.
## Order layers for the cache

That cache rule decides how to write a Dockerfile. The docs advise putting steps that change rarely, and are expensive, near the beginning, and steps that change often near the end. The standard example: copy only the dependency file first and install dependencies, then copy the rest of the source. The docs show it with package.json for Node. For Python it is requirements.txt. Then editing application code only invalidates the final layers, and the dependency install stays cached.
Add a .dockerignore file, which works like .gitignore, so the build context does not include unnecessary files such as .git, virtual environments and local databases.
## A Django Dockerfile

Start from a slim Python base image, set the working directory, copy requirements.txt, install, copy the code, and run the app with Gunicorn rather than runserver. Docker's best-practices guide backs several habits: if a service can run without privileges, use USER to switch to a non-root user; pin base image versions (it describes pinning to a specific digest as the strongest form); and use multi-stage builds, which reduce the size of the final image. It also warns that an environment variable set in the image persists in that layer and its value can be dumped, so never put secrets in ENV. Pass secrets at run time instead.
## Docker Compose: the whole stack

A real app needs more than one process: the web app, a database, a cache, a worker. Docker Compose describes them in one YAML file and starts them together with one command. Compose creates a default network and attaches every service to it, and each service registers its name with an internal DNS server, so the web app reaches the database at host 'db'. Container IP addresses change when containers are recreated, so always use the name. Database files belong in a named volume, because a container's own filesystem disappears with the container. Check the Compose documentation for the file format your version expects.
## Things interviewers ask

- Image versus container, and container versus VM.
- Why layer order matters, and how you would speed up a slow build.
- How data persists (volumes).
- How containers talk to each other (a shared network and service names).
- Where configuration and secrets come from (environment variables or a secret store, not the image).
- Multi-stage builds, a common technique that builds in one stage and copies only the result into a smaller final image.
keyPoints: Image = template, container = running instance. Containers share the host kernel.
Each Dockerfile instruction is a layer. A changed layer invalidates every layer after it.
Copy requirements first and install, then copy the source, so code edits reuse the cached install.
Use .dockerignore, run Gunicorn (not runserver), run as non-root, keep secrets out of the image.
Compose runs web, database and cache together. Use a named volume for database data.

sql.title: Dockerfile for Django
sql.code:
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app

# 1. dependencies first: this layer is rebuilt only when requirements.txt changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# 2. source last: it changes on every commit
COPY . .

RUN useradd --create-home app && chown -R app /app
USER app

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "config.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

sql.title: .dockerignore
sql.code:
.git
.venv
__pycache__/
*.pyc
db.sqlite3
.env
node_modules/

sql.title: docker-compose.yml
sql.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_HOST: db            # the service name is the hostname
      POSTGRES_DB: app
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}   # read from your shell or .env, not hard-coded
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: app
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data       # keeps data when the container is replaced
volumes:
  pgdata:

exercise: Containerise a Django project: write the Dockerfile and .dockerignore above, then a compose file with web and Postgres. Time a clean build, change one line of a view and rebuild, and confirm the dependency layer shows as cached. Then reorder the Dockerfile the wrong way, rebuild after the same edit, and compare the times. Finally recreate the database container and confirm your data is still there.
pitfalls: Copying the whole project before installing dependencies, so every edit reinstalls them.
Putting secrets in the Dockerfile, in an ENV line or in the image.
Running with runserver, or as root, in the container.
Keeping database data only in the container filesystem.
Forgetting .dockerignore so .git, virtual environments and local databases bloat the build.

interview.q: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
interview.a: An image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile, made of layers. A container is a running instance of an image with a writable layer on top.

interview.q: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
interview.a: A VM runs a whole guest operating system on virtualised hardware. Containers share the host's kernel and isolate processes, so they are lighter and start faster.

interview.q: How do you make Docker builds faster?
interview.a: Order the Dockerfile so rarely changing, expensive steps come first: copy the dependency file and install before copying the source. A changed layer invalidates every later layer, so this keeps the install cached. Also use a .dockerignore and slim base images.

interview.q: How do you persist database data in Docker?
interview.a: Use a named volume mounted at the database's data directory. A container's own filesystem disappears when the container is removed, but a volume survives.

interview.q: How do containers in Compose talk to each other?
interview.a: Compose puts them on a shared network and each service name resolves as a hostname, so the web app connects to the database at host 'db'.

interview.q: Where should secrets and configuration come from?
interview.a: From environment variables or a secret store supplied at run time, not baked into the image or committed to the repository.

basis: Priority 2 is my judgment: Docker is expected for a backend role but at a basic level, and the questions are mostly about layers, volumes and Compose. The layer, cache-invalidation, ordering and .dockerignore statements come from the Docker docs pages I opened. The non-root USER, base-image pinning, multi-stage and ENV-persistence guidance comes from Docker's best-practices page, and the Compose default network and service-name DNS from its networking page, both of which I opened. The container-versus-VM comparison and the Compose file itself are standard practice, so check the Compose docs for your version's file format.

A container is a lunch box for an app: your code, the right Python version and libraries, all inside. 'It works on my machine' stops being a problem.

Packing a box the same way each time
