title: CI/CD and Deploying Django: Nginx, Gunicorn and Production Settings
tagline: Test every change automatically, then run the app on a real server with safe settings.
explain: Writing the app is half the job. Interviewers also ask how code gets from a commit to a running service: how it is tested automatically, what runs in production, and which settings must change. This lesson covers the pipeline and the production request path.
## CI and CD

Continuous integration (CI) means every change is built and tested automatically, so a broken change is caught within minutes. Continuous delivery means every passing change is ready to release, and continuous deployment goes further and releases it automatically. The idea is the same: small changes, automatic checks, and a pipeline that stops when a check fails.

GitHub Actions is one common CI system. Its docs define a workflow as a configurable automated process that runs one or more jobs, defined in YAML in .github/workflows. An event (such as a push) triggers it. A job is a set of steps executed on the same runner (the server that runs it), and each step runs a script or an action. By default, jobs run in parallel, and a job can wait for another with needs.
A typical pipeline: check out the code, install dependencies, lint, run the tests, build the image, then deploy only if everything passed. Put the fast checks first so failures appear quickly.
## The production request path

In production you do not use runserver. The Django deployment checklist says the runserver command is not designed for production and tells you to switch to a production-ready WSGI or ASGI server. A common setup is: Browser, then Nginx, then Gunicorn, then Django, then the database.

- Gunicorn runs your Django code in several worker processes. Its docs strongly recommend running it behind a proxy server. With the default synchronous workers, you must make sure the proxy buffers slow clients, otherwise Gunicorn becomes vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks, because slow clients tie up workers.
- Nginx terminates HTTPS, serves static files, buffers slow clients and forwards requests to Gunicorn. It passes the original host and scheme in headers (Host, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto) so the app knows who called and over which protocol.
- Django needs to be told to trust those headers only from your proxy.
## The settings that must change

The Django deployment checklist says: keep SECRET_KEY secret and out of source control, load it from the environment; never enable DEBUG in production; set ALLOWED_HOSTS; enforce site-wide HTTPS and set CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE and SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE to True; define STATIC_ROOT and run collectstatic so your web server can serve static files; protect database and cache credentials like the secret key. Run python manage.py check --deploy against your production settings, because it automates some of these checks.
## Releasing safely

- Deploy by replacing instances gradually (rolling), so there is no downtime. Old and new code run together briefly, which is why schema changes must be compatible with both (see the production-ops lesson).
- Have a health-check endpoint so the platform only sends traffic to instances that started correctly.
- Know how to roll back: keep the previous image and keep migrations backward compatible.
- Keep secrets in the environment or a secret manager, and never in the repository or the image.
keyPoints: CI runs the tests on every push and blocks a failing change. CD ships passing changes.
GitHub Actions: workflow, event, job, runner, step. Jobs run in parallel unless one needs another.
Production path: Nginx (HTTPS, static, buffering) in front of Gunicorn workers in front of Django.
Gunicorn should sit behind a proxy because slow clients can tie up its workers.
DEBUG False, SECRET_KEY from the environment, ALLOWED_HOSTS, secure cookies, collectstatic, check --deploy.

sql.title: A CI workflow (GitHub Actions)
sql.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - name: Run tests
        run: python manage.py test
      - name: Deployment checks
        run: python manage.py check --deploy

sql.title: Nginx in front of Gunicorn

django.title: Production settings from the environment
django.code:
import os

SECRET_KEY = os.environ['SECRET_KEY']             # never committed to the repo
DEBUG = False                                      # never True in production
ALLOWED_HOSTS = os.environ['ALLOWED_HOSTS'].split(',')

CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True                          # cookies only over HTTPS
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ('HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO', 'https')   # trust the proxy's header

STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'staticfiles'             # collectstatic copies files here

# then:  python manage.py collectstatic && python manage.py check --deploy
django.note: Only set SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER when your proxy always overwrites that header. Otherwise a client could forge it. Read the Django docs for it before enabling.

exercise: Add the CI workflow to a repository and push a commit with a deliberately failing test: confirm the pipeline stops and shows red. Fix it and see it pass. Then run the app with Gunicorn behind Nginx using the snippet above (locally or in Docker Compose), set DEBUG = False, fill in ALLOWED_HOSTS and run manage.py check --deploy. Exposing Gunicorn directly to the internet with no proxy.
Forgetting collectstatic, so static files are missing in production.

Deploying a schema change that old running code cannot handle.

interview.q: What is the difference between continuous integration, delivery and deployment?
interview.a: CI builds and tests every change automatically. Continuous delivery keeps every passing change in a releasable state. Continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically without a manual approval step.

interview.q: How would you deploy a Django app to production?
interview.a: Run it with Gunicorn behind Nginx, with DEBUG off, SECRET_KEY and database credentials from the environment, ALLOWED_HOSTS and secure cookies set, static files collected, and HTTPS enforced. Check settings with manage.py check --deploy and release through a pipeline that runs tests first.

interview.q: Why not use runserver in production?
interview.a: The Django docs say it is not designed for production. It is not built for performance or security, so you switch to a production-ready WSGI or ASGI server such as Gunicorn.

interview.q: Why put Nginx in front of Gunicorn?
interview.a: Gunicorn's docs recommend a proxy because slow clients can occupy its workers and make it vulnerable to denial of service. Nginx buffers those clients, terminates HTTPS, serves static files and forwards the original host and scheme in headers.

interview.q: What would your CI pipeline contain?
interview.a: Triggered by push and pull request: checkout, install dependencies, lint, run the tests, run the deployment checks, then build the image and deploy only if everything passed. Fast checks come first so failures appear quickly.

interview.q: How do you deploy without downtime?
interview.a: Replace instances gradually with health checks so traffic only goes to healthy ones, keep database changes compatible with both the old and new code, and keep a rollback path such as the previous image.

basis: Priority 2 is my judgment: deployment basics are expected for a backend role and CI/CD is a recurring interview topic, but depth varies by company. The checklist items, the Gunicorn-behind-a-proxy advice and the proxy headers, and the GitHub Actions concepts and syntax shown come from the Django, Gunicorn and GitHub pages I opened. The GitHub page I read did not cover service containers, so the example avoids them. Release strategy advice is general practice.

everyday.story: A factory checks each product on a belt before it is packed. If a product fails, the belt stops and a worker looks at it. Only checked products reach the shop. CI is the checking belt for code: every change is tested automatically. CD is the delivery truck that takes passed changes to the shop (the live site).

A failed build stops the release
Truck taking it to the shop

Continuous delivery: passed changes are released automatically.

A web server placed in front of the app to handle connections and files.

title: DRF Internals: Serializers, ViewSets, Routers and Permissions
tagline: How a request becomes data, gets checked, and where the access checks really happen.
explain: The earlier DRF lesson covered API design: pagination, status codes and idempotency. This lesson opens the box and explains the four parts you configure every day: serializers, viewsets, routers and permissions. Interviewers ask 'what does a serializer do?' and 'where do permission checks run?' because the answers expose whether you understand the framework or only copy snippets.
## Serializers: conversion and validation in one place

The DRF docs describe a serializer as something that converts complex data such as querysets and model instances to native Python types, which can then be rendered as JSON. It works in the other direction too: it validates incoming data and turns it back into objects. A ModelSerializer generates its fields and validators from the model, including unique_together validators, and gives you default create() and update() methods. The docs add that the defaults do not support writable nested representations, so nested writes need explicit code.

- Field-level validation: add a validate_<field_name> method that returns the value or raises serializers.ValidationError.
- Object-level validation: add validate(self, data) for rules that involve several fields. On a partial update it receives only the fields sent in the request.
- is_valid(raise_exception=True) raises a ValidationError on bad data, and DRF turns that into an HTTP 400 response. Without raise_exception, serializer.errors holds the messages keyed by field name.
- read_only_fields in Meta stops clients from writing fields such as total or status. Never trust client-sent prices or states.
- save() calls create() or update(), depending on whether you passed an instance. Extra keyword arguments to save(), such as owner=request.user, arrive in validated_data. That is the safe way to set the owner.
## ViewSets and routers

A ViewSet is a class-based view that does not provide get() or post() methods. It provides actions such as list(), create(), retrieve(), update(), partial_update() and destroy(), and you register it with a router that works out the URLs for you. ModelViewSet provides all of the actions. ReadOnlyModelViewSet provides only list and retrieve. GenericViewSet supplies helpers such as get_queryset and get_object but no actions, so you add the ones you want with mixins. The @action decorator adds extra routes, on the collection (detail=False) or on one object (detail=True).

The router's table is worth memorising. For a registered prefix 'orders': GET and POST on orders/ map to list and create, and GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on orders/{pk}/ map to retrieve, update, partial_update and destroy. If the viewset has no queryset attribute, because you define get_queryset instead, you must pass a basename when registering it.
## Permissions: when and where they run

The DRF docs say permission checks always run at the very start of the view, before any other code. There are two hooks on a custom permission class. has_permission(request, view) is the view-level check. has_object_permission(request, view, obj) is the object-level check, and it runs only when the view calls get_object() or check_object_permissions(). The docs also state plainly that the generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to each instance in a queryset on a list view.

That last sentence is the source of a common vulnerability. If GET /orders/ is protected only by an object-level permission, nothing filters the list, so a logged-in user sees everyone's orders. The fix is to filter the queryset in get_queryset() so the list contains only objects the user may see, and keep has_object_permission for detail actions. Also note the defaults: if DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES is not set, access is unrestricted, so set IsAuthenticated globally and open specific views on purpose.

DRF returns 403 when the user is authenticated but not permitted, and also when authentication fails if the highest-priority authentication class does not use a WWW-Authenticate header (SessionAuthentication is an example). It returns 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header when authentication fails and the first authentication class uses that header (TokenAuthentication does). So the status you see depends on the authentication class.
keyPoints: A serializer converts objects to JSON types and validates incoming data. ModelSerializer generates fields and validators from the model.
validate_<field> checks one field, validate() checks across fields, is_valid(raise_exception=True) leads to a 400.
Set the owner with serializer.save(owner=request.user), never from client data. Mark computed fields read-only.
A router maps a ViewSet's actions to URLs: list and create on prefix/, retrieve, update, partial_update and destroy on prefix/{pk}/.
Object-level permissions run in get_object(), not on lists. Filter get_queryset() to protect list endpoints.

sql.title: Serializer with both kinds of validation
sql.code:
from rest_framework import serializers
from .models import Order

class OrderSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Order
        fields = ['id', 'items', 'total', 'status', 'created_at']
        read_only_fields = ['total', 'status', 'created_at']   # the client cannot set these

    def validate_items(self, value):             # one field
        if not value:
            raise serializers.ValidationError('An order needs at least one item.')
        return value

    def validate(self, data):                    # several fields together
        if data.get('coupon') and data.get('is_gift'):
            raise serializers.ValidationError('Coupons cannot be used on gifts.')
        return data

sql.title: Tests for the permission rules
sql.code:
from rest_framework.test import APITestCase

class OrderPermissionTests(APITestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='x')
        self.bob = User.objects.create_user('bob', password='x')
        self.order = Order.objects.create(owner=self.alice)

    def test_list_shows_only_my_orders(self):
        self.client.force_authenticate(self.bob)
        resp = self.client.get('/api/orders/')
        self.assertEqual(resp.json()['results'], [])      # get_queryset filters

    def test_cannot_read_someone_elses_order(self):
        self.client.force_authenticate(self.bob)
        resp = self.client.get(f'/api/orders/{self.order.pk}/')
        self.assertEqual(resp.status_code, 404)            # not in bob's queryset

Setting the owner from request data instead of serializer.save(owner=request.user).

Letting clients write totals, prices or statuses because they were not read-only.
Forgetting basename on a router registration for a viewset that has no queryset attribute.

interview.q: What does a DRF serializer do?
interview.a: It converts model instances and querysets into native Python types that render as JSON, and in the other direction it validates incoming data and turns it into validated objects. ModelSerializer generates the fields and validators from the model.

interview.q: What is the difference between validate_<field> and validate()?
interview.a: validate_<field> checks one field and returns the value or raises ValidationError. validate() receives the whole dictionary of field values and checks rules that involve several fields.

interview.q: What is a ViewSet and how does it differ from an APIView?
interview.a: A ViewSet provides actions such as list, create, retrieve and destroy instead of HTTP-verb methods, and a router maps those actions to URLs. ModelViewSet gives full CRUD with very little code, whereas an APIView gives full control.

interview.q: Which URLs and methods does a DefaultRouter generate for a registered ViewSet?
interview.a: GET and POST on prefix/ for list and create, and GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on prefix/{pk}/ for retrieve, update, partial_update and destroy. It also adds an API root view and optional format suffixes.

interview.q: Where do DRF permission checks run, and what is the pitfall with object-level permissions?
interview.a: They run at the very start of the view. has_permission is view-level, has_object_permission is checked when get_object() runs. Object permissions are not applied to each item in a list, so list endpoints must filter get_queryset() or they can leak other users' objects.

interview.q: When does DRF return 401 and when 403?
interview.a: 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header when authentication fails and the first authentication class uses that header, such as TokenAuthentication. Otherwise 403, which is also what an authenticated but forbidden user gets.

interview.q: How do you set the owner of a new object safely?
interview.a: Pass it into save(), for example serializer.save(owner=request.user) in perform_create, so it comes from the authenticated request and never from client-supplied data.

title: Testing Django Applications
tagline: Write small checks that tell you when a change has broken something.
explain: Tests are what let you change code without fear, and 'how do you test your Django code?' is asked in almost every backend interview. A good answer covers what you test, which tools you use, and why your tests do not interfere with each other.
## What Django's test tools give you

Django's tests use Python's standard unittest module. The docs describe django.test.TestCase as a subclass of unittest.TestCase that runs each test inside a transaction to provide isolation. Tests that need the database never use your real one: separate, blank databases are created for the tests, and the docs say they are destroyed when all the tests have run, whether the tests pass or fail. By default the runner discovers files named test*.py.

- SimpleTestCase disallows database queries. Use it for pure logic.
- TestCase wraps each test in a transaction that is rolled back at the end. It is the default choice and it is fast.
- TransactionTestCase resets the database by truncating all tables after each test. It is slower and is needed only when the code under test manages transactions itself (for example testing on_commit behavior or select_for_update across transactions).
Because each test is rolled back, a row created inside one test is gone before the next test starts. Data that many tests share can be built once per class in setUpTestData.
## The test client

The docs describe the test client as a dummy web browser that lets you exercise your views programmatically, and it does not need a web server. Because it goes through the whole stack, one client.get() exercises middleware, URL routing, the view and the ORM together. Use force_login(user) to skip the login steps, and follow=True to follow redirects. It can only request pages from your Django project, not external URLs.
For DRF, APIClient and APITestCase work the same way, with force_authenticate.
## What to assert

- Behavior that users or other code depends on: status codes, response data, database state, side effects.
- The failure paths: invalid input, missing permission, unauthenticated access, duplicate submission.
- Query counts: assertNumQueries fails if someone introduces an N+1 query.
- Not implementation details such as the name of a private helper. Tests that mirror the code break on every refactor.
## Isolating the outside world

A test must not call a real payment API or send real email. Django's test runner already redirects email to an in-memory outbox. For other services replace the call with unittest.mock.patch so you control what it returns, including failures and timeouts. Use override_settings to change a setting for one test, and never edit django.conf.settings directly, because Django will not restore the value.
## Keeping the suite healthy

Most tests should be small and fast. A common model is a pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests that cross layers (the client tests above), and a few end-to-end tests through a real browser, which are slow and break more easily. Fix or delete flaky tests, because a suite nobody trusts gets ignored. Run the suite in CI on every push (see the CI/CD lesson). Third-party tools such as pytest-django and factory_boy are popular for less boilerplate, but plain Django TestCase is enough for an interview and for most projects.
keyPoints: TestCase runs each test inside a transaction that is rolled back, against a separate test database.
SimpleTestCase for no-database logic, TestCase by default, TransactionTestCase only when transactions themselves are under test.
The test client runs the whole stack with no web server: middleware, URLs, view, ORM.
Test behavior and failure paths. Use assertNumQueries to catch N+1 regressions.
Mock external services with unittest.mock.patch. Use override_settings, never edit settings directly.

sql.title: A request-level test
sql.code:
from django.test import TestCase
from django.urls import reverse

class OrderListTests(TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpTestData(cls):                 # built once for the class, shared read-only
        cls.user = User.objects.create_user('asha', password='x')
        Order.objects.bulk_create([Order(owner=cls.user, total=10) for _ in range(5)])

    def test_requires_login(self):
        resp = self.client.get(reverse('order-list'))
        self.assertEqual(resp.status_code, 302)           # redirected to login

    def test_lists_my_orders_in_three_queries(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.user)                # skips the login steps
        with self.assertNumQueries(3):                    # fails if an N+1 appears
            resp = self.client.get(reverse('order-list'))
        self.assertContains(resp, 'Order', count=5)

interview.q: How does Django's TestCase keep tests isolated?
interview.a: It runs each test inside a database transaction that is rolled back at the end, against a separate test database that is created and destroyed by the runner. So data created in one test is not visible to the next.

interview.q: What is the difference between TestCase, TransactionTestCase and SimpleTestCase?
interview.a: SimpleTestCase forbids database queries. TestCase wraps each test in a rolled-back transaction, which is fast. TransactionTestCase truncates tables after each test and is needed when the code under test manages transactions itself.

interview.q: How do you test a view?
interview.a: Use the test client, which acts like a browser without needing a server, so the request goes through middleware, URL routing, the view and the ORM. I assert on status code, response content and database state, and use force_login for authenticated cases.

interview.q: How do you test code that calls an external API?
interview.a: I replace the call with unittest.mock.patch, patched where the code looks it up, and make it return success, an error or a timeout so I can test each path without a network.

interview.q: How do you stop N+1 queries coming back?
interview.a: I add assertNumQueries around the request in a test, so a regression that adds queries fails the build.

interview.q: What is the testing pyramid?
interview.a: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests across layers, and a small number of slow end-to-end tests. It balances confidence against speed and fragility.

title: HTTP and Networking Basics
tagline: What happens between typing a web address and seeing the page.
explain: 'What happens when you type a URL into a browser?' is one of the most common backend and DevOps interview questions, and the answer is the foundation of debugging anything on the web. This lesson walks the path and then focuses on the parts you control as a backend developer: status codes, headers and caching.
## The journey of a request

- DNS: the browser turns the host name into an IP address by asking a resolver. Results are cached.
- TCP: the client opens a reliable connection to that address and port (443 for HTTPS).
- TLS: for HTTPS, the two sides agree on encryption and the server proves its identity with a certificate, so the traffic cannot be read or altered on the way.
- HTTP: the client sends a request. The server sends a response.
- Rendering: the browser reads the response and fetches more resources, repeating the process.

The MDN docs describe HTTP as an application-layer protocol sent over TCP, or over a TLS-encrypted TCP connection. It is a client-server protocol in which the browser is always the one that initiates the request. HTTP/2 wraps messages in binary frames, which allows header compression and multiplexing several messages over one connection, but the principle of request and response stays the same.
## Requests and responses

A request has a method (GET, POST and so on), a path, a version, optional headers and, for some methods, a body. A response has a version, a status code, a short status message, headers and optionally a body. HTTP itself is stateless: there is no link between two successive requests. Cookies are what allow stateful sessions on top of it, which is how Django sessions work.

- GET reads and should not change anything. POST creates or triggers work. PUT replaces a resource, PATCH changes part of it, DELETE removes it. GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent, meaning repeating them has the same effect as doing them once, and POST is not, which is why payments need idempotency keys.
## Status codes you must know

The classes are 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error. The common codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found (temporary), 304 Not Modified, 400 Bad Request, 401, 403, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable and 504 Gateway Timeout.

The pair people confuse is 401 and 403. MDN says 401 'Unauthorized' semantically means unauthenticated: the client must authenticate to get the response. 403 means the server knows who you are and refuses access. When you see 502 or 504, a gateway (such as Nginx) could not get a good or timely answer from the server behind it (such as Gunicorn). A 503 means the service is not ready, for example overloaded or down for maintenance.
## Caching

Caching is how most pages become fast, and a favourite interview topic. The server controls it with the Cache-Control header. max-age says how long a response is fresh. When it is stale, the client can revalidate: it sends the ETag it saved in an If-None-Match header, and the server answers 304 Not Modified if nothing changed, so no body is sent again. Two directives are often mixed up: no-store means do not store the response at all, while no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation before every reuse. Use private for personalised content so only the user's own browser cache keeps it, because a shared cache could otherwise serve one user's data to another.
## A debugging habit

Use curl -v (or the browser's network tab) to see the actual request and response headers instead of guessing. Most 'it works locally' problems become obvious once you can see the status code, the redirects, the cookies and the cache headers.
keyPoints: URL → DNS → TCP → TLS (for HTTPS) → HTTP request and response → rendering.
HTTP is stateless and client-initiated. Cookies add sessions. HTTP/2 multiplexes messages over one connection.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST is not, so retry-safe POSTs need an idempotency key.
401 means not authenticated, 403 means authenticated but forbidden. 502 and 504 point to a failing gateway upstream.
no-store: never stored. no-cache: stored but revalidated before use. private: only the browser may cache it. ETag with 304 saves the body.

sql.title: See the real headers with curl
sql.code:
curl -v https://example.com/api/orders/ -H 'Authorization: Token abc123'
# > GET /api/orders/ HTTP/2            <- the request line you sent
# > authorization: Token abc123
# < HTTP/2 200                          <- the status
# < content-type: application/json
# < cache-control: private, max-age=60
# < etag: "33a64df5"

# revalidate with the ETag: a 304 means 'your copy is still good, no body sent'
curl -i https://example.com/api/orders/ -H 'If-None-Match: "33a64df5"'

pitfalls: Returning 200 with an error message in the body instead of a proper 4xx or 5xx status.
Using 401 and 403 interchangeably.
Caching personalised pages without private, so a shared cache can leak them.
Using no-cache when you meant no-store for sensitive data.
Retrying POST requests blindly without an idempotency key.

interview.q: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
interview.a: The browser resolves the host name with DNS, opens a TCP connection, does a TLS handshake for HTTPS, sends an HTTP request, receives the response, then renders the page and fetches further resources such as scripts, styles and images.

interview.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
interview.a: 401 means the client is not authenticated and must authenticate. 403 means the client is identified but not allowed to access the resource.

interview.q: What does 502 mean compared with 504?
interview.a: Both come from a gateway or proxy. 502 means it received an invalid response from the server behind it, for example because the app crashed. 504 means that server did not answer in time, for example because of a slow query or a hung worker.

interview.q: Which HTTP methods are idempotent?
interview.a: GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent, so repeating them has the same effect as one call. POST is not, which is why creating operations such as payments need an idempotency key to be safe to retry.

interview.q: How do ETag and 304 work?
interview.a: The server sends an ETag identifying the content. When the cached copy is stale, the client sends it back in If-None-Match. If the content has not changed the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, so the client reuses its copy.

interview.q: What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
interview.a: no-store means do not store the response anywhere. no-cache allows storing it but requires revalidating with the server before each reuse.

interview.q: HTTP is stateless. How do websites keep you logged in?
interview.a: With cookies. The server sets a cookie, for example a session ID, and the browser sends it on every request, which lets the server recognize the user across otherwise unrelated requests.

basis: Priority 2 is my judgment: the URL-to-page question and status codes are standard in backend and DevOps interviews but are quick to learn. The description of HTTP (client-initiated, stateless, over TCP or TLS, HTTP/2 frames and multiplexing), the status code meanings including 401 versus 403, and the caching directives (max-age, no-store versus no-cache, ETag and 304, private versus shared caches) come from the MDN pages I opened. title: TCP, TLS and HTTP Connections
tagline: What happens between typing an address and getting the first byte, and why reusing connections makes pages faster.
explain: A web request is not one step. Before any HTTP message travels, the browser looks up the address, opens a connection, and secures it. Understanding the order explains page speed, HTTPS, and why HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 exist.
## The order of events

The MDN pages put it in this order: a DNS lookup, then the TCP handshake, then the TLS handshake, then the HTTP request. DNS turns a name into an address. TCP makes a reliable connection. TLS makes it private. Only then does the request go.
## The TCP three-way handshake

MDN calls it SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. The initiator, usually the browser, sends SYN. The server answers SYN-ACK. The initiator sends ACK, and when the server receives it, the connection is established. Closing uses a four-way exchange of FIN and ACK in each direction, after which a half-closed connection can still carry data one way. The page does not cover sequence numbers, timeouts, retransmission, or how long the handshake takes, so those are not claimed here.
## What TLS adds

TLS lets a client talk securely to a server across an untrusted network. It gives three guarantees: encryption, so others cannot read; integrity, so others cannot change the data unnoticed; and authentication, so the client knows it is talking to the real server. In the handshake the two sides agree on a TLS version and a cipher suite, the server proves its identity with a certificate that ties its public key to its domain name, and they agree on a secret key used for everything after. TLS 1.3 is the current and most used version, TLS 1.2 is still used, and 1.1 and 1.0 should no longer be used.
## Persistent connections

HTTP/1.0 opened a new connection for each request, paying the handshakes every time. HTTP/1.1 made persistent connections the default, so a connection can serve several requests. A request can still ask for Connection: close. Pipelining, sending several requests without waiting for the replies, exists but is not active by default in modern browsers, and it suffers from head-of-line blocking: one slow reply holds up the ones behind it.
## Six connections, then multiplexing

To get around the one-at-a-time limit, browsers open several connections to a site, commonly 6 in parallel. HTTP/2 is a binary protocol that is multiplexed, so many requests share one connection at the same time, and it compresses headers. HTTP/3 keeps the same meaning for requests but replaces TCP with QUIC, which runs multiple streams over UDP and handles loss per stream, so one lost packet does not stall all the streams.
## HSTS and mixed content

A redirect from HTTP to HTTPS can be intercepted on the first visit. The Strict-Transport-Security header tells the browser to use HTTPS from then on, and the preload list covers the very first visit. Loading plain HTTP resources inside an HTTPS page is called mixed content, and browsers upgrade or block it.
## How to talk through it

Walk the order: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP. State what each step costs and which can be skipped on a reused connection. Explain how HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 reduce waiting, and what HTTPS guarantees. Do not quote round-trip counts unless you have checked them.
keyPoints: Order: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, then the HTTP request.
TCP handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK; the server considers it established on the final ACK.
TLS gives encryption, integrity and authentication; prefer TLS 1.3.
Persistent connections (HTTP/1.1 default) skip repeated handshakes; browsers also open about 6 connections per site.
HTTP/2 multiplexes requests on one connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

sql.title: Persistent connections skip the repeated setup
sql.code:
def steps_for(n_requests, persistent):
    """What happens before each HTTP request. A persistent connection pays the setup cost once."""
    steps = ["DNS lookup"]
    for i in range(n_requests):
        if i == 0 or not persistent:
            steps += ["TCP handshake", "TLS handshake"]
        steps.append("request")
    return steps

assert steps_for(3, persistent=True).count("TCP handshake") == 1       # connection reused: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive
assert steps_for(3, persistent=False).count("TCP handshake") == 3      # one request per connection: HTTP/1.0 style
assert steps_for(1, persistent=True) == ["DNS lookup", "TCP handshake", "TLS handshake", "request"]   # the order in the pages

Thinking HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 change what a request means: they change how it travels.

interview.q: What happens when you type a URL in the browser?
interview.a: The browser looks up the address with DNS, opens a TCP connection with the SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK handshake, performs the TLS handshake for HTTPS, then sends the HTTP request and receives the response.

interview.q: What does TLS provide?
interview.a: Encryption (nobody can read the traffic), integrity (nobody can change it unnoticed) and authentication (the server proves who it is with a certificate).

interview.q: Why are persistent connections faster?
interview.a: A connection that serves several requests pays the TCP and TLS setup only once, instead of for every request.

interview.q: What problem does HTTP/2 solve?
interview.a: It multiplexes many requests over one connection, so they do not wait for each other, and compresses headers. HTTP/1.x with pipelining suffered from head-of-line blocking.

interview.q: How is HTTP/3 different from HTTP/2?
interview.a: HTTP/3 keeps the same semantics but uses QUIC over UDP instead of TCP, so a lost packet stalls only its own stream.

basis: Why it is here: what happens when you type a URL is one of the most common interview questions, and connection setup explains real performance. The order DNS, TCP, TLS and the SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK and FIN steps are from the MDN TCP handshake page I read; it does not give sequence numbers, timeouts or timings. The three TLS guarantees, the handshake outline, versions, certificates, HSTS and mixed content are from the MDN TLS page I read. Persistent connections, pipelining, head-of-line blocking and six connections per domain are from the MDN HTTP/1.x connection page, and the history, HTTP/2 multiplexing, HTTP/3 and QUIC are from the MDN evolution page; both were read from the part before the fetch tool cut them. The code is my own simplified model, not real TCP. How to order the explanation is my own judgment. Hours and priority are my judgment.

title: Cloud Basics: Regions, Zones, Managed Services and Access
tagline: What the cloud is: renting computers in big data centers, and giving each person only the access they need.
explain: Cloud providers rent you computing, storage and databases by the hour instead of you buying servers. Backend interviews at 5 or more years often include 'how would you deploy this on the cloud?'. You do not need to know every service. You need the vocabulary, the failure model and the security basics. This lesson uses AWS terms as the example, and the ideas apply to every major provider.
## What you can rent

- Virtual machines (for example EC2): you manage the operating system and the app.
- Managed platforms and containers: you give the provider your container or code and it runs and scales it.
- Managed databases (for example RDS): the provider handles backups, patching and failover for PostgreSQL or MySQL.
- Object storage (for example S3): cheap, durable storage for files, images and backups, accessed by key over HTTP.
- Load balancers and queues: spread traffic across instances and decouple slow work.
The trade-off is control against effort. The more managed the service, the less you operate and the less you can tune.
## Regions and availability zones

AWS defines a Region as a physical location where it clusters data centers, and an Availability Zone (AZ) as one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking and connectivity within a Region. AZs in a Region are physically separated, by many kilometres, and are connected by high-bandwidth, low-latency networking. Each Region has at least three AZs. The point of AZs is high availability: if one fails because of a power outage or a similar event, an application spread across AZs keeps running in the others.

Region choice affects latency (pick one near your users), data-residency rules, price and which services exist. Design so that a single AZ failure is survivable: run application instances in at least two AZs behind a load balancer.
## Managed databases and failover

A Multi-AZ deployment of a managed database keeps a standby copy in a different AZ and fails over to it automatically. AWS documents two shapes: a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with one standby that provides failover support but does not serve read traffic, and a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment whose standbys provide failover and can also serve reads. So high availability and read scaling are different features, and a standby is not automatically a read replica (see the Replication lesson).
## Access: least privilege and temporary credentials

The AWS IAM best-practice guide says to apply least-privilege permissions: grant only the permissions needed for a task, by naming the actions on specific resources under specific conditions. It says to require workloads to use temporary credentials through IAM roles instead of long-term access keys, to require multi-factor authentication for human users and the root user, and to follow best practices for protecting root-user credentials. It also recommends regularly reviewing and removing unused users, roles and credentials. In practice this means an application server gets a role that can read one storage bucket, and nobody commits access keys to a repository.
## The shared responsibility idea

The provider secures the underlying infrastructure. You secure what you put on it: your code, your configuration, your data and who can access it. Most cloud breaches are misconfigurations, such as a public bucket or a leaked key, rather than failures of the provider.
## Cost
Cloud bills grow with use. Habits that matter: size instances to the load, turn off unused resources, set billing alerts, and remember that data transfer out and idle managed databases cost money.
keyPoints: A Region is a cluster of data centers. An Availability Zone is one or more separate data centers inside it, with at least three per Region.
Run across at least two AZs behind a load balancer so one AZ failing does not take you down.
Multi-AZ gives failover. A standby in a DB instance deployment does not serve reads. Read replicas or a cluster do that.
Least privilege: name specific actions on specific resources. Use IAM roles with temporary credentials, not long-term keys. Require MFA.
You secure your code, data and configuration (shared responsibility). Watch costs.

interview.q: What is the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?
interview.a: A Region is a physical location where a provider clusters data centers. An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power and networking inside a Region, physically separated from the other AZs but connected by fast links. A Region has at least three of them.

interview.q: How do you make an application highly available on the cloud?
interview.a: Run it in at least two Availability Zones behind a load balancer, keep servers stateless so any instance is replaceable, use a managed database with a Multi-AZ standby for failover, and store files in object storage.

interview.q: Does a Multi-AZ database standby serve reads?
interview.a: Not in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment: the standby is there for failover and does not serve read traffic. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has standbys that can also serve reads, and read replicas are a separate feature.

interview.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
interview.a: Grant only the permissions needed for a task: the specific actions on the specific resources under specific conditions. It limits the damage if a credential is leaked.

interview.q: How should an application authenticate to cloud services?
interview.a: With an IAM role that gives it temporary credentials, instead of long-lived access keys stored in code or configuration.

interview.q: What does shared responsibility mean?
interview.a: The provider secures the underlying infrastructure, and you secure what you put on it: your code, configuration, data and access control. Most breaches come from misconfiguration on the customer side.

AWS is used as the example; the concepts exist at every major provider but the names differ. The shared-responsibility summary and the cost habits are general knowledge.

title: JavaScript: the Event Loop, Promises and async/await
tagline: JavaScript does one job at a time. This explains why some code runs later and why a long loop freezes the page.
explain: JavaScript in the browser runs on one thread, yet it can wait for network responses, timers and clicks without freezing. The mechanism is the event loop. 'What is the output of this code?' with a setTimeout and a Promise is one of the most common frontend interview questions, and the same model explains why a slow function makes a page feel stuck.
## The model: stack, queues and the loop

The MDN docs describe an agent as a thread, which means the interpreter can only process one statement at a time. Three pieces matter. The call stack holds the functions currently running, and every job enters by pushing a frame onto the empty stack and finishes by emptying it. The queue of jobs is what the HTML spec calls the event loop. Each time, the agent pulls a job from the queue and runs it, and a job is complete when the stack is empty. The key rule is run to completion: each job is processed completely before any other job is processed, so nothing can interrupt a running function.
## Tasks and microtasks

Not all jobs have equal priority. MDN says HTML event loops split jobs into two categories, tasks and microtasks, and that microtasks have higher priority: the microtask queue is drained first before the task queue is pulled. Timer callbacks (setTimeout) and events such as clicks are tasks. Promise callbacks (.then, and the code after an await) are microtasks.

> console.log('sync'); setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('microtask')); prints sync, then microtask, then timeout. The synchronous code finishes first, then the microtask queue is drained, and only then does the loop take the next task, which is the timer, even though its delay was 0.
## Promises and async/await

A Promise represents a value that will arrive later. async/await is syntax that lets you write the code that handles one in a straight line. An async function returns a promise, and when it reaches await it hands control back and continues later as a microtask, once the awaited promise has settled. Errors are handled with try/catch around await, or .catch on the promise. Promise.all runs several operations at the same time and waits for all of them, which is how you avoid awaiting independent requests one after another.
## Why long jobs freeze the page

Rendering and event handling also need the same thread. If one job runs for 300 ms, for example a big loop, the browser cannot paint or react to a click until it finishes, because each job runs to completion. MDN's practical advice is to make job processing short and, if possible, cut one job into several jobs. In practice: do heavy work in chunks that yield between pieces, move it to a Web Worker, or avoid doing it at all. This connects directly to the Interaction to Next Paint metric in the performance lesson.
## Other fundamentals interviewers pair with this

- Closures: a function remembers the variables of the scope where it was created.
- this depends on how a function is called, and arrow functions take this from the surrounding scope.
- Events bubble from the target up through its ancestors, which is what makes event delegation (one listener on a parent) work.
- == converts types and === does not, so prefer ===.
- var is function-scoped and let and const are block-scoped.

Microtasks (promise callbacks) run before the next task (timers, events). So setTimeout(0) runs after a resolved promise.

A long synchronous job blocks painting and clicks. Cut it into pieces, or use a Web Worker.
Promise.all runs independent operations concurrently instead of awaiting them one by one.

interview.q: Explain the JavaScript event loop.
interview.a: JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack. Callbacks from timers, events and network responses wait in queues. When the stack is empty, the event loop takes the next job and runs it to completion. Microtasks, such as promise callbacks, are drained before the next task.

interview.q: What is the output of a script that logs, sets a setTimeout of 0, resolves a promise and logs again?
interview.a: The synchronous logs first, then the promise callback because the microtask queue is drained when the stack empties, and finally the timeout callback because timers are tasks that run after the microtasks.

interview.q: What is the difference between a task and a microtask?
interview.a: Tasks are things like timers and user events, taken one per loop turn. Microtasks are promise callbacks and run to completion before the next task, so they have higher priority.

interview.q: How does async/await relate to promises?
interview.a: async/await is syntax over promises. An async function returns a promise, and code after an await resumes as a microtask once the awaited promise settles. Errors are caught with try/catch.

interview.q: Why can a long-running function make a page unresponsive and how do you fix it?
interview.a: Each job runs to completion on the one thread, so rendering and event handling wait. Fix it by splitting the work into short pieces that yield, moving it to a Web Worker, or reducing the work.

interview.q: How do you run several independent API calls at once?
interview.a: Start them all and await Promise.all, which resolves when every promise has resolved, so the total time is about that of the slowest instead of the sum.

MDN does not give the setTimeout(0) versus Promise.then example; I derived it by applying those rules. The closures, this, bubbling and == notes are general knowledge I did not verify here.

title: React: Rendering, State Snapshots, Keys and Effects
tagline: Why React redraws the screen, why a change seems to arrive late, and what keys and effects are for.
explain: Most React bugs and most React interview questions come from not knowing when and why React runs your code. Learn the rendering model once and 'why did this re-render?', 'why is my state stale?' and 'why did my input lose its text?' stop being mysteries.
## Trigger, render, commit

The React docs describe three steps. First a render is triggered, for example by the first mount or by a state update. Second, React renders the component, which the docs define simply as: 'Rendering is React calling your components.' Third, React commits to the DOM. The docs add that React only changes the DOM nodes if there is a difference between renders, which is why re-rendering a component is usually cheap even when the function runs again.

Because React may call a component at any time, rendering must be a pure calculation: the same inputs give the same JSX, and a component must not change objects or variables that existed before rendering. Side effects belong in event handlers or in effects, not in the body of the component.
## State is a snapshot

Calling a state setter does not change the variable in the code that is running. The docs say setting state does not change the state variable you already have, but triggers a re-render, and that when you call useState, React gives you a snapshot of the state for that render. A state variable's value never changes within a render, even if an event handler is asynchronous.

> Calling setNumber(number + 1) three times in one handler only adds 1, because in that render number is always 0, so you set the state to 1 three times. To make each update build on the previous one, use the updater form, setNumber(n => n + 1), which React applies in order. The docs cover this on their next page about queueing state updates.
## Keys

When you render a list, each item needs a key. The docs say keys let React uniquely identify an item between its siblings and tell React which array item each component corresponds to, so it can match them up later. The rules: keys must be unique among siblings, and keys must not change, so do not generate them while rendering with something like Math.random(), which makes keys never match between renders so everything is recreated. Using the array index is tempting, and the docs warn that when items are inserted, deleted or reordered it often leads to subtle and confusing bugs. Use a stable id from your data.
The classic symptom of wrong keys: you reorder or delete rows that contain inputs, and the text a user typed stays at the same position instead of moving with its row.
## Effects

An Effect lets you run code after rendering to synchronize your component with a system outside of React, such as a network connection, a timer or a browser API. The dependency array controls when it runs: with no array it runs after every render, and with an empty array it runs only when the component first appears. The cleanup function you return runs before the effect runs again and once more when the component unmounts, which is where you close connections and cancel timers.

In development, React remounts each component once right after its first mount to check that your effect cleans up properly. The docs say this is correct behavior and that in production you would see the effect once. If a fetch inside an effect can race, make the cleanup ignore stale responses. Do not use an effect to compute something you could calculate during rendering.
## Common interview questions

- Props versus state: props are inputs passed from a parent and read-only, state is memory owned by the component.
- What causes a re-render: a state change, a new value from a parent re-rendering it, or a changed context value.
- useMemo and useCallback cache a value or a function between renders. They are optimizations to use after you measure, not by default.
keyPoints: React renders in three steps: trigger, render (call your components), commit (update the DOM if something changed).
Render must be pure: same inputs, same JSX, no changing outside variables.
State is a snapshot per render. setX(x + 1) three times adds one. Use the updater form setX(n => n + 1) to build on the previous value.
Keys must be unique among siblings and stable. Do not use Math.random, and avoid the array index when the list can change.
An Effect synchronizes with an outside system. The dependency array controls when it runs, and the cleanup function undoes it.

sql.title: State snapshot vs updater
Keys: stable id, not index
An effect with cleanup and a stale-response guard
sql.code:
useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;                       // set when this effect is cleaned up
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${query}`)
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(data => { if (!ignore) setResults(data); });   // drop answers to old queries
  return () => { ignore = true; };         // cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount
}, [query]);                                // re-run only when query changes

interview.q: What happens when state changes in React?

title: Web Performance and Accessibility
tagline: Make pages fast, steady and quick to respond, and usable by everyone.
explain: Two things separate a working page from a good one: how fast it feels, and who can use it. Interviews for frontend roles at 2 or more years ask how you would measure and improve performance, and whether your interface works with a keyboard and a screen reader.
## Core Web Vitals

Google's web.dev defines three metrics that describe the user's experience. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading, and a good LCP is within 2.5 seconds of when the page first starts loading. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures interactivity, and a good INP is 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability, and a good CLS is 0.1 or less. These are assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, and a page passes only when it meets all three.

- Improving LCP: make the largest element (often a hero image or heading) arrive sooner. Compress and size images properly, serve them from a CDN, avoid blocking the page with large scripts and styles, and cache what you can.
- Improving INP: keep the main thread free. Long tasks delay the response to a click (see the event-loop lesson), so split heavy work, debounce expensive handlers and avoid unnecessary re-renders.
- Improving CLS: stop things moving after they appear. Give images and embeds explicit width and height so the browser reserves space, and avoid inserting content above what the user is already reading.

Measure before optimizing: lab tools such as Lighthouse and the browser's performance panel help you find causes, and real-user data shows what visitors actually experience. Set a budget, change one thing, and measure again.
## Accessibility

Accessibility means people with disabilities, and also people with a broken mouse, a bright screen or a slow connection, can use your interface. The W3C's guidance organizes it into four principles: perceivable information and user interface, operable user interface and navigation, understandable information and user interface, and robust content and reliable interpretation.

- Perceivable: text alternatives for non-text content such as images and icon buttons, and captions or transcripts for audio.
- Operable: many people do not use the mouse and rely on the keyboard, so every control must be reachable and usable by keyboard, and keyboard focus must not get trapped.
- Understandable: readable text, predictable behavior, clear errors.
- Robust: content that works with different browsers and assistive technologies.
## Practical rules that cover most cases

- Use the right HTML element. A real <button> is focusable, responds to Enter and Space and is announced as a button. A clickable <div> gets none of that for free.
- Label every form control with a <label>, and give images useful alt text (empty alt for purely decorative ones).
- Keep a visible focus outline. Do not remove it without a replacement.
- Do not rely on color alone to convey meaning, and keep enough contrast between text and background.
- Use headings in order so assistive technology users can navigate by structure.
- Test with the keyboard only, then with a screen reader. Automated tools find only part of the problems.
keyPoints: Core Web Vitals: LCP within 2.5 s (loading), INP at most 200 ms (interactivity), CLS at most 0.1 (stability), at the 75th percentile.
Improve LCP with smaller, well-sized images and less blocking code. INP with short tasks. CLS by reserving space.
Measure first, change one thing, measure again.
Accessibility: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust.
Use semantic HTML, labels, alt text, visible focus, and test with the keyboard.

interview.q: What are the Core Web Vitals?
interview.a: LCP, INP and CLS. Largest Contentful Paint measures loading and should be within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness and should be 200 ms or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability and should be 0.1 or less, at the 75th percentile.

interview.q: How would you improve a slow LCP?
interview.a: Find the largest element, usually an image or heading, then make it arrive sooner: compress and correctly size the image, serve it from a CDN, load it with high priority, and avoid large blocking scripts and styles. Then measure again.

interview.q: What causes layout shift and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: Content that loads late and pushes other content, such as images without dimensions or injected banners. Reserve space with width and height or fixed containers, and avoid inserting content above what the user is reading.

interview.q: How do you keep a page responsive to input?
interview.a: Keep the main thread free: split long tasks, debounce heavy handlers, avoid needless re-renders and move heavy computation to a Web Worker.

interview.q: What are the principles of web accessibility?
interview.a: Perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. For example text alternatives for images, full keyboard operability, readable and predictable content, and compatibility with assistive technologies.

interview.q: Why use a button instead of a clickable div?
interview.a: A real button is keyboard focusable, activates with Enter and Space and is announced as a button by assistive technology. A div has none of that without extra code.

title: Analytical SQL: Window Functions and CTEs
tagline: Rank rows, add running totals and compare months, without losing your rows.
explain: Data and analytics roles are tested on SQL more than anything else, and the questions go beyond joins: 'find the top 3 per group', 'running total', 'compare with the previous month'. The tools are window functions and common table expressions (CTEs).
## GROUP BY collapses rows, window functions keep them

The PostgreSQL docs define a window function as a calculation across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. It is comparable to an aggregate, but window functions do not cause rows to become grouped into a single output row. Instead the rows retain their separate identities. So GROUP BY answers 'what is each department's average salary?' with one row per department, while a window function can show every employee next to their department's average.

- A window function call always contains an OVER clause directly after the function name.
- PARTITION BY inside OVER divides the rows into groups that share the same value. Without it, the window is the whole result.
- ORDER BY inside OVER controls the order rows are processed in the window, which is what makes ranks and running totals possible.

> SELECT depname, empno, salary, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM empsalary; numbers the employees within each department from highest salary to lowest. This is the example shape in the PostgreSQL tutorial. Filter on that number in an outer query to get the top N per group.
## Evaluation order and where they are allowed

The docs state that the rows a window function sees are those of the virtual table produced by FROM as filtered by WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING. Window functions are permitted only in the SELECT list and ORDER BY, and are forbidden in WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, because they logically run after those clauses. That is why you cannot write WHERE row_number() = 1, and instead wrap the query in a subquery or a CTE and filter outside.
## The window functions to know

- Ranking: row_number() gives 1, 2, 3 with no ties. rank() gives ties the same number and leaves gaps. dense_rank() gives ties the same number with no gaps.
- Running totals: sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) accumulates as the window moves.
- Previous and next row: lag(value) and lead(value) read the row before or after. Use lag to compute change from the previous period.
- Shares: amount / sum(amount) OVER () gives each row's share of the total.
## CTEs: name your steps

A WITH query, the docs say, provides a way to write auxiliary statements for use in a larger query. They are often called common table expressions and can be thought of as temporary tables that exist just for one query. Using them turns a deeply nested query into a list of named steps that read top to bottom. WITH RECURSIVE lets a query refer to its own output, which is how you walk a hierarchy such as an org chart or category tree. The docs also describe how a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE can be folded into the parent query for joint optimization, and that MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED let you override that choice.
## Think in grain

Before writing the query, say the grain of the result: one row per what? One row per customer per month is a different query from one row per order. Most wrong analytics numbers come from joining at the wrong grain and double counting. State the grain, check the row count at each step, and test totals against a number you know.
keyPoints: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group. A window function keeps every row and adds a calculation across related rows.
OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) defines the window. Window functions go only in SELECT and ORDER BY.
To filter on a window result (for example top 3 per group), compute it in a CTE or subquery and filter outside.
row_number has no ties, rank has gaps after ties, dense_rank has none. lag and lead read neighbouring rows.
CTEs name each step. Always state the grain, and check row counts after each join.

sql.title: Top 2 products per category
sql.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category,
         product,
         revenue,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rn
  FROM product_sales
)
SELECT category, product, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 2          -- a window function cannot be in WHERE, so filter in the outer query
ORDER BY category, rn;

sql.title: Running total and month-over-month change
sql.code:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at) AS month,
         sum(total)                      AS revenue          -- grain: one row per month
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)                      AS running_total,
       revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)            AS change_vs_prev,
       round(100.0 * (revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1)           AS pct_change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

sql.title: Walk a hierarchy with WITH RECURSIVE
sql.code:
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth          -- non-recursive term: start at the CEO
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, r.depth + 1   -- recursive term refers to 'reports'
  FROM employees e
  JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
)
SELECT * FROM reports ORDER BY depth, name;

django.title: Window functions in the Django ORM
django.code:
from django.db.models import F, Window
from django.db.models.functions import RowNumber

ranked = Sale.objects.annotate(
    rn=Window(expression=RowNumber(), partition_by=[F('category')], order_by=F('revenue').desc())
)
# Django 4.2+ lets you filter on a window annotation directly:
top2 = ranked.filter(rn__lte=2)
django.note: Raw SQL or a database view is often clearer for complex analytics, and you can run it with connection.cursor() or Model.objects.raw().

interview.q: What is the difference between GROUP BY and a window function?
interview.a: GROUP BY collapses rows into one row per group. A window function performs a calculation across rows related to the current row but keeps every row, so you can show detail and the group calculation together.

interview.q: How do you get the top N rows per group?
interview.a: Number the rows with row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) in a CTE or subquery, then filter the number in the outer query. You cannot filter it in WHERE of the same query.

interview.q: What is the difference between row_number, rank and dense_rank?
interview.a: row_number gives unique sequential numbers even for ties. rank gives ties the same number and skips the following numbers. dense_rank gives ties the same number without gaps.

interview.q: How do you calculate month-over-month change?
interview.a: Aggregate to one row per month, then use lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) to read the previous month and subtract or divide.

interview.q: What is a CTE and why use one?
interview.a: A WITH query defines a named temporary result that exists for one statement. It turns nested subqueries into readable steps, and WITH RECURSIVE can walk hierarchies.

interview.q: Why are window functions not allowed in WHERE?
interview.a: They logically run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING have been applied, so their result does not exist yet when WHERE is evaluated.

basis: Priority 1 is my judgment: analytical SQL is the most-tested skill in data roles in the skill tables I read. The definition of a window function, OVER, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, the row_number example, where window functions are allowed and why, the definition of WITH and WITH RECURSIVE, and the MATERIALIZED options come from the PostgreSQL pages I opened. The behavior of rank, dense_rank, lag, lead and the running-total patterns is standard SQL knowledge that I did not look up on those pages.

everyday.plain: Window functions let you rank, total and compare rows without losing the rows themselves.

title: Data Pipelines: Idempotency, Batch vs Streaming and Quality
tagline: Move data so that running the job twice changes nothing, choose batch or live, and stop bad data early.
explain: A data pipeline moves data from where it is produced to where people analyse it, on a schedule or continuously. The interesting engineering is not the move itself. It is making the pipeline safe to re-run, deciding how fresh the data must be, and catching bad data before it reaches a dashboard.
## ETL and ELT

ETL extracts data, transforms it, then loads it into the destination. ELT loads the raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse using SQL, which is the common modern pattern because warehouses are powerful and you keep the raw data for reprocessing. Either way the stages are extract, load, transform, and test.
## Idempotency: the most important property

Pipelines fail and get re-run. The Airflow best-practices guide says tasks should produce the same outcome on every re-run, and warns against plain INSERTs, which can create duplicate rows when a task runs again, recommending an upsert instead. That property is called idempotency. It is the same idea as the idempotent Celery tasks and idempotency keys you met earlier.

In PostgreSQL the upsert is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. The docs say ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING simply avoids inserting a row, while ON CONFLICT (column) DO UPDATE updates the existing row that conflicts and guarantees an atomic insert-or-update outcome even under high concurrency. The row proposed for insertion is available as the special excluded table. For this to work the target needs a unique key that identifies a record, so choose the key before building the load.

- Load a day at a time into a partition or with a delete-then-insert for that day inside one transaction, so a re-run replaces that day instead of adding to it.
- Do not read the current time inside a task. Airflow's guide says never to use now() for the critical computation, and suggests using the data interval start as the partition. A job re-run next week must process the same day as the original run.
- Keep top-level orchestration code light. Do database access and heavy work inside tasks, not when the pipeline definition is loaded.
## Batch versus streaming

Batch pipelines process data in chunks on a schedule, for example every night. They are simpler, cheaper and easy to re-run. Streaming pipelines process each event as it arrives, so results are minutes or seconds old, at the cost of more complexity. Apache Kafka is the usual streaming backbone. Its docs describe it as an event streaming platform where an event records the fact that something happened, producers publish events, consumers subscribe to them, and producers and consumers are fully decoupled. Topics are partitioned across brokers, and events are not deleted after consumption: they can be read as often as needed until the retention period ends. That replay ability is what lets you fix a bug and reprocess history.

Choose from the requirement, not fashion: if a daily report is enough, batch is the right answer. Use streaming when the business really needs data in seconds, such as fraud detection or live inventory.
## Data quality

Bad data is worse than late data, because people trust it. Add checks between stages and make them fail the run: row counts within an expected range, no unexpected nulls in key columns, uniqueness of keys, values within allowed ranges, and freshness. Quarantine rejected rows with the reason instead of silently dropping them. Add schema checks too, because upstream systems change columns without warning.
## Backfills and late data

A backfill reprocesses a past period, for example after a bug fix. It only works safely if the pipeline is idempotent and parameterized by date. Late-arriving data is normal, so decide how long you wait and how corrections are applied.
keyPoints: Make every load idempotent: re-running the same day gives the same result, with no duplicates.
Use upserts (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT) keyed on a unique business key, and process by the data interval, never by now().
Batch is simpler and cheaper. Use streaming only when freshness in seconds is a real requirement.
Kafka topics are durable, partitioned logs. Events are not deleted on consumption, so you can replay.
Put quality checks between stages and fail the run. Quarantine bad rows with reasons.

CREATE TABLE daily_sales (
  sale_date date    NOT NULL,
  store_id  int     NOT NULL,
  revenue   numeric NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (sale_date, store_id)
);

-- running this twice for the same day leaves exactly the same rows

SELECT sale_date, store_id, sum(amount)
FROM staging_orders
WHERE sale_date = '2026-03-01'
GROUP BY sale_date, store_id
ON CONFLICT (sale_date, store_id)
DO UPDATE SET revenue = EXCLUDED.revenue;   -- EXCLUDED is the row we tried to insert

interview.q: What does it mean for a pipeline to be idempotent and how do you achieve it?
interview.a: Running it again for the same input produces the same result, with no duplicates or drift. You achieve it with upserts keyed on a unique business key or by replacing a whole partition atomically, and by processing a logical date instead of the current time.

interview.q: What is an upsert and how do you do it in PostgreSQL?
interview.a: Insert a row, or update it if it already exists. In PostgreSQL it is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE, which is atomic even under concurrency, and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING simply skips existing rows.

interview.q: Batch or streaming: how do you choose?
interview.a: From the freshness requirement. Batch is simpler, cheaper and easy to re-run, so I use it unless the business needs results in seconds, such as fraud detection, where streaming is worth the added complexity.

interview.q: What is Kafka and why is replay useful?
interview.a: An event streaming platform where producers publish events to partitioned topics and consumers subscribe. Events are not deleted when consumed, so a consumer can re-read history to fix a bug or rebuild a downstream table.

interview.q: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
interview.a: ETL transforms data before loading it. ELT loads raw data into the warehouse first and transforms it there with SQL, keeping the raw data available for reprocessing.

interview.q: What data-quality checks would you add to a pipeline?
interview.a: Row counts in an expected range, no nulls in key columns, unique keys, values within valid ranges, freshness and schema checks. They fail the run before bad data is published, and rejected rows are quarantined with a reason.
