title: Observability, SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets
tagline: See what a service is doing, decide how reliable it must be, and wake people only for real problems.
explain: You cannot run a service you cannot see, and you cannot improve reliability you have not defined. This lesson covers the two halves: observability (how you see inside a system) and service level objectives (how you decide what 'reliable enough' means). They are the core of DevOps and SRE interviews.
## Observability: logs, metrics and traces

The OpenTelemetry docs say observability lets you understand a system from the outside. It rests on three kinds of signal. Logs are timestamped messages emitted by services. Metrics are aggregations over a period of time of numeric data about your infrastructure or application. A trace records the path taken by a single request as it moves through multiple services, and it is made of spans, each a single unit of work.

- Metrics answer 'is something wrong, and how much?' They are cheap and good for dashboards and alerts.
- Traces answer 'where in the chain is it slow or failing?'
- Logs answer 'what exactly happened?' Make them structured (JSON with fields) so you can search them, and include a request or trace id so one request can be followed across services.
## What to measure: the four golden signals

The Google SRE book names four signals to monitor for any user-facing system. Latency is the time it takes to service a request. Traffic is a measure of how much demand is placed on the system. Errors is the rate of requests that fail, either explicitly (such as HTTP 500s) or in other ways. Saturation is how full your service is. A good starting dashboard for any service is those four.
## Alert on symptoms, not causes

The SRE book frames monitoring around two questions, what is broken and why, and says paging should focus on symptoms, the problems users can see, while causes are debugging aids. It says it is better to spend much more effort catching symptoms than causes. It also states a rule worth memorising: every page should be actionable, and if a page merely merits a robotic response, it should not be a page. A CPU at 90 percent with no user impact is a ticket or a dashboard, not a 3 a.m. phone call. An elevated error rate or high latency that users feel is a page.
## SLI, SLO and SLA

The SRE book defines the terms precisely. A service level indicator (SLI) is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided, for example the fraction of requests that succeed or that complete in under 300 ms. A service level objective (SLO) is a target value or range of values for a service level measured by an SLI, for example 99.9 percent of requests succeed over 30 days. A service level agreement (SLA) is a contract with users that includes consequences of meeting or missing the SLOs it contains. Typical SLI types are latency, error rate and availability.
## Why not 100 percent, and the error budget

The SRE book says 100 percent availability is impossible and that it is both unrealistic and undesirable to insist that SLOs be met 100 percent of the time. Instead it recommends allowing an error budget, a rate at which the SLOs can be missed, and tracking it daily or weekly. If your SLO is 99.9 percent over 30 days, you may fail 0.1 percent of requests, which for time-based availability is about 43 minutes of downtime in 30 days (0.001 x 43,200 minutes). While budget remains, you can ship features and take risks. When it is spent, you slow down and fix reliability. This turns an argument between 'ship faster' and 'be safer' into a number both sides can read.
## Choosing a good SLI

Measure what users experience, at the edge, as close to the user as you can (a load balancer or client measurement beats a database metric). The SRE book says ideally an SLI directly measures the service level of interest, but sometimes only a proxy is available. Pick a small number of SLIs per user journey, such as 'checkout succeeds' and 'search returns in under 500 ms', not dozens.
keyPoints: Logs (what happened), metrics (how much, aggregated) and traces (the path of one request) are the three observability signals.
The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
Page on symptoms users feel. Every page must be actionable. Causes are for dashboards and debugging.
SLI is the measurement, SLO is the target for it, SLA is the contract with consequences.
The error budget is 100 percent minus the SLO. 99.9 percent over 30 days is about 43 minutes. Spend it on shipping, and slow down when it is gone.

sql.title: Compute an SLI and the remaining error budget
sql.code:
def slo_report(total_requests, failed_requests, slo=0.999):
    sli = 1 - failed_requests / total_requests           # the measurement (success rate)
    budget = (1 - slo) * total_requests                  # failures we are allowed in this window
    return {
        'sli': round(sli, 5),
        'allowed_failures': round(budget),
        'failures_so_far': failed_requests,
        'budget_remaining': round(budget - failed_requests),
        'burned_pct': round(100 * failed_requests / budget, 1),
    }

print(slo_report(total_requests=10_000_000, failed_requests=6_500))
# sli 0.99935, allowed 10,000, remaining 3,500, 65 percent of the budget burned

sql.title: Structured log line with a trace id
sql.code:
import json, logging, time, uuid

logger = logging.getLogger('app.requests')

def request_logging_middleware(get_response):
    def middleware(request):
        trace_id = request.headers.get('X-Request-ID') or uuid.uuid4().hex   # follow one request across services
        start = time.perf_counter()
        response = get_response(request)
        logger.info(json.dumps({
            'trace_id': trace_id, 'method': request.method, 'path': request.path,
            'status': response.status_code,
            'latency_ms': round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000, 1),
        }))
        return response
    return middleware

interview.q: What are the three pillars of observability?
interview.a: Logs, metrics and traces. Logs are timestamped messages, metrics are numeric aggregations over time, and traces record the path of a single request through multiple services as spans.

interview.q: What are the four golden signals?
interview.a: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation: how long requests take, how much demand there is, how many requests fail, and how full the service is.

interview.q: What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA?
interview.a: An SLI is a quantitative measurement of service level, such as the success rate. An SLO is a target for that measurement, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with users that has consequences if SLOs are missed.

interview.q: What is an error budget and how do you use it?
interview.a: It is the allowed amount of unreliability, 100 percent minus the SLO, for example 0.1 percent. While there is budget left you can ship and take risks, and when it is spent you prioritize reliability work. It makes the trade-off between speed and stability measurable.

interview.q: What should trigger a page?
interview.a: A symptom users feel, such as a high error rate or latency, that needs a human to act. Causes like high CPU are for dashboards and debugging, and anything that needs only a scripted response should be automated rather than paged.

interview.q: Why is 100 percent availability a bad target?
interview.a: It is impossible and it would freeze all change, because any deploy carries risk. A realistic SLO plus an error budget lets the team balance new features against reliability.

title: Incident Management and Blameless Postmortems
tagline: When something breaks: call it early, share the roles, keep notes, and learn without blaming anyone.
explain: Every system fails eventually. What separates mature teams is how they respond and what they learn. Interviews for DevOps, SRE and senior backend roles ask 'tell me about an incident' and 'how would you run one', and they listen for structure and for a blameless attitude.
## What counts as an incident, and when to declare one

The Google SRE book advises that it is better to declare an incident early and then find a simple fix and close out the incident. It gives three tests, and if any is true the event is an incident: do you need to involve a second team in fixing the problem, is the outage visible to customers, and is the issue unsolved even after an hour's concentrated analysis. Declaring early costs little. Declaring late costs customers.
## Roles

The SRE book's incident management structure separates responsibilities so that people can act without stepping on each other. The incident commander holds the high-level state of the incident and assigns responsibilities. The operations team is the only group modifying the system during an incident, so changes do not collide. The communications role is the public face of the response and sends periodic updates to responders and stakeholders. The planning role supports operations with longer-term issues, such as filing bugs and tracking how the system has diverged from normal so it can be reverted. The book notes, a little counterintuitively, that a clear separation of responsibilities gives individuals more autonomy.

- Keep a living incident document. The book calls this the incident commander's most important responsibility: a document that several people can edit at once, recording the timeline and decisions, kept for the postmortem.
- Hand off clearly. If the commander changes, say so out loud and do not leave until the new commander acknowledges.
- In a small team one person may hold several roles. Name them anyway.
## Mitigate first, then find the cause

During an incident the goal is to stop the customer impact, which may mean rolling back a deploy, turning off a feature flag or failing over, rather than understanding the root cause. Investigate deeply afterwards, once users are no longer affected.
## Blameless postmortems

A postmortem is a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root causes and the follow-up actions that prevent recurrence. The SRE book states three goals: the incident is documented, all contributing root causes are well understood, and effective preventive actions are put in place to reduce the likelihood or impact of recurrence.

The key principle is blamelessness. A postmortem should identify contributing causes without indicting any individual or team for bad or inappropriate behavior. It assumes everyone involved had good intentions and acted on the information they had. The book gives the reason: without it, people will not bring issues to light for fear of punishment, so you stop learning. Writing a postmortem is not punishment. Practically this means writing 'the deploy pipeline allowed a change without a test' rather than 'Sam deployed untested code'.
## What a good postmortem contains

The book's review questions are a good template: was key incident data collected for posterity, are the impact assessments complete, was the root cause sufficiently deep, is the action plan appropriate and are the resulting bug fixes at the right priority, and was the outcome shared with relevant stakeholders. In practice that means a timeline, the impact in numbers, contributing causes (often several), what went well, what went badly, where you got lucky, and action items with an owner and a due date.
keyPoints: Declare early. It is an incident if you need a second team, customers can see it, or it is unsolved after an hour.

interview.q: Walk me through how you would handle a production incident.
interview.a: Detect it from a symptom alert, declare an incident early, assign an incident commander and an operations lead who alone changes the system, plus communications, keep a live incident document, mitigate first (roll back, disable or fail over), then write a blameless postmortem with owned action items.

interview.q: When do you declare an incident?
interview.a: Early. If I need to involve a second team, if customers can see the outage, or if it is unsolved after an hour of focused analysis. It is cheaper to declare and close it quickly than to declare late.

interview.q: What are the main incident roles?
interview.a: The incident commander holds the state and assigns work, operations is the only group modifying the system, communications updates responders and stakeholders, and planning handles longer-term items like bugs and tracking changes to revert.

interview.q: What does blameless mean in a postmortem?
interview.a: Identifying contributing causes without blaming an individual or team, assuming everyone acted with good intentions on the information they had. It keeps people willing to report problems, so the organization learns.

interview.q: Why mitigate before finding the root cause?
interview.a: Customer impact is the priority, and the quickest safe action such as a rollback usually stops it. Deep analysis is easier and safer once the pressure is off.

interview.q: What makes a postmortem useful?
interview.a: Key data was collected, impact is quantified, the root causes are deep rather than superficial, action items are specific with owners and priorities, and the learnings are shared.

title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
tagline: Write your servers and networks as files, preview each change, and rebuild them the same way every time.
explain: Clicking through a cloud console creates infrastructure nobody can reproduce, review or roll back. Infrastructure as code (IaC) replaces that with files in version control. Terraform is the most widely asked-about tool, and the ideas transfer to others.
## What it is

HashiCorp describes Terraform as an infrastructure as code tool that lets you build, change and version cloud and on-prem resources. Its configuration files are declarative, meaning they describe the end state of your infrastructure rather than the steps to reach it. You say 'there should be one bucket with this name and these settings', and Terraform works out what to create, change or delete to make reality match.
## The core workflow: write, plan, apply

The Terraform docs say the core workflow has three stages. You write the configuration. You plan: Terraform creates an execution plan describing the infrastructure it will create, update or destroy, so you can review the changes before it makes them. Then you apply, and approved changes are carried out in dependency order. The plan is the safety net. In a team, the plan is posted on the pull request and reviewed like code before anyone applies it.
## State

Terraform records your real infrastructure in a state file, which the docs call a source of truth for your environment. It compares your configuration with the state (and the real resources) to decide what changes will bring infrastructure in line. In a team the state is stored remotely and locked so two people cannot apply at once. State can contain sensitive values, so treat it as a secret and restrict access to it.
## Declarative versus imperative

A shell script that runs 'create a server' creates a second server if you run it twice. A declarative description says 'one server exists', so applying it twice changes nothing the second time. That repeatability (idempotence) is what lets you run the same code to create staging, production and a disaster-recovery copy, and re-apply safely after a failure.
## Drift

Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches the code, usually because someone changed it by hand in the console. The next plan shows the difference, and applying either restores the declared state or you update the code to adopt the change. Many teams forbid manual changes so the code stays the truth.
## Good habits

- Keep all infrastructure changes in pull requests, with the plan output reviewed.
- Split large configurations into modules you can reuse for each environment.
- Never put secrets in the code. Read them from a secret manager or the environment.
- Keep separate state per environment so a staging mistake cannot touch production.
- Make the pipeline run plan automatically on every change and apply only after approval.
## Related ideas

Configuration management tools (such as Ansible) configure what runs inside machines, while Terraform-style tools create the machines and networks. Containers (see the Docker lesson) and an orchestrator such as Kubernetes then run your applications on top. In an interview, be ready to explain declarative versus imperative, what the plan is for, and what state is and why it is dangerous to lose or leak.
keyPoints: IaC means infrastructure described in version-controlled, reviewable files. Terraform configuration is declarative: it describes the end state.
Workflow: write, plan (preview what will be created, updated or destroyed), apply.
State is Terraform's record of real infrastructure. Store it remotely with locking, and treat it as sensitive.
Declarative apply is repeatable: running it twice changes nothing the second time.
Drift is manual change that diverges from the code. The plan reveals it. Review plans in pull requests.

interview.q: What is infrastructure as code and why use it?
interview.a: Describing infrastructure in version-controlled files instead of clicking in a console. It makes environments reproducible, reviewable and auditable, and lets you recreate or roll back safely.

interview.q: What is the difference between declarative and imperative?
interview.a: Declarative describes the desired end state and the tool computes the steps, so applying twice changes nothing the second time. Imperative lists the steps, so running them twice repeats the work.

interview.q: What do terraform plan and apply do?
interview.a: Plan creates an execution plan describing what will be created, updated or destroyed so it can be reviewed. Apply carries out the approved changes in dependency order.

interview.q: What is Terraform state and why does it matter?
interview.a: A record of the real infrastructure Terraform manages, used as a source of truth to work out what to change. It should be stored remotely with locking, and protected because it can hold sensitive values.

interview.q: What is configuration drift?
interview.a: When real infrastructure differs from the code, usually from manual changes. The next plan shows the difference, and you either restore the declared state or update the code.

interview.q: How would you manage several environments?
interview.a: The same modules with different variables, a separate state per environment, changes through pull requests with the plan reviewed, and approval before apply in production.

title: Batch Processing with Spark
tagline: Why Spark waits before it works, why moving data between machines is slow, and when saving results helps.
explain: When data no longer fits on one machine, or one machine is too slow, you split the work across many. Apache Spark is the standard engine for that kind of batch processing, and data engineering interviews ask how it works: what 'lazy' means, what a shuffle is, and how you make a job fast.
## Transformations and actions

The Spark docs say datasets support two types of operations. Transformations create a new dataset from an existing one, for example map and filter. Actions return a value to the driver program after running a computation on the dataset, for example count, collect and reduce. The crucial rule: all transformations in Spark are lazy, meaning they do not compute their results right away. They only record what to do, and the transformations are computed only when an action requires a result.

This laziness lets Spark see the whole chain before running it and plan the work efficiently. It also explains a common surprise: your filter and map lines run instantly because nothing has happened yet, and the real work, and any error in it, appears when the first action runs.
## DataFrames and Spark SQL

Spark SQL is a Spark module for structured data processing. A DataFrame is a Dataset organized into named columns, conceptually equivalent to a table in a relational database, with richer optimizations under the hood. The docs explain that the structured interfaces give Spark more information about the structure of the data and the computation, which it uses to perform extra optimizations. That is why you should prefer DataFrames and SQL over low-level RDD code for most jobs. You can run SQL queries directly, and the result comes back as a DataFrame.
## The shuffle: the expensive part

Data is split into partitions that are processed in parallel on different machines. Operations such as groupBy, join or distinct need rows with the same key to end up together. The docs call this event the shuffle: Spark's mechanism for re-distributing data so that it is grouped differently across partitions. It typically involves copying data across executors and machines, and the docs say it is an expensive operation because it involves disk I/O, data serialization and network I/O. Most Spark tuning is about reducing shuffles: filter and select columns early so less data moves, avoid unnecessary groupBy and distinct, and watch for one key that has far more rows than the others (skew), which makes one machine do most of the work.
## Caching

The docs describe persisting or caching a dataset in memory across operations as one of Spark's most important capabilities. It makes future actions much faster, often by more than 10 times, which suits iterative algorithms and reusing an intermediate result. The cache() shorthand uses the default MEMORY_ONLY level. Their guidance is to leave things at the default if the data fits comfortably, and not to spill to disk unless the computation is expensive, because recomputing a partition may be as fast as reading it from disk. Cache a result only if you use it more than once.
## Batch, files and when not to use Spark

Store analytical data in a columnar file format such as Parquet, partitioned by a column you often filter on, so a query reads only the columns and folders it needs. And be honest about scale: if the data fits on one machine, a database or pandas job is simpler, cheaper and faster to develop. Spark pays off when data is large, when you need to scale out, or when the organization already runs it.
keyPoints: Transformations (map, filter) are lazy and only describe the work. Actions (count, collect, reduce) trigger computation.
Prefer DataFrames and Spark SQL: Spark knows the structure and can optimize.
A shuffle redistributes data across partitions and is expensive (disk, serialization, network). Reduce them.
Filter and select early, and watch for skewed keys.
Cache a dataset only when it is reused. Do not use Spark when one machine is enough.

sql.title: A PySpark job: transformations are lazy until the action
sql.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName('daily-sales').getOrCreate()

orders = spark.read.parquet('s3://lake/orders/')            # nothing is read yet

daily = (orders
    .filter(F.col('status') == 'paid')                        # transformation (lazy)
    .select('order_date', 'store_id', 'amount')               # drop columns early
    .groupBy('order_date', 'store_id')                        # needs a SHUFFLE
    .agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue')))                   # transformation (lazy)

daily.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://lake/daily_sales/')   # ACTION: now it all runs

''')                                            # returns a DataFrame

interview.q: What does it mean that Spark transformations are lazy?
interview.a: They do not compute anything when called. Spark only records the operations, and computes the result when an action such as count, collect or write needs it, which lets it optimize the whole chain first.

interview.q: What is the difference between a transformation and an action?
interview.a: A transformation (map, filter, groupBy) creates a new dataset from an existing one and is lazy. An action (count, collect, reduce, write) returns a value or writes output and triggers the computation.

interview.q: What is a shuffle and why is it expensive?
interview.a: It is Spark's mechanism for redistributing data so it is grouped differently across partitions, needed by operations like groupBy and join. It is expensive because it involves disk I/O, data serialization and network I/O between machines.

interview.q: How do you make a Spark job faster?
interview.a: Reduce shuffles and the data moved: filter and select early, avoid unnecessary groupBy, distinct and joins, deal with skewed keys, use DataFrames so Spark can optimize, use columnar partitioned storage, and cache results that are reused.

interview.q: When would you cache a DataFrame?
interview.a: When it is used by more than one action and is expensive to recompute. Caching keeps it in memory so later actions are much faster. If it is used once, caching is just wasted memory.

interview.q: Spark or a database for a 5 GB dataset?
interview.a: Usually a database or a single-machine tool, because it is simpler and faster to develop. Spark is worth it when the data is large, needs to scale out, or the platform already runs it.

title: ML Fundamentals: Splits, Overfitting, Leakage and Metrics
tagline: Why a perfect score on data the model already saw means nothing, and how to measure real performance.
explain: Machine learning interviews start with evaluation, because a model that looks good for the wrong reason is worse than no model. Four ideas cover most of it: hold out data, recognize overfitting, avoid leakage, and choose a metric that matches the cost of mistakes.
## Learning from examples

In supervised learning you have examples with inputs (features) and known answers (labels), and you fit a model that predicts the label for new inputs. Classification predicts a category (fraud or not fraud). Regression predicts a number (a delivery time). The model is only useful if it works on data it has not seen.
## Overfitting and the hold-out set

The scikit-learn docs say that learning the parameters of a prediction function and testing it on the same data is a methodological mistake: a model that just repeated the labels of the samples it has seen would have a perfect score but would fail to predict anything useful on unseen data. This is called overfitting. The standard remedy is to hold out part of the data as a test set, which scikit-learn does with the train_test_split helper. You fit on the training part and report the score on the held-out part.

The docs go on to point out that you can still overfit to the test set if you keep tweaking parameters until it looks best, because knowledge about the test set leaks into the model and the metrics no longer report generalization. The fix is a separate validation set for tuning, with the test set used once at the end. Because splitting into three sets reduces the data available for learning, cross-validation is the usual alternative: the test set is still held out, but the training data is split into k folds, the model is trained on k minus 1 of them and checked on the remaining one in turn, and the reported performance is the average over the loop.
## Data leakage

Leakage means information from outside the training data sneaks into training, so your scores are too optimistic and the model fails in production. The scikit-learn docs give a concrete case: preprocessing such as standardisation or feature selection should be learned from the training set and then applied to the held-out data. If you scale using the mean of all the data, the test set has influenced the model. They recommend using a Pipeline so the preprocessing is fitted inside each cross-validation fold automatically. Other typical leaks: a feature that is only known after the outcome happened, duplicates of the same row in both train and test, and shuffling time series randomly instead of splitting by time.
## Metrics: accuracy is not enough

Accuracy, the fraction of predictions that are right, misleads when classes are imbalanced. If 1 percent of transactions are fraud, a model that always says 'not fraud' is 99 percent accurate and useless. For a positive class use precision and recall. The scikit-learn docs define precision as the true positives over the true positives plus the false positives, and recall as the true positives over the true positives plus the false negatives. In words: high precision means few false positives in the results returned, and high recall means few false negatives among the relevant items. A system with high recall but low precision returns most relevant items but many wrong ones, and the reverse returns few relevant items but mostly correct ones.

The two trade off through the decision threshold. Lowering the threshold returns more results, which can increase recall, but if the threshold was already about right it adds false positives and lowers precision. Choose the point from the cost of each mistake: for cancer screening a missed case is far worse than a false alarm, so favour recall, while for a spam filter that deletes mail a false positive may be worse, so favour precision.
## Always compare with a baseline

Before celebrating a number, compare it with something simple: predicting the majority class, last period's value, or a basic rule. A model must beat the baseline by enough to justify its cost and complexity.
keyPoints: Never judge a model on its training data. Hold out a test set, and use it once at the end.
Tune on a validation set or with k-fold cross-validation, not on the test set.
Leakage: fit preprocessing on the training data only. Use a Pipeline. Split time series by time.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Recall = TP / (TP + FN). Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.
Lowering the threshold usually raises recall and can lower precision. Pick by the cost of each mistake and compare with a baseline.

sql.title: Split, pipeline, cross-validate, report
sql.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, confusion_matrix

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0)   # hold out a test set (stratify keeps the class ratio)

# the scaler lives INSIDE the pipeline, so it is fitted on training folds only: no leakage
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))

scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='recall')   # tune with CV, not the test set
print('CV recall', scores.mean())

model.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = model.predict(X_test)                                # touch the test set ONCE, at the end
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, pred))
print('precision', precision_score(y_test, pred), 'recall', recall_score(y_test, pred))

sql.title: A baseline to beat
sql.code:
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent').fit(X_train, y_train)
print('baseline accuracy', baseline.score(X_test, y_test))   # on 1% fraud data this is already ~0.99
# if your model's accuracy is not clearly better, or its recall on the positive class is zero, it adds nothing

exercise: On any labeled dataset (for example a fraud or spam dataset), first train a decision tree with no depth limit and show the train-test gap. Then fit a baseline (most frequent class) and compare. Deliberately introduce leakage by scaling before splitting and see the score rise, then fix it with a Pipeline. Finally compute the confusion matrix, precision and recall at three thresholds and decide which threshold you would ship and why.
pitfalls: Reporting accuracy on an imbalanced dataset.
Tuning hyperparameters on the test set until it looks good.
Fitting scalers, imputers or feature selection on all the data before splitting.
Randomly splitting time series data so the model sees the future.
Never comparing against a simple baseline.

interview.q: What is overfitting and how do you detect it?
interview.a: The model learns the training data, including noise, and fails on unseen data. I detect it by comparing training and held-out scores: a large gap means overfitting. Remedies include more data, a simpler model, regularisation and cross-validation.

interview.q: What is the difference between a validation set and a test set?
interview.a: The validation set is used to tune and choose models. The test set is held out and used once at the end to estimate how the final model generalizes. Tuning on the test set leaks information about it into the model.

interview.q: What is cross-validation?
interview.a: A way to estimate performance without a separate validation set: split the training data into k folds, train on k minus 1 and evaluate on the remaining fold in turn, and average the scores.

interview.q: What is data leakage? Give an example.
interview.a: Information from outside the training data influencing the model, making scores unrealistically good. For example scaling or selecting features using the whole dataset before splitting, or using a feature that is only known after the outcome.

interview.q: Define precision and recall and when you would favour each.
interview.a: Precision is true positives over true positives plus false positives, so how many flagged items were right. Recall is true positives over true positives plus false negatives, so how many real items were found. Favour recall when missing a case is costly, such as disease screening, and precision when false alarms are costly.

interview.q: Why is accuracy a bad metric for imbalanced data?
interview.a: A model that always predicts the majority class gets a high accuracy while finding none of the rare class. Precision, recall, or a cost-based metric describes performance on the class that matters.

basis: Priority 1 is my judgment: evaluation methodology is the first thing ML interviews test in the guides I read. Overfitting, the hold-out test set, the validation set and cross-validation, the preprocessing-leakage guidance with the Pipeline recommendation, and the precision, recall and threshold trade-off come from the scikit-learn pages I opened. The email numbers are an illustrative example I computed, the overfitting score tables are illustrative, and the extra leakage examples and baseline advice are general practice.

title: ML in Production: Skew, Drift, Monitoring and Rollback
tagline: A model that worked in testing can slowly get worse in real use. Learn what to record, watch and undo.
explain: Training a model is the easy part. Keeping it correct for months while the world changes is the hard part, and it is what ML engineering interviews focus on at 2 or more years. Software fails loudly with errors. Models fail silently by returning confident, wrong answers.
## Start simpler than you think

Google's Rules of Machine Learning begin with Rule 1: do not be afraid to launch a product without machine learning. A simple heuristic can often get a large share of the value, so you can wait until you have data. Shipping the heuristic first also gives you a baseline that any model must beat, and the plumbing (logging, serving, evaluation) you will need anyway.
## Training-serving skew

The Rules of ML define training-serving skew as a difference between performance during training and performance during serving. It can come from data handled differently in training and serving, from the data changing between the two, or from a feedback loop. The classic cause is computing a feature in two places with two bits of code, say in SQL for training and in Python at request time, so they disagree subtly. The guide's advice is to monitor skew explicitly so that system and data changes do not introduce it unnoticed. Rule 29 adds a practical habit: save the set of features used at serving time and log them for use in training, even logging a small fraction lets you verify that serving and training are consistent. Where possible share one feature-computation code path between training and serving.
## Drift

Drift is the world changing after the model was trained. Data drift means the distribution of the inputs changes, for example a new product line or a new customer segment. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes, for example fraudsters change tactics. Either one erodes accuracy without any error message. You detect it by comparing recent inputs and predictions with a reference period (means, spreads, category frequencies, the share of nulls), and by measuring real performance once true labels arrive, which may be days or weeks later.
## Freshness and retraining

Rule 8 of the guide asks you to know the freshness requirements of your system: how much does performance degrade if you have a model that is a day old, a week old? The answer tells you how often to retrain and how closely to monitor. Retrain on a schedule or when a monitor trips, and always evaluate the new model against the current one before replacing it.
## Monitoring checklist

- Inputs: missing values, ranges, category frequencies, schema changes.
- Outputs: the distribution of predictions and scores. A sudden shift is a red flag even without labels.
- Performance: precision, recall or your business metric, computed when labels become available.
- Service health: latency, error rate, throughput (see the observability lesson).
- Business outcome: the metric the model was built to improve.
## Shipping and rolling back safely

Treat a model like any release. Version every model with the data, code and parameters that produced it, so you can reproduce it and roll back. Run the new model in shadow mode first, where it makes predictions that are logged but not used, then give it a small share of traffic (a canary) and compare against the current model, then expand. Keep the previous version deployed and make rollback one action. Decide in advance what happens if the model service is down or times out: a safe fallback such as the baseline rule is better than an error.
keyPoints: Launch a heuristic baseline first (Rule 1). A model must beat it.
Training-serving skew is a difference between training and serving performance. Share feature code and log serving-time features to monitor it.
Data drift: inputs change. Concept drift: the right answer changes. Both degrade accuracy silently.
Monitor inputs, prediction distributions, delayed performance, service health and the business metric.
Version models, roll out via shadow and canary, keep the previous version and a safe fallback for instant rollback.

interview.q: What is training-serving skew and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: A difference between how the model performs in training and in serving, often because features are computed differently in the two places or data changes between them. Prevent it by sharing the feature code, logging serving-time features, and monitoring the difference.

interview.q: What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?
interview.a: Data drift is a change in the distribution of the inputs. Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the correct output. Both silently reduce accuracy, so you monitor input and prediction distributions and measure real performance when labels arrive.

interview.q: How do you monitor a model in production?
interview.a: Input quality and distributions, the distribution of predictions, delayed performance metrics once labels arrive, the service's latency and errors, and the business metric the model is meant to improve.

interview.q: How would you roll out a new model safely?
interview.a: Version it, run it in shadow mode, then a small canary compared with the current model, then expand. Keep the previous version deployed for instant rollback, and have a safe fallback if the model is unavailable.

interview.q: Why start with a non-ML baseline?
interview.a: Rule 1 of Google's Rules of ML: a simple heuristic can capture much of the value, gives you a baseline the model must beat, and lets you build the logging and serving infrastructure before you need the model.

interview.q: How often should you retrain a model?
interview.a: It depends on freshness requirements: measure how much performance drops if the model is a day or a week old. Retrain on a schedule or when monitoring shows drift, and always compare the candidate with the current model first.

title: ML System Design Interviews
tagline: Plan a machine learning product: the goal, a simple first version, the data, how to measure, and how it runs live.
explain: An ML system design interview asks 'design a system that detects fraudulent payments' or 'recommends videos'. As with other design interviews, you are not expected to know one answer. You are expected to follow a method, ask questions, and make trade-offs explicit. The method below reuses ideas from the previous two lessons.
## A seven-step structure

- Frame the problem: what decision does the model support, and what business metric improves if it works? Clarify scale, latency and who is affected by mistakes.
- Start with a baseline: a simple rule or heuristic. Google's Rules of ML begins with the advice not to be afraid to launch without machine learning.
- Data and labels: where do labels come from, how reliable are they, and how long after the event do they arrive? Labels for fraud may take weeks (chargebacks).
- Features: which inputs are available at the moment of prediction? Anything only known later is a leak.
- Model: start simple and justify any added complexity.
- Evaluate: offline with a proper split, then online with an experiment.
- Serve and monitor: latency budget, batch or real time, monitoring for drift and skew, fallback and rollback.
## Worked example: flag fraudulent payments

Framing: the decision is approve, review or block a payment, and the cost of mistakes is asymmetric. Blocking a good customer loses a sale and trust, and approving fraud loses money. The prediction must arrive within about 100 milliseconds because the customer is waiting.

Baseline: rules such as 'block if more than 5 attempts in a minute' catch the obvious cases and give you something to beat. Data: fraud is rare, so the classes are heavily imbalanced, accuracy is the wrong metric and you will track precision and recall. Labels are delayed by chargeback reports, so recent data has incomplete labels, and your training window must account for it.

Features: only information available at authorization time, such as amount, merchant, device, country mismatch, and counts of recent attempts for this card. Computing 'attempts in the last minute' fast needs a low-latency store, and the same definition must be used in training (see training-serving skew). Evaluation: split by time, so you train on the past and test on the future, which matches deployment. Pick the decision threshold from costs, and use a human review band between approve and block. Online, run a shadow period and then an experiment.
## Trade-offs interviewers like to hear

- Precision versus recall, set by the cost of each mistake and adjustable through the threshold.
- Batch versus real-time features and predictions: batch is cheap and simple but stale, real time is fresh but costly and brings skew risk.
- Complexity versus maintainability: a gradient-boosted tree with solid features often beats a deep model for tabular data and is far easier to operate.
- Feedback loops: the system's decisions shape future data. If you block certain transactions you never learn whether they were fraud, which the Rules of ML list as one source of skew. Keep a small random sample unblocked, or review blocked cases, to keep learning.
- Failure plan: what happens when the model times out, drifts or is wrong. A rule-based fallback and a fast rollback.
## Mistakes to avoid
Jumping to a deep model before a baseline, ignoring label delay and leakage, using accuracy on imbalanced data, forgetting latency and serving, and describing training but never monitoring.
keyPoints: Follow the structure: frame, baseline, data and labels, features, model, evaluation, serving and monitoring.
Start with a heuristic baseline and justify any added complexity.
Use only features available at prediction time. Watch label delay. Split by time.
Choose the threshold from the cost of each mistake. Add a human review band where useful.
Plan for feedback loops, drift, a fallback and rollback.

sql.title: A design outline to reuse
sql.code:
1. Problem   : decision supported (approve / review / block), business metric, latency 100 ms, scale 500 tx/s
2. Baseline  : rules (velocity, amount, country mismatch). Measure its precision and recall first.
3. Data      : labels from chargebacks (delayed ~30 days), 0.3% positive -> imbalanced
4. Features  : only at authorisation time: amount, merchant, device, tx counts in last 1 min / 1 h (from a fast store)
5. Model     : gradient-boosted trees; compare with the baseline
6. Evaluation: time-based split; precision/recall at a cost-chosen threshold; then shadow, then A/B
7. Serve     : real-time scoring in <100 ms, feature store shared with training, fallback to rules, one-click rollback
   Monitor   : input drift, score distribution, delayed recall, latency, review-queue size

interview.q: How do you approach an ML system design question?
interview.a: Frame the decision and the business metric, propose a simple baseline, discuss labels and features available at prediction time, choose and justify a model, evaluate offline with a proper split and then online, and finish with serving, monitoring, a fallback and rollback.

interview.q: Why start with a baseline?
interview.a: A simple heuristic can capture a large share of the value, gives you a number the model must beat, and lets you build logging and serving first. Google's Rules of ML start with not being afraid to launch without machine learning.

interview.q: How do you handle delayed labels?
interview.a: Account for the delay when building training sets so recent data with incomplete labels is not treated as negative, evaluate on matured data, and use early proxy signals or monitoring on predictions while true labels arrive.

interview.q: How do you choose a decision threshold?
interview.a: From the cost of each mistake. Lowering it raises recall and can lower precision. Often I add a manual-review band between auto-approve and auto-block.

interview.q: What is a feedback loop in an ML system?
interview.a: The system's decisions influence the data it later learns from, for example blocked transactions are never confirmed as fraud or not. It can bias the model, so keep a small unbiased sample or review outcomes of decisions to keep learning.

interview.q: How do you make sure the model keeps working after launch?
interview.a: Monitor input and prediction distributions and delayed performance, keep a fallback and a one-step rollback, version every model, and retrain based on freshness requirements and drift.

title: Caching: Cache-Aside, Staleness and Stampedes
tagline: Keep the most asked answers somewhere much faster than the database, and know what it costs.
explain: A cache is a small, fast store that holds copies of answers so you do not have to compute or fetch them again. It is not the source of truth. The database is. The cache is a copy that can be wrong, can disappear, and must be rebuildable from the truth at any time. Everything hard about caching follows from that one fact.
## When a cache is worth it

A cache helps when the same data is read many times and changes rarely. The signs are repeated identical queries, a small set of rows that gets most of the reads, and a database whose CPU is busy doing the same work again and again. If every request is different, or the data changes on every read, a cache adds complexity and gives nothing back.
## Cache-aside, the pattern you will use most

In cache-aside the application owns the logic. To read: look in the cache. On a hit, return it. On a miss, read the database, store the answer in the cache with a time limit, and return it. To write: change the database, then remove the cached copy so the next read rebuilds it.

> product = cache.get('product:42')
if product is None:
    product = Product.objects.get(pk=42)
    cache.set('product:42', product, timeout=300)

Django ships this as a framework with several backends (Memcached, Redis, database, file system, local memory). Its default timeout is 300 seconds, timeout=None caches forever and timeout=0 means do not cache. The local-memory backend is private to each process, so it is fine for development but it cannot share entries between your gunicorn workers.
## The number that matters: hit rate

Hit rate is hits divided by hits plus misses. Only misses reach the database, so database load is reads times (1 minus hit rate). At 90% a tenth of reads still land on the database; at 99% only a hundredth do. Redis reports keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses so you can compute it. If the rate is lower than you expected, the usual causes are a time limit that is too short, keys that are too specific, or a cache too small for the hot set.
## Staleness: the price you pay

Because the cache is a copy, it can disagree with the database. There are two tools. Expiry puts a time limit on every entry, so a stale value lives at most that long. Invalidation deletes the key when the underlying row changes. Use both: delete on write for freshness, and keep a time limit as a safety net for the writes you forgot about. Prefer deleting over overwriting, because a delete cannot store an old value over a newer one.

In Django, do the delete after the transaction commits (transaction.on_commit). Deleting before the commit lets another request refill the cache with the old row in between, which leaves the stale value in place until it expires.
## Memory is finite: eviction

A cache has a size limit. When it is full, an eviction policy decides what to drop. Least recently used (LRU) drops the entry untouched for the longest time. Least frequently used (LFU) drops the one used least often. Redis offers allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-ttl and noeviction, and its documentation suggests allkeys-lru as a sensible default when a small subset of keys gets most of the reads. Redis approximates LRU by sampling a few keys.
## Failure modes to name in an interview

- Stampede (dog-pile): a hot key expires and many requests rebuild it at once. Fix with a rebuild lock (cache.add), jittered time limits, or refreshing before expiry.
- Stale reads: the cache outlives a write. Fix with delete on write plus a time limit.
- Cold start: after a restart the cache is empty and the database takes the full load until it warms. Warm popular keys first, and bring caches back gradually.
- Wrong key: a personalised answer cached under a shared key. Put user, language and version in the key.
- Cache as a crutch: if the database falls over whenever the cache is cold, the cache is hiding a query that needs an index.
## What to say about it

A strong answer names what is cached, the key, the time limit and why that staleness is acceptable, how entries are invalidated on write, what happens on a stampede, and how you would watch the hit rate. Then say what you would check before adding a cache at all: could an index or a better query fix the slow read for less?
keyPoints: A cache is a disposable copy. The database stays the source of truth.
Cache-aside: read the cache, on a miss read the database and store the answer with a time limit; on a write change the database and delete the key.
Database load is reads times (1 minus hit rate), so small gains near 99% matter a lot. Measure hits and misses.
Combine delete-on-write with a TTL. Delete after the transaction commits.
Name the failure modes: stale reads, stampede, cold start, wrong key.

sql.title: Cache-aside in Django
sql.code:
from django.core.cache import cache
from django.db import transaction

def get_product(pk):
    key = f'product:{pk}'
    product = cache.get(key)
    if product is None:
        product = Product.objects.get(pk=pk)
        cache.set(key, product, timeout=300)   # 5 minutes
    return product

def set_price(pk, price):
    with transaction.atomic():
        Product.objects.filter(pk=pk).update(price=price)
        # delete only after the commit succeeds
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: cache.delete(f'product:{pk}'))

sql.title: Rebuild lock
sql.code:
def get_hot(pk):
    key = f'product:{pk}'
    value = cache.get(key)
    if value is not None:
        return value
    if cache.add(f'lock:{key}', 1, timeout=10):   # only one caller gets True
        try:
            value = Product.objects.get(pk=pk)
            cache.set(key, value, timeout=300)
        finally:
            cache.delete(f'lock:{key}')
        return value
    time.sleep(0.05)               # someone else is rebuilding
    return cache.get(key) or Product.objects.get(pk=pk)

django.title: settings.py: a shared cache
django.note: Use a cache shared by every process (Redis or Memcached). LocMemCache is per-process, so each gunicorn worker would have its own copy and its own hit rate.

steps.title: Every page hits the database
body: Your shop is popular. Every product page asks the database for the same kind of thing (name, price, photos) and the database is now 92% busy.
Reads queue up and pages slow to nearly half a second at p95. All the numbers in this lesson are illustrative: they are chosen to show the shape of the problem, not measured from a real system.

callout.text: The database holds the only copy of the truth, so it is usually the hardest part to scale. Protect it from repeated work.

steps.title: The same questions, again and again
body: Look at what the database is being asked. A handful of products account for most reads, and their answers barely change from one second to the next.
A small set of items that is read far more often than the rest is exactly the pattern that makes a cache worth having.

callout.text: A cache pays off when reads greatly outnumber writes and a small hot set gets most of the reads.

steps.title: Add a cache beside the app
body: A cache is a fast store, usually in memory, that keeps copies of recent answers. The app asks it first.
At the start it is empty, so the first read is a miss: the app falls back to the database exactly as before.
changes: + A cache next to the app servers
~ Every read now starts with a cache lookup

steps.title: Cache-aside: the read path
body: This pattern is called cache-aside: the application, not the cache, loads data on a miss. Look in the cache. On a miss read the database. Store the answer with a time limit. Return it.
The next reader of the same key skips the database entirely.

callout.text: Django's default cache timeout is 300 seconds (5 minutes). You can pass timeout=None to cache forever, or 0 to not cache at all.

steps.title: Hit rate decides everything
body: Only misses reach the database, so database traffic is reads times (1 minus the hit rate). At a 90% hit rate, 10 of every 100 reads still miss. At 99%, only 1 does.
That is why a few points near the top matter so much: going from 90% to 99% sends one tenth as many reads to the database.

callout.text: Measure it: hits divided by hits plus misses. Redis reports keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses in INFO stats for exactly this.

predict.question: The hit rate rises from 90% to 99%. How much less traffic does the database receive?
predict.why: Misses are what reach the database: 10 in every 100 reads at 90%, but only 1 in every 100 at 99%. That is one tenth as many.

steps.title: The price changed. The cache did not.
body: An admin raises a price from $20 to $25. The database has the new price, but the cache still holds the old copy, so shoppers keep seeing $20 until something removes it.
A cache is a second copy of the truth. Keeping that copy honest is the hard part of caching.

callout.text: Every cache trades freshness for speed. Decide, per piece of data, how stale is acceptable: seconds for a price, minutes for a blog post.

steps.title: Two ways to remove stale data
body: Expire: every entry has a time limit, so stale data lives at most that long. Cheap, and you can state the worst case: no more than 5 minutes old.
Invalidate: when the app changes the row, it also deletes the cache key, so the next read rebuilds it from the database. Most systems do both: delete on write, with the time limit as a safety net.

callout.text: Deleting the key is usually safer than writing the new value into the cache yourself: the next reader rebuilds it from the database, so you cannot overwrite a newer value with an older one.

changes: + Write path deletes the cache key
~ Next read refills it from the database

steps.title: Memory is finite: eviction
body: The cache is full. To add something new it must remove something old, and the eviction policy chooses the victim.

LRU removes what was used longest ago. LFU removes what is used least often. The Redis docs call allkeys-lru a good default when you have no reason to prefer another, because a small subset of keys usually gets most of the reads.

callout.text: Redis approximates LRU by sampling a few keys rather than tracking every one, because exact LRU costs more memory.

changes: - The least recently used keys are dropped to make room

steps.title: A hot key expires: the stampede
body: The time limit on the most popular key runs out. For a moment the cache has nothing, so every request that arrives sees a miss. Thousands of them all go to the database to rebuild the same value.
The more popular the key and the slower the query, the worse this is, and it happens exactly when load is highest.

callout.text: This is called a cache stampede (or dog-pile). The cache did its job right up to the moment it expired.

steps.title: One rebuild, everyone else waits
body: Let one request rebuild the value while the others wait a moment, or serve the slightly old value. Other defences: add a little random jitter to time limits so hot keys do not all expire together, and refresh popular keys shortly before they expire.
In Django, cache.add stores a value only if the key is absent and tells you whether it did, which is the building block for a rebuild lock.

callout.text: A lock needs a cache shared by every process. Django's LocMemCache is private to each process, so it cannot coordinate them.

card.title: A rebuild lock
lines: wait briefly, read the cache again

changes: + A lock so only one request rebuilds

steps.title: A key must say everything the answer depends on
body: If the answer differs by user, language or version, all of that must be part of the key. Otherwise one user's cached page is served to another.
Django helps: KEY_PREFIX separates cache keys between sites or servers that share a cache, and VERSION lets you invalidate a whole family of keys at once by bumping a number.

callout.text: Never cache a personalised response under a shared key. This is how one customer sees another customer's basket.

changes: + User, language and version are part of the key

steps.title: Recap: what you bought and what it cost
body: You bought speed and relief for the database: most reads never reach it. You paid with staleness, one more moving part, and a cold start while the cache fills.
Checklist: reads far outnumber writes; cache-aside with a time limit; delete on write; watch the hit rate; protect hot keys; put the owner in the key.

exercise: Pick the slowest read endpoint in a project you know. Write down the key, the time limit and what happens on a write. Add cache-aside, then log hits and misses for an hour and compute the hit rate. Finally expire the key during a load test and watch how many requests rebuild it at once.
pitfalls: Caching before measuring: first check whether an index or a better query fixes the slow read.
Deleting the key before the transaction commits, so a concurrent read refills the old value.
Using LocMemCache in production with several workers: each process has its own private cache.
A key that omits the user or language, so one person is served another person's data.
No time limit at all, so a missed invalidation stays wrong forever.

interview.q: Walk me through cache-aside.
interview.a: The app checks the cache first. On a hit it returns the value. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a time limit and returns it. On a write it updates the database and deletes the cached key, so the next read rebuilds it. The application, not the cache, loads the data.

interview.q: How do you keep a cache from serving stale data?
interview.a: Two tools together. Expire every entry with a TTL so staleness is bounded, and delete the key when the row changes so it is usually fresh. In Django I delete inside transaction.on_commit so another request cannot refill the old value before the commit lands. Then I decide, per field, how stale is acceptable.

interview.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: When a hot key expires, many requests miss at once and all rebuild the same value against the database. Prevent it with a rebuild lock so one caller rebuilds, with random jitter on TTLs so hot keys do not expire together, or by refreshing popular keys shortly before they expire.

interview.q: Your hit rate is 60% and you expected 95%. What do you check?
interview.a: Whether the time limit is too short, whether keys are too specific (a timestamp or user id in a key that should be shared), whether the cache is too small and evicting the hot set (look at evicted keys), and whether the access pattern really has a small hot set.

interview.q: LRU or LFU?
interview.a: LRU evicts what was used longest ago and works well when recent use predicts future use. LFU evicts what is used least often and can keep a steadily popular key through a burst of one-off reads. Redis docs suggest allkeys-lru as a default when a subset of keys is hot; I would measure the hit rate before switching.

basis: Verified against the Django cache page (backends, 300 s default, LocMemCache is per-process, add and get_or_set, KEY_PREFIX and VERSION) and the Redis eviction page (policy names, approximated LRU, hit-rate formula). My own judgment, not from a source: the staleness trade-off advice, 'delete rather than overwrite', the stampede defences (jitter, early refresh) and the illustrative numbers in the animation. The Django page does not state that cache.add is atomic; on Redis and Memcached it normally is, so check your backend before relying on it as a lock.

everyday.plain: A cache keeps answers you use often close by, so you do not look them up again.
everyday.story: A tea stall owner remembers that most people ask for 'masala chai'. He keeps a flask ready instead of making each cup from scratch. It is much faster. But the flask can go cold or run out. If the recipe changes, the flask still has the old tea. A cache has the same trade: fast, but sometimes out of date.
maps: Everyone rushing when the flask is empty
words: A fast store of copies of answers.
The share of requests answered from the cache.
Time to live: how long a cached item stays before it expires.
Many requests all rebuilding the same expired item at once.

title: Load Balancing and Health Checks
tagline: One front door for many servers: how requests are shared, and what happens when a server dies.
explain: A load balancer sits in front of several identical servers and spreads incoming requests across them. Users see one address. Behind it you can add or remove machines without anyone noticing. That gives you two things at once: more capacity than one machine has, and survival when one machine fails.
## What makes it work: interchangeable servers

Any server must be able to answer any request. That means the servers are stateless: they do not keep anything a later request needs in their own memory or disk. State goes to shared places, such as the database, a cache or a session store. The Twelve-Factor guidance says this directly: processes are stateless and share nothing, and sticky sessions should never be relied upon.
## Choosing a rule

- Round robin: take turns. Cheap and fair when requests cost about the same. It is the nginx default when you configure no method.
- Least connections: send to the server with the fewest active connections. Better when some requests are much slower than others.
- IP hash: the same client address goes to the same server. This is a form of stickiness and brings the problems of stickiness with it.
- Weights: give bigger servers a larger share. With weights 3, 1, 1, three of every five requests go to the first server.
> Heavy exports land on server A three times in a row under round robin. A reaches 91% CPU while B and C idle at 30%. Switching to least connections sends new work to B and C until A catches up.
## Health checks

A balancer must stop sending traffic to a dead server. Passive checks watch real requests: nginx marks a server failed after max_fails consecutive failures and avoids it for fail_timeout, then probes it with live requests. The weakness is that real users are the probe. Active checks call a health endpoint in the background and avoid that. A good health endpoint checks that the app can reach what it needs, but not so much that one slow dependency takes every server out at once.
## The balancer is a single point of failure too

Putting one balancer in front of many servers moves the single point of failure; it does not remove it. Run the balancer redundantly. Managed cloud balancers are built across several machines. With your own, use a standby with failover (a floating address or DNS failover) and test it.
## Layer 4 and layer 7

A layer 4 balancer forwards connections by address and port without reading the request. A layer 7 balancer reads HTTP, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS and retry on another server. Most web applications use layer 7 for the routing flexibility.
## Sessions in a Django app

If sessions live in one process's memory, a user is logged out whenever the balancer sends them elsewhere. Django stores sessions in the database by default, which works across servers. cached_db adds a cache in front for speed, and the cache backend alone is only as durable as your cache. The local-memory cache is not safe across processes, so use Redis or Memcached for shared sessions.
## What to say about it

Name the rule and why it fits the workload, say how failures are detected and how fast, point out that the balancer itself needs redundancy, and state where session and other state lives. Mention deploys: with a pool you can drain one server at a time and roll out with no downtime.
keyPoints: A balancer needs interchangeable, stateless servers. Move state to a shared store.
Round robin for equal work, least connections when cost varies, weights for unequal machines.
Health checks remove failed servers. Passive checks use real requests as probes, active checks probe in the background.
The balancer is also a single point of failure: run it redundantly and test the failover.
Sticky sessions are a workaround. Shared session storage is the fix.

A health endpoint
sql.code:
from django.db import connection
from django.http import JsonResponse

def health(request):
    # cheap check: can we reach the database?
    with connection.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute('SELECT 1')
    return JsonResponse({'status': 'ok'})

django.title: settings.py: sessions that survive a balancer
django.note: With the default database sessions nothing extra is needed. Do not use LocMemCache for sessions behind a balancer: each process would have its own.

Health checks that remove a failed server
The balancer as a single point of failure

steps.title: One server, one very busy day
body: A single server handles every request. It is at 96% CPU, responses crawl, and some requests fail outright. You could buy a bigger machine, but there is a ceiling on that, and one machine is still one point of failure.
Numbers in this lesson are illustrative. They show the shape of the problem, not measurements.

callout.text: One server means no headroom for a spike and no way to deploy or reboot without downtime.

steps.title: Add a load balancer in front
body: A load balancer gives users one address and spreads their requests over several identical servers. Users never need to know how many servers there are.
Two more servers join the pool. Now capacity grows by adding machines, and one machine can fail without taking the site down.
changes: + A load balancer: one front door
+ Servers B and C behind it

steps.title: Round robin: take turns
body: The simplest rule: first request to A, second to B, third to C, then A again. It is cheap and fair as long as every request costs about the same.
nginx uses round robin when you do not configure a method, so a plain upstream block already does this.

callout.text: A pool of identical, stateless servers is what makes any simple rule work: any server can answer any request.

steps.title: Not every request costs the same
body: Round robin counts requests, not work. If a heavy request (a big report, a slow export) lands on the same server a few times in a row, that server drowns while the others idle.
The balancer is being fair about the wrong thing.

callout.text: Watch for it when request cost varies a lot: uneven CPU across identical servers is the symptom.

changes: ~ Server A at 91%, B and C near 30%

steps.title: Least connections: pick the least busy
body: Instead of taking turns, send the next request to the server with the fewest active connections. A server stuck on slow requests gets fewer new ones.
The nginx docs describe least_conn as giving fairer control of load when some requests take longer to complete.

steps.title: Weights for unequal servers
body: Servers are not always the same size. A weight tells the balancer how big a share each should get. With weights 3, 1 and 1, out of every 5 new requests three go to A, one to B and one to C.
nginx accepts weights with round robin, least connections and ip_hash.
changes: ~ A is a bigger machine and gets 3 of every 5 requests

steps.title: Health checks: stop sending to a dead server
body: Server C crashes. If the balancer keeps sending it traffic, one in three users sees an error. So the balancer watches for failures and takes the server out of rotation.
nginx does this passively: when a request to a server fails, it marks the server failed for a while and avoids it, then probes it again with live requests after the timeout.

callout.text: A passive check learns about a failure from a real request, so the first few users can still hit it. Active health checks probe in the background to avoid that.

card.title: nginx
lines: # max_fails: consecutive failures to mark it failed
# fail_timeout: how long it stays out

changes: ~ Traffic shifts to A and B, no user-visible outage

steps.title: The load balancer is now the single point of failure
body: You removed the single point of failure behind the balancer and created one in front of it. If the load balancer dies, all three healthy servers are unreachable.
Reliability is only as good as the weakest part every request must pass through.
changes: ~ 100% of requests fail although A, B and C are healthy

steps.title: Run two: a standby takes over
body: Run the balancer as a pair. The standby watches the active one and takes over its address when it fails. Managed cloud load balancers do this across several machines for you; with your own, you need a failover mechanism such as a floating IP or DNS failover.
A short blip is normal while clients reconnect.

callout.text: Wherever you put redundancy, test the failover. An untested standby is a hope, not a plan.

steps.title: Sticky sessions or shared state?
body: Alice logs in on server A. Her next request goes to B. If B does not know about her session, she is logged out. One fix is stickiness: always send her to A. The Twelve-Factor guidance says sticky sessions should never be relied upon, because a server restart loses the state.
The better fix is to keep sessions out of the server's memory: in a shared store with expiration. Any server can then answer any request.

callout.text: Django's local-memory cache is not multi-process safe, so cache-based sessions need Redis or Memcached. cached_db keeps the database as the durable copy.

pill.text: shared by A, B and C

card.title: Django settings
lines: # reads from the cache, falls back to the database

changes: ~ Any server can serve any user

steps.title: Layer 4 or layer 7?
body: A layer 4 balancer routes on addresses and ports without reading the request. A layer 7 balancer understands HTTP, so it can send /static to one pool and /api to another, terminate TLS, and make smarter decisions.
The price of layer 7 is more work per request. Most web setups use it because the routing options are worth it.

callout.text: This split into L4 and L7 is a general networking distinction. Check your own load balancer's documentation for the exact features it offers.

changes: + Static files served by their own pool

steps.title: Recap: one front door, many identical servers
body: A balancer adds capacity and removes single points of failure, if the servers are interchangeable. That needs stateless servers, health checks and a redundant balancer.
Pick the rule by the workload: round robin for equal work, least connections when cost varies, weights for unequal machines.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 2 a rule that matches the work
5 sessions live in a shared store

exercise: Run two gunicorn processes on different ports behind nginx. Log in, then use curl against each port directly to confirm the session works on both (database sessions). Kill one process during a request loop and watch nginx mark it failed. Then change to least_conn and compare CPU on both under a mixed fast and slow load.
pitfalls: Keeping sessions or uploads in one server's memory or disk, so the next request lands on a server that does not know them.
A health endpoint that checks too much, so one slow dependency removes every server at once.
One load balancer with no standby.
Round robin with very uneven request cost.
Forgetting that the client IP is now the balancer's: read the forwarded header your balancer sets.

interview.q: How does a load balancer pick a server?
interview.a: Common rules are round robin (take turns), least connections (fewest active), IP hash (same client, same server) and weighted variants. Round robin is fine when requests cost about the same. Least connections suits uneven request cost. Weights handle servers of different sizes.

interview.q: What happens when a backend server dies?
interview.a: Health checks detect it. Passive checks mark a server failed after consecutive failed requests and avoid it for a while; active checks probe a health endpoint in the background. The balancer stops sending traffic and users are served by the remaining servers.

interview.q: Is the load balancer a single point of failure?
interview.a: It can be. You run it redundantly: managed cloud balancers span several machines, and self-managed ones use an active and standby pair with a floating address or DNS failover. I would also test the failover.

interview.q: What are sticky sessions and why avoid them?
interview.a: The balancer sends a user to the same server each time so in-memory session data is found. It breaks when that server restarts or is removed and it spreads load unevenly. Keep sessions in a shared store instead, so any server can answer.

interview.q: Layer 4 versus layer 7?
interview.a: Layer 4 forwards connections by address and port without reading the request. Layer 7 reads HTTP, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS and do smarter retries, at the cost of more work per request.
