title: Consistent Hashing: Adding Servers Without Reshuffling
tagline: Decide which server holds which data, so adding a server moves only a little of it.
explain: When data is spread across many servers (a cache cluster, a sharded database, a pool of workers that each own some users) you need a rule that says which server owns which key. Every client must be able to compute the answer on its own, because asking a central directory for every lookup would make that directory the bottleneck.
## The obvious rule and why it breaks

The simplest rule is server = hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of servers. It spreads keys evenly and costs nothing to compute. The trouble starts when N changes. Going from 3 servers to 4 changes the answer for most keys: with sequential keys only 1 in 4 keeps its server, so 75% move. In a cache each moved key is a miss, and a cluster that adds one server suddenly sends most of its reads to the database.
## The ring

Consistent hashing fixes this. Treat the output range of the hash function as a circle: the largest value wraps round to the smallest. Hash each server onto the circle, and hash each key onto it too. A key belongs to the first server you meet walking clockwise from the key. Dynamo's paper describes it this way: each node gets a random position on the ring, and a key is assigned by walking the ring clockwise to the first node with a larger position.

> Servers A, B and C sit on the ring. Key k3 hashes between B and C, so walking clockwise it reaches C first: C owns k3. Add server D between B and C and only the keys between B and D move to D. Everything else is untouched.
## What moves when the cluster changes

- Adding a server takes over one arc from its clockwise neighbour. On average about 1 / N of the keys move.
- Removing a server hands its arc to the next server clockwise. Again, only that arc moves.
- Nothing else moves, so most caches stay warm and most data stays where it is.
## The weakness and its fix: virtual nodes

With one point per server, positions are random, so some servers get much bigger arcs than others, and when one fails its entire arc lands on a single neighbour. The basic scheme also ignores that machines have different capacity. Dynamo's answer is virtual nodes: each physical node is assigned several positions (tokens) on the ring. The paper lists the benefits: if a node becomes unavailable its load is dispersed across the remaining nodes, a new node takes a roughly equal share from each of the others, and the number of virtual nodes can follow each node's capacity.
## Fixed slots: a close cousin

Redis Cluster does not use a ring. It divides the key space into 16384 hash slots, computes the slot as CRC16(key) mod 16384, and assigns slots to master servers. Moving a slot moves only its keys. The idea is the same: decouple the number of servers from where a key lives, so a membership change touches a small part of the data.
## What to say about it

State the problem (mod N reshuffles almost everything), the ring, the next-clockwise rule, what moves on add and remove, the uneven-load weakness, and virtual nodes as the fix. Mention replication: a key is often stored on the next few distinct servers clockwise so that a failure loses nothing.
keyPoints: hash(key) mod N moves almost every key when N changes. Going from N to N+1 keeps only 1 key in N+1.
On a ring, a key belongs to the next server clockwise. Adding or removing a server moves only one arc, about 1 / N of the keys.
One point per server gives uneven shares. Virtual nodes (many tokens per server) even the load and spread a failure.
Redis Cluster uses 16384 fixed hash slots (CRC16(key) mod 16384) assigned to servers, a related idea.
Use it for caches, key-value stores and sharded services where membership changes must not reshuffle everything.

sql.title: A tiny hash ring
sql.code:
import bisect, hashlib

def h(s):  # position on the ring, 0 .. 2**32 - 1
    return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest()[:8], 16)

class Ring:
    def __init__(self, servers, tokens=100):
        self.points = sorted((h(f'{s}#{i}'), s) for s in servers for i in range(tokens))
        self.keys = [p for p, _ in self.points]

    def owner(self, key):
        i = bisect.bisect(self.keys, h(key)) % len(self.points)   # next clockwise, wrap round
        return self.points[i][1]

r3 = Ring(['A', 'B', 'C'])
r4 = Ring(['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'])
keys = [f'user:{i}' for i in range(10_000)]
moved = sum(r3.owner(k) != r4.owner(k) for k in keys)
print(moved / len(keys))   # roughly 0.25, not 0.75

sql.title: Modulo for comparison
sql.code:
keys = range(10_000)
moved = sum((k % 3) != (k % 4) for k in keys)
print(moved / len(keys))   # about 0.75

django.title: Where this shows up in a Django project
django.note: With a multi-server cache, the client library decides which server holds each key. Check how yours maps keys to servers before adding or removing one, because a plain modulo mapping would flush most of the cache.

scenes.title: Consistent hashing, step by step

legend.label: key moves to a new owner

learn.text: The hash ring and the next-clockwise rule
Adding and removing a server moves one arc

steps.title: The problem: hash(key) % N
body: A cache cluster has three servers. A simple way to decide which server holds a key is key mod 3. Each server gets one third of the keys, and every client can compute the answer without asking anyone.
That works until the number of servers changes. Here the dots are 12 keys and the color shows the server that owns each one.

callout.text: The goal: any client computes the owner of a key by itself, and a change in the number of servers moves as few keys as possible.

steps.title: Add one server and most keys move
body: A fourth server joins, so the rule becomes key mod 4. Compare the owner before and after: only 3 of the 12 keys keep their server. Nine have to move.
In a cache every moved key is a miss, so adding one server throws away most of the cache and sends a flood to the database. In general, going from N to N+1 servers keeps only 1 key in N+1.

callout.text: This is why plain modulo hashing is a poor fit for a cluster that grows or shrinks.

card.title: key mod 3 vs key mod 4
lines: k3 k4 k5 k6 k7 k8 k9 k10 k11 move

changes: ~ 9 of 12 keys now live on a different server

predict.question: With keys assigned by key mod N, going from 3 to 4 servers: how many of the 12 keys keep their server?
predict.why: Only keys 0, 1 and 2 have the same owner under mod 3 and mod 4. The other 9 move, which is 75%.

steps.title: Bend the hash space into a ring
body: Hash every key to a position on a circle, and hash every server to a position too. The largest hash value wraps round to the smallest, which is what makes it a ring.
The keys are the same 12 dots, but now they sit where their hash puts them. Servers sit on the ring at their own positions.

callout.text: In Dynamo's words, the output range of the hash function is treated as a fixed circular space, and each node is assigned a position on it.

changes: ~ Keys and servers are placed by their hash
- Server D is not part of the ring yet

steps.title: A key belongs to the next server clockwise
body: To find the owner of a key, start at the key and walk clockwise until you meet a server. That server owns the key. Anyone with the list of server positions gets the same answer, with no central lookup.
Follow k3 clockwise: its owner is Server B.

steps.title: Add a server: only one arc moves
body: Server D lands on the ring. Only the keys between D and the previous server, walking back, change owner: 3 of 12. Everyone else keeps their server and their cache.
Compare with modulo: 9 of 12 keys moved. On a ring, adding a server moves only about 1 / N of the keys on average.

callout.text: Incremental scalability: Dynamo lists consistent hashing as the technique that lets it add nodes one at a time.

steps.title: Remove a server: its keys go to the next one
body: Server B fails. Its keys move to whoever is next clockwise, which is A. No other key moves.
Again only 4 of 12 keys moved. But look at who received them.
changes: ~ 4 keys moved to the next server clockwise

steps.title: But random positions make uneven shares
body: Server A now holds 67% of all keys because it sits right after the gap B left. With only one point per server, the shares are lumpy and a failure dumps everything on one neighbour.
The Dynamo paper names two problems with the basic scheme: random positions give non-uniform data and load, and it ignores differences in server capacity.

callout.text: A neighbour that suddenly takes double load may fail too, and then its neighbour inherits both. This is a known risk of the basic ring.

steps.title: Virtual nodes: many points per server
body: Instead of one point, give each server several (Dynamo calls them virtual nodes, or tokens). Each colored dot on the ring is one token. A server owns every arc that ends at one of its tokens.
Now the keys are spread across all four servers, three each, and the servers can sit anywhere because the tokens do the work.

callout.text: You can give a bigger machine more tokens. The Dynamo paper says the number of virtual nodes can follow a node's capacity.

changes: + Three tokens per server on the ring

steps.title: A failure now spreads over many servers
body: Server C fails and its three tokens disappear. Each of its arcs falls to a different next token, so the load spreads across the other servers: no server holds more than 4 of 12 keys.
This is the benefit Dynamo lists for virtual nodes: when a node becomes unavailable, its load is dispersed over the remaining nodes.

steps.title: Where you will meet it
body: Dynamo (Amazon's key-value store) partitions data with consistent hashing and virtual nodes. Redis Cluster uses a related but different idea: it splits the key space into 16384 fixed hash slots, computes the slot as CRC16(key) mod 16384, and assigns slots to servers.
Moving a slot to another server moves only that slot's keys. Fixed slots make the bookkeeping explicit instead of computing a ring position.

card.title: Redis Cluster
lines: each master serves a subset of the 16384 slots

steps.title: Recap: change the cluster, move few keys
body: Modulo hashing reshuffles almost everything when N changes. A ring moves roughly 1 / N of the keys. Virtual nodes even out the shares and spread a failure's load.
Use it where a change in the number of nodes must not invalidate everything: caches, key-value stores, sharded services.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 hash keys and servers onto one ring
3 add or remove: only one arc moves

exercise: Run the Ring class above with 3 then 4 servers and 10,000 keys, with 1 token and then with 100 tokens per server. Record the fraction of keys that move and the biggest and smallest server shares. Explain the difference between 1 token and 100.
pitfalls: Using hash mod N for a cluster whose size changes.
One point per server: lumpy shares and a failure dumping onto one neighbour.
Using a hash with poor distribution so keys cluster on the ring.
Forgetting replication: the data of a failed server must also exist elsewhere, or it is lost, not merely moved.
Treating consistent hashing as a load balancer: it keeps keys sticky to servers, which also makes a very hot key hot on one server.

interview.q: Why not just use hash(key) % N?
interview.a: Because when N changes almost every key maps to a different server. Going from 3 to 4 servers keeps only 1 key in 4, so a cache loses about 75% of its entries and the database takes the load.

interview.q: Explain consistent hashing.
interview.a: Hash keys and servers onto the same circle. A key belongs to the first server clockwise from its position. When a server is added or removed only the keys on one arc change owner, about 1 / N of them, so the rest stay where they are.

interview.q: What are virtual nodes and why use them?
interview.a: Each physical server gets several positions on the ring. It evens out shares, spreads a failed server's keys over many others instead of one neighbour, and lets a bigger machine take more tokens.

interview.q: How does Redis Cluster differ?
interview.a: It does not use a ring. It splits the key space into 16384 hash slots, uses CRC16(key) mod 16384 to find a key's slot, and assigns slots to masters. Resharding moves whole slots.

interview.q: What happens to data when a server leaves?
interview.a: Its arc goes to the next server clockwise, so with no replication its data is gone unless it was copied. Stores like Dynamo replicate each key to the next few servers on the ring so the data survives.

references.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store

basis: Verified against the Dynamo paper (ring, first node clockwise, non-uniform load and capacity problems, virtual nodes and their benefits) and the Redis Cluster specification (16384 slots, CRC16 mod 16384). The 75% figure for modulo hashing is arithmetic: going from N to N+1 servers keeps 1 key in N+1. The 12-key positions in the animation are chosen for clarity and are not random measurements; the ownership shown is computed from them. My own judgment: the 'about 1 / N of keys move' summary and the interview framing.

everyday.plain: It decides which server stores which data, so that adding a server moves only a little data.
everyday.story: Imagine houses around a circular road, and a post office van delivering to the nearest depot clockwise. If a new depot opens, only the houses just before it change depot. The rest stay the same. If we had assigned houses by simple counting (house 1 to depot 1, house 2 to depot 2), adding a depot would change almost every house.
maps: Only a few houses change depot
Only a small part of the data moves
words: Turning a value into a number using a fixed rule.
A circle of positions where servers and keys are placed.
Extra positions given to one server so that load spreads evenly.

title: Message Queues and Background Workers
tagline: Reply right away, do the slow work later, and never lose a job or do it twice by mistake.
explain: A message queue sits between the part of your system that asks for work and the part that does it. The web server writes a small message, such as resize photo 42, and replies immediately. A separate worker process reads the message and does the slow work. This is how Django projects use Celery with Redis or RabbitMQ, and how cloud services use SQS.
## What a queue buys you

- Fast responses: the user does not wait for slow work.
- Absorbing spikes: a burst becomes a backlog that drains, instead of an outage.
- Independent scaling: add workers without touching the web tier.
- Isolation: a worker crash does not take the website down.
## Pull, not push

Workers pull messages when they are ready. A busy worker is never handed more than it can take, and adding workers simply adds more pullers. The queue's depth and the age of its oldest message are the two numbers to watch and alert on.
## Never lose a job: acknowledgements

When a queue hands a message to a worker it does not delete it. It waits for an acknowledgement (ack). If the worker dies first, the message comes back. RabbitMQ requeues a message that was not acknowledged when the connection closes. In Amazon SQS the message is hidden for a visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default, and becomes visible again if it has not been deleted by then.

The timing of the ack is a choice. Acknowledge before the work (Celery's default) and a crash loses the job: at most once. Acknowledge after the work (acks_late in Celery) and a crash means it runs again: at least once. RabbitMQ also warns that automatic acknowledgement is unsafe, because a crash after delivery loses the message.
## Duplicates are normal, so be idempotent

At-least-once delivery means a job can run twice. Redelivered messages carry a redelivered flag in RabbitMQ, and the docs tell consumers to be ready for them. Make each job idempotent: record that job id X is done in the same transaction as its side effect, and have a repeat do nothing. Celery's documentation says ideally task functions should be idempotent for this reason.

> Job 77 sends a receipt. The worker sends the email, crashes before acknowledging, and the job is redelivered. get_or_create on a Receipt row for order 77 finds it already exists and returns without sending again.
## Retries, poison messages and dead letters

Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter so that many failing jobs do not all retry at once. Cap the attempts. A message that keeps failing is a poison message: after the limit move it to a dead-letter queue so it stops blocking work, and alert someone to inspect it.
## Limits and backpressure
A queue can hide trouble. If workers never catch up, the backlog grows and jobs get very old. Set a limit and decide what happens beyond it: reject or slow new work, or scale workers on queue depth.
## What to say about it

Say what you would move to a queue and why, how a crash is handled (acks), how duplicates are handled (idempotency), what happens to failing jobs (retries and dead letters), and what you would monitor (depth, age, failures). Mention the trade-off: results are eventual, and there is another system to run.
keyPoints: A queue turns slow, deferrable work into background work and turns spikes into delay instead of failure.
A message is deleted only after an acknowledgement. Without one it is redelivered (RabbitMQ requeues, SQS visibility timeout defaults to 30 s).
Ack early is at most once; ack late is at least once. Most systems choose at least once and make jobs idempotent.
Cap retries, back off with jitter, and move poison messages to a dead-letter queue.
Watch backlog depth and the age of the oldest message.

sql.title: A Celery task done safely
Enqueue after the commit
sql.code:
from django.db import transaction

def place_order(data):
    with transaction.atomic():
        order = Order.objects.create(**data)
        # queue the job only once the row is visible to the worker
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(order.id))
    return order

django.title: settings.py: Celery with a broker
django.code:
CELERY_BROKER_URL = 'redis://redis.internal:6379/0'
CELERY_TASK_ACKS_LATE = True            # ack after the task runs: at least once
CELERY_TASK_REJECT_ON_WORKER_LOST = True  # redeliver if the worker process is killed
django.note: Enqueue inside transaction.on_commit: a worker that starts before the web request commits would not find the row. Keep task arguments small (ids, not objects).

scenes.title: Queue and workers, step by step

learn.text: Why slow work leaves the request
The queue as a buffer for spikes
At least once delivery and idempotent jobs

steps.title: Slow work blocks the request
body: Users upload photos. The web server resizes each one before it answers, and that takes 8 seconds. The user stares at a spinner, and the web server is tied up doing work instead of serving other pages.
All numbers in this lesson are illustrative; they show the shape of the problem.

callout.text: Anything slow that the user does not need immediately (resizing, emailing, reports, calling a third party) is a candidate to move out of the request.

steps.title: Answer right away, do the work later
body: The web server now writes a small message, resize photo 42, to a queue and replies at once. A separate worker process picks the job up and does the slow part.
The user waits 80 ms instead of 8 seconds, and the web server is free again.
changes: + A job queue between web and workers

steps.title: The queue is a buffer
body: The queue decouples the rate work arrives from the rate it is done. Producers add messages whenever they like. Workers take messages when they are ready: they pull, so a busy worker is never pushed more than it can handle.
That is the whole value: bursts are absorbed by waiting instead of by failing.

callout.text: A queue turns a spike in load into a delay. It does not make the work cheaper, it makes it patient.

steps.title: A spike becomes a backlog, not an outage
body: A viral post triggers thousands of uploads in a minute. The web server still answers in 80 ms because it only enqueues. The single worker cannot keep up, so the queue grows and photos appear a few minutes late.
Late is much better than down. And the backlog is a number you can watch.

callout.text: Queue depth and the age of the oldest message are the two metrics to alert on.

steps.title: Add workers to drain it
body: Workers are independent, so you drain the backlog by adding more. Two more workers join and the queue shrinks.
This is the scaling lever a queue gives you: web servers and workers scale separately, each to the size of its own job.

steps.title: A worker dies mid-job
body: Worker 2 crashes halfway through resizing photo 42. If the queue had already thrown the message away, that photo would be lost.
Queues avoid this by not deleting a message when it is handed out. The message is hidden for a while. If the worker never confirms, it reappears for someone else.

callout.text: RabbitMQ requeues an unacknowledged message when its connection closes. In Amazon SQS the message becomes visible again when its visibility timeout (default 30 seconds) runs out.

changes: ~ Job 42 goes back to the queue

steps.title: Acknowledge when the work is done
body: The worker sends an acknowledgement (ack) when it has finished. Only then does the queue delete the message. Ack early and a crash loses the job. Ack late and a crash means the job runs again.
Celery's default is to acknowledge just before the task runs. With acks_late the message is acknowledged after the task has run.

callout.text: Celery's docs warn that with acks_late a task may be executed multiple times if the worker crashes in the middle. Ack early: at most once. Ack late: at least once.

card.title: Celery
lines: ...   # may run twice after a crash

steps.title: At least once means sometimes twice
body: After a crash and a redelivery, job 77 (send a receipt email) runs twice and the customer gets two emails. RabbitMQ's docs say consumers must be prepared to handle redeliveries and mark them with a redelivered flag. SQS documents at-least-once delivery for the same reason.
No queue can promise exactly once for free. You get at least once, and you make the work safe to repeat.

callout.text: Redelivery is not a bug in the queue. It is the price of never losing a job.

predict.question: A worker sends the receipt email, then crashes before acknowledging the job. What happens to the job?
options: It is redelivered and may send the email again
It goes straight to the dead-letter queue
predict.why: No acknowledgement arrived, so the queue redelivers the job. The email can be sent twice, which is why jobs must be idempotent.

steps.title: Make the job safe to repeat
body: An idempotent job gives the same result however many times it runs. Give every job an id and record that it is done in the same transaction as its side effect. A repeat finds the record and does nothing.
Idempotency is the most important property of a background job.
changes: + A done-record keyed by job id

steps.title: A poison message
body: One job always crashes: its input is corrupt. The queue keeps redelivering it, a worker keeps failing on it, and it never leaves.

Give each job a retry limit. After the limit it moves to a dead-letter queue, where you can inspect it, fix the cause and replay it. SQS supports exactly this: messages that cannot be processed after several retries are captured separately instead of circulating forever.

callout.text: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Celery supports retry_backoff and retry_jitter on autoretry, and jitter is on by default.

changes: ~ Job 91 is parked, not retried forever

steps.title: Backpressure: do not let it grow forever
body: A queue hides overload, which is good until it hides it too long. If workers can never catch up, the backlog grows without limit and jobs become uselessly old.
Decide a limit. When the backlog passes it, the web layer can reject or slow new work (return a clear error), or you scale the workers out automatically on queue depth.

callout.text: Watch the age of the oldest message. A short queue of very old jobs is as bad as a long one.

changes: + A backlog limit and an alert on queue age

steps.title: Recap: patient, safe, observable
body: A queue makes slow work asynchronous, absorbs spikes as delay, and lets web and workers scale independently. To stay safe it needs acknowledgements, idempotent jobs, retry limits with a dead-letter queue, and a watched backlog.
It costs you a new moving part and eventual rather than immediate results.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 2 ack when done, not when received

exercise: Run Celery with Redis. Write a task that sleeps 5 s and sends an email, then call it from a view with .delay inside transaction.on_commit. Kill the worker mid-task with acks_late on and off and observe whether the task is re-run. Make the task idempotent and prove a double delivery does nothing.
pitfalls: Enqueueing before the transaction commits, so the worker cannot find the row.
Assuming exactly-once delivery and writing jobs that are not idempotent.
Retrying immediately and forever instead of backing off and dead-lettering.
Passing whole objects into the message instead of ids.
No alert on queue depth or age, so the backlog grows unnoticed.

interview.q: Why use a message queue?
interview.a: To take slow or unreliable work out of the request path, absorb traffic spikes as a backlog instead of an outage, and scale the workers independently of the web tier. The trade-off is eventual results and another system to operate.

interview.q: What happens if a worker crashes mid-job?
interview.a: The message was not acknowledged, so the broker redelivers it: RabbitMQ requeues it when the connection closes, and SQS makes it visible again after the visibility timeout (30 seconds by default). That is why delivery is at least once, and why jobs must be idempotent.

interview.q: What does idempotent mean for a job, and how do you do it?
interview.a: Running it twice has the same effect as once. Give each job an id, record completion in the same transaction as the side effect, and have a repeat detect the record and do nothing.

interview.q: How do you handle a message that always fails?
interview.a: Retry a limited number of times with exponential backoff and jitter, then move it to a dead-letter queue so it stops blocking the queue, and alert so someone can inspect and replay it.

interview.q: When would you not use a queue?
interview.a: When the user needs the result in the same response, when the work is fast, or when you cannot tolerate the added delay or the extra infrastructure. A queue also makes debugging harder, so I would not add one without a reason.

basis: Verified against the RabbitMQ acknowledgements page (requeue on closed connection, redelivered flag, handle redeliveries, automatic ack unsafe), the Amazon SQS visibility timeout page (30 s default, reappears if not deleted, at-least-once delivery, dead-letter queues) and the Celery tasks page (default early ack, acks_late may run twice after a crash, idempotent tasks, retry_backoff and retry_jitter). My own judgment: when to move work to a queue, the backpressure advice, which metrics to alert on, and all numbers in the animation, which are illustrative.

everyday.plain: A queue lets one part of a system hand work to another part, which does it when ready.
everyday.story: At a courier office, the clerk writes your parcel on a slip and puts it in a tray. Delivery boys pick slips from the tray one by one. The clerk can quickly serve the next customer, and if many parcels arrive, the tray just fills up for a while. If a boy drops a slip by mistake, another will pick it up.
maps: Tray filling up on a busy day
A job delivered twice, so it must be safe to repeat
words: A line of messages waiting to be handled in order.
The part that puts messages in the queue.
The part that takes messages out and handles them.
A place for messages that keep failing, so someone can look at them.

title: Rate Limiting: Token Buckets, Windows and 429
tagline: Stop one noisy user from taking the service away from everyone, without blocking normal bursts.
explain: A rate limiter caps how much a client may ask of a service in a period. Its job is fairness and survival: one buggy script, one scraper or one attacker must not be able to use up capacity that everyone shares. It also protects what is behind your API, such as the database and paid third-party calls.
## Decide who a client is

You count requests per key. The key might be an API key, a user id, an IP address, or a combination. Each has trade-offs. IP addresses are shared by whole offices and mobile networks, and a determined attacker can change them. User ids need authentication first. The HTTP specification for 429 says explicitly that it does not define how the server identifies the user or counts requests, so this is your design decision.
## Token bucket

Imagine a bucket with a capacity of 10 tokens that gains 2 tokens a second. Each request removes a token. If the bucket is empty the request is refused. An idle client's bucket fills up, so a quick burst of up to 10 requests passes, but the sustained rate cannot exceed 2 a second. Two numbers describe it: capacity (burst size) and refill rate (sustained speed). Stripe describes using the token bucket algorithm for its request limiter, one bucket per user, and reports allowing brief bursts for events like flash sales.
## Fixed windows and their seam

A fixed window counts requests in each calendar minute and resets at the boundary. It is simple, but a client can send the full allowance at the end of one minute and the full allowance at the start of the next. With a limit of 100 per minute that is 200 requests in about two seconds. A sliding window counts the last 60 seconds measured back from now and removes the seam, at the cost of storing more per client. Token buckets avoid the seam too.
## Saying no politely

The standard response is 429 Too Many Requests. The specification says it may include a Retry-After header that tells the client how long to wait. Return 429 before doing any expensive work, and document the limits so clients can adapt. In Django REST framework a throttled request raises Throttled, and Retry-After is included when the throttle class implements wait().
## Counters shared across servers

If each of three API servers has its own counter, a client gets three times the limit. Keep counters in one shared store and update them atomically. Redis INCR is an atomic increment; the Redis documentation describes a per-client counter with an expiry and shows that incrementing and setting the expiry must happen together (MULTI and EXEC, or a Lua script), because a naive read-then-write has a race.
> Limit 10 per second per IP. Key = ip:unix_second. Every request runs INCR on that key and sets a short expiry in the same transaction. If INCR returns more than 10, return 429.
## Rate limiting is one tool among several

Stripe describes four protections used together: a request rate limiter, a concurrent requests limiter, a fleet usage load shedder and a worker utilization load shedder. Per-client limits protect against one noisy client. Load shedding protects against too much total demand, which no single client caused.
## What to say about it

Name the key, the algorithm and why, where the counters live and how they are kept atomic, what the client sees (429 and Retry-After), and how you would choose the numbers: from observed legitimate usage, with headroom, and reviewed when they cause complaints.
keyPoints: Count per client key. You choose the key: API key, user, IP. Each has trade-offs.
Token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity and caps the sustained rate at its refill speed.
Fixed windows let a client double its rate across the boundary. Sliding windows and token buckets avoid that.
Answer 429 with Retry-After before doing expensive work.
Counters must be shared and atomic across servers. DRF's built-in throttles are not atomic, so treat them as approximate.

sql.title: Token bucket in plain Python
Redis counter with expiry
sql.code:
import redis, time
r = redis.Redis()

def allow(client_id, limit=10):
    key = f'rl:{client_id}:{int(time.time())}'   # one counter per client per second
    pipe = r.pipeline(transaction=True)         # MULTI / EXEC
    pipe.incr(key)
    pipe.expire(key, 10)
    count, _ = pipe.execute()
    return count <= limit

django.title: DRF throttling
django.note: Throttle state lives in Django's cache. The default local-memory cache is per process, so use a shared cache with several servers. The built-in throttles use non-atomic operations, so under heavy concurrency a few extra requests can pass.

scenes.title: Rate limiting, step by step

learn.text: Why one client must not starve the rest

steps.title: One client floods the API
body: A buggy script (or an attacker) sends 500 requests a second. The API is at 100% CPU and Alice, a normal user, gets errors and timeouts.
The numbers in this lesson are illustrative. They show the shape of the problem.

callout.text: Without limits, one noisy client can take the service away from everyone else, whether it is malicious or just a bug.

steps.title: Limit each client, not everyone together
body: A rate limiter sits in front of the API and counts requests per client. Each client gets an allowance, for example 100 requests a minute. Beyond it, requests are refused before they cost the API anything.
You choose what identifies a client: an API key, a user id or an IP address. The HTTP specification for 429 leaves that choice and the way requests are counted to the server.
changes: + A rate limiter in front of the API
~ The bot is refused, Alice is served

steps.title: Token bucket: a bucket that refills
body: Picture a bucket that holds up to 10 tokens and gains 2 tokens a second. Each request takes one token. If the bucket is empty, the request is refused. An idle client's bucket fills up to its capacity.
Stripe describes using the token bucket algorithm for its request rate limiter, with one bucket per user and a token removed on every request.

callout.text: Two numbers define it: capacity (how big a burst is allowed) and refill rate (the sustained speed).

steps.title: Bursts pass, floods do not
body: Alice clicks around quickly and sends 6 requests at once. The bucket had 10 tokens, so all 6 pass and 4 remain. A moment later it has refilled a little.
The bot drains its bucket in a few milliseconds and then runs at the refill rate: 2 requests a second, however fast it sends. The bucket allows normal bursts and caps the sustained rate.

callout.text: Stripe reports adding the ability to briefly burst above the normal cap for real-time events like flash sales.

steps.title: A fixed window has a seam
body: A simpler limiter counts requests per calendar minute and resets the counter at :00. The weakness is the seam. A client can send the whole allowance in the last second of one minute and the whole allowance again in the first second of the next.
With a limit of 100 a minute, that is 200 requests in about 2 seconds, twice the rate you meant to allow.

callout.text: Counters that reset on a clock boundary let clients double their rate across the boundary.

predict.question: A limit of 100 requests per minute is enforced by a counter that resets at each minute boundary. What is the most a client can send in 2 seconds?
predict.why: 100 in the last second of one minute and 100 in the first second of the next: 200 in about 2 seconds.

steps.title: A sliding window smooths it
body: Instead of resetting on a boundary, a sliding window counts the requests in the last 60 seconds, measured back from now. The seam disappears: 200 requests in 2 seconds is rejected after the first 100.

The cost is tracking more information per client, such as timestamps or two adjacent counters. Token buckets and sliding windows both avoid the seam, and the choice is a trade-off between precision, memory and burst behavior.

steps.title: Refuse politely: 429 and Retry-After
body: The standard answer is HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. The specification says a 429 response may include a Retry-After header telling the client how long to wait before trying again.
A clear 429 lets well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering harder. Return it before doing any expensive work.

callout.text: Retry-After is optional in the specification. In Django REST framework it is sent only when the throttle implements wait().

steps.title: Counters must be shared
body: With three API servers each keeping its own counter, a client can get three times the limit by being spread across them. The counters need to live in one shared place, and updating them must be atomic.

Redis is the usual choice. INCR is an atomic increment, and the Redis docs describe a per-client counter with an expiry. They also show a naive read-then-increment version that has a race, and fix it by incrementing and setting the expiry in a single MULTI and EXEC, or with a Lua script.

callout.text: Read-then-write is not atomic. Two requests can both read 99, both pass, and both write 100.

card.title: Redis counter, per client per second

steps.title: In Django REST framework
body: DRF ships throttle classes. AnonRateThrottle limits unauthenticated users by IP address, and UserRateThrottle limits authenticated users by user id. Rates are written as a count per period: '100/day', '1000/day'.

Throttle state lives in Django's cache. The default LocMemCache is fine for simple setups; with several servers use a shared cache. DRF also warns that its built-in throttles use non-atomic operations, so under high concurrency a few extra requests may slip through.

callout.text: Treat DRF throttling as protection against abuse and accidents, not as a precise meter. For exact limits, build on an atomic store.

steps.title: Limits are not the only protection
body: Stripe describes four kinds of protection working together. A request rate limiter caps requests per user. A concurrent requests limiter caps how many run at once. Two load shedders, a fleet usage shedder and a worker utilization shedder, drop lower-priority traffic when the system as a whole is under pressure.
Per-client limits protect against one noisy client. Load shedding protects against too much total demand, which no single client caused.

steps.title: Recap: who, how much, and what to say
body: Pick the key (who is a client), the algorithm (token bucket for bursts, sliding window for smoothness), a shared atomic store, and a clear 429 with Retry-After.
Decide limits from real usage, return headers so clients can adapt, and monitor how often you refuse, because a rising refusal rate is a signal worth reading.

exercise: Add UserRateThrottle at '5/minute' to one DRF view. Hit it with a loop of 10 requests and note the status codes and whether Retry-After is present. Then run two server processes with the default LocMemCache and show how the effective limit changes. Switch to a shared cache and repeat.
pitfalls: Counting per IP behind a proxy without reading the real client address, so every user shares the proxy's limit.
Per-process counters: with N servers the real limit is N times higher.
Read-then-write counters with a race, so bursts slip past the limit.
Fixed windows that allow double the rate across the boundary.
Returning 429 with no Retry-After or documentation, so clients retry immediately.

interview.q: Explain the token bucket algorithm.
interview.a: A bucket holds up to a fixed number of tokens and gains tokens at a steady rate. Each request takes one. If the bucket is empty the request is refused. Capacity sets the allowed burst and the refill rate sets the sustained speed.

interview.q: What is wrong with a fixed-window counter?
interview.a: The counter resets at a clock boundary, so a client can send a full allowance at the end of one window and another at the start of the next, up to double the intended rate in a short time. A sliding window or token bucket removes the seam.

interview.q: How do you rate limit across several servers?
interview.a: Keep the counters in one shared store such as Redis and update them atomically (INCR with an expiry in the same transaction or a Lua script). Per-server counters would multiply the limit by the number of servers.

interview.q: What should a rate-limited response look like?
interview.a: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header, returned before any expensive work, with the limits documented so clients can back off.

interview.q: How is load shedding different from rate limiting?
interview.a: Rate limiting caps each client. Load shedding drops lower-priority work when the whole system is overloaded, regardless of which client sent it. Stripe uses both, along with a concurrent requests limiter.

title: Timeouts, Retries and Circuit Breakers
tagline: Calls to other systems can be slow or fail. When to wait, when to try again and when to stop.
explain: In a system of several services, any call over the network can be slow, fail, or succeed after you stopped waiting. How you handle that decides whether a small problem stays small. Three tools do most of the work: timeouts, retries and circuit breakers, and each one is harmful on its own.
## Timeouts: do not wait forever

A call without a timeout can hang for as long as the other side does, and every waiting call holds a thread or connection. A slow dependency can use up all of its caller's capacity and spread the failure upstream. Set a timeout on every remote call. The AWS Builders' Library suggests choosing it from data: pick an acceptable rate of false timeouts, then use the matching latency percentile of the downstream service. Its example uses p99.9.
## Retries: only for what is safe

Many failures are brief, so trying again often succeeds. But a timeout means unknown, not failed. The work may have happened and only the reply was lost. AWS says APIs with side effects are not safe to retry unless they provide idempotency. A common approach is an idempotency key: the caller sends a unique key per logical operation, the server stores the result under it, and a repeat returns the stored result without redoing the work.
> Orders asks Inventory to reserve one item with key 7f3a. The reply is lost, Orders retries with the same key, and Inventory returns the first result. One item is reserved, not two.
## Retry storms

If every layer retries, the multiplication is brutal. Three layers that each try three times send 27 calls to the bottom service for one user request, and they arrive when that service is weakest. The AWS article makes the same point, that retries at each layer multiply. Retries help with brief failures and make sustained failures worse.
## Backoff, jitter and a budget

- Exponential backoff: wait longer after each failure, for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms.
- Jitter: add randomness to the wait so clients do not all retry at the same instant. The AWS article describes jitter as spreading retries around in time.
- One layer: for cheap operations, retry at a single point in the stack and let the lower layers fail fast.
- A budget: limit retries locally, for example with a token bucket, so they stay a small share of normal traffic.
## Circuit breakers

A circuit breaker wraps a call. While calls succeed it is closed. Failures are counted, and when they reach a threshold it trips and opens. While open, calls are rejected immediately without being made. After a reset timeout it goes half-open and lets one trial call through: success closes it, failure restarts the timeout. This protects the struggling service from more load and gives callers an instant answer to turn into a fallback. Alert when a breaker changes state.
## In a Django project

Set timeouts on every requests call (requests has no default timeout), on database connections and on gunicorn workers. For Celery tasks use autoretry_for with retry_backoff and retry_jitter, and keep tasks idempotent. If you call a payment provider, send its idempotency key and store your own record of the attempt.
## What to say about it

Walk through the failure: slow dependency, timeout, a retry that duplicated a side effect, idempotency key, the multiplication across layers, backoff with jitter, a budget, and the breaker. Say which layer owns retries and how you would see a storm starting (retry rate, latency, error rate).
keyPoints: Set a timeout on every remote call. Choose it from the downstream latency percentile you can accept as a false-timeout rate.
A timeout means unknown, not failed. Retry only idempotent operations, using an idempotency key for side effects.
Retries multiply across layers: 3 layers of 3 tries is 27 calls at the bottom.
Back off exponentially with jitter, retry in one place and keep a retry budget.
A circuit breaker (closed, open, half-open) stops calling a failing dependency and tests recovery with a trial call.

scenes.title: Timeouts and retries, step by step

learn.text: Timeouts stop a slow service spreading
Retries repeat side effects, idempotency keys fix it

steps.title: A slow dependency
body: Orders calls Inventory, and Inventory has become slow: each call takes 30 seconds because its database is struggling. Orders has no timeout, so every call waits.
Waiting requests hold threads and connections. Soon Orders has nothing left to serve anyone, and the failure spreads upstream. All numbers are illustrative.

callout.text: Without a timeout, one slow dependency can use up every thread of its caller. The problem spreads from the slow service to the ones that depend on it.

steps.title: Set a timeout
body: A timeout caps how long you wait. Orders gives Inventory 800 ms. After that it gives up, frees the thread and tells the caller promptly.

How to choose the number: the AWS Builders' Library suggests picking an acceptable rate of false timeouts, then using the matching latency percentile of the downstream service (it uses p99.9 as its example).

callout.text: Fail fast. A quick error that frees resources is better than a slow success that nobody is waiting for anymore.

steps.title: Retry the transient failure
body: Many failures are brief: a dropped packet, a server restarting. Trying again a moment later often succeeds, and the user never notices.
That is the case for retries. The next steps are about how retries go wrong.

steps.title: Retries can repeat a side effect
body: Orders asked Inventory to reserve one item. Inventory did it, but the reply was lost, so Orders timed out and retried. Now two items are reserved.
The AWS guidance is blunt: APIs with side effects are not safe to retry unless they provide idempotency.

callout.text: A timeout means unknown, not failed. The work may have happened.

steps.title: Idempotency key: safe to repeat
body: Orders sends a unique key with the request. Inventory records the result under that key. If the same key arrives again, it returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.
Now a retry is harmless, and you can retry after any timeout without fear.
changes: + An idempotency key per logical operation
~ A repeat returns the stored result

steps.title: Retry storm: layers multiply
body: Inventory is overloaded and failing. Now every layer retries: Gateway tries 3 times, each Orders call tries 3 times, each Inventory call tries 3 times against the database. One user request becomes 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls at the bottom.
The failing service gets more load exactly when it is weakest, so it cannot recover. The AWS article gives the same warning: retries at each layer multiply.

callout.text: Retries help with brief failures and hurt with sustained ones. They turn a partial failure into a total one.

hud.k: Calls per user request at the database

predict.question: The gateway, orders and inventory each try a failing call 3 times (1 attempt plus 2 retries). How many calls reach the database for one user request?
predict.why: Retries multiply across layers: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27.

steps.title: Back off, with jitter
body: Wait before retrying, and wait longer each time: for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms. That is exponential backoff.
If every client waits exactly the same time they all come back together. Jitter adds randomness to the wait to spread the retries out in time.

callout.text: The AWS article describes jitter as adding randomness to the backoff to spread retries around in time. Celery's retry_jitter does the same for task retries.

hud.k: Calls per user request at the database

steps.title: Retry in one place, with a budget
body: Do not retry at every layer. For cheap operations the AWS article recommends retrying at a single point in the stack. Lower layers fail fast and let one caller decide.
Also cap the total. A local token bucket for retries allows some while tokens remain and then drops to a low fixed rate, so retries can never exceed a fraction of normal traffic.

callout.text: A retry budget keeps retries to a small share of normal traffic, so they can help with blips and cannot swamp a struggling service.

hud.k: Calls per user request at the database

changes: ~ 27 calls per request becomes at most 3

steps.title: Circuit breaker: stop calling a failing service
body: A circuit breaker wraps a call. While calls succeed it is closed. Each failure is counted, and when failures reach a threshold the breaker trips and becomes open.
While open, calls are rejected immediately without reaching the failing service. That gives it room to recover and gives callers an instant answer instead of a slow failure.

callout.text: Martin Fowler's description: once failures reach a threshold the breaker trips, and all further calls return an error without the protected call being made at all.

hud.k: Calls per user request at the database

steps.title: Half-open: test the water
body: After a reset timeout the breaker lets one trial call through. If it succeeds the breaker closes and traffic returns. If it fails, the timeout starts again.
Fowler also recommends alerting when a breaker changes state, so people see that a dependency is in trouble.

hud.k: Calls per user request at the database

changes: ~ One trial call decides whether to close the breaker

steps.title: Recap: timeout, idempotent retry, backoff, breaker
body: Set a timeout on every remote call. Retry only what is safe to repeat, in one place, with backoff and jitter and a budget. Trip a circuit breaker when a dependency is clearly down.
Each tool alone is dangerous: timeouts without retries drop blips, retries without backoff cause storms, retries without idempotency repeat side effects.

lines: 4 backoff, jitter and a retry budget

exercise: Write a client for a flaky endpoint (return a 500 half the time and sleep 5 s sometimes). First call it with no timeout and note what happens under 20 parallel calls. Add a timeout, then backoff with jitter, then an idempotency key on a POST. Count the calls the server receives per logical request.
pitfalls: No timeout: requests defaults to waiting forever.
Retrying non-idempotent calls, so one payment or reservation happens twice.
Retrying at every layer, so failures multiply into a storm.
Backoff without jitter, so clients retry in lockstep.
A circuit breaker with no alert, so nobody knows a dependency is down.

interview.q: How do you choose a timeout?
interview.a: From the downstream service's latency distribution: decide the false-timeout rate you can tolerate and use that percentile (the AWS Builders' Library example uses p99.9), plus allowance for network latency. Then check it fits inside the caller's own deadline.

interview.q: When is it safe to retry?
interview.a: When the operation is idempotent, or you make it so with an idempotency key. A timeout means unknown, so a retried side effect can happen twice. Also only for failures that are likely transient.

interview.q: What is a retry storm?
interview.a: When failing calls are retried at several layers, the load multiplies (three layers of three tries is 27 calls at the bottom) and arrives when the service is weakest, so it cannot recover. The fixes are retrying in one layer, exponential backoff with jitter, and a retry budget.

interview.q: Why add jitter?
interview.a: Without it, clients that failed together wait the same time and retry together. Randomness spreads the retries in time, which reduces bursts.

interview.q: Explain a circuit breaker.
interview.a: A wrapper with three states. Closed: calls pass and failures are counted. Open: after a threshold, calls are rejected immediately. Half-open: after a timeout one trial call decides whether to close it. It protects a failing service and gives callers a fast failure.

everyday.story: You call a friend and he does not pick up. You wait a few rings, not forever (timeout). You try again a minute later, then after longer gaps, not every second (backoff). If his phone is clearly off, you stop calling and try later (circuit breaker). Calling non-stop would not help anyone.

title: Consensus and Leader Election (Raft)
tagline: How a group of servers agrees on one leader, and keep agreeing when some of them fail.
explain: Copying data to several servers protects you from losing it, but it raises a question: when the servers disagree, who is right? And when the leader stops responding, who takes over? Consensus algorithms answer both. Raft is the one designed to be easy to understand, and its ideas appear in most explanations of distributed systems.
## The problem: split brain

A node cannot tell the difference between a dead peer and one it simply cannot reach. If you promote a new leader whenever the old one goes silent, a network partition can leave two leaders, each accepting writes. The data then has two histories that cannot be merged safely. Split brain is worse than being down.
## The core idea: majorities

Require a majority of all the servers for every decision. With three servers a majority is two. Two disjoint groups can never both contain a majority, so there can be at most one leader and one history. The Raft website puts it this way: typical consensus algorithms make progress when any majority of servers is available, so a cluster of five can keep operating when two fail. If more fail they stop making progress, but they never return an incorrect result.
## Terms and elections

Raft divides time into terms, numbered with consecutive integers. Every term starts with an election. Servers are in one of three states: follower, candidate or leader. A leader sends heartbeats. If a follower hears nothing for its election timeout, it increments its term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself and asks the others for votes. A candidate that gets votes from a majority for the same term becomes leader. Each server votes for at most one candidate per term, so at most one can win.

Terms act as a logical clock. If a server sees a larger term it updates to it, and if a leader or candidate finds its term is out of date it steps down at once. A request with a stale term is rejected. This is how an old leader that comes back from a partition is made harmless.
## Random timeouts

If two followers time out together they can split the vote. Raft chooses election timeouts at random from a fixed interval (the paper's example is 150 to 300 ms), so usually one server times out first, wins and sends heartbeats before the others start. A split vote is resolved by waiting for a new random timeout.
## Commit

A write is committed once its log entry is stored on a majority of servers. Only then does the leader confirm it to the client. Because any future leader must have the committed entries, a confirmed write is not lost when the leader crashes. An entry that never reached a majority was never confirmed, so a returning old leader can safely discard it and copy the new leader's log.

> Three nodes, A leads in term 1. A is partitioned away. B times out, becomes a candidate in term 2, gets C's vote and leads. A write goes to B and C: committed. The partition heals, A sees term 2, steps down, drops its unconfirmed entry and catches up.
## How many nodes

Use an odd number. A cluster of N needs a majority of N/2 + 1: three nodes tolerate one failure, five tolerate two, and four tolerate only one, the same as three. More nodes means more tolerance but slower commits, because each write waits for a majority. Keep consensus groups small and use them for small critical data: configuration, leader election, locks. Raft is implemented in many systems; the Raft website lists them.
## What to say about it

Explain split brain first, then the majority rule, terms and elections, randomized timeouts, commit on a majority, and what happens when an old leader returns. Say what you would do if a majority is lost: the system pauses rather than risk wrong answers, and you must restore a majority.
keyPoints: Naive failover can create two leaders (split brain). Silence does not mean death.
Every decision needs a majority of all servers. Two groups cannot both hold one, so there is at most one leader.
Time is split into numbered terms. A higher term wins, a stale term is rejected, and an out-of-date leader steps down.
Elections use random timeouts (e.g. 150 to 300 ms) so split votes are rare.
A write is committed when stored on a majority. Use odd cluster sizes: 3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2.

sql.title: Majority and fault tolerance
sql.code:
def majority(n):          # how many nodes must agree
    return n // 2 + 1

def tolerates(n):         # how many nodes may fail
    return n - majority(n)

for n in (3, 4, 5, 7):
    print(n, majority(n), tolerates(n))
# 3 2 1
# 4 3 1   <- same tolerance as 3, higher cost
# 5 3 2
# 7 4 3

django.code:
# You rarely implement consensus. You rely on it.
# - a managed database's automatic failover
# - a coordination service holding locks or configuration
# - Kubernetes' control plane state
#
# What you do decide: how many nodes, and what your app does while

scenes.title: Leader election and consensus, step by step

learn.text: Why replicas need exactly one leader

steps.title: One server, one point of failure
body: A single database server holds the data. If it dies, writes stop and the data may be lost. You can copy the data to other servers, but then a harder question appears: who is in charge?
Raft is an algorithm for getting several servers to agree, and to keep agreeing when some of them fail.

callout.text: Consensus means multiple servers agreeing on values. Once they decide on a value, the decision is final.

steps.title: Replicas need exactly one leader
body: Add two replicas. Writes go to one leader, which copies each change to the followers. All three then hold the same log of changes, in the same order.
Raft makes sure there is at most one leader in any given term. Followers only answer requests from other servers; a leader sends regular heartbeats to keep its authority.
changes: + Nodes B and C as followers
~ A replicates every write to both

steps.title: Naive failover: two leaders
body: The network between A and the others breaks. B and C stop hearing A, so a simple script promotes B to leader. But A is still alive and still believes it is the leader.
Now two nodes accept writes. They store different values and the data has two histories. This is split brain, and it is worse than being down.

callout.text: A node cannot tell whether a silent peer is dead or just unreachable. Treating silence as death is how you get two leaders.

changes: - Network between A and B, C is cut

steps.title: A majority decides
body: The fix is simple to state: a node may act as leader only if a majority of all the servers agree. With 3 servers a majority is 2.
Two groups cannot both hold a majority, so there can be at most one leader. Isolated A has only itself (1 of 3) and cannot commit anything. B and C together have 2 of 3 and can carry on.

callout.text: Consensus algorithms make progress when any majority of servers is available. A cluster of 5 servers keeps working if 2 fail. If more fail it stops making progress, but it never returns an incorrect result.

changes: + A quorum rule: 2 of 3 must agree

steps.title: Terms: a logical clock
body: Raft divides time into numbered terms. Each term begins with an election. If a candidate wins, it leads for the rest of the term. If the vote is split, the term ends with no leader and a new term begins.
Terms act as a logical clock. Servers swap term numbers in every message. A server that sees a larger term updates to it, and a server that receives a request with a stale term rejects it.

callout.text: No clock times are compared between servers. The only question is: whose term number is higher?

steps.title: Election: timeout, then votes
body: B hears no heartbeat for its election timeout, so it assumes there is no viable leader. It increments its term to 2, becomes a candidate, votes for itself and asks the others for votes.

Each server votes for at most one candidate in a term, first come, first served. C grants its vote. B now has 2 of 3, a majority, and becomes leader. It immediately sends heartbeats so nobody else starts an election.
changes: ~ B starts term 2 and wins with 2 of 3 votes
~ At most one leader per term

steps.title: Randomised timeouts avoid split votes
body: If two followers time out at the same moment they split the vote and nobody wins. Raft prevents this by giving every server a different, random election timeout, chosen from a fixed interval such as 150 to 300 ms.
Usually only one server times out first, wins and sends heartbeats before the others even start. If a vote is split anyway, each candidate waits for a fresh random timeout and tries again.

card.title: Election timeouts (illustrative)
lines: B wins before C and A start

steps.title: A write counts when a majority has it
body: Alice writes x = 5. The leader appends it to its log and sends it to the followers. Once the entry is stored on a majority of servers it is committed and the leader replies to the app.
Committed entries are safe: any future leader must hold them, so a committed write cannot be lost or undone by a later election.

callout.text: The app is told 'done' only after a majority has the entry. That is what makes a successful write survive the leader crashing.

steps.title: The old leader returns and steps down
body: The network heals. A, still in term 1, receives a message from B with term 2. Because the term is larger, A reverts to follower at once.
A's log holds one entry that never reached a majority, so it was never confirmed to anyone. A discards it and copies B's log. All three nodes are identical again, and nothing confirmed has been lost.

callout.text: If a candidate or leader discovers its term is out of date, it immediately reverts to follower.

changes: ~ A steps down and discards its unconfirmed entry

steps.title: How many nodes?
body: The cluster can lose as many nodes as it can spare while still leaving a majority. With 3 nodes a majority is 2, so it survives 1 failure. With 5 nodes a majority is 3, so it survives 2. The Raft site gives the same example: 5 servers can keep operating if 2 fail.
Always use an odd number. A cluster of 4 needs 3 for a majority, so it also tolerates only 1 failure, the same as 3 nodes, and costs more.
changes: ~ Now 5 nodes: any 3 are a majority

predict.question: How many node failures can a 4-node cluster survive and still make progress?
predict.why: A majority of 4 is 3, so only 1 node can fail. That is the same tolerance as 3 nodes, which is why you run an odd number.

steps.title: More nodes are not faster
body: Every commit needs a majority to answer, so adding nodes means more messages and the commit waits for the slowest member of the majority. A bigger cluster tolerates more failures and is slower to write.
Most deployments choose 3 or 5 nodes. Use consensus for the small, critical data that must be right (configuration, leadership, locks), not for bulk data.

callout.text: Keep the consensus group small and use it for coordination. Store big data elsewhere.

changes: ~ A, B and C still form a majority of 5 (3 of 5)

steps.title: Recap: majorities, terms and one leader
body: Raft keeps replicas agreeing by electing one leader per term with a majority vote, committing writes only when a majority has them, and rejecting stale terms. That makes it safe through crashes and partitions: it may pause, but it does not give wrong answers.
You will rarely write it yourself. You will use systems built on it, and you should be able to say why they need an odd number of nodes and what happens when a majority is lost.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 one leader per term, by majority vote
4 higher term wins, stale leaders step down

exercise: Draw a 5-node cluster and mark which nodes are in each side of a 2 vs 3 partition. Say which side can elect a leader and commit writes and which cannot, and what the isolated side does when the partition heals. Then do the same for a 4-node cluster split 2 and 2.
pitfalls: Treating silence as death and promoting a second leader without a majority.
Running an even number of nodes: the same tolerance as one fewer, at a higher cost.
Putting bulk data through consensus: every write waits for a majority.
Ignoring what the application does during an election.
Comparing wall-clock times between servers instead of using terms.

interview.q: What is split brain and how is it prevented?
interview.a: Two parts of a cluster each believe they are the leader after a partition and accept conflicting writes. Consensus algorithms prevent it by requiring a majority of all servers for a leader and for a commit, because two disjoint groups cannot both be a majority.

interview.q: How does Raft elect a leader?
interview.a: A follower that hears no heartbeat before its election timeout increments its term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself and requests votes. Each server votes once per term. A candidate with a majority becomes leader and sends heartbeats. Random timeouts make split votes rare.

interview.q: What is a term?
interview.a: A numbered period that begins with an election and acts as a logical clock. Servers exchange terms in every message, a higher term wins, a stale term is rejected and an out-of-date leader steps down.

interview.q: When is a write considered committed?
interview.a: When its log entry is stored on a majority of servers. Only then is the client told it succeeded, which is why a confirmed write survives a leader crash.

interview.q: Why use an odd number of nodes?
interview.a: Majority is N/2 + 1. Three nodes tolerate one failure, five tolerate two, and four also tolerate only one, so the fourth node adds cost without adding tolerance.

The arithmetic for majority sizes is standard. everyday.plain: A group of servers agrees on one leader, even when some fail.
everyday.story: Five friends are planning a trip and need one person to decide the plan, but anyone could be away. They vote. Whoever gets more than half the votes becomes the leader. If the leader goes quiet, they vote again. Because a majority is needed, two leaders cannot be chosen at the same time.

The one machine that is in charge right now.
More than half of the machines, enough to make a decision.
A numbered period in which one leader is in charge.

title: Design a URL Shortener
tagline: A full example: numbers, API, short codes, storage, speed, and what happens when things fail.
explain: A URL shortener turns a long link into a short code and redirects anyone who visits the short link to the original. It is a popular interview design question because it is small enough to finish in 45 minutes and exercises most of the basics: estimation, an API, id generation, storage, caching, scaling and failure.
## Start with requirements and numbers

Ask what is in scope: creating links, redirecting, expiry, custom codes, click analytics, accounts. Then estimate load. Assume 100 million new links a month and 100 reads for each write. A month has about 2.6 million seconds, so writes are roughly 40 a second and reads roughly 4,000 a second. At about 500 bytes a record, that is 50 GB a month or around 600 GB a year. These are assumptions to state out loud and check with the interviewer, not facts. The conclusion that matters is that the system is read-heavy.
## The API

Two calls cover the core. POST /links takes a long URL and returns a short code. GET /{code} looks it up and answers with a redirect: a 3xx status and a Location header with the destination. The browser follows it at once.
## Making the short code

The code must be short, unique and cheap to produce. Random codes need a collision check. A truncated hash of the URL is deterministic but still collides after truncation. A counter written in base 62 never collides. With 62 symbols, 6 characters give 56,800,235,584 codes and 7 characters give 3,521,614,606,208, so 7 characters cover six billion links over five years with plenty of room.

Redis INCR is an atomic increment, so concurrent writers each get a different number. A single counter is enough at 40 writes a second. To avoid a call per link, each service instance can take a block of numbers and hand them out locally. Counters make codes guessable in sequence, so for private links shuffle the number or use random codes with a collision check.
## Storage

One row per link: the code as primary key, the long URL, creation time and optional expiry. The only access pattern is a lookup by code. Most stores can do that. A relational database like Postgres handles this volume with an index on the code and gives you transactions and easy analytics queries.
## The read path and the cache

Redirects dominate, and the popular links are read over and over without changing. That is the situation for cache-aside: look in the cache, on a miss read the table and store the result. If 20% of links take most of the traffic, a day's hot set at these numbers is around 35 GB, which fits in one cache instance. Aim for a hit rate above 90% and use a rebuild lock so a popular link that expires does not cause a stampede.

A 301 Moved Permanently is meant to last forever and crawlers update the URL. A 302 is temporary and crawlers do not memorise the new URL. For a shortener the trade-off is yours: a permanent redirect lets clients and caches remember it, which cuts load but hides repeat visits and stops you changing the target; a temporary redirect keeps every visit flowing through you, which allows click counting and editing or disabling links. This recommendation is design judgment, not an HTTP rule.
## Abuse, scaling and failure

Rate-limit link creation per key and check destinations against a blocklist. Scale by running several stateless service instances behind a load balancer, and the database by read replicas and later by sharding on the code with consistent hashing. If the cache fails the database takes every read, so guard it with a rebuild lock and a standby. If the counter fails only creation is affected, and id blocks hide short outages.
## What to say about it

Follow the order above and spend the most time on the part the numbers point to, the read path. Name your assumptions, say what you would measure (hit rate, redirect latency, database CPU), and be ready to change an assumption: for example, how the design changes if the ratio is 1000 to 1, or if links must be private.
keyPoints: State assumptions and do the arithmetic: 100 M links a month is about 40 writes a second; with 100 reads per write, about 4,000 redirects a second.
API: POST /links returns a code, GET /{code} answers with a 3xx redirect and a Location header.
Use an atomic counter written in base 62: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion codes. Counters are guessable, so scramble if links are private.
The system is read-heavy: put a cache-aside cache in front of the table and watch the hit rate.
301 (permanent, remembered) versus 302 (temporary, every visit counted) is a judgment about analytics and control.

class Link(models.Model):
    code = models.CharField(max_length=10, primary_key=True)
    url = models.URLField(max_length=2048)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
