scenes.title: URL shortener, step by step

learn.text: Short codes from an atomic counter

steps.title: Start with the numbers
body: Design a URL shortener: paste a long link, get a short one, and anyone who opens the short one lands on the long one. First state your assumptions, then do the arithmetic. Every figure here is an assumption you would confirm with the interviewer.
Say 100 million new links a month and 100 reads for every write. That is about 40 new links a second but about 4,000 redirects a second.

callout.text: The ratio decides the design. Reads outnumber writes 100 to 1, so the read path is what you must make cheap.

card.title: Back-of-envelope (assumptions)
lines: x 100 reads per write      ~ 4,000 reads / s
500 B x 100 M / month      ~ 50 GB / month
~ 600 GB a year, ~ 3 TB in 5 years

steps.title: The API: two calls
body: Two operations. POST /links takes a long URL and returns a short code. GET /{code} looks the code up and redirects the visitor to the long URL.
A redirect is an HTTP response with a 3xx status code and a Location header holding the URL to go to. The browser then loads that address immediately.

steps.title: Choosing the short code
body: The code must be short, unique and quick to generate. Three options. A random code: simple, but you must check for collisions. A hash of the URL, truncated: same URL gives the same code, but truncation causes collisions. A counter converted to base 62: no collisions, ever.
With 62 symbols (a-z, A-Z, 0-9), 6 characters give 62^6 = 56,800,235,584 codes and 7 characters give 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208. Six billion links over five years fits easily in 7.

callout.text: Check the arithmetic against your numbers: 100 M a month for 5 years is 6 billion codes. 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion.

predict.question: How many different codes can 7 characters from a 62-symbol alphabet make?

steps.title: A counter gives unique ids
body: Keep one counter and take the next number for every new link, then write it in base 62. Redis INCR is an atomic increment: even many clients incrementing the same key never race, so no two links get the same number.
At 40 writes a second one counter is plenty. Each app server can also fetch a block of numbers at once (say 1,000) and hand them out locally, so the counter is touched rarely.

callout.text: A plain counter makes codes guessable in order. If links are private, mix the number (a reversible shuffle) or use random codes with a collision check.

card.title: Create a link
lines: INSERT INTO links (code, url) VALUES (code, url)

changes: + A counter service for unique ids

steps.title: Store it
body: One row per link: the code (primary key), the long URL, when it was created and optionally when it expires. The access pattern is simple: look up one row by its code.
Any store that does key lookups well will do. A relational database such as Postgres handles this volume with an index on the code, and it gives you transactions and easy queries for analytics.

pill.text: lookup by code: one index hit

steps.title: The read path is 100 times busier
body: Redirects dominate: 4,000 a second against 40 writes. Every redirect reads the database, so it is busy doing the same lookups. And a link that goes viral is read thousands of times a minute but never changes.
This is the pattern from the caching lesson: a small set of rows gets most of the reads, and the answers hardly change.

steps.title: Cache the hot codes
body: Put a cache in front of the table and use cache-aside: look in the cache, on a miss read the database and store the answer. Short links almost never change, so a long time limit is fine.
If 20% of the links get most of the traffic, caching that 20% of a day's reads (about 35 GB at 500 bytes each, 4,000 reads a second) fits in a single Redis instance. Aim for a hit rate above 90%.

card.title: Why it fits (assumptions)
lines: x 500 B ~ 173 GB/day of redirect data
hot 20% ~ 35 GB: fits in one cache

changes: + A cache of hot short codes

steps.title: 301 or 302?
body: A 301 Moved Permanently means the move is meant to last forever, and crawlers update the original URL. A 302 is a temporary redirect: crawlers do not memorise the new URL.

For a shortener the choice is a trade-off. A permanent redirect invites clients and caches to remember it, which cuts load but means you may never see repeat visits, and you cannot change the target later. A temporary one keeps every visit flowing through you, so you can count them and edit or disable the link.

callout.text: The 301 versus 302 recommendation here is design judgment, not something the HTTP docs decide. Pick based on whether you need click analytics and the ability to change or remove links.

card.title: Redirect
lines: 302 Found              temporary, every visit hits you

steps.title: Abuse: spam, enumeration and cost
body: Shorteners attract abuse: people hide malicious links behind a short code, and scripts create millions of links or scan every code to find private ones.
Put a rate limit on link creation per user or key, check destination URLs against a blocklist, and make codes hard to guess if links may be private.

callout.text: See the rate limiting lesson: a token bucket per API key answers 429 with Retry-After before a single row is written.

steps.title: Scale out
body: The service keeps no state of its own, so you run several copies behind a load balancer. Reads scale with the cache and, if needed, read replicas of the database.
If one database ever becomes too small, shard it by code: hash the code to pick a shard, with consistent hashing so that adding a shard moves only a fraction of the rows.
changes: ~ Reads come from the cache, writes go to one database

steps.title: What breaks, and what then?
body: The cache fails: every redirect reads the database at once and it can fall over. Protect it with a rebuild lock, a warm standby cache and a rate limit on cache misses.
The ID counter fails: nobody can create links, but redirects keep working. Give each service a block of ids so a short counter outage goes unnoticed. Redirects never depend on the counter.
changes: ~ Redirects fall back to the database, creation is limited

steps.title: Recap: how to present it
body: Present in this order: requirements and numbers, API, code generation, data model, the read path and cache, the redirect choice, abuse, scaling and failure.
The shape to remember is a read-heavy key lookup: unique ids from an atomic counter, a cache in front of a simple table, and a stateless service you can copy.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 4 cache-aside in front of the table

exercise: Build the two endpoints in Django with SQLite and a counter table. Time 1,000 redirects with and without cache-aside using the local-memory cache, then reason about what changes with several processes. Write one paragraph that justifies 301 or 302 for a product with click analytics.
pitfalls: Skipping the numbers and designing without knowing the read to write ratio.
Truncating a hash and ignoring collisions.
Sequential codes for links that must stay private.
Using 301 when you need click analytics or the ability to edit links.
No plan for the cache failing, so the database takes every redirect.

interview.q: How would you generate the short codes?
interview.a: A counter written in base 62. Redis INCR is atomic, so concurrent creators get distinct numbers and there are no collisions. 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes. If codes must not be guessable, scramble the number or use random codes with a collision check.

interview.q: Estimate the load.
interview.a: State assumptions: 100 million new links a month is about 40 writes a second, and with 100 reads per write about 4,000 redirects a second. At around 500 bytes each, storage is about 600 GB a year. The design follows from reads being 100 times writes.

interview.q: How do you make redirects fast?
interview.a: Cache-aside in front of the links table. Hot links are read repeatedly and almost never change, so a cache with a long time limit gives a high hit rate and takes load off the database. Add a rebuild lock to avoid a stampede on an expiring popular link.

A 301 is permanent and clients may remember it, which lowers load but hides repeat visits and stops you changing the target. A 302 is temporary so every visit reaches you, which lets you count clicks and edit or disable links. For analytics I would use 302.

interview.q: What happens if the cache goes down?
interview.a: Every redirect falls through to the database, so it must be protected: a rebuild lock, a warm standby cache and a limit on misses. Redirects stay available, just slower. If only the id counter goes down, creating links is affected but redirects are not.

basis: Verified against the MDN redirections page (301 meant to last forever, crawlers update the URL, 302 temporary, Location header) and the Redis INCR page (atomic increment). The powers of 62 and the per-second arithmetic are computed from the stated assumptions. All the traffic, storage and cache-size figures are assumptions for practice, not measurements. The 301 versus 302 recommendation, the shuffle advice for private links, id blocks and the abuse controls are my own design judgment.

everyday.story: Think of a notebook where you write long addresses and give each one a short number: '1: a very long address'. When someone says 'take me to 1', you look up the notebook and send them there. The main questions are how to hand out new numbers without repeating, and how to answer quickly when millions ask.

title: How a Request Travels: Where the Time Goes
tagline: Follow one page load from the address bar to the screen, and find the slowest step.
explain: Before you can make a system faster you need to know where the time goes. The easiest way to find out is to follow one request all the way from the browser to the database and back, and write down what each step costs. This lesson does that with illustrative numbers so you can do the same arithmetic on a real system.
## The steps

- DNS: turn the name you typed into the server's real address. MDN describes DNS as special servers that match a web address like mozilla.org to the site's real IP address, a number such as 192.0.2.172. Answers are cached, so repeat visits are quicker.
- Connect: the browser and server set up a connection. HTTP messages travel over TCP/IP, and setting up a connection, with encryption for HTTPS, costs round trips before any page data moves.
- Request: the browser sends an HTTP request message, such as GET /products.
- Server work: the server builds the page. This is usually where your code and database queries run.
- Response: the server sends 200 OK and the page in small packets, and the browser assembles it.
> DNS 20 ms + connect 60 ms + request and server 55 ms + download 20 ms = 155 ms. The server and database part is 55 of those 155 ms, and it is the part you control most.
## A page is many requests

The first response is only the HTML. A page is made of code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and assets (images, fonts, video), and each one is another request. Browsers fetch several in parallel and reuse cached copies, but every request that is made pays for what it needs. Fewer, smaller and cacheable files make pages faster.
## Find the biggest piece

If a query takes 350 ms instead of 35, the total rises from 155 ms to 470 ms and nothing else changed. Improving a 20 ms step can never save you more than 20 ms. Always measure first and attack the largest part. For a Django backend that usually means the database: check the number of queries and their plans before touching anything else.
## Distance

Signals in optical fibre travel at about 200,000 km per second. For 10,000 km that is at least 50 ms each way, so a round trip is at least 100 ms before any work is done. Connection setup needs several round trips, so distance is paid several times over. You cannot speed up light, but you can bring content closer with caches and content delivery near users, and reduce the number of round trips.
## Latency, throughput and percentiles

Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests per second you handle. As a server nears its limit, requests queue and latency climbs sharply even though each request needs the same work. Averages hide this, so look at percentiles: p95 is the time that 95% of requests beat, and the slow tail is what unhappy users actually feel.
## What to say about it

In an interview, walk the path in order and put a rough number on each step, say which you would measure first (browser network tab, server timing, slow query log), and explain how you would reduce the biggest one. Distinguish latency from throughput and name a percentile rather than an average.
keyPoints: A request passes DNS, connection setup, the HTTP request, server and database work, and the download. Each costs time.
Measure where the time goes and fix the biggest step first. A slow database query can dominate everything else.
A page needs many requests. Fewer, smaller, cached files are faster.
Distance costs round trips: light in fibre needs at least about 100 ms for a 10,000 km round trip.
Latency is one request's time, throughput is requests per second. Watch p95, not only averages.

sql.title: Log slow requests in Django
sql.code:
import logging, time
log = logging.getLogger('slow')

class TimingMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        response = self.get_response(request)
        ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        if ms > 300:                                   # your threshold
            log.warning('%s %s took %.0f ms', request.method, request.path, ms)
        return response

django.title: Find the slow part: queries per request
django.code:
from django.db import connection
from django.test.utils import CaptureQueriesContext

with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as ctx:
    client.get('/products')
print(len(ctx), 'queries')
for q in ctx.captured_queries:
    print(q['time'], q['sql'][:80])
django.note: Most of the server's share of a Django page is usually database time. Count queries first (N+1 problems), then read the slowest query's plan.

scenes.title: How a request travels, step by step

learn.text: Why a connection costs round trips
The path browser, server, database and back

steps.title: Type a URL and press Enter
body: Users say the shop feels slow. Before you can make anything faster you need to know where the time goes. So follow one page load, hop by hop.

You type shop.example and press Enter. A fraction of a second later a page appears. A lot happens in between. All times in this lesson are illustrative round numbers, chosen so the arithmetic is easy to follow.

callout.text: Every web request is a conversation between machines, and every step has a cost. The costs add up.

steps.title: Find the address: DNS
body: Computers talk to numbers, not names. The browser asks the Domain Name System to turn shop.example into the server's real address. MDN describes DNS as special servers that match the address you type to the website's real IP address, a number like 192.0.2.172.
Answers are cached, so repeat visits skip most of this. Here the lookup takes 20 ms.

callout.text: Large sites run on many servers, so the address you get can depend on where you are.

steps.title: Open a connection
body: The browser and the server must set up a connection before any page data moves. MDN notes that HTTP messages and all other data travel over TCP/IP.

Setting up a connection takes round trips: messages going out and coming back. An HTTPS connection also negotiates encryption first. With a 30 ms round trip, assume this costs 60 ms before a single byte of the page is requested.

callout.text: The number of round trips is general networking knowledge, not from the MDN page. Check it for your own protocol versions. The point to keep is that setup cost is paid in round trips.

steps.title: Send the request
body: Now the browser sends an HTTP request message asking the server for a copy of the page. The first line says what it wants: a method, a path and the protocol version.
The server reads it and starts working. Whatever the server does next is the part you control most.

steps.title: The server fetches data
body: To build the page, the server asks the database for the products. It takes 20 ms to cross the network and the request, and 35 ms of that is the query itself.
Request plus server time comes to 55 ms in this example.

steps.title: The response
body: If the server accepts the request it replies with 200 OK and starts sending the page's files, split into small packets. The browser assembles them and shows the page.
Here the download takes 20 ms, so the total is 20 + 60 + 55 + 20 = 155 ms.

steps.title: A page is many requests
body: The first response is only the HTML. A real page is made of code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and assets (images, fonts, video), and each of those is another request. A product page may need dozens.
Browsers fetch several in parallel, and caches avoid repeats. But every extra request pays again for what it needs, so fewer and smaller files make a page faster.

callout.text: A cache in the browser or in front of your server turns a request into a quick local hit. See the caching lesson.

steps.title: One slow query dominates
body: The products query now scans a big table with no index and takes 350 ms instead of 35. The request and server time grows from 55 ms to 370 ms, and the total goes from 155 ms to 470 ms.
Nothing else changed. The lesson: measure where the time goes, then fix the biggest piece first. Here that is the query, not the network.

callout.text: Speeding up a step that takes 20 ms cannot save you much. Look for the step that takes most of the time.

predict.question: The database query gets 10 times slower, 35 ms to 350 ms. The total page load was 155 ms. Roughly what is it now?
predict.why: Only the query got slower: 155 - 35 + 350 = 470 ms, about 3 times. The slow step dominates, but the other steps still count.

steps.title: Distance costs time
body: The same page requested from the other side of the world. Signals in optical fibre travel at roughly 200,000 km per second, so 10,000 km takes at least 50 ms each way, and a round trip at least 100 ms, even before any server work.
Setup needs several round trips, so distance is paid several times. With a 150 ms round trip, connect alone costs about 300 ms.

callout.text: You cannot speed up light. You can bring the content closer with caches near users, or reduce the number of round trips.

steps.title: Latency is not throughput
body: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests per second the system handles. A fast road with too much traffic still has queues.

As a server gets busy, requests wait their turn and latency rises sharply even though each one takes the same work. That is why you watch percentiles such as p95 (95% of requests were faster than this), not only averages.

card.title: Two different questions
lines: latency     how long for one request?
throughput  how many requests per second?
p95         the slow tail users feel

steps.title: Recap: where the time goes
body: A page load is DNS, connection setup, the request, server work (often a database query), the download, and then many more requests. Distance multiplies the round trips.
To speed things up: measure first, fix the biggest piece, reduce round trips, cache, and move content nearer to users.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 5 watch p95, not just the average

exercise: Open your browser's network tab on a real page and write down DNS, connect, waiting (time to first byte) and download for the main document. Then repeat with curl -w. Identify the biggest piece and propose one change. Try the same page through a VPN to another continent and compare the connect time.
pitfalls: Optimizing a step that takes a tiny share of the total.
Ignoring the number of requests: one big fast request can be cheaper than thirty small ones.
Quoting averages instead of percentiles.
Forgetting distance: a server far from users pays round trips many times.
Measuring only on a fast office network.

interview.q: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
interview.a: The browser looks up the server's IP address using DNS, sets up a connection (with encryption for HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, the server does its work (often database queries) and returns a response, and the browser assembles the page and fetches the other files it needs.

interview.q: A page takes 3 seconds. How do you investigate?
interview.a: Measure each step: the browser network tab or curl timings for DNS, connect, time to first byte and download. If the wait is on the server, check the number and plan of database queries. Fix the biggest share first and measure again.

interview.q: Why is distance a problem?
interview.a: Signals travel at a finite speed, roughly 200,000 km per second in fibre, so a long round trip costs at least tens of milliseconds, and connection setup needs several round trips. Caches and content delivery near users remove some of that.

interview.q: Latency versus throughput?
interview.a: Latency is the time one request takes. Throughput is how many requests are handled per second. When a server is near capacity requests queue and latency rises even though throughput is flat.

interview.q: Why use p95 instead of the average?
interview.a: The average hides a slow tail. p95 says 95% of requests were faster than this value, so it shows what the unluckiest regular users experience.

basis: Verified against the MDN page for DNS mapping a web address to an IP address, the HTTP request over TCP/IP, the 200 OK response with the files in packets and the example content-length of 45227. My own judgment or general knowledge, not from a source I read: how many round trips connection setup and encryption need (the page I opened does not cover it, and the Cloudflare page I tried returned 403), the speed of light in fibre (about 200,000 km per second, standard physics), and the advice on percentiles. All timings in the animation are illustrative round numbers.

everyday.plain: A web page load takes many small steps, and it helps to know which one takes the longest.
everyday.story: Ordering a parcel online goes through many hands: the shop gets the order, the warehouse packs, the courier picks up, the truck travels, the delivery boy walks to your door. If delivery feels slow, you want to know which step is slow. Page loading is the same: DNS, connection, server, database, and the browser drawing the page.
words: The delay between asking and getting an answer.
One trip to the server and back.
The directory that turns a name like example.com into a computer's address.

title: Scaling Out: Vertical, Horizontal and Stateless Servers
tagline: Add more machines instead of one bigger one, and keep every server interchangeable.
explain: Every service eventually outgrows its first server. There are two ways to add capacity. Scaling up (vertical scaling) replaces the machine with a bigger one. Scaling out (horizontal scaling) adds more machines of the same kind. Most interview answers and most real systems end up using both, in that order.
## Scaling up

A bigger machine needs no change to the code, which makes it the cheapest first move. Its limits are clear. There is a biggest machine you can buy, the price rises quickly near the top, and it is still one machine: if it fails or restarts, everything is down. Treat it as a way to buy time.
## Scaling out

With several servers behind a load balancer, capacity grows in small steps and a failed server only costs you a share of capacity. The catch is that any server must be able to answer any request. If a server remembers something a later request needs, requests start failing in confusing ways.
## State is the enemy

State is anything a server keeps in its own memory or on its own disk between requests: a logged-in session, an uploaded file, a counter, a cache that others rely on. The Twelve-Factor guidance describes processes as stateless and share-nothing, says that anything that must persist belongs in a stateful backing service such as a database, and warns never to assume that something cached in memory or on disk will be there on a future request, because a different process will probably serve it.

> Alice logs in on Server 1, which keeps her session in memory. Her next request goes to Server 2 and she is logged out. Bob uploads a photo to Server 2's disk and the next request lands on Server 1 and cannot find it.
## The fixes

- Sessions: keep them in a shared store. Django stores sessions in the database by default; cached_db adds a cache for speed; cache-only sessions need a persistent cache such as Redis, and the local-memory cache is not safe across processes.
- Files: use object storage (S3 or similar) for uploads and generated files, and keep only the name in the database. In Django that is a storage backend setting.
- Sticky sessions (always send a user to the same server) are a workaround. Twelve-Factor says they should never be relied upon, because losing that server loses the state.
- Configuration and secrets come from the environment, so every server is identical.
## What you get

When servers hold nothing that cannot be rebuilt, losing one is a non-event, deploys can replace servers one at a time, and capacity can follow demand. Autoscaling adds servers when load rises and removes them when it falls. New servers take time to start, so scale early, and scale down by draining connections first.
## The next limit

Web servers scale almost without limit, but they share the database. Its CPU, connections and storage become the next ceiling. That is where caching, read replicas, queues and partitioning come in, covered in the other lessons of this track.
## What to say about it

Say that you would scale up while it is cheap, then scale out, and state the precondition: stateless servers, with sessions, files and config moved out. Name the next bottleneck before the interviewer does.
keyPoints: Scale up (bigger machine) is simple but capped and still a single point of failure. Scale out (more machines) needs interchangeable servers.
State in a server's memory or disk breaks scale out. Move sessions to a shared store, files to object storage, config to the environment.
Django sessions default to the database; cached_db adds a cache; the local-memory cache is not safe across processes.
Stateless servers make failure, deploys and autoscaling routine.
The database is usually the next bottleneck after the web tier.

sql.title: Settings for a stateless Django server
sql.code:
import os

# config from the environment, so every server is identical
SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']
DATABASES = {'default': dj_database_url.parse(os.environ['DATABASE_URL'])}

# sessions in a shared place, not in process memory
SESSION_ENGINE = 'django.contrib.sessions.backends.cached_db'
CACHES = {'default': {'BACKEND': 'django.core.cache.backends.redis.RedisCache',
                      'LOCATION': os.environ['REDIS_URL']}}

sql.title: Uploads to object storage
sql.code:
# pip install django-storages boto3
STORAGES = {
    'default': {'BACKEND': 'storages.backends.s3.S3Storage',
                'OPTIONS': {'bucket_name': os.environ['MEDIA_BUCKET']}},
    'staticfiles': {'BACKEND': 'django.contrib.staticfiles.storage.StaticFilesStorage'},
}
# FileField and ImageField now save to the bucket, so every server sees the same files

django.title: Checklist: is my Django app stateless?
django.code:
# 1. Sessions: database, cached_db, or Redis. Not locmem cache, not files on one disk.
# 2. Uploads (MEDIA_ROOT): object storage, not a local folder.
# 3. Caches other servers must see: Redis or Memcached, not LocMemCache.
# 4. Background work: Celery, not threads inside a web process.
# 5. Config and secrets: environment variables, the same on every server.
django.note: A quick test: run two copies of the app on different ports behind nginx, log in, upload a file, and click around. If anything breaks depending on which copy answers, you have state.

scenes.title: Scaling up and out, step by step

learn.text: Why state in memory breaks scale out
Surviving the loss of a server
The database as the next limit

steps.title: One server, all quiet
body: The shop starts on a single server that runs the app and talks to a database. For a few thousand users that is fine, and it is the right place to start: simple to build, simple to understand.
The numbers here are illustrative. The question is what happens as traffic grows.

steps.title: Traffic grows and the server runs out
body: Ten times as many users arrive. The server is at 96% CPU, pages are slow and some requests fail. You have to add capacity.
There are two directions: make the server bigger, or add more servers.

callout.text: One machine is also a single point of failure: when it is down, everything is down.

steps.title: Scale up: a bigger machine
body: Vertical scaling means replacing the server with a bigger one: more CPU, more memory. It is the easiest fix because nothing in the code changes.
It has limits: there is a largest machine you can buy, prices rise faster than capacity at the top end, and it is still one machine, so one failure still takes everything down.

callout.text: Scaling up is often the right first move. It buys time cheaply while you build the harder, more flexible option.

changes: ~ Server 1 replaced by a bigger machine
- Still a single point of failure

steps.title: Scale out: more servers
body: Horizontal scaling adds more machines of the same kind and puts a load balancer in front of them. Capacity grows by adding servers, and when one fails the others carry on.
This only works if any server can answer any request. That is the real work, and it is what the next steps are about.

callout.text: Scaling out turns capacity into something you can adjust in small steps. The price is that servers must be interchangeable.

steps.title: The trap: state in server memory
body: Alice logs in. Server 1 stores her login in its own memory. Her next request goes to Server 2, which has never heard of her, so she appears logged out.
Anything a server remembers in its own memory or disk is state, and state breaks the idea that any server can answer any request.

callout.text: The Twelve-Factor guidance says never to assume that anything cached in memory or on disk will be available on a future request, because that request will likely be served by a different process.

predict.question: Alice logs in on Server 1, which keeps her session in its own memory. Her next request goes to Server 2. What does she see?
predict.why: Server 2 has no record of her session, so she appears logged out. Sessions must live in a shared store.

steps.title: Stateless servers, shared state
body: Move the state out of the servers into a shared place: the database or a fast store such as Redis. Now any server can look up Alice's session, so it does not matter which one answers.

Twelve-Factor describes processes as stateless and share-nothing: data that must persist belongs in a stateful backing service, and session data suits a datastore with expiration. Django stores sessions in the database by default, and its cached_db backend adds a cache.
changes: ~ Any server can serve any user

steps.title: Files are state too
body: Bob uploads a profile photo. Django writes it to Server 2's local disk. When the next request lands on Server 1, the file is not there.
Local disk is state in the same way memory is. Uploaded files, generated reports and temporary files must live somewhere every server can reach.
changes: ~ The file exists on one server only

steps.title: Object storage for shared files
body: Store uploads in an object store (Amazon S3 or similar) that every server uses. The app keeps only the file's name in the database. In Django this is a change of storage backend, not of the code that saves files.
Now servers hold nothing that cannot be rebuilt. They are cattle, not pets: you can add, replace or remove them freely.

steps.title: Any server can die
body: Server 2 crashes. The balancer stops sending it traffic and the other servers serve everyone, because nothing important lived on Server 2. Users notice nothing.
That is the payoff for statelessness: failure of one machine is a non-event, and so are deployments, since you can replace servers one at a time.

steps.title: Autoscaling: follow the demand
body: Because servers are interchangeable, a platform can add them when load rises and remove them when it falls, instead of you keeping a fleet sized for the busiest hour.

Watch the details: new servers take time to start, so scale up early; and scaling down must drain connections first. Choose a metric that reflects real load, such as requests per server, not just CPU.

callout.text: Whether and how a platform scales automatically depends on the platform. The principle is the same: capacity follows demand.

changes: + Servers added or removed with demand

steps.title: The next bottleneck: the database
body: You can add web servers almost without limit, but they all share one database. As traffic grows, the database CPU climbs and it becomes the new ceiling.
The usual next moves are the subject of other lessons: cache reads (caching), add read replicas, move slow work to a queue, and later partition the data.

steps.title: Recap: stateless first, then scale out
body: Scale up first if it is cheap. To grow further and survive failures, scale out: interchangeable servers behind a balancer, with sessions, files and other state moved to shared services.
Each step solves one limit and reveals the next. Knowing the next limit is what makes your answer sound like experience.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 scale up while it is cheap
2 scale out behind a load balancer
5 expect the database to be next

exercise: Run two gunicorn instances behind nginx with the default round-robin. Log in with database sessions and confirm it works on both. Switch SESSION_ENGINE to the local-memory cache and watch it break. Upload a file with FileSystemStorage and show it is missing on the other instance, then fix it with a shared storage backend.
pitfalls: Keeping sessions in process memory (local-memory cache) behind a load balancer.
Saving uploads to a local folder when running more than one server.
Using sticky sessions instead of fixing the state.
Scaling the web tier and ignoring that the database is shared.
Config baked into the server image, so servers differ.

interview.q: Vertical versus horizontal scaling?
interview.a: Vertical means a bigger machine: easy, no code change, but there is a ceiling, cost rises steeply and it remains a single point of failure. Horizontal means more machines behind a load balancer: capacity grows in steps and failures are survivable, but servers must be interchangeable.

interview.q: What does stateless mean and why does it matter?
interview.a: The server keeps nothing between requests that a later request needs. State lives in shared services such as a database, cache or object storage. Then any server can answer any request, so you can add, remove or lose servers freely.

interview.q: Users get logged out randomly behind the load balancer. What is wrong?
interview.a: Probably sessions stored in one process's memory (for example the local-memory cache backend). Fix by using database, cached_db or a shared Redis session store, so any server can read the session.

interview.q: Where do uploaded files go in a scaled-out Django app?
interview.a: Into object storage such as S3 through a storage backend, with only the file name in the database, so every server sees the same files.

interview.q: What is the next bottleneck after scaling the web tier?
interview.a: The database. Move reads to a cache and replicas, move slow work to a queue, and later partition the data.

basis: Verified against the Twelve-Factor processes page (stateless, share-nothing, persistent data in a backing service, never assume memory or disk cache survives, sticky sessions should not be relied upon, session data suits a datastore with expiration) and the Django sessions page (database default, cached_db, cache backend durability, local-memory cache not multi-process safe). My own judgment: the order 'scale up while cheap, then out', the autoscaling cautions, the state checklist and the figures in the animation, which are illustrative. The django-storages setting is my recollection of that library's usage and was not verified here.

everyday.plain: To serve more people, add more machines, and make sure any machine can serve any person.
everyday.story: A restaurant that gets busy can buy one huge kitchen (vertical), or open more small kitchens (horizontal). More small kitchens work well only if any cook can make any customer's order. If your order details are kept in one cook's head, you must go back to that cook. So keep orders on a shared board instead.
maps: State kept in a shared database or cache
words: Not remembering anything between requests, so any server can handle any request.
A shared place where login information is kept.

title: Arrays and Hash Maps
tagline: Most speed-ups come from using a set or a dictionary instead of searching inside a loop.
explain: Arrays and hash tables are the two structures behind the largest share of interview problems. In Python they are the list and the dict or set. Knowing what each operation costs is what lets you say 'O(n) time, O(n) space' and mean it.
## What each one costs

- list: index O(1), append O(1) amortized, pop() from the end O(1), insert or pop at the front O(n), 'x in list' O(n).
- dict and set: add, remove and look up by key are O(1) on average. The worst case is O(n) if many keys collide, which is rare in practice.
- A dict keeps insertion order in modern Python, but it cannot answer 'the next larger key'.
## The patterns

- Seen-set: one pass, check then add. Finds duplicates, first repeated item, whether two collections overlap.
- Complement lookup (two-sum): store value to index; for each item ask whether target minus the item was already seen.
- Counting and grouping: a dict of counts, or a dict from a hashable key to a list of items (anagrams, buckets).
- Prefix sums: precompute running totals so any range sum is one subtraction. With a dict of prefix counts you can count subarrays that sum to k in one pass.
## A worked example: first non-repeating character

Brute force: for each character call s.count(ch), which scans the string, so the whole thing is O(n^2). Better: one pass to count every character with a Counter, then a second pass to return the first character whose count is 1. That is O(n) time and O(k) space, where k is the number of distinct characters. Two passes are still O(n); the constant does not matter in Big-O.
## Variations to practice

- Longest consecutive sequence: put the numbers in a set and only start counting from a number whose predecessor is not in the set, so every run is walked once: O(n).
- Product of the array except self: build prefix products and suffix products instead of dividing.
- Top-k frequent elements: a Counter, then heapq.nlargest or a bucket per count.
- Contains duplicate within distance k: keep a set or dict of the last k items.
## How to talk through it

Start with the brute force and its cost (usually two nested loops, O(n^2)). Name what you are searching for inside the loop, and replace that search with a hash lookup. Then say the new time and the extra space, and test empty input, one element and duplicates.
keyPoints: list: index and append are O(1); insert at the front and 'x in list' are O(n).
dict and set: add and lookup are O(1) on average.
A search inside a loop is the signal to use a set or dict.
Prefix sums give range sums in O(1) after an O(n) build.
Always state time and space.

sql.title: Two-sum, one pass
Group anagrams
Subarrays that sum to k (prefix sums + dict)
sql.code:
def count_subarrays(nums, k):
    seen = {0: 1}                  # prefix sum -> how many times
    total = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        count += seen.get(total - k, 0)
        seen[total] = seen.get(total, 0) + 1
    return count

assert count_subarrays([1, 1, 1], 2) == 2
assert count_subarrays([1, 2, 3], 3) == 2

exercise: Solve these without looking: contains-duplicate, two-sum, valid-anagram, group-anagrams, top-k-frequent (use a Counter), subarray-sum-equals-k. For each, write the brute force and its complexity first, then the hash-table version, then three edge-case tests (empty, one item, all equal). Aim for 25 minutes per medium problem.
pitfalls: Checking 'x in some_list' inside a loop and calling the result O(n).
Using a list or a set as a dict key (not hashable); use a tuple or a frozenset.
Inserting into the dict before checking, so an item pairs with itself.
Forgetting duplicates: [3, 3] with target 6 must work.
Giving the time but not the extra space.

interview.q: Why is a set lookup O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case?
interview.a: A set hashes the key to find a bucket, so on average one step. If many keys land in the same bucket (collisions), the lookup must compare against each of them, which is O(n) in the worst case. Good hash functions make that rare.

interview.q: How do you solve two-sum in O(n)?
interview.a: Walk the list once keeping a dict from value to index. For each item x, check whether target - x is already in the dict; if so return both indices, otherwise store x. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, instead of O(n^2) for checking every pair.

interview.q: When is a hash table the wrong tool?
interview.a: When you need order or ranges, such as the smallest key greater than x, or the sorted contents. Then sort the data (O(n log n)) or use a structure that keeps order. Also when keys are not hashable or memory is tight.

interview.q: What is a prefix sum and when does it help?
interview.a: prefix[i] is the sum of the first i items. The sum of any range a[l:r] is prefix[r] - prefix[l], in O(1) after an O(n) build. It helps when you answer many range-sum queries or count subarrays with a target sum.

scenes.title: Arrays and hash maps, step by step

steps.title: Two structures do most of the work
body: A Python list is an array: indexing is O(1), appending is amortized O(1), but inserting at the front is O(n) because every item shifts.
A dict or set is a hash table: looking up a key is O(1) on average. Most speed-ups in coding interviews come from trading a little memory for a hash table.

card.title: Costs to remember
lines: list   a[i]  O(1)   append  O(1) amortized   insert(0, x)  O(n)   x in a  O(n)
dict   d[k]  O(1) average   set add / in  O(1) average
worst case for a hash table is O(n), but it is rare

steps.title: Seen-set: find a duplicate in one pass
body: Keep a set of values you have seen. For each item, check the set first (O(1)), then add it. One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space.
The slow version checks 'x in list' inside a loop, which is O(n) per check and O(n^2) overall.

predict.question: You check 'if x in seen_list' for each of n items. What is the total time?
predict.why: Each 'in' on a list scans it, O(n), and it runs n times. With a set the check is O(1) on average and the whole loop is O(n).

steps.title: Complement lookup: two-sum
body: Find two numbers that add to a target. For each x, the number you need is target - x. Look it up in a dict of values seen so far (value to index). O(n) time and O(n) space, instead of checking every pair in O(n^2).
Check before you insert, so an element is never paired with itself.

steps.title: Counting and grouping
body: Count frequencies with a dict (or collections.Counter). Group items by a key that is the same for items that belong together: sorted letters for anagrams, a tuple for a coordinate.
The key must be hashable: use a tuple or string, never a list.

steps.title: Prefix sums: range sums in O(1)
body: Build prefix[i] = sum of the first i items once, in O(n). The sum of a[l:r] is then prefix[r] - prefix[l], in O(1).
With a dict of prefix-sum counts you can count the subarrays that add to k in one pass.

steps.title: Know when it is not enough
body: A hash table does not keep order, cannot answer 'the smallest key above x', and needs hashable keys. If you need order or ranges, sort the data or use a different structure.
Also state the cost: extra memory, and O(n) to build.

callout.text: Say both time and space. 'O(n) time, O(n) space' is a complete answer; 'O(n)' alone is not.

steps.title: Recap
body: Reach for a set or dict when you are searching inside a loop. Name what the key and the value mean before you write the code, then test empty input, one item and duplicates.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 'x in list' inside a loop? use a set
2 pair or complement? dict of seen values

everyday.plain: A list is checked item by item, but a dictionary jumps straight to what you want.
everyday.story: To find whether a name is in a class, you can read the register from the top, which is slow for a big class. Or you keep a seating chart where each name points to a seat, so you jump straight to it. A list is the register. A dictionary or set is the seating chart. Most speed-ups in interviews are just swapping the register for the chart.

A dictionary or set, about O(1)
words: A row of items stored one after another, found by position.

title: Stacks and Queues
tagline: A stack gives back the last item put in. A queue gives back the first. Each suits a different job.
explain: A stack and a queue are not new storage, they are rules about which end you may touch. The rule is the whole point: it matches the shape of a problem.
## Stack: last in, first out

Push and pop at one end. In Python a list does this in O(1) with append() and pop(). Use a stack when the most recent unresolved thing must be handled first: matching brackets, evaluating expressions, undo, depth-first search without recursion.
## Queue: first in, first out

Add at the back, remove from the front. Use collections.deque so that append and popleft are O(1); a list's pop(0) is O(n) because every item shifts. Queues drive breadth-first search and any 'process in arrival order' task.
## The monotonic stack

To find, for each item, the next larger item to its right, keep a stack of indices whose answer is still unknown. When a larger value arrives, pop and answer every smaller index. Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the total is O(n), even though a while-loop sits inside a for-loop.
## A worked example: evaluate a postfix expression

In '3 4 + 2 *' the operator comes after its operands. Scan left to right: push numbers; on an operator pop the top two, apply it (the first popped is the right-hand operand), and push the result. '3 4 +' leaves 7, then '2 *' leaves 14. The stack holds the values still waiting for an operator, which is why the same idea evaluates any expression once you convert it to postfix.
## Variations to practice

- Min-stack: keep a second stack of running minimums so get_min() is O(1).
- Daily temperatures and next greater element: a monotonic stack.
- Sliding window maximum: a monotonic deque, popping smaller values from the back.
- Largest rectangle in a histogram: a monotonic stack of increasing heights.
- Implement a queue with two stacks (amortized O(1)).
## How to talk through it
Say which end each operation uses and why that rule fits the problem. Mention the empty-stack case before it bites: popping from an empty list raises IndexError.
keyPoints: Stack = LIFO: use a list with append and pop.
Queue = FIFO: use collections.deque with append and popleft.
list.pop(0) is O(n); deque.popleft() is O(1).
Matching or nested structure is the signal for a stack.
A monotonic stack solves 'next greater element' in O(n).

sql.title: Valid brackets
Next greater element (monotonic stack)
A queue with deque
sql.code:
from collections import deque

q = deque()
q.append('a'); q.append('b')
assert q.popleft() == 'a'
assert list(q) == ['b']

exercise: Solve valid-parentheses, min-stack (a stack that also returns the minimum in O(1)), daily-temperatures (monotonic stack) and implement-queue-using-two-stacks. For each, write the invariant of the stack in one sentence before you code, and test the empty input.
pitfalls: Popping from an empty list without checking.
Using list.pop(0) as a queue.
Forgetting to check that the stack is empty at the end of bracket matching.
Saying a loop inside a loop is O(n^2) without counting how often each item is touched.

interview.q: Why use deque instead of a list for a queue?
interview.a: A list's pop(0) shifts every remaining item, so it is O(n). A deque supports append and popleft in O(1) at both ends.

interview.q: How would you check balanced brackets?
interview.a: Push each opening bracket. For a closing bracket, pop the top and check it is the matching opener (fail if the stack is empty). At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) time, O(n) space.

interview.q: A monotonic stack has a while loop inside a for loop. Why is it O(n)?
interview.a: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total number of pops across the whole run is at most n. The inner loop does not restart from scratch, it consumes items that are never seen again.

interview.q: Implement a queue with two stacks.
interview.a: Push onto an 'in' stack. To dequeue, if the 'out' stack is empty, pour everything from 'in' into 'out' (reversing order), then pop from 'out'. Each item moves at most twice, so operations are O(1) amortized.

steps.title: A stack is last in, first out
body: A stack lets you add and remove at one end only: push puts an item on top, pop takes the top item. The last item in is the first out (LIFO).
In Python a list is a stack: append() pushes and pop() pops, both O(1).

steps.title: Matching brackets
body: Scan the string. On an opening bracket, push it. On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its opening partner; pop it. At the end the stack must be empty.
The stack remembers 'what is still open, innermost last', which is exactly what nesting needs.

steps.title: Closing pops the matching opener
body: Reading ')' pops '(' (match), then ']' pops '[', then '}' pops '{'. The stack empties, so the string is valid.
'(]' fails: the top is '(' but ']' needs '['. '(' alone fails: the stack is not empty at the end.

predict.question: For the input '([)]', what does the algorithm return?
predict.why: After '(' and '[' are pushed, ')' arrives but the top is '[', which is not its partner, so the answer is False. The brackets overlap instead of nesting.

steps.title: A queue is first in, first out
body: A queue adds at the back and removes from the front, so the first item in is the first out (FIFO). Use it when order of arrival matters: tasks, breadth-first search.
Use collections.deque: append and popleft are both O(1). list.pop(0) is O(n) because every item shifts.

steps.title: A monotonic stack: next greater element
body: For 'the next larger value to the right', keep a stack of indices whose answer is still unknown, with values decreasing from bottom to top. When a bigger value arrives, pop and answer every smaller one.
Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the whole scan is O(n) even though there is a loop inside a loop.

steps.title: Recap
body: Stack for nesting and 'undo' and 'most recent unresolved'. Queue for order of arrival. Use deque, never list.pop(0). A while-loop inside a for-loop can still be O(n) if each item is handled once.

title: Linked Lists
tagline: A chain of items that each point to the next: walking it, finding loops and reversing it.
explain: A linked list stores each value in a node with a pointer to the next one. You hold the head and follow pointers. There is no index, so reaching the k-th node costs k steps, but inserting or deleting next to a node you already hold costs O(1).
## Why it is in interviews
It tests whether you can keep several pointers straight without losing part of the list. The code is short, and the bugs are in the order of assignments and in forgetting None.
## The techniques

- Traverse: cur = head; while cur: ...; cur = cur.next.
- Fast and slow pointers: slow moves one node, fast moves two. When fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle. If fast ever meets slow, there is a cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space.
- Dummy head: put a fake node before the real head so inserting or deleting at the head is not a special case.
- Reverse in place: keep prev, flip head.next to prev, then advance. Save head.next in a variable first, or you lose the rest of the list.
## Compared with a Python list

A Python list is an array: indexing is O(1) and inserting in the middle is O(n). A linked list is the reverse: no indexing, O(1) insert once you hold the node. In practice arrays are faster because of memory locality, so linked lists mainly appear in interviews and inside structures like an LRU cache.
## A worked example: merge two sorted lists

Create a dummy head and a tail pointer. While both lists have nodes, attach the smaller head to tail.next and advance that list and the tail. When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other. Return dummy.next. It takes O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space because you relink existing nodes instead of creating new ones. The dummy head means you never special-case 'which list supplies the first node'.
## Variations to practice

- Remove the n-th node from the end: two pointers n apart.
- Add two numbers stored as digit lists: walk both lists with a carry.
- Reorder list: find the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave the halves.
- Copy a list with random pointers: first map each old node to its copy in a dict, then wire the pointers.
- Doubly linked lists appear inside the LRU cache lesson.
## How to talk through it
Draw three or four nodes with arrows. Say what each pointer variable means. Walk one step by hand before coding. Then test the empty list, a single node and two nodes.
keyPoints: Each node has a value and a next pointer; you keep the head.
Access by position is O(n); insert after a held node is O(1).
Fast and slow pointers give the middle and detect cycles in O(1) space.
A dummy head removes head special cases.
When reversing, save next before overwriting it.

sql.title: Node, build, reverse
Middle and cycle with fast and slow pointers
Remove the n-th node from the end (dummy head, two pointers)
sql.code:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = Node(0, head)
    fast = slow = dummy
    for _ in range(n):
        fast = fast.next
    while fast.next:
        fast, slow = fast.next, slow.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next
    return dummy.next

assert to_list(remove_nth_from_end(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)) == [1, 2, 3, 5]
assert to_list(remove_nth_from_end(build([1]), 1)) == []

exercise: Implement from scratch: reverse a list, find the middle, detect a cycle, merge two sorted lists, remove the n-th node from the end. For each one, draw the nodes first, and test the empty list, one node and two nodes. Time yourself: 20 minutes each.
pitfalls: Overwriting head.next before saving it, which loses the rest of the list.
Calling .next on None: guard with 'while cur and cur.next'.
Forgetting to return the new head after reversing or removing the first node.
Not using a dummy head, then special-casing the first node with bugs.

interview.q: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
interview.a: Use two pointers: slow moves one step, fast moves two. If there is a cycle, fast eventually catches slow inside it, so they meet. If fast reaches None there is no cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space. A set of visited nodes also works but uses O(n) space.

interview.q: How do you find the middle node in one pass?
interview.a: Move slow by one and fast by two. When fast reaches the end (fast or fast.next is None), slow is at the middle.

interview.q: Why does reversing need a temporary variable?
interview.a: Setting head.next = prev overwrites the only pointer to the rest of the list. Save nxt = head.next first, otherwise the remaining nodes are lost.

interview.q: When would you choose a linked list over an array in practice?
interview.a: When you need O(1) insert or delete at a known node and do not need indexing, for example inside an LRU cache (a doubly linked list plus a dict). Otherwise arrays are usually faster because their memory is contiguous.

scenes.title: Linked lists, step by step

steps.title: Nodes joined by pointers
body: A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. You keep only the head, and every other node is reached by following pointers.
There is no index: reaching the k-th node takes k steps.

hud.k: Insert after a node you hold

steps.title: Traversal
body: Walk with a pointer: cur = head; while cur: ...; cur = cur.next. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
Always guard against None, or you will call .next on nothing.

steps.title: Fast and slow pointers: find the middle
body: Move slow by one node and fast by two. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. One pass, O(1) space.
For 1 to 5, fast ends at 5 while slow stands on 3.

predict.question: In a list of 5 nodes, slow moves 1 step and fast moves 2 steps per turn. Where is slow when fast reaches the last node?
predict.why: After 2 turns fast is on node 5 (1 to 3 to 5) and slow is on node 3, the middle.

steps.title: A cycle: the same two pointers catch it
body: If the last node points back to an earlier one, a plain traversal never ends. With slow and fast pointers, fast laps slow inside the cycle, so they meet if and only if a cycle exists. O(n) time, O(1) space.
The other way is a set of visited nodes: simpler, but O(n) space.

callout.text: Floyd's cycle detection: if fast ever equals slow, there is a cycle; if fast hits None, there is not.

steps.title: Insert and delete are pointer changes
body: Given a node, inserting after it is two assignments: new.next = node.next; node.next = new. Deleting the next node is node.next = node.next.next. Both are O(1), but finding the node first is O(n).
A dummy head node before the real head removes special cases when the head itself changes.

steps.title: Reverse in place
body: Walk once and flip each pointer to point backwards, keeping a 'prev' and a 'next' reference so you do not lose the rest. O(n) time and O(1) space.
After the loop prev is the new head.

title: Sorting, Searching and Intervals
tagline: Sort first, then search the sorted data fast, and know one good sorting method well.
explain: Sorting turns many O(n^2) problems into O(n log n) ones, and binary search turns a scan into O(log n). Both are common building blocks, and interviewers can ask you to write them from scratch.
## Sorting

- Comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n) in general. Merge sort is O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space and is stable. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n^2) in the worst case.
- In Python, sorted() and list.sort() use Timsort, are guaranteed stable, and take a key= function that is called once per item.
- Say the cost of a sort when you use one: it often dominates.
## Binary search

On sorted data compare with the middle and discard half: O(log n). Keep lo <= hi and use mid + 1 or mid - 1 so the range always shrinks. Python's bisect module does the search part: bisect_left gives the insertion point.

Binary search also works on an answer: if a yes/no check flips exactly once as a candidate grows, search for the boundary.
## Intervals
Sort by start, then sweep once, extending the current interval while the next start is no later than the current end. This pattern covers merging intervals, meeting-room counts and insertion.
## A worked example: can one person attend every meeting?

Given meetings as (start, end) pairs, sort them by start time, then check each meeting's start against the previous meeting's end: if a start is earlier than the previous end, they overlap and the answer is no. Sorting is O(n log n) and the check is O(n), so the whole answer is O(n log n). Without sorting you would compare every pair, which is O(n^2). The sort is what makes a single pass enough.
## Search variations to practice

- First and last position of a value: bisect_left finds the start, and bisect_right minus one finds the end.
- Search in a rotated sorted array: one half is always sorted, so check which half holds the target.
- Search a sorted 2D matrix: treat it as one flattened sorted list, or step from a corner.
- Kth largest: a heap of size k is O(n log k); sorting is O(n log n); say which you chose and why.
- Merge intervals and insert interval build directly on the sweep shown above.
## How to talk through it

Ask whether the input may be sorted or modified in place, since sorting copies or changes it. Mention the cost, then give the loop condition for binary search and test the one-element and not-found cases.

interview.q: Why can't a comparison sort beat O(n log n)?
interview.a: With n items there are n! possible orders, and each comparison gives one bit of information, so you need at least log2(n!) comparisons, which is on the order of n log n.

interview.q: Explain merge sort and its cost.
interview.a: Split the list in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. There are log n levels and each does O(n) work, so O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space. It is stable.

interview.q: What does it mean that Python's sort is stable, and why does it matter?
interview.a: Items with equal keys keep their original relative order. That lets you sort by a secondary key first and the primary key second, to get a multi-key order.

interview.q: How do you merge overlapping intervals?
interview.a: Sort by start. Walk through them keeping the last merged interval: if the next start is at most its end, extend the end with max, otherwise append a new interval. O(n log n) for the sort and O(n) for the sweep.

title: Trees and Binary Search Trees
tagline: A family-tree shape for data: how to walk it, and why its height decides the speed.
explain: A tree is a set of nodes linked from a root with no cycles. A binary tree has at most two children per node. A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller values on the left and larger on the right, so a search can discard a whole subtree at each step.
## Cost is the height

Search, insert and delete on a BST cost O(h), where h is the height. A balanced tree has h of about log n. If you insert already-sorted values into a plain BST it becomes a chain with h = n. Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) rebalance to avoid this; you rarely implement one in an interview, but you should say why they exist.
## Traversals

- Depth-first (DFS), by recursion or an explicit stack: pre-order (node, left, right), in-order (left, node, right), post-order (left, right, node). In-order on a BST gives sorted order.
- Breadth-first (BFS), by a queue: visit level by level. Use it for 'level order', minimum depth and shortest paths.
- Time is O(n) because each node is visited once. Space is O(h) for DFS recursion and O(width) for BFS.
## The recursive template

Almost every tree problem is: if the node is None return the base value; get the answer for the left and right subtrees; combine them with the node. Height, size, sum, diameter, symmetric and path-sum all fit.
## A worked example: diameter of a binary tree

The diameter is the longest path between any two nodes. For each node, the longest path through it is height(left) plus height(right). Compute heights recursively and, at each node, update a running maximum with that sum. One traversal does both jobs, so it is O(n) time and O(h) space. A common mistake is to call height() again at every node, which turns O(n) into O(n^2) on a skewed tree.
## Variations to practice

- Symmetric tree and same tree: recurse on pairs of nodes.
- Path sum: pass the remaining target down the recursion.
- Kth smallest in a BST: in-order traversal, stop after k items.
- Lowest common ancestor of a general binary tree: if the node is p or q return it; otherwise combine the answers from both sides.
- Serialize and deserialize a tree: pre-order with a marker for None.
## How to talk through it

Draw a small tree. State the base case first, then what each recursive call returns. Check the empty tree, a single node and a skewed tree. When validating a BST pass down a lower and upper bound; comparing only with the direct children misses violations deeper down.
keyPoints: BST: left smaller, right larger; search is O(height).
In-order traversal of a BST is sorted.
DFS uses recursion or a stack; BFS uses a queue.
Recursive template: base case None, solve both sides, combine.
A balanced tree has height about log n; a skewed one has height n.

interview.q: What is the time complexity of searching a BST?
interview.a: O(h), where h is the height. It is O(log n) when the tree is balanced and O(n) in the worst case, when the tree degenerates into a chain.

interview.q: What is the difference between DFS and BFS on a tree?
interview.a: DFS goes deep first and uses recursion or a stack (O(h) space). BFS goes level by level and uses a queue (O(width) space). Both visit every node once, O(n). Use BFS for shortest or level-based answers.

interview.q: How do you check that a tree is a valid BST?
interview.a: Pass a lower and upper bound down the recursion and check lo < node.val < hi at every node, narrowing the bound on each side. Or do an in-order traversal and check the values are strictly increasing.

interview.q: Why do balanced trees exist?
interview.a: A plain BST can become a chain if values are inserted in order, which makes operations O(n). AVL and red-black trees rotate on insert and delete to keep the height about log n, guaranteeing O(log n) operations.

scenes.title: Trees and BSTs, step by step

steps.title: Root, children, leaves
body: A tree is nodes with parent-to-child links and no cycles. The top node is the root, nodes with no children are leaves, and the height is the longest path from the root down.
A binary tree allows at most two children per node: left and right.

steps.title: Binary search tree: smaller left, larger right
body: In a binary search tree (BST), every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in its right subtree is larger. That ordering is what makes search fast.
Here 3, 1, 6 and 4 are all smaller than 8, and 10 and 14 are larger.

steps.title: Search follows one path
body: To find 4: at 8 go left (4 < 8), at 3 go right (4 > 3), at 6 go left (4 < 6), found. Each comparison discards a whole subtree, so the cost is the height h: O(h).
In a balanced tree h is about log n; in a lopsided one it can be n.

steps.title: Depth-first traversal: in-order
body: Depth-first search (DFS) goes all the way down before coming back. In-order visits left subtree, the node, then the right subtree. On a BST it visits values in sorted order: 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14.
Pre-order (node first) copies a tree; post-order (node last) computes things from the leaves up, like the height.

predict.question: In-order traversal of a binary search tree prints the values in which order?
predict.why: Left, node, right on a BST always yields ascending order. That is also how you check a tree is a valid BST.

steps.title: Breadth-first traversal: level order
body: Breadth-first search (BFS) visits level by level using a queue: take a node from the front, add its children to the back. Level order here is 8, then 3 and 10, then 1, 6, 14, then 4.
Use it for shortest paths and anything described by levels.

steps.title: Recursion: answer from the children
body: Most tree code has the same shape: handle the empty tree, solve the left and right subtrees, combine. Height is 1 + max(height(left), height(right)); the base case is 0 for None.
Every node is visited once, so O(n) time; the recursion stack uses O(h) space.

steps.title: Balanced or lopsided
body: If you insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order into a BST, each value goes to the right of the last one and the tree becomes a linked list: height n, search O(n).
Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) rebalance on insert so the height stays about log n. Python's standard library has no balanced tree; sorted lists with bisect, or a heap, cover most needs.

title: Graphs: BFS, DFS and Topological Order
tagline: A map of connected places: explore it wave by wave, or deep along one path.
explain: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) and edges. It is the most general structure in the track: a tree, a grid, a social network, a set of course prerequisites and a road map are all graphs. Many problems become easy once you say what the nodes and edges are.
## Representation

Use an adjacency list: a dict from each node to a list of its neighbours. It takes O(V + E) space and lets you list a node's neighbours directly. An adjacency matrix takes O(V^2) and is only worth it for dense graphs.
## BFS and DFS

- BFS uses a queue and visits nodes in rings of increasing distance. With equal edge costs the first time you reach a node is by a shortest path.
- DFS uses recursion or a stack and follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking. It suits exploring everything reachable, counting components, detecting cycles and topological order.
- Both need a visited set, and both run in O(V + E).
## Directed graphs and ordering

A topological order lists each node after all of its prerequisites. It exists exactly when the directed graph has no cycle. Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly remove nodes with no remaining prerequisites) or DFS finds it. In Python, graphlib.TopologicalSorter does it and raises CycleError if there is a cycle.
## A worked example: shortest path in a grid

Treat each open cell as a node connected to its four neighbours. Put (row, col, distance) in a queue, mark cells as seen when you enqueue them, and stop when you reach the target. Time is O(rows x cols) because each cell is processed once. Check bounds and blocked cells before enqueueing, and handle the case where the start is already the target.
## Variations to practice

- Connected components: start a DFS from every unvisited node and count the starts.
- Clone a graph: a dict from old node to its copy.
- Word ladder: the graph is implicit (words one letter apart) and BFS gives the fewest changes.
- Bipartite check: BFS with two colors; a neighbour with the same color means no.
- Weighted shortest path: Dijkstra with a heap, or union-find when the question is only 'are these connected'.
## How to talk through it

First say what the nodes and edges are, whether edges are directed or weighted, and whether cycles are possible. Choose BFS or DFS and justify it. Mark visited when you enqueue, not when you dequeue. For weighted shortest paths name Dijkstra and say it needs non-negative weights.
keyPoints: Use an adjacency list: O(V + E) space.
BFS (queue) gives fewest edges; DFS (stack or recursion) explores or orders.
Always keep a visited set; mark it when you enqueue.
Both traversals are O(V + E).
Topological order exists only for graphs without cycles.

interview.q: When do you choose BFS over DFS?
interview.a: When you need the fewest steps in an unweighted graph, because BFS reaches nodes in order of distance. DFS is better when you need to explore everything, find any path, detect cycles, or produce a topological order, and it uses less memory on wide graphs.

interview.q: What is the complexity of BFS and DFS?
interview.a: O(V + E) time with an adjacency list, since each node and each edge is processed once, and O(V) extra space for the visited set and the queue or stack.

interview.q: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
interview.a: Run a topological sort (Kahn's algorithm or DFS). If you cannot order all nodes, or the DFS reaches a node that is still on the current path, there is a cycle. Python's graphlib raises CycleError.

interview.q: How would you find the shortest path when edges have weights?
interview.a: Use Dijkstra's algorithm: BFS with a priority queue keyed by distance so far. It requires non-negative weights. For negative weights use Bellman-Ford.

steps.title: BFS: explore in rings

Mark nodes visited when you add them to the queue, not when you pop them, or the same node can be queued twice.

A B C D E F

predict.why: BFS finishes each ring before moving on: A; then B, C; then D, E; then F. The other first option is a depth-first order.

steps.title: BFS gives shortest paths when every step costs the same
body: Because BFS reaches nodes in order of distance, the first time it reaches a node is by a path with the fewest edges. Store the distance as you go.
This is the right tool for 'minimum number of moves' on a grid or word ladder. For weighted edges use Dijkstra's algorithm, which is BFS with a priority queue.

steps.title: DFS: go deep, then back up
body: Depth-first search follows one path as far as it can, then backtracks. From A it goes A, B, D, F, E, C. It uses recursion or a stack, and the same visited set.
Use it to explore everything reachable, count connected components, detect cycles and do topological sorts.

steps.title: The visited set stops infinite loops
body: An undirected edge appears in both directions, and graphs can have cycles. Without a visited set the search walks A to B to A to B forever.
Add each node to the set the first time you reach it and skip nodes already in it. Then each node and edge is processed once: O(V + E).

callout.text: A missing visited set is the most common graph bug: the program never ends or runs out of memory.

title: Heaps and Priority Queues
tagline: Always know the smallest item quickly: top few, merging lists and scheduling.
explain: A heap is a tree-shaped structure that keeps the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) item at the root. It is the standard implementation of a priority queue: a queue where the next item out is the highest priority, not the oldest.
## What it costs
Peeking at the smallest item is O(1). Push and pop are O(log n), because an item moves at most one level per swap and the tree has about log n levels. heapify builds a heap from a list in O(n).
## In Python

The heapq module is a min-heap kept in a plain list. heap[0] is the smallest. Push negated numbers for a max-heap (Python 3.14 added dedicated max-heap functions). To order tasks by priority push tuples (priority, counter, task) so equal priorities never make Python compare the tasks themselves. Note that heapq's sort is not stable.
## Where it appears

- Top-k elements and kth largest: a min-heap of size k, O(n log k) time.
- Merging k sorted lists: push the head of each list, pop the smallest, push its successor.
- Scheduling and 'next event': always take the earliest or highest-priority item.
- Dijkstra's shortest path uses a heap to take the closest unvisited node.
## A worked example: k closest points to the origin

Keep a max-heap of size k by pushing the negated squared distance. For each point push it, and if the heap holds more than k items pop the largest distance (the root, because the values are negated). What remains are the k closest points. That is O(n log k) time and O(k) space, and you never take a square root because squared distances sort the same way.
## Variations to practice

- Median of a data stream: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept within one item of each other; the median is at the top of one or both.
- Task scheduler and reorganize string: always take the most frequent remaining item.
- Connect ropes with minimum cost: repeatedly merge the two shortest.
- Merge k sorted lists and Dijkstra use the same pop-smallest-then-push-successor loop.
## How to talk through it
Say why a heap and not sorting: items keep arriving, or you only need the top k, so you avoid sorting everything. State the heap size and the cost: O(n log k).
keyPoints: Min-heap: parent <= children; heap[0] is the smallest.
Peek O(1); push and pop O(log n); heapify O(n).
heapq is a min-heap: negate values for a max-heap.
Top-k: keep a heap of size k, O(n log k).
For priorities use tuples with a tie-break counter.

sql.title: heapq basics and top-k
sql.code:
import heapq

heap = [5, 3, 8]
heapq.heapify(heap)
heapq.heappush(heap, 1)
assert heap[0] == 1 and heapq.heappop(heap) == 1

def kth_largest(nums, k):
    heap = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, x)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return heap[0]

assert kth_largest([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2) == 5

max_heap = []
for x in [4, 9, 2]:
    heapq.heappush(max_heap, -x)         # max-heap by negation
assert -heapq.heappop(max_heap) == 9

sql.title: Merge k sorted lists
sql.code:
import heapq

def merge_k(lists):
    heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        val, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(val)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out

assert merge_k([[1, 4, 5], [1, 3, 4], [2, 6]]) == [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6]

sql.title: Task queue with a tie-break counter
sql.code:
import heapq, itertools

counter = itertools.count()
queue = []
for priority, task in [(2, 'write'), (1, 'plan'), (2, 'test')]:
    heapq.heappush(queue, (priority, next(counter), task))

assert [heapq.heappop(queue)[2] for _ in range(3)] == ['plan', 'write', 'test']

pitfalls: Using a sort when only the top k are needed, or a heap of size n when a heap of size k would do.
Forgetting heapq is a min-heap and getting the smallest when the largest was needed.
Pushing tasks as tuples without a counter, so equal priorities compare the tasks and raise an error.
Modifying an item inside the heap in place: remove and re-push, or use lazy deletion.
Believing heappop returns items in insertion order.

interview.q: What are the costs of a binary heap?
interview.a: Peek the min is O(1). Push and pop are O(log n) because an item moves up or down at most the height of the tree. Building a heap from n items with heapify is O(n).

interview.q: How do you find the k largest elements of a large stream?
interview.a: Keep a min-heap of size k. For each item push it, and if the heap has more than k items pop the smallest. The heap then holds the k largest, with the k-th largest at the root. O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

interview.q: Python's heapq is a min-heap. How do you get a max-heap?
interview.a: Push negated values (or tuples with a negated key) and negate when popping. Python 3.14 also adds heappush_max, heappop_max and related functions.

interview.q: Why add a counter to heap entries?
interview.a: Tuples compare element by element. If two priorities are equal Python compares the next element, which may be a task object that cannot be ordered and raises TypeError. A unique counter makes the comparison never reach the task and keeps first-in order among equals.
