scenes.title: A min-heap, step by step

steps.title: A heap always knows its smallest item
body: A min-heap is a binary tree where every parent is no larger than its children, so the smallest item is always at the root. Python's heapq is a min-heap stored in a plain list: heap[0] is the smallest.
The children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, so no pointers are needed.

steps.title: Push: add at the end
body: heappush adds the new item at the end, which is the next free slot in the tree, then compares it with its parent. We push 0.
The tree stays complete (filled left to right), so the height stays about log n.

steps.title: Sift up: swap with a larger parent
body: 0 is smaller than its parent 2, so they swap. Repeat while the item is smaller than its parent. Each swap moves one level up, so push is O(log n).
Swapping up cannot break the other branch, because the moved parent was larger than both of its children.

predict.question: After pushing 0, how many swaps does it take to reach the root in this heap?
predict.why: 0 swaps with its parent 2, then with the root 1: two swaps. It becomes the new smallest item.

steps.title: The new minimum reaches the root
body: 0 swaps with the root 1 and stops because it has no parent. The heap is now [0, 3, 1, 7, 4, 5, 2], and heap[0] is the smallest.
The heap invariant (parent <= children) holds everywhere again.

steps.title: Pop: take the root, move the last item up
body: heappop returns the root, then moves the last item to the root to keep the tree complete. Here the last item is 2 and 0 is returned.
The root may now be too large, so it sifts down.

steps.title: Sift down: swap with the smaller child
body: Compare the root 2 with its children 3 and 1 and swap with the smaller one (1). Repeat until the item is no larger than both children. Each swap goes one level down, so pop is O(log n).
Always swap with the smaller child, or the other child would be smaller than its new parent.

steps.title: Top-k with a heap of size k
body: To keep the k largest items of a stream, hold a min-heap of size k. For each new item, push it and pop the smallest if the heap has more than k items. The root is the k-th largest so far.
Time O(n log k) and space O(k), better than sorting everything when k is small.

steps.title: Max-heap and priorities with heapq
body: heapq is a min-heap only. For a max-heap push negated values (Python 3.14 adds heappush_max and friends). For priorities, push tuples: (priority, counter, task); the counter stops Python comparing the tasks when priorities tie.
heapify turns a list into a heap in O(n).

steps.title: Recap
body: Use a heap when you repeatedly need the smallest or largest item while items keep arriving: top-k, merging sorted streams, scheduling, Dijkstra. Peek is O(1), push and pop are O(log n).

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 repeatedly the min or max? heap
2 top-k: heap of size k, O(n log k)
5 sorted order of everything? just sort

everyday.story: In a hospital emergency room, patients are not served in arrival order. The most serious is seen first, even if he came last. The nurse always knows who is most urgent without sorting everyone again. A heap does that for data: pick the smallest (or the biggest) quickly.
maps: The smallest or largest item, on top
words: A tree-like structure that always keeps the smallest (or biggest) item on top.
A queue where the most important item comes out first.
The k biggest or smallest items.
A heap with the smallest item on top.

title: Recursion and Backtracking
tagline: Solve a big problem with a smaller copy of itself, and undo choices that did not work.
explain: Recursion solves a problem by solving a smaller copy of it. Backtracking is recursion over a tree of choices: make a choice, explore what follows, then undo the choice and try the next. It generates all subsets, permutations, combinations and solutions to puzzles such as N-queens and sudoku.
## Recursion basics

Write the base case first, then the step that moves toward it. Each call waits on the call stack, so the space cost is the depth. Python limits recursion depth (sys.getrecursionlimit, commonly 1000 by default in CPython), and a too-high limit can crash the interpreter, so very deep inputs need a loop or an explicit stack.
## The backtracking template

Keep a path of choices made so far. If the path is a complete answer, record a copy of it. Otherwise loop over the remaining choices: append one, recurse, then pop it. Copy the path when recording, or every saved answer will change as the search continues.
## Pruning and cost

Return early when a branch cannot succeed, for example when a running total already exceeds the target. Pruning helps in practice, but the worst case is still exponential: 2^n subsets, n! permutations. Say that, and note that if the same smaller problem appears many times, dynamic programming is the better tool.
## A worked example: generate parentheses

To list all valid strings with n pairs: add an opening bracket while fewer than n have been used, and add a closing bracket only while closings are fewer than openings. Those two rules prune every invalid prefix, so every path reaches a valid answer. For n = 3 there are 5 strings; the counts are the Catalan numbers, so the work grows roughly like 4^n.
## Variations to practice

- N-queens: sets of used columns and diagonals make the check O(1).
- Word search in a grid: mark a cell as used, recurse, then unmark it (the undo step).
- Subsets and combinations with duplicates: sort first and skip a value equal to the previous one at the same level.
- Palindrome partitioning and letter combinations of a phone number.
- Turn a deep recursion into a loop with an explicit stack when the depth could exceed Python's limit.
## How to talk through it
State the choice at each step, what the path holds, and the stopping condition. Draw the first two levels of the decision tree. Then give the cost as the number of leaves times the work per leaf.
keyPoints: Every recursion needs a base case and progress toward it.
Depth costs stack space; Python limits recursion depth.
Backtracking: choose, explore, undo.
Record a copy of the path, not the path.
Cost is exponential (2^n subsets, n! permutations); prune early.

sql.title: Subsets
sql.code:
def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        path.append(nums[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop()
        go(i + 1)
    go(0)
    return res

assert sorted(subsets([1, 2, 3])) == sorted([[], [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3]])
assert subsets([]) == [[]]

sql.title: Permutations
Combination sum with pruning

exercise: Write subsets, permutations and combination-sum from memory, then solve: letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number, generate-parentheses, n-queens and word-search. For each, say what a choice is, what the path holds and the worst-case count of leaves before you code.
pitfalls: Appending the path itself instead of a copy.
Forgetting to undo the choice (pop) before trying the next one.
No base case, or a base case that is never reached.
Not pruning, then timing out on an input that pruning would cut by a large factor.
Ignoring duplicates in the input and returning repeated answers.

interview.q: What is backtracking?
interview.a: A depth-first search over a tree of choices. At each step you make a choice, recurse to explore what follows, then undo the choice and try the next one. It systematically generates all candidate solutions and abandons a branch as soon as it cannot lead to a valid one.

interview.q: What is the complexity of generating all subsets?
interview.a: O(2^n) subsets, and copying each takes up to O(n), so O(n * 2^n) time. The recursion depth is n, so the extra stack space is O(n) besides the output.

interview.q: Why must you copy the path when you record a result?
interview.a: The same list is modified for the rest of the search. If you store the list itself, every stored answer refers to that one list and ends up showing its final state (usually empty). A copy freezes the answer at that moment.

interview.q: What if the recursion is too deep for Python?
interview.a: Python raises RecursionError beyond its recursion limit. Convert the recursion to a loop with an explicit stack, or restructure the problem (for example iterate bottom-up in dynamic programming). Raising the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit is risky because too high a value can crash the interpreter.

scenes.title: Recursion and backtracking, step by step

steps.title: Recursion: a function that calls itself on a smaller problem
body: Every recursive function needs a base case that stops it and a step that moves toward it. Factorial: n! = n * (n-1)!, with 0! = 1.
Each call waits on the call stack until the smaller call returns, so depth costs memory: O(depth).

steps.title: The call stack has a limit
body: Python limits recursion depth (see sys.getrecursionlimit and sys.setrecursionlimit); the default in CPython is commonly 1000. Going past it raises RecursionError, so a loop or explicit stack is safer for very deep inputs.
Raising the limit too high can crash the interpreter.

callout.text: Python does not optimize tail calls, so a deep recursion that would be a loop elsewhere can fail here.

steps.title: Backtracking: build a choice, explore, undo it
body: Backtracking tries every choice for the next position, recurses, then undoes the choice (backtracks) to try the next. It is a depth-first search over a tree of decisions.
For subsets of [1, 2, 3] each element is either taken or not: 2^3 = 8 subsets.

steps.title: The template
body: Keep a path (the choices so far). At each call: if the path is complete, record a copy; otherwise loop over the remaining choices, append one, recurse, then pop it.
Record a copy of the path, not the path itself, or later changes will rewrite your answers.

card.title: Python
lines: path.append(nums[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop()   # take, explore, undo

predict.question: In backtracking, why do you append path[:] (a copy) to the results instead of path?
options: Because path keeps changing after you record it
predict.why: The same list object is modified as the search continues. Storing it directly means every saved answer ends up pointing at the one final, empty list. Copy it at the moment you record it.

pill.text: record a COPY of the path

steps.title: Prune to avoid wasted work
body: Stop a branch as soon as it cannot lead to an answer. In combination-sum, if the running total already exceeds the target, return. Sorting the candidates first lets you break out of the loop early.
Pruning does not change the worst case but often cuts the real running time a lot.

steps.title: Know the cost
body: Backtracking is exponential or factorial: subsets 2^n, permutations n!. It is fine for n around 10 to 20, and not beyond.
If a smaller problem repeats, store its answer instead: that is dynamic programming (next lesson).

steps.title: Recap
body: Recursion: base case plus a smaller problem. Backtracking: choose, explore, undo, record a copy. Prune early and state the exponential cost honestly.

4 record a copy of the path

title: Dynamic Programming
tagline: Remember the answer to each small part, so you never work it out twice.
explain: Dynamic programming (DP) speeds up recursive problems whose subproblems repeat. Instead of recomputing an answer every time it is needed, you compute it once and reuse it. It is often the hardest topic in an algorithm round, but it follows a fixed recipe.
## Two ways to write it

- Top-down (memoization): write the plain recursion, then cache results in a dict. In Python, functools.cache does this; the arguments must be hashable.
- Bottom-up (tabulation): fill a table from the smallest subproblem to the answer, in the order the dependencies allow. It avoids recursion depth limits and lets you keep only the last row or two when that is enough.
## The recipe

Define the state in one sentence (dp[i] means ...). Write the recurrence that builds a state from smaller ones. Write the base cases. Decide the fill order. The time is the number of states times the work per state.
## Common families

- 1-D: climbing stairs, house robber, longest increasing subsequence.
- Coins and knapsack: fewest coins for an amount, subset sum.
- Two sequences: longest common subsequence, edit distance.
- Grids: unique paths, minimum path sum.
## Greedy versus DP

A greedy algorithm takes the best local choice. It is faster but only correct when that choice is provably safe. With coins 1, 3 and 4 and amount 6, greedy gives 3 coins but the best is 2. If you cannot prove greedy works, use DP.
## A worked example: house robber

You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Let dp[i] be the most money from the first i houses. Either skip house i (dp[i-1]) or rob it and add dp[i-2]. So dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i-1]). Each state depends only on the previous two, so two variables replace the table: O(n) time, O(1) space. For [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] the best is 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.
## Variations to practice

- Longest increasing subsequence: O(n^2) with a table, or O(n log n) with bisect on a list of tails.
- 0/1 knapsack and partition equal subset sum.
- Edit distance and unique paths: two-dimensional tables.
- Word break: dp[i] is true if some earlier break point j has dp[j] true and s[j:i] is a word.
- Whenever the table has one row that depends only on the previous row, keep just that row.
## How to talk through it
Start with the brute-force recursion and its exponential cost. Point out the repeated subproblems, then name the state and the recurrence. Only then write the code, and finish with time and space.
keyPoints: DP applies when subproblems overlap: compute each once.
Define the state in one sentence, then recurrence and base cases.
Top-down uses a cache (functools.cache); bottom-up fills a table.
Time = number of states x work per state.
Greedy is only correct if the local choice is provably safe.

interview.q: What is dynamic programming?
interview.a: A technique for problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure: solve each subproblem once, store the answer and reuse it. It turns exponential recursion into polynomial time.

interview.q: Memoization versus tabulation?
interview.a: Memoization is top-down: write the recursion and cache results, solving only the subproblems you need. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table from the smallest case in dependency order. Tabulation avoids recursion limits and makes it easy to save space; memoization is often quicker to write.

interview.q: Why does greedy fail for coin change with coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6?
interview.a: Greedy takes the largest coin that fits: 4, then 1, then 1, using 3 coins. The best is 3 + 3, using 2. The locally best choice (the biggest coin) is not part of an optimal solution, so you must compare options with DP.

interview.q: How do you get the time complexity of a DP solution?
interview.a: Multiply the number of distinct states by the work done per state. For coin change that is (amount + 1) states times the number of coins. For LCS it is m * n states times O(1).

scenes.title: Dynamic programming, step by step

steps.title: The same subproblem, solved again and again
body: Naive Fibonacci calls itself twice per call. fib(5) computes fib(3) twice and fib(2) three times, and the number of calls grows exponentially, O(2^n).
Dynamic programming (DP) is for problems where smaller subproblems overlap: solve each one once and reuse the answer.

predict.question: In naive recursive fib(5), how many times is fib(2) computed?
predict.why: fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3). fib(4) calls fib(3) and fib(2); each fib(3) calls fib(2) again. In total fib(2) is computed 3 times; for larger n the repeats explode.

steps.title: Memoization: remember the answers
body: Store each result in a dict the first time you compute it, and look it up next time. Each subproblem is now solved once: O(n) time for Fibonacci.
In Python, functools.cache (or lru_cache) does it with one decorator; the arguments must be hashable.

steps.title: Tabulation: fill a table from the bottom
body: Instead of recursing, build the answers from the smallest case up in a loop. dp[i] depends only on earlier entries, so you fill the table in order. No recursion, no depth limit.
If only the last few entries matter, keep just those and save space.

card.title: Python
lines: def climb(n):             # ways to climb n stairs, 1 or 2 steps

steps.title: Define the state and the recurrence
body: Every DP has three parts: the state (what dp[i] means), the recurrence (how it follows from smaller states) and the base cases. Writing the meaning of dp[i] in a sentence is the most important step.
Coin change: dp[a] is the fewest coins that make amount a. dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c, with dp[0] = 0.

steps.title: Greedy is not always right
body: For amount 6 with coins 1, 3, 4, taking the largest coin first gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 uses only 2. When local best choices can be wrong, you need DP to compare the options.
Use greedy only when you can prove the local choice is safe.

steps.title: Two sequences: a grid of subproblems
body: Longest common subsequence of 'abcde' and 'ace': let dp[i][j] be the answer for the first i and j characters. If the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, otherwise the larger of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. The answer here is 3 ('ace').
The table has m * n cells and each takes O(1): O(m * n) time and space.

steps.title: How to recognize DP
body: Signals: you are asked for a count, a minimum, a maximum or whether something is possible, and the choice at each step depends on earlier choices. Try brute-force recursion first, spot repeated subproblems, then add a cache.
Typical families: 1-D (stairs, house robber), coins and knapsack, two strings (LCS, edit distance), grids (unique paths).

body: DP = overlapping subproblems solved once. State, recurrence, base cases. Memoize or tabulate. State time as (number of states) times (work per state) and the space you used.

title: Object-Oriented Design and SOLID
tagline: Organize code so one change does not break many things: one job per class.
explain: Low-level design (LLD), also called object-oriented design, is the part of an interview where you turn a small problem statement (a parking lot, a library, a vending machine) into classes, relationships and methods that are easy to change. The ideas below are the vocabulary you use to explain your choices.
## The four ideas

- Encapsulation: keep data private and expose behavior through methods, so the class can change inside.
- Abstraction: callers depend on what something does (an interface), not how.
- Polymorphism: different classes answer the same method call in their own way.
- Inheritance versus composition: 'is a' versus 'has a'. Prefer composition unless the base class is stable and the relationship is a true 'is a'.
## SOLID

- Single responsibility: there should be one reason for a class to change.
- Open-closed: open for extension, closed for modification: add behavior by adding code.
- Liskov substitution: instances of a subclass must be usable wherever the base class is expected, without the caller noticing.
- Interface segregation: clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.
- Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions.
## In Python

Use abc.ABC with @abstractmethod, or typing.Protocol for structural interfaces. Python is duck-typed, so an interface is a convention more than a requirement; the value is in the design, not the syntax. Use @dataclass for plain data holders.
## Smells that tell you to redesign

- A long if/elif or switch on a type or a string (use polymorphism or a strategy).
- A class whose methods do not share any data (it has several responsibilities).
- A subclass that overrides a method only to raise 'not supported' (the inheritance is wrong).
- A constructor that creates its own collaborators (inject them).
- A test that needs many mocks to run one method (too many dependencies).
## Python notes

Python has no private keyword: a leading underscore means 'internal, do not touch', and @property lets you add validation later without changing callers. @dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and equality for plain data classes. Protocols (typing.Protocol) describe an interface by shape, so a class does not have to inherit from anything to fit it.
## How to talk through it

Name the principle when you apply it: 'I put notification behind an interface so a new channel does not edit OrderService'. Avoid over-engineering: add an interface when there is a second implementation or a clear need, not for every class.
keyPoints: Single responsibility: one reason to change.
Open-closed: add a class instead of editing a working one.
Liskov: a subclass must work wherever the base class is expected.
Depend on abstractions and inject them through the constructor.
Prefer composition to inheritance.

exercise: Take this prompt: 'design a notification system with email, SMS and push, where users can turn channels on or off'. Draw the classes, say which SOLID principle each boundary protects, then write the code with a fake notifier and two tests. Finally add a fourth channel and count how many existing classes you had to edit; the goal is zero.
pitfalls: Creating the concrete dependency inside the class (EmailNotifier() inside OrderService), which makes it hard to swap or test.
Using inheritance for code reuse when the relationship is not 'is a'.
Making an interface for every class, before there is a second implementation.
A subclass that narrows what the base class accepts, which breaks callers.
Naming principles without saying what change they protect against.

interview.q: Explain the single responsibility principle.
interview.a: A class should have only one reason to change. If a class both formats a report and sends it by email, a change to either forces you to edit it. Split them so each change touches one class.

interview.q: Composition versus inheritance?
interview.a: Inheritance models 'is a' and binds the child to its parent's internals. Composition models 'has a': an object holds other objects and delegates to them. Composition is more flexible because the parts can be swapped (often through an interface), so prefer it unless the base class is stable and the relationship is a real 'is a'.

interview.q: What is dependency injection and why use it?
interview.a: Passing a class its dependencies from outside (usually through the constructor) instead of creating them inside. It keeps high-level code dependent on an abstraction, lets you swap implementations, and lets tests pass in fakes.

interview.q: What does the Liskov substitution principle mean?
interview.a: Any place that expects the base type must work correctly with a subtype, without special cases. A Square that inherits from Rectangle but changes both sides when you set the width breaks code written for rectangles, so the subtype is not substitutable.

steps.title: A class that does everything
body: OrderService saves the order, charges the card, builds the email text and sends it. When the email format changes, or SMS is added, you edit this one class, and you risk breaking the payment code next to it.
Object-oriented design is about making each change touch as little code as possible.

lines: if channel == 'email': ...  # build and send an email
elif channel == 'sms': ... # every new channel edits here

steps.title: S: single responsibility
body: A class should have one reason to change. Split the work: one part owns orders and payment, another owns sending notifications. A change to the email text no longer touches payment.
This is the first of the five SOLID principles (named by Michael Feathers from Robert Martin's principles).

steps.title: O: open for extension, closed for modification
body: Define an interface, Notifier with send(). OrderService depends on that interface. Email and SMS are two implementations. Adding a channel means adding a class, not editing OrderService.
In Python an abstract base class (abc.ABC) or a typing.Protocol expresses the interface.

steps.title: Add a channel without touching OrderService
body: Adding push notifications is a new class, PushNotifier, that implements Notifier. No existing class changes, so nothing that already works can break.
That is the payoff of the open-closed principle.

predict.question: You add PushNotifier(Notifier). Which existing class must you edit to support it?
predict.why: OrderService only knows the Notifier interface, so a new implementation plugs in without editing any existing class. You pass the new object in where the service is created.

steps.title: L: substitutable subclasses
body: Wherever a Notifier is expected, any implementation must work without surprises. A subclass that raises an error for input the base class accepts, or ignores the contract, breaks callers.
The classic example: a Square that inherits from Rectangle breaks code that sets width and height separately.

callout.text: If a subclass needs 'if isinstance(...)' checks around it, the inheritance is probably wrong. Prefer composition.

steps.title: I: small interfaces
body: Do not force a class to implement methods it does not use. A Notifier that also has print_receipt() and refund() makes every channel implement them. Prefer several small interfaces.
In Python, small Protocols or abstract classes with one or two methods keep this natural.

card.title: Smell and fix
lines: class Notifier: send(), refund(), print_receipt()   # too wide

steps.title: D: depend on abstractions
body: High-level code (OrderService) should depend on an abstraction (Notifier), not on a concrete class (EmailNotifier). The concrete object is passed in from outside: dependency injection, in practice a constructor argument.
It also makes testing easy: pass a fake notifier that records messages.

card.title: Python
lines: self.notifier = notifier         # injected, not created here

steps.title: Prefer composition to inheritance
body: Inheritance says 'is a'; composition says 'has a'. Deep inheritance trees couple a child to everything above it. Compose small objects and delegate to them.
Use inheritance for a true 'is a' with a stable base, and composition for everything else.

callout.text: OrderService has a Notifier. It is not a kind of notifier.

steps.title: Recap
body: SOLID is a set of heuristics for keeping change local, not a law. In an interview name the principle you are applying and the change it protects against.
Do not over-engineer: introduce an interface when there is a second implementation or a real need to swap one.

title: Design Patterns That Come Up in Interviews
tagline: Ready-made solutions to problems that keep coming up.
explain: Design patterns are named solutions to problems that keep coming up in object-oriented code. In an LLD round they give you short names for design decisions. Do not apply them for their own sake: describe the problem first, then the pattern.
## Strategy

Problem: a class chooses between several ways of doing the same job with if/elif. Fix: put each way behind the same interface and pass the chosen one in. refactoring.guru defines it as a family of algorithms, each in its own class, made interchangeable. In Python a function is often enough.
## Factory
Problem: which class to create depends on input. Fix: one function (or a dict from name to class) makes the decision, so callers never name the concrete classes.
## Observer

Problem: when one object changes, several others must react, and the first should not know about them. Fix: a subscription list. The publisher notifies every subscriber. Watch for slow or failing listeners and decide on error handling and ordering.
## Decorator
Problem: add behavior (logging, caching, auth) without editing the class. Fix: wrap the object or function. Python's @ syntax and functools.wraps make this natural.
## State

Problem: behavior depends on state and you have conditionals in every method. Fix: one class per state that handles the events for that state. The State pattern is closely related to finite-state machines; the next lessons use it in a vending machine.
## Singleton: handle with care

One instance, globally reachable. It hides dependencies and shares state between tests. Prefer creating one object at start-up and passing it in; a module-level object is already a single instance in Python.
## Other patterns you may be asked to name

- Builder: construct a complex object step by step; in Python, keyword arguments and dataclasses often replace it.
- Adapter: wrap an incompatible interface so it fits the one you expect (a payment SDK behind your own PaymentGateway).
- Facade: one simple entry point in front of a complicated subsystem.
- Command: represent a request as an object so you can queue, log or undo it.
- Iterator: Python builds it in through __iter__ and generators.
## Strategy or State?

Both swap behavior by delegating to another object. In Strategy the client chooses which algorithm to use, and the choice usually stays put (a pricing rule). In State the object changes its own behavior as events happen (a vending machine moving from idle to dispensing). If the 'strategy' changes itself in response to events, you probably want State.
keyPoints: Name the problem, then the pattern.
Strategy: swap algorithms behind one interface.
Factory: one place chooses the class to create.
Observer: publisher notifies subscribers it does not know.
Singleton is global state: prefer injecting one shared object.

exercise: For each of Strategy, Factory, Observer and Decorator write (1) a three-line problem statement in your own words, (2) the code that has the problem (a long if/elif, a hard-coded class), (3) the refactored version and (4) one cost of the pattern. Then pick a domain (a ride-hailing app) and name where each pattern would fit and where it would be over-engineering.
pitfalls: Applying a pattern because it is on a list, not because of a problem.
A class per tiny strategy when a function would do.
An observer whose subscriber raises an error and stops the others.
Using a singleton for something that should be passed in, then having tests share state.
Forgetting functools.wraps, so decorated functions lose their name and docstring.

interview.q: When would you use the Strategy pattern?
interview.a: When a class has a large conditional choosing between variants of the same algorithm, or you want to swap the algorithm at run time. Each variant goes behind a common interface and the class receives the one to use. Pricing rules and routing algorithms are typical.

interview.q: What is the Observer pattern and what can go wrong?
interview.a: A publisher keeps a list of subscribers and notifies them when something happens, so the publisher need not know who they are. Problems: a slow or failing subscriber can block or break the rest, notification order may matter, and forgetting to unsubscribe leaks objects.

interview.q: Why is a singleton considered a smell?
interview.a: It is global state: it hides the dependency from the caller's signature, makes unit tests share and leak state, and complicates threading. Prefer creating one instance at start-up and injecting it.

interview.q: How is a decorator different from inheritance for adding behavior?
interview.a: A decorator wraps an existing object or function at run time and can be stacked, without creating a new subclass for each combination. Inheritance fixes the combination at class definition and couples the child to its parent.

body: When a class contains a big if/elif choosing between ways of doing the same thing (pricing rules, sort orders, routing), move each way into its own object or function with the same interface and pass it in.
refactoring.guru describes it as defining a family of algorithms, putting each in a separate class, and making them interchangeable. In Python a plain function often is the strategy.

title: The LLD Method, Worked on a Parking Lot
tagline: From a one-line request to classes and flows: a method for small design questions.
explain: An LLD interview gives you a short, vague prompt and asks for classes, their relationships and the key methods, usually with some code. Interviewers look at how you structure the problem more than at a perfect final answer. This lesson gives a repeatable method and applies it to a parking lot.
## The method

1. Clarify: vehicle types, sizes, fees, scale, concurrency. Write the requirements down.
2. Nouns become classes, verbs become methods.
3. Draw the relationships: has-many, refers-to, and what each object must remember.
4. Write the main flow and the error cases. Raise clear errors for a full lot and an unknown ticket.
5. Add patterns only where change is likely (pricing is a strategy; spot assignment can be one too).
6. Discuss extension (a new vehicle type) and concurrency (two entrances).
## The design here

ParkingLot holds Spots and a map of active Tickets. A Spot has an id and a vehicle type and knows whether it is free. A Ticket records the spot, the vehicle plate and the entry time. park(plate, type) finds a free matching spot, marks it, and returns a ticket. unpark(ticket_id) frees the spot and returns the fee from a PricingStrategy.
## Where the marks are

Clear requirements, sensible class boundaries, no god class, errors handled, and a design that absorbs a new requirement without editing working code. The concurrency discussion matters: finding a free spot and marking it must be atomic.
## The same method on other prompts

Practise on a library system, hotel booking, ATM, elevator, tic-tac-toe or chess, an expense splitter and a rate limiter. For each one write the requirements, list the nouns, draw relationships, write the main flow and its errors, and name where a new requirement would plug in. The nouns change but the steps do not, so after three or four problems the method becomes automatic.
## What a good answer sounds like

'I'll assume cars and motorcycles, one entrance, hourly pricing; tell me if that is wrong.' 'A Ticket ties the vehicle, the spot and the entry time together, so unpark needs only the ticket.' 'Pricing changes often, so it is a strategy; adding trucks is data, not code.' 'Two entrances can race for a spot, so finding and marking it must be atomic.' Each sentence states a requirement, a design choice and the reason for it.
## How to talk through it
Think aloud and draw. State assumptions. Keep the first version small and say 'I would add X next'. Run a few tests by hand on your code before the interviewer asks.
keyPoints: Clarify requirements before drawing anything.
Nouns are classes, verbs are methods.
Write the happy path and the error cases.
Use a pattern (strategy) only where requirements are likely to change.
Finding and marking a spot must be atomic.

Then extend it with a new member type (a student with a lower limit) and count how many existing classes you edited.

A single god class that holds spots, tickets and pricing rules together.
Ignoring error cases: full lot, ticket reuse, unknown ticket.

interview.q: How do you approach a low-level design question?
interview.a: Clarify the requirements and write them down. Turn nouns into classes and verbs into methods. Draw relationships and what each object remembers. Write the main flow plus error cases, add design patterns only where change is likely, then discuss extension and concurrency, and test with a few examples.

interview.q: How would you add a new vehicle type to the parking lot?
interview.a: Add a VehicleType value and create spots of that type. Because park matches spots by type, park and unpark do not change. If pricing differs, add a pricing strategy for it. The point is to extend by adding, not editing.

interview.q: What can go wrong with two entrances parking at once?
interview.a: Both can find the same free spot before either marks it taken, a race that double-books the spot. Make find-and-mark atomic: a lock in one process, or a database transaction with a unique constraint on the spot across servers.

interview.q: Why is pricing a separate strategy object?
interview.a: Fee rules change often (hourly, flat, weekend). Putting them behind one interface keeps park and unpark stable and lets you add a rule by adding a class, and it makes the fee logic easy to test on its own.

title: Design an LRU Cache
tagline: Keep recent items handy and throw out the one unused for longest, quickly.
explain: The LRU (least recently used) cache is one of the most common design-plus-coding questions, because it combines a data-structure insight with clean class design. The requirement: a cache of fixed capacity where get and put run in O(1), and a full cache evicts the entry that was used longest ago.
## Why two structures

A dict gives O(1) lookup but no usage order. A linked list keeps order and lets you move or remove a node in O(1), but finding a node by key is O(n). Together: the dict maps key to node, and the doubly linked list orders the nodes from most recently used (front) to least recently used (back).
## The operations

- get(key): if absent return -1; otherwise unlink the node, link it at the front, return its value.
- put(key, value): if present, update and move to the front. If absent and full, remove the back node and its key from the dict. Then add a new node at the front and in the dict.
- Use sentinel head and tail nodes so you never special-case an empty list.
## Shortcuts to mention

collections.OrderedDict has move_to_end and popitem(last=False), which makes a short LRU; the docs say it suits LRU caches. functools.lru_cache is a ready-made version for function results (arguments must be hashable). For a shared cache you need a lock, or a store like Redis.
## Variations interviewers ask for

- LFU cache (least frequently used): you need counts as well as recency, usually a map from key to node and a map from count to a recency-ordered list, to keep O(1).
- TTL: store an expiry time on each entry; check it lazily on get, and optionally sweep with a heap of expiry times.
- Capacity by size in bytes instead of by count: evict until the total fits.
- Thread safety: one lock around get and put, or sharded locks to reduce contention.
- Write-through versus write-back when the cache sits in front of a database.
## Invariants worth stating

The dict and the list always hold the same keys. head.next is the most recently used node and tail.prev is the least recently used. After every get or put, the touched node is at the front. If you can state these three sentences, you can check your code against them line by line.
## How to talk through it

State the requirements and the O(1) targets. Explain why one structure is not enough. Draw the list with sentinels. Write the helper methods (remove node, add to front) first, then get and put. Test capacity 1, updating an existing key and eviction order.
keyPoints: Hash map for lookup plus doubly linked list for order.
Front = most recent, back = least recent: evict the back.
Both get and put count as a use and move the node to the front.
Sentinel head and tail nodes remove edge cases.
OrderedDict.move_to_end and popitem(last=False) give a short version.

sql.title: LRU cache from a dict and a doubly linked list
sql.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=None, val=None):
        self.key, self.val = key, val
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.map = {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()           # sentinels
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev

    def _add_front(self, node):
        node.prev, node.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return -1
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_front(node)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            node = self.map[key]
            node.val = value
            self._remove(node)
            self._add_front(node)
            return
        if len(self.map) >= self.cap:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._add_front(node)

c = LRUCache(2)
c.put('a', 1); c.put('b', 2)
assert c.get('a') == 1          # a is now the most recent
c.put('c', 3)                   # evicts b, the least recent
assert c.get('b') == -1 and c.get('c') == 3 and c.get('a') == 1
c.put('a', 10)
assert c.get('a') == 10
c1 = LRUCache(1)
c1.put('x', 1); c1.put('y', 2)
assert c1.get('x') == -1 and c1.get('y') == 2

functools.lru_cache for function results
sql.code:
from functools import lru_cache

calls = []

@lru_cache(maxsize=2)
def square(n):
    calls.append(n)
    return n * n

assert [square(2), square(2), square(3)] == [4, 4, 9]
assert calls == [2, 3]                      # the second square(2) came from the cache
info = square.cache_info()
assert info.hits == 1 and info.misses == 2 and info.maxsize == 2

exercise: Implement the LRU cache with a dict and a doubly linked list, with no OrderedDict. Write tests for capacity 1, updating an existing key, and eviction order after several gets. Then add a TTL (entries expire after N seconds) and say what that does to your invariants. Finally make it thread-safe and explain what the lock protects.
pitfalls: Using a singly linked list, so removing a node needs a scan to find its predecessor.
Forgetting to delete the evicted key from the dict.
Not treating get as a use, so the order goes stale.
Not updating the order when put is called with an existing key.
Missing edge cases that sentinels would remove: capacity 1 and an empty list.

interview.q: How do you build an LRU cache with O(1) get and put?
interview.a: A hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency. get moves the node to the front; put updates or inserts at the front and, when over capacity, removes the back node and its map entry. All steps are pointer updates or dict operations, so O(1).

interview.q: Why a doubly linked list and not a singly linked one?
interview.a: To remove a node you already hold in O(1) you need its predecessor. A doubly linked list stores it in node.prev. A singly linked list would need an O(n) scan to find it.

interview.q: What would you change to make it thread-safe?
interview.a: get mutates the order, so even reads need exclusive access. Guard get and put with a lock (or use a concurrent library). Across processes or machines use an external store such as Redis with an eviction policy.

interview.q: What does Python provide for this?
interview.a: collections.OrderedDict has move_to_end and popitem(last=False), which makes a compact LRU, and functools.lru_cache caches a function's results with a maxsize (arguments must be hashable).

steps.title: The requirement
body: Design a cache of fixed capacity with get(key) and put(key, value), both in O(1). When it is full, put evicts the least recently used entry.
'Used' means read or written: both count as a use.

steps.title: A hash map alone cannot answer 'least recent'
body: A dict finds a key in O(1) but does not know which entry was used longest ago. Scanning for the oldest would be O(n) on every eviction.
We need a second structure that keeps the usage order and lets us move an entry to the front in O(1).

steps.title: Add a doubly linked list for the order
body: Keep the entries in a doubly linked list: most recently used at the front, least recently used at the back. The map stores key to node, so we reach any node in O(1).
Doubly linked means each node knows its previous and next, so removing a node you hold is O(1) with no scan.
changes: + Doubly linked list ordered by recency

steps.title: get: move the node to the front
body: get('b') finds B through the map, unlinks it and links it at the front, then returns its value. B is now the most recently used; A, which was first, becomes second.
All pointer changes, so O(1).

predict.question: After get('b'), which key is the least recently used (next to be evicted)?
predict.why: The order before was a, b, c from most to least recent. Reading b moves it to the front: b, a, c. The back of the list, c, is next to go.

steps.title: put on a full cache: evict the back
body: put('d', 4) with capacity 3: the cache is full, so remove the node at the back (C) and delete its key from the map, then add D at the front and the map. Everything stays O(1).
If the key already exists, update its value and move it to the front instead.

steps.title: The same idea with OrderedDict

title: Design a Vending Machine: State Machines
tagline: Model something that moves through steps, like a vending machine: states, events and moves.
explain: Many LLD prompts (vending machine, ATM, elevator, traffic light, order status) are really finite-state machines: an object that is always in exactly one of a fixed set of states, and moves between states in response to events by predetermined rules. Naming that early shapes the whole design.
## Start with the table

List the states and the events. For every (state, event) pair decide the next state, or decide it is invalid (ignore it, or raise a clear error). The table is the specification; the code is a way to implement it.
## Two ways to implement it

- State pattern: one class per state implements the events. The machine delegates to its current state object. Adding a state means adding a class. refactoring.guru notes that state machines built from conditionals get harder to change as states are added, which is what this avoids.
- Table-driven: a dict from (state, event) to the next state, with a default for invalid events. Shorter when states only move and do little.
## What interviewers look for
That you find the states and transitions, handle invalid events deliberately, keep each state's behavior in one place, and can add a state (out of stock, maintenance mode) without editing the others.
## A worked example: order status

States: created, paid, shipped, delivered, canceled. Allowed transitions: created to paid or canceled, paid to shipped or canceled, shipped to delivered. A refund after shipping is not allowed here. In Django store the status as a CharField with choices and keep the allowed transitions in one dict next to it.

Two requests can try to move the same order at once. Make the change a conditional UPDATE (for example filter on status='paid' and set it to shipped) and check how many rows changed; if none changed, the order was already moved. That keeps the state machine correct under concurrency, using the database as the arbiter.
## How to talk through it
Draw the diagram first. Ask about money handling (coins, change, refund), stock and concurrency. State what an invalid event does. Test every arrow and an invalid event in each state.
keyPoints: Model the object as states, events and transitions.
Decide what every invalid event does.
State pattern: one class per state; add a state by adding a class.
A transition table is a compact alternative.
Test every arrow and at least one invalid event per state.

sql.title: Vending machine with the State pattern

exercise: Design an elevator controller (one elevator, N floors) as a state machine. List the states (idle, moving up, moving down, doors open), the events (request, arrive, door timeout), and the transition table. Implement it with the State pattern, then with a table, and compare. Test every transition and one invalid event per state. Then add 'maintenance mode' and count how many existing classes you edited.
pitfalls: Not listing the invalid (state, event) pairs, so behavior is undefined.
Flags and nested if/else in every method instead of one place per state.
Letting the machine hold state that belongs to a single state class.
Forgetting to handle 'out of stock' or 'refund' paths.
Not testing transitions, only the happy path.

interview.q: When is a design problem a state machine?
interview.a: When an object's behavior depends on what happened before and it moves between a fixed set of modes by predetermined rules: vending machines, ATMs, elevators, order and payment statuses. List states, events and transitions, and decide what an invalid event does.

interview.q: How does the State pattern help?
interview.a: Each state is its own class that implements all the events; the context delegates to the current state. State-specific behavior lives in one place, and adding a state is adding a class instead of editing a conditional in every method.

interview.q: State pattern or transition table?
interview.a: Use a table when states only decide the next state, it is compact and easy to test. Use state classes when each state has real behavior (different side effects and checks) and you want to extend it without editing the others.

interview.q: How do you handle an invalid event?
interview.a: Decide explicitly per (state, event): ignore it (stay in the same state), or raise or report a clear error. Never leave it undefined, and test at least one invalid event per state.

basis: Why it is here: vending-machine and elevator style prompts are common LLD exercises, and Amazon lists object-oriented design among its technical topics. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard. title: Design an Elevator System
tagline: Several lifts, many buttons: decide which car answers each call, and make each car move without wasting trips.
explain: The elevator is a favourite low-level design question because it mixes a small state machine with a scheduling rule. Do not start with code. Start with what the system must do.
## Requirements to ask for

How many elevators and floors? Is there a hall call (up or down button on a floor) and a car call (a floor button inside)? Do doors, weight limits and emergency stop matter? Is the goal the shortest wait or the least energy? State your assumptions. A reasonable first version is a few cars, hall and car calls, and the shortest average wait.
## The entities

Elevator holds its floor, its direction and the set of floors it must stop at. Request is a hall call: a floor and a direction. Controller receives hall calls and decides which Elevator takes each. Keep movement inside Elevator and assignment inside Controller, so each class has one reason to change. That is the single-responsibility idea from SOLID.
## How one car moves: keep going, then turn round

A car that reverses for every new call wastes trips. The usual rule, called SCAN or LOOK, is to keep moving in the current direction, stop at every requested floor on the way, and reverse only when nothing is left ahead. A car at floor 3 going up with stops at 5, 2 and 7 serves 5, then 7, then turns round for 2. This ordering falls out of one test: are any stops ahead of me?
## Which car answers a hall call

Compute a cost for each car and pick the lowest. An idle car costs its distance. A moving car costs its distance only if it is heading toward the floor in the direction the caller wants; otherwise add a large penalty, because it must finish its trip and come back. The cost function follows the Strategy pattern: you can swap in a different policy without touching Elevator. Ties break by car id so the result is predictable and testable.
## States of one car

A car is in a state: idle, moving up, moving down, or doors open. What happens on a button press depends on the state, which is the State pattern. In a first version a direction field is enough. Name the full state machine if the interviewer asks about doors, overload or fire mode, and say it would become a State class per state.
## What the interviewer probes

Concurrency: calls arrive while cars move, so the stop set needs a lock or a single thread that owns the car. Extensibility: express priorities (a fire key, a VIP floor) as a different cost function. Failure: if a car goes out of service, its stops are re-dispatched. Testing: with a fake clock and no real motion, each rule above is a plain unit test.
## How to talk through it

Requirements, entities, the movement rule, the assignment rule, then states and extensions. Say which parts are patterns (Strategy for assignment, State for modes) and which are plain classes. Write the movement test first, because it proves the rule.
keyPoints: Elevator moves and holds stops; Controller assigns hall calls. Keep the two jobs apart.
Keep going in one direction, serve stops on the way, reverse only when nothing is ahead (SCAN or LOOK).
Assign a hall call by lowest cost: distance, plus a big penalty for a car going the wrong way.
The cost function is a Strategy; a car's modes are a State.
Calls arrive while cars move, so protect the stop set with a lock or one owning thread.

sql.title: One car: keep going, then turn round
The controller picks a car by cost
sql.code:
class Controller:
    """Strategy: how a hall call is assigned. Swap cost() to change the policy."""
    def __init__(self, elevators):
        self.elevators = elevators

    def cost(self, e, floor, direction):
        distance = abs(e.floor - floor)
        if e.dir == Dir.IDLE:
            return distance
        coming_my_way = (floor - e.floor) * e.dir.value > 0 and direction == e.dir
        return distance if coming_my_way else distance + 100   # a car going away makes a long detour

    def request(self, floor, direction):
        best = min(self.elevators, key=lambda e: (self.cost(e, floor, direction), e.id))
        best.add_stop(floor)
        return best.id

a, b = Elevator(1, floor=0), Elevator(2, floor=9)
c = Controller([a, b])
assert c.request(8, Dir.DOWN) == 2          # the idle car on 9 is nearer than the one on 0
b2 = Elevator(1, floor=2); b2.add_stop(10)  # already heading up past floor 5
far = Elevator(2, floor=9)
assert Controller([b2, far]).request(5, Dir.UP) == 1   # it is passing floor 5 on its way up

exercise: Extend the elevator code. Add a car call inside the elevator and a door-open step that takes two ticks. Then replace the cost function with a policy that prefers the car with fewer pending stops, and write a test that shows the two policies choose different cars in one situation. Finally say how you would stop two threads from changing the same stop set.
pitfalls: Starting to write classes before agreeing what the system must do.
Reversing the car for every new call instead of finishing the direction first.
Putting assignment logic inside Elevator, so it cannot be changed without touching movement.
Ignoring that calls arrive while the car is moving, so the stop set is shared state.
Forgetting a deterministic tie-break, which makes tests flaky.

interview.q: How does one elevator decide where to go next?
interview.a: It keeps moving in its current direction and serves requested floors on the way. Only when no stop is ahead does it reverse. This is the SCAN or LOOK idea and avoids wasting trips.

interview.q: How do you choose which elevator answers a hall call?
interview.a: Give each car a cost and pick the lowest. An idle car costs its distance. A moving car costs its distance if it is heading toward the caller in the right direction, otherwise distance plus a penalty. Break ties by id.

interview.q: Which design patterns fit, and why?
interview.a: Strategy for the assignment policy, so it can be swapped. State for the car's modes (idle, moving, doors open, out of service). They are fits, not requirements: a simple version needs only a direction field.

interview.q: What changes if there are many calls at once?
interview.a: The stop set and the assignment need protection: a lock around each car, or one thread that owns each car and receives calls through a queue.

interview.q: How would you test it without real time?
interview.a: Make motion a step() call driven by the test. Each rule then becomes a unit test: the visiting order, the turn-round, and the assignment cost.

basis: Why it is here: an elevator is a standard low-level design prompt that tests class responsibilities, a scheduling rule and the State and Strategy patterns. The elevator design, the SCAN-style movement rule, the cost function and its penalty of 100 are my own worked example, not a copy of any company's answer, and the numbers are illustrative. It is my judgment that a direction field is enough for a first version. No page I read says how often this question is asked. Hours and priority are my judgment.

title: Design a Ticket Booking System
tagline: Two people click the same seat at the same moment. Make sure exactly one of them gets it, and that a seat nobody pays for comes back.
explain: A ticket booking system looks easy until two buyers choose the last seat at once. The whole design is about one promise: a seat is never sold twice. Everything else is detail.
## Requirements and entities

Ask how many shows and seats, whether a buyer picks seats or takes any, how long a seat is reserved while the buyer pays, and what happens on payment failure. The main entities are Show, Seat, a Hold (a temporary claim with an expiry), and a Booking (the final sale). A seat moves through three states: available, held and booked.
## Why a hold exists

Payment takes time. If you marked a seat booked at the first click, abandoned carts would block seats forever. If you waited until payment finished, two people could pay for the same seat. A hold sits between: it claims the seat for a few minutes, and if the buyer does not pay, the hold expires and the seat becomes available again.
## The race and how to stop it

Check-then-set is the bug, a race condition: two requests both see the seat available, and both mark it held. The check and the change must happen as one step. In one process that is a lock around the code. Across many servers the lock must live in the database. In PostgreSQL a row-level lock such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE makes other writers and lockers of that row wait. A unique constraint on show and seat is the final safety net, because the database rejects a second booking of the same seat no matter what the code did.
## All or nothing

A buyer often wants several seats together. Hold them in one step: if any seat is taken, hold none. Sort the seats before locking them, so two buyers who want the same seats in different orders cannot wait on each other forever. The PostgreSQL documentation says to prevent deadlocks by locking objects in a consistent order.
## Expiry

Store an expiry time on every hold and treat an expired hold as no hold. The simplest approach is lazy: each request first clears expired holds, as in the code here. A background job can also sweep. Inject the clock, so tests can move time forward instead of sleeping.
## Payment and retries

Confirm a booking only if the buyer still holds every seat, and make the confirm step safe to repeat, because a payment callback can arrive twice. An idempotency key on the payment request lets a retry return the same result instead of charging twice.
## How to talk through it

State the promise (no double sale). Show the states and the hold. Name the race, show the single locked step that closes it, then add the database constraint as the backstop. Finish with expiry, all-or-nothing and retries.
keyPoints: The promise: a seat is never sold twice. Check and change must be one atomic step.
A hold claims a seat for a few minutes; if nobody pays, it expires and the seat is available again.
Hold several seats all or nothing, in sorted order, to avoid deadlock.
In a database use a row lock (FOR UPDATE) and a unique constraint on show and seat as the backstop.
Inject the clock so expiry can be tested, and make confirm safe to repeat.

sql.title: Seat map with holds, expiry and confirm
sql.code:
import threading

class SeatMap:
    """Seats are AVAILABLE, HELD (until a deadline) or BOOKED. All changes happen under one lock."""
    def __init__(self, seats, hold_seconds=300, clock=None):
        self.hold_seconds = hold_seconds
        self.clock = clock or (lambda: 0)
        self.booked = {}                     # seat -> user
        self.held = {}                       # seat -> (user, expires_at)
        self.seats = set(seats)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def _expire(self):
        now = self.clock()
        for seat in [s for s, (_, until) in self.held.items() if until <= now]:
            del self.held[seat]

    def hold(self, user, seats):
        """All or nothing: either every seat is held for this user, or none."""
        with self.lock:
            self._expire()
            wanted = sorted(set(seats))      # a fixed order avoids deadlocks if you later lock per seat
            for s in wanted:
                if s not in self.seats or s in self.booked or s in self.held:
                    return False
            for s in wanted:
                self.held[s] = (user, self.clock() + self.hold_seconds)
            return True

    def confirm(self, user, seats):
        with self.lock:
            self._expire()
            if any(self.held.get(s, (None, 0))[0] != user for s in seats):
                return False
            for s in seats:
                del self.held[s]
                self.booked[s] = user
            return True

now = [0]
m = SeatMap({"A1", "A2", "A3"}, hold_seconds=300, clock=lambda: now[0])
assert m.hold("ann", ["A1", "A2"]) is True
assert m.hold("bob", ["A2", "A3"]) is False          # A2 is taken, so bob gets nothing
assert m.hold("bob", ["A3"]) is True                 # A3 was not touched by the failed attempt
assert m.confirm("ann", ["A1", "A2"]) is True
now[0] = 301                                         # bob never paid: his hold expires
assert m.hold("cy", ["A3"]) is True
assert m.confirm("bob", ["A3"]) is False

sql.title: Fifty threads, one seat

exercise: Add a release(user, seats) method and a rule that one user can hold at most six seats at a time. Write a test where a hold expires between hold and confirm. Then describe the same design with a database: which table holds the seats, which statement takes the row lock, and which unique constraint is the final guard.
pitfalls: Check-then-set without a lock, so two buyers both succeed.
Booking at the first click, so abandoned carts block seats for ever.
Locking seats in different orders for different buyers, which can deadlock.
Never expiring holds, or expiring them with a real sleep in tests.
Confirming a booking twice when a payment callback is repeated.

interview.q: How do you stop two users booking the same seat?
interview.a: Make the check and the change one atomic step: a lock in one process, or a database row lock or conditional update across servers. Add a unique constraint on show and seat as the final guard.

interview.q: Why use a hold with an expiry instead of booking at click?
interview.a: A hold gives the buyer time to pay without selling the seat twice, and the expiry returns unpaid seats to the pool so they are not blocked for ever.

interview.q: How do you hold several seats at once?
interview.a: All or nothing: check every seat, and only if all are free hold them in the same locked step. Lock in a fixed order so two buyers cannot deadlock.

interview.q: What does SELECT ... FOR UPDATE do?
interview.a: It locks the selected rows until the transaction ends, so other transactions that try to update or lock those rows must wait.

interview.q: How do you handle a repeated payment callback?
interview.a: Make confirm idempotent: if the booking already exists for that hold, return success without booking again, and use an idempotency key on the payment request.

references.title: Stripe: Designing robust APIs with idempotency

basis: Why it is here: seat booking is a classic design prompt about concurrency, and the lesson turns it into a testable class. The row-level lock modes and the advice to prevent deadlocks by locking objects in a consistent order are from the PostgreSQL explicit locking page I read; that page does not cover NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED, so they are not used here. The Lock and Thread facts are from the Python threading page and the idempotency-key idea is from the Stripe post, both of which I read. The three-state design, the five-minute hold, the lazy expiry and the unique-constraint backstop are my own worked example and judgment, not a copy of any company's answer; the numbers are illustrative assumptions. Hours and priority are my judgment.

title: Design a Vending Machine
tagline: A machine that behaves differently depending on whether it has money: the State pattern in its simplest useful form.
explain: The vending machine is the textbook State pattern problem. The same button press means different things depending on what has already happened: pressing a product button with no money does nothing useful, while with enough money it dispenses.
## Requirements

Ask which coins and notes are accepted, whether the machine gives change, what happens when an item is sold out, whether a refund is allowed before choosing, and how stock is refilled. A sound first version: insert money, select a slot, dispense and return change, or refund.
## The trap: a pile of if statements

The first attempt is a VendingMachine class with a status field and methods full of if status == 'idle' ... elif status == 'has_money' .... Every new state or action touches every method. This is the shape the State pattern removes.
## The State pattern

Make each state its own class with the same methods: insert, select, refund. The machine holds a reference to its current state object and forwards every call to it. The state does the work and may switch the machine to another state. Adding an 'out of service' state means adding one class, and no existing method changes.
## Entities

VendingMachine owns the stock, the credit and the current state. A slot has a price and a quantity. States are Idle and HasMoney, and later OutOfService or Dispensing. Money is stored as integer cents, not floating point, because 0.1 plus 0.2 is not 0.3 in binary arithmetic.
## Making change

Pay back with the fewest coins by taking the largest coin first. This greedy method is correct for common coin systems such as 100, 50, 25, 10, 5 and 1, but not for every system, so say that out loud. Also say what you do when the machine lacks the coins for exact change.
## Related patterns

A Strategy is for swapping one algorithm (how to make change). A State is for an object whose behavior changes with its mode. The two look alike in code, and the intent differs. A Factory could create the product objects. Mention them, and do not force them in.
## How to talk through it

Requirements, the if-statement trap, the state classes and their transitions as a small table, money in cents, change, and what you would add next (payment cards, out of service, restock). Draw the transitions: Idle to HasMoney on insert, HasMoney to Idle on refund or when credit reaches zero.
keyPoints: The State pattern: one class per state, the machine forwards calls to its current state.
Replaces a growing tangle of if status == ... in every method.
Adding a state means adding a class; existing states stay unchanged.
Store money as integer cents, never as floats.
Greedy change works for common coin sets, but say it is not true for every coin system.

sql.title: States: idle and has-money
Making change

exercise: Add an OutOfService state that rejects every action and a restock() method on the machine that is only allowed in that state. Then make make_change aware of limited coin stock: return None if exact change is impossible and let HasMoney refuse the sale with 'exact change only'. Write a test for each new transition.
pitfalls: A giant status variable checked with if statements in every method.
Using floats for money.
Letting the state objects share mutable data in a way that is hard to follow, instead of passing the machine in.
Assuming greedy change works for every coin system.
Forgetting the sold-out and exact-change cases.

interview.q: Why use the State pattern for a vending machine?
interview.a: Behavior depends on mode (idle, has money, out of service). One class per state keeps each mode's rules together, removes big if chains, and lets you add states without editing existing ones.

interview.q: How is State different from Strategy?
interview.a: Both delegate to an object. A Strategy is a swappable algorithm chosen from outside. A State is the object's current mode, and states usually switch the object to another state themselves.

interview.q: How do you represent money?
interview.a: As integer cents (or the smallest unit). Floating point cannot store most decimals exactly, so sums can be slightly wrong.

interview.q: Is greedy coin change always correct?
interview.a: No. It is correct for many real coin systems, such as 100, 50, 25, 10, 5, 1, but some coin sets need dynamic programming. State the assumption.

interview.q: How would you add an out-of-service mode?
interview.a: Add an OutOfService state class whose methods reject every action, and a transition into and out of it. No existing state needs to change.

basis: Why it is here: the vending machine is the standard teaching example for the State pattern and appears in many low-level design lists. The State and Strategy descriptions, and the Factory Method relations, are from the Refactoring Guru pages I read. The machine, the transition table and the integer-cents choice are my own worked example, not a copy of any company's answer. The remark that floating point cannot store most decimals exactly and the point about greedy coin change are general knowledge that I did not check against a page. No page I read says how often this question is asked. Hours and priority are my judgment.

title: Design Splitwise (Expense Sharing)
tagline: Friends pay for things in turn. Record who paid and who owes, and settle everyone with as few payments as possible.
explain: Splitwise-style problems test whether you can model money correctly, choose a clean way to vary the rules, and then solve a small algorithm problem on top. It is a good example of why design and algorithms meet in interviews.
## Requirements

Users form groups. An expense has a payer, a total and a split rule: equal, exact amounts, or percentages. The system keeps balances (who owes whom) and can show a simplified set of payments that settles everything. Ask about currencies, rounding, and whether expenses can be edited or deleted.
## Entities

User, Group, Expense, and a Ledger of balances. An Expense holds the payer, the total in cents and a map from each user to the amount they owe. The Ledger turns expenses into balances. Keep the split rules out of Expense, in their own functions or classes.
## Splits are a Strategy

Equal, exact and percent are three algorithms for one job: turn a total into a map of amounts per user. That is the Strategy pattern. A new rule, such as splitting by shares, is a new strategy, and nothing else changes. A simple function per rule is often enough in Python. Use classes if the rules carry configuration.
## Money is whole cents

Store amounts as integer cents. Equal splitting then needs care: 100 cents among three people cannot be 33.33 each. Give each person the base amount and hand the leftover cents to the first few, so the parts always add up to the total. The same idea fixes percentages: round down each share, then give out the leftover cents. Always assert that the parts sum to the total.
## Balances

Keep one net number per user: positive means others owe them, negative means they owe others. When someone pays, add the total to their net, then subtract each person's share from that person's net. All nets always add up to zero, which is a good invariant to test.
## Simplifying debts

Without simplification, a group can end up with a web of small debts. The net balances are enough to settle everyone: repeatedly take the biggest creditor and the biggest debtor, pay the smaller of the two amounts, and put back whoever still has a balance. A heap gives each pick in logarithmic time. This greedy approach gives few payments, but it is not guaranteed to be the very fewest. Finding the true minimum is a harder problem, and it is fair to say so.
## How to talk through it

Requirements, entities, split strategies, cents and the leftover rule, the net balance and its zero-sum invariant, then simplification with a heap. Mention concurrency (two expenses added at once) and storage (expenses are the source of truth, balances can be recomputed).
keyPoints: Model amounts as integer cents; split rules must always add up to the total.
Equal, exact and percent are strategies: one job, swappable algorithms.
Keep a net balance per user; all nets sum to zero.
Simplify by matching the biggest creditor with the biggest debtor using heaps.
The greedy simplification gives few payments, not guaranteed the fewest.

sql.title: Split rules that always add up
A ledger and simplified payments
sql.code:
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

class Ledger:
    def __init__(self):
        self.net = defaultdict(int)          # positive: is owed money, negative: owes money

    def add_expense(self, paid_by, total, shares):
        """shares: user -> cents owed for this expense (must add up to total)."""
        assert sum(shares.values()) == total
        self.net[paid_by] += total
        for user, owed in shares.items():
            self.net[user] -= owed

    def simplify(self):
        """Few payments that settle everyone: repeatedly match the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor."""
        owed = [(-v, u) for u, v in self.net.items() if v > 0]      # max-heap by amount
        owes = [(v, u) for u, v in self.net.items() if v < 0]       # most negative first
        heapq.heapify(owed); heapq.heapify(owes)
        payments = []
        while owed and owes:
            credit, creditor = heapq.heappop(owed)
            debt, debtor = heapq.heappop(owes)
            amount = min(-credit, -debt)
            payments.append((debtor, creditor, amount))
            if -credit > amount:
                heapq.heappush(owed, (-(-credit - amount), creditor))
            if -debt > amount:
                heapq.heappush(owes, (-(-debt - amount), debtor))
        return payments

g = Ledger()
g.add_expense("ann", 3000, split_equal(3000, ["ann", "bob", "cy"]))     # ann paid dinner
g.add_expense("bob", 900, split_equal(900, ["ann", "bob", "cy"]))       # bob paid a taxi
assert sum(g.net.values()) == 0
pays = g.simplify()
assert pays == [("cy", "ann", 1300), ("bob", "ann", 400)]
settled = defaultdict(int)
for debtor, creditor, amount in pays:
    settled[debtor] += amount; settled[creditor] -= amount
assert all(settled[u] == -g.net[u] for u in g.net)                       # everyone ends at zero

exercise: Add a split-by-shares rule (for example 2 shares and 1 share) that always adds up to the total. Add a settle(debtor, creditor, amount) method that records a real payment. Then build an example where the greedy simplification uses more payments than the true minimum, or explain why you could not find one, and say what you would do if the group had thousands of users.
pitfalls: Using floats for money and seeing totals that are off by a cent.
Splitting 100 equally among three and losing or inventing a cent.
Putting the split rules inside Expense, so every new rule edits it.
Storing only balances and losing the expense history.
Claiming the greedy simplification is always minimal.

interview.q: How do you split 100 cents equally among 3 people?
interview.a: Give each 33 cents and give the leftover cent to the first person, so the amounts are 34, 33, 33 and add up to exactly 100.

interview.q: Which design pattern fits the split rules?
interview.a: Strategy: equal, exact and percent are different algorithms for the same job, and a new rule is a new strategy without changing the rest.

interview.q: How do you keep track of who owes whom?
interview.a: Keep a net balance per user: positive means they are owed, negative means they owe. Every expense adds the total to the payer and subtracts each person's share. The nets always sum to zero.

interview.q: How do you simplify the debts in a group?
interview.a: Take the biggest creditor and the biggest debtor, settle the smaller amount between them, and repeat with whoever still has a balance. Heaps make each pick fast. It gives few payments, not provably the fewest.

interview.q: Why store expenses and not only balances?
interview.a: Expenses are the source of truth: they let you show history, fix mistakes and recompute balances. Balances alone cannot be audited or corrected.

basis: Why it is here: expense sharing is a common low-level design prompt that combines modeling, a Strategy for the split rules and a small heap algorithm. The Strategy description is from the Refactoring Guru page, and the heapq and defaultdict behavior used here is from the Python heapq and collections pages, all of which I read. The design, the leftover-cent rule and the net-balance invariant are my own worked example, not a copy of any company's answer. The claim that finding the true minimum number of payments is harder than the greedy method is general knowledge that I did not check against a page. No page I read says how often this question is asked. Hours and priority are my judgment.
