title: How Interview Loops Are Structured, by Role
tagline: What the interview rounds look like at big companies, and how they differ by role.
explain: Before you plan your study time, find out what the interview contains. No company publishes how many hours each topic deserves or how rounds are weighted. They do publish the rounds and the topics, and that is enough to see the shape of a loop.
## Big-company software engineer loops

Amazon (SDE II): an online assessment with 90 minutes for two coding questions, 20 minutes of system design scenarios and an 8-minute work-style survey, then a loop of four 55-minute interviews. SDE III: a 60-minute phone screen, half Leadership Principles, then five 55-minute interviews. Each interviewer asks two or three behavioral questions, and you should expect at least one systems design question. Amazon's topic list names data structures, algorithms, coding, object-oriented design, databases, distributed computing, operating systems, internet topics and general machine learning.

Meta (an older blog post, so check it): a screen of about 35 minutes with two coding problems, then coding, a 45-minute design round and a 45-minute behavioral round. Microsoft: common data structures, at least one n log n sort, complexity, testing your own code and designing a system from scratch. Google (candidate-reported, not official): mostly data structures and algorithms, with system design stronger at senior levels.
## Frontend

The Front End Interview Handbook lists five round types: JavaScript coding, UI coding, algorithmic coding, quiz questions and system design. Its table shows Amazon, Google and Microsoft asking all five. Amazon's front end page names data structures and algorithms as a core focus.
## ML and AI engineer

Chip Huyen's book describes onsites of 4 to 8 interviews including coding, ML theory, ML implementation and behavioral, and says almost every company asks an ML system design question. A 2026 article (one author's opinion, without data) says coding leans toward LLM application pieces and evaluation harnesses, and that 'design an LLM-based system' is the usual design prompt.
## Backend and Django
Django prep guides and job posts emphasise the framework, databases, APIs and deployment. The big-company loops above apply if you target them. The right study mix depends on the employer.
## What follows for your plan

Coding on data structures and algorithms is the most numerous round, then system and low-level design, then behavioral in every loop. Databases are a topic inside those, not a track of their own. The platform's SDE roadmap follows this shape. Always confirm your own loop with the recruiter, because formats change, for example whether an AI assistant is part of coding rounds.
keyPoints: Companies publish rounds and topics, not hours or weights.
Coding on data structures and algorithms is in every big-company loop described here.
System design is common and grows with seniority; behavioral is in every loop.
Frontend adds JavaScript and UI coding rounds; ML adds ML theory and ML system design.
Confirm the format with your recruiter, since it changes.

sql.title: Turn a loop into a study budget

exercise: Pick three companies you would apply to. For each, find the official interview page and write the rounds, their lengths and the topics listed. Mark each fact as 'official page', 'candidate-reported' or 'unknown'. Then decide your own split of study hours across data structures and algorithms, system design, low-level design, database and behavioral, and write one sentence per share saying why.
pitfalls: Preparing for one format (for example only system design) because it is the one you like.
Treating candidate-reported summaries as official requirements.
Not asking the recruiter which rounds apply, then over-preparing a round that does not exist.
Giving behavioral little time because the hours look small, when it is in every loop.
Assuming a role title tells you the loop: a 'backend' role may be a Django product job or a big-company SDE loop.

interview.q: What does a typical big-company SDE loop contain?
interview.a: Coding rounds on data structures and algorithms, at least one system or product design round (more at senior levels), and behavioral questions in every interview. Amazon adds an online assessment with two coding questions and a short design section, and asks two or three behavioral questions in each loop interview.

interview.q: How is a frontend loop different?
interview.a: The Front End Interview Handbook lists JavaScript coding, UI coding, algorithmic coding, quiz questions and front end system design. Big companies such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft ask all five; some other companies skip algorithms or quizzes.

interview.q: How is an ML engineer loop different?
interview.a: Coding stays close to software-engineering coding, and there are extra rounds on ML theory or implementation and, almost always, ML system design. Recent claims say design prompts increasingly involve LLM-based systems, but the evidence for that is one author's opinion.

interview.q: How would you decide how to split your study time?
interview.a: Count the rounds by type for the loops you target, weigh each by how hard it is for you, keep a floor for behavioral, treat databases as a topic inside design and fundamentals, and confirm the format with the recruiter.

basis: Sources and how sure I am: Amazon's SDE II, SDE III, topics and front end pages, Meta's preparation blog post (older) and Microsoft's technical-interviewing page were opened and read. The Front End Interview Handbook and Chip Huyen's book were read. Google's loop, Meta's current AI-assistant note and the 2026 LLM-era claims come from search summaries or a single author's opinion and are labeled so. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard: no company page I read gives hours, weights or pass rates, only the rounds and topics. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises or lowers it for other roles (for example, data structures and algorithms are core in the SDE plan).

body: Chip Huyen's book describes ML onsites of 4 to 8 interviews with a coding question, ML theory, ML implementation and behavioral questions, and says almost every company she talked to asks an ML system design question. Coding challenges are typically 1 to 3 questions.

One 2026 article claims the coding rounds now lean toward implementing parts of an LLM application and writing evaluation harnesses, and that 'design an LLM-based system' is the most common design prompt. The author gives no data, so treat it as opinion.

steps.title: Backend and Django roles
body: Django and backend job posts and prep guides I read emphasise the framework, databases, APIs, testing and deployment more than algorithms. The big-company loops above still apply if you target them.
So the right mix depends on where you apply: a product company's Django role weights the database and framework; a big-company SDE loop weights coding and design.

callout.text: Decide the target first. The same learner needs a different study mix for a Django role at a startup and an SDE loop at a large company.

steps.title: Turning the loop into a study budget
body: Counting rounds: coding is the most numerous round type, design (system and low-level) is next, behavioral is in every loop, and databases are a topic inside design and fundamentals. The platform's SDE roadmap follows that shape.

Measured for a 1.5-year learner at 2 hours a day, 6 days a week over 10 weeks: about 45% data structures and algorithms, 19% system design, 12% low-level design, 14% database, 8% behavioral. These shares are my judgment, not a published standard.

callout.text: Behavioral is a modest share of hours but a large share of the decision at Amazon. Do not skip it because the hours look small.

steps.title: Ask the recruiter
body: Formats differ by company, level and team, and they change. Ask the recruiter which rounds you will have, how long each is, which languages are allowed and whether AI tools are part of the interview. Then adjust the plan.
A short checklist of those questions is worth sending the day you get the call.

card.title: Questions to send
lines: Which rounds, and how long is each?
Coding, system design, low-level design, behavioral?
Which languages and tools are allowed?
Is an AI assistant part of any round?
Is there an online assessment first?

everyday.plain: A job interview usually has several rounds, each testing something different.
everyday.story: Getting into a college may need an entrance exam, a group discussion and a personal interview. Each checks a different thing. Software interviews work like that too: a coding round, a design round, and a talk about your past work. What is in the loop depends on the company and the role.

A short first interview that filters candidates.
A round where you plan a large system out loud.

title: How to Run a Coding Round
tagline: A routine for coding rounds: understand, example, simple solution, better solution, code, test.
explain: A coding round is a short test of how you solve a problem in front of another person. The sources I read agree on the habits that count, and none of them is about being clever. Meta says to think out loud, Microsoft wants clarifying questions and a plan before you code, and Amazon asks for correct, well-tested code that handles edge cases.
## The seven steps

1. Restate the problem and ask clarifying questions (input size, duplicates, empty input, what to return when there is no answer).
2. Work a small example by hand and list edge cases.
3. Say the brute force and its cost.
4. Name the bottleneck and choose a pattern (hash map, two pointers, binary search, BFS and so on).
5. Write real code in a language you know, with clear names, not pseudocode.
6. Test your own code by tracing the example and the edge cases.
7. State time and space complexity, and say what you would change under other constraints.
## Practise it the way it is tested

Write code in a plain editor without autocomplete (Meta suggests this) and with a timer, for example 30 minutes for a medium problem. Practise out loud, even alone. Record yourself once and listen for silences.
## When you are stuck

Go back to the brute force and find the repeated work. Try a smaller input. Ask for a specific hint, instead of going silent, because your reasoning is part of what is being assessed. Correct but slow code is a better place to stand than half of a clever solution.
## Design rounds follow the same shape

For system and low-level design the routine is: requirements, numbers or entities, the main flow, trade-offs, then failure modes and extension. The system-design and low-level-design tracks of this platform each walk through it.
## A worked example of the whole routine

Prompt: 'find the first character that does not repeat'. Clarify: lowercase letters only? What to return if none (say -1 for the index)? Example: 'leetcode' gives 'l', index 0; 'aabb' gives none. Brute force: for each character count it with s.count(ch), O(n^2). Bottleneck: repeated counting. Pattern: count once with a Counter, then scan again for the first count of 1: O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters. Code it, then trace 'aabb' (no answer) and '' (empty).
## A practice schedule

Do one timed problem a day for the topic you are weakest in, and one untimed review of a problem you failed last week. After each problem write one line: where you lost time (understanding, pattern, bug, complexity). After ten problems, count which reason repeats and train that step on purpose.
keyPoints: Think out loud; interviewers assess how you reason.
Clarify and work an example before coding.
Brute force first, then name the bottleneck.
Write real, correct code; test it yourself; state time and space.
If stuck, narrate and ask for a specific hint.

sql.title: The routine applied: two-sum with its own tests
sql.code:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                       # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:
            return seen[target - x], i
        seen[x] = i
    return None

# step 6: tests from the clarifying questions and edge cases
assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == (0, 1)     # the worked example
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == (0, 1)             # duplicates
assert two_sum([], 5) is None                   # empty input
assert two_sum([1, 2], 10) is None              # no solution

exercise: Pick five medium problems from different topics. For each, set a 30-minute timer, use a plain editor, and speak aloud. Write the seven steps as comments before you code: your clarifying questions, an example with edge cases, the brute force and its cost, the bottleneck, the pattern. After coding, trace one example and write the final time and space. Afterwards note the step where you lost the most time.
pitfalls: Coding before clarifying what to return and what the input can contain.
Going silent when stuck.
Jumping to a clever solution you cannot finish instead of finishing the brute force.
Not testing, then being told about a bug you could have found.
Giving a time complexity without the space, or none at all.

interview.q: How do you approach an unfamiliar coding problem?
interview.a: Restate it and ask clarifying questions, work a small example and list edge cases, state the brute force and its cost, name the bottleneck and match it to a pattern, write clean code, trace it on the example and edge cases, and finish with time and space complexity. Narrate throughout.

interview.q: What do you do if you cannot see the optimal solution?
interview.a: Write the brute force and say its cost, then look for repeated work or a structure that removes the slow step. Try a smaller input by hand. If still stuck, say where you are blocked and ask for a specific hint. A correct slow solution is better than an incomplete clever one.

interview.q: Why do interviewers ask you to think out loud?
interview.a: They are assessing how you reason, not only the final code. Meta says to think out loud so the interviewer can follow your approach, and silence hides your reasoning and is read as a red flag.

interview.q: What makes code 'good' in a coding round?
interview.a: It is syntactically correct (not pseudocode), clear, handles edge cases and invalid input, and you have tested it yourself. Amazon says the most important thing an SDE writes is scalable, robust, well-tested code.

references.title: Preparing for your software engineering interview at Meta

basis: Sources: Microsoft's technical-interviewing page (clarifying questions, a plan before implementing, testing your own code), Meta's preparation post (think out loud, practice in a plain editor, review complexity) and Amazon's SDE II page (syntactically correct code, edge cases and invalid input, no brain teasers) were opened and read. The seven-step ordering is my synthesis of those pages, not a published procedure. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard: no company page I read gives hours, weights or pass rates, only the rounds and topics. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises or lowers it for other roles (for example, data structures and algorithms are core in the SDE plan).

scenes.title: Running a coding round, step by step

steps.title: The answer is how you get there
body: Interviewers watch your process as much as your result. Meta tells candidates to think out loud so the interviewer can follow, and Microsoft says it looks at how you break a problem down.
A calm, repeatable routine is more reliable than inspiration.

card.title: The seven steps
lines: 2 work an example and list edge cases
3 state a brute force and its cost
4 name the bottleneck, pick a pattern

steps.title: 1 and 2: clarify, then work an example
body: Restate the problem in your own words. Ask about input size, duplicates, negative numbers, sorted or not, empty input and what to return when there is no answer. Microsoft recommends clarifying questions and a plan before you implement.
Work a small example by hand and write down three edge cases: empty, one item, and the largest sensible input.

card.title: Two-sum: questions and cases
lines: Can numbers repeat? Can I use one element twice?
What if no pair exists? (return None)

steps.title: 3 and 4: brute force first, then the bottleneck
body: Say the simplest correct solution aloud and its cost: two nested loops, O(n^2). Then name what is slow: the inner loop is searching for a complement. A hash map replaces that search with a lookup.
A correct but slow solution is a good start. Jumping to a clever one you cannot finish is worse.

predict.question: In two-sum the brute force checks every pair. What is the bottleneck a hash map removes?
options: The inner search for the matching value
predict.why: For each x the inner loop searches for target - x, which costs O(n). A dict gives that lookup in O(1) on average, so the whole thing is O(n).

steps.title: 5: write real code
body: Amazon and Microsoft both say to write syntactically correct code in a language you know, not pseudocode. Amazon also asks for code that is robust and well tested. Use clear names, small helper functions and no clever one-liners you cannot explain.
Practise in a plain editor without autocomplete, as Meta suggests.

steps.title: 6: test it yourself before they ask
body: Trace your example line by line, then the edge cases. At Microsoft you test your own code; Amazon checks edge cases and invalid input. Finding your own bug and fixing it calmly is a positive signal.
Say what you are checking: 'with [3, 3] and target 6 the first 3 is stored, so the second finds it'.

card.title: Trace [3, 3], target 6
lines: i=0 x=3: 6-3=3 not in seen -> seen = {3: 0}

steps.title: 7: state time and space, then offer improvements
body: End with 'O(n) time, O(n) space', and say what you would change under different constraints: if memory were tight, sort and use two pointers for O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space.
Mention what you would test next. It shows you think past the first answer.

callout.text: Complexity is not decoration. 'O(n)' without space is half an answer.

steps.title: When you are stuck
body: Say what you know and what is blocking you. Return to the brute force and look for repeated work. Try a smaller input by hand. If you still cannot see it, ask for a specific hint rather than going silent: silence hides your reasoning, which is what is being assessed.
Design rounds use the same habit: ask questions to complete and validate your design, as Amazon puts it.

callout.text: Going silent is the most common avoidable mistake. Narrate even when you are unsure.

pill.text: stuck? go back to brute force

steps.title: Recap
body: Clarify, example, brute force, bottleneck, code, test, complexity. Practise the whole routine on every problem, with a timer and no autocomplete, until it is automatic.

everyday.plain: Follow the same steps every time, so you do not panic.
everyday.story: A driver follows a routine: check mirrors, indicate, then turn. In a coding round, the routine is: understand the question, try an example, think of a simple solution, find a faster one, write it, test it, and say how fast it is. A routine stops you from freezing.
maps: Take the slow safe route first
words: The simple solution that tries everything.
An unusual input, like an empty list, that can break code.
How the time and memory grow with the size of the input.

title: JavaScript Utility Functions: Debounce, Throttle, Promises
tagline: Small JavaScript helpers that control when functions run: debounce, throttle and promises.
explain: The Front End Interview Handbook lists JavaScript coding as one of five front end round types: you implement a function in JavaScript, often a utility such as throttle or a polyfill for a language or DOM API. Amazon's front end page names JavaScript, CSS and HTML as tested skills. The functions are short, so interviewers look at correctness, edge cases and how well you explain the language.
## Closures and timers

Most utilities are a function that returns a function and keeps some state in a closure: a timer id, a cache, a handler list. Debounce clears and restarts a timer on every call, so a burst of calls ends in one call after the pause. Throttle lets one call through per interval and keeps the latest arguments for a trailing call. Pass this and the arguments through with fn.apply(this, args).
## Caching and composition

memoize stores results by a key made from the arguments. once runs a function a single time. curry collects arguments until it has fn.length of them. Each is a few lines; the discussion is about keys, memory growth and what happens with this.
## Promises

Promise.all returns an array in input order whatever order the promises finish, rejects immediately with the first rejection, and fulfils at once for an empty input; values that are not promises are kept as they are. Writing it yourself checks that you understand the order, the counter and the rejection rule. A retry helper adds loops, await and exponential backoff.
## Emitters and cloning

An event emitter maps event names to handler lists. Iterate a copy of the list when emitting so unsubscribing inside a handler is safe. For deep copies, JSON round trips lose functions, undefined and Dates and fail on circular references; structuredClone preserves cycles and throws DataCloneError for values it cannot serialize.
## How to talk through it

Say what state the closure keeps, then trace three calls: first, repeated, and last. Write asserts for the behavior before the implementation if you can. State what you did not handle (cancel methods, immediate option) and offer to add it.
keyPoints: Utilities are closures that keep state: a timer, a cache, handlers.
Debounce: one call after a pause. Throttle: at most one call per interval, with a trailing call.
Promise.all keeps input order and rejects with the first rejection.
Iterate a copy of the handlers when emitting.
structuredClone handles cycles; JSON round trips do not.

sql.title: Debounce and throttle, tested
Memoize, once and curry
Promise.all and retry with backoff
Event emitter and structuredClone

exercise: Write each of these from a blank file, with asserts, in 15 minutes each: debounce (with a cancel method), throttle (leading and trailing), memoize with a custom key function, once, curry, Promise.all, Promise.race, retry with backoff, an event emitter with once(), and flatten for nested arrays. After each one list the edge cases you did not handle.
pitfalls: Forgetting to pass this and the arguments through to the wrapped function.
Debounce that never clears the previous timer.
Throttle that drops the last call, so the final state is never applied.
Promise.all that returns results in completion order instead of input order.
Using JSON round trips for deep clone and losing Dates and functions or crashing on cycles.

interview.q: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
interview.a: Debounce waits until calls stop for a given time and then runs once, so a burst produces one call at the end. Throttle limits the rate: at most one call per interval, usually with an immediate first call and a trailing call with the latest arguments. Use debounce for search-as-you-type and throttle for scroll handlers.

interview.q: How does Promise.all behave?
interview.a: It fulfils with an array of the results in input order, regardless of completion order, once all inputs fulfil. It rejects immediately with the first rejection reason and does not cancel the other work. An empty iterable fulfils immediately, and values that are not promises are kept as they are.

interview.q: How would you implement memoize and what are the pitfalls?
interview.a: Keep a Map in a closure from a key built from the arguments to the result, and check it before calling the function. Pitfalls: building the key (JSON.stringify ignores functions and fails on cycles), unbounded cache growth, and functions that are not pure.

interview.q: How do you deep copy an object in JavaScript?
interview.a: structuredClone copies nested objects, Dates, Maps, Sets and circular references, and throws a DataCloneError if a value, such as a function, cannot be cloned. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) drops functions and undefined, turns Dates into strings and throws on cycles.

basis: Round type: the Front End Interview Handbook (read) lists JavaScript coding as one of five round types and gives throttle and polyfills as examples; Amazon's front end page (read) names JavaScript, CSS and HTML. Promise.all's order, rejection and empty-input behavior and structuredClone's cycle support and DataCloneError are from the MDN pages I read. The debounce and throttle definitions are standard practice, stated as general knowledge, and every code sample is executed with Node and passes its asserts. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard. The Front End Interview Handbook and Amazon's front end page tell me which round types exist; no page I read says how long to prepare for each.

scenes.title: JavaScript utility functions, step by step

steps.title: The round: implement a utility
body: The Front End Interview Handbook describes the JavaScript coding round as 'implement a function in JavaScript': a utility such as throttle, or a polyfill for a language or DOM API. You are judged on correct behavior, edge cases and how clearly you explain closures and timers.
These functions are small, so the interview is about details: what happens on a second call, which arguments and `this` are passed on, what happens at the end.

steps.title: Problem: every keystroke calls the API
body: A search box fires a request on each keystroke. Typing 'react' sends five requests; four are wasted and they can come back out of order.
We want to wait until typing pauses, or to cap how often the function runs.

steps.title: Debounce: run after the pause
body: Debounce delays a call until a quiet period (wait ms) has passed since the last call. Each new call clears the previous timer and starts a new one, so a burst produces one call, at the end.
Use it for search-as-you-type, window resize handlers and auto-save.

steps.title: Throttle: at most once per interval
body: Throttle lets a call through at most once every wait ms. The first call runs immediately; calls during the wait are collapsed into one trailing call with the latest arguments.
Use it for scroll and mousemove handlers, where you want regular updates, not just one at the end.

card.title: Debounce versus throttle
lines: debounce  waits for silence; one call at the end of a burst
throttle  steady rate; one call per interval

predict.question: throttle(fn, 100) is called five times in a row within 1 ms, with arguments 1 to 5. Which calls reach fn?
predict.why: The first call runs at once (leading edge). The calls with 2 to 4 are overwritten, and the last arguments (5) run once the interval has passed (trailing edge).

steps.title: Memoize, once and curry
body: memoize caches results keyed by the arguments, so a pure function is not recomputed. once runs a function the first time and returns that result afterwards. curry turns f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c) by collecting arguments until fn.length are present.
Mention the cost: memoize needs a cache key (JSON.stringify is simple but ignores functions and breaks on cycles) and can grow without bound.

steps.title: Promise.all and retry
body: Promise.all fulfils with an array in the order of the input, regardless of which finishes first, and rejects as soon as any input rejects, with that first reason. An empty input fulfils immediately; non-promise values are kept as they are (MDN).
A retry helper loops over attempts, waits longer each time (exponential backoff) and rethrows the last error if every attempt fails.

card.title: Rules to implement
lines: result[i] = value of input i (order preserved)

steps.title: Event emitter and deep clone
body: An event emitter keeps a map from event name to a list of handlers; on adds, off removes, emit calls each. Iterate over a copy so a handler that unsubscribes does not skip another handler.

For deep clone, JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) drops functions, undefined and Dates and fails on cycles. structuredClone copies cycles and many built-in types and throws DataCloneError for values it cannot serialize, such as functions.

callout.text: In the interview say which edge cases you handle (cycles, Dates, functions) and which you do not.

steps.title: Recap
body: Closures hold the state (the timer, the cache, the handler map). Say what each call does, what the edge cases are and what you did not handle. Write the test calls first: they show you understand the behavior.
Practise by writing each utility from memory, then run it with asserts.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 what state does the closure keep?
2 are this and the arguments passed on?
3 first call, repeated call, last call

everyday.plain: Small helper functions that control when and how often other functions run.
everyday.story: A lift's door button: if people press it ten times quickly, the door still closes just once, after they stop pressing (debounce). A security guard who lets only one person in per minute, no matter how many arrive (throttle). These are common helpers in web pages, for example for a search box.
words: A function that remembers the variables around it.
Wait until calls stop for a while, then run once.
Run at most once in a given time.
An object that stands for a result that arrives later.

title: UI Coding Round: Autocomplete, Modal, Tabs
tagline: Build a search box, a pop-up or tabs that work with a keyboard and a screen reader.
explain: The Front End Interview Handbook describes the user interface coding round as building a UI component, an app or a game with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The components are small (tabs, a modal, an autocomplete, a paginated table). The way to stand out is to cover what a demo skips: keyboard use, accessibility, loading and error states, and out-of-order responses.
## A plan

Clarify the requirements and what is out of scope. Write down the state: what changes, and who owns it. List the events a user can cause. Then write markup with the right roles, and finally handle loading, empty and error. Everything on screen should be a function of the state.
## Races and stale responses

Asynchronous requests can return out of order. In an autocomplete, a slow response for an earlier query can arrive after the response for the current one. Fix it by tagging each request with an increasing id and applying a response only if its id is the latest, or by aborting the previous request. Debouncing the input reduces requests but does not remove the race.
## Accessibility patterns (W3C ARIA Authoring Practices)

- Combobox: the input has role combobox; aria-expanded shows whether the popup is open; aria-controls points to it; aria-activedescendant names the highlighted option while focus stays in the input. Down Arrow moves into the popup, Enter accepts, Escape closes it.
- Modal dialog: role dialog and aria-modal true, a visible title referenced with aria-labelledby. Focus moves inside on open, Tab and Shift+Tab wrap inside, Escape closes, and focus returns to the opener.
- Tabs: roles tablist, tab and tabpanel; aria-selected and aria-controls on tabs; aria-labelledby on panels; Left and Right Arrow move between tabs and wrap; Home and End are optional.
## The four states
Success is only one of four. Show loading, empty (no results) and error (with a retry) as well. Keep fetching separate from rendering so each state is a short branch.
## How to talk through it
Narrate the plan, say what you will skip and why, and mention what you would test: a stale response, an empty result and keyboard-only use.
keyPoints: State first: everything on screen is a function of it.
Guard against stale responses with request ids or an AbortController.
Combobox, dialog and tabs each have documented roles and keys (W3C APG).
A modal must move focus in, trap Tab, close on Escape and return focus.
Handle loading, empty and error, not only success.

sql.title: Stale-response guard
Keyboard logic for tabs and a listbox
Accessible markup (W3C APG attributes)

exercise: Build each of these in a plain HTML file in 45 minutes without a framework: an autocomplete (debounced, with a stale-response guard, keyboard navigation and loading, empty and error states), a modal dialog (focus in, Tab trap, Escape, focus returned), and a tabs component. Test with the keyboard only, then with a screen reader if you have one. Write down what you would add with more time.
pitfalls: Setting the list from whichever response arrives last.
A modal that does not move focus in, trap Tab or return focus to the opener.
Making arrow keys scroll the page instead of moving the highlight (call preventDefault).
Only building the success state.
Starting with CSS before the state and events are clear.

interview.q: How do you handle out-of-order responses in an autocomplete?
interview.a: Tag each request with an increasing id and apply a response only if its id is still the latest, or abort the previous request with an AbortController. Also debounce the input so fewer requests are made, but the guard is still needed.

interview.q: What makes a modal dialog accessible?
interview.a: role=dialog with aria-modal=true and a visible title referenced by aria-labelledby. Focus moves into the dialog when it opens, Tab and Shift+Tab wrap inside it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. Content outside must really be unreachable when aria-modal is set.

interview.q: Which ARIA roles and keys does a tabs component need?
interview.a: A tablist containing tab elements with aria-selected and aria-controls, and tabpanels with aria-labelledby. Tab focuses the active tab; Left and Right Arrow move between tabs and wrap; Home and End jump to the first and last (optional). Space or Enter activates a tab if it is not activated on focus.

interview.q: What would you cover first with 10 minutes left?
interview.a: The error and empty states and keyboard support, because they show correctness and accessibility, before polishing styles. Then state what you would test.

basis: Round type from the Front End Interview Handbook (read); the roles, attributes and keyboard behavior for dialog, tabs and combobox are from the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices pages I read. The stale-response guard is standard practice (general knowledge). The plan and the four states are my synthesis, and all code samples run in Node and pass their asserts. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard. The Front End Interview Handbook and Amazon's front end page tell me which round types exist; no page I read says how long to prepare for each.

scenes.title: A UI coding round, step by step

steps.title: What a UI coding round tests
body: In a UI coding round you build a small component or app (tabs, modal, autocomplete, a paginated table) with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Interviewers look for working behavior first, then the things that separate a demo from a component: keyboard use, accessibility, loading and error states, and clean state handling.
Plan before you type: requirements, the state, the events, then markup.

card.title: A plan that works
lines: 1 requirements and what is out of scope
2 state: what changes and who owns it
3 events: what the user can do

steps.title: Model the state first
body: For an autocomplete the state is small: the query, the list of suggestions, the highlighted index, whether the list is open, and the request status (idle, loading, error). Everything on screen is a function of that state.
Writing it down first avoids the tangle of DOM updates that makes these rounds go wrong.

steps.title: The race: a slow old answer arrives last
body: The user types 'ab', then 'abc'. The request for 'ab' is slow and answers after the request for 'abc'. If you set the list from whichever response arrives last, the box shows suggestions for 'ab' under a query of 'abc'.
Debouncing reduces requests but does not remove this race.

predict.question: Two requests are in flight: 'ab' (slow) and 'abc' (fast). 'ab' answers last and the code just sets items from each response. What does the user see?
predict.why: The late response overwrites the newer one. Each response must be checked against the latest request, or the older request canceled.

steps.title: Fix: ignore stale responses
body: Give every request an increasing id (or use an AbortController to cancel the previous request) and apply a response only if its id is still the latest. Late answers are dropped.
Also debounce the input to send fewer requests.

card.title: JavaScript
lines: if (id === latest) onResult(res);   // drop stale answers

steps.title: Combobox keyboard and ARIA
body: The ARIA Authoring Practices combobox pattern: the input has role combobox, aria-expanded says whether the popup is open, aria-controls points to it, and aria-activedescendant names the highlighted option while real focus stays in the input. Down Arrow moves into the list, Enter accepts, Escape closes it.
Move the highlight with the arrow keys and keep it inside the list.

card.title: Roles and keys (APG)
lines: focus   stays in the input; aria-activedescendant = option

steps.title: Modal dialog: focus is the hard part
body: APG for a modal dialog: role=dialog, aria-modal=true, and a visible title named with aria-labelledby. When it opens, focus moves inside. Tab and Shift+Tab wrap inside the dialog. Escape closes it. On close, focus returns to the element that opened it.
Most home-made modals forget the last two.

card.title: Checklist (APG)
lines: on open: move focus into the dialog
on close: focus back to the opener

pill.text: focus moves in, Tab wraps, Escape closes

steps.title: Tabs: roles and arrow keys
body: APG for tabs: a tablist containing tabs, each with aria-selected and aria-controls pointing at a tabpanel; each tabpanel has aria-labelledby. Tab moves focus to the active tab; Left and Right Arrow move between tabs and wrap; Home and End are optional shortcuts.
Only the active tab is in the page's tab order, so arrow keys do the navigation inside the group.

card.title: Roles and keys (APG)
lines: Left / Right: previous and next tab, wrapping

steps.title: Every component has four states
body: Show loading, empty (no results), error (with a retry) and success. Interviewers notice when only the success path exists. Keep the data fetch separate from the markup so each state is one small branch.
Then mention what you would test: a stale response, an empty result, keyboard-only use.

callout.text: If you have 10 minutes left, add the error state and keyboard support before polishing styles.

steps.title: Recap

title: Frontend System Design: Feeds, Caching, Real Time
tagline: Plan a web app: how it gets data, stores it, shows long lists and updates live.
explain: Frontend system design asks you to design the architecture of a client application, for example a news feed, a chat or an autocomplete. The Front End Interview Handbook lists it as one of five round types. It is not about writing code; it is about choosing the pieces, drawing how data moves and stating the trade-offs.
## Clarify and draw the data flow

Ask about users and scale, platforms and network conditions, what updates live and what must work offline. Draw the path: browser, CDN and static assets, API, database. Decide what the client owns (view state, cache) and what the server owns (the source of truth).
## Client data: cache and pagination

Cache fetched data on the client and serve it immediately while refetching in the background (stale-while-revalidate). In TanStack Query data is stale after staleTime (default 0) and an unused query is garbage collected after gcTime (default five minutes). Paginate with a cursor, not a page number, because a feed changes while you read it.
## Rendering large lists

A very large DOM makes style calculation and updates slower. Windowing (virtualisation) renders only the visible items, plus a few extra, and reuses nodes while scrolling, so the DOM size follows the viewport, not the data (web.dev).
## Updates: optimistic and real time

Optimistic UI shows the result at once and rolls back on failure; React's useOptimistic shows the optimistic value only while the action is pending and reverts if it throws. For live data, server-sent events are one-way with automatic reconnect (without HTTP/2, browsers limit open connections per domain), and WebSocket is two-way without polling but has no backpressure.
## Quality
Lazy-load code and images, avoid layout shifts, keep handlers cheap, support keyboard and screen readers, and plan for offline, slow networks, retries and expired sessions.
## A worked example: search autocomplete

Requirements: suggestions as the user types, under about 200 ms feel, keyboard and screen-reader support, works on slow phones. Data flow: input, debounce, request, results. Client: a small cache keyed by the query (the second time someone types 'rea' there is no request), a request id or abort so a slow old response cannot overwrite a new one, and a limit on the number of suggestions rendered. Server: prefix index and a short cache. Accessibility: the combobox pattern. Failure: show recent searches when offline and an inline error with retry. Every choice has a cost you should state: a bigger client cache uses memory and can show stale suggestions.
## Numbers worth stating

Say how many items, how big each response is and how often it changes, even as rough figures. 'About 20 items of 1 KB per page, 10 pages scrolled in a session, so around 200 KB held in the cache' is more useful than 'it should be fast'. Label them as assumptions and say which one would change the design if it were wrong.
## How to talk through it
Follow a fixed order: requirements, data flow, client state and cache, rendering and performance, updates, quality. For each choice name the alternative and the trade-off.
keyPoints: Clarify, then draw the data flow before choosing pieces.
Client cache with stale-while-revalidate: show cached data, refetch in the background.
Virtualise long lists: DOM size follows the viewport.
Cursor pagination does not repeat or skip items when the feed changes.
SSE is one-way push; WebSocket is two-way with no backpressure.

For each, write down two alternatives you rejected and why, and one failure case (offline, slow network, stale data) with what the user sees.

interview.q: How would you build an infinite-scrolling feed?
interview.a: Fetch pages with a cursor, prefetch the next page when the last rows near the viewport, keep a client cache keyed by request, and virtualise the list so the DOM stays small. Add loading and error states, and an optimistic update for actions like likes with a rollback on failure.

interview.q: What is stale-while-revalidate on the client?
interview.a: Return cached data immediately and refetch in the background, then update the screen when fresh data arrives. In TanStack Query data is stale after staleTime (default 0) and unused cache entries are garbage collected after gcTime (default five minutes).

interview.q: SSE or WebSocket?
interview.a: Server-sent events are one-way (server to client), plain HTTP, reconnect automatically, but without HTTP/2 browsers limit open connections per domain (MDN says 6). WebSocket is a two-way channel without polling, but has no backpressure, so a fast sender can overwhelm a slow client. Use SSE for push-only feeds and WebSocket for frequent two-way messaging.

interview.q: What is an optimistic update and what can go wrong?
interview.a: Updating the UI before the server confirms, so the app feels instant. It must be rolled back if the request fails, and it can conflict with changes made elsewhere in the meantime. React's useOptimistic shows the optimistic value only while the action is pending and reverts if it throws.

basis: Round type: the Front End Interview Handbook (read). Windowing is from the web.dev article, optimistic updates from the React useOptimistic reference, SSE and WebSocket behavior (one-way, reconnect, the per-domain limit without HTTP/2, no backpressure) from the MDN pages, and staleTime and gcTime defaults from the TanStack Query caching guide, all read. The six-part order of the answer is my own framework, and the numbers in the diagram are illustrative. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard. The Front End Interview Handbook and Amazon's front end page tell me which round types exist; no page I read says how long to prepare for each.

steps.title: The prompt: design a feed

body: Keep fetched data in a client cache keyed by what was requested. A stale-while-revalidate policy returns cached data immediately and refetches in the background. body: A feed changes while you read it, so page 2 by offset can repeat or skip items when new posts arrive. A cursor (the id or time of the last item) continues exactly where you stopped, and stays fast for deep scrolling.

It makes the app feel instant but you must handle failure.

WebSocket is a two-way channel with no polling, but it has no built-in backpressure, so a fast sender can overwhelm a slow client.

title: Design an LLM Application (RAG, Evals, Cost)
tagline: An AI assistant that answers from your own documents: find the pages, write the answer, check it, control the cost.
explain: A growing share of ML design interviews ask you to design an LLM-based system, for example a support assistant that answers from a company's documents. One 2026 article says this is now the most common ML design prompt; it is one author's opinion with no data, so treat it as a signal rather than a fact. The structure of a good answer is stable even as tools change.
## Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

Instead of asking the model to remember your documents, look up relevant passages and put them in the prompt. Offline, split documents into chunks and index them with embeddings for meaning and a keyword index for exact terms. Online, embed the question and fetch the best chunks. When documents change you re-index; the model is not retrained.
## Making retrieval good

Chunks lose context: a sentence about 'the quarter' does not say which company. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval prepends generated context to each chunk before indexing, and reports from its own experiments that the top-20 failure rate fell from 5.7% to 3.7% with contextual embeddings, to 2.9% adding keyword search, and to 1.9% adding a reranker (not independently verified). The general lesson: combine meaning and keyword search, rerank, and tune how many chunks go in the prompt.
## Guardrails

Retrieved text and user input are untrusted and can contain instructions (prompt injection). Check access rights at retrieval time, give the model only the powers it needs, validate outputs, show sources, and refuse or escalate when the answer is not supported.
## Cost and latency

Cost scales with tokens. A long stable prefix repeated on every call can be cached: Anthropic's docs describe a 1.25 times cache write price for the 5-minute lifetime and a 0.1 times read price (some models differ), a default lifetime of 5 minutes and a requirement that the prefix match exactly. Other levers are a smaller model for easy questions, caching whole answers and trimming the retrieved context. Check current prices before quoting any figure.
## Evaluation

Define specific, measurable success criteria, build evals that mirror the real task including edge cases, automate grading (exact match, code-graded, model-graded), and favour more automatically graded questions over a few hand-graded ones. Grade with a different model from the one being evaluated. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.
## How to talk through it

Follow the order: requirements and the cost of a wrong answer, indexing, retrieval, prompt, guardrails, cost and latency, evaluation, monitoring. Name what you would measure and the first thing you would try if quality is poor (usually retrieval).
keyPoints: RAG puts retrieved passages in the prompt; re-index documents, do not retrain.
Combine meaning (embeddings) and keyword search, then rerank.
Treat retrieved text and user input as untrusted; check access at retrieval time.
A stable prompt prefix can be cached; check the provider's current pricing.
Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, with an automated eval set.

sql.title: Chunking and a toy retriever, with a recall@k check
sql.code:
import math, re
from collections import Counter

def chunk(text, size=40, overlap=10):
    words = text.split()
    step = size - overlap
    return [' '.join(words[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, max(len(words) - overlap, 1), step)]

words = ' '.join(f'w{i}' for i in range(105))
parts = chunk(words)
assert len(parts) == 4 and parts[0].startswith('w0 ') and parts[-1].endswith('w104')
assert parts[1].startswith('w30 ')                       # chunks overlap by 10 words

def vec(t):
    return Counter(re.findall(r'[a-z]+', t.lower()))

def cos(a, b):
    dot = sum(a[k] * b.get(k, 0) for k in a)
    na = math.sqrt(sum(v * v for v in a.values()))
    nb = math.sqrt(sum(v * v for v in b.values()))
    return dot / (na * nb) if na and nb else 0.0

def retrieve(query, docs, k=2):
    q = vec(query)
    ranked = sorted(range(len(docs)), key=lambda i: -cos(q, vec(docs[i])))
    return ranked[:k]

docs = ['Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase if the item is unused.',
        'Shipping takes 3 to 5 business days within the country.',
        'Our office is closed on public holidays.']
assert retrieve('how long do refunds take', docs, k=1) == [0]
assert retrieve('how many days does shipping take', docs, k=1) == [1]

evalset = [('how long do refunds take', 0), ('when is shipping delivered business days', 1), ('are you open on public holidays', 2)]
recall_at_1 = sum(retrieve(q, docs, 1)[0] == want for q, want in evalset) / len(evalset)
assert recall_at_1 == 1.0

sql.title: Prompt caching arithmetic (illustrative prices)
sql.code:
def cost(calls, prefix, new, out, in_price, out_price, cache=False, write=1.25, read=0.1):
    """Prices are $ per million tokens. write and read are multipliers of the base input price."""
    per_m = 1_000_000
    if not cache:
        return calls * ((prefix + new) * in_price + out * out_price) / per_m
    first = (prefix * in_price * write + new * in_price + out * out_price) / per_m   # the first call writes the cache
    rest = (prefix * in_price * read + new * in_price + out * out_price) / per_m     # later calls read it
    return first + (calls - 1) * rest

no_cache = cost(100, 10_000, 500, 300, in_price=4, out_price=20)
with_cache = cost(100, 10_000, 500, 300, in_price=4, out_price=20, cache=True)
assert round(no_cache, 3) == 4.8
assert round(with_cache, 3) == 1.246
assert with_cache < no_cache / 3              # large saving when the prefix is long and reused within the cache lifetime

sql.title: A tiny exact-match eval harness
sql.code:
def run_evals(answer_fn, cases):
    results = []
    for question, expected in cases:
        got = answer_fn(question)
        results.append({'question': question, 'ok': got.strip().lower() == expected.strip().lower()})
    return sum(r['ok'] for r in results) / len(results), results

fake_model = {'capital of france?': ' Paris ', 'capital of spain?': 'Barcelona'}.get
score, detail = run_evals(lambda q: fake_model(q, ''), [('capital of france?', 'paris'), ('capital of spain?', 'madrid')])
assert score == 0.5
assert [d['ok'] for d in detail] == [True, False]      # regressions show up as a drop in the score

exercise: Design an assistant that answers questions from 5,000 internal policy documents. Write: the requirements and the cost of a wrong answer; the chunking and indexing plan; how you retrieve (and what k you start with); the prompt; the checks for access rights and prompt injection; a cost estimate for 10,000 questions a day using made-up token counts and prices; an evaluation set of 30 questions with expected sources and answers; and the first change you would try if recall@5 is 70%.
pitfalls: Skipping evaluation, so no change can be shown to help.
Putting too many chunks in the prompt, adding cost and burying the answer.
Ignoring access rights: the retriever returns documents the user may not read.
Trusting retrieved text or user input as if it were instructions.
Quoting prices from memory instead of checking the provider's pricing page.

interview.q: What is RAG and why use it?
interview.a: Retrieval-augmented generation looks up relevant passages in your documents and puts them in the prompt, so the model answers from your data. It lets you update knowledge by re-indexing instead of retraining, lets you cite sources, and reduces made-up answers when the model is told to answer only from the passages.

interview.q: How do you improve retrieval quality?
interview.a: Combine embeddings with keyword search, add context to chunks before indexing, rerank a wider candidate set and keep the best, and tune chunk size and k with a labeled evaluation set. Anthropic reports a drop in top-20 retrieval failures from 5.7% to 1.9% using contextual embeddings, contextual keyword search and a reranker, from its own experiments.

interview.q: How would you evaluate an LLM application?
interview.a: Define specific, measurable success criteria, build a task-specific eval set with edge cases, automate grading (exact match, code-graded, model-graded with a different model), and evaluate retrieval (is the right chunk returned?) separately from generation (is the answer correct and grounded?). Track latency and cost as well.

interview.q: How do you reduce the cost of an LLM feature?
interview.a: Cut tokens (shorter retrieved context, tighter prompts), use prompt caching for a long stable prefix reused within its lifetime, route easy questions to a smaller model, and cache repeated answers. Measure cost per answer in your evals, and check current prices.

references.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations (Anthropic docs)

basis: Why it is here: a 2026 article (one author, no data; read) says 'design an LLM-based system' is now the usual ML design prompt, and Chip Huyen's book says almost every company asks an ML system design question. The 5.7%, 3.7%, 2.9% and 1.9% figures are Anthropic's own experiments, not independently verified. The cache multipliers (1.25 write for 5 minutes, 0.1 read, 5-minute default, exact prefix match) and the evaluation guidance are from Anthropic's docs pages I read; model-specific prices change, so the code uses illustrative prices. Prompt injection is described from general security knowledge. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard.

title: Operating Systems: Processes, Scheduling, Virtual Memory
tagline: How the computer shares time and memory between programs.
explain: Amazon's list of interview topics includes operating systems. Interviews ask for the concepts, not kernel code: what a process is, how the scheduler decides, what virtual memory does and what happens on a page fault. The free textbook Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (OSTEP) organizes the subject into virtualization, concurrency and persistence; this lesson covers the first part.
## Processes and time sharing

A process is a running program with its own address space and registers. The OS shares the CPU by running one process for a short slice, saving its registers, restoring another's and continuing: a context switch. Switching is overhead, so slices that are too short waste time.
## Scheduling

- First-in-first-out: simple, but a long job delays everything behind it.
- Shortest job first: lowest average turnaround, but needs job lengths and can starve long jobs.
- Round robin: each process gets a time slice in turn: good response time, worse average turnaround.
The right choice depends on whether you care about throughput, response time or fairness.
## Virtual memory and paging

Each process gets a private address space. Hardware and the OS translate virtual addresses to physical frames through a page table, which isolates processes and lets the address space exceed RAM. When a needed page is not in RAM the access faults and the OS loads it from disk, which is far slower than memory.
## Page replacement

When RAM is full the OS evicts a page. LRU evicts the least recently used; FIFO evicts the oldest. For the sequence 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO takes 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4: more memory gave more faults (Belady's anomaly). Real systems approximate LRU.
## Processes, threads and system calls

Threads in a process share its address space and have their own stacks; processes are isolated and heavier to create. A system call moves from user mode to kernel mode so the kernel can provide a service, such as file access.
## How to talk through it
Define the term, give the trade-off, then an example with numbers. Interviewers often hand you a small table of jobs or page references to simulate on paper.
keyPoints: A process is a running program with its own address space; the scheduler time-shares the CPU.
A context switch saves and restores state and is pure overhead.
Scheduling trades turnaround, response time and fairness.
Virtual memory isolates processes; a page fault loads a page from slow disk.
LRU does not suffer Belady's anomaly; FIFO can.

sql.title: Scheduling simulation: FIFO and round robin
sql.code:
def fifo(bursts):
    t, done, first = 0, [], []
    for b in bursts:
        first.append(t)
        t += b
        done.append(t)
    return done, first

def round_robin(bursts, quantum):
    remaining, t = list(bursts), 0
    done, first = [0] * len(bursts), [None] * len(bursts)
    queue = list(range(len(bursts)))
    while queue:
        i = queue.pop(0)
        if first[i] is None:
            first[i] = t
        run = min(quantum, remaining[i])
        t += run
        remaining[i] -= run
        if remaining[i]:
            queue.append(i)
        else:
            done[i] = t
    return done, first

bursts = [5, 3, 8]
fd, ff = fifo(bursts)
rd, rf = round_robin(bursts, 2)
assert fd == [5, 8, 16] and rd == [12, 9, 16]
avg = lambda xs: sum(xs) / len(xs)
assert round(avg(fd), 2) == 9.67 and round(avg(rd), 2) == 12.33      # round robin: worse turnaround
assert round(avg(ff), 2) == 4.33 and avg(rf) == 2.0                  # round robin: better response time
