Address translation with a tiny page table

exercise: By hand, then in code: for jobs with burst times 6, 2, 4, 8 arriving together, compute the completion time of each job under FIFO, shortest-job-first and round robin with a slice of 3, and the average turnaround and response time of each. Then take the page reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 and count the faults with 3 frames under FIFO and LRU. Write one sentence on which policy you would choose for an interactive system and why.
pitfalls: Mixing up a process and a thread: threads share the address space, processes do not.
Saying virtual memory is 'extra RAM' instead of translation plus isolation, backed by disk.
Forgetting that a context switch has a cost.
Claiming one scheduling policy is best without naming the metric.
Believing more frames can never increase FIFO faults.

interview.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
interview.a: A process is a running program with its own address space and resources. Threads in the same process share its address space and have their own stacks and registers. Threads are cheaper to create and switch, and communicate through shared memory, which needs synchronization; processes are isolated.

interview.q: What is a context switch?
interview.a: Saving the state (registers) of the running process and restoring another's so it can resume. It is how the OS time-shares the CPU, and it is overhead because no useful work happens during the switch and caches may be cooled.

interview.q: What happens on a page fault?
interview.a: The process accessed a virtual page that is not mapped to a frame in RAM. The OS handles the trap, finds the page (on disk or a new zeroed page), loads it into a free or evicted frame, updates the page table and restarts the instruction. Disk access is much slower than RAM, so frequent faults hurt performance.

interview.q: Compare FIFO and LRU page replacement.
interview.a: FIFO evicts the oldest page, LRU the least recently used. LRU matches typical locality better. FIFO can show Belady's anomaly: for 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 it takes 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4. LRU never gets worse with more frames. Exact LRU is costly, so systems approximate it.

basis: Why it is here: Amazon's interview-topic page (read) lists operating systems. OSTEP's table of contents (read) gives the structure (virtualization with chapters on processes, scheduling, address spaces, paging, TLBs and swapping; then concurrency). The specific scheduling and page-replacement numbers in this lesson are computed by the code samples, which run and pass their asserts, and the definitions are standard operating-systems knowledge. Priority 3 is my judgment: interviews ask the concepts, rarely in depth, so it comes after coding and design. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard.

scenes.title: Processes and virtual memory, step by step

steps.title: A process is a running program
body: A program is a file on disk. A process is that program running: it has its own memory, registers and open files. The operating system lets many processes appear to run at once on few CPUs.

OSTEP, the free textbook by Arpaci-Dusseau, organizes operating systems into three pieces: virtualization, concurrency and persistence. This lesson covers the first; the next lesson covers concurrency.

steps.title: Time sharing and the context switch
body: The OS runs one process for a short time, then saves its registers and restores another's: a context switch. Switching fast enough gives each process the illusion of its own CPU.
A switch is overhead: it saves and restores state and can cool CPU caches, so switching too often wastes time.

steps.title: Scheduling: what to run next
body: The scheduler decides. First-in-first-out is simple but one long job delays everyone behind it. Shortest-job-first minimizes average turnaround but needs to know job lengths and can starve long jobs. Round robin gives each process a time slice in turn, which gives good response time but a worse average turnaround.
There is no best policy, only a trade-off between turnaround time, response time and fairness.

predict.question: Three jobs need 5, 3 and 8 time units and all arrive at once. Compared with first-in-first-out, what does round robin with a slice of 2 do to the AVERAGE turnaround time?
predict.why: FIFO finishes at 5, 8 and 16 (average 9.67). Round robin finishes at 12, 9 and 16 (average 12.33): worse turnaround, but every job starts within 4 units (better response time).

steps.title: Virtual memory: each process has its own addresses
body: Each process sees a private, large address space, as if it owned the memory. The OS and hardware translate each virtual address to a physical one, so processes cannot read each other's memory, and a process can use more address space than there is RAM.
The mapping is kept in a page table.

hud.v: a process cannot see another's memory

steps.title: Paging and page faults
body: Memory is split into fixed-size pages. A page table maps a process's virtual pages to physical frames. If a page is not in RAM, the access causes a page fault: the OS fetches the page from disk, which is thousands of times slower than RAM.
Because disk access is so slow, a program that touches memory in a scattered way (thrashing) can crawl.

steps.title: Page replacement: what to evict
body: When RAM is full, the OS must evict a page. LRU evicts the page unused for longest; FIFO evicts the oldest. For one famous sequence, FIFO with 3 frames takes 9 faults but with 4 frames takes 10: more memory made it worse (Belady's anomaly). LRU does not do this.
Real systems approximate LRU because tracking exact recency is expensive.

steps.title: Process or thread, and system calls
body: A process has its own address space. Threads inside a process share its address space (and so can talk through memory, and need locks) but have their own stack and registers. A system call is how a program asks the kernel for a service, such as reading a file; it switches from user mode to kernel mode.
Creating a process is heavier than creating a thread; a crash in one process does not take down others.

card.title: Compare
lines: process  own address space, heavier, isolated
thread   shares the process's memory, lighter, needs locks
syscall  user mode to kernel mode for a kernel service

steps.title: Recap
body: Virtualization: the OS gives each process the illusion of its own CPU (time sharing, scheduling) and its own memory (virtual memory, paging). Know the vocabulary and the trade-offs, and be able to simulate a scheduler and a page replacement by hand.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 4 virtual memory, page table, page fault

everyday.plain: The operating system shares the computer among programs and keeps their memory separate.
everyday.story: A teacher with one board serves many classes. He gives each class a short slot (time sharing), so all seem to move forward. Each class has its own notebook, and they cannot read each other's. If the board is full, old content is stored in a cupboard and brought back when needed (virtual memory).
words: A running program with its own memory.
The part of the system that decides which program runs next.
A trick that gives each program its own large, private memory space.
A moment when needed data is not in memory and must be loaded.

title: Concurrency: Threads, Locks, Deadlock, the GIL
tagline: What goes wrong when many things run at once, and the tools that prevent it.
explain: Concurrency comes up in system design (shared state, workers), in LLD questions (a thread-safe cache or parking lot) and as a topic on its own. You need the vocabulary and a few patterns you can write correctly. OSTEP's concurrency part covers threads, locks, condition variables, semaphores and concurrency bugs.
## Threads and shared memory

Threads in a process share its address space and have their own stack and registers. Sharing makes communication cheap and makes bugs easy. counter += 1 is really load, add, store; if the OS switches threads between those steps, two threads can both read 50 and both write 51, losing an update. OSTEP calls this a race condition: the result depends on timing.
## Critical sections and locks

Code that touches shared data is a critical section. Mutual exclusion means only one thread executes it at a time. A lock provides it: acquire before, release after. In Python use 'with lock:' so the lock is released even on an exception. Keep critical sections short and keep slow work, such as I/O, outside them.
## Deadlock

A deadlock is a state where threads wait for each other forever. It needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and a circular wait. Break the circular wait by taking locks in one global order. Other defences: acquire with a timeout, hold fewer locks, or use a queue instead of shared variables.
## Python specifics

CPython's global interpreter lock allows one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time and is released during I/O. Threads therefore suit I/O-bound work; for CPU-bound Python use multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor. Free-threaded builds (3.13 onwards) can disable the GIL but are not the default. The GIL does not make your own read-modify-write sequences safe.
## Primitives by purpose

- Lock and RLock: mutual exclusion (an RLock can be re-acquired by the same thread).
- Condition: wait for a state change; always wait in a while loop that rechecks the condition.
- Semaphore: allow at most N threads into a section.
- Event: one thread signals, others wait.
- queue.Queue: a thread-safe producer-consumer queue, usually the best first choice.
## How to talk through it
Say what is shared and mutable, name the race, choose the smallest protection that fixes it, and say what you would test. Mention deadlock whenever you take more than one lock.
keyPoints: A race condition is a result that depends on thread timing; counter += 1 is not atomic.
A lock gives mutual exclusion; use 'with lock:' and keep the section short.
Deadlock needs a circular wait: acquire locks in one global order.
CPython threads suit I/O-bound work; use processes for CPU-bound code.
Condition.wait goes in a while loop; queue.Queue is the safest hand-off.

sql.title: A deterministic lost update, and the lock that fixes it
Deadlock, detected with timeouts, and avoided with lock ordering
sql.code:
import threading

a, b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()
barrier, barrier2 = threading.Barrier(2), threading.Barrier(2)
results = []

def grab(first, second):
    with first:
        barrier.wait()                                    # both threads now hold one lock each
        got = second.acquire(timeout=0.2)                 # the circular wait: nobody can get the second lock
        results.append(got)
        barrier2.wait()                                   # neither releases its lock before both have tried
        if got:
            second.release()

t1 = threading.Thread(target=grab, args=(a, b))
t2 = threading.Thread(target=grab, args=(b, a))
t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join()
assert results == [False, False]                          # deadlock detected by timeout

def ordered(l1, l2):
    return sorted([l1, l2], key=id)                       # every thread takes locks in the same global order

done = []
def safe(x, y):
    first, second = ordered(x, y)
    with first, second:
        done.append(1)
ts = [threading.Thread(target=safe, args=(a, b)), threading.Thread(target=safe, args=(b, a))]
[t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
assert done == [1, 1]                                     # both finish

sql.title: Producer and consumer with a Condition, a Semaphore and a Queue
sql.code:
import threading, queue, time

# Condition: wait in a loop that rechecks the state
items, cv, got = [], threading.Condition(), []
def consumer():
    with cv:
        while not items:
            cv.wait()
        got.append(items.pop())
c = threading.Thread(target=consumer); c.start()
time.sleep(0.05)
with cv:
    items.append('job')
    cv.notify()
c.join()
assert got == ['job']

# Semaphore: at most 2 threads inside at once
sem, lock, active, peak = threading.Semaphore(2), threading.Lock(), [0], [0]
def limited():
    with sem:
        with lock:
            active[0] += 1; peak[0] = max(peak[0], active[0])
        time.sleep(0.02)
        with lock:
            active[0] -= 1
ts = [threading.Thread(target=limited) for _ in range(6)]
[t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
assert peak[0] <= 2

# Queue: the thread-safe hand-off
q, out = queue.Queue(), []
def worker():
    while (job := q.get()) is not None:
        out.append(job * 2)
w = threading.Thread(target=worker); w.start()
for n in (1, 2, 3):
    q.put(n)
q.put(None)                                              # sentinel: stop
w.join()
assert out == [2, 4, 6]

exercise: Write a thread-safe bank account class with deposit, withdraw (never below zero) and transfer(a, b, amount) between two accounts. First write it without locks and show a lost update with the interleaving simulator. Then add locks, make transfer take both locks in a global order, and test with 8 threads doing 10,000 random transfers: the total must stay constant and no balance may go negative. Finally replace the shared account list with a queue of transfer requests handled by one worker, and compare.
pitfalls: Assuming counter += 1 is atomic.
Holding a lock while doing I/O or calling unknown code.
Taking two locks in different orders in different threads.
Using if instead of while around Condition.wait().
Using threads to speed up CPU-bound pure Python code.

interview.q: What is a race condition?
interview.a: A bug where the result depends on the timing or interleaving of threads. For example, two threads each do counter += 1, which is load, add, store: both may load the same value and one update is lost. Fix it with mutual exclusion (a lock), an atomic operation, or by avoiding shared mutable state.

interview.q: What are the conditions for deadlock and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Prevent it by breaking one of them, most simply by acquiring locks in a single global order so a circular wait cannot form. Other options: acquire with a timeout and retry, hold fewer locks at once, or use a queue instead of shared locks.

interview.q: What does the GIL mean for Python threads?
interview.a: In CPython only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, and the GIL is released during I/O. Threads therefore help with I/O-bound work, but not with CPU-bound Python code, for which you use multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor. Free-threaded builds can disable the GIL from Python 3.13 but it is not the default. The GIL does not make your own multi-step updates atomic.

interview.q: When do you use a Condition versus a Semaphore versus a Queue?
interview.a: A Condition lets threads wait until some state becomes true (wait in a while loop that rechecks it). A Semaphore limits how many threads may enter a section at once. A queue.Queue is a thread-safe hand-off between producers and consumers and is usually the simplest correct choice.

basis: Why it is here: Amazon's topic list (read) includes operating systems and distributed computing, and concurrency underlies the thread-safe designs asked in LLD rounds. The race-condition example (a counter at 50 ending at 51), the critical-section and mutual-exclusion definitions come from the OSTEP threads chapter, which I extracted and read locally. The GIL behavior (one thread runs bytecode at a time, released during I/O, free-threaded builds from 3.13) is from the Python glossary; Lock, RLock, Condition (while-loop rule), Semaphore and Event behavior is from the threading docs. The four deadlock conditions are standard operating-systems knowledge. Every sample runs and passes its asserts. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard.

scenes.title: Concurrency, step by step

steps.title: Threads share memory
body: Threads in one process share its memory and each has its own stack and registers. That makes communication cheap, and it makes bugs possible: two threads can change the same variable at the same time.
OSTEP's concurrency chapters cover threads, locks, condition variables, semaphores and concurrency bugs.

steps.title: Two threads add 1: both read 50
body: counter += 1 looks like one step but is three: load the value, add one, store it back. A context switch can happen between those steps.
Thread 1 loads 50, then the OS switches to thread 2, which also loads 50.

steps.title: Both write 51: an update is lost
body: Each thread adds 1 to its own copy (51) and stores it. The counter ends at 51, not 52. This is a race condition: the result depends on the timing of the threads. OSTEP's example starts the counter at 50 for exactly this reason.
It may pass a thousand runs and fail the next, which is what makes races hard to debug.

predict.question: Two threads each run counter += 1 on a counter that starts at 50 and the unlucky interleaving happens. What is the final value?
predict.why: Both threads read 50 and both write 51. One increment is lost, so the result is 51, not 52.

steps.title: The critical section and mutual exclusion
body: The code that touches shared data is a critical section. Mutual exclusion means only one thread is inside it at a time. A lock (mutex) provides it: acquire before the critical section, release after.
In Python use 'with lock:' so the lock is released even if the code raises.

card.title: Python
lines: with lock:            # acquire; release on exit

steps.title: With a lock the result is always right
body: Thread 1 acquires the lock, reads, adds and writes 51, and releases. Thread 2 was blocked and now reads 51 and writes 52. The updates are serialized, so no update is lost.
The cost: threads wait. Keep critical sections short and do slow work, like I/O, outside the lock.

steps.title: Deadlock: waiting for each other
body: Thread 1 holds lock A and wants B. Thread 2 holds B and wants A. Neither can proceed: a deadlock. It needs four conditions together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular wait.
The program does not crash; it simply stops.

steps.title: Avoid it: a global lock order
body: The usual fix is to break the circular wait: every thread acquires locks in the same global order (for example by an id). Then no thread can hold B while waiting for A. Other tools: acquire with a timeout and back off, hold fewer locks, or avoid shared state with queues.
Prefer message passing (a queue between threads) to shared variables when you can.
changes: ~ Both threads lock A then B

steps.title: Python: the GIL, threads and processes
body: In CPython the global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, and it is released during I/O. So threads help with I/O-bound work (network, files) but not with CPU-bound Python code; for that use multiprocessing or concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor. Since Python 3.13 free-threaded builds can disable the GIL, but not by default.
The GIL protects the interpreter, not your logic: counter += 1 across threads can still lose updates, so you still need locks.

card.title: Which tool?
lines: shared data between threads   Lock, or a queue.Queue

steps.title: Producer and consumer
body: A producer adds work to a queue and a consumer takes it. queue.Queue is already thread-safe, so it is the first thing to reach for. With a Condition you must wait in a while loop that rechecks the condition, because wait() can return when the condition no longer holds. Semaphores limit how many threads use a resource at once; an Event signals 'ready'.
Know the primitives by their purpose: Lock for exclusion, Condition to wait for a state, Semaphore to count, Event to signal.

card.title: Python
lines: cv.wait()          # releases the lock while waiting

steps.title: Recap
body: Shared mutable state needs protection. A race is a result that depends on timing; a lock gives mutual exclusion; deadlock needs a circular wait, so impose a lock order. In Python, threads for I/O, processes for CPU, and a queue where you can.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 4 acquire locks in one global order
5 prefer a queue to shared variables

everyday.plain: When many things run at once and share something, they can trip over each other.
everyday.story: Two people try to withdraw money from the same account at the same moment. Both check the balance (500), both see enough, and both take 400. The account ends up wrong. To prevent this, only one person at a time may use the account window. That is a lock. But if two people each hold one key and wait for the other's, they wait forever (deadlock).
maps: One at a time at the window
Each waiting for the other's key
words: A line of work inside a program; several can run in turn or together.
A bug where the result depends on the timing of two things.
A lock that lets only one thread in at a time.
Threads waiting for each other forever.

title: How to Answer a System Design Question
tagline: A routine for design questions: needs, things, API, big picture, then details.
explain: A system design round is a short, open prompt and about 45 minutes. Interviewers are not looking for one correct architecture. They assess whether you can structure an open problem, state assumptions, justify components and discuss trade-offs. Amazon's SDE II page says to expect at least one systems design question and lists practicality, accuracy, efficiency, reliability, optimization and scalability as the qualities it looks for.
## A six-step delivery framework

Hello Interview's guide gives six steps with rough time budgets: requirements (about 5 minutes), core entities (about 2), API or system interface (about 5), an optional data flow (about 5), high-level design (about 10 to 15) and deep dives (about 10). Together they add up to roughly 37 to 42 minutes.

- Requirements: functional (what users can do) and non-functional (availability, latency, consistency, scale). Do capacity estimation only if the numbers will change the design.
- Core entities: the nouns that become your data model.
- API: the contract with users, usually REST, one endpoint per requirement.
- Data flow: the sequence of processing steps, only if the system is a long chain.
- High-level design: the components and how data moves, one endpoint at a time. Satisfy the functional requirements simply first.
- Deep dives: non-functional requirements, edge cases and bottlenecks, guided by the interviewer.
## Other guides say the same thing

The System Design Primer's approach has four steps: outline use cases, constraints and assumptions; create a high-level design; design core components; scale the design. Alex Xu's first volume opens with scaling from zero, back-of-the-envelope estimation and a framework chapter (table of contents known from search summaries only). The order is always requirements, a simple design, then depth.
## Where levels differ

At mid level you are expected to drive requirements, the API and a sound high-level design. At senior level you go deep in two or three places, give numbers, and flag the limits of your own design (Hello Interview's levels page, which this project already cites).
## How to talk through it
Say the step you are on. Write assumptions where both of you can see them. After each design choice say the alternative you rejected and why. End by listing what you would improve with more time.
keyPoints: Run the same six steps every time: requirements, entities, API, data flow (optional), high-level design, deep dives.
Satisfy functional requirements simply before optimizing.
Estimate only when the numbers change the design.
Every design choice needs a stated trade-off.
Say the failure mode and the consistency requirement out loud.

sql.title: A time budget for the six steps
sql.code:
STEPS = [('requirements', 5, 5), ('core entities', 2, 2), ('api', 5, 5), ('data flow (optional)', 5, 5), ('high-level design', 10, 15), ('deep dives', 10, 10)]

def budget(skip_data_flow=False):
    lo = sum(a for name, a, b in STEPS if not (skip_data_flow and 'data flow' in name))
    hi = sum(b for name, a, b in STEPS if not (skip_data_flow and 'data flow' in name))
    return lo, hi

assert budget() == (37, 42)                    # the 37 to 42 minutes quoted by the guide
assert budget(skip_data_flow=True) == (32, 37) # skipping the optional step buys time for deep dives
assert budget()[1] <= 45                       # leaves a few minutes for questions and wrap-up

exercise: Pick three prompts (a news feed, a chat app, a file-sharing service). For each, spend exactly the time budget above, on paper: write the requirements (functional and non-functional, with what is out of scope), the entities, three API endpoints, the high-level boxes and two deep dives. Afterwards circle every claim in the design that you could not defend with a number or a trade-off.
pitfalls: Starting to draw before asking what the system must do.
Spending 25 minutes on requirements and entities and running out of time for deep dives.
Listing components without saying why each is there.
Not stating non-functional requirements, so every choice looks arbitrary.
Never saying what you would change with more time.

interview.q: How do you structure a system design answer?
interview.a: Requirements (functional and non-functional), core entities, the API, an optional data flow, a simple high-level design that satisfies the functional requirements one endpoint at a time, then deep dives on non-functional requirements, bottlenecks and failure modes, stating trade-offs throughout.

interview.q: When do you do capacity estimation?
interview.a: Only when the numbers will influence the design, for example to decide whether one database can handle the writes or whether you need to partition. Convert daily numbers to per second and plan for a peak of two to three times the average.

interview.q: What changes between a mid-level and a senior answer?
interview.a: Mid level drives requirements, the API and the schema and shows breadth across components. Senior goes deep in a couple of places with numbers, recognizes what makes the system hard, and points out the limits of their own design.

interview.q: What do you do if you realize a choice was wrong halfway through?
interview.a: Say so, explain what you learned, and change it. Revising a design in response to a constraint you missed is a good signal; defending a mistake silently is not.

references.title: System Design Primer: how to approach a system design interview question
Hello Interview: system design delivery framework

basis: Sources I read: Hello Interview's delivery framework (six steps and time budgets), the System Design Primer README (four steps and the full topic list), Amazon's SDE II page (at least one design question; the qualities assessed), and Hello Interview's levels page. Alex Xu's table of contents is known only from search summaries. The step names I use are Hello Interview's; the mapping to the Primer's steps is my own reading. Priorities, hours and every number in the animations are judgment calls or illustrative assumptions, not measurements; where a figure comes from a page I read, the source is named above. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises it for roles whose loops contain a design round (for example, the SDE plan).

scenes.title: A system design answer, step by step

steps.title: A system design round is a conversation with a shape
body: You get a short prompt ('design a news feed') and about 45 minutes. Nobody expects the one right architecture. They watch whether you can structure an open problem, make assumptions explicit, and explain trade-offs.
A framework keeps you from jumping to boxes and arrows before you know what the system must do.

steps.title: 1. Requirements (about 5 minutes)
body: Split them into functional requirements (what users can do: post, follow, view a feed) and non-functional ones (availability, latency, consistency, scale). Ask which are most important: a feed can be eventually consistent, a payment cannot.
Hello Interview's guide says to do capacity estimation only if the numbers will change your design.

card.title: Two lists
lines: non-functional  available, low latency, eventual consistency is fine
out of scope    say it aloud: no search, no ads

steps.title: 2 and 3. Core entities and the API (about 7 minutes)
body: List the main nouns (User, Post, Follow) as a first draft of the data model. Then define the interface between users and system, usually a REST API: one endpoint per requirement, with inputs and outputs.
The API is a contract. Writing it early fixes what the rest of the design must serve.

steps.title: 4. Data flow (optional, about 5 minutes)
body: If the system is a long chain of actions (a crawler, a pipeline), write the sequence of steps first: fetch, parse, deduplicate, store. If it is a simple request and response, skip this step.
It is optional in the framework for a reason: spend time where the problem is hard.

pill.text: only if there is a long chain

steps.title: 5. High-level design (about 10 to 15 minutes)
body: Draw the components and how data moves, one endpoint at a time: clients, load balancer, services, database, cache, queue. Keep it simple and satisfy the functional requirements before optimizing.
Say what each box is for. A box you cannot justify should not be on the board.

predict.question: What should the high-level design do first?
predict.why: Get a working design for each endpoint first. Optimizations belong in the deep dives, where you can tie each one to a non-functional requirement.

steps.title: 6. Deep dives (about 10 minutes)
body: Now take on the non-functional requirements, the edge cases and the bottlenecks, guided by the interviewer's questions. Examples: what happens with a user who has 50 million followers? What if the cache is down?
This is where senior candidates show depth: numbers, failure modes, and the trade-off behind each choice.

steps.title: The same shape in other guides
body: The System Design Primer's four steps are: outline use cases, constraints and assumptions; create a high-level design; design the core components; scale the design. Alex Xu's book opens with a chapter on a framework for system design interviews, after chapters on scaling from zero and back-of-the-envelope estimation (table of contents from search summaries).
The names differ and the order is the same: requirements first, a simple design second, depth and scale last.

card.title: Primer versus Hello Interview
lines: Primer 1  use cases, constraints, assumptions   = requirements
Primer 2  high-level design                     = API + high-level design
Primer 3  design core components                 = deep dives
Primer 4  scale the design                      = deep dives

steps.title: Common mistakes
body: Drawing boxes before asking what the system must do. Quoting daily numbers and never converting them to per second. Reaching for sharding or a new database before the numbers need it. Treating every part of the system as needing the same consistency. Not saying the trade-off of a choice. Going silent.
Name the failure mode out loud: it is what senior interviewers listen for.

callout.text: A design with no stated trade-offs is a list of components, not an answer.

steps.title: Recap
body: Requirements, core entities, API, optional data flow, high-level design, deep dives. Budget the time, keep notes of the assumptions, and finish with trade-offs and what you would do next.
The rest of this track gives you the building blocks (caching, load balancing, queues) and the classic designs (feed, chat, crawler) to practice this routine on.

everyday.plain: Answer a design question in the same order every time: what is needed, what are the things, how do people use it, the big picture, then the details.
everyday.story: If a friend asks, 'plan a wedding for us', you do not start by choosing flowers. You ask: how many guests, what budget, which city? Then you list the main parts (venue, food, music), then draw the big plan, and only then go deep on the parts that matter. A design interview follows the same order.
words: Something the system must do, such as 'post a message'.
How well it must work, such as speed or uptime.
The big picture of the main parts and how they connect.
Going into detail on one important part.

title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
tagline: Do rough sums on speed, requests and storage, and see which decision each number points to.
explain: Estimation in a system design round is quick arithmetic that tells you which problem you actually have. It is not about precision; it is about the order of magnitude and about using the result to choose a design. Both the System Design Primer and Alex Xu's book give it its own section or chapter.
## The numbers to remember

- Powers of two: 2^10 is about a thousand (1 KB), 2^20 about a million (1 MB), 2^30 about a billion (1 GB), 2^40 about a trillion (1 TB).
- Time: the Primer uses about 2.5 million seconds in a month. A day is 86,400 seconds, which you can round to 100,000.
- Latency (Primer, 'latency numbers every programmer should know'): main memory reference 100 ns, random 4 KB SSD read 150 microseconds, datacenter round trip 500 microseconds, HDD seek 10 ms, a trip from California to the Netherlands and back 150 ms. The ratios matter more than the exact values.
## The chain of estimates

Users, then actions per user per day, then requests per second, then a peak factor of two to three. Items times size gives storage over the retention period. Requests per second times response size gives bandwidth. In the Primer's Twitter example, 500 million tweets a day is about 6,000 writes a second and 250 billion reads a month is about 100,000 reads a second, and at about 10 KB a tweet new content is about 150 TB a month.
## Turn it into a decision

State what the number implies: reads dominate, so cache; the write rate is high for one primary, so partition or queue; the data is large, so object storage and a CDN. If a number does not change the design, you did not need it.
## Availability in numbers
From the Primer: 99.9% availability allows about 8 hours 45 minutes of downtime a year; 99.99% allows about 52 minutes. Each extra nine is ten times less downtime and costs more.
## How to talk through it
Write the assumption, the arithmetic and the unit on each line. Round aggressively. If the interviewer changes an assumption, recompute that line. Label everything as an assumption.
keyPoints: Know 2^10 (KB), 2^20 (MB), 2^30 (GB), 2^40 (TB) and about 2.5 million seconds a month.
Memory is orders of magnitude faster than SSD, which beats a disk seek and a cross-continent trip.
Users to QPS to peak (2 to 3 times) to storage to bandwidth.
Estimate only what changes the design; end with a one-sentence decision.
Each extra nine of availability is ten times less downtime.

sql.title: An estimator you can check by hand
sql.code:
SECONDS_PER_MONTH = 2_500_000          # the Primer's rounding

def per_second(per_month):
    return per_month / SECONDS_PER_MONTH

def storage(items_per_month, bytes_each, months=1):
    return items_per_month * bytes_each * months

# The Primer's Twitter assumptions
tweets_per_month = 15e9
reads_per_month = 250e9
assert round(per_second(tweets_per_month)) == 6000           # about 6,000 writes a second
assert round(per_second(reads_per_month)) == 100_000         # about 100,000 reads a second
assert storage(tweets_per_month, 10_000) == 150e12           # 150 TB a month at 10 KB a tweet
assert storage(tweets_per_month, 10_000, 36) == 5.4e15       # 5.4 PB over three years
assert reads_per_month / tweets_per_month > 16               # read-heavy

def downtime_per_year_seconds(availability):
    return (1 - availability) * 365.25 * 24 * 3600

assert round(downtime_per_year_seconds(0.999)) == 31558      # about 8 h 46 min (the Primer: 8h 45min 57s)
assert round(downtime_per_year_seconds(0.9999) / 60, 1) == 52.6   # about 52.6 min

exercise: Estimate for a photo-sharing app with 50 million daily users who each view 40 photos and upload 0.5 photos a day (assumptions: 2 MB per uploaded photo, 200 KB per displayed thumbnail). Compute reads and writes per second with a 3 times peak, storage per year, and outbound bandwidth at peak. Then write three sentences saying what each number means for the design (database, cache, CDN, object storage).
pitfalls: Mixing KB, MB and GB in one line.
Quoting daily numbers and never converting to per second.
Planning for the average instead of the peak.
Producing numbers and then not using them to choose anything.
Too much precision: spending five minutes on exact arithmetic.

interview.q: How do you estimate requests per second from daily active users?
interview.a: Multiply users by actions per user per day, divide by about 100,000 seconds (86,400 rounded), and apply a peak factor of two to three. Separate reads and writes because they drive different design decisions.

interview.q: Roughly how long do a memory reference, an SSD read and a cross-continent round trip take?
interview.a: From the Primer's list: main memory about 100 nanoseconds, a random 4 KB SSD read about 150 microseconds, a round trip within a datacenter about 500 microseconds, and a packet across continents and back about 150 milliseconds. The ratios (memory much faster than SSD, SSD much faster than a disk seek or a long-haul trip) are what you use.

interview.q: How would you estimate storage?
interview.a: Items per period times average size times the retention period, then multiply by the replication factor. Separate small metadata from large blobs, because they go in different stores.

interview.q: What do you do with an estimate?
interview.a: Conclude something that changes the design: reads dominate so add a cache, write rate needs partitioning or a queue, data size needs object storage and a CDN. If the estimate does not change the design, say so and move on.

steps.title: From users to requests per second

title: Latency, Throughput and Availability
tagline: How long one thing takes, how many things per second, and how often it works.
explain: The first topics in the System Design Primer are performance versus scalability, latency versus throughput and availability. They give you the vocabulary for every non-functional requirement you will be asked about, and the arithmetic to make claims about them.
## Performance versus scalability

A service has a performance problem if it is slow for a single user. It has a scalability problem if it is fast for one user but slow under heavy load. Making a request cheaper helps the first; adding capacity or removing a shared bottleneck helps the second.
## Latency versus throughput

Latency is the time one request takes, throughput is the number of requests completed per second. Batching raises throughput and adds latency per item. Say which the product cares about and design for the maximum throughput with acceptable latency.
## Availability in numbers

The Primer's figures: 99.9% availability allows 8 hours 45 minutes 57 seconds of downtime a year (43 minutes 49.7 seconds a month) and 99.99% allows 52 minutes 35.7 seconds a year (4 minutes 23 seconds a month). Each extra nine is ten times less downtime and usually much more cost.
## Series and parallel

If a request needs components A, B and C, all must work: multiply their availabilities (three components at 99.9% give about 99.7%). If you run two independent copies and either can serve, the tier fails only if both fail: 1 minus (1 minus a) squared, which for 99.9% is 99.9999%. Every extra component in the path lowers availability unless it is redundant, and redundancy only helps when failures are independent.
## Fail-over
In active-passive, a standby takes over when the active server's heartbeat stops. In active-active, both serve traffic. Replication that is asynchronous can lose recent writes on failover.
## Measuring it

Define an indicator (the fraction of successful requests), an objective (99.9% over 30 days) and use the error budget to make release decisions, as the Google SRE book describes in its chapter on service level objectives.
## How to talk through it
State the target and what downtime it allows. Walk the request path and name every single point of failure. Add redundancy where the arithmetic says it matters and say what the extra copy costs.
keyPoints: Performance is slow for one user; scalability is slow under load.
Latency is time per request; throughput is requests per second; batching trades one for the other.
99.9% allows about 8 h 46 min of downtime a year; 99.99% about 53 minutes.
Availabilities multiply in series and combine as 1 - (1-a)^n in parallel.
Remove single points of failure: balancer, database and region too.

sql.title: Series and parallel availability
sql.code:
def series(*a):
    p = 1.0
    for x in a:
        p *= x
    return p

def parallel(*a):
    p = 1.0
    for x in a:
        p *= (1 - x)
    return 1 - p

assert round(series(0.999, 0.999, 0.999), 4) == 0.997      # three 99.9% parts in a row: about 99.7%
assert round(parallel(0.999, 0.999), 6) == 0.999999        # two independent copies: 99.9999%

# the whole path: balancer -> (two app servers) -> database
path = series(0.999, parallel(0.999, 0.999), 0.999)
assert round(path, 4) == 0.998                              # now limited by the balancer and the database

def downtime_minutes_per_year(a):
    return (1 - a) * 365.25 * 24 * 60

assert round(downtime_minutes_per_year(0.999)) == 526       # 8 h 46 min (the Primer: 8h 45min 57s)

exercise: Draw the request path for a web app (DNS, load balancer, two app servers, a primary database and a replica). Assign each component 99.9% availability and compute the path availability, once with a single load balancer and once with two. Identify the single points of failure in your diagram and write what each fix costs. Then write an SLI and SLO for the checkout endpoint.
pitfalls: Confusing a performance problem with a scalability problem.
Adding a second server and claiming 100% availability while the load balancer is a single point of failure.
Assuming failures are independent when both copies share a power source or a deploy.
Quoting nines without saying what downtime they allow.
Forgetting that async replication can lose data on failover.

interview.q: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
interview.a: Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many requests the system completes per second. You can raise throughput by batching or parallelism at the cost of latency per request. State which one the requirement is about.

interview.q: How much downtime does 99.9% allow?
interview.a: About 8 hours 46 minutes a year (the Primer gives 8h 45min 57s), around 43 minutes a month. 99.99% allows about 52 minutes a year.

interview.q: How does redundancy change availability?
interview.a: In series, availabilities multiply, so more components lower the total. Running independent copies in parallel makes the tier fail only if all copies fail, which raises availability a lot. You still need redundancy for the other parts of the path, and failures must be independent.

interview.q: Active-passive versus active-active?
interview.a: Active-passive keeps a standby that takes over (usually by heartbeat) while only the active one serves. Active-active runs both and shares load, which uses capacity better but needs clients or DNS to know both and needs state to be shared safely.

steps.title: Performance versus scalability
body: A service has a performance problem if it is slow for one user. It has a scalability problem if it is fast for one user but slow under heavy load. The first is fixed by making one request cheaper, the second by adding capacity or removing a bottleneck.
The System Design Primer lists these as the first topics for that reason: they tell you which kind of problem you have.

steps.title: Latency versus throughput
body: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests per second the system completes. They trade off: batching raises throughput and raises latency for each item; handling requests one at a time lowers latency and may lower throughput.
Aim for the maximum throughput with acceptable latency, and say which one the product cares about.

card.title: Two different numbers
lines: batching: more throughput, more latency per item

steps.title: Availability in numbers
body: Availability is the fraction of time a service works. The Primer: 99.9% allows 8 hours 45 minutes 57 seconds of downtime a year, and 99.99% allows 52 minutes 35.7 seconds. Each extra nine is ten times less downtime.
Targets come from what users need and what you can afford: an internal tool and a payment API do not need the same.

steps.title: Components in series multiply
body: If a request must pass through a load balancer, an app server and a database, each at 99.9%, the whole path works only when all three work: 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 99.7%. Every component you add in series lowers the availability of the path.
Three nines for each part gives fewer than three nines in total.

predict.question: A request passes through three components, each 99.9% available. What is the availability of the path?
predict.why: Probabilities multiply: 0.999 cubed is about 0.997, so 99.7%, which is roughly 26 hours of downtime a year instead of under 9.

steps.title: Redundancy in parallel
body: Two independent app servers behind the load balancer: the app tier fails only if both fail. At 99.9% each, the tier is 1 minus 0.001 times 0.001, which is 99.9999%. Redundancy in parallel raises availability a lot, as long as failures are independent.
The load balancer and database are still single points of failure: they need redundancy too.

steps.title: Fail-over: active-passive and active-active
body: Active-passive: a standby takes over the active server's role when heartbeats stop; only the active one serves traffic. Active-active: both serve traffic and share load, so clients or DNS must know both. (System Design Primer)
Failover can lose data if replication is asynchronous, which is covered with replication in the database track.

steps.title: Availability needs a measure
body: A target is useless unless you measure it. The SRE book's approach: define a service level indicator (for example, the fraction of requests that succeed), set an objective (99.9% over 30 days) and use the error budget to decide how much risk a release can take.
See the observability and reliability lessons for the full model.

steps.title: Recap
body: Performance is one request, scalability is many. Latency and throughput trade off. Nines multiply in series and improve with independent redundancy in parallel. Say your target, what it costs, and how you measure it.

everyday.plain: Latency is how long one thing takes, throughput is how many things per second, and availability is how often it works.

A restaurant can serve many dishes per hour yet make each customer wait. These are different things and you can improve one without the others.

title: CAP, Consistency Patterns and Quorums
tagline: When the network breaks, do you stay available or stay in sync? And how voting between copies helps.
explain: Almost every distributed design question reaches the same point: 'what happens if the network between two replicas breaks?'. The CAP theorem frames the answer. This lesson gives you the vocabulary the System Design Primer lists (CAP, CP, AP, consistency patterns, fail-over, replication) and the quorum arithmetic from the Dynamo paper.
## CAP in practice

When data is on more than one machine a partition will eventually happen, so partition tolerance is not optional. You then choose between consistency and availability for each piece of data. The Primer describes CP as waiting on a partitioned node, which may time out, suitable for systems that need atomic reads and writes, and AP as returning the most available data, which may be stale, with writes propagating once the partition resolves, suitable for systems that accept eventual consistency.
## Consistency patterns

- Weak: after a write, a read may or may not see it. Used in real-time chat and games.
- Eventual: reads will see the write after some time, usually within milliseconds. Used in DNS and email.
- Strong: after a write, all reads see it. Used in file systems and relational databases.
A design usually mixes them, for example strong for a balance and eventual for a feed.
## Reconciling divergence

AP systems must merge conflicting writes after a partition: last write wins by timestamp (simple, can lose a write), merging structures such as sets, or asking the application. Dynamo uses version vectors to detect conflicting versions and read repair to fix them.
## Quorums

With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read contacts R replicas. When R + W is greater than N the sets overlap, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write. Smaller W or R is faster and may return stale data. Dynamo exposes N, R and W as tunable parameters.
## Replication and fail-over

Synchronous replication waits for the copy, which is safer but slower and blocks when the copy is unreachable. Asynchronous replication does not wait, which is faster but can lose the latest writes on failover. Active-passive and active-active fail-over are described in the availability lesson.
## How to talk through it

Go through each feature and say what it does during a partition and why. 'Orders: reject writes on the minority side. Feed: serve stale and merge later.' Then name the replication mode and quorum that implements it.
keyPoints: Partitions will happen: choose CP or AP per feature.
CP refuses requests it cannot confirm; AP answers and reconciles later.
Weak, eventual and strong consistency are different promises about reads after writes.
R + W > N makes reads see the latest write; smaller values trade it for speed.
Async replication can lose writes on failover; sync replication can block.

sql.title: Quorum reads and writes over three replicas
Last write wins loses a write; a set merge does not

exercise: For a ride-hailing app list five data items (driver location, ride request, payment, rating, user profile) and for each write: what should happen in a network partition (CP or AP), which consistency pattern you need, and the replication and quorum settings you would use. Then write the conflict rule for any item you made AP.
pitfalls: Saying 'CA' is an option for a distributed system on a real network.
Choosing one consistency level for the whole system instead of per feature.
Using last write wins without saying what it can lose.
Forgetting that R + W > N needs the sets to overlap in at least one replica holding the latest write.
Claiming strong consistency while reading from an async replica.

interview.q: Explain the CAP theorem.
interview.a: In a distributed data store, when a network partition occurs you must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write, so some requests are refused) and availability (every request gets an answer, which may be stale). Partition tolerance is not optional on real networks, so the real choice is CP or AP, ideally per feature.

interview.q: What are weak, eventual and strong consistency?
interview.a: Weak: a read after a write might not see it. Eventual: reads will see it after a short time if there are no new writes (DNS, email). Strong: every read after a write sees it (relational databases, file systems), at a cost in latency and availability.

interview.q: What does R + W > N guarantee?
interview.a: With N replicas, W write acknowledgements and R replicas read, the read set and write set always overlap, so a read includes at least one replica with the latest acknowledged write. It is how Dynamo-style systems offer tunable consistency.

interview.q: How do you reconcile conflicting writes after a partition?
interview.a: Use version vectors to detect that the writes are concurrent, then apply a rule: last write wins by timestamp (simple, may lose data), a merge function for mergeable types such as sets or counters, or surface the conflict to the application. Pick per data type.

scenes.title: CAP and consistency, step by step

steps.title: The question CAP answers
body: When data lives on more than one machine, a network partition (A cannot reach B) will eventually happen. The CAP theorem says you then have to choose: stay consistent (refuse some requests) or stay available (answer, possibly with stale or divergent data). Partition tolerance is not optional on a real network.
So the practical question is: when the network splits, do you give up consistency or availability?

steps.title: A partition splits the replicas
body: The link between A and B fails. Both replicas are up, and each client can still reach its own replica, but A and B cannot exchange updates. Client 1 now writes x = 2 to A.
Client 2 reads x from B. What should B answer?

steps.title: Choose CP: refuse to answer
body: A CP system keeps consistency: B cannot be sure it has the latest value, so it refuses (or times out) until the partition heals. Reads and writes are atomic, at the price of unavailability on the minority side.
Suitable when a wrong answer is worse than no answer: balances, inventory counts, leader election.

predict.question: During the partition B must keep reads consistent. What does it do?
options: Refuses or times out until it can reach A
predict.why: A consistent system cannot return a value that might be stale, so it rejects the request. That is the availability cost of choosing consistency.

steps.title: Choose AP: answer, accept divergence
body: An AP system stays available: B answers with what it has (x = 1, which is stale) and accepts writes, so A and B may now hold different values and must reconcile after the partition heals.
Suitable when stale data is acceptable: timelines, likes, shopping carts, DNS.

steps.title: Healing: reconcile
body: When the link returns, replicas exchange updates. Conflicts (two different writes to x) are resolved by a rule: last write wins by timestamp, merge (for example a set union), or ask the application. Dynamo-style stores use version vectors and read repair.
Choose the rule per data type; last write wins can silently lose a write.

steps.title: Consistency patterns
body: Weak: after a write a read may or may not see it (video chat, games). Eventual: reads will see the write after some time, usually milliseconds (DNS, email). Strong: after a write every read sees it (file systems, relational databases). (System Design Primer)
Most real systems mix them: strong for the balance, eventual for the feed.

card.title: Patterns (Primer)
lines: weak       a read may miss a recent write
eventual   reads converge after a short time
strong     every read sees the latest write

steps.title: Quorums: tune it per request
body: With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write. Dynamo lets you tune N, R and W per use.
N=3, W=2, R=2 is common; W=1, R=1 is fast and may return stale data.

card.title: N=3
lines: W=2, R=2  R+W=4 > 3  reads see the latest write
W=1, R=1  R+W=2 < 3  fast, may read stale
W=3, R=1  slow writes, fast reads

steps.title: Fail-over and replication
body: Replication copies data to survive failures and spread reads. With synchronous replication the primary waits for the copy: safer, slower, and blocked if the copy is unreachable. With asynchronous replication it does not wait: faster, but a failover can lose the latest writes.
That is CAP's trade-off again, applied to one decision.

callout.text: Say it as a requirement: 'for orders I need no lost writes, so synchronous to one replica; for the feed async is fine'.

steps.title: Recap
body: Partitions happen, so choose per feature: CP when a wrong answer costs more than no answer, AP when availability matters more. Know weak, eventual and strong consistency, and use quorums or sync versus async replication to dial it.
