More than half of the copies, enough to decide.
Copies may differ for a while but will agree later.

title: DNS, CDN and the Reverse Proxy
tagline: How a request finds your servers, why copies live near users, and what sits in front of your servers.
explain: Before any of your code runs, a request has to find your servers. The System Design Primer lists the Domain Name System, content delivery networks and reverse proxies as the first layers of every design. They cut latency and protect your origin, and each has well-known limits that interviewers like to probe.
## DNS

DNS is a hierarchical, decentralised naming system that maps human-friendly names such as mozilla.org to IP addresses (MDN). Resolvers cache answers for a time to live, so most lookups are local. DNS can also steer traffic: it can answer differently by location or by the health of a region. Failover by DNS is limited by the TTL and by clients that cache longer than they should.
## CDN

MDN defines a CDN as a group of servers spread over many locations that store duplicate copies of data so requests can be answered by the nearest server. It notes that most CDNs have servers worldwide, that distance affects latency proportionally, and that serving static assets over a CDN lowers the load on your own servers. It also warns that a CDN can reduce performance if it adds extra DNS lookups and connections to a third party, and because browsers no longer share caches across origins.
## Push and pull

In a pull CDN the edge fetches an object from the origin on the first request and caches it for a TTL, so the first request is slow. In a push CDN you upload content when it changes, which gives control and suits content that rarely changes. The Primer lists both. Either way, Cache-Control headers tell the edge how long a copy is valid, and versioned file names make purging unnecessary.
## Reverse proxy and load balancer

A reverse proxy forwards client requests to the right backend and can terminate TLS, compress, cache and hide the servers. A load balancer is a reverse proxy that also distributes load across servers. The Primer discusses the overlap between the two.
## What to cache

Static assets and video segments belong at the edge. Personalised or authenticated responses must be marked private or bypass the cache, because serving one user's page to another is a security incident.
## How to talk through it
Walk the path: DNS, CDN edge, reverse proxy, origin. At each hop say what is cached, for how long, and what happens on a miss.
keyPoints: DNS maps names to IPs; answers are cached for a TTL and can steer traffic.
A CDN keeps copies near users: lower latency and lower origin load.
Pull CDN: fetch on first request. Push CDN: you upload content.
Never cache private responses at a shared cache.
A reverse proxy fronts servers for TLS, caching and routing; a load balancer is a reverse proxy that spreads load.

sql.title: A pull CDN with TTL: hit ratio and origin load
A resolver cache with TTL
sql.code:
class Resolver:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cache, self.lookups = {}, 0
    def resolve(self, name, now, authoritative):
        hit = self.cache.get(name)
        if hit and hit[1] > now:
            return hit[0]
        self.lookups += 1
        ip, ttl = authoritative(name)
        self.cache[name] = (ip, now + ttl)
        return ip

records = {'example.com': ('203.0.113.5', 30)}
r = Resolver()
assert r.resolve('example.com', 0, records.get) == '203.0.113.5'
r.resolve('example.com', 10, records.get)           # cached: no lookup
assert r.lookups == 1
records['example.com'] = ('203.0.113.9', 30)         # the address changes (failover)
assert r.resolve('example.com', 20, records.get) == '203.0.113.5'   # clients still use the old IP until the TTL ends
assert r.resolve('example.com', 31, records.get) == '203.0.113.9'

exercise: Design the delivery path for a photo site with users on three continents. Write: what DNS returns and the TTL you choose and why; which URLs go through the CDN (and the Cache-Control headers); what never goes through it; what the reverse proxy does; and what happens, step by step, when the origin in one region fails. Estimate the hit ratio you expect and say what it does to origin load.
pitfalls: Caching personalised pages at a shared edge.
Very long DNS TTLs, which make failover slow.
No versioned file names, so a bad asset stays cached.
Assuming a CDN always improves performance.
Treating the load balancer and reverse proxy as unrelated.

interview.q: How does a CDN reduce latency and load?
interview.a: It keeps copies of content on servers in many locations so a request is answered by a nearby edge instead of the distant origin. That shortens the round trip and removes most requests from your origin servers. Pull CDNs fill the cache on first request; push CDNs are loaded by you.

interview.q: Push CDN or pull CDN?
interview.a: Pull is simpler: content is fetched on the first request and cached for its TTL, at the cost of a slow first request. Push gives control and suits content that rarely changes and is large, but you must upload and manage it.

interview.q: What is the difference between a reverse proxy and a load balancer?
interview.a: A reverse proxy forwards client requests to backend servers, optionally terminating TLS, caching and compressing. A load balancer is a reverse proxy whose main job is spreading requests across several servers, with health checks. One component can do both.

interview.q: How does DNS affect failover?
interview.a: DNS can point clients to a healthy region, but resolvers and clients cache answers for the TTL, so failover is only as fast as the TTL (plus any caching beyond it). Shorter TTLs speed failover and raise lookup load.

basis: Sources: MDN's CDN and DNS glossary pages (definitions, latency proportional to distance, origin load, the caveats about third-party lookups and cache partitioning), MDN's HTTP caching pages read earlier, and the System Design Primer (push versus pull CDNs, reverse proxy versus load balancer, DNS records), all read. TTL values and hit ratios in the code are illustrative assumptions, and DNS caching behavior is stated as general knowledge because the MDN glossary page does not cover it. Priorities, hours and every number in the animations are judgment calls or illustrative assumptions, not measurements; where a figure comes from a page I read, the source is named above. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises it for roles whose loops contain a design round (for example, the SDE plan).

scenes.title: DNS, CDN and reverse proxy, step by step

steps.title: Before any request: DNS
body: The Domain Name System translates a human-friendly name (mozilla.org) into a numeric IP address: a DNS lookup (MDN). It is a hierarchical, decentralised system. Resolvers cache answers for a time to live (TTL), so most lookups never leave your ISP or device.
DNS is also the first routing decision: it can return different addresses for different users, which is how traffic is steered to the nearest region.

steps.title: A far-away origin is slow
body: Latency grows with distance: MDN notes that geographic distance affects latency proportionally, and a round trip across continents costs about 150 ms in the Primer's latency table. Serving every image and script from one origin makes users far away wait and puts every request on your servers.
The idea of a content delivery network is to move copies of content near users.

steps.title: A CDN serves copies from the edge
body: A CDN is a group of servers in many locations that store copies of data so requests are answered by the server closest to the user (MDN). It cuts latency and lowers the load on your origin.
The edge server answers from its cache when it has the object; otherwise it asks the origin.

steps.title: Push CDN versus pull CDN
body: Pull CDN: the edge fetches content from the origin the first time it is requested and caches it for a TTL. Simple, but the first request is slow. Push CDN: you upload content to the CDN when it changes. More control and good for content that rarely changes, but you manage the uploads. (System Design Primer)
Set cache headers (Cache-Control) so the edge knows how long a copy is valid.

pill.text: miss: fetch from origin, then cache

predict.question: A new user is the first to request a file from this edge on a pull CDN. What happens?
options: The edge fetches it from the origin and caches it
The file is pushed in advance
The user is redirected to DNS
predict.why: A pull CDN populates its cache on demand: the first request goes to the origin (a miss), later requests hit the edge.

steps.title: Reverse proxy and load balancer
body: A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers: clients talk to it and it forwards to the right server. It can terminate TLS, cache, compress and hide your servers. A load balancer is a reverse proxy that also spreads requests across several servers; the Primer notes the two roles overlap.
Put them between the CDN and the origin.

steps.title: What not to cache
body: Cache static assets (images, scripts, video segments) at the CDN. Personalised pages, authenticated API responses and anything that must be fresh need care: set Cache-Control correctly, or bypass the CDN. MDN also warns that a CDN can hurt performance: extra DNS lookups and connections to a third-party host, and browsers no longer share caches across origins.
Purging a stale object takes time, so version your file names (app.3f2a.js).

callout.text: A CDN that caches a logged-in user's page and serves it to someone else is a security incident.

steps.title: DNS-based traffic steering
body: DNS can return different IPs depending on the resolver's location or the health of a region, which is how traffic reaches the closest healthy data center. Short TTLs make failover faster and increase lookups.
Failover by DNS is only as fast as the TTL plus client caching.

steps.title: Recap
body: DNS maps names to IPs and steers traffic. A CDN serves cached copies near users (pull or push), lowering latency and origin load. A reverse proxy or load balancer fronts the servers. Be clear about what is cacheable.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 2 static content on a CDN (pull by default)
3 cache headers and versioned file names
4 reverse proxy for TLS and routing
5 never cache private pages by accident

everyday.plain: DNS finds the address, a CDN keeps copies near you, and a reverse proxy stands in front of your servers.
everyday.story: Imagine a famous bookshop. DNS is the directory that tells you its address. A CDN is like small branches in every city that keep copies of popular books, so you do not have to travel to the main shop. A reverse proxy is the receptionist at the main shop who takes your request and decides who inside should handle it.
words: The directory that turns names into addresses.
A network of servers near users that keep copies of your files.
A server in front of your servers that receives requests for them.
Your real server, where the original content lives.

title: Microservices, APIs and Communication
tagline: Many small programs instead of one big one: where to split, and how they talk.
explain: Interviewers often ask 'would you use microservices here?' and 'how do the services talk?'. Good answers weigh costs, not fashion. The System Design Primer's application layer and communication sections list microservices, service discovery, TCP, UDP, RPC and REST, and Martin Fowler's article gives the trade-offs.
## Monolith first

Fowler suggests beginning with a monolith, keeping it modular, and splitting it into services once it becomes a problem. He notes that monolithic applications can be successful, that team skill matters more than the style, and that many teams have found microservices a productivity-sapping burden.
## What microservices are

Fowler lists common characteristics rather than a definition: services as independently deployable components, organized around business capabilities, owned by teams for the whole product lifetime, with smart endpoints and simple communication, decentralised governance and data management, infrastructure automation, design for failure and evolutionary design.
## The costs

Remote calls are more expensive than in-process calls; chains of synchronous calls multiply downtime; distributed transactions are hard, so services lean on eventual consistency and compensating actions; each service needs monitoring, logging and a pipeline; changing an interface can break consumers.
## Discovery and the gateway

Because instances come and go, callers use service discovery (a registry or the platform's DNS) rather than fixed addresses. An API gateway is the single entry point that routes, authenticates and rate limits; run several instances and keep business logic out of it.
## REST, RPC and gRPC

REST over HTTP with JSON is simple and works for public APIs and browsers. RPC calls a remote method as if it were local. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers both as its interface definition language and as its message format, which gives typed contracts and compact messages for internal calls.
## TCP, UDP and asynchronous messaging

TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is connectionless with no guarantee and lower overhead, used for live media and games. A queue between services decouples producer and consumer; a growing queue signals back pressure.
## How to talk through it

Start from team size, scale and rate of change. If you choose services, name the boundaries (business capabilities), how they find each other, how they call each other (and what happens on a timeout), and who owns each service's data.
keyPoints: Start with a modular monolith; split when it hurts.
Services follow business capabilities and own their data.
Remote calls cost more, and synchronous chains multiply downtime.
REST for public APIs; RPC (gRPC with Protocol Buffers) for internal calls.
Queues decouple services but make results eventual.

sql.title: A service registry with round-robin and failover
Synchronous chains multiply availability; a queue breaks the chain
sql.code:
def chain(*availabilities):
    p = 1.0
    for a in availabilities:
        p *= a
    return p

# Orders -> Payments -> Bank, all called synchronously
assert round(chain(0.999, 0.999, 0.999), 4) == 0.997

# With a queue, Orders only needs itself and the queue to accept the order
assert round(chain(0.999, 0.9999), 4) == 0.9989

from collections import deque
q, processed = deque(), []
def place_order(o):
    q.append(o)                                      # returns immediately
def payments_worker():
    while q:
        processed.append(q.popleft())
place_order('A'); place_order('B')
assert processed == []                               # accepted, not yet paid: the result is eventual
payments_worker()
assert processed == ['A', 'B']

exercise: Take a monolithic shop (catalogue, cart, orders, payments, notifications). Decide which parts you would split first and which you would leave together, and justify it with team size and rate of change. Draw the services, the gateway and the registry; mark each call as sync or async and write what happens on a timeout. Compute the availability of the checkout path if every sync call is 99.9%.
pitfalls: Splitting into many services for a small team with no operational maturity.
Sharing one database between services, so they are coupled anyway.
Long synchronous chains with no timeouts or fallbacks.
Calling every internal call 'REST' without saying why.
Putting business logic into the API gateway.

interview.q: When would you choose microservices over a monolith?
interview.a: When independent deployment and team autonomy are worth the operational cost: a large organization, parts of the system with very different scaling or release rates, or clear business boundaries. For a small team, start with a modular monolith and split when it becomes a problem.

interview.q: What are the costs of microservices?
interview.a: Remote calls are slower and fail, synchronous chains multiply downtime, distributed transactions are hard so you accept eventual consistency, every service needs deployment, monitoring and on-call, and interface changes can break consumers.

interview.q: REST or gRPC?
interview.a: REST over HTTP and JSON is simple, human readable, cacheable and works with browsers, which suits public APIs. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers as the interface definition language and message format, giving typed contracts and compact messages, which suits internal service-to-service calls. Both still need timeouts, retries and idempotency.

interview.q: Why put a queue between two services?
interview.a: To decouple them: the producer returns without waiting, a slow or failed consumer does not block it, and the queue absorbs bursts. The cost is eventual results and the need to handle retries and duplicates, and a growing queue is a signal to apply back pressure or add consumers.

basis: Sources, all read: Martin Fowler's microservices article (characteristics, the costs including distributed complexity, eventual consistency and multiplicative downtime, and the advice to begin with a monolith), the gRPC introduction (Protocol Buffers as both interface definition language and message format; the page does not mention HTTP/2 or call types, so I do not attribute those to it), and the System Design Primer (service discovery, TCP versus UDP, RPC versus REST, back pressure). The shop example and availability figures are illustrative assumptions, and when to split is my judgment. Priorities, hours and every number in the animations are judgment calls or illustrative assumptions, not measurements; where a figure comes from a page I read, the source is named above. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises it for roles whose loops contain a design round (for example, the SDE plan).

scenes.title: Microservices and communication, step by step

steps.title: Start with a monolith
body: A monolith is one deployable application. Martin Fowler's advice is to begin with a monolith, keep it modular, and split it into services once it becomes a problem. Many teams find microservices a heavy burden when they do not need them.
In an interview this is the answer to 'would you use microservices?': it depends on team size and scale, and you say why.

steps.title: Split along business capabilities
body: Microservices (Fowler's common characteristics): independently deployable services organized around business capabilities, owned by teams end to end, with smart endpoints and simple pipes, and each service managing its own data.
Users, Orders and Payments become three services behind one entry point.

steps.title: Service discovery
body: Instances come and go, so callers cannot hard-code addresses. A registry keeps the list of healthy instances (the Primer describes service discovery as registering and finding services); callers or a gateway look up an address and retry on another instance if one fails.
In practice this is built into the platform (Kubernetes services, DNS) rather than hand-built.

steps.title: The cost: a distributed system
body: Fowler: remote calls are more expensive than in-process calls, and a chain of synchronous calls multiplies downtime. Distributed transactions are hard, so services favour eventual consistency and compensating actions. Each service needs its own monitoring and deployment pipeline.
So the benefits (independent deploys, team autonomy) come with real operational costs.

predict.question: Orders calls Payments, which calls a bank, each at 99.9% availability, all synchronously. What happens to Orders' availability?
predict.why: Synchronous dependencies multiply: Orders is only as available as the product of the services it needs. That is Fowler's 'multiplicative effect of downtime'.

steps.title: Choose how services talk: REST or RPC
body: REST over HTTP and JSON is simple, human-readable and works everywhere, which suits public APIs. RPC lets a client call a method on a remote server as if it were local; gRPC uses Protocol Buffers as both the interface definition language and the message format, which gives compact messages and strongly typed contracts for internal calls.
Choose by audience: public and browser clients use REST; internal service-to-service calls often use RPC.

card.title: Compare
lines: REST   resources + HTTP verbs, JSON, cacheable, browsers
gRPC   typed methods from a .proto file, compact binary
both    need timeouts, retries and idempotency

steps.title: Asynchronous messaging decouples services
body: Instead of Orders waiting on Payments, it publishes an event to a queue and carries on. Payments consumes it later. A slow consumer no longer slows the producer, and a failed consumer can retry. Back pressure (a queue that grows) signals that consumers are too slow; limit the queue or add consumers.
The cost: the result arrives later, so the user experience and consistency model must allow it.

steps.title: TCP and UDP
body: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: ordered delivery, retransmission, congestion control; it suits requests and responses. UDP is connectionless with no delivery guarantee but lower overhead: it suits live video, voice and games where a late packet is worse than a lost one. (System Design Primer)
Most service calls run over TCP; gRPC runs over HTTP/2, which uses TCP.

card.title: Choose
lines: TCP  ordered, reliable, retransmits   web, APIs, databases
UDP  no guarantee, low overhead          live video, voice, DNS, games

steps.title: API gateway
body: A gateway is the single entry for clients: it routes to services, authenticates, applies rate limits, terminates TLS and aggregates responses. It also becomes a critical dependency, so run several instances and keep business logic out of it.
Use it so clients do not need to know the service layout.

steps.title: Recap
body: Monolith first, split on business capabilities when needed. Add discovery, a gateway and an async path, and pay attention to the costs: remote calls, chains of availability, eventual consistency. Choose REST for public APIs, RPC for internal, queues to decouple.

everyday.plain: Instead of one big program, you can have many small ones that talk to each other.
everyday.story: A hospital is not one person doing everything. There is a reception, a pharmacy, a lab, a billing desk. Each does one job and they pass notes to each other. This helps when each team works alone. But passing notes takes time and can go wrong, so you should not split into small desks too early.
words: One program that holds the whole application.
A small program that does one job and talks to others.
A style of API that uses web addresses and simple actions like GET and POST.
Finding where a service currently runs.

title: Forward and Reverse Proxies
tagline: A proxy is a go-between. Which side it stands for decides what it is for, what it hides, and what it can break.
explain: A proxy is a server that sits between two parties and passes messages along. The word alone does not say which side it works for, so interviewers ask you to separate two kinds: a forward proxy and a reverse proxy.
## Forward proxy: stands for the clients

A forward proxy sits in front of clients. The clients send their requests to it, and it fetches from the internet on their behalf. The website sees the proxy, not the client. Typical uses are filtering what employees may visit, caching popular downloads, and hiding the client's address. No page I read defines a forward proxy, so this paragraph is general knowledge.
## Reverse proxy: stands for the servers

A reverse proxy sits in front of servers. Clients talk to it, believing it is the website, and it passes each request to a server behind it. The NGINX documentation describes it this way: it sends the client request to a proxied server, fetches the response, and sends it back to the client. The docs list typical uses as distributing load and passing requests to application servers. The client never sees how many servers there are or where they are.
## What a reverse proxy does for you

It ends HTTPS (TLS termination), so app servers speak plain HTTP on a private network. It spreads requests over several servers (load balancing, see the load balancing lesson). It can serve static files and cache responses. It can reject bad requests or apply rate limits before they reach the app. With buffering on, which is the NGINX default, it reads the whole response from the app and then sends it to a slow client at the client's pace, freeing the app early.
## How it passes requests

In NGINX you write proxy_pass inside a location block, for example proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000. By default NGINX sets the Host header to the proxy_host variable and the Connection header to close, so use proxy_set_header to pass the original Host and anything else the app needs. If proxy_pass has a URI, it replaces the matching part of the request path.
## The cost: the app no longer sees the client

Behind a proxy, every connection comes from the proxy's address. To recover the real client address, proxies add a header such as X-Forwarded-For. That header is easy to forge, so the app must trust it only when the direct connection comes from a proxy you run. Django has the same warning: SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER should be set only if you understand the risk, because a forgeable header can lead to CSRF problems. The NGINX page I read does not cover X-Forwarded-For; that part is general knowledge.
## Single point of failure
One reverse proxy is one thing that can fail and take the whole site down. Run two or more behind a load balancer or a floating address. Keep its config simple, because everything flows through it.
## How to talk through it

Say which side the proxy serves. Then list what it gives (TLS termination, load balancing, caching, protection) and what it costs (an extra hop, hidden client IP, a possible single point of failure). Mention that an API gateway is a reverse proxy with extras such as authentication and routing.
keyPoints: A forward proxy stands for clients (outbound); a reverse proxy stands for servers (inbound).
A reverse proxy gives TLS termination, load balancing, caching, buffering and protection.
The app sees the proxy's address; recover the client from X-Forwarded-For, but only from a trusted proxy.
NGINX: proxy_pass sends the request on; proxy_set_header passes the Host and other headers; buffering is on by default.
One proxy is a single point of failure: run more than one.

sql.title: Trust the forwarded header only from our own proxy

exercise: Set up NGINX in front of a small web app with proxy_pass and proxy_set_header Host. Print the client address the app sees with and without X-Forwarded-For. Then send a request with a forged X-Forwarded-For header straight to the app and to the proxy, and show that only the version that trusts the proxy alone survives. Finally add a second app server and explain what changes for the proxy.
pitfalls: Trusting X-Forwarded-For from any client, so anyone can fake their address.
Forgetting proxy_set_header Host, so the app sees the proxy's host name.
Putting one proxy in front and treating it as if it cannot fail.
Mixing up the two kinds: a forward proxy hides clients, a reverse proxy hides servers.
Caching responses that differ per user at the proxy.

interview.q: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
interview.a: A forward proxy acts for clients: clients send requests to it and it fetches from the internet, hiding the client from the site. A reverse proxy acts for servers: clients talk to it and it passes requests to servers behind it, hiding the servers.

interview.q: Why put a reverse proxy in front of an application server?
interview.a: It can end TLS, spread load over several servers, serve static files, cache, buffer slow clients and filter bad requests, so the app server only does application work.

interview.q: How does an app find the real client IP behind a proxy?
interview.a: From a header the proxy adds, such as X-Forwarded-For. Because clients can send that header too, the app should trust it only when the direct connection is from a proxy it controls.

interview.q: What is TLS termination?
interview.a: The proxy handles the encrypted HTTPS connection with the client and passes plain HTTP to the servers behind it, usually over a private network.

interview.q: What are the downsides of a reverse proxy?
interview.a: An extra hop, the app loses the client's address unless forwarded, and a single proxy is a single point of failure, so you run several.

basis: Why it is here: forward versus reverse proxy is a standard warm-up in system design rounds, and the project's own deployment puts NGINX in front of the app. How a reverse proxy works, proxy_pass and its URI rule, the default Host and Connection headers, proxy_set_header and buffering are from the NGINX reverse proxy page I read; it does not mention X-Forwarded-For. What TLS provides is from the MDN page I read. The warning about trusting a proxy header is from the Django security page I read. The description of a forward proxy and the X-Forwarded-For header are general knowledge that I did not check against a page. The step-by-step picture, the idea of one proxy failing, and the choice of what to stress are my own judgment; the numbers shown in the animation are illustrative assumptions, not measurements. Hours and priority are my judgment.

scenes.title: Two proxies, two sides

steps.title: Without a proxy the client talks straight to the site
body: The website sees each client's address. Servers are reachable directly, so every server must handle HTTPS, slow clients and attacks itself.
A proxy is a go-between that takes some of these jobs.

steps.title: A forward proxy stands in front of the clients
body: Clients send requests to the forward proxy, and it fetches from the internet for them. The website sees the proxy, not the client.
Typical uses: filtering, caching downloads, hiding the client's address (general knowledge).

steps.title: A reverse proxy stands in front of the servers
body: Clients talk to the reverse proxy as if it were the website. It sends each request to a server behind it, fetches the response and sends it back.
The client cannot see how many servers there are.

predict.question: Which proxy hides the servers from the clients?
predict.why: A reverse proxy stands in front of the servers, so clients only see the proxy.

steps.title: The proxy ends HTTPS so the app does not have to
body: TLS termination: the proxy handles the encrypted connection and passes plain HTTP to the app on a private network.
TLS gives encryption, integrity and authentication on the public side.

steps.title: It spreads requests over several servers
body: With two app servers behind it, the proxy can alternate or pick the least busy one. This is load balancing, covered in its own lesson.
Clients still see one address.

steps.title: It buffers for slow clients
body: With buffering on (the NGINX default), the proxy reads the whole response from the app quickly, then hands it to a slow phone at the phone's pace.
The app server is free sooner.

callout.text: Turning proxy_buffering off streams the response, but then a slow client holds the app.

steps.title: Behind a proxy the app sees the proxy's address
body: Every connection now comes from the proxy. To find the real client, the proxy adds X-Forwarded-For.
But clients can send that header too, so trust it only when the direct connection is from a proxy you run.

callout.text: Django gives the same warning for SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER.

predict.question: A client sends its own X-Forwarded-For header straight to your app. Should the app trust it?
options: No, only when the direct peer is your own proxy
predict.why: Anyone can send the header. Trust it only when it comes through a proxy you control.

steps.title: One proxy is a single point of failure
body: If the only proxy dies, the whole site is unreachable. Run at least two behind a floating address or another load balancer.
Keep its configuration small, because everything passes through it.

callout.text: A proxy that protects the servers must not become the weakest part.

everyday.plain: A go-between that passes messages along. Whose side it stands on decides what it is for.
everyday.story: A receptionist in a big office takes every visitor's request and sends it to the right person inside. Visitors never learn who sits where. A school guard at the gate, by contrast, lets students out only to approved places. One protects the inside, the other controls the outside.
words: A server that passes requests and responses between two parties.
A proxy that stands in front of clients and fetches from the internet for them.
A proxy that stands in front of servers and passes client requests to them.
Ending the encrypted connection at the proxy and passing plain traffic behind it.
A header that carries the original client address through a proxy.

title: Partitioning and Sharding in Practice
tagline: Cut one huge table into pieces. Choose the piece boundaries well, or one piece does all the work.
explain: When one table becomes too big or too busy, you cut it into pieces. Two words describe this and they are often mixed up. Partitioning splits a table into parts that usually live on one server. Sharding spreads the pieces over several servers. The cutting rule is similar, and the cost of getting it wrong is bigger when the pieces are on different machines.
## Partitioning inside one database

PostgreSQL supports range, list and hash partitioning. You declare the table with PARTITION BY and the partition key, then create partitions for value ranges or lists. The partitioned table has no storage of its own: a row goes to the partition its key belongs to. A range includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound. If a row fits no partition, the insert fails until you add one.
## Why partition

The PostgreSQL docs list the benefits. A query that filters on the key reads only the matching partitions, which is called partition pruning, and you can check it with EXPLAIN. Old data can be removed by dropping or detaching a partition, which is much cheaper than a huge DELETE. Cold data can move to cheaper storage. The docs give a rule of thumb that a table is worth partitioning when its size exceeds the memory of the server. The limits are real: a unique or primary key must include every partition key column.
## Sharding across servers

When one machine cannot hold the data or take the writes, you shard: each shard is a separate database holding part of the data, and a router sends each request to the right one. The core decision is the shard key, the column whose value picks the shard.
## Choosing the shard key

MongoDB's documentation names the tests, and they apply to any system. Cardinality: a key with only 7 distinct values (continents) can have at most 7 chunks, so more than 7 shards are useless. Frequency: if most rows share a few values, those chunks become hot and cannot be split. Monotonic change: a key that always increases, such as a timestamp or counter, sends every new insert to the last chunk, so one shard takes all the writes. Query pattern: a query that includes the shard key goes to one shard; one that does not is broadcast to all shards and the answers are combined (scatter-gather).
## Hashed or ranged

A ranged key keeps neighbours together, so range queries are efficient, but it suits keys with high cardinality, low frequency and no steady increase. A hashed key spreads values evenly and fits increasing keys, but neighbouring values land on different shards, so range queries are broadcast. The docs also warn that floating-point values are truncated before hashing, so 2.3 and 2.9 collide.
## Changing your mind

A shard key is hard to change. MongoDB can refine a key by adding suffix fields, or reshard to a different key from version 5.0, but both move large amounts of data. Pick the key against the queries you expect, and choose a key you will not regret. The consistent-hashing lesson shows how to add shards with less data movement.
## How to talk through it

Say whether you need partitioning or sharding. Name the shard key and test it against cardinality, frequency, monotonic change and the main queries. Say what you give up: cross-shard joins and transactions, and the cost of resharding.

sql.title: Range vs hash: where do new ids land?
sql.code:
import zlib

def hash_shard(key, n):
    """Deterministic hash sharding (Python's built-in hash() changes between runs)."""
    return zlib.crc32(str(key).encode()) % n

def range_shard(key, boundaries):
    """boundaries = upper bounds of each shard except the last, e.g. [100, 200] -> 3 shards."""
    for i, upper in enumerate(boundaries):
        if key < upper:
            return i
    return len(boundaries)

def spread(shard_of, keys, n):
    counts = [0] * n
    for k in keys:
        counts[shard_of(k)] += 1
    return counts

ids = range(1000, 1300)                                   # new ids always increase
by_range = spread(lambda k: range_shard(k, [1100, 1200]), ids, 3)
by_hash = spread(lambda k: hash_shard(k, 3), ids, 3)
assert by_range == [100, 100, 100]                        # even over all ids...
newest = range(1290, 1300)                                # ...but a burst of NEW ids all lands on the last shard
assert spread(lambda k: range_shard(k, [1100, 1200]), newest, 3) == [0, 0, 10]
assert max(spread(lambda k: hash_shard(k, 3), newest, 3)) < 10    # hashing spreads the same burst
assert sum(by_hash) == 300

continents = ["asia", "europe", "africa"] * 100               # low cardinality: only 3 distinct keys
assert len(set(hash_shard(c, 8) for c in continents)) <= 3    # at most 3 shards can ever be used, however many exist

exercise: Create a table of orders partitioned by month in PostgreSQL. Insert a year of data, then use EXPLAIN to show that a query for one month reads one partition. Drop the oldest partition. Then, for a sharded version, pick a shard key for orders, test it against cardinality, frequency, monotonic change and your top three queries, and explain which query becomes scatter-gather.
pitfalls: Using an always-increasing key as a ranged shard key and sending every insert to one shard.
A shard key with too few distinct values, so extra shards stay empty.
Sharding before trying indexes, caching and a bigger machine.
Forgetting that queries without the shard key hit every shard.
Assuming joins and transactions across shards work like they do on one server.

interview.q: What is the difference between partitioning and sharding?
interview.a: Partitioning splits one table into parts, usually inside one database server. Sharding spreads data over several independent servers, with a router choosing the server. Both cut the data by a key.

interview.q: How do you choose a shard key?
interview.a: Check cardinality (many distinct values), frequency (no value dominates), monotonic change (the key should not always increase) and whether your main queries include it, so they go to one shard.

interview.q: Why is a timestamp a poor ranged shard key?
interview.a: It always increases, so every new write goes to the shard holding the newest range. That shard becomes a hot spot and the others idle. Hashing the key, or adding a prefix, spreads the writes.

interview.q: What is scatter-gather?
interview.a: A query that does not include the shard key is sent to all shards and the results are combined. It works but costs more as the shard count grows.

interview.q: What does partition pruning do?
interview.a: The planner skips partitions that cannot contain matching rows, based on the filter on the partition key, so the query reads less data.

basis: Why it is here: sharding and partitioning come up in almost every system design round about scale. Range, list and hash partitioning, pruning and EXPLAIN, the benefits, the rule of thumb about table size and memory, the limits on unique keys, and what happens when no partition matches are from the PostgreSQL partitioning page I read; the last section of that page came through a summary. The shard key tests (cardinality, frequency, monotonic change, query pattern), hashed versus ranged sharding, the floating-point warning and refine or reshard are from the MongoDB pages I read. The page on shard keys is an overview, and the detail came from five linked sub-pages. The code sample and the numbers in it and in the animation are illustrative assumptions, not measurements. How to order the explanation is my own judgment. Hours and priority are my judgment.

title: Read Replicas and Replication Lag
tagline: Copy the database so many readers can share the load, and learn why a copy can be a little behind.
explain: Most systems read far more than they write. One database server takes all the writes. Read replicas are copies that follow it and answer read queries. Add replicas and the read load spreads. The price is that a copy can be slightly behind.
## How a replica works

In PostgreSQL a standby server replays the changes (the write-ahead log) of the primary. With hot standby on, which is the default, the standby accepts read-only queries while it replays. It accepts connections once it has reached a consistent state. The primary is the single place where writes happen, so replicas help reads, not writes.
## Read-only means read-only

A hot standby session is strictly read-only. SELECT, cursors, SHOW and transaction control work. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, DDL, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and sequence functions such as nextval are rejected with errors, and the session cannot change its read-only setting. Even temporary tables cannot be written. So a replica is for reporting, search pages, dashboards and any read that can tolerate a short delay.
## Eventually consistent

A change becomes visible on a standby once its commit record has been replayed there. Between the commit on the primary and that moment, a reader of the replica sees the old data. That gap is replication lag. The data is eventually consistent, as the PostgreSQL docs put it. The CAP and consistency lesson explains why asynchronous copies behave this way.
## The bug users notice: not seeing your own write

A user saves a profile, the page reloads and reads from a replica that has not caught up, and the old value appears. It looks like the save failed. The fix is read-your-writes: after a user writes, send that user's reads to the primary for a short time, or until the replica has reached the write's position. The code here uses a five-second window, which is an illustrative choice. Pick the window from your measured lag.
## Query conflicts

Replaying changes can conflict with a long query on the standby: for example, VACUUM on the primary removes old row versions that the standby's query still needs. The standby then waits up to max_standby_streaming_delay and cancels the query if the delay is exceeded. Setting hot_standby_feedback avoids the cancellations but can make tables on the primary bloat. The docs also warn that a long delay can stop other sessions from seeing recent changes. Set limits to suit the workload.
## Operating replicas

Watch the lag, because a replica that falls far behind serves old data and may never catch up. Watch cancellation counts in pg_stat_database_conflicts. Each standby's connection limits must be at least those of the primary. If the primary fails you can promote a replica, but anything the replica had not yet received is lost in asynchronous setups, which is the fail-over trade-off covered in the CAP lesson.
## How to talk through it

Start from a read-heavy workload. Add replicas and route reads to them. Then name the cost: lag, stale reads, the read-your-writes fix, query conflicts, and that writes are still limited to one primary. If writes are the bottleneck, replicas do not help and you look at sharding.
keyPoints: Replicas replay the primary's changes and serve read-only queries; they scale reads, not writes.
A hot standby rejects INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
Replication lag means a reader can see old data; the data is eventually consistent.
Read-your-writes: send a user's reads to the primary briefly after they write.
Long standby queries can be canceled by replay conflicts; watch lag and conflict counts.

Then add a router that sends a user's reads to the primary for five seconds after a write, and show that the stale-read bug disappears.

interview.q: What do read replicas give you, and what do they not give you?
interview.a: They spread read load and give a warm copy for fail-over. They do not increase write capacity, because all writes still go to one primary, and they can be slightly out of date.

interview.q: What is replication lag?
interview.a: The delay between a change being committed on the primary and being visible on a replica. During that gap, a reader of the replica sees the old data.

interview.q: How do you fix a user not seeing their own update?
interview.a: Read-your-writes: after a user writes, route their reads to the primary for a short time or until the replica has caught up to that write.

interview.q: Why can a long query on a standby be canceled?
interview.a: Replaying changes from the primary, such as clean-up of old row versions, can conflict with the rows the query still needs. After the allowed delay the standby cancels the query.

interview.q: When are replicas the wrong answer?
interview.a: When writes are the bottleneck, or when every read must see the latest data. Then you need sharding, a bigger primary, or strongly consistent reads from the primary.

The five-second read-your-writes window and every number in the animation are illustrative assumptions, not recommendations or measurements. The routing design is my own judgment. The remark that an asynchronous replica can miss recent writes on promotion is from the consistency discussion in the earlier lessons of this track, not from this page. Hours and priority are my judgment.

title: Event Streaming with Kafka
tagline: Keep every event in an ordered log that many readers can replay, instead of handing each message to one reader and throwing it away.
explain: The message queue lesson showed a queue where a message is given to a worker and then removed. An event stream is different. Events are written to a log and stay there. Many readers can read the same log, each at its own pace, and can go back and read it again. Apache Kafka is the best-known system built this way.
## Events and topics

The Kafka introduction defines an event as having a key, a value, a timestamp and optional metadata headers. Events are stored in topics. A topic is multi-producer and multi-subscriber: many writers can append to it and many readers can read from it. Events are not deleted after they are consumed. How long they are kept is a setting per topic, and after that old events are discarded.
## Partitions give scale and order

A topic is split into partitions spread across servers, so one topic can be larger and faster than one machine. Events with the same key are written to the same partition. Kafka guarantees that a reader of a partition sees its events in exactly the order they were written. There is no promise about order across different partitions. So pick the key to keep related events together: all events for one order or one user share a key.
## Replication

Each partition is replicated. The introduction says a common production setting is a replication factor of 3, so a partition survives the loss of a server. Producers never need to wait for consumers: writing and reading are decoupled, and a slow reader does not slow a writer.
## Readers, positions and groups

A reader remembers its position in each partition, called an offset, and can move it back to replay. Several instances of one application can share the work by forming a consumer group, where each partition is read by one member. The Kafka introduction page I read does not mention offsets or consumer groups, so this paragraph is general knowledge that you should confirm in the Kafka documentation.
## Delivery guarantees

The introduction says Kafka provides guarantees such as the ability to process events exactly-once, with no detail. The detailed rules for at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery were on a documentation page I could not read. Treat this as an open question to check, and design readers to be idempotent anyway, as in the message queue lesson.
## Queue or log?

Use a queue when each job should be done once by one worker and then forgotten. Use a log when many systems need the same events, when you want to replay history (rebuild a search index, fix a bug and reprocess), or when order per key matters. A log holds data for a retention period, so it is also a buffer between fast writers and slow readers.
## How to talk through it

Say what the events are and what the key is. Explain partitions for scale, per-partition order, retention, and replication. Name the cost: no order across partitions, a new system to run, and readers that must handle duplicates.
keyPoints: An event stream is an ordered log: events stay after being read, and many readers can read at their own pace.
Events have a key, a value, a timestamp and headers; topics are multi-producer and multi-subscriber.
Same key goes to the same partition; order is guaranteed only within a partition.
Retention is per topic; replication factor 3 is common in production.
Use a log when many consumers or replay are needed; use a queue for one-time jobs.

sql.title: A tiny partitioned log
sql.code:
import zlib

class Topic:
    """A tiny partitioned log. Events are appended and never removed by reading."""
    def __init__(self, partitions):
        self.partitions = [[] for _ in range(partitions)]

    def produce(self, key, value):
        p = zlib.crc32(str(key).encode()) % len(self.partitions)      # same key -> same partition
        self.partitions[p].append((key, value))
        return p, len(self.partitions[p]) - 1                          # partition and position

    def read(self, partition, offset):
        """Reading does not delete: any reader can start from any position."""
        return self.partitions[partition][offset:]

t = Topic(3)
placed = [t.produce("user-1", f"event{i}") for i in range(4)]
assert len({p for p, _ in placed}) == 1                                # one key, one partition
p = placed[0][0]
assert [v for _, v in t.read(p, 0)] == ["event0", "event1", "event2", "event3"]   # order kept within a partition
assert [v for _, v in t.read(p, 2)] == ["event2", "event3"]                       # a second reader can replay from 2
assert len(t.read(p, 0)) == 4                                                     # nothing was deleted by reading

Start a reader, stop it halfway, and restart it from where it left off. Then reset its position to the start and replay everything. Write one paragraph on why order across partitions is not guaranteed and how your key choice works around it.

interview.q: What is the difference between a message queue and an event log like Kafka?
interview.a: A queue hands each message to one worker and removes it. A log keeps events for a retention period, so many readers can read the same events, each at its own position, and can replay them.

interview.q: Why does Kafka partition a topic?
interview.a: To spread a topic over many servers for scale. Events with the same key go to the same partition, and order is guaranteed within a partition.

interview.q: Is order guaranteed across a whole topic?
interview.a: No. Order is guaranteed only within a partition. If related events must stay in order, give them the same key so they share a partition.

interview.q: How does Kafka survive a server failure?
interview.a: Each partition is replicated to other servers. A common production replication factor is 3.

interview.q: When would you choose a log over a queue?
interview.a: When several systems need the same events, when you need to replay history, or when ordering per key matters.

title: Real-Time Updates: Polling, SSE and WebSockets
tagline: How a server tells a browser that something changed, without the browser asking again and again.
explain: HTTP was built so that the client asks and the server answers. A chat message, a score update or a progress bar needs the opposite: the server speaks first. There are four common ways to get there, and a system design answer names the trade-offs.
## Polling and long polling

Polling is the simplest: the client asks 'anything new?' every few seconds. It works everywhere, but most answers are 'no', and an update waits up to one interval. Long polling holds each request open until there is news or a timeout, then the client asks again. It cuts the empty answers and the wait, at the cost of many open requests. These two are general knowledge; no page I read describes them.
## Server-sent events (SSE)

SSE is a one-way stream from server to browser. The client uses EventSource, and the server replies with the content type text/event-stream, a UTF-8 stream where each message ends with a blank line. A message can have the fields event, data, id and retry, and a line starting with a colon is a comment, which is handy as a keep-alive. If the connection drops, the browser reconnects by default. The page is clear that you cannot send events from the client to the server over it.
## The connection limit

Over HTTP/1.1 a browser allows 6 connections per domain, shared across tabs, and each open SSE stream uses one. The MDN page says this is marked 'Won't fix' in Chrome and Firefox. Under HTTP/2 the number of streams is negotiated and defaults to 100. Open many tabs on plain HTTP/1.1 and later requests wait.
## WebSockets

A WebSocket is a two-way session between browser and server. It starts as a normal HTTP request: a GET using HTTP 1.1 or later with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, Sec-WebSocket-Key and Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept, a value made by adding a fixed GUID to the key, taking SHA-1 and encoding in base64. After that, both sides send frames. Client frames must be masked. Ping and pong frames check that the other side is alive. Browsers generally require a secure connection, and ports other than 80 and 443 may have trouble with firewalls and proxies.
## What WebSockets do not give you

The MDN page warns that the WebSocket API has no backpressure: if messages arrive faster than you process them, memory can fill or the CPU can reach 100 percent. It points to WebTransport as an alternative. Reconnection is also not automatic, unlike SSE, so you write that logic. An open WebSocket can keep a page out of the browser's back-forward cache, so close it when done.
## Scaling many connections

Each user holds a connection to one server, so a message for user A must reach the server that holds A. A common design puts a publish and subscribe layer (a message broker or Redis) between servers: the server that receives a message publishes it, and every server forwards it to its own connected users. Load balancers must keep a connection on one server. That is my own judgment on a common design, not a rule from the pages.
## How to talk through it

Ask how fast updates must arrive and which direction messages flow. Server to client only, such as notifications or live scores: SSE is simple and reconnects by itself. Two-way and frequent, such as chat or games: WebSockets. Rare updates or the simplest possible option: polling. Then cover the connection count, reconnection, heartbeats and backpressure.
keyPoints: Polling asks repeatedly; long polling holds the request open; SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream; WebSocket is two-way.

interview.q: What is the difference between SSE and WebSockets?

interview.q: How does a WebSocket connection start?
interview.a: The client sends an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket and a Sec-WebSocket-Key. The server replies 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept, and both sides then exchange frames.

interview.q: When would you choose polling?
interview.a: When updates are rare, delays of a few seconds are fine, and you want the simplest thing that works through every proxy. Long polling is a step up with fewer empty replies.

interview.q: What is a problem with WebSockets at scale?
interview.a: A user's connection is on one server, so a message must reach that server, usually through a publish and subscribe layer. Also no backpressure and no automatic reconnect, so you handle both.

interview.q: What limits SSE in a browser?
interview.a: Over HTTP/1.1 a browser allows about 6 connections per domain, shared across tabs. HTTP/2 raises the number of streams, which defaults to 100.

title: Sagas: Transactions Across Services
tagline: When one business action touches several databases, you cannot use one transaction. A saga replaces it with small steps and a plan to undo them.
explain: Inside one database, a transaction makes several changes succeed or fail together. When each service owns its own database, one transaction cannot span them. Placing an order may need the order service, the customer service and the stock service to each change their own data. A saga is the usual answer.
## What a saga is

The microservices.io page defines a saga as a reliably coordinated sequence of local transactions. Each step is an ordinary transaction inside one service. If a step fails because of a business rule, the saga runs compensating transactions that undo the steps already finished. The page's example is an order that must not exceed the customer's credit limit, where orders and customers live in different databases.
## Why not two-phase commit
The page lists the force bluntly: two-phase commit is not an option. A distributed transaction across services couples them and holds locks across a network. A saga trades that for design work.
## Compensation is not rollback

A database rollback erases a change as if it never happened. A compensating transaction is a new action that cancels the effect: refund a payment, release a reservation, mark the order canceled. The page names this as a drawback: no automatic rollback, so you must design the compensations. Some actions cannot be undone, such as an email already sent, so order the steps so that the hardest step to undo comes last.
## Two ways to coordinate

In choreography each service publishes an event when its step finishes and the next service reacts. The order service creates the order as PENDING and emits Order Created. The customer service reserves credit and emits the result. The order service then approves or rejects. In orchestration a saga orchestrator tells each participant what to do, step by step, and handles the replies. Choreography has no central piece but is hard to follow. Orchestration is easier to read and test, and the orchestrator is one more component to run.
## Lack of isolation

The page names a second drawback: sagas lack the I in ACID. While a saga runs, other requests can see its half-finished changes, which can cause anomalies. It says countermeasures exist, and points to a book chapter for them, so I do not list them as sourced. A common practical step is a visible state such as PENDING, so other code knows the order is not final.
## Publishing the event safely

A service must update its database and publish an event, and a distributed transaction between the two is not available. The page names event sourcing and the transactional outbox as the options. An outbox writes the event into a table in the same transaction as the data change, and a separate process publishes it.
## What the client sees

The page gives three choices. Reply only when the saga finishes. Reply at once with the order id and let the client poll for the result. Or reply with the id and push the result later, for example by WebSocket or webhook. How to talk through it: describe the steps and their compensations, pick choreography or orchestration with a reason, and say what happens when a compensation itself fails: retry it until it works, so make every step and compensation idempotent.
keyPoints: A saga is a sequence of local transactions, with a compensating transaction for each step that can be undone.
Two-phase commit across services is not an option; a saga trades it for design work.
Choreography: services react to each other's events. Orchestration: a coordinator tells each one what to do.
Sagas lack isolation: show a PENDING state and expect other requests to see half-finished work.
Use a transactional outbox to update data and publish the event together; make steps and compensations idempotent.

sql.title: A tiny orchestrated saga with compensation
sql.code:
class Saga:
    """Run local steps in order. If one fails, run the compensations of the finished steps in reverse."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.steps = []

    def add(self, name, action, compensate):
        self.steps.append((name, action, compensate))
        return self

    def run(self):
        done, log = [], []
        for name, action, compensate in self.steps:
            try:
                action()
                done.append((name, compensate))
                log.append(f"{name}: ok")
            except Exception as e:                       # a step failed: undo what finished, newest first
                log.append(f"{name}: failed ({e})")
                for done_name, undo in reversed(done):
                    undo()
                    log.append(f"{done_name}: compensated")
                return False, log
        return True, log

state = {"order": None, "credit": 100, "stock": 1}

def create_order(): state["order"] = "PENDING"
def cancel_order(): state["order"] = "CANCELLED"
def reserve_credit():
    if state["credit"] < 150:
        raise ValueError("credit limit")
    state["credit"] -= 150
def release_credit(): state["credit"] += 150

ok, log = Saga().add("create order", create_order, cancel_order).add("reserve credit", reserve_credit, release_credit).run()
assert ok is False
assert log == ["create order: ok", "reserve credit: failed (credit limit)", "create order: compensated"]
assert state["order"] == "CANCELLED" and state["credit"] == 100         # the first step was undone

state["credit"] = 500
ok, log = Saga().add("create order", create_order, cancel_order).add("reserve credit", reserve_credit, release_credit).run()
assert ok is True and state["credit"] == 350

Then make a compensation fail once, and add a retry so that it still completes. Finally list one step in your design that cannot be undone, and say how you would reorder the saga because of it.
pitfalls: Treating a compensation like a rollback and forgetting that it is a new action that can also fail.
Ignoring that other requests see half-finished state while a saga runs.
Updating the database and then publishing an event in two separate steps, so one can succeed without the other.
Putting the step that cannot be undone first instead of last.
Non-idempotent steps, so a retry applies the effect twice.

interview.q: What is a saga and why use it?
interview.a: A sequence of local transactions across services, coordinated so that either all steps complete or the finished ones are undone by compensating transactions. It is used because one ACID transaction cannot span several services' databases.

interview.q: What is a compensating transaction?
interview.a: A new action that cancels the effect of an earlier step, such as refunding a payment or releasing a reservation. It is not a database rollback, so it must be designed and may itself need retries.

interview.q: What is the difference between choreography and orchestration?
interview.a: In choreography services publish events and react to each other with no central controller. In orchestration a central orchestrator sends commands to each participant and handles their replies.

interview.q: What is the main weakness of sagas?
interview.a: Lack of isolation: concurrent requests can see the saga's intermediate state. There is also no automatic rollback, so compensations must be written by hand.

interview.q: How do you update data and publish an event reliably?
interview.a: Use the transactional outbox: write the event to a table in the same local transaction as the data change, and have a separate process publish it. Event sourcing is the other option.

title: API Design: Resources, Methods and Retries
tagline: A good API says clearly what each call does, what is safe to repeat, and what happens when a call is sent twice.
explain: An API is a contract between your service and every client. Interviewers ask about it because the same few decisions decide whether it is pleasant to use and whether it survives failures: names, methods, status codes, paging, and retries.
## Resources and methods

In a REST-style API, nouns are resources (/orders/42) and the HTTP method is the verb. MDN's table lists the properties that matter. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe, which means read-only, and idempotent. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe. POST and PATCH are neither. GET is cacheable. POST and PATCH are cacheable only in narrow cases. GET should only retrieve data, PUT replaces the whole resource, PATCH applies a partial change, and POST usually causes a change or side effect.
## What idempotent really means

A method is idempotent if the intended effect of many identical requests equals the effect of one. It does not mean the response is identical: the first DELETE may return 200 and the next 404. It also does not mean there are no side effects such as logging. The rule that matters for design is in RFC 9110: an idempotent request can be repeated automatically after a communication failure, a proxy must not retry a non-idempotent request, and clients should not either unless they know it is safe.
## Making POST safe to retry

A network timeout leaves the client unsure whether a charge happened. For POST, let the client send an idempotency key. The server stores the result under the key and returns the same result for a repeat, as in the Stripe design. The code here is a tiny version. Keys need an expiry and a check that the repeat has the same body.
## Status codes

Use the classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. Common choices are 200 OK, 201 Created after a create, 204 No Content with no body, 400 for malformed requests, 401 when unauthenticated, 403 when authenticated but refused, 404 not found, 409 conflict with current state, 422 when the request is well formed but semantically invalid, 429 when rate limited, 500 for a server fault and 503 for temporary unavailability. 429 and 503 can carry Retry-After.
## Paging lists

Offset paging (page=3) is simple, but if a row is inserted between requests, a row can appear twice or be skipped. Cursor paging returns an opaque cursor, such as the last id seen, and the next request continues after it, so inserts do not shift the pages. It also stays fast for big tables. This advice is my own judgment and general knowledge; the pages I read do not cover it.
## Caching and conditional requests
Send Cache-Control and an ETag on responses that can be cached. A client that sends If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified when nothing changed, with no body.
## Versioning and errors

Plan for change: put a version in the path or a header, never break old clients in place, and add fields rather than changing them. Return errors in one consistent shape with a machine-readable code and a human message. If you need streaming or a strict typed contract between services, gRPC is an alternative to REST.
## How to talk through it

List the resources and the calls. For each call say the method, the success and failure statuses, whether it is idempotent, and how a client retries. Cover paging, rate limits with 429 and Retry-After, caching, and versioning.
keyPoints: Resources are nouns, methods are verbs: GET/HEAD/OPTIONS safe; PUT/DELETE idempotent; POST/PATCH neither.
Idempotent means one effect, not one response; only retry automatically when the request is idempotent.
Make POST retryable with an idempotency key that stores and returns the first result.
Use status classes and the right codes: 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, 503 with Retry-After.
Page big lists with cursors; use ETag and 304 for caching; version the API.

sql.title: An idempotency key stops double charges
Cursor pagination survives inserts
sql.code:
def page(items, limit, after=None):
    """Cursor pagination: 'after' is the last id the client saw, so inserts do not shift the pages."""
    start = 0 if after is None else next((i + 1 for i, it in enumerate(items) if it["id"] == after), len(items))
    chunk = items[start:start + limit]
    next_cursor = chunk[-1]["id"] if start + limit < len(items) else None
    return {"data": chunk, "next": next_cursor}

rows = [{"id": i} for i in range(1, 8)]
p1 = page(rows, 3)
assert [r["id"] for r in p1["data"]] == [1, 2, 3] and p1["next"] == 3
rows.insert(0, {"id": 0})                          # a new row appears at the front between requests
p2 = page(rows, 3, after=p1["next"])
assert [r["id"] for r in p2["data"]] == [4, 5, 6]  # no repeats and no gaps; offset paging would repeat row 3

exercise: Design an API for a to-do app with users, lists and items. Write the table of endpoints with method, success status, failure statuses, and whether each is idempotent. Add an Idempotency-Key to the create endpoint and implement it with a dictionary. Then page the item list with a cursor, insert rows while paging, and show that no item repeats or disappears.
pitfalls: Using GET for something that changes data, which crawlers and prefetchers will trigger.
Retrying a POST automatically without an idempotency key and charging twice.
Returning 200 with an error message in the body.
Offset paging on a list that changes while the client pages through it.
Breaking clients by changing a field's meaning without a new version.

interview.q: What is the difference between safe and idempotent?
interview.a: Safe means the request does not change server state (read-only). Idempotent means repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once. GET is both; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST is neither.

interview.q: How do you make a payment endpoint safe to retry?
interview.a: Require an idempotency key. Store the result under the key and return the stored result if the same key arrives again, so a retry after a timeout does not charge twice.

interview.q: When do you return 401 and when 403?
interview.a: 401 means the client is not authenticated. 403 means the client's identity is known but it is not allowed to do this.

interview.q: Why prefer cursor pagination to offset pagination?
interview.a: With offsets, an insert or delete between requests shifts the rows, so items repeat or vanish, and large offsets get slow. A cursor continues after a known row, so pages stay stable.

interview.q: What does a 429 response tell the client?
interview.a: It has sent too many requests in a given time and is being rate limited. A Retry-After header can say how long to wait.

basis: Why it is here: every system design answer includes an API, and interviewers probe idempotency, status codes and paging. The method table (safe, idempotent, cacheable), the descriptions of GET, PUT, POST, PATCH and DELETE, and the footnote about POST and PATCH are from the MDN methods page I read. The status classes and the meaning of the common codes are from the MDN status page I read. The definition of idempotent, its caveats, and the retry rules are from the RFC 9110 section, the MDN glossary pages and the MDN 429 page, all of which I read. The idempotency key idea is from the Stripe post I read. Cursor versus offset paging, versioning advice and the gRPC remark are general knowledge and my own judgment, not taken from those pages. The animation values are illustrative assumptions. Hours and priority are my judgment.

A unique value a client sends so the server can recognize a repeated request.
A marker for where to continue a list, instead of a page number.
