title: Generating Unique IDs at Scale
tagline: Every row, order and message needs an ID that is unique, and often sortable by time, with no server asking another for permission.
explain: A single database can hand out ids 1, 2, 3 with an auto-increment column. Once data is spread over many servers, that counter becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure. The question 'how do you generate unique ids?' appears in many designs: URL shorteners, feeds, chat, orders.
## What we want from an id

Twitter's Snowflake README lists the requirements that shaped its design: at least 10,000 ids per second per process, machines generating ids should not have to coordinate with each other, and the ids should be directly sortable. Those three are a good checklist: unique, fast, no coordination, and sortable by time.
## Option 1: UUIDs

A UUID is 128 bits (RFC 9562). Version 4 is random, with 122 random bits, so any machine can make one with no coordination. The cost is that random ids do not sort by time, and the RFC notes that versions which are not time ordered have poor database-index locality: new rows land all over the index. Version 7 puts a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp first, so ids sort by time, which fixes that. The layout of version 7 came to me through a summary of a long page, so check the RFC before quoting bit sizes.
## Option 2: Snowflake-style ids

Pack three fields into one 64-bit number: 41 bits of time in milliseconds from a custom epoch (about 69 years), 10 bits for a machine id (up to 1024 machines) and 12 bits for a sequence number that rolls over every 4096 ids per machine. That is 63 bits, so it fits a signed 64-bit integer. Ids are roughly time ordered, with no coordination except giving each machine a unique id once. The README says the ordering is k-sorted: it promises one second and aims for tens of milliseconds.
## The clock is the weak spot

Snowflake depends on the clock. If the clock moves backwards, ids could repeat. The README says the system refuses to generate ids until a time later than the last one it used, and it recommends NTP set up so it never steps the clock backwards. Other failure modes are two machines given the same machine id and a sequence that runs out inside one millisecond, which the generator handles by waiting for the next millisecond.
## Option 3: a ticket server or database sequence

One server hands out ranges of ids (1 to 1000) to application servers, which then use them locally. It is simple and ids are small, but the ticket server is a single point of failure unless replicated, and ids are not time sorted across servers. This option is general knowledge, not from a page I read.
## Choosing

Need no coordination and a 128-bit id is fine: UUID (version 7 if you want order). Need 64-bit, sortable, compact ids: Snowflake style. Need small sequential numbers and a modest scale: a database sequence. Also say what an id reveals: a time-ordered id leaks when something was created, which may matter.
## How to talk through it
Start with the requirements, name the three options with their costs, choose one for the system at hand, and finish with the failure mode of that choice, which for Snowflake is the clock.
keyPoints: Good ids: unique, fast, no coordination between machines, and sortable by time.
UUIDv4 is random (122 random bits) and sorts badly in indexes; UUIDv7 starts with a millisecond timestamp.
Snowflake: 41 bits time + 10 bits machine + 12 bits sequence = 63 bits, roughly time ordered.
The clock is the weak spot: refuse to generate ids if it moves backwards.
A ticket server gives ranges but is a single point of failure.

sql.title: A Snowflake-style id generator
sql.code:
class Snowflake:
    """41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of worker id, 12 bits of sequence (the layout in Twitter's README)."""
    EPOCH = 1_288_834_974_657          # a custom epoch (ms); any fixed past time works

    def __init__(self, worker, clock_ms):
        assert 0 <= worker < 1024
        self.worker, self.clock = worker, clock_ms
        self.last, self.seq = -1, 0

    def next_id(self):
        now = self.clock()
        if now < self.last:
            raise RuntimeError("clock moved backwards: refuse to generate ids")
        if now == self.last:
            self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & 0xFFF          # 12 bits: 4096 ids per millisecond per worker
            if self.seq == 0:                          # sequence used up: wait for the next millisecond
                while now <= self.last:
                    now = self.clock()
        else:
            self.seq = 0
        self.last = now
        return ((now - self.EPOCH) << 22) | (self.worker << 12) | self.seq

def decode(i):
    return {"ms": (i >> 22) + Snowflake.EPOCH, "worker": (i >> 12) & 0x3FF, "seq": i & 0xFFF}

t = [Snowflake.EPOCH + 1000]
g1, g2 = Snowflake(1, lambda: t[0]), Snowflake(2, lambda: t[0])
a, b = g1.next_id(), g1.next_id()                      # same millisecond: the sequence separates them
assert a < b and decode(b)["seq"] == decode(a)["seq"] + 1
assert g1.next_id() != g2.next_id()                    # different workers never collide
t[0] += 1
c = g1.next_id()
assert c > b and decode(c) == {"ms": Snowflake.EPOCH + 1001, "worker": 1, "seq": 0}    # later time sorts later
t[0] -= 5
try:
    g1.next_id()
    assert False, "should have refused"
except RuntimeError:
    pass                                               # a backwards clock is refused, as the README describes
assert (1 << 63) > a                                   # 41 + 10 + 12 = 63 bits fits a signed 64-bit integer

exercise: Implement the generator above and add a test where 5,000 ids are requested within one millisecond, so the sequence overflows, and show the generator waits for the next millisecond. Then write down the bit layout for a different design, 5 bits of datacenter and 5 bits of machine, and say how many ids per millisecond per machine you still get.
pitfalls: Using auto-increment ids across several database servers and getting collisions.
Giving two machines the same machine id.
Letting the clock go backwards without noticing.
Random UUIDs as a primary key in a huge table, causing scattered index writes.
Showing sequential ids to users, which leaks volume and creation order.

interview.q: How would you generate unique ids across many servers?
interview.a: Pick a scheme that needs no per-id coordination: UUIDs, or Snowflake-style ids that pack a timestamp, a machine id and a sequence into 64 bits. A ticket server handing out ranges is a simpler alternative.

interview.q: How is a Snowflake id built?
interview.a: 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits for the machine, and 12 bits for a per-millisecond sequence. They add up to 63 bits, so the id fits a signed 64-bit integer and is roughly time ordered.

interview.q: What happens if the clock goes backwards?
interview.a: The generator could repeat ids, so it should refuse to generate until the clock passes the last time it used. NTP should be set so it does not step the clock backwards.

interview.q: Why are random UUIDs bad as database keys?
interview.a: They are not ordered by time, so new rows are inserted at random places in the index, which hurts locality. A time-ordered id such as UUIDv7 avoids this.

interview.q: What happens if more than 4096 ids are needed in one millisecond on one machine?
interview.a: The 12-bit sequence is used up, so the generator waits until the next millisecond and starts again from 0.

The Snowflake layout (41, 10 and 12 bits), the requirements, k-sorted ordering and the behavior on a backwards clock are from the archived Snowflake README I read; it does not mention the epoch value, a sign bit or a comparison with UUIDs. The UUID facts (128 bits, version 4 layout and 122 random bits, poor index locality of non-time-ordered versions) are from the RFC 9562 text I read before it was cut; the version 7 layout and sortability came from a summary. The ticket server option and the advice on which option to choose are general knowledge and my own judgment. The numbers used in the animation are illustrative assumptions. Hours and priority are my judgment.

title: Distributed Locks and Fencing Tokens
tagline: Let only one machine at a time do a job, and learn why a lock that can expire is not enough to protect your data.
explain: A lock inside one program is easy. A lock shared by many machines is hard, because machines pause, networks delay and clocks drift. Interviewers ask about it when two workers must not do the same job, or two writers must not corrupt the same record.
## Two reasons for a lock

Martin Kleppmann separates them. An efficiency lock saves work: if two workers both do a job, you waste a little money, but nothing breaks. A correctness lock prevents concurrent processes from stepping on each other, and failure means data loss or permanent inconsistency. The same tool can be fine for one and unsafe for the other. Decide which you need first.
## A lock in Redis

The Redis documentation describes the single-instance recipe: SET resource_name my_random_value NX PX 30000. NX sets the key only if it does not exist, and PX gives an expiry of 30,000 milliseconds. The value must be unique across clients and requests. To release, delete the key only if its value still matches yours, atomically. A plain DEL is unsafe because a client may remove another client's lock. The expiry matters: it frees the lock if the holder crashes.
## The trouble with expiry

A lock with a lease can expire while its holder is still working. Kleppmann's example is a long garbage-collection pause, and he notes a network packet delayed for about 90 seconds in a GitHub incident. Client A takes the lock, pauses past its lease, client B takes the lock, then A wakes and writes, believing it still holds the lock. Checking the lease just before writing does not help, because a pause can happen right after the check.
## Fencing tokens

The fix is a fencing token: a number that increases each time the lock is granted. The client sends the token with every write, and the storage rejects any write with a token lower than one it has already seen. If A held token 33 and B was granted 34, A's late write with 33 is refused. This only works if the resource itself checks the token. ZooKeeper's zxid or a znode version can serve as the token.
## Redlock

Redlock uses N=5 independent Redis masters. A client tries all five and holds the lock only if a majority (three) accept within a time that leaves part of the lease. The Redis page itself says you should implement fencing tokens, and admits that with asynchronous replication a failover can break mutual exclusion. Kleppmann's critique is that Redlock has no facility for generating fencing tokens and depends on clocks, and that for correctness you should use a consensus system such as ZooKeeper, or a database with reasonable transactional guarantees.
## Practical advice

For efficiency locks, a single Redis lock with a random value and an expiry is usually enough. For correctness, prefer a database constraint or transaction, or a coordination service, and enforce fencing tokens at the resource. A unique constraint or a compare-and-set update often removes the need for a lock at all. That last point is my own judgment.
## How to talk through it
Ask what happens if two workers both run. Choose efficiency or correctness. Show the SET NX PX recipe, then the pause problem, then fencing tokens, and say what Redlock does and does not guarantee.
keyPoints: Efficiency locks save work; correctness locks protect data. Decide which you need.
Redis lock: SET key random_value NX PX ttl, and release with an atomic compare-and-delete.
A lease can expire while the holder is paused, so two clients may both believe they hold the lock.
A fencing token (a number that only goes up) checked by the storage rejects stale writers.
For correctness use a consensus service or database transactions, and fencing, not Redlock alone.

sql.title: Fencing tokens reject a stale writer
A lock with a random value and compare-and-delete
sql.code:
import secrets

class TinyRedis:
    """Just enough of SET key value NX PX and compare-and-delete to show why the random value matters."""
    def __init__(self, clock):
        self.clock, self.data = clock, {}
    def set_nx(self, key, value, ttl):
        if key in self.data and self.data[key][1] > self.clock():
            return False
        self.data[key] = (value, self.clock() + ttl)
        return True
    def delete_if_equal(self, key, value):
        if key in self.data and self.data[key][0] == value:
            del self.data[key]
            return True
        return False

now = [0]
r = TinyRedis(lambda: now[0])
mine = secrets.token_hex(8)
assert r.set_nx("lock:report", mine, ttl=30) is True
assert r.set_nx("lock:report", "someone else", ttl=30) is False       # held
now[0] = 31                                                            # my lease expired
theirs = secrets.token_hex(8)
assert r.set_nx("lock:report", theirs, ttl=30) is True                 # another client took the lock
assert r.delete_if_equal("lock:report", mine) is False                 # my late release must NOT remove their lock
assert r.delete_if_equal("lock:report", theirs) is True

Remove the fencing and show the corruption. Finally replace the whole lock with a compare-and-set update (UPDATE ... WHERE version = n) and say when that is better than a lock.
pitfalls: Releasing a lock with a plain delete, removing another client's lock.
Assuming the lease cannot expire while you are working.
Using Redlock for a correctness guarantee and no fencing tokens.
Holding a lock across a slow network call with no timeout.
Using a lock when a unique constraint or compare-and-set would do.

interview.q: How do you take a lock in Redis?
interview.a: SET key random_value NX PX ttl: set only if absent, with an expiry. Release with an atomic compare-and-delete so you only remove your own lock.

interview.q: What is wrong with a lock that expires?
interview.a: The holder may be paused past the lease, so a second client gets the lock and both write. Checking the lock just before writing does not fix it, because the pause can come after the check.

interview.q: What is a fencing token?
interview.a: A number that increases each time the lock is granted. The client sends it with writes, and the resource rejects any write whose token is lower than one it has seen.

interview.q: When is Redlock not enough?
interview.a: When correctness depends on it. It has no fencing tokens, relies on clocks, and a failover with asynchronous replication can break mutual exclusion. Use a consensus system or database transactions plus fencing.

interview.q: Is a lock always the right tool?
interview.a: No. A unique constraint, a conditional update or an idempotent operation often removes the need for a lock.

Martin Kleppmann: How to do distributed locking

title: Design a News Feed (Twitter Timeline)
tagline: Prepare each person's feed early or when asked, and mix both for celebrities.
explain: The news feed is one of the most common design prompts. The System Design Primer solves it as the Twitter timeline, and Alex Xu's first volume has a news feed chapter (table of contents from search summaries only). The central decision is when to do the work: when a post is written, or when a feed is read.
## Numbers first

The Primer's assumptions: 100 million active users, 500 million tweets a day (about 6,000 writes a second), 250 billion reads a month (about 100,000 a second), roughly 10 KB per tweet including media, about 150 TB of new content a month. Reads outnumber writes by about 16 to 1.
## Fan-out on read

Compute the feed when the user asks: look up everyone they follow, fetch their latest posts, merge and sort. Writes are cheap and reads are expensive, which is the wrong way round for a read-heavy product.
## Fan-out on write

Precompute. When a post is created, a fan-out service looks up the author's followers and inserts the post into each follower's timeline in a cache. A read is then one cache lookup plus hydration of the ids. The cost is one insert per follower, so an author with 1,000 followers causes 1,000 inserts. The Primer counts about 5 billion deliveries a day, about 60,000 a second.
## The timeline cache

Each timeline is a list in an in-memory store such as Redis, holding compact entries (a tweet id, a user id and a byte of metadata in the Primer). Keep a few hundred per user and only for active users; rebuild from the database for inactive ones.
## Celebrities and the hybrid

An account with millions of followers makes fan-out a bottleneck: it could take minutes. The Primer suggests skipping fan-out for highly followed users, fetching their recent tweets at read time, merging with the precomputed timeline, and reordering when serving.
## Consistency, pagination and scaling
A feed can be a few seconds stale, so eventual consistency is acceptable. Use cursor pagination. Scale the database with federation, sharding, denormalisation and tuning, and say what you shard by.
## How to talk through it
Give the read-to-write ratio, choose fan-out on write, immediately raise the celebrity problem yourself and present the hybrid, then discuss the cache, pagination and failure modes.
keyPoints: Reads dominate a feed, so precompute the timeline (fan-out on write).
Fan-out on write costs one insert per follower and runs asynchronously.
Skip fan-out for celebrities; merge their posts at read time.
Cache timelines of active users only; rebuild others from the database.
Use cursor pagination; eventual consistency is acceptable.

sql.title: Fan-out on write with a celebrity pull path
sql.code:
from collections import defaultdict

class Feed:
    def __init__(self, celeb_threshold=3):
        self.followers = defaultdict(set)          # author -> followers
        self.following = defaultdict(set)
        self.timeline = defaultdict(list)          # user -> [post ids], newest first (the cache)
        self.posts = {}                            # post id -> (author, clock)
        self.by_author = defaultdict(list)
        self.clock = 0
        self.threshold = celeb_threshold

    def follow(self, user, author):
        self.followers[author].add(user)
        self.following[user].add(author)

    def post(self, author):
        self.clock += 1
        pid = f'p{self.clock}'
        self.posts[pid] = (author, self.clock)
        self.by_author[author].insert(0, pid)
        if len(self.followers[author]) < self.threshold:     # normal account: fan out on write
            for f in self.followers[author]:
                self.timeline[f].insert(0, pid)
        return pid

    def read(self, user, limit=10):
        ids = list(self.timeline[user])
        for a in self.following[user]:                         # celebrities: pull at read time and merge
            if len(self.followers[a]) >= self.threshold:
                ids += self.by_author[a][:limit]
        ids.sort(key=lambda p: -self.posts[p][1])
        return ids[:limit]

feed = Feed(celeb_threshold=3)
for u in ['u1', 'u2', 'u3']:
    feed.follow(u, 'star')                                      # 'star' has 3 followers: treated as a celebrity
feed.follow('u1', 'friend')
p1 = feed.post('friend')
p2 = feed.post('star')
p3 = feed.post('friend')
assert feed.timeline['u1'] == [p3, p1]                          # friend's posts were fanned out
assert p2 not in feed.timeline['u1']                            # the celebrity post was not
assert feed.read('u1') == [p3, p2, p1]                          # merged at read time, newest first
assert feed.read('u2') == [p2]

sql.title: Why a cursor beats an offset when new posts arrive
sql.code:
feed = ['p9', 'p8', 'p7', 'p6', 'p5', 'p4']      # newest first

def page_offset(feed, offset, size):
    return feed[offset:offset + size]

def page_cursor(feed, after, size):
    start = 0 if after is None else feed.index(after) + 1
    return feed[start:start + size]

first = page_offset(feed, 0, 3)                 # ['p9', 'p8', 'p7']
feed = ['p10'] + feed                           # a new post arrives while the user scrolls
assert page_offset(feed, 3, 3) == ['p7', 'p6', 'p5']      # p7 is shown twice
assert page_cursor(feed, first[-1], 3) == ['p6', 'p5', 'p4']   # the cursor continues exactly after p7

Write the read and write rates (with assumptions), compare fan-out on read and on write with numbers, choose a threshold for celebrities and justify it, describe the timeline cache layout and its memory size for 20 million active users with 300 entries of 17 bytes each, and list what you would shard by. Then say what the user sees if the cache is down.
pitfalls: Choosing fan-out on write for everyone and ignoring celebrities.
Computing the feed at read time at 100,000 reads a second.
Caching timelines for inactive users, wasting memory.
Offset pagination on a feed that changes while you scroll.
Doing the fan-out inside the post request instead of asynchronously.

interview.q: Fan-out on write or on read for a news feed?
interview.a: Feeds are read-heavy, so precompute: on write, insert the post into each follower's cached timeline so a read is one lookup. The cost is one insert per follower, run asynchronously. For accounts with millions of followers skip fan-out and merge their recent posts at read time (a hybrid).

interview.q: How do you handle a user with 50 million followers?
interview.a: Do not fan out their posts: it would take minutes and flood the cache. Store the post once, and when a follower reads, fetch the recent posts of the celebrities they follow, merge them with the precomputed timeline and sort. Choose a follower threshold for 'celebrity'.

interview.q: What goes in the timeline cache and how large is it?
interview.a: A list of compact post references per active user (for example an id and a little metadata), a few hundred per user, hydrated from the post and user services on read. Inactive users' timelines are rebuilt from the database on return. Size is users times entries times bytes per entry.

interview.q: What consistency does a feed need?
interview.a: Eventual consistency is fine: a new post may take a few seconds to appear. State it as a requirement, use cursor pagination so scrolling is stable, and reserve stronger consistency for things like the follow action's confirmation.

steps.title: Fan-out on read: compute the feed when asked
body: The simplest design: when a user opens the app, look up everyone they follow and query the latest posts of each, merge and sort them. Nothing extra happens at write time.
At 100,000 reads a second, each doing a many-way merge across the database, the reads are the expensive part, which is the wrong place for the cost.

steps.title: Fan-out on write: precompute each timeline
body: Do the work at write time. When a post is created, a fan-out service looks up the author's followers and inserts the post into each follower's timeline in a cache. Reading a timeline becomes one cache lookup.
This is what the Primer's design does: store the tweet, then fan out to followers' home timelines in a memory cache.

steps.title: What the timeline cache holds
body: Each home timeline is a list in a memory store such as Redis, holding compact entries (the Primer uses an 8-byte tweet id, an 8-byte user id and one byte of metadata). On read, the timeline service takes the ids and hydrates them with multigets to the tweet and user services.
Keep only a few hundred entries per timeline and only for active users. Rebuild an inactive user's timeline from the database when they return.

pill.text: list of post ids per user

card.title: Per timeline entry (Primer)
lines: keep a few hundred; active users only

steps.title: The cost of fan-out
body: Fan-out on write costs one insert per follower. An author with 1,000 followers causes 1,000 writes. With 500 million posts a day each reaching about 10 followers, the Primer counts about 5 billion fan-out deliveries a day, roughly 60,000 a second.
That is affordable if followers are few and the work is asynchronous.

predict.question: A user with 2 million followers posts once. How many timeline inserts does fan-out on write perform?
predict.why: One insert per follower: about 2 million. Doing that in the request would be far too slow, so it runs asynchronously, and it is the reason celebrities need special handling.

steps.title: The celebrity problem and the hybrid
body: For accounts with millions of followers, skip fan-out. At read time, fetch their recent posts and merge them with the precomputed timeline, then sort. The Primer describes exactly this: skip fan-out for highly followed users, search their recent tweets at read time, merge and reorder.
Pick a threshold (for example, over 100,000 followers) and treat only those accounts as 'pull'.
changes: ~ Celebrity posts merged at read time

steps.title: Pagination and freshness
body: Page with a cursor (the id of the last item seen), not a page number, because new posts arrive while the user scrolls and an offset would repeat or skip items. A feed may be a few seconds stale: that is acceptable for this feature, so the design is eventually consistent.
Push notifications for new posts go through a queue, outside the read path.

steps.title: Scaling the stores
body: Replicas absorb reads but cache misses and the write volume still reach the primary. The Primer's advice for the database tier is federation (split by function), sharding, denormalisation, SQL tuning, and moving some data to NoSQL. Shard posts by author or post id, and the follow graph by user.
Always say what you are sharding by and which queries that makes expensive.

steps.title: Recap
body: Reads dominate, so precompute: fan-out on write into a timeline cache, a hybrid for celebrities, cursor pagination and eventual consistency. Name the cost of each choice: write amplification, cache memory and merge-at-read for hot authors.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 2 fan-out on write for most accounts

everyday.plain: A feed shows you the latest posts from people you follow, and the key choice is when to prepare it.
everyday.story: A newspaper boy can either prepare a bundle for each house in the morning (work done early, reading is fast), or collect papers only when you ask (work done late). For ordinary people, preparing early works well. For a celebrity with ten million followers, preparing ten million bundles is too much, so you collect their posts only when asked.
maps: Preparing the bundle in the morning
words: Spreading one post out to many followers.
Preparing each follower's feed when a post is made.
Building the feed only when someone opens it.
The list of posts a person sees.

title: Design a Web Crawler
tagline: Visit billions of pages without repeats, without being rude, and keep them fresh.
explain: A web crawler downloads pages starting from seed URLs, extracts links and repeats, usually to feed a search index. It appears in both the System Design Primer's solved problems and Alex Xu's first volume (title from search summaries). It is a good prompt because the interesting problems are scale, duplicates and good behavior, not fetching a page.
## Scale from the Primer

The Primer's design assumes 1 billion links to crawl, refreshed about once a week, so 4 billion links a month, at about 500 KB per page: roughly 2 PB of content a month and 72 PB over three years, about 1,600 writes a second.
## The crawl loop and the frontier

Take the top-ranked URL from a frontier, fetch the page, store it, extract links and add unseen ones. The frontier is a ranked queue of URLs to crawl (the Primer ranks by site popularity using a Redis sorted set). This is breadth-first search over the web graph, so you need a visited set to stop cycles.
## Deduplication

Normalize URLs and keep a seen set; at a billion URLs shard it or use a Bloom filter. For content, compute signatures: a hash for exact duplicates and a similarity measure such as the Jaccard index for near duplicates. The Primer compares page signatures with Jaccard or cosine similarity and lowers the priority of similar pages.
## Politeness

RFC 9309 defines robots.txt: a UTF-8 file at the top level with user-agent groups and allow and disallow rules, where the most specific matching rule is used. Crawlers are requested to honour it and should not use a cached copy for more than 24 hours. The RFC states it is not an access-control mechanism. Also rate-limit per host: keep one queue per host with a delay, so parallelism is across hosts.
## Freshness and scaling

Record a timestamp per page and refresh after a default period (a week in the Primer), more often for popular or frequently changing pages, using conditional requests. Partition the frontier by host so each node owns hosts and politeness stays local. Cache DNS lookups, reuse connections, keep pages in an object store and the index in sharded stores.
## How to talk through it
State the scale, draw the loop, then spend the deep-dive time on duplicates, politeness and freshness, because those are where real crawlers fail.
keyPoints: A crawler is breadth-first search over the web with a frontier and a seen set.
Normalize URLs; shard the seen set or use a Bloom filter at scale.
Honour robots.txt (RFC 9309), cache it at most 24 hours; it is not security.
Rate-limit per host: parallel across hosts, serial within one.
Detect duplicate content with signatures and Jaccard similarity; re-crawl by change rate.

sql.title: Normalization, a polite frontier and robots.txt rules
Near-duplicate pages with Jaccard similarity
sql.code:
def shingles(text, k=3):
    words = text.lower().split()
    return {' '.join(words[i:i + k]) for i in range(len(words) - k + 1)}

def jaccard(a, b):
    return len(a & b) / len(a | b) if a | b else 1.0

doc1 = 'the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'
doc2 = 'the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog today'
doc3 = 'completely different words about databases and queues here now'
assert jaccard(shingles(doc1), shingles(doc1)) == 1.0
assert jaccard(shingles(doc1), shingles(doc2)) > 0.8      # near duplicate
assert jaccard(shingles(doc1), shingles(doc3)) == 0.0

exercise: Design a crawler for 500 million pages refreshed weekly. Compute fetches per second and bandwidth, size the seen-URL set and say whether it fits in memory (and what you do if not), write the per-host politeness rule with numbers, choose how you partition the frontier and what happens when a crawler node dies, and specify how you decide how often to re-crawl a page. Then list three ways a crawler gets trapped (infinite calendars, session ids in URLs, redirect loops) and your defense for each.
pitfalls: No per-host rate limit, so the crawler behaves like an attack.
Ignoring robots.txt, or treating it as access control.
Crawling duplicates because URLs were not normalized.
A single machine's frontier and seen set at a billion URLs.
Re-crawling every page at the same interval.

interview.q: How do you avoid crawling the same page twice?
interview.a: Normalize URLs and keep a seen set (sharded, or a Bloom filter at very large scale). For different URLs with the same content, compute content signatures: a hash for exact duplicates and shingles with Jaccard similarity for near duplicates.

interview.q: How do you make a crawler polite?
interview.a: Fetch and honour robots.txt (RFC 9309: user-agent groups, allow and disallow, the most specific rule wins, cache at most 24 hours), and keep a queue per host with a minimum delay so requests to one host are spaced out while many hosts are crawled in parallel.

interview.q: How do you decide when to re-crawl?
interview.a: Record when each page was crawled and how often it changed. Refresh all pages after a default period and more often for pages that change frequently or are popular, using conditional requests (ETag, If-Modified-Since) so unchanged pages are cheap.

interview.q: How do you scale the crawler?
interview.a: Partition the frontier by host hash so each node owns hosts (politeness stays local), run many fetchers, cache DNS and reuse connections, store pages in object storage and metadata in sharded stores, and benchmark to find the next bottleneck.

references.title: System Design Primer: design a web crawler

basis: Sources, both read: the System Design Primer's web crawler solution (the 1 billion link, weekly refresh, 500 KB, 2 PB a month figures, frontier ranking with a Redis sorted set, page signatures with Jaccard or cosine similarity, DNS caching and connection pooling) and RFC 9309 (robots.txt location, groups, most specific rule, honour request, 24 hour cache recommendation, not access control). The Primer's treatment of politeness is thin, so the per-host queue design, the Bloom filter and conditional requests are my own judgment and standard practice. Animation figures are illustrative. Priorities, hours and every number in the animations are judgment calls or illustrative assumptions, not measurements; where a figure comes from a page I read, the source is named above. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises it for roles whose loops contain a design round (for example, the SDE plan).

scenes.title: A web crawler, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: crawl the web
body: A web crawler starts from seed URLs, downloads pages, extracts links and repeats. It feeds a search index. The Primer's design assumes 1 billion links to crawl, refreshed about once a week, so about 4 billion links a month, at about 500 KB per page, which is about 2 PB of content a month.
The hard parts are not fetching one page; they are scale, duplicates, politeness and freshness.

card.title: Requirements
lines: crawl pages, extract links, store content
do not crawl the same page twice
be polite: respect robots.txt and rate limits
stay fresh: re-crawl on a schedule
do not get stuck in a loop

steps.title: The crawl loop
body: Take the top URL from the frontier, fetch the page, store it, extract its links, and add the new ones to the frontier. A frontier is a queue of URLs still to crawl, ranked by priority (the Primer ranks by site popularity, using a Redis sorted set).
This is breadth-first search over the web graph, with a visited set to stop cycles.

steps.title: Do not crawl the same URL twice
body: Normalize every URL (lowercase the host, remove fragments, resolve relative paths, sort query parameters) and keep a set of seen URLs. Without it a link cycle makes the crawler loop forever.
At a billion URLs the set no longer fits in one machine's memory: shard it by URL hash, or use a compact structure such as a Bloom filter (accepting rare false positives).

steps.title: Politeness: robots.txt
body: Before fetching from a site, read its /robots.txt. The Robots Exclusion Protocol (RFC 9309) defines it: a UTF-8 text file at the top level, with user-agent groups and allow and disallow rules; when several rules match, the most specific one wins. Crawlers are requested to honour it, and should not use a cached copy for more than 24 hours.
It is not access control: the RFC says it is not a substitute for real security measures.

card.title: RFC 9309
lines: user-agent group, allow and disallow lines

steps.title: Politeness: do not overload a host
body: If the frontier hands 1,000 URLs from one site to 1,000 fetchers, you have launched a denial of service. Keep a queue per host and a minimum delay between requests to the same host. Order work so fetchers rotate across hosts.
Many fetchers in parallel, but one at a time per host.

predict.question: 1,000 fetcher threads all pull URLs for the same host at once. What is the problem?
options: The host is overloaded and may block you
robots.txt is ignored by the host
predict.why: Parallelism must be across hosts, not within one. Per-host queues with a delay keep the crawl polite and avoid being blocked.

steps.title: Duplicate content
body: Different URLs often serve the same or nearly the same content (mirrors, tracking parameters). Compute a signature of each page's content (a hash for exact duplicates, shingle-based similarity such as the Jaccard index for near duplicates) and compare with already crawled pages. The Primer uses page signatures with Jaccard or cosine similarity.
If a similar signature exists, lower the page's priority instead of storing it again.

card.title: Jaccard similarity
lines: J(A, B) = |A intersect B| / |A union B|
set of word shingles per page

steps.title: Freshness: when to re-crawl
body: Store a timestamp with each crawl. Refresh all pages after a default period (the Primer uses a week) and more often for pages that change often or are popular. Use HTTP conditional requests (If-Modified-Since, ETag) so an unchanged page costs a few bytes.
Mine your own history: a page that changed on every visit should be visited more often.

steps.title: Scaling the crawler
body: Partition the frontier by host hash so each crawler node owns a set of hosts (which also makes per-host politeness local). Cache DNS lookups, because resolving the host for every URL is slow, and reuse connections. Store pages in an object store and metadata in a sharded database.
The Primer's advice: benchmark and fix the next bottleneck rather than designing the final system at once.

steps.title: Recap
body: Frontier plus fetchers plus parser, URL normalization and a seen set, robots.txt and per-host politeness, content signatures for duplicates, scheduled re-crawl, a frontier partitioned by host. Name the numbers: billions of URLs and petabytes a month.

lines: 2 normalize URLs, seen set / Bloom filter

title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (Dynamo)
tagline: A giant dictionary on many machines that keeps working when some fail.
explain: Designing a distributed key-value store is a classic prompt (Alex Xu's first volume, the Primer's query-cache and key-value discussions) and has a canonical answer: Amazon's Dynamo, described in its 2007 paper. The design shows how a handful of ideas combine to give high availability and horizontal scale.
## Partitioning with consistent hashing

Hash keys onto a ring where each node owns an arc; a key belongs to the first node clockwise. When a node joins or leaves only its arc moves, unlike hash-mod-N which reshuffles almost everything. Virtual nodes give each machine many points on the ring to balance load.
## Replication and quorums

Store each key on its owner and the next N-1 nodes. A write succeeds after W acknowledgements and a read contacts R replicas; if R + W > N, a read overlaps the latest acknowledged write. Dynamo makes N, R and W configurable per application: N=3, W=2, R=2 is a common choice that tolerates one failure.
## Keeping writes available

If a replica is unreachable, Dynamo writes to the next healthy node with a hint naming the intended owner and hands the data back when the owner returns (hinted handoff). This keeps writes available, with weaker guarantees during failures.
## Conflicts

Because any replica can accept a write, concurrent updates happen. Dynamo uses vector clocks to tell whether one version descends from another or the two are concurrent; concurrent versions are returned for the application to merge, or resolved by last write wins, which is simple and can lose a write.
## Repair and membership
Merkle trees let two replicas find which key ranges differ cheaply; read repair fixes stale replicas found during reads; gossip spreads membership information without a central master.
## A cache variant

The Primer's key-value cache for search queries combines an LRU (hash table plus doubly linked list) with sharding by hash(query) across machines, preferring consistent hashing, and a TTL for refresh. Use that when data can be recomputed on a miss.
## How to talk through it
Start with the CAP choice (availability and latency over strong consistency), then partitioning, replication, quorums, failure handling, conflicts and repair, in that order.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes partitions the keys; only one arc moves on a change.
Replicate to N nodes; R + W > N makes reads see the latest write.
Hinted handoff keeps writes available when a replica is down.
Vector clocks detect concurrent versions; resolve by merge or last write wins.
Merkle trees, read repair and gossip converge replicas without a master.

sql.title: A tiny Dynamo: ring, N replicas, quorum and hinted handoff
Version vectors: ordered or concurrent?
sql.code:
def compare(a, b):
    nodes = set(a) | set(b)
    ge = all(a.get(n, 0) >= b.get(n, 0) for n in nodes)
    le = all(a.get(n, 0) <= b.get(n, 0) for n in nodes)
    if ge and le:
        return 'equal'
    return 'a newer' if ge else 'b newer' if le else 'concurrent'

assert compare({'n1': 2}, {'n1': 1}) == 'a newer'
assert compare({'n1': 1}, {'n1': 1, 'n2': 1}) == 'b newer'
assert compare({'n1': 1}, {'n2': 1}) == 'concurrent'        # two writers, neither saw the other: needs a merge

sql.title: The cache variant: an LRU with a hash map and a linked list order

exercise: Design a session store for 50 million users with 2 KB per session and 200,000 operations a second at peak. Choose N, W and R and justify them; compute the memory needed with replication; say what happens when a node dies, a datacenter loses connectivity, and a user's two devices write the same session at once; and say which of these answers would change if the store held bank balances instead.
pitfalls: Using hash mod N, so adding a node moves almost every key.
Claiming strong consistency while using W=1 and R=1.
Last write wins without saying what it can lose.
No story for node failure or for a replica that missed writes.
Forgetting virtual nodes, so the load is uneven.

interview.q: How does consistent hashing help a key-value store?
interview.a: Keys and nodes are hashed onto a ring and each key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node only moves the keys of one arc, so the cluster scales without reshuffling everything. Virtual nodes spread load evenly and let bigger machines own more.

interview.q: Explain N, W and R.
interview.a: N is the number of replicas per key, W the number of replicas that must acknowledge a write and R the number contacted on a read. If R + W > N a read always overlaps the latest acknowledged write. Lower W or R gives faster, more available operations and weaker consistency.

interview.q: How does Dynamo keep accepting writes when a replica is down?
interview.a: It writes to the next healthy node on the ring with a hint naming the intended owner (a sloppy quorum) and hands the data back when the owner recovers (hinted handoff). The trade-off is weaker guarantees during the failure.

interview.q: How are conflicting versions handled?
interview.a: Each version carries a vector clock. If one dominates the other, the older is discarded; if they are concurrent, both are kept and returned to the client to merge, or resolved by a rule like last write wins, which is simple but can drop a write.

steps.title: The prompt: a distributed key-value store
body: Design a store with get(key) and put(key, value) that spreads data over many machines, stays available when machines fail and scales by adding nodes. The model answer is the Dynamo design from Amazon's 2007 paper, which the System Design Primer and Alex Xu's book both draw on.
State the trade-off at the start: highly available, eventually consistent, tunable per request.

card.title: Requirements
lines: get(key) and put(key, value), small values

steps.title: Partition with consistent hashing
body: Hash each key onto a ring. Each node owns an arc of the ring, so a key belongs to the first node clockwise from its hash. Adding or removing a node moves only the keys of one arc, instead of reshuffling everything as hash mod N would.
Virtual nodes (many points per machine) even out load and let stronger machines take more.

steps.title: Replicate to N successors
body: Store each key on its owner and the next N-1 nodes on the ring (N is often 3). A node can fail without losing data, and reads can be served by any replica.
Choose replicas on different racks or zones.

steps.title: Quorums: W and R
body: A write succeeds when W replicas acknowledge, a read contacts R replicas and takes the newest. If R + W > N the sets overlap and a read sees the latest acknowledged write. With N=3, W=2, R=2 you tolerate one failed node for both. Dynamo lets applications tune N, R and W.
Lower W gives faster, more available writes and weaker consistency.

predict.question: N=3 with W=2 and R=2. One replica is down. Can writes and reads still succeed?
options: Yes, 2 of 3 are enough for both
predict.why: Two replicas still acknowledge, so W=2 and R=2 are both met. R + W = 4 > 3, so reads still overlap writes.

steps.title: Failures: sloppy quorum and hinted handoff
body: Dynamo avoids refusing writes when replicas are temporarily down: it writes to the next healthy node on the ring instead, with a hint saying who the data belongs to, and hands it back when the owner returns (hinted handoff).
This keeps writes available at the cost of weaker guarantees during failures.
changes: ~ Write goes to the next healthy node with a hint

steps.title: Conflicts: version vectors
body: Without a single writer, two clients can update the same key on different replicas. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (a list of node and counter pairs) so it can tell whether one version descends from another or the two are concurrent. Concurrent versions are returned to the client to merge, or resolved by a rule such as last write wins.
Last write wins is simple and can silently drop a write.

steps.title: Anti-entropy and membership
body: Replicas that missed writes are repaired in the background by comparing Merkle trees (hash trees over key ranges) so only differing ranges are exchanged, and by read repair when a read finds a stale replica. Nodes learn who is alive through gossip, with no central master.
These keep replicas converging without any node being special.

steps.title: A cache variant: sharded LRU
body: The Primer's query-cache design is a smaller cousin: each machine keeps an LRU cache (a hash table plus a doubly linked list), and the cache is sharded by hash(query) across machines, with consistent hashing preferred. Compare the three options: each node caches its own (low hit rate), each holds a full copy (wasteful), or shard (best).
Use this version when the data can be recomputed on a miss.

lines: 3 W, R with R + W > N for reads to see writes

If one cabinet is damaged, the others still have the card. Staff may disagree briefly about the newest version of a card, and they need a rule to sort that out.

title: Design a Chat System
tagline: Deliver messages quickly and in order, also to people who are offline.
explain: Chat is a standard prompt (Alex Xu's first volume has a chat system chapter; title from search summaries). It tests real-time delivery, ordering, storage and the handling of offline users. Discord's engineering blog on how it stores trillions of messages is a good primary source for the storage part.
## Persistent connections

Polling is wasteful and slow. A WebSocket gives a two-way interactive session between browser or app and server without polling (MDN), so the server can push a message immediately. Connection gateways hold many long-lived connections and are scaled separately from the chat logic. MDN notes WebSocket has no backpressure, so a fast sender can overwhelm a slow client; plan for it.
## Send path and delivery

The gateway passes the message to the chat service, which validates it, assigns an id, stores it durably and routes it to the recipients' gateways. Store before delivering so an acknowledged message is never lost. Acknowledge 'sent' when stored and 'delivered' when the recipient's device confirms. Retries mean at-least-once delivery, so deduplicate by message id.
## Ordering and ids
Use server-assigned ids that sort by time. Discord uses Snowflake ids so messages are chronologically sortable; a common layout is timestamp, worker id and sequence. Never order by client clocks.
## Storage

The main query is 'latest messages in this conversation', so partition by conversation and a time bucket. Discord partitions by channel plus a bucket (a fixed time window), replicated across three nodes by default. It started on MongoDB, moved to Cassandra and then to ScyllaDB; reads can create hot partitions, and it added data services that coalesce identical concurrent requests and route by channel with consistent hashing. Its reported results: 177 Cassandra nodes became 72 ScyllaDB nodes, historical fetch p99 fell from 40 to 125 ms to 15 ms and insert p99 from 5 to 70 ms to a steady 5 ms.
## Presence and offline users

Presence is small, frequent, disposable data: keep it in memory with a TTL refreshed by connection heartbeats and send it only to relevant contacts. For offline users, store the message (they sync from their last seen id) and send a push notification. In FCM a trusted server sends a message request to the FCM backend, which relays through the platform transport (Android transport, APNs, web push). Push is best effort; the stored history is the source of truth.
## How to talk through it
Clarify scale and group size, then connection, send path, ordering, storage, presence and push, and raise hot partitions yourself.
keyPoints: WebSocket gateways hold the connections; scale them separately.
Store first, then deliver; ack sent and delivered; dedupe by message id.
Server-assigned, time-sortable ids give conversation order.
Partition messages by conversation and a time bucket; watch for hot partitions.
Presence is in-memory with TTL; offline users get push, history is the source of truth.

sql.title: A Snowflake-style id generator
sql.code:
import time

class Snowflake:
    """41 bits of milliseconds since an epoch, 10 bits of worker id, 12 bits of sequence."""
    EPOCH = 1_600_000_000_000
    def __init__(self, worker, clock=lambda: int(time.time() * 1000)):
        assert 0 <= worker < 1024
        self.worker, self.clock, self.last, self.seq = worker, clock, -1, 0
    def next(self):
        now = self.clock()
        if now == self.last:
            self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & 0xFFF
            if self.seq == 0:                          # sequence exhausted this millisecond: wait for the next
                while now <= self.last:
                    now = self.clock()
        else:
            self.seq = 0
        self.last = now
        return ((now - self.EPOCH) << 22) | (self.worker << 12) | self.seq
    @staticmethod
    def parts(i):
        return (i >> 22) + Snowflake.EPOCH, (i >> 12) & 0x3FF, i & 0xFFF

t = [1_700_000_000_000]
gen = Snowflake(worker=7, clock=lambda: t[0])
a, b = gen.next(), gen.next()                         # same millisecond
t[0] += 1
c = gen.next()
assert a < b < c                                       # ids sort by creation time
assert Snowflake.parts(c) == (1_700_000_000_001, 7, 0)
assert Snowflake.parts(b)[2] == 1

sql.title: Messages partitioned by channel and time bucket
sql.code:
from collections import defaultdict

BUCKET_MS = 10 * 24 * 3600 * 1000                       # a fixed time window (an illustrative size)

class MessageStore:
    def __init__(self):
        self.parts = defaultdict(list)                 # (channel, bucket) -> [(id, text)]
    def add(self, channel, msg_id, ts_ms, text):
        self.parts[(channel, ts_ms // BUCKET_MS)].append((msg_id, text))
    def latest(self, channel, now_ms, limit):
        out, bucket = [], now_ms // BUCKET_MS
        while bucket >= 0 and len(out) < limit:        # walk back one bucket at a time
            out += sorted(self.parts.get((channel, bucket), []), reverse=True)
            bucket -= 1
            if bucket < now_ms // BUCKET_MS - 5:
                break
        return [text for _id, text in out[:limit]]

m = MessageStore()
day = 24 * 3600 * 1000
for i in range(1, 6):
    m.add('general', i, i * 4 * day, f'msg{i}')       # messages every 4 days
assert m.latest('general', 5 * 4 * day, 3) == ['msg5', 'msg4', 'msg3']
assert len({k for k in m.parts if k[0] == 'general'}) >= 2     # data is spread over time buckets

exercise: Design chat for 50 million daily users, groups up to 500 members and 40 messages per user per day. Estimate messages per second and storage per year, size the number of gateway servers if one holds 100,000 connections, choose the message partition key and say what makes a hot partition in your design, define delivery semantics and how duplicates are handled, and describe what happens when a user reconnects after two days offline.
pitfalls: Ordering messages by client timestamps.
Delivering before storing, so a crash loses acknowledged messages.
Storing presence in the main database.
No plan for a very large or very active conversation.
Relying on push notifications as the only way to receive missed messages.

interview.q: How do clients receive messages in real time?
interview.a: Over a persistent two-way connection such as a WebSocket held by a gateway tier, so the server can push a message as soon as it is stored, instead of the client polling. Gateways are stateless apart from the connection and scale horizontally.

interview.q: How do you order messages in a conversation?
interview.a: Assign each message a server-side, time-sortable id (Snowflake-style: timestamp, worker, sequence) and order by it within a conversation. Do not trust client clocks.

interview.q: How would you store the messages?
interview.a: Partition by conversation plus a time bucket, since the main query is the latest messages of one conversation, and replicate for durability. Discord used channel plus a fixed time bucket, and had to deal with hot partitions on busy channels.

interview.q: What happens to a user who is offline?
interview.a: The message is stored; a push notification tells the device (best effort); on reconnect the client asks for messages after its last seen id. Stored history, not push, is the source of truth.

scenes.title: A chat system, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: a chat system
body: Design one-to-one and group chat: send a message, receive it in near real time, see history, know who is online, and get a notification when the app is closed. Ask about scale, group size and whether history must be searchable.
Non-functional: low latency, messages never lost, ordered within a conversation, available.

card.title: Requirements
lines: send and receive in near real time

steps.title: A persistent connection
body: With plain HTTP the client would have to poll for new messages: wasteful and slow. A WebSocket opens a two-way channel between client and server, so the server pushes a message the moment it arrives, and the client sends over the same connection (MDN).
Gateways hold millions of connections, so they are separate from business logic and scale horizontally.

steps.title: The send path
body: Alice's message reaches her gateway, goes to the chat service, which validates it, assigns an id, stores it durably and finds Bob's gateway to push it. Store first, then deliver, so a crash cannot lose a message that was already acknowledged.
Acknowledge to Alice when it is stored (sent), and again when Bob's device confirms receipt (delivered).

steps.title: Message ids give order
body: Order matters inside a conversation. Use ids that sort by time. Discord uses Snowflake ids, so messages are chronologically sortable; the common layout is a timestamp, a worker id and a sequence number, generated without coordination.
Do not rely on client clocks. Order within a conversation by the server-assigned id.

card.title: Snowflake-style id (common layout)
lines: sorts by time, unique, no central counter

predict.question: Two clients send at almost the same moment from phones with different clock settings. What should decide the order?
options: The id assigned by the server
predict.why: Client clocks disagree. A server-assigned, time-sortable id gives one agreed order for everyone in the conversation.

steps.title: Storing messages: partition by channel and time
body: Chat storage is write-heavy and read by conversation, newest first. Discord partitions messages by channel plus a bucket, a fixed time window, so all messages for a channel-and-bucket live together and are replicated across three nodes by default. They started on MongoDB, moved to Cassandra, and later to ScyllaDB.
Choose the partition key from the main query: 'last 50 messages of this channel'.

steps.title: Presence and typing
body: Presence (online, last seen) is a stream of small, frequent, disposable updates. Keep it in memory with a short TTL refreshed by heartbeats from the connection, and fan updates out only to the user's active contacts. Do not write presence to the main message store.
If a heartbeat stops, the status expires on its own.

steps.title: Offline users: push notifications
body: If Bob has no connection, store the message (he gets it on reconnect, from his last seen id) and ask a push service to notify the device. With Firebase Cloud Messaging a trusted server sends a message request to the FCM backend, which relays it through the platform transport (Android, APNs for Apple devices, web push).
Push is best effort, so the stored history is the source of truth.

steps.title: Hot partitions and scale
body: A very busy channel is a hot partition: many concurrent reads and writes to one partition raise latency for everything on those nodes. Discord reports reads cost more than writes in Cassandra, and added data services in front that coalesce identical concurrent requests and route by channel with consistent hashing.

Its reported results after moving messages to ScyllaDB: 177 Cassandra nodes became 72, historical fetch p99 went from 40 to 125 ms down to 15 ms, and insert p99 from 5 to 70 ms down to a steady 5 ms (Discord's own figures).

steps.title: Recap
body: WebSocket gateways, a chat service that stores before delivering, time-sortable ids for order, a store partitioned by conversation and time, presence with heartbeats and TTLs, push for offline devices, and a plan for hot partitions. Say your delivery guarantee: at least once, deduplicated by message id.

everyday.plain: A chat app must deliver messages quickly, in order, and also work when the other person is offline.
everyday.story: Think of a postman who can walk straight into a house if the person is home (a live connection), and otherwise leaves a note at the post office for later (stored message, plus a notification). Each message gets a number, so the conversation is always read in the right order.
maps: Storing the message and sending a push notification
words: A connection that stays open so messages can flow both ways at any time.
Whether a user is online right now.
A message sent to a phone even when the app is closed.
Making sure messages appear in the order they were sent.

title: Design a Notification System
tagline: Send alerts on many channels without losing them or sending them twice.
explain: A notification system sends push notifications, email and SMS on behalf of other services. Alex Xu's first volume has a chapter on it (the title is known from search summaries). It is a good prompt for queues, retries and idempotency, which are the practical heart of reliable messaging.
## The shape

Producers call one API with a template, a user and parameters. The API authenticates, checks the user's preferences and quiet hours, renders the template, assigns a notification id and puts it on a queue, one queue per channel and usually per priority. Workers pull from the queues and call the providers. Queues decouple producers from slow or rate-limited providers and absorb bursts.
## Providers

For push, Firebase Cloud Messaging's architecture has a trusted server environment send a message request to the FCM backend, which does fan-out and generates message ids, then relays through platform transport layers: Android's transport, APNs for Apple devices and the web push protocol. A client registers and receives a registration token that identifies the app instance. Email and SMS use their own providers.
## Reliability

Providers time out. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, as the AWS Builders' Library recommends, so retries do not synchronize; do not retry permanent failures such as an invalid token. In a queue like Amazon SQS a message that is not deleted reappears after its visibility timeout, which provides retry. After a maximum number of attempts, move the message to a dead-letter queue for inspection and replay.
## Duplicates

Queues deliver at least once, so a retry can cause a duplicate. Give each notification an id and record it in a dedupe store (a conditional insert) before sending; if the id is already there, skip. This is the idempotency idea Stripe describes for API requests: the client sends a unique key and the server returns the stored result for a repeat.
## Protecting users and providers

Cap notifications per user per period, honour opt-outs and quiet hours, batch where it helps, and respect provider rate limits. Put urgent classes such as security codes on their own queue and workers so a promotional flood cannot delay them.
## How to talk through it
Clarify channels, volume and guarantees, then walk the path from API to provider, naming the failure at each hop and the mechanism that handles it.
keyPoints: Queue per channel and priority; producers do not wait for providers.
Retry transient failures with backoff and jitter; never retry permanent ones.
At-least-once queues need an idempotent consumer: dedupe by notification id.
A dead-letter queue stops a poison message from blocking the queue.
Rate-limit per user and per provider; give urgent traffic its own queue.

sql.title: A worker with retries, backoff, dedupe and a dead-letter queue
Per-user rate limiting and priority queues

exercise: Design notifications for an e-commerce site: 20 million users, 3 notifications per user per day on average, a 10x burst during a sale. Compute the average and peak rate per second, size the number of workers if one worker sends 200 notifications a second, define queues and priorities, specify the retry policy (which errors, how many attempts, the backoff), the dedupe key, and what you show support when a user says they never got an order notification.
pitfalls: Calling the provider from the producer's request path.
One shared queue, so a promotional flood delays security codes.
Retrying permanent errors forever.
No dedupe, so retries send duplicates.
No dead-letter queue or status store, so failures are invisible.

interview.q: How do you design a notification system?
interview.a: An API that validates, applies user preferences and templates, and enqueues; queues per channel and priority; workers that call providers (FCM, APNs, email and SMS vendors); retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient failures; idempotent delivery using a notification id; a dead-letter queue and a status store; and per-user and per-provider rate limits.

interview.q: How do you avoid sending duplicates?
interview.a: Queues deliver at least once, so the consumer must be idempotent: give each notification an id and record it (a conditional insert) before sending; if it already exists, skip. This is the same idea as an idempotency key on an API request.

interview.q: What do you retry and what do you not?
interview.a: Retry transient failures such as timeouts and 5xx responses with exponential backoff and jitter up to a limit. Do not retry permanent errors such as an invalid or unregistered device token; mark the token invalid instead.

interview.q: How do you handle a spike of a million notifications?
interview.a: The queues absorb the spike while workers drain it at the rate the providers allow; scale workers with the backlog; keep urgent traffic on separate queues so it is not delayed; and apply per-user caps so users are not flooded.

references.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library)

scenes.title: A notification system, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: notify millions of users
body: A notification system sends push notifications, emails and SMS on behalf of other services: order shipped, new message, password reset. It must be reliable (important ones are not lost), not duplicate, respect user preferences and not overwhelm users or providers.
Alex Xu's first volume has a notification system chapter (title from search summaries). The design is mostly queues, workers and careful failure handling.

steps.title: The API validates and checks preferences
body: Producers call one API with a template id, a user id and parameters. The API authenticates the caller, checks the user's preferences (channel, opt-out, quiet hours), renders the template and assigns a notification id.
Keep producers simple: they say what happened, the system decides how and whether to notify.

steps.title: Queues decouple producers from delivery
body: Put each notification on a queue, one queue per channel (and often per priority), and return immediately. A burst of one million notifications waits in the queue instead of overwhelming the providers, and a slow provider does not block the producers.
Separate queues stop a flood of promotional emails from delaying a password-reset SMS.

steps.title: Workers call the providers
body: Workers pull from a queue and call the external provider: for push, a service such as Firebase Cloud Messaging, where a trusted server sends a request to the FCM backend, which relays it through the platform transport (Android, APNs for Apple devices, web push); for email and SMS, an email or SMS provider.
Scale workers per queue with the backlog. The provider's own rate limits set the pace.

steps.title: Failures: retry with backoff and jitter
body: Providers time out and fail. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and random jitter so retries do not arrive in a synchronized wave (the AWS Builders' Library recommends this). Stop after a maximum number of attempts, and do not retry permanent errors such as an invalid token.
With a queue like SQS, a message that is not deleted after processing reappears after its visibility timeout, which gives retry for free.

predict.question: A provider returns 'invalid device token'. Should the worker retry?
options: No, it is a permanent failure: mark the token invalid
predict.why: Retrying cannot fix a permanently bad token. Retry only transient failures (timeouts, 5xx), and remove or flag the token.

steps.title: Duplicates: make delivery idempotent
body: Queues deliver at least once, and retries can send the same notification twice. Give every notification an id and record it in a dedupe store before sending (or use a conditional insert): if the id was already handled, skip. Stripe's idempotency-key approach is the same idea for API requests.
Users forgive a late message more easily than the same message five times.

steps.title: Dead-letter queue and visibility
body: Notifications that still fail after the retry limit go to a dead-letter queue for inspection and replay, so one bad message cannot block a queue forever. Store the status of each notification (queued, sent, failed) so support can answer 'did my user get it?'.
Alert on the size and age of the dead-letter queue.

steps.title: Rate limits and priority
body: Limit notifications per user per period (a user should not get 50 pushes in a minute), and respect each provider's rate limits. Give urgent classes (security codes, payment) their own high-priority queue and workers.
Allow users to choose categories and digests; batching is kinder than a stream.

steps.title: Recap
body: API with preferences and templates, queues per channel and priority, workers calling providers, retries with backoff and jitter, idempotent delivery with a dedupe store, a dead-letter queue, per-user rate limits. Say the guarantee: at least once, deduplicated, best effort for push.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 3 retry transient failures only, with jitter

everyday.plain: Send alerts like SMS, email and app notifications reliably, without sending the same one twice.
everyday.story: A school office sends messages to parents: some by phone, some by email. The messages are put in a tray for each type, and staff send them one by one. If a phone line is busy, they try again after a little time. A note is kept of each message sent, so a parent does not get the same message twice.
maps: Keeping a record of what was sent
words: A way to reach someone, like SMS, email or app.
Safe to do twice: the second time changes nothing.
A place for messages that keep failing.

title: Design Search Autocomplete (Typeahead)
tagline: Suggest words as people type, very fast.
explain: Search autocomplete suggests completions as the user types. Alex Xu's first volume has a chapter on it (title known from search summaries); the data structure behind it is the trie from the data structures track. This lesson is my own worked design, using that structure and the caching and pipeline ideas from this track.
## The requirement

Given a prefix, return the top few completions ranked by popularity, within an interactive latency budget. The data should reflect real searches and be refreshed regularly. Spelling correction and personalisation are out of scope unless asked.
## A trie with top-k at every node

A trie stores prefixes as paths. Walking a prefix of length L costs O(L), regardless of how many queries are stored. To avoid collecting everything below a node on each keystroke, precompute at every node its top k completions with their counts. Then a lookup is: walk the prefix and return the stored list. The price is memory: k entries per node.
## Caching

A few short prefixes receive a large share of traffic and their answers change slowly. Cache them in memory and let browsers or a CDN cache responses briefly. On the client, debounce keystrokes so a request is not sent for every character.
## Updating the data

Do not write to the serving trie on every search. Log queries, aggregate counts in batches, build a fresh trie with top-k lists and swap it in. The serving path stays read-only. For trending queries, merge in a small recent-window structure, or rebuild the hottest prefixes more often. Filter unwanted suggestions both at build time and at serve time.
## Scaling

A trie of every query may exceed one machine. Shard by prefix range, balanced by measured query volume instead of the alphabet because letters are used unevenly, and replicate shards for read capacity and availability.
## How to talk through it

State the freshness you accept. Walk the data structure, then the serving path with caches, then the offline pipeline, then sharding. Mention what you would measure: latency, the cache hit rate and the click-through rate of suggestions.
keyPoints: A trie finds a prefix in O(length); store the top k completions at each node.
Cache hot prefixes in memory, at a CDN, and debounce on the client.
Build the trie offline from aggregated query logs and swap it in.
Merge a small recent window to show trending queries.
Shard by prefix range balanced by load, and replicate.

sql.title: A trie with top-k lists built from query counts
Merging a small trending window into the stable ranking

exercise: Design autocomplete for a site with 100 million searches a day and 10 million distinct queries a month. Estimate suggestion requests per second (assume 5 keystroke requests per search before debouncing and 2 after), the trie size if the average query is 20 characters with top-5 lists, the number of shards, the cache you add and its expected hit rate, and the refresh schedule. Describe what happens when a new celebrity story breaks.
pitfalls: Searching all stored queries on every keystroke.
Updating the serving trie synchronously on each search.
No client debounce, multiplying the request rate.
Sharding by alphabet position when letter usage is very uneven.
No plan for trending or for removing inappropriate suggestions.

interview.q: Why a trie for autocomplete?
interview.a: A trie stores every prefix as a path, so finding the node for a prefix costs O(prefix length) regardless of data size. Storing the top k completions at each node means a lookup returns a precomputed list without searching below the node.

interview.q: How do you keep suggestions fresh?
interview.a: Log queries, aggregate counts in batches, build a new trie offline and swap it in so the serving path stays read-only. Add a small recent-window structure for trending queries, or rebuild hot prefixes more often, and say the staleness you accept.

interview.q: How do you reduce latency and load?
interview.a: Cache hot prefixes in memory and let a CDN or the browser cache responses for a short time; debounce keystrokes on the client; keep responses tiny; and replicate shards so reads are spread out.

interview.q: How do you shard it?
interview.a: By prefix range, but balance by measured query volume rather than by letter because usage is uneven, and replicate each shard. Route using the first characters of the prefix.

Unlike the other designs in this track I found no primary source that describes a production autocomplete in detail, so the design is my own synthesis of the trie, caching and offline-pipeline ideas from this platform, and the numbers and the trending boost are illustrative assumptions and my judgment. scenes.title: Search autocomplete, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: suggest as you type
body: As a user types 'ha', show the most likely completions ('harry potter', 'hair salon', ...). It must feel instant, so the response has to be tiny and fast, and the data must reflect what people actually search.
Alex Xu's first volume has a search autocomplete chapter (title from search summaries). This lesson is my own synthesis, using the trie from the data structures track.

card.title: Requirements
lines: prefix in, top k completions out
out of scope: spelling correction, personalisation

steps.title: A trie stores prefixes
body: A trie is a tree where each edge is a character, so every prefix is a path from the root. To find completions of 'ha', walk two edges and then collect words below that node.
Walking is O(length of the prefix), independent of how many queries are stored.

card.title: Idea
lines: root -> h -> a -> r -> r -> y ...

steps.title: Precompute the top k at every node
body: Collecting all words below 'h' on every keystroke is too slow. Instead each node stores its top k completions (say 5) with their counts, computed ahead of time. A lookup is then: walk the prefix, return the stored list. O(prefix length), no search below the node.
The cost is memory: each node holds k entries.

predict.question: Each trie node stores its top 5 completions. What does a lookup for 'ha' cost?
options: Walking 2 nodes and returning a stored list
predict.why: The answer is precomputed at the node: walk two edges and return its list, so the cost depends on the prefix length, not on the data size.

steps.title: Cache the hot prefixes
body: A small number of short prefixes ('a', 'th', 'how') account for a large share of requests, and their answers change slowly. Cache them in memory, and let browsers and a CDN cache responses with a short Cache-Control lifetime.
Add a client side debounce so the browser does not send a request on every keystroke.

steps.title: Build the trie offline from query logs
body: Do not update the trie on every query: it would make reads and writes fight. Log queries, aggregate counts in batches (hourly or daily), build a new trie with top-k lists, and swap it in. The query path stays read-only.
The trie can be rebuilt in parallel by prefix range.

steps.title: Freshness and trending
body: A daily rebuild misses what is trending now. Add a small, fast path: a recent-window counter over the last hour whose top items are merged into the results, or rebuild more often for the hottest prefixes.
Filter inappropriate or removed items at serve time as well as at build time.

callout.text: State the staleness you accept: 'suggestions may be an hour out of date; trending items are merged within minutes'.

steps.title: Scaling and sharding
body: A trie of all queries may not fit in one machine. Shard by prefix range (a to f on node 1, and so on), though letters are unevenly used, so split by measured load (balance by query volume, not by the alphabet). Replicate each shard for reads and availability.
Route by the first one or two characters of the prefix.

steps.title: Recap
body: Trie with top-k per node for O(prefix) lookups, hot-prefix and CDN caching, an offline pipeline from query logs, a fast path for trending, and sharding by prefix with load-aware ranges. Say the freshness trade-off.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 trie, top k at each node

title: Design a File Sync Service (Dropbox)
tagline: Keep files in sync on all devices by sending only the pieces that changed.
explain: File storage and sync (Dropbox, Google Drive) is a standard prompt; Alex Xu's first volume has a Google Drive chapter (title from search summaries). Dropbox's engineering posts are a primary source for the design and describe the mechanism in detail.
## Blocks and hashes

Dropbox's streaming file synchronization post says every file is partitioned into 4 MB blocks, with the last block possibly smaller, and each block is hashed with SHA-256 and stored. A file is identified by its ordered list of block hashes, a blocklist. Because blocks are named by their content hash, identical blocks are stored once.
## Commit and need-blocks

To upload, the client sends the blocklist in a commit. If the server lacks some blocks it replies 'need blocks' with the missing ones; the client uploads only those, subject to a per-request byte limit, and a final commit adds the file to the metadata journal. Editing a small part of a large file therefore uploads only the changed blocks, and a retry after a failure asks again for what is still missing.
## Two stores

Metadata (names, folders, versions, blocklists, sharing) is small, changes often and needs transactions, so it belongs in a database sharded by user or namespace. Blocks are large and immutable, so they belong in an object store addressed by hash. They scale and fail differently.
## Sync across devices

After a commit, a notification channel tells other devices that something changed. A device fetches the new metadata and downloads only blocks it does not already have. Dropbox also describes streaming sync, where downloading clients prefetch blocks of an uncommitted file; in its 500 MB example sync took 293 seconds against 383 without, and the post says up to 2x improvement while its own two-machine test showed about 25%.
## Conflicts, versions and durability

If two offline devices edit the same file, keep both as a conflicted copy instead of overwriting. Keep a history of blocklists for versions and undelete. Replicate blocks, verify by hash, encrypt them (Dropbox's whitepaper describes per-block encryption) and tier cold data to cheaper storage.
## How to talk through it
Start with the large-file problem and the block idea, then commit and need-blocks, then the two stores, then sync, conflicts and durability.
keyPoints: Split files into fixed-size blocks and name each by its content hash.
A file is an ordered blocklist; the server replies with the blocks it needs.
Metadata in a transactional database; blocks in an object store.
Notify devices of changes, then let them pull only missing blocks.
Keep both versions on conflict; replicate and verify blocks.
