Estimate total storage, blocks, metadata rows, uploads per second (assume 2 uploads per user per day with a 3x peak), and the bandwidth saved by block-level sync when 10% of each file changes per edit. Then describe how you shard metadata, what notification channel you use, and what you do on a conflict.

interview.q: How do you sync large files efficiently?
interview.a: Split into fixed-size blocks, hash each block, and represent the file as a blocklist. The client commits the blocklist; the server replies with which blocks it lacks; only those are uploaded. A small edit changes few blocks, so little data moves, and identical blocks across files and users are stored once.

interview.q: Why separate metadata from block storage?
interview.a: Metadata is small, frequently changing and needs transactions and consistency (a sharded database). Blocks are large, immutable and addressed by hash (an object store). They have different scale, access and durability needs.

interview.q: How do other devices learn about a change?
interview.a: A notification (long-lived connection or push) tells the device that the metadata journal changed; the device fetches the new metadata and downloads only the blocks it does not have. Keeping the notification small and pulling details is more robust.

interview.q: What happens when two devices edit the same file offline?
interview.a: Their version histories diverge from the same parent. Detect it from the histories and keep both as a conflicted copy for the user to resolve, rather than silently overwriting.

basis: Sources: Dropbox's streaming file synchronization post (read: 4 MB blocks, SHA-256, blocklist, the commit and need-blocks protocol, the per-request byte limit, streaming sync and the 293 versus 383 second and up-to-2x figures, which are Dropbox's own). A search summary also mentioned Dropbox's security whitepaper (content-addressable block storage, per-block encryption); I did not open it, so those two claims are from summaries. Alex Xu's Google Drive chapter is known from its title only. The code uses 4-byte blocks for readability, and the sizing exercise numbers are assumptions. Priorities, hours and every number in the animations are judgment calls or illustrative assumptions, not measurements; where a figure comes from a page I read, the source is named above. scenes.title: A file sync service, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: a file sync service
body: Design something like Dropbox or Google Drive: upload files, keep them in sync across devices, share, and keep versions. Files can be large and edited often, users have flaky connections, and the service stores a huge amount of data.
The central question: how do you move and store large files efficiently when only a small part usually changes?

card.title: Requirements
lines: efficient: do not resend unchanged data

steps.title: Split files into blocks and hash them
body: Dropbox's engineering post describes it: every file is partitioned into 4 MB blocks (the last may be smaller), each block is hashed with SHA-256 and stored. A file's identity is its ordered list of block hashes, called a blocklist.
Because blocks are identified by their content hash, identical blocks are stored once, whoever uploaded them.

card.title: Blocklist (Dropbox)
lines: block id = SHA-256 of its content
file = ordered list of block ids

steps.title: Commit the blocklist; the server says what it needs
body: The client sends the blocklist to the metadata service in a commit. The server compares it with the blocks it already has and replies 'need blocks' listing the missing ones. Only those are uploaded to the block servers, in requests with a byte limit. A final commit then adds the file to the metadata journal.
A file that only exists elsewhere in the system uploads zero bytes.

predict.question: You edit one paragraph in a 40 MB document (ten 4 MB blocks) and the edit changes one block. How much does the client upload?
predict.why: Only the changed block hash is new, so the server's 'need blocks' reply lists just that one: about 4 MB. That is the benefit of content-addressed blocks.

steps.title: Separate metadata from blocks
body: Two kinds of data behave differently. Metadata (names, folders, versions, the blocklist per file, sharing) is small, changes often and needs transactions and consistency: a database. Blocks are large, immutable and addressed by hash: an object store. Dropbox calls its history of file changes a journal.
Scale each independently: shard the metadata database by user or namespace, and scale block storage by capacity.

steps.title: Sync to the other devices
body: When the commit lands, other devices must learn of it. A notification channel (a long-lived connection or push) tells your phone that the journal changed; the phone fetches the new metadata and then downloads only the blocks it does not already have.
Notifications say 'something changed', the device then pulls the details. That keeps notifications small and reliable.
changes: + Change notifications and a second device

steps.title: Streaming sync
body: Dropbox describes an optimization, streaming sync: instead of waiting for the full upload and commit, downloading clients prefetch blocks of an uncommitted file, so the other device is almost done when the commit happens. For a 500 MB file their test showed 293 seconds with it versus 383 without; the post claims up to a 2x improvement, though in their two-machine test it was about 25%.
It applies to large new files that need many requests.

steps.title: Conflicts and versions
body: Two devices edit the same file while offline. When both sync, their blocklists diverge from the same parent version. Do not silently overwrite: keep both and create a 'conflicted copy', and let the user choose.
Keep a version history (a list of blocklists), which also gives undo and recovery from deletion.

callout.text: Last writer wins is the simplest rule and it loses someone's work. For files, keep both versions.

steps.title: Durability, security and cost
body: Replicate blocks across failure domains and verify them by hash, since a block's id is its checksum. Encrypt blocks (Dropbox's security whitepaper describes per-block encryption keys) and control access in the metadata service. Move old or rarely read blocks to cheaper storage tiers.
Large uploads should be resumable: the 'need blocks' protocol gives that for free, because retrying the commit asks again for what is missing.

card.title: Checklist
lines: blocks replicated and verified by hash
encryption at rest and in transit

steps.title: Recap
body: 4 MB content-addressed blocks, a blocklist per file, 'need blocks' commits so only missing data is sent, metadata in a database and blocks in an object store, notifications plus pull to sync devices, conflict copies, and replicated, encrypted storage.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 2 commit blocklist; upload only needed blocks

everyday.plain: A file sync service keeps your files the same on all your devices.
everyday.story: Imagine sending a big photo album by post. If you change one page, you send only that page, not the whole album. The receiver checks which pages he already has and asks for just the new ones. File sync does this by cutting files into pieces and sending only the changed pieces.
maps: The receiver listing the pages he has
words: A small piece of a file.
A short fingerprint made from data, used to tell whether it changed.
Information about a file, such as its name and version.
Making the files match on every device.

title: Design a Video Streaming Service (YouTube)
tagline: Upload, convert to many qualities, and play smoothly on any connection.
explain: Video streaming (YouTube, Netflix) is a standard prompt; Alex Xu's first volume has a YouTube chapter (title from search summaries). The key is to see two separate paths: a heavy, asynchronous processing pipeline for uploads, and a cheap, cacheable delivery path for viewers. MDN's page on adaptive streaming is a primary source for the delivery mechanics.
## Upload

Videos are large and uploads fail, so upload in chunks that can be retried, directly to object storage with a short-lived signed URL so bytes bypass application servers. Record metadata and queue the video for processing; it becomes watchable when processing finishes.
## Transcoding

A phone on a slow connection cannot play a very high bitrate file. Convert the original into several qualities and cut each into short segments. MDN says that to stream adaptively you split media into chunks and provide several quality files over several time points; the more qualities and time points, the more adaptive the stream, balanced against size, encoding time and adaptiveness. This is CPU heavy work, so run it as a queued pipeline of idempotent steps on a pool of workers.
## Manifests and formats

MPEG-DASH uses a media presentation description (an XML .mpd file) listing the streams, their bandwidths and where the pieces are. HLS, implemented by Apple, uses an index (an .m3u8 file) pointing to media segments. For adaptive streaming over HTTP, MDN states that no special server-side components are required: segments are ordinary files served over HTTP.
## Delivery

Segments are small, static and immutable, which suits a CDN. Popular segments sit at edges near viewers; the long tail comes from the origin. Egress bandwidth is the main cost, so CDN strategy is a cost decision as much as a latency one.
## Adaptive playback

The player downloads the manifest, measures throughput and buffer, and chooses the quality of the next segment. Segments of all qualities share time boundaries, so it can switch without a break. MDN's page does not describe the exact switching algorithm, so any rule you give is your own design.
## How to talk through it

Separate the upload and processing path from the delivery path, give the bitrate ladder and segment idea, then the manifest, CDN and player. Mention cost, and what you would do about the failed or slow encode.
keyPoints: Chunked, resumable uploads straight to object storage.
Transcode into several bitrates and cut into short segments, in a queued pipeline.
A manifest (MPD for DASH, m3u8 for HLS) lists the segments and bandwidths.
Segments are static files: serve them from a CDN; egress is the main cost.
The player picks the quality for each next segment from throughput and buffer.

sql.title: A bitrate ladder, segment math and a manifest
An illustrative adaptive bitrate rule

exercise: Design a video service with 1 million uploads a day (average 5 minutes) and 100 million views a day. Choose a bitrate ladder and compute storage per video and per day; compute the transcoding capacity needed if encoding one minute of video takes 30 seconds of one CPU core per quality; estimate peak egress bandwidth (assume 2 Mbps average and 10% of views concurrent at peak); decide what to cache at the CDN; and describe how a failed encode is retried without re-uploading.
pitfalls: Proxying uploads through application servers.
Serving one fixed bitrate to all devices.
Mixing processing and delivery paths, so uploads slow playback.
No CDN, so every view hits the origin.
Marking a video ready before every quality is encoded.

interview.q: How does adaptive streaming work?
interview.a: The video is encoded at several bitrates and each is cut into short segments with aligned time boundaries. A manifest (MPD for DASH, m3u8 for HLS) lists the streams and segment locations. The player reads it, measures throughput and buffer, and requests the next segment at the quality it can sustain, switching between segments as conditions change.

interview.q: Why transcode into several qualities?
interview.a: Devices and connections vary widely. A single high bitrate buffers on slow links and wastes bandwidth on small screens. A ladder of qualities lets each viewer get the best one their connection supports.

interview.q: Why use a CDN for video?
interview.a: Segments are static, immutable files, so edges can cache popular ones near viewers, reducing start-up time and keeping most traffic off the origin. Egress bandwidth is the main cost, so it is also a cost control.

interview.q: How do you build the processing pipeline?
interview.a: A queue and workers running idempotent steps (inspect, split, encode each quality, thumbnails, manifests), retrying failures without re-uploading, running qualities in parallel and marking the video ready only when all steps finish. Prioritise short or popular videos.

references.title: Setting up adaptive streaming media sources (MDN)

basis: Source, read: MDN's page on setting up adaptive streaming media sources (splitting media into chunks in several qualities, MPEG-DASH .mpd and HLS .m3u8 manifests, no special server components over HTTP; it does not describe the switching algorithm). The CDN reasoning follows MDN's CDN glossary page, read for the CDN lesson. Alex Xu's YouTube chapter is known from its title only. The bitrate ladder, the switching rule and every exercise figure are illustrative assumptions and my own judgment. Priorities, hours and every number in the animations are judgment calls or illustrative assumptions, not measurements; where a figure comes from a page I read, the source is named above. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises it for roles whose loops contain a design round (for example, the SDE plan).

scenes.title: A video streaming service, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: upload and stream video
body: Design a video platform: users upload videos, others watch them on any device and network. Alex Xu's first volume has a YouTube chapter (title from search summaries). The constraints: videos are huge, devices and connection speeds vary a lot, and delivery bandwidth is the main cost.
Two paths: an upload and processing pipeline, and a delivery path optimized for read.

card.title: Requirements
lines: play smoothly on any device and speed
out of scope: recommendations, comments, search

steps.title: Upload: chunked and resumable
body: Large files fail halfway. Upload in chunks so a retry resends only what was missing (the same idea as block-level sync), straight to object storage using a short-lived signed URL so the bytes do not pass through your application servers. Then record the video's metadata and queue it for processing.
Return quickly: the video becomes watchable after processing, not at upload.

card.title: Why chunks
lines: bytes go to object storage, not app servers

steps.title: Transcode into several qualities and segments
body: A phone on a slow link cannot play a 4K file. Convert the original into several resolutions and bitrates and split each into short segments. MDN: to stream adaptively you split media into chunks and provide several quality files over several time points; more qualities and time points means a more adaptive stream, balanced against size and time to encode.
This is heavy CPU work, so it runs in a pipeline of queued jobs on a pool of workers.

steps.title: A manifest describes the segments
body: Both MPEG-DASH and HLS use a playlist or manifest. A DASH media presentation description (.mpd, XML) lists the streams, their bandwidths and where the pieces are; an HLS index (.m3u8) lists the segment locations and metadata. The player loads the manifest first, then fetches segments.
For adaptive streaming over HTTP, MDN says no special server-side components are required: segments are ordinary files.

predict.question: Which component tells the player where the video segments are and at what bitrates?
predict.why: The manifest lists the available streams with their bandwidths and segment locations. The player reads it and then requests segments over plain HTTP.

steps.title: Deliver through a CDN
body: Segments are small, static, immutable files: perfect for a CDN. The edge caches popular segments near viewers, which cuts start-up time and moves almost all the traffic off your origin. Popular videos are cached everywhere; a long tail is fetched from the origin on demand.
Bandwidth egress is the dominant cost, so CDN strategy is a cost decision as much as a latency one.

steps.title: The player adapts
body: The player measures how fast segments download and picks the quality for the next segment: if the buffer is filling, step up; if it is draining, step down. Because every quality is split at the same time points, it can switch at a segment boundary without a visible break. MDN's page does not describe the switching algorithm, so treat the rule below as an illustration.
Start low for a quick first frame, then climb.

card.title: An illustrative rule
lines: buffer low or throughput falling -> lower quality
buffer healthy and throughput high -> higher quality
never choose a bitrate above measured throughput

steps.title: The processing pipeline
body: Transcoding is a pipeline of steps (inspect, split, encode each quality, make thumbnails, write manifests, publish). Drive it with a queue and workers; make each step idempotent and retryable; run quality encodes in parallel, and mark the video 'ready' only when all steps finish.
Prioritise: short videos and popular uploaders first; big files in the background.

callout.text: A failed encode must not lose the upload: the raw file stays, and the job is retried.

steps.title: Recap
body: Resumable chunked uploads to object storage, a transcoding pipeline producing several bitrates split into segments, a manifest per video, delivery from a CDN, and an adaptive player. State that egress bandwidth is the main cost and that quality is chosen per segment on the client.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 chunked, resumable upload with a signed URL
2 transcode to a bitrate ladder, split into segments

everyday.plain: Video apps cut a video into small pieces in several qualities, and play the best one your internet can handle.
everyday.story: A cook sends a long meal to a customer in small boxes instead of one huge pot. He also packs a light version and a full version. If the road gets bad, the next box is the light version, so the customer is not left waiting. The boxes are kept in nearby kitchens, so they arrive quickly.
words: Converting a video to other sizes and qualities.
How much data per second a video uses; higher means better quality.
A short piece of a video, a few seconds long.
Switching video quality up or down to match your connection.

title: Design a Proximity Service (Uber, Nearby)
tagline: Find nearby places or drivers fast by dividing the map into squares.
explain: Proximity problems ('find drivers near me', 'restaurants within 2 km', 'nearby friends') appear in Alex Xu's second volume (proximity service, nearby friends, maps; titles from search summaries). The central idea is to turn two-dimensional closeness into something an index handles well: cells.
## Why SQL range queries struggle

With latitude and longitude columns, a B-tree index sorts by one column, so a bounding-box query scans the whole latitude band and filters by longitude. Constantly changing positions also make index updates expensive. You need a structure that puts nearby points in the same or neighbouring buckets.
## Cells

Divide space into cells and index each point by its cell id. Uber's H3 is a grid of hexagons: a latitude, longitude and resolution map to a 64-bit index naming a cell. Resolutions run from 0 (coarsest) to 15 (finest), and each finer resolution has cells with one seventh the area; truncating an index gives its coarser parent. Uber's post says hexagons minimize quantisation error as users move and that all of a hexagon's neighbours are equidistant from its center. Geohash and quadtrees are alternatives with the same shape of solution.
## The live index

Drivers ping every few seconds. Compute the new cell; if it changed, move the driver between cell sets. Keep this hot index in memory, with a TTL so drivers that stop pinging disappear, and write the durable location history separately and asynchronously.
## The query

Compute the rider's cell at a resolution where a cell is about the size of the search radius, read that cell and its neighbours, filter by exact distance, sort by distance, and widen the ring if there are too few. The number of cells read is a handful regardless of the total number of drivers.
## Reuse and scale

Uber's post says it uses hexagons to compute surge pricing from supply and demand per cell and to match nearby riders and drivers. Dense areas create hot cells: use finer resolution there, shard the index by cell or region, and replicate, accepting that positions are a few seconds stale.
## How to talk through it
State the read and write rates, explain why a naive range query is poor, choose a cell scheme and its resolution, then walk the update and query paths and the hot-cell problem.
keyPoints: Bucket points by cell; a query reads the cell and its neighbours, then filters by exact distance.
H3 maps lat, lng and resolution to a 64-bit cell id; finer resolutions have 1/7 the area.
Keep the live index in memory with a TTL; log history asynchronously.
Use finer cells in dense areas and shard by cell.
Reuse cells for matching, surge pricing and analytics.

sql.title: A cell index with a neighbour ring (a square grid as an illustrative stand-in for H3)
Supply and demand per cell for surge pricing
sql.code:
from collections import Counter

def surge(drivers_by_cell, requests_by_cell, base=1.0, cap=3.0):
    out = {}
    for c, demand in requests_by_cell.items():
        supply = drivers_by_cell.get(c, 0)
        ratio = demand / max(supply, 1)
        out[c] = round(min(cap, max(base, ratio)), 2)         # an illustrative pricing rule
    return out

drivers = Counter({(1, 1): 10, (1, 2): 2})
requests = Counter({(1, 1): 8, (1, 2): 6, (2, 2): 1})
assert surge(drivers, requests) == {(1, 1): 1.0, (1, 2): 3.0, (2, 2): 1.0}   # a busy cell with few drivers gets the cap

exercise: Design 'nearby drivers' for a city with 200,000 active drivers pinging every 5 seconds and 5,000 ride requests per second at peak. Compute location updates per second, the memory for the in-memory index (assume 100 bytes per driver), choose a cell size for a 2 km search and justify it, describe the query step by step, say how you handle a stadium emptying (a hot cell), how you shard, and how stale the answers can be.
pitfalls: Using a latitude-and-longitude range query on a relational table for moving objects.
Updating a durable database on every ping.
Searching only the rider's own cell, so nearby drivers just across a cell edge are missed.
One cell size for both a city center and the countryside.
Forgetting to expire drivers that stopped reporting.

interview.q: How do you find nearby points efficiently?
interview.a: Bucket points by a cell id from a grid such as geohash, a quadtree or H3. A query computes the cell for the search location, reads that cell and its neighbours, filters by exact distance and sorts. The cost depends on the number of cells read, not on the total number of points.

interview.q: Why does the query include neighbouring cells?
interview.a: A point just across a cell boundary is close to the user but in a different cell. Reading the neighbour ring catches those; the exact-distance filter removes false candidates.

interview.q: How do you handle drivers moving constantly?
interview.a: Keep a live in-memory index from cell to drivers; on each ping, move the driver if the cell changed and refresh a timestamp; expire entries that stop updating; log history to durable storage asynchronously.

interview.q: What is a hot cell and what do you do about it?
interview.a: A dense area (a city center, a stadium) puts a very large number of points in one cell, overloading its shard. Use finer resolution there, shard by cell or region, and replicate; accept slightly stale positions.

references.title: H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index

basis: Source, read: Uber's H3 post (64-bit cell indexes from latitude, longitude and resolution 0 to 15, each finer resolution one seventh the area, truncation to parents, hexagons minimizing quantisation error and having equidistant neighbours, use for surge pricing and dispatch). Alex Xu's second volume chapters are known from titles only. The code uses a square grid and a haversine distance as a clearly simplified stand-in for H3; the cell size, TTL, pricing rule and exercise numbers are illustrative assumptions and my judgment. scenes.title: A proximity service, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: who is near me?
body: Find drivers near a rider, restaurants near a user, friends nearby. Alex Xu's second volume covers proximity service, nearby friends and maps (titles from search summaries). The problem: a very large set of points on the Earth, many of them moving, and a query that asks 'what is within r of here?'.
Two workloads: lots of location updates (writes) and many nearby queries (reads).

card.title: Requirements
lines: return places or drivers within a radius
out of scope: routing and ETA

steps.title: Why a plain SQL range query is slow
body: With latitude and longitude columns you can ask for rows where lat is between a and b and lon is between c and d. But a B-tree index sorts by one column, so the database scans all rows in the latitude band and filters by longitude, and the band can hold a large share of the data. Updating the index for every move is also costly.
We need an index that groups nearby points together.

predict.question: Which index idea groups points that are close in 2D into the same bucket?
options: Splitting space into cells and bucketing points by cell
A hash of the user's name
predict.why: A grid or tree over space puts nearby points in the same or adjacent cells, so a query looks only at a few cells instead of the whole table.

steps.title: Divide the world into cells
body: Split space into cells and index each point by its cell id. Uber's H3 does this with hexagons: a location (latitude, longitude, resolution) becomes a 64-bit index naming a cell; resolution runs from 0 (coarsest) to 15 (finest), and each finer resolution has cells with one seventh the area. Other schemes: geohash (string prefixes), quadtrees, S2.
The resolution is a trade-off: small cells give precise results and many cells, big cells give few cells and more false candidates.

card.title: H3 (Uber)
lines: truncate an index to get its parent cell

steps.title: Why hexagons
body: Uber's post says hexagons minimize the quantisation error introduced when users move through a city, and that every neighbour of a hexagon is the same distance from its center (a square has two distances, a triangle three), which makes radius approximation and smoothing simpler.
For an interview you can use a square grid or geohash and explain the same ideas: cell id, neighbours, resolution.

card.title: Neighbours
lines: hexagon: 6 neighbours, all the same distance
same algorithm: look at the cell and its neighbours

steps.title: Update the index as drivers move
body: A driver pings every few seconds. The location service computes the new cell; if it changed, move the driver from the old cell's set to the new one, otherwise just refresh the timestamp. Keep the hot index in memory (a hash map from cell id to a set of drivers), because it is small and rewritten constantly, and drop entries that stop updating (a TTL).
Write the durable trail (for analytics) asynchronously, separate from this live index.

steps.title: Query: the cell and its neighbours
body: To find drivers within r of the rider: compute the rider's cell at a resolution where a cell is about the size of r, take that cell and its neighbours (a ring), collect their drivers, and filter by exact distance, sorted nearest first. If too few are found, widen the ring.
The query touches a handful of cells, independent of the total number of drivers.

steps.title: Matching and surge use the same cells
body: Uber's post says it computes surge pricing by measuring supply and demand in hexagons, and uses cells to match nearby riders and drivers. Once locations are bucketed, demand and supply per cell are a simple count, and the same index serves pricing, dispatch and analytics.
Design the index as a shared building block.

steps.title: Dense cells and sharding
body: A city center cell can hold thousands of drivers while a rural cell holds none. Hot cells overload one node. Use finer resolution in dense areas (hierarchical cells), shard the index by cell id or region, and keep each shard's set small. Replicate for availability, accepting that a driver's position is a few seconds stale.
Say the consistency you need: nearby results may be a few seconds old.

steps.title: Recap
body: Bucket points by cell (H3, geohash or a quadtree), keep a live in-memory cell index with TTLs, query the cell and its neighbours then filter by distance, use finer cells where it is dense, shard by cell, and reuse the cells for matching and pricing.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 cell id per point; pick the resolution
2 in-memory index, TTL for stale drivers
3 query: cell + neighbours, filter by distance

everyday.plain: Finding nearby places or drivers by dividing the map into small squares.
everyday.story: To find the nearest tea stall, you do not measure the distance to every stall in the country. You look at your own street block and the blocks around it. A map divided into small blocks, each keeping a list of what is inside, gives a fast answer.
maps: Grid cells (such as geohash or H3)
Looking at your block and the ones around
A list of what is in each block

title: Design a Payment System
tagline: Never charge twice, and keep exact records that always add up.
explain: Payments are a favourite senior-level prompt because correctness matters more than scale. The rules are simple to state and hard to guarantee: never lose money, never charge twice. Stripe's engineering post on idempotency is a primary source for the central technique.
## The problem

Your service calls an external payment provider you do not control. If the call times out you cannot tell whether the charge happened. A blind retry might charge the customer twice. You cannot include the provider's call in your database transaction either, so any step can fail halfway.
## Idempotency keys

Stripe's post describes it: the client generates a unique value for each operation and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header on mutating requests (anything under POST). The server correlates the key with the request's state; if the key is new it processes the request, and on a retry with the same key it replies with the cached result of the successful operation. The post recommends exponential backoff with random jitter for retries, and notes that exact recovery behavior is heavily dependent on implementation. It does not cover key expiry, reuse with different parameters or concurrent duplicates, so you must decide those yourself.
## Concurrent duplicates

Two identical requests at once can both pass a 'does the key exist?' check. Insert the key first with a unique constraint and a state of processing: one insert wins, and the other returns the stored result or an 'in progress' answer.
## State machine and ledger

Model a payment as a state machine (created, processing, succeeded, failed, refunded) with conditional updates so two workers cannot move the same payment. Record money movement in an immutable double-entry ledger: every transfer is a debit and an equal credit in one transaction, balances are derived, corrections are new entries. This makes the data auditable and its total always zero.
## Recovery and reconciliation

Record the payment as processing with its key, call the provider with the same key, and on restart retry unfinished payments, which is safe because of the key. Compare your ledger with the provider's settlement report to find charges that exist on only one side. Reconciliation is what makes the design acceptable when the steps cannot be atomic.
## How to talk through it
State the two invariants, show the double-charge failure, introduce idempotency keys, then handle concurrency, states, the ledger, recovery and reconciliation, naming the guarantee at the end.
keyPoints: Retries after timeouts can charge twice; make the operation idempotent.
A client-generated idempotency key; a unique insert wins races; a repeat returns the stored result.
A payment is a state machine with conditional transitions.
A double-entry ledger: debit equals credit, immutable, auditable.
The provider call is outside your transaction: recover with the key and reconcile.

sql.title: An idempotent charge with a unique key, retries and a ledger
A payment state machine with conditional transitions
Reconciling the ledger with the provider's report

exercise: Design payments for a marketplace with 5 million orders a day. Write the invariants, the API with the idempotency key, the unique-insert logic for concurrent duplicates, the payment states and transitions, the ledger accounts for a sale with a platform fee (customer, merchant, platform), what your service does when it crashes between calling the provider and saving the result, and the daily reconciliation report with the three kinds of discrepancy and who handles each.
pitfalls: Retrying a charge without an idempotency key.
Checking whether the key exists and then inserting, which races.
Updating a balance column instead of writing ledger entries.
Marking the payment succeeded before the provider confirms.
No reconciliation, so charges that exist on only one side go unnoticed.

interview.q: How do you prevent double charges?
interview.a: Make the operation idempotent: the client generates a unique key per operation and sends it with the request; the server inserts the key (unique) with state processing, calls the provider with the same key, and stores the result under the key. A retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging again. Stripe describes this with an Idempotency-Key header.

interview.q: What if two identical requests arrive at the same time?
interview.a: Insert the key with a unique constraint before doing the work, so one insert wins. The other request either waits and returns the stored result or gets an 'in progress' response. A check-then-insert has a race.

interview.q: Why a double-entry ledger?
interview.a: Every movement is an immutable debit on one account and an equal credit on another, written in one transaction, so the total is always zero, balances are derived and history is auditable. Corrections are new entries, never edits.

interview.q: What do you do when you cannot make the provider call atomic with your database?
interview.a: Record the payment as processing with its key first, call the provider with the same key, and on restart retry unfinished payments, which is safe because of the key. Then reconcile your ledger against the provider's settlement reports to find any discrepancy.

references.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe)

basis: Source, read: Stripe's idempotency post (client-generated Idempotency-Key header on mutating endpoints, server stores state and replays the cached result, exponential backoff with jitter, recovery behavior depends on implementation, and what it does not cover: key expiry, parameter mismatch and concurrent duplicates). The double-entry ledger, the state machine, the unique-insert approach to races and reconciliation are standard payments engineering practice stated as my own judgment and general knowledge, not taken from that post. The code is a simplified model, and amounts and volumes are illustrative. Priorities, hours and every number in the animations are judgment calls or illustrative assumptions, not measurements; where a figure comes from a page I read, the source is named above. The priority shown is the baseline for a Django backend learner; the roadmap raises it for roles whose loops contain a design round (for example, the SDE plan).

scenes.title: A payment system, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: take a payment
body: Design the backend for card payments in a shop: a customer pays, the order is confirmed, the merchant is credited. Money has two rules that most systems can relax: it must not be lost and it must not be created or charged twice.
A payment goes through an external provider (a payment service provider or bank), which you do not control and which can time out.

card.title: Requirements
lines: charge a customer once per order
out of scope: fraud scoring, refunds, multi-currency

steps.title: Timeouts create double charges
body: The client sends 'pay 50'. The API calls the provider, which charges the card, but the response is lost (a timeout). The client retries. Without protection, the second request charges again.
You cannot tell the difference between 'the charge failed' and 'the charge succeeded but I did not hear back'.

predict.question: A payment request times out after the bank may have charged the card. The client retries the same request. What is the risk?
predict.why: The server cannot know whether the first attempt succeeded, so a blind retry can charge again. The fix is to make the operation idempotent.

steps.title: Idempotency keys
body: The client generates a unique key for each operation and sends it with the request (Stripe uses an Idempotency-Key header on mutating requests). The server stores the key with the request's state and result. A retry with the same key returns the stored result without repeating the side effect.
Stripe's post also recommends exponential backoff with jitter for retries. It notes that the exact mid-operation recovery behavior depends on implementation.

steps.title: Concurrent duplicates
body: Two identical requests can arrive at the same moment (a double click). Both check the store, both find nothing, and both charge. Insert the key with a unique constraint before doing the work, so one insert wins and the other waits or receives 'in progress'.
The Stripe article does not cover this case: it is a design decision you must make and state.

card.title: Order of steps
lines: 2 if the insert fails: return the stored result or 409
3 call the provider with the same key
4 save the result under the key

steps.title: A payment is a state machine
body: Model each payment as states: created, processing, succeeded, failed (and later refunded). Allow only valid transitions, and make each transition a conditional update, so two workers cannot both move the same payment. The state-machine lesson in the low-level design track shows the pattern.
Never mark a payment succeeded before the provider confirms it.

steps.title: Record movements in a double-entry ledger
body: Do not just update a balance column. Write immutable ledger entries: every transfer is a debit on one account and an equal credit on another, in one database transaction. The sum of all entries is always zero, balances are derived from the entries, and the history is auditable.
Corrections are new entries, never edits.

steps.title: We cannot make the provider call transactional
body: Your database transaction cannot include the provider's call. If you charge, then crash before recording it, you have taken money without a record. If you record first and the charge fails, the record is wrong.

Handle it with states and recovery: record 'processing' with the key first, call the provider with the same key, and on restart retry the unfinished payments (safe because of the key). Reconcile against the provider's own reports to catch anything left.

callout.text: Any step that crosses a system boundary can fail halfway. Design for recovery, not for perfection.

steps.title: Reconciliation
body: Compare your ledger with the provider's settlement report (usually daily). Matching entries are fine; entries on one side only are investigated: charged but not recorded, or recorded but not charged. Automatic fixes for known cases, alerts and a human for the rest.
Reconciliation is the safety net that makes the rest of the design acceptable.

steps.title: Recap
body: Idempotency keys with a unique insert, a payment state machine with conditional transitions, a double-entry ledger in a transaction, recovery of unfinished payments, and reconciliation against the provider. The guarantee to state: at most one charge per key, and every discrepancy eventually found.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 5 retry unfinished payments with the same key

everyday.plain: A payment system must never charge twice and must always keep exact records.
everyday.story: When you pay a shopkeeper and the network drops, you press pay again. The shopkeeper's machine sees the same bill number and says 'already paid', not 'charge again'. And the bank writes every movement twice, once as money out of one account and once as money into another, so the books always balance.
maps: Checking the books against the bank
words: A unique ID sent with a request so repeating it does not charge twice.
A record of every money movement.
Writing each movement twice: once out of one account, once into another.
Checking your records against the bank's records.

title: Generalization, Cross-Validation and Regularization
tagline: Make a model learn the pattern, not the examples, and test it fairly.
explain: The ML theory round asks one family of questions in many forms: how do you know a model will work on new data, and what do you do when it will not? The answers are overfitting, honest evaluation and regularization. scikit-learn's own guides are good primary sources for the definitions and the pitfalls.
## Overfitting and the test set

scikit-learn's cross-validation guide says that learning the parameters of a prediction function and testing it on the same data is a methodological mistake: a model that just repeats the labels of the samples it has seen would have a perfect score but would fail to predict anything useful on unseen data. This is overfitting. The common practice is to hold out part of the data as a test set.
## Validation and cross-validation

When you tune hyperparameters there is still a risk of overfitting on the test set, because the parameters can be tweaked until the estimator performs optimally, so knowledge of the test set leaks into the model. The guide suggests a validation set for tuning and the test set for the final evaluation, and notes the cost: fewer samples for learning and results that depend on one random split. k-fold cross-validation avoids the separate validation set: split the training set into k folds, train on k-1 and validate on the remaining one in turn, and report the average. A test set is still held out for the final evaluation.
## Leakage through preprocessing

Standardisation, feature selection and similar transformations must be learnt from the training set and applied to held-out data. A Pipeline composes them with the estimator so that under cross-validation they are refit inside each training fold.
## Bias, variance and regularization

A model that is too simple underfits (both scores are poor); a model that is too flexible overfits (training is excellent, validation much worse). Regularization limits the flexibility. Ridge regression penalises the size of the coefficients with an L2 term; the larger alpha, the greater the shrinkage, and the more robust the coefficients are to collinearity. Lasso uses an L1 penalty and estimates sparse coefficients, setting some exactly to zero, so it can perform feature selection. Elastic net mixes both and is useful when several features are correlated: Lasso tends to pick one of them at random, elastic net is likely to pick both.
## How to talk through it

State the split strategy first (train, validation or folds, test), then how you tune, then how you prevent leakage, and finally what the train and validation gap says. Use the words 'held-out' and 'honest estimate'.
keyPoints: Never evaluate on the data you trained on; hold out a test set.
Tune with a validation set or k-fold cross-validation, never against the test set.
Fit preprocessing on training data only; a Pipeline does it inside each fold.
A big train/validation gap means overfitting; two poor scores mean underfitting.
Ridge shrinks coefficients (L2); Lasso can zero them (L1); elastic net mixes both.

sql.title: k-fold splits, and a ridge coefficient that shrinks with alpha
sql.code:
def kfold(n, k):
    """Yield (train_indices, validation_indices) for k folds over n items, without shuffling."""
    sizes = [n // k + (1 if i < n % k else 0) for i in range(k)]
    start = 0
    for size in sizes:
        val = list(range(start, start + size))
        train = [i for i in range(n) if i < start or i >= start + size]
        yield train, val
        start += size

folds = list(kfold(10, 5))
assert len(folds) == 5 and all(len(v) == 2 and len(t) == 8 for t, v in folds)
assert sorted(i for _t, v in folds for i in v) == list(range(10))      # every item is validated exactly once
assert all(set(t).isdisjoint(v) for t, v in folds)                    # never trained on what it is validated on

# ridge for one feature through the origin: w = sum(xy) / (sum(x^2) + alpha)
xs, ys = [1, 2, 3, 4], [2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8]
def ridge(alpha):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / (sum(x * x for x in xs) + alpha)
ws = [ridge(a) for a in (0, 1, 10, 100)]
assert [round(w, 2) for w in ws] == [1.99, 1.93, 1.49, 0.46]
assert ws == sorted(ws, reverse=True)                                  # a larger alpha shrinks the coefficient

sql.title: Leakage: scaling before the split changes the held-out data's view of the world
sql.code:
def standardize_fit(xs):
    mean = sum(xs) / len(xs)
    var = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in xs) / len(xs)
    return mean, var ** 0.5

train = [10, 12, 11, 13, 9]
test = [30, 31]                                              # held-out data from a shifted period

wrong = standardize_fit(train + test)                         # fitted on everything: the test set influenced the scaler
right = standardize_fit(train)                                # fitted on training data only
assert wrong != right
z_wrong = (test[0] - wrong[0]) / wrong[1]
z_right = (test[0] - right[0]) / right[1]
assert z_right > 3 * z_wrong                                   # the honest scaler exposes how unusual the test data is; the leaky one hides it

exercise: Take any small dataset. (1) Split off a 20% test set and do not look at it. (2) With 5-fold cross-validation on the rest, choose the best alpha for Ridge from [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100] and plot the training and validation scores against alpha. (3) Repeat with a Pipeline that includes standardisation, and again with the scaler fitted before the split, and compare the scores. (4) Evaluate once on the test set. Write two sentences on what the gap between training and validation told you.
pitfalls: Reporting the training score, or the best validation score after many tries, as the expected performance.
Fitting a scaler or imputer on all the data before splitting.
Tuning repeatedly against the test set, which spends it.
Not shuffling ordered data before k-fold cross-validation.
Saying 'add regularization' without saying what it controls or how you would choose its strength.

interview.q: What is overfitting and how do you detect it?
interview.a: The model fits noise in the training data and fails on new data. You detect it by a large gap between the training score and the score on held-out data (validation or test). Remedies: more data, a simpler model, regularization, early stopping.

interview.q: Why not tune hyperparameters on the test set?
interview.a: Repeatedly tweaking parameters until the test score is good leaks knowledge of the test set into the model, so the score no longer estimates generalization. Tune with a validation set or cross-validation and use the test set once at the end.

interview.q: How does k-fold cross-validation work?
interview.a: Split the training data into k folds. For each fold, train on the other k-1 and validate on it. The reported score is the average of the k validation scores. It uses the data more efficiently than one fixed validation split and shows the variability of the score.

interview.q: What is the difference between Ridge and Lasso?
interview.a: Both add a penalty to the least-squares objective. Ridge penalises the squared L2 norm of the coefficients, shrinking them all and stabilising them under collinearity. Lasso penalises the L1 norm and can set coefficients exactly to zero, giving a sparse model and feature selection. Elastic net combines them and handles correlated features better than Lasso.

references.title: Linear models: Ridge, Lasso, elastic net (scikit-learn)

basis: Sources, both read: scikit-learn's cross-validation guide (overfitting, the test set, validation sets, k-fold, leakage through preprocessing, pipelines) and its linear models guide (Ridge's L2 penalty and alpha, Lasso's sparse coefficients, elastic net with correlated features; I read the first part of that long page). The bias and variance framing is standard practice stated as general knowledge. The numbers in the code are my own small examples, and animation scores are illustrative. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard. The priority shown is the baseline; the roadmap raises it for roles that need it (the frontend plan makes the CSS and React lessons core, the ML plan makes generalization and metrics core).

scenes.title: Generalization and regularization, step by step

steps.title: A perfect training score proves nothing
body: Learning the parameters of a prediction function and testing it on the same data is a methodological mistake: a model that just repeats the labels of the samples it has seen would score perfectly and still fail on new data. This is overfitting (scikit-learn's cross-validation guide).
So hold out part of the data as a test set that the model never trains on.

steps.title: Tuning on the test set leaks it
body: Hyperparameters (regularization strength, tree depth) are tweaked until the score looks good. If you tweak them against the test set, knowledge of the test set leaks into the model and the score no longer measures generalization.

The guide's fix: a validation set for tuning, and the test set only for the final evaluation. Its drawback: splitting three ways leaves fewer samples for learning, and results can depend on one random split.

steps.title: k-fold cross-validation
body: Cross-validation removes the separate validation set. Split the training set into k folds; train on k-1 of them and validate on the remaining one, k times; the reported score is the average of the k values. A test set is still held out for the final evaluation.
By default no shuffling occurs, so shuffle explicitly when the data is ordered.

card.title: Folds
lines: score = mean of the 5 validation scores

predict.question: With 5-fold cross-validation, how many models are trained, and on what share of the training data each?
predict.why: Each fold takes a turn as the validation set while the other four (4/5 of the data) are used for training, so five models are trained and the five scores are averaged.

steps.title: Preprocessing must learn from the training part only
body: Standardising, selecting features or imputing missing values also learn from data. If you fit them on everything before splitting, held-out data influences training. The guide says transformations should be learnt from a training set and applied to held-out data.
A Pipeline refits the preprocessing inside each training fold, which keeps the held-out fold out of it.

callout.text: A score that is too good to be true is often leakage: ask what the model could see that it should not.

steps.title: Underfitting and overfitting
body: A model that is too simple misses the pattern (high bias): training and validation scores are both poor. A model that is too flexible memorises noise (high variance): training is excellent and validation is much worse. The gap between them is the signal.
More data, simpler models, early stopping and regularization all reduce variance. (This framing is standard machine learning practice, stated as general knowledge.)

steps.title: Ridge: penalise large coefficients
body: Ridge regression adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients: it minimizes the residual sum of squares plus alpha times the squared L2 norm. The larger alpha, the greater the shrinkage, and the more robust the coefficients are to collinearity (scikit-learn's linear model guide).
Collinear features otherwise make the least-squares estimate highly sensitive to random errors and give a large variance.

steps.title: Lasso and elastic net
body: Lasso uses an L1 penalty and estimates sparse coefficients: it can set some exactly to zero, so it also works as feature selection. Elastic net mixes L1 and L2: when several features are correlated, Lasso tends to pick one at random while elastic net is likely to pick both.
Logistic regression in scikit-learn applies regularization by default.

card.title: Penalties
lines: Ridge        alpha * sum(w^2)    shrinks all weights
Lasso        alpha * sum(|w|)    can zero some weights
Elastic net  mixes both          stable with correlated features

steps.title: Choose alpha by cross-validation, then test once
body: Pick alpha (and other hyperparameters) with cross-validation on the training data, refit on all of the training data, and evaluate on the test set a single time. That one number is the honest estimate of how the model will do on new data.
If the test score disappoints, resist the urge to tune against it again: that spends the test set.

steps.title: Recap
body: Hold out a test set, tune with validation or cross-validation, keep preprocessing inside the training folds (a Pipeline), watch the train/validation gap, and use regularization to control variance. Report the test score once.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 1 test set held out, touched once
2 tune with CV, not the test set

everyday.plain: A model should learn the pattern, not the exact examples.
everyday.story: A student who memorises each solved example fails a new question. A student who understands the pattern passes. To push a model toward understanding, you can penalise it for being too complicated, like a teacher saying 'explain it simply'. That is regularisation.
words: How well a model works on data it has not seen.
Learning the examples so closely that new data goes badly.
Testing several times, each time on a different slice kept aside.
A penalty that keeps a model simple so it does not overfit.

title: ML Metrics and A/B Testing
tagline: Pick the right score for a model, and test changes without fooling yourself.
explain: Two questions follow every model: how good is it, and does it help? The first is metrics, the second is experiments. Interviewers ask for the definitions and then probe the traps, such as accuracy on imbalanced data and stopping a test early.
## The confusion matrix and its ratios

scikit-learn defines entry i, j of a confusion matrix as the number of observations actually in group i but predicted to be in group j. For a binary problem the four counts are true negatives, false positives, false negatives and true positives. Precision, the ability of the classifier not to label a negative sample as positive, is tp / (tp + fp). Recall, the ability to find all the positive samples, is tp / (tp + fn). F-beta is (1 + beta^2) * precision * recall / (beta^2 * precision + recall); with beta = 1 precision and recall are equally important.
## Imbalanced data and the threshold

If 1% of examples are positive, predicting 'negative' for everything is 99% accurate. scikit-learn's documentation recommends balanced accuracy, the macro-average of recall per class, which avoids inflated estimates on imbalanced data and drops to 1 / n_classes when accuracy is only above chance because of the imbalance. A classifier outputs a score, and the threshold turns it into a decision: lowering it raises recall and usually lowers precision. Choose it from the cost of each kind of mistake.
## ROC AUC
The ROC AUC summarizes the ROC curve in one number and, the documentation notes, does not require optimizing a threshold for each label. It measures how well scores rank positives above negatives.
## A/B testing

Randomly split users into control and variant and compare a metric. Evan Miller's article 'How Not To Run An A/B Test' makes the central point: repeated significance testing always increases the false positive rate. With a true 50% conversion rate in both groups and no real effect, stopping at the first 5% significance within 150 observations gave a false positive rate of 26.1%, more than five times the nominal 5%. His advice is to decide on a sample size in advance and wait until the experiment is over, with a rule of thumb of n = 16 sigma^2 / delta^2, where delta is the minimum effect to detect and sigma^2 = p(1 - p) for conversion rates. Sequential or Bayesian designs allow valid early stopping.
## How to talk through it

Name the class balance and the cost of each error before choosing a metric, give the threshold you would pick and why, and for an experiment state the primary metric, guardrails, minimum effect, sample size and stop rule up front.
keyPoints: Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data; use precision, recall, F1 or balanced accuracy.
precision = tp / (tp + fp); recall = tp / (tp + fn).
The threshold trades precision for recall; choose it from the cost of errors.
ROC AUC measures ranking without choosing a threshold.
A/B tests: fix the sample size in advance; peeking inflates false positives.

sql.title: Metrics from a confusion matrix, and the accuracy trap
sql.code:
def metrics(tp, fp, fn, tn):
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    accuracy = (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn)
    balanced = (recall + tn / (tn + fp)) / 2                 # macro-average of recall per class
    return {'precision': precision, 'recall': recall, 'f1': f1, 'accuracy': accuracy, 'balanced_accuracy': balanced}

m = metrics(tp=15, fp=5, fn=85, tn=9895)
assert m['precision'] == 0.75 and m['recall'] == 0.15
assert round(m['f1'], 3) == 0.25
assert round(m['accuracy'], 4) == 0.991                      # looks excellent
assert round(m['balanced_accuracy'], 3) == 0.575             # the honest view of a classifier that misses most spam

lazy = metrics(tp=0, fp=0, fn=100, tn=9900)                  # always predicts 'not spam'
assert lazy['accuracy'] == 0.99 and lazy['balanced_accuracy'] == 0.5      # balanced accuracy drops to 1 / n_classes

sql.title: The threshold trade-off, and why peeking at an A/B test is dangerous
sql.code:
import math, random

scores = [(0.95, 1), (0.80, 1), (0.60, 0), (0.55, 1), (0.40, 0), (0.30, 0), (0.20, 1), (0.10, 0)]   # (score, is_spam)
def at(threshold):
    tp = sum(1 for s, y in scores if s >= threshold and y)
    fp = sum(1 for s, y in scores if s >= threshold and not y)
    fn = sum(1 for s, y in scores if s < threshold and y)
    return tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 1.0, tp / (tp + fn)

(p_strict, r_strict), (p_loose, r_loose) = at(0.9), at(0.25)
assert p_strict > p_loose and r_strict < r_loose              # raising the threshold buys precision and costs recall

def significant(a, b, n):
    p = (a + b) / (2 * n)
    se = math.sqrt(2 * p * (1 - p) / n) or 1e-9
    return abs((a - b) / n / se) > 1.96                      # two-sided test at about 5%

def false_positive_rate(peek, trials=2000, n=150, every=10, seed=7):
    rng, wrong = random.Random(seed), 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        a = b = 0
        hit = False
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            a += rng.random() < 0.5                          # both groups have the SAME true rate
            b += rng.random() < 0.5
            if peek and i % every == 0 and significant(a, b, i):
                hit = True
                break
        wrong += hit or significant(a, b, n)
    return wrong / trials

assert false_positive_rate(peek=False) < 0.08                  # one look at a fixed sample size: about 5%
assert false_positive_rate(peek=True) > 0.15                   # looking every 10 observations: several times worse

def sample_size(p, delta):
    return 16 * p * (1 - p) / delta ** 2                       # Evan Miller's rule of thumb, per group
assert round(sample_size(0.5, 0.05)) == 1600

exercise: Using any binary classifier you build or are given scores for: (1) compute the confusion matrix at threshold 0.5, then at 0.3 and 0.7, and the precision and recall at each; (2) say which threshold you would choose for a fraud detector and for a spam filter, and why; (3) for an experiment with a 4% baseline conversion where you care about a 0.5 percentage point change, compute the sample size per group with n = 16 p(1-p) / delta^2 and write the stop rule and two guardrail metrics.
pitfalls: Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
Choosing a threshold of 0.5 without saying why.
Checking an A/B test every day and stopping at the first significant result.
No guardrail metrics, so a win on one metric hides harm on another.
Confusing precision with recall.

interview.q: Why is accuracy a poor metric for imbalanced classes?
interview.a: A model that always predicts the majority class gets a high accuracy and finds none of the minority class. Use precision, recall, F1, balanced accuracy (the average of per-class recall, which falls to 1 / n_classes for such a model) or the precision-recall curve, and look at the confusion matrix.

interview.q: Explain precision and recall.
interview.a: Precision = tp / (tp + fp): of the items flagged positive, how many were right. Recall = tp / (tp + fn): of the real positives, how many were found. Lowering the decision threshold raises recall and usually lowers precision; choose from the costs of false positives and false negatives.

interview.q: What does ROC AUC measure?
interview.a: The area under the curve of true positive rate against false positive rate across all thresholds. It summarizes how well the model ranks positives above negatives and needs no threshold. For rare positives also check precision and recall.

interview.q: How do you run a valid A/B test?
interview.a: Randomise users, choose a primary metric and guardrails, decide the minimum effect and the sample size in advance (roughly n = 16 p(1-p) / delta^2 per group), run to that size and test once. Peeking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives well above the nominal 5%; use a sequential design if you need early stopping.

references.title: How Not To Run an A/B Test (Evan Miller)

basis: Sources, both read: scikit-learn's model evaluation page (confusion matrix, precision and recall definitions, F-beta, ROC AUC without a threshold, balanced accuracy for imbalanced data; I read the first part of that very long page) and Evan Miller's article (the 26.1% false positive example, the peeking table, deciding the sample size in advance, n = 16 sigma^2 / delta^2, sequential and Bayesian alternatives). The simulation in the code is mine and gives about 23% with peeking and about 5% without. The caution about AUC on rare positives and the guardrail advice are general practice and my judgment. Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard. The priority shown is the baseline; the roadmap raises it for roles that need it (the frontend plan makes the CSS and React lessons core, the ML plan makes generalization and metrics core).

scenes.title: Metrics and A/B tests, step by step

steps.title: Accuracy can hide a useless model
body: In a data set where 1% of the emails are spam, a classifier that says 'not spam' for everything is 99% accurate and catches nothing. Accuracy alone says little when the classes are imbalanced.

scikit-learn recommends balanced accuracy for this case: the macro-average of recall per class, which drops to 1 divided by the number of classes when a classifier only exploits an imbalanced test set.

steps.title: Start from the confusion matrix
body: Count four outcomes: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Entry i, j of a confusion matrix is the number of observations actually in group i but predicted to be in group j.
Every metric below is a ratio of these four numbers.

steps.title: Precision and recall
body: Precision is the ability not to label a negative sample positive: tp / (tp + fp) = 15 / 20 = 75%. Recall is the ability to find all the positive samples: tp / (tp + fn) = 15 / 100 = 15%.
Precision asks 'of what I flagged, how much was right?'; recall asks 'of what was there, how much did I find?'.

predict.question: tp = 15, fp = 5, fn = 85. What are precision and recall?
predict.why: precision = 15 / (15 + 5) = 75%. recall = 15 / (15 + 85) = 15%. High precision with low recall is the signature of a cautious classifier.

steps.title: The threshold trades one for the other
body: A classifier outputs a score; you choose a threshold above which it predicts positive. Lowering the threshold flags more emails: recall rises and precision usually falls. Raising it does the opposite. F1 combines them (with beta = 1 precision and recall are equally important); a different beta weights one over the other.
Pick the threshold from the cost of each mistake: a missed fraud costs more than a false alarm; a spam filter that hides a real email costs more than a spam in the inbox.

steps.title: ROC AUC: one number, no threshold
body: The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across all thresholds. The area under it (ROC AUC) summarizes the curve in one number, and, scikit-learn notes, does not require choosing a threshold. It measures how well the score ranks positives above negatives.

For very rare positives, look at precision and recall (or a precision-recall curve) as well; AUC can look comfortable while precision is poor. (That caution is general practice, not from the scikit-learn page I read.)

steps.title: From offline metrics to an experiment
body: An offline metric says the model is better on past data. To know if it helps users, run an A/B test: randomly split users into a control group (A) and a variant group (B) and compare a business metric, such as conversion.
The question is not 'is B ahead?' but 'is the difference larger than chance would produce?'.

steps.title: Peeking inflates false positives
body: If you check the result every day and stop as soon as it looks significant, the real false positive rate is much higher than 5%. Evan Miller's article gives an example: with a true conversion rate of 50% in both groups, stopping at the first 5% significance within 150 observations gives a false positive rate of 26.1%, more than five times the nominal 5%.
The same article notes that peeking ten times at a reported 1% significance really means about 5%.

predict.question: Both groups have the same true rate. You check significance at 5% after every 10 observations and stop the first time it shows. What happens to the false positive rate?
predict.why: Every extra look is another chance to be fooled by noise. Repeated significance testing always increases the false positive rate; in a simulation of this kind it rises to about a quarter.

steps.title: Decide the sample size in advance
body: Evan Miller's advice: decide on a sample size before the experiment and wait until it is over. His rule of thumb is n = 16 sigma^2 / delta^2 per group, where delta is the smallest effect worth detecting and sigma^2 = p(1 - p) for a conversion rate. Committing in advance mitigates the problem.
If you must monitor continuously, use a sequential design with pre-set checkpoints, or a Bayesian design, which allow valid early stopping.

pill.text: n fixed in advance, then test once

steps.title: Metrics for the business, guardrails for harm
body: Pick one primary metric that the change should move, and guardrail metrics it must not harm (latency, error rate, revenue per user). A model that improves click rate and lengthens page load may not be a win.
Write the decision rule before the test: 'ship if the primary metric improves by at least X and no guardrail drops by more than Y'.

callout.text: State the metric, the minimum effect, the sample size and the stop rule before you launch.

steps.title: Recap
body: Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, the threshold trade-off, ROC AUC and balanced accuracy for imbalanced data. Then validate with an A/B test: fixed sample size, one look, a primary metric and guardrails.

lines: 2 confusion matrix, then precision and recall
3 threshold from the cost of errors
4 AUC ranks; check precision for rare events
5 A/B test: fixed n, one look, guardrails

everyday.story: A smoke alarm that rings for every cooking smell (many false alarms) is annoying. One that stays silent in a real fire (a miss) is dangerous. Which mistake matters more decides how you set it. And to test a new alarm, you compare it with the old one on similar houses at the same time, and you decide how many houses to test before you start looking at the results.

Of all the real cases, how many the model found.

title: Design a Recommender System
tagline: Suggest things people will like: pick a short list, then rank it.
explain: Recommendation and ranking are among the most common ML system design prompts. Chip Huyen's interview book says almost every company asks an ML system design question, and prep guides recommend practicing recommendation systems, ranking pipelines and feature stores. Google's machine learning course on recommendation systems is a primary source for the architecture.
## Three stages

The course describes a common architecture with three stages: candidate generation, scoring and re-ranking. Candidate generation is the first stage. Its model must evaluate queries quickly given the enormous size of the corpus; the course's example reduces billions of videos to hundreds or thousands. Scoring then ranks those candidates with a richer model, and re-ranking adjusts the final list.
## Candidate generation

Content-based filtering uses similarity between items to recommend items similar to what the user likes. Collaborative filtering uses similarities between queries and items simultaneously, recommending an item to a user because a similar user liked it. Both approaches map each item and each query to an embedding vector in a common embedding space where similar items end up close together, with closeness defined by a similarity measure such as cosine, dot product or Euclidean distance. In production you search for nearest neighbours with an approximate index, and combine several candidate generators.
## Scoring and re-ranking

A ranking model predicts the probability of a click, watch or purchase for each candidate using user, item and context features. It can be expensive per item because there are few items. Re-ranking looks at the list as a whole: remove seen items, apply policy, add diversity and freshness, and leave room for exploration.
## Cold start and feedback

New users and new items have no history, so collaborative filtering has nothing to use (general knowledge): fall back to content features and popularity, and explore deliberately. Log impressions and outcomes to train the next model, evaluate offline and then with an A/B test, and watch for feedback loops where the model learns from its own earlier choices.
## How to talk through it
Start with the objective and constraints, draw the three stages with the size of the set at each step, then discuss features, training data, cold start, evaluation and what can go wrong online.
keyPoints: Three stages: candidate generation, scoring, re-ranking; each narrows the set.
Content-based: similar items. Collaborative: similar users. Embeddings make both a nearest-neighbour search.
Scoring is a richer model on few items; re-ranking handles diversity and policy.
Cold start needs content features, popularity and exploration.
Evaluate offline, then with an A/B test; beware feedback loops and training-serving skew.

sql.title: Embeddings, nearest neighbours and item-to-item collaborative filtering
Re-ranking: remove seen items and keep the list diverse

exercise: Design recommendations for a short-video app with 500 million items and 50 million daily users, with a 100 ms budget. Draw the three stages with the size of the item set after each, say which candidate generators you would combine and why, list the features for the ranking model and how training and serving features stay consistent, define the re-ranking rules, describe how a brand-new video and a brand-new user are handled, and write the offline metric and the A/B test (primary metric and two guardrails).
pitfalls: Trying to score the whole corpus with the heavy model.
Ignoring cold start for new users and new items.
Optimizing clicks alone, which rewards clickbait; no guardrail metrics.
Training on features that cannot be computed at serving time.
No exploration, so the model only learns from what it already showed.

interview.q: How is a recommender system structured?
interview.a: Three stages: candidate generation narrows a huge corpus to hundreds or thousands using fast methods (content-based, collaborative, embedding nearest-neighbour search); scoring ranks them with a richer model using user, item and context features; re-ranking adjusts the final list for diversity, freshness and policy.

interview.q: What is the difference between content-based and collaborative filtering?
interview.a: Content-based filtering recommends items similar to ones the user liked, using item features. Collaborative filtering uses the behavior of similar users, recommending what they liked. Both can be expressed as embeddings in a shared space with a similarity measure such as cosine or dot product.

interview.q: What is the cold start problem and how do you handle it?
interview.a: New users and items have no interaction history, so collaborative signals are missing. Use content features, popularity and context, ask for preferences at sign-up, and reserve some traffic for exploring new items so they collect data.

interview.q: How do you evaluate a recommender?
interview.a: Offline with ranking metrics on held-out interactions to compare models cheaply, then online with an A/B test on a business metric (watch time, purchases) with guardrails (latency, diversity, complaints). Watch for feedback loops from training on the model's own recommendations.

references.title: Candidate generation overview (Google ML recommendation course)

steps.title: Three stages: generate, score, re-rank
body: Google's recommendation course describes a common architecture with three stages: candidate generation, scoring and re-ranking. You cannot score millions of items per request, so candidate generation narrows the corpus (the course's example is a billion videos down to hundreds or thousands), scoring ranks those with a more expensive model, and re-ranking adjusts the final list.
Each stage can use a different, increasingly precise and expensive technique.

steps.title: Content-based filtering
body: Content-based filtering uses similarity between items to recommend items similar to what the user likes: a user who watched cute cat videos is shown other cute animal videos. It needs item features and works for new items, but it only recommends more of what the user already likes.
Both approaches map each item and each query (user or context) to an embedding vector in a common space where similar items are close together.

pill.text: items similar to what you liked

steps.title: Collaborative filtering
body: Collaborative filtering uses similarities between queries and items simultaneously: it recommends video 1 to user A because user A is similar to user B, who likes video 1. It needs no item features and can recommend surprising items, but needs interaction data.
A new user or new item has no history: the cold start problem (general knowledge). Fall back to content features, popularity and exploration.

predict.question: User A and user B have liked many of the same videos. B also liked video 7, which A has not seen. What does collaborative filtering do?
predict.why: Collaborative filtering assumes similar users like similar items, so it recommends what similar users liked that this user has not seen.

steps.title: Embeddings and similarity
body: Put users and items into the same embedding space; the closeness of two embeddings is a similarity measure such as cosine, dot product or Euclidean distance. For a user, the candidates are the items with the nearest embeddings. At large scale you search them with an approximate nearest-neighbour index rather than comparing against every item.
Several candidate generators (popular items, nearest neighbours, items from followed creators) are usually combined and their outputs merged.

pill.text: item embeddings in an ANN index

steps.title: Scoring with a ranking model
body: For the few hundred candidates, a richer model predicts how likely the user is to click, watch or buy, using many features (user history, item, context such as time and device). It can afford more computation per item because there are few items.
Train on logged interactions; take care that features available at training time are also available at serving time (training-serving skew).

steps.title: Re-ranking: the list, not the items
body: The final list must work as a whole: remove items the user has seen, enforce policy (age, region, safety), add diversity so the page is not ten near-duplicates, and mix in fresh or exploratory items to learn about them.
Business rules belong here, after the model, where they are easy to change.

steps.title: Feedback loop and evaluation
body: Log what was shown and what happened (impressions, clicks, watch time) to train the next model. Evaluate offline with ranking metrics on held-out data, then confirm with an online A/B test on the business metric, with guardrails.
Beware feedback loops: a model trained on what it already showed learns its own bias. Reserve some traffic for exploration.

steps.title: Recap
body: Clarify the objective, then three stages: candidate generation (content-based, collaborative, embeddings with nearest-neighbour search), scoring with a ranking model, re-ranking for diversity and policy. Close the loop with logging, offline and online evaluation, and a plan for cold start.

Then he puts the best at the top of the table. New customers, about whom he knows nothing, are a harder case, because he has no history to go on.
