title: CSS Layout: Box Model, Flexbox, Grid, Responsive
tagline: How sizes add up, how rows and grids share space, and how one page fits every screen.
explain: Front end interviews include CSS and HTML as well as JavaScript: Amazon's front end page names JavaScript, CSS and HTML as tested skills, and the UI coding round expects you to build a layout that looks right and works at different widths. The MDN guides are the primary source for the rules below.
## The box model

MDN lists four layers: the content box, the padding box, the border box and the margin box. In the standard box model, width and height set the content box and padding and border are added: width 350, height 150, padding 25 and border 5 give 410 by 210 (350 + 25 + 25 + 5 + 5). The margin is not counted. With box-sizing: border-box the width is the visible box, so the same declarations take 350 by 150. MDN's recommended pattern sets html { box-sizing: border-box } and *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: inherit }.
## Margin collapsing

Two positive vertical margins combine into one equal to the largest, so a margin-bottom of 50px and a margin-top of 30px produce a 50px gap, not 80px. Two negative margins collapse to the smallest value (furthest from zero), and a negative margin is subtracted from the total.
## Flexbox

Setting display: flex on an element makes it a flex container and its children flex items. The main axis runs in the direction of flex-direction (a row by default) and the cross axis is perpendicular to it. flex-wrap: wrap moves overflowing items to a new line; justify-content places items on the main axis (space-between leaves no space at either end, space-around leaves a little at both); align-items places them on the cross axis (the default behaves as stretch; center keeps their size and centers them). The flex shorthand sets flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis, and a unitless value such as flex: 1 shares the free space in proportion.
## Grid

display: grid with grid-template-columns creates columns; the fr unit is a fraction of the available space, so 2fr 1fr 1fr in a 1000px container with a 20px gap gives 480, 240 and 240. gap sets the space between tracks (not in fr units). grid-column: 1 / 3 makes an item span from line 1 to line 3. MDN describes grid as a two-dimensional layout system, and flexbox as the tool to lay items out in a row or a column.
## Responsive design

Responsive sites use flexible grids, relative units and media queries. A media query applies CSS when a condition holds, for example @media screen and (width >= 80rem); the points where the layout changes are breakpoints. MDN recommends mobile first: a single-column layout for narrow screens, then more columns for wider ones. Always include the viewport meta tag, because mobile browsers otherwise report a wider viewport than the device. Use max-width: 100% on images and video, and srcset and sizes to avoid downloading oversized images.
## How to talk through it
Say which layout system you use for which dimension and why, set border-box first, build mobile first and name the breakpoints, then check keyboard and screen reader behavior.
keyPoints: Box width = content + padding + border (the default); border-box makes width the visible box.
Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the largest.
Flexbox is one-dimensional: main and cross axis; grid is two-dimensional.
fr shares the available space; gap is the space between tracks.
Mobile first, media queries with relative units, the viewport meta tag, max-width: 100% images.

Check it at 320, 768 and 1440 px, and with only the keyboard.

Using absolute pixel breakpoints taken from one device.
Expecting margins to add instead of collapse.
Using grid for a single row of items, or flexbox for a two-dimensional page layout.
No viewport meta tag, so media queries seem to do nothing on phones.

interview.q: Explain the CSS box model and box-sizing.
interview.a: Each element is a box with content, padding, border and margin. By default width and height set the content box, so padding and border add to the total (350 wide with 25 padding and 5 border is 410). With box-sizing: border-box the width includes padding and border, so it is 350. Margins are outside the box and are not counted in its size.

interview.q: Flexbox or grid?
interview.a: Flexbox lays items out along one axis (a row or a column) and shares the free space between them; grid is two-dimensional, defining rows and columns together. Use flexbox for toolbars and rows of cards, grid for page layouts and galleries, and nest them freely.

interview.q: What does the fr unit do?
interview.a: It is a fraction of the available space in a grid container after fixed sizes and gaps are removed. With 2fr 1fr 1fr in 1000px and a 20px gap, 960px is shared as 480, 240 and 240. It distributes available space, not all space.

interview.q: How do you make a layout responsive?
interview.a: Use flexible layouts (flexbox, grid), relative units and mobile first CSS, adding media queries at breakpoints where the content needs it; include the viewport meta tag; keep images within their containers with max-width: 100% and serve appropriately sized images with srcset and sizes.

Amazon's front end page (read) names CSS and HTML as tested skills. The advice on when to use flexbox versus grid is a common rule of thumb; MDN's grid page does not state it directly. The priority shown is the baseline; the roadmap raises it for roles that need it (the frontend plan makes the CSS and React lessons core, the ML plan makes generalization and metrics core).

steps.title: Every element is a box
body: MDN lists four layers of a box: the content box (sized with width and height), the padding box, the border box and the margin box, the outermost layer, which is whitespace between this box and other elements.
Layout problems are very often box-size problems, so know how the sizes add up.

steps.title: box-sizing: which width do you mean?
body: By default (the standard box model) width and height set the content box, and padding and borders are added: width 350, height 150, padding 25 and border 5 give a box 410 px wide and 210 px high (350 + 25 + 25 + 5 + 5). The margin is not counted.
With box-sizing: border-box, the width is the visible box, so the same CSS takes exactly 350 by 150 and the content shrinks to fit.

steps.title: Margins collapse
body: When two vertical margins touch, positive margins combine into one equal to the largest: a margin-bottom of 50 px and a margin-top of 30 px give a 50 px gap, not 80. If one margin is negative its value is subtracted from the total.
If you do not get the space you expect, margin collapsing is a likely reason.

steps.title: Flexbox: one dimension
body: display: flex makes an element a flex container and its children flex items. They are laid out along the main axis (a row by default; flex-direction can make it a column), with the cross axis perpendicular to it. If items overflow, flex-wrap: wrap moves them to a new line.
flex: 1 and flex: 2 share the available space in proportion: the second item gets two of three units.

steps.title: Align along both axes

justify-content: center with align-items: center centers an item both ways.

steps.title: Grid: two dimensions
body: display: grid with grid-template-columns defines columns. The fr unit is a fraction of the available space: 2fr 1fr 1fr in a 1000 px container with a 20 px gap leaves 960 px, so the columns are 480, 240 and 240. gap sets the space between tracks. Items can span lines: grid-column: 1 / 3.
MDN notes fr distributes available space, not all space: a large item in one track leaves less to share.

steps.title: Flexbox or grid?
body: Use flexbox to lay out items in one line or one direction and let them share space (a toolbar, a row of cards). Use grid when you need rows and columns together (a page layout, a gallery). They combine: a grid of cards, each card a flex column.
MDN describes grid as a two-dimensional layout system, organizing content into rows and columns.

steps.title: Responsive design: one page, many screens
body: Responsive sites are built on flexible grids, relative units and media queries. A media query applies CSS only when a condition holds (for example width >= 80rem); the points where the layout changes are breakpoints. Flexbox and grid are responsive by default.
Mobile first: start with a simple single-column layout for narrow screens, then add columns when there is room.

steps.title: The viewport tag and flexible images
body: Without <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width"> mobile browsers report a wide fake viewport and your breakpoints may not work, so MDN says to always include it. Keep media inside its container with img, picture, video { max-width: 100% }, and use srcset and sizes so small screens do not download huge images.
Test at real widths and with the keyboard.

callout.text: A page that needs sideways scrolling on a phone usually has a fixed-width element or a missing viewport tag.

steps.title: Recap
body: Know the box (content, padding, border, margin) and box-sizing, margin collapsing, flexbox for one dimension, grid for two, and responsive design with relative units, media queries, a viewport tag and flexible images.

title: React State: Structure, Lifting, Reducers and Context
tagline: Decide where each piece of data lives so bugs cannot happen, and share it without passing it down every level.
explain: State questions in a React interview are really design questions: where does this value live, and how is it shaped? The react.dev guides give clear principles. This lesson follows three of those guides: choosing the state structure, sharing state between components, and scaling up with a reducer and context.
## Choosing the state structure

react.dev lists five principles. Group related state: if you always update two or more variables together, merge them into one, such as a position object with x and y. Avoid contradictions: replace isSending and isSent with a single status variable with the values typing, sending and sent, so both cannot be true at once. Avoid redundant state: if you can calculate something from props or existing state during rendering, do not put it in state, for example fullName from firstName and lastName. Avoid duplication: store a selectedId and find the item in the list instead of a copy of the item. Avoid deeply nested state: prefer a flat table keyed by id, with each record holding childIds. The goal is to make state easy to update without introducing mistakes.
## Lifting state up

Sometimes you want the state of two components to change together. Remove the state from both, move it to their closest common parent and pass it down via props together with the event handlers: lifting state up. For each unique piece of state you choose the component that owns it: a single source of truth, which does not mean all state in one place but a specific owner for each piece. A component driven by props is controlled; one with its own local state is uncontrolled. Uncontrolled components are easier to use, controlled components are maximally flexible but need the parent to configure them fully. Most components are a mix, and you can refactor later.
## Reducers and context

A reducer consolidates the state update logic of a component: handlers dispatch actions such as added, changed and deleted and the reducer function computes the next state, which keeps event handlers short and concise. If the state is needed deep in the tree, passing it and the handlers through many intermediate components (prop drilling) becomes frustrating. Put the state and the dispatch function into context in three steps: create the context, put the state and dispatch into it, and use it anywhere in the tree. The state still lives in the top-level component, managed with useReducer, but is available to every component below it.
## How to talk through it
For any state question say what the minimum state is, what you derive in render, who owns it, how it changes (which events), and what you would do if it were needed far down the tree.
keyPoints: Group related state; use one status value instead of several booleans.
Derive what you can in render; store ids, not copies.
Prefer flat state keyed by id.
Lift state to the closest common parent: one owner, a single source of truth.
Reducer for update logic; context to avoid prop drilling.

exercise: Build a small shop page in React (or plain JavaScript functions first): a product list, a filter, a cart and a checkout status. Write the minimal state on paper (what is stored, what is derived), give each piece an owner, replace any pair of booleans with a status, put the cart logic in a reducer with add, remove and change quantity actions, and test the reducer with asserts. Then say where context would help and where plain props are clearer.
pitfalls: Storing derived values (a filtered list, a total) in state, then forgetting to update them.
Two booleans that can contradict each other.
Copying an object into state when an id would do, so the copy goes stale.
Mutating state in a reducer instead of returning a new value.
Reaching for context for everything, including values only a neighbour needs.

interview.q: How do you decide what belongs in state?
interview.a: Keep the minimum: values that change over time and cannot be computed from other state or props. Derive everything else during rendering. Group values that change together, use one status instead of several booleans, store ids instead of duplicated objects, and keep nested data flat.

interview.q: What is lifting state up?
interview.a: When two components must stay in sync, move their state to the closest common parent and pass it down as props with the handlers that change it. The parent is then the single source of truth for that piece of state.

interview.q: Controlled or uncontrolled component?
interview.a: A controlled component's important information is driven by props from its parent, so the parent can coordinate it fully, at the cost of configuring it. An uncontrolled one keeps local state: simpler to use, less flexible. Most components mix the two.

interview.q: When would you use a reducer and context?
interview.a: A reducer when several handlers update the same complex state and you want the logic in one testable pure function. Context when many components, possibly deep in the tree, need the state or dispatch and passing props through the middle would be prop drilling. The state still lives in one top-level owner.

Priorities and hours are my own judgment, not a published standard. steps.title: State is the part of the UI that changes
body: Where state lives and how it is shaped decides how many bugs you will have. react.dev gives principles for structuring state; its goal is to make state easy to update without introducing mistakes, and its summary is 'make your state as simple as it can be, but no simpler'.
The five principles: group related state, avoid contradictions, avoid redundancy, avoid duplication, avoid deep nesting.

hud.v: easy to update, hard to get wrong

steps.title: Group related state
body: If you always update two or more state variables at the same time, merge them into one: a position { x, y } instead of separate x and y. They can then never be updated out of step.
The same applies to form fields that change together.

steps.title: Avoid contradictions
body: isSending and isSent can both be true at once, which makes no sense. Replace them with a single status variable with values 'typing', 'sending' and 'sent': only one can hold, so contradictions are impossible.
Whenever a combination of booleans has a meaningless state, use one variable with named values.

predict.question: State has isSending and isSent booleans. How many combinations are possible, and how many make sense?
predict.why: Two booleans give four combinations, but 'sending and sent at the same time' is impossible in reality, which leaves three meaningful states. One status variable has exactly the three real values.

steps.title: Avoid redundant and duplicated state
body: If you can calculate something from existing state during rendering, do not store it: fullName is firstName + ' ' + lastName, computed on each render. Do not duplicate data either: store selectedId and find the item in the list, instead of a copy of the selected item that can drift out of sync with the list.
Derived values are always right; copies need synchronizing.

pill.text: selectedId, not a copy of the item

steps.title: Prefer flat state
body: Deeply nested state is awkward to update. Store records in a flat table keyed by id, with child ids instead of nested child objects: { 1: { title, childIds: [2, 3] }, 2: {...} }. Updating one record then touches one entry.
This is the same normalization idea as in databases.

steps.title: Lift state up
body: When two components must always change together, remove the state from both, move it to their closest common parent and pass it down as props, with the event handlers. This is lifting state up. For each piece of state, choose the single component that owns it: a single source of truth.
Lifting state often changes what you store: a boolean per panel became a single activeIndex, which ensured only one panel is active.

steps.title: Controlled and uncontrolled components
body: A component with its own local state is 'uncontrolled': its parent cannot influence it. A component driven by props is 'controlled': the parent specifies its behavior fully. Uncontrolled components are easier to use; controlled ones are more flexible when you need to coordinate components.
In practice most components mix both. Decide for each piece of information whether props or local state should control it; you can refactor later.

steps.title: A reducer collects the update logic
body: When many handlers update the same state, move the logic into one reducer function: (state, action) returns the new state. Handlers only dispatch actions such as added, changed, deleted. A reducer helps keep event handlers short and concise (react.dev).
A reducer is a pure function, so it is easy to test without rendering.

steps.title: Context: skip the prop drilling
body: Passing state and handlers through tens of components in the middle is frustrating prop drilling. Put the state and the dispatch function into context so any component below can read and update them. The three steps: create the context, put state and dispatch into it, use it anywhere in the tree. The state still lives in the top-level component.
Context is for what many components need; passing props is still the clearest way for nearby components.
changes: + Context provider and a deep consumer

steps.title: Recap
body: Structure state simply (group, no contradictions, derive instead of copying, keep it flat), give each piece one owner and lift it to the nearest common parent, choose controlled or uncontrolled per component, use a reducer when logic grows and context when many components need it.

card.title: Checklist
lines: 3 derive in render; store ids not copies
5 lift to the common parent: one owner
6 reducer for logic, context for reach

everyday.plain: Decide where each piece of data lives, so that only one place owns it.
everyday.story: In a family, the shopping list is kept on the fridge, not copied in every room. If two people need it, they both look at the fridge. When someone adds something, everyone sees it. In React, the data should live in one place, with the parts that need it getting it from there.
words: Data a component remembers, which makes it redraw when it changes.
Moving state to a shared parent so several children can use it.
A function that takes the old state and an action and gives the new state.
A way to share a value with many components without passing it down every level.

title: Two Pointers and Sliding Window in Depth
tagline: Turn nested loops into one pass by moving two indexes with a rule, and say why the rule is safe.
explain: Two pointers and the sliding window are the two patterns that turn an O(n^2) nested loop into an O(n) scan. Interviewers like them because the code is short but the reasoning is easy to get wrong, so you are graded on explaining why the pointer moves are safe.
## Two pointers from both ends

Use it when the data is sorted (or can be sorted) and you are looking for a pair or a condition on both ends: pair sum, three sum, container with most water, checking a palindrome. Put one pointer at each end. Compare, then move the pointer whose value cannot be part of any better answer. Every step discards at least one candidate for ever, so the loop runs at most n times.

The sentence to say out loud is the invariant: "if an answer exists, it is between the two pointers". When the sum is too big, the right value is too big with every remaining partner, so it can be dropped. If you cannot state why a value can be dropped, the pattern does not apply.
## Two pointers in the same direction

A slow pointer marks where the next good item goes, and a fast pointer scans ahead. This removes duplicates from a sorted list in place, moves zeros to the end, or filters a list in O(n) time and O(1) space. A variant is the slow and fast pointer on a linked list, used to find the middle or detect a cycle.
## The sliding window
A window is a contiguous range [left, right]. Keep a summary of what is inside (a sum, a count dictionary, a set) and update it as the window moves instead of recomputing it.

- Fixed size k: add the value entering, subtract the value leaving. Maximum sum of k values, or the number of distinct values in every window of k.
- Variable size, longest valid window: move right every step; while the window is invalid, move left. Longest substring without repeating characters is the classic.
- Variable size, shortest valid window: move right until the window becomes valid, then move left as far as it stays valid, recording the length each time. Minimum size subarray with sum at least S.
The total work is O(n) even though there is a loop inside a loop, because left and right each move forward at most n times. This is an amortized argument, and interviewers expect you to say it.
## Which pattern?

- Sorted input, a pair or triple: two pointers from both ends.
- Contiguous subarray or substring, with a size or a validity rule: sliding window.
- Contiguous subarray with negative numbers and a target sum: a window does not work, because adding a value no longer makes the sum only grow; use a prefix sum and a hash map instead.
- Not contiguous (subsets, choices): backtracking or dynamic programming.
## What to say in the interview

State the brute force and its cost, name the pattern and why it applies (sorted, or contiguous), state the invariant, then code it. Finish with the time and space cost and two edge cases: an empty input and a window larger than the input.
keyPoints: Two pointers from both ends needs sorted data; state the invariant: an answer, if any, lies between the pointers.
Same-direction pointers (slow and fast) filter or deduplicate in place in O(n) time and O(1) space.
A fixed window updates its sum in O(1): add the entering value, subtract the leaving value.
A variable window grows the right end and shrinks the left end; each moves forward at most n times, so the total is O(n).
Negative numbers break the window for sum targets: use prefix sums and a hash map instead.

sql.title: Two pointers from both ends, and in the same direction
Fixed and variable sliding windows
sql.code:
def max_sum_of_k(nums, k):
    if k > len(nums):
        return None
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

assert max_sum_of_k([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3) == 9
assert max_sum_of_k([1, 2], 3) is None

def longest_unique_substring(s):
    """Longest window with no repeated character: grow right, shrink left while invalid."""
    last_seen = {}
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last_seen and last_seen[ch] >= left:
            left = last_seen[ch] + 1
        last_seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

assert longest_unique_substring("abcabcbb") == 3
assert longest_unique_substring("bbbb") == 1
assert longest_unique_substring("") == 0
assert longest_unique_substring("pwwkew") == 3

def min_subarray_len(target, nums):
    """Shortest window with sum >= target (positive numbers only)."""
    left = total = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        total += x
        while total >= target:
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

assert min_subarray_len(7, [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]) == 2
assert min_subarray_len(100, [1, 2, 3]) == 0

exercise: Solve these without looking: valid-anagram is a warm-up, then three-sum, container-with-most-water, longest-substring-without-repeating and best-time-to-buy-sell from the problem bank. For each, write the brute force and its cost first, say which pattern applies and why, state the invariant in one sentence, then code it. Finally take min_subarray_len and explain in two sentences why a nested loop still gives O(n).
pitfalls: Using two pointers on unsorted data without saying that sorting (O(n log n)) comes first.
Off-by-one errors: lo < hi or lo <= hi, and whether the window is [left, right] inclusive.
Forgetting to shrink the window with a while loop; an if only removes one item.
Using a sliding window when the array has negative numbers and the target is a sum.
Claiming O(n^2) because of the nested loop, or claiming O(n) without explaining that each pointer only moves forward.

interview.q: When do you use two pointers, and what do you say to justify it?
interview.a: When the data is sorted (or can be) and the answer is a pair or a condition on both ends. I state the invariant: if an answer exists it lies between the pointers. Each comparison tells me which end cannot be part of any answer, so I move that pointer and drop that value for good, which makes the scan O(n).

interview.q: How is a nested while loop in a sliding window still O(n)?
interview.a: The right pointer moves forward n times and the left pointer also only moves forward, at most n times in total, because it never goes back. So the combined work is at most 2n steps. This is an amortized argument: the inner loop is not O(n) every time.

interview.q: Longest substring without repeating characters: how do you solve it?
interview.a: Slide a window over the string and keep a dict of the last index of each character. Move right every step. If the current character was seen inside the window, jump left to one past its last index. Track the largest window length. O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

interview.q: Why does a sliding window fail for "subarray with sum equal to k" when there are negative numbers?
interview.a: A window relies on the sum only growing when you extend it and only shrinking when you shrink it, so you know which end to move. Negative numbers break that. Use prefix sums with a hash map from prefix value to count: the number of subarrays ending here with sum k is the count of earlier prefixes equal to prefix - k.

interview.q: How would you remove duplicates from a sorted array in place?
interview.a: Use a slow and a fast pointer. The fast pointer scans every element; whenever it finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, advance slow and copy the value there. The unique values end up in the prefix of length slow + 1. O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

scenes.title: Two pointers on a sorted array

steps.title: The prompt: find a pair that sums to 10
body: The list is sorted: [1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11]. Find two numbers whose sum is 10.
Checking every pair costs O(n^2). Because the list is sorted, two pointers can do it in O(n): one at each end, and every comparison throws away at least one candidate for good.

card.title: Idea
lines: left starts at the smallest value
right starts at the largest value
sum too big: move right inwards
sum too small: move left inwards

steps.title: 1 + 11 = 12: too big
body: The sum is 12, above the target 10. 11 is the largest value, so paired with anything else (all at least 1) it is 12 or more. It cannot be part of the answer.
Move right one step left. One value is gone for good.

card.title: Python
lines: hi -= 1      # the largest is too big
lo += 1      # the smallest is too small

predict.question: The sum is 12 and the target is 10. Which pointer should move?
predict.why: The sum is too big and the list is sorted, so only a smaller right value can help. 11 can never be in a pair that sums to 10, so right moves in.

steps.title: 1 + 8 = 9: too small
body: 9 is below 10. The smallest value, 1, paired with the largest remaining value is still too small, so 1 cannot work with anything. Move left to the right.

steps.title: 3 + 8 = 11: too big
body: 11 is above 10, so 8 is discarded. Each step removes one value, so there are at most n steps in total: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

steps.title: 3 + 6 = 9: too small
body: Move left. Notice that the invariant never changes: if an answer exists, it lies between the two pointers.

steps.title: 4 + 6 = 10: found
body: The sum equals the target. Return the pair. Five comparisons for six values, never more than n.
This works only because the list is sorted. For an unsorted list, either sort first (O(n log n)) or use a hash set of seen values (O(n) time, O(n) space).

callout.text: State that the input must be sorted. If it is not, say what you would do instead.

scenes.title: Sliding window of size 3

steps.title: The prompt: best sum of 3 neighbours
body: Find the largest sum of any 3 consecutive values in [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]. Recomputing each window from scratch costs O(n * k).
A sliding window keeps the current sum and updates it as the window moves: add the value entering, subtract the one leaving. That is O(1) per move, O(n) overall.

steps.title: First window: 2 + 1 + 5 = 8
body: Build the first window by adding its k values. Remember the sum, 8, as the best so far.

steps.title: Slide right: add 1, drop 2
body: Move the window one step. New sum = old sum + entering value - leaving value = 8 + 1 - 2 = 7. No loop over the window is needed.

predict.question: The window sum is 7 and the window slides: 3 enters and 1 leaves. What is the new sum?
predict.why: 7 + 3 - 1 = 9. Add the entering value and subtract the leaving value; the window is never summed again.

steps.title: Slide again: add 3, drop 1
body: 7 + 3 - 1 = 9. This is the new best. Window [5, 1, 3].

steps.title: Last slide: add 2, drop 5
body: 9 + 2 - 5 = 6, below the best. The scan is finished: the answer is 9 after n - k slides, O(n) time and O(1) space.
For a variable-size window (longest substring without repeats, shortest subarray with sum at least S) the idea is the same: grow the right end, and shrink the left end while the window is invalid.

everyday.story: Two friends look for a pair of books on a sorted shelf that cost exactly 10 together. One starts at the cheapest book, the other at the dearest. If the pair costs too much, the friend at the expensive end steps in. If too little, the cheap-end friend steps in. They meet in the middle having touched each book once.

title: Tries and Union-Find
tagline: Two structures for two questions: "does any word start with this?" and "are these two things connected?"
explain: Hash maps, heaps and trees cover most interview problems, but two more structures appear often enough to learn: the trie for questions about prefixes, and union-find for questions about groups. Each is short to code and each has a clear sentence that justifies it.
## Trie (prefix tree)

A trie stores strings one character per edge, from a root. Words that share a prefix share a path, and a flag on a node marks the end of a word. Searching for a key of length m costs O(m), no matter how many words are stored. A balanced search tree costs O(m log n) for the same lookup, and a hash set cannot answer a prefix question at all without scanning.

- Insert, exact search and prefix search are all one walk down the tree: O(m).
- Autocomplete: walk to the prefix node, then collect the words below it with a depth-first search. Production systems store a top-k list per node so they do not search on each key press.
- Common questions: implement a trie, word search with many words (prune the search when no word has the current prefix), longest common prefix, replace words with their shortest root.
- Cost: many small nodes, so memory use is higher than a plain set of strings for few or very different words. A radix tree compresses chains of single-child nodes.

In Python the simplest trie is nested dictionaries with a special key such as "$" for the end of a word. A class with a children dict and an is_end flag is just as good, and clearer to read when you are nervous.
## Union-find (disjoint set union)

Union-find keeps a collection of items split into groups, with two operations: find(x) returns the representative (root) of x's group and union(a, b) merges the groups of a and b. Two items are connected exactly when their roots are equal.

Each group is a tree stored in a parent array. Quick-find updates every item on a union (slow union); quick-union only links two roots, but trees can become long chains. The standard fix uses two ideas together: weighted union (attach the smaller tree under the larger, so depth is at most log n) and path compression (point every item on a find path directly at the root). Together the cost per operation is almost constant, the inverse Ackermann function, which is below 5 for any practical size.

- Count connected components: start with n and subtract one for every union that joins two different roots.
- Detect a cycle in an undirected graph: an edge whose endpoints already share a root closes a cycle (redundant connection).
- Kruskal's minimum spanning tree: sort edges by weight, add an edge only if it joins two different components.
- Limits: it answers connected or not, not the path, and it cannot undo a union.
## Choosing between them and the alternatives

Prefix questions suggest a trie. "Are these connected" questions on a growing set of edges suggest union-find; on a fixed graph BFS or DFS gives the same answer for components, and is the safer choice when you also need paths or distances. Say which you chose and what you give up.
keyPoints: A trie answers prefix questions in O(length of the prefix), independent of the number of words.
Prefer a hash set for exact matches; use a trie only when prefix queries matter.
Union-find = parent array + find + union; two items are connected when their roots are equal.
Weighted union (small under large) and path compression together give almost constant time per operation.
Union-find detects cycles and counts components, but cannot give paths or undo a union.

Using a trie for exact lookups, where a hash set is simpler and uses less memory.
Writing union(a, b) so it links a and b instead of their roots, which corrupts the groups.
Implementing find without path compression and union without weights, so a long chain makes operations O(n).
Using union-find when the question needs the path between two nodes, or edge removal.

interview.q: What is a trie and when is it better than a hash set?
interview.a: A trie is a tree where each edge is one character, so words sharing a prefix share a path. Lookups cost O(length of the key). It is better when you need prefix operations such as autocomplete or longest common prefix, which a hash set cannot answer without scanning every word. For exact matches only, a hash set is simpler and lighter.

interview.q: How would you build autocomplete for a search box?
interview.a: Store queries in a trie and keep a short top-k list by popularity at each node, so a request is one walk to the prefix node plus reading that list. Update counts offline in batches. For very large scale the trie is split across servers by prefix, with caching of hot prefixes.

interview.q: What is union-find and what are its two operations?
interview.a: A structure that tracks which items are in the same group. find(x) returns the root of x's tree; union(a, b) links the roots of a and b if they differ. Two items are connected when find returns the same root for both.

interview.q: Which two optimizations make union-find fast, and what is the result?
interview.a: Union by size or rank (attach the smaller tree under the larger, keeping depth at most log n) and path compression (point nodes on the find path straight at the root). Together they give amortized cost per operation close to constant, the inverse Ackermann function.

interview.q: How do you detect a cycle in an undirected graph with union-find?
interview.a: Process the edges one at a time. For edge (a, b), if find(a) equals find(b) the endpoints are already connected, so this edge closes a cycle. Otherwise union them. It runs in near O(E) time.

scenes.title: A trie holding car, cat and cow

steps.title: The prompt: fast prefix lookups
body: Typing "ca" should list every word that starts with "ca". A hash set answers "is this exact word present" in O(1), but it cannot answer a prefix question without scanning every word.
A trie (prefix tree) stores one character per edge, so words with the same start share the same path.

steps.title: Insert "car"
body: Start at the root and follow or create one child per character: c, a, r. Mark the last node as the end of a word.
Insert costs O(m) for a word of length m, no matter how many words are stored.

card.title: Python
lines: node["$"] = True   # end of a word

steps.title: Insert "cat": the prefix is shared
body: "cat" starts with c, a, which already exist, so only a new node t is added. Shared prefixes are stored once; that is where a trie saves space compared with storing every word separately.

predict.question: A trie already holds "car". How many new nodes does inserting "cat" create?
predict.why: Only one: the t node. The path c, a already exists and is reused.

steps.title: Insert "cow": a new branch
body: "cow" shares only c with the others, so the trie branches at c: o, then w.

steps.title: Prefix search: "ca"
body: Walk c then a. If a step has no child, the prefix does not exist. If you reach the end, the prefix exists: this took 2 steps, no matter how many words are stored. Cost is O(length of the prefix).

body: After walking to the node for "ca", run a depth-first search below it and collect every end-of-word marker: car and cat. The cost is the prefix length plus the size of the part of the trie you visit.
Real autocomplete usually stores a precomputed top-k list per node (by popularity) so it does not need to search below the node on every key press.

steps.title: When not to use a trie
body: A trie spends memory on many small nodes, so for exact-match lookups a hash set is simpler and faster. Reach for a trie when prefix queries are the point: autocomplete, spell check, longest common prefix, word search on a grid with pruning.
Memory can be reduced by compressing chains of single-child nodes (a radix tree).

callout.text: Say "I would use a hash set unless I need prefix queries" before you reach for a trie.

scenes.title: Union-find with weighted union and path compression

steps.title: The prompt: are these two connected?
body: Given a stream of "connect a and b" operations, answer "are a and b in the same group?" quickly. Examples: friend groups, network components, finding a cycle in an undirected graph, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.
Union-find (disjoint set union) keeps each group as a tree and uses the root as the group's name. find(x) walks up to the root. union(a, b) joins two roots.

steps.title: Start: five separate groups
body: Every item is its own root: parent[i] = i, and the size of each group is 1. Number of groups: 5.

steps.title: union(0, 1)
body: Find the root of each side, 0 and 1. They differ, so attach one root under the other. Groups: 4. With a weighted union you always attach the smaller tree under the larger, which keeps trees shallow: depth at most log n.

steps.title: union(2, 3)
body: Same again for 2 and 3. Groups: 3. Two trees of size 2.

steps.title: union(1, 3): join the two trees
body: find(1) = 0 and find(3) = 2 are different roots, so join them: root 2 goes under root 0 (equal sizes, so either choice works). Now 0, 1, 2 and 3 share root 0. Groups: 2.
Notice that 3 is now two steps from the root: 3, then 2, then 0.

predict.question: union(1, 3) is called. What does it compare?
options: The sizes of the two groups only
predict.why: It calls find on both items and compares their roots. If the roots are equal the items are already connected; otherwise it links the roots.

steps.title: find(3) with path compression
body: find(3) walks 3, 2, 0 and finds the root. While going back, path compression points every visited item straight at the root, so 3 now has parent 0. The next find(3) takes one step.
Weighted union plus path compression makes each operation cost almost constant time (the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for any practical n). Either trick alone gives O(log n) amortized.

steps.title: Using it in an interview
body: Detect a cycle in an undirected graph: for each edge (a, b), if find(a) == find(b) the edge closes a cycle; otherwise union them. Count connected components: start with n and subtract one for every successful union.
Union-find only answers "connected or not". It cannot tell you the path between two nodes, and it does not support removing an edge.

callout.text: If the question needs shortest paths or removal of edges, use BFS or a different structure.

everyday.plain: A trie finds words by their first letters. Union-find tells you which things belong to the same group.
everyday.story: In a dictionary you find "car" by turning to C, then CA, then CAR. All words starting with CA sit together. For groups, think of friend circles at a party: when two circles meet and merge, everyone in them is now in one circle, and you ask only who the circle leader is.

Words starting with CA sit together
words: A tree that stores words one letter per step, so words with the same start share a path.
The first letters of a word, such as "ca" in "car".
A structure that tracks which items belong to the same group.
Pointing every item on a search path straight at the group root, so later searches are short.

title: Greedy Algorithms and Interval Problems
tagline: Know when taking the best-looking choice is provably safe, and when it is a trap that needs dynamic programming.
explain: A greedy algorithm builds an answer one step at a time and always takes the choice that looks best right now, never going back. When it works, it is the shortest and fastest solution. When it does not, it returns a wrong answer that looks confident. Interviewers test both: can you apply it, and can you tell when it is not valid?
## When greedy is correct

Two properties are needed. First, the greedy choice property: some optimal solution contains the locally best choice. Second, optimal substructure: after making the choice, what remains is a smaller problem of the same kind. You usually justify the first property with an exchange argument: take any optimal solution, swap in the greedy choice, and show it is no worse.
## Interval scheduling

To attend the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings, sort by end time and take each meeting whose start is not before the end of the last chosen one. Earliest finish leaves the most room for the future, and it is optimal. Earliest start and shortest first are not: a very long early meeting, or a short meeting in the middle, can block two others. The cost is O(n log n) for the sort.

- Non-overlapping intervals (remove the fewest so none overlap): n minus the maximum number you can keep.
- Minimum arrows to burst balloons: sort by end and shoot at the end of the first balloon.
- Meeting rooms II (how many rooms are needed): sort by start and keep a min-heap of end times; reuse a room if the earliest end is not after the next start.
- Merge intervals: sort by start and extend the last interval while the next one overlaps.
## Other greedy problems that come up

- Jump game: track the furthest reachable index; if you fall behind it, fail.
- Gas station and task scheduler: a running balance or a counting argument.
- Assigning cookies, or boats to carry people: sort, then pair with two pointers.
- Huffman coding: repeatedly join the two least frequent symbols, using a heap.
## When greedy fails

Coin change with coins 1, 3 and 4 and amount 6: greedy takes 4, 1, 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 is two coins. For arbitrary coins, use dynamic programming. The same pattern holds for 0/1 knapsack (greedy by value per weight fails; it works only for the fractional version). If you see "count the ways" or "the best of every combination", suspect dynamic programming.
## What to say in the interview

Propose the greedy rule, say why it should be safe (one sentence of exchange argument), test it on a small counterexample attempt, state the cost (usually O(n log n) because of sorting), and be ready to say what you would use if the rule failed.
keyPoints: Greedy needs the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure; justify it with an exchange argument.
Interval scheduling: sort by end time, take each interval that starts at or after the last chosen end.
Earliest start and shortest interval first are wrong for maximizing the number of intervals.
Meeting rooms: sort by start and use a min-heap of end times.
Greedy fails for general coin change and 0/1 knapsack; use dynamic programming there.

exercise: Solve from the problem bank: jump-game and merge-intervals. Then implement erase-overlap-intervals, minimum-arrows-to-burst-balloons and meeting-rooms-II yourself. For each, write the greedy rule in one sentence and a two-line exchange argument for why it is safe. Finish by finding your own counterexample that breaks "shortest interval first" for interval scheduling.
pitfalls: Choosing a greedy rule because it feels right, without a counterexample check or an exchange argument.
Sorting by start time when the correct rule sorts by end time (and the other way round for meeting rooms).
Treating intervals that only touch ([1, 2] and [2, 3]) as overlapping, without asking the interviewer.
Using greedy for general coin change or 0/1 knapsack, where dynamic programming is required.
Forgetting the cost of the sort and claiming O(n).

interview.q: How do you know a problem can be solved greedily?
interview.a: It needs the greedy-choice property (some optimal answer includes the locally best choice) and optimal substructure. I try to prove the first with an exchange argument: take any optimal answer, swap in the greedy choice, and show it is no worse. I also try a few small counterexamples before I commit.

interview.q: Maximum number of non-overlapping meetings: what is the algorithm and why is it correct?
interview.a: Sort by end time and take every meeting whose start is not before the last chosen end. Ending earliest leaves the most time for the rest, and an exchange argument shows some optimal answer starts with that meeting. O(n log n) for the sort, then O(n).

interview.q: How many meeting rooms are needed for a list of meetings?
interview.a: Sort by start time and keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use. For each meeting, if the earliest-ending room is free by its start, reuse it (replace the top); otherwise add a room. The heap size at the end is the answer. O(n log n).

interview.q: Give an example where greedy fails.
interview.a: Coin change with coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6. Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 uses two. The greedy choice of the biggest coin is not safe for these denominations, so you use dynamic programming. Greedy also fails for 0/1 knapsack.

interview.q: What is the difference between greedy and dynamic programming?
interview.a: Greedy commits to one choice at each step and never revisits it, so it is fast but only valid when the choice is provably safe. Dynamic programming considers all choices by combining the answers to overlapping subproblems, so it is correct for more problems but costs more time and memory.

basis: Sources, all read: the Wikipedia interval-scheduling article (earliest-finish-time greedy is optimal; earliest-start and shortest-first are not; O(n log n)) and the Python heapq documentation. scenes.title: Greedy interval scheduling: pick the earliest finish

steps.title: The prompt: attend as many meetings as possible
body: You have six meetings with start and end times: A 1-3, B 2-5, C 4-6, D 5-8, E 7-9, F 8-10. You can attend one at a time. Which ones maximize the number you attend?
A greedy algorithm makes the best-looking local choice at each step and never reconsiders it. It is fast but only correct when you can prove the local choice is safe.

steps.title: Candidate rules: which greedy is right?
body: Three tempting rules: take the earliest start, take the shortest meeting, or take the earliest end. The first two fail: one very long early meeting, or a short meeting in the middle that blocks two others, can lead to fewer meetings.
The rule that works is earliest finish time: it leaves the most room for what comes next.

predict.question: Which greedy rule gives the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings?
predict.why: Always taking the meeting that ends first leaves the largest remaining time for the others, and an exchange argument proves it is optimal. The other two have counterexamples.

callout.text: In an interview, name the rule and give one counterexample for a rule you reject.

steps.title: Sort by end time and take A
body: Sort by end time: A(3), B(5), C(6), D(8), E(9), F(10). Take A, the earliest to finish. Remember its end time, 3.

steps.title: B starts at 2 < 3: skip
body: B overlaps A (it starts before A ends), so skip it. Skipping costs nothing: A ended earlier than B, so A is at least as good.

steps.title: C starts at 4 >= 3: take
body: C starts after A ends, so take it. The last end becomes 6.

steps.title: D starts at 5 < 6: skip
body: D overlaps C, so skip it.

steps.title: E starts at 7 >= 6: take
body: E is free, take it. The last end becomes 9, and F starts at 8, before 9, so F is skipped.

steps.title: Why it is optimal, and the cost
body: Exchange argument: take any optimal answer. Replace its first meeting by the earliest-finishing meeting. It still does not overlap the rest, because it ends no later. So some optimal answer starts with our choice; repeat for the remaining meetings.
Cost: O(n log n) for the sort, then one O(n) pass. "Minimum number of meetings to remove so none overlap" is the same problem: n minus the answer.

everyday.plain: Greedy means always taking the best-looking choice now, and only trusting it when you can show it is safe.
everyday.story: You want to see as many films as possible in one day at a festival. If you always pick the film that finishes first, you are free sooner and can fit more films after it. Picking the shortest film, or the one that starts first, can leave you blocked.
maps: Intervals with start and end times
Pick the film that finishes first
Leaving the most room for later choices
words: Always taking the choice that looks best right now, without reconsidering it later.
A proof that swaps the greedy choice into any best answer without making it worse.
A range with a start and an end, such as a meeting from 2 to 5.
After one choice, what is left is a smaller problem of the same kind.

title: Design a Leaderboard (Sorted Sets)
tagline: Rank millions of players in real time: why a database count is slow and how a sorted set answers rank in O(log N).
explain: The leaderboard is a favourite system design question because it looks like a simple table and hides a real data structure problem. Players submit scores, and everyone wants the top N, their own rank and the players near them, fast and fresh. The answer is to use the right structure for ranked reads, then protect it with a durable store.
## Requirements and numbers

Ask: how many players, how many score updates and reads per second, how fresh must ranks be, is it global or per game, are there daily or weekly boards, and do ties matter. State your assumptions out loud and compute from them; the numbers decide whether one node is enough.
## Why SQL alone struggles

ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10 is fine with an index. A player's rank is the problem: COUNT(*) WHERE score > mine has to walk every row ahead of the player, so cost grows with the number of players, and every update must also maintain the index. At a few thousand reads a second on millions of rows this is the bottleneck.
## The sorted set

A Redis sorted set is a collection of unique members ordered by an associated score. Its documented costs are ZADD and ZINCRBY at O(log N), ZRANK and ZREVRANK at O(log N), ZRANGE at O(log N + M) for M returned members, and ZSCORE and ZCARD at O(1). Internally it combines a skip list (order) with a hash table (member lookup). That gives you the three reads you need: the top N, my rank, and my neighbours.

- Update a score: ZADD or ZINCRBY.
- Top 10: ZRANGE key 0 9 REV WITHSCORES.
- My rank: ZREVRANK key member (zero based, add one).
- Neighbours: ZRANGE key (rank - 5) (rank + 5) REV.
## Durability and the data flow

Redis is an in-memory store, so treat the sorted set as a fast view and keep a database as the source of truth. A common flow: the API validates the score and writes an event to a queue; a worker stores the row in SQL and updates the sorted set. If Redis is lost, rebuild it from SQL. Make updates idempotent with an event id so a retry cannot count twice.
## Ties, time windows and scale

- Ties: equal scores sort by member name. To rank earlier achievers higher, fold a timestamp into the score, keeping the value exact within the precision of a double.
- Windows: one key per day or week, with an expiry, updated by the same event as the all-time key.
- Scale: split players over several sorted sets by hash of the id. Top N is scatter and gather. Exact rank is the sum of higher counts per shard, so large products show exact ranks for the top and a percentile for the rest.
## Follow-up questions to prepare
Friends-only leaderboards, anti-cheat (validate scores server side), what happens when a hot key gets many writes, and how you would test a rebuild of Redis from the database.
keyPoints: Rank is a count of rows ahead of you, which SQL computes by scanning; a sorted set keeps the order ready.
Sorted set costs: ZADD, ZINCRBY, ZREVRANK are O(log N); ZRANGE is O(log N + M).
Keep SQL as the source of truth and treat Redis as a rebuildable view; use a queue and idempotent events.
Daily and weekly boards are separate keys with expiry; fold time into the score to break ties by who was first.
To scale past one node, shard by player id and merge the top N from every shard; show percentile instead of exact rank far down.

sql.title: A sorted-set style leaderboard in plain Python (ranks and ties)
sql.code:
import bisect

class Leaderboard:
    """Keeps (-score, tie_breaker, player) in a sorted list: the same read pattern as a sorted set.
    Insert and rank are O(log N) to find, O(N) to shift here; a skip list removes the shifting."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.rows = []
        self.by_player = {}
        self.clock = 0

    def set_score(self, player, score):
        if player in self.by_player:
            self.rows.remove(self.by_player[player])
        self.clock += 1
        row = (-score, self.clock, player)            # earlier arrival wins a tie
        bisect.insort(self.rows, row)
        self.by_player[player] = row

    def top(self, n):
        return [(p, -s) for s, _, p in self.rows[:n]]

    def rank(self, player):
        return bisect.bisect_left(self.rows, self.by_player[player]) + 1

    def around(self, player, k):
        r = self.rank(player) - 1
        lo = max(0, r - k)
        return [(p, -s) for s, _, p in self.rows[lo:r + k + 1]]

lb = Leaderboard()
for name, score in [("ana", 120), ("bo", 300), ("cy", 300), ("di", 90)]:
    lb.set_score(name, score)
assert lb.top(2) == [("bo", 300), ("cy", 300)]       # tie: bo reached 300 first
assert lb.rank("ana") == 3 and lb.rank("di") == 4
lb.set_score("di", 500)
assert lb.top(1) == [("di", 500)] and lb.rank("ana") == 4
assert lb.around("ana", 1) == [("cy", 300), ("ana", 120)]

sql.title: Merging the top N of several shards (scatter and gather)
sql.code:
import heapq

def merge_top(shards, n):
    """Each shard returns its own top list sorted by score descending; the global top n is a k-way merge."""
    merged = heapq.merge(*shards, key=lambda row: -row[1])
    return list(merged)[:n]

shard_a = [("ana", 900), ("bo", 500), ("cy", 100)]
shard_b = [("di", 800), ("ed", 700)]
assert merge_top([shard_a, shard_b], 3) == [("ana", 900), ("di", 800), ("ed", 700)]
assert merge_top([[], shard_b], 1) == [("di", 800)]

def weekly_key(prefix, iso_year, iso_week):
    return f"{prefix}:{iso_year}-w{iso_week:02d}"

assert weekly_key("board", 2026, 7) == "board:2026-w07"

exercise: Design the leaderboard on paper in 25 minutes: write your assumptions and the read and write rates, then draw the API, the sorted set, the queue and the SQL table. Write the Redis commands for top 10, my rank and my neighbours. Then answer out loud: what happens if Redis restarts, how do two players with the same score rank, how do you add a weekly board, and what changes at 500 million players?
pitfalls: Computing rank with COUNT(*) on a SQL table that has millions of rows.
Treating Redis as the only copy of the scores.
Forgetting ties and time windows until the interviewer asks.
Making updates non-idempotent, so a queue retry adds points twice.
Jumping to sharding before checking that one node is not enough.

interview.q: Why is a Redis sorted set good for a leaderboard?
interview.a: It keeps members ordered by score, so ZADD or ZINCRBY updates a score in O(log N), ZREVRANK gives a player's rank in O(log N) and ZRANGE reads the top N in O(log N + M). The same queries on SQL need a COUNT over every higher score or a scan, which grows with the number of players.

interview.q: What is your source of truth, and what if Redis loses its data?
interview.a: SQL (or another durable store) holds every score. Redis is a fast view built from it. If Redis is lost I rebuild the sorted set from the database, and in the meantime reads can degrade to a slower query or a cached copy. Events go through a queue with ids so updates are idempotent.

interview.q: How do you handle ties?
interview.a: Equal scores in a sorted set are ordered by member name, which is arbitrary for users. To make the earlier player rank higher, encode the time in the score, such as score * 10^6 + (max_time - time), as long as the value stays exact in a double, or break ties in the application after fetching a slightly larger range.

interview.q: How would you add daily and weekly leaderboards?
interview.a: One sorted set per window, with the date in the key (board:2026-w47) and an expiry set when the window ends. The score update writes to the all-time key and to the current window keys in the same worker step.

interview.q: How do you scale a leaderboard beyond one Redis node?
interview.a: Split the players over several sorted sets by hash of the player id. The top N is scatter and gather: take the top N from each shard and merge. An exact global rank is the sum of the number of higher scores in every shard, which is costly, so show exact rank for the top and an approximate percentile (from score buckets) for the rest.

The numbers in the animation (10 million players, 5,000 updates a second, 2,000 reads a second) are illustrative assumptions chosen for clarity, not measurements. steps.title: The prompt: a live leaderboard for a game
body: Design a leaderboard: players submit scores, everyone can see the top 10, and each player can see their own rank and the players around them. Ranks should be fresh within about a second.

The numbers here are assumptions for the animation, chosen for clarity: 10 million players, about 5,000 score updates a second and 2,000 leaderboard reads a second. State your own assumptions to the interviewer in the same way.

card.title: Requirements
lines: submit a score for a player
my rank, and the players around me
out of scope: anti-cheat, friends-only boards

steps.title: First attempt: a SQL table
body: Store (player_id, score) and run: SELECT ... ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10. With an index on score, the top 10 is cheap.

The trouble is a player's rank: SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE score > my_score has to count every row above you. For a player near the bottom of 10 million rows that is a huge range scan on every request, and every score update also has to update the index.

steps.title: A sorted set keeps the order for you
body: A Redis sorted set is a collection of unique members, each with a score, kept ordered by score. ZADD sets or updates a score, and ZINCRBY adds to it; both are O(log N). Redis implements it as a skip list plus a hash table, so finding a member and its position are both fast.
The database now does the ranking work when a score is written, so reads do not have to scan.

predict.question: A sorted set holds 10 million players. What is the cost of ZINCRBY on one player?
predict.why: Redis documents ZADD and ZINCRBY as O(log N): the skip list finds the position and the hash table finds the member. It does not re-sort the whole set.

steps.title: Top N and my rank
body: Top 10: ZRANGE board 0 9 REV WITHSCORES, O(log N + 10). My rank: ZREVRANK board "ana", O(log N), which is zero based, so add 1. The players around me: take my rank r and read ZRANGE board (r - 5) (r + 5) REV.
Both reads are cheap and do not depend on how many millions of players there are.

steps.title: Redis is memory: what if it restarts?
body: A sorted set lives in memory. If the node is lost, the scores must be recoverable. Redis persistence helps but is not the source of truth you want for a game economy.
Keep the database as the system of record and treat the sorted set as a fast, rebuildable view.

callout.text: Always answer "what is the source of truth, and how do you rebuild the cache or index from it?"

steps.title: Write the event once, update both stores
body: The API puts a score event on a queue. A worker writes the durable row to SQL and updates the sorted set. If Redis is lost, rebuild it from SQL; if the worker is down, events wait in the queue.
Updates stay idempotent when the event carries an id and the worker applies the highest score or the increment exactly once.

steps.title: Ties, and daily or weekly boards
body: Equal scores are ordered by member name in a sorted set, which is rarely what players expect. To rank the player who reached the score first higher, fold the time into the score, for example score * 1,000,000 + (max_time - time), as long as the number stays exact in a double.
A weekly leaderboard is just another sorted set with a date in the key, such as board:2026-w47, given an expiry. All-time and weekly boards are separate keys updated by the same event.

steps.title: When one sorted set is not enough
body: One sorted set on one node is comfortable for millions of members. Beyond that, split the players into several sorted sets by a hash of the player id. The top N is then scatter and gather: ask every shard for its top N and merge the lists.

An exact global rank is harder: it is the sum of the count of higher scores on every shard. Many products show the exact rank only for the top thousand, and an approximate percentile (bucket the scores) for everyone else.

hud.v: merge the top N of every shard

steps.title: Recap: what to say
body: Requirements, then a sorted set for ordered reads in O(log N), the database as the source of truth, a queue to update both, time-windowed keys, and sharding with scatter and gather when one set is too big. Name the failure cases: Redis lost, duplicate events, hot keys.
Interviewers often follow with "how would you show the top 10 among my friends?": a small sorted set per player or a query of the friends' scores, because the friend list is small.

everyday.plain: A leaderboard shows who is ahead. A sorted set keeps the list in order so you never recount.
everyday.story: In a school race, a teacher can tally everyone's time at the end and sort the list, which takes ages. Or the teacher can keep a list on a board where each runner is slotted into the right place the moment they finish. Then "who is third?" is just a glance.

Slotting runners in as they finish
ZADD placing a member in order

A player's position in the ordered list; first place is rank 1.
The store whose data is trusted when copies disagree.

title: Design Full-Text Search (Inverted Index)
tagline: How keyword search stays fast over millions of documents: analysis, inverted indexes, ranking and shards.
explain: Search comes up in many designs (product search, site search, log search), and interviewers expect you to know why a database LIKE query is the wrong tool and what replaces it. The core answer is the inverted index. Explain it, then show how it is built, queried, ranked and scaled.
## Requirements and scale

Ask what is searched (products, posts, logs), the number of documents and queries per second, the latency target, how quickly new documents must appear, and whether you need typo tolerance, filters and facets. State your assumptions as numbers; they drive the number of shards.
## Why LIKE does not work

A condition such as text LIKE '%word%' with a leading wildcard cannot use a normal index. The database scans every document for every query, and it has no notion of relevance. Search engines flip the model: instead of storing, per document, its words, they store, per word, the documents that contain it.
## Analysis

Text is analyzed before it is indexed: split into tokens, lower-cased, often stripped of very common words, and reduced to word stems so that "running" and "runs" meet at "run". The same analysis runs on the query. Elasticsearch's documentation states that text fields are analyzed and indexed for full-text search, and returns results by relevance rather than exact match only.
## The inverted index

The index maps each term to a sorted postings list of document ids, often with term counts and positions. Looking up a term is one dictionary lookup. A query with two terms intersects two sorted lists by walking them together, in time proportional to their lengths; OR is a union and NOT removes ids. Phrase queries use the stored positions.
## Ranking

Matches need an order. TF-IDF-style scoring gives a higher score to a document that contains the term often and to a term that is rare across the collection, and BM25 refines it with a limit on repeated terms and normalization by document length. Production ranking usually adds freshness, popularity or a learned model over the top few hundred candidates, so retrieval is cheap and ranking is expensive but narrow.
## Shards, replicas and freshness

- Split the index by document id into shards. A query is sent to all shards, each returns its top results, and a coordinator merges them (scatter and gather). Latency is set by the slowest shard.
- Replicas serve reads and survive failures.
- New documents go into small immutable segments that are searched together and merged in the background; searchable after a short refresh interval, about a second in Elasticsearch by default.
- Cache popular queries briefly.
## What to say at the end

Say what you left out: spelling correction, autocomplete (a trie or an edge n-gram index), personalised ranking and how you measure relevance (click-through, human judgments). Naming the gaps shows you know the real problem is larger than the diagram.
keyPoints: A LIKE with a leading wildcard scans every row; search engines store, per term, the documents that contain it.
Analysis (tokens, lower-case, stop words, stems) must be identical at index time and query time.
AND is an intersection of sorted postings lists; OR is a union.
Rank with TF-IDF or BM25 ideas: term frequency, term rarity, length normalization; then re-rank the top candidates.
Shard by document id and scatter-gather; latency is the slowest shard; new documents live in small segments merged later.

pitfalls: Proposing a LIKE query or a SQL full scan for text search.
Applying different analysis at index time and at query time, so terms never match.
Forgetting that a query must hit every shard, so tail latency is the slowest shard.
Calling the search index the source of truth, instead of a derived copy that can be rebuilt.
Ignoring relevance: returning matches in id order.

interview.q: What is an inverted index?
interview.a: A map from each term to the sorted list of the documents that contain it (a postings list), often with counts and positions. A query looks up its terms and combines the lists, so the work depends on the matching documents, not on the whole collection. It is called inverted because it flips the usual document-to-words direction.

interview.q: Why can a database LIKE '%word%' query not power search?
interview.a: A leading wildcard cannot use a normal B-tree index, so the database scans every row for every query. It also cannot rank by relevance. At large scale this is too slow and expensive; a search engine builds an inverted index once and answers from it.

interview.q: What does analysis do and why must it match at query time?
interview.a: It converts text to the tokens that are indexed: split, lower-case, remove stop words, reduce words to stems. A query must go through the same steps, otherwise its tokens will not equal the stored ones and nothing matches.

interview.q: How do you combine "fast" AND "car"?
interview.a: Take the two sorted postings lists and intersect them by walking both with two pointers, advancing the smaller id; the cost is proportional to the list lengths. Starting with the shortest list and using skip pointers speeds this up. OR is a merge into a union, NOT removes ids.

interview.q: How does a distributed search system answer a query?
interview.a: The index is sharded by document id. A coordinator sends the query to every shard, each shard returns its top results using its local inverted index, and the coordinator merges and re-ranks them. Replicas add availability and read capacity. Total latency is set by the slowest shard, so timeouts and replicas are important.

scenes.title: A full-text search engine, step by step

steps.title: The prompt: search over many documents
body: Design search for a site with hundreds of millions of documents (products, posts, pages). Users type a few words and expect relevant results in well under a second, with new documents searchable soon after they are published.
The numbers in this animation are assumptions chosen for clarity: 300 million documents, 3,000 queries a second, and about a second of delay before a new document is searchable.

card.title: Requirements
lines: results fast, even for common words
out of scope: spelling, personalisation, ads

steps.title: Why not WHERE text LIKE '%word%'?
body: A leading wildcard cannot use a normal index, so the database scans every document for every query. 300 million documents at 3,000 queries a second is not workable, and a scan also has no idea which results are more relevant.
Search engines reverse the problem: instead of "for each document, which words does it have", they store "for each word, which documents have it".

steps.title: Analysis: turn text into tokens
body: Before indexing, text is analyzed: split into tokens (words), lower-cased, often with very common words removed and words reduced to a stem, so "Running" and "runs" both become "run". Elasticsearch describes text fields as analyzed and indexed for full-text search.
The same analysis must be applied to the query, or "Running" would never match the stored "run".

predict.question: Why must the query pass through the same analyzer as the documents?
options: So its tokens match the stored tokens
predict.why: The index contains analyzed tokens such as "run". If the query kept "Running", it would not match. Index and query must use the same analysis.

steps.title: The inverted index
body: The index maps each term to the sorted list of ids of the documents that contain it (a postings list). Looking up a term is a dictionary lookup, then you read its list. The cost no longer depends on how many documents do not contain the word.
Postings often also store how many times the word appears and its positions, which is needed for ranking and phrase queries.

steps.title: A two-word query: intersect the lists
body: The query "fast car" means documents containing both words. Take the two sorted lists and walk them together, advancing the pointer with the smaller id: [1, 3, 7, 12] and [3, 4, 12, 20] give [3, 12]. Cost is proportional to the list lengths, and you can start from the shortest list.
OR queries are a union of the lists, and NOT removes ids.

if a[i] == b[j]: out.append(a[i]); i += 1; j += 1

steps.title: Ranking: which match comes first?
body: Thousands of documents may match, so results need a relevance score. The classic idea (TF-IDF, and its successor BM25, the default in Lucene-based engines) rewards a document when the query term appears often in it and when the term is rare across all documents, and normalizes for document length.
Real systems add signals such as freshness, popularity and click data, often with a learned ranking model applied to the top few hundred candidates.

steps.title: Shards: split the index and scatter the query
body: 300 million documents do not fit one machine, so the index is split into shards by document id. Each shard holds a complete inverted index for its documents. A query goes to every shard (scatter), each returns its own top results, and the coordinator merges them (gather).
Replicas of each shard add availability and read capacity. Latency is set by the slowest shard, so one slow shard hurts every query: use timeouts and hedged requests.

steps.title: Freshness: new documents become searchable
body: Rewriting a big index for each new document is far too slow. Engines like Lucene write new documents into small immutable segments and search across all segments, merging them in the background. Elasticsearch makes new documents searchable after a refresh, about a second by default.
Deletes are marked, not removed, until a merge rewrites the segment. The cost is extra disk and merge work, in return for fast, lock-free reads.

steps.title: Caching and recap
body: Many queries repeat, so cache popular query results for a short time, and invalidate or let them expire as the index changes. Know the trade-off: a cached result can be a few seconds stale.

Summary: analyze, build an inverted index, intersect postings, rank, shard and scatter-gather, add replicas and a cache. Name the hard parts: relevance quality, slow shards, and keeping the index in step with the source data.
