title: Resume Bullets and Project Walkthroughs
tagline: Turn each resume line into a story you can defend for ten minutes of follow-up questions.
explain: Most interviews begin with your resume and a project walkthrough, and the follow-up questions often decide the round. The goal is not to impress with a long list of tools; it is to show that you understand what you built, why you built it that way, and what happened. Every line on your resume must survive five minutes of "why?".
## Write bullets that start a story

A strong bullet has four parts: an action verb, what you built or changed, how you did it (the main technology or method) and a result you can measure. Compare "Worked on the payments API" with "Cut checkout p95 latency from 800 ms to 120 ms by adding a Redis cache and removing an N+1 query". The second one makes the interviewer ask exactly the question you want.

- Lead with verbs such as built, cut, migrated, designed and led, not "responsible for" or "helped with".
- Put one number in most bullets: latency, cost, error rate, users, time saved.
- Name the technology only where it is part of the result.
- Drop anything you could not discuss for five minutes.
## The 90-second project walkthrough

Use the same order every time. First, the problem and why it mattered. Second, your role and the size of the team. Third, the key decision and the alternative you rejected, with the reason. Fourth, the result with a number. Fifth, what you would do differently. This takes about a minute and a half. Stop there. A short, clear answer leads to the follow-up questions you have prepared for.
## Prepare for the probes

Interviewers dig where the story is thin. Expect: why this technology and what else you considered, the hardest bug, what broke first as it scaled, how you measured the result, what you would change, and which part you did yourself. Write one honest answer for each, with a real detail. Failures and trade-offs are good material: they show judgment.
## Numbers you can defend

Every number is a question: where did it come from, over what period, and what else changed? Know the source (a dashboard, a load test, a before and after). If you cannot defend a number, soften it or remove it. An exaggeration found in the first follow-up makes the rest of the story less believable.
## We and I

Say "we" for the team outcome and "I" for what you personally decided, wrote or fixed. If you only say "we", the interviewer cannot see your contribution. If you only say "I", the story sounds unrealistic. Be honest about what you did not do.
## Map stories to common questions

Prepare four to six stories and note which questions each can answer: a conflict, a failure, a deadline, a decision with missing data, a time you led or influenced someone. Companies publish what they look for; Amazon's leadership principles include Ownership, Dive Deep, Deliver Results, Learn and Be Curious, Have Backbone and Disagree and Commit, so tag stories to those if you interview there. One story can serve several questions if you change the emphasis.
keyPoints: A good bullet = verb + what + how + a measured result.
Tell the project in about 90 seconds: problem, role, key decision and rejected alternative, result, what you would change.
Prepare the follow-ups: why this tool, what broke, how you measured, what you would change, what you did yourself.
Only keep numbers you can explain; never invent or round up results.
Say "we" for the team result and "I" for your part; prepare four to six stories mapped to common questions.

sql.title: A small resume bullet checker
sql.code:
import re

WEAK_STARTS = ("responsible for", "worked on", "helped with", "involved in", "assisted")

def lint_bullet(text):
    """Return a list of problems with a resume bullet."""
    issues = []
    lowered = text.lower().strip()
    if lowered.startswith(WEAK_STARTS):
        issues.append("starts with a weak phrase: use a verb such as built, cut or led")
    if not re.search(r"\d", text):
        issues.append("no number: add a measured result")
    if len(text.split()) > 30:
        issues.append("too long: aim for one or two lines")
    if len(text.split()) < 6:
        issues.append("too short: say what and how")
    return issues

assert lint_bullet("Worked on the payments API") != []
good = "Cut checkout p95 latency from 800 ms to 120 ms with a Redis cache and an N+1 fix"
assert lint_bullet(good) == []
assert "no number: add a measured result" in lint_bullet("Built a recommendation service for the mobile app team")

exercise: Take your three strongest resume bullets and rewrite each as verb + what + how + result. For each one, write the 90-second walkthrough in five lines (problem, role, decision and rejected alternative, result, what you would change). Then write one honest answer for each probe: why this tool, what broke, how you measured it, what you would change, what you did yourself. Practise out loud with a timer, then ask a friend to interrupt with "why?" every 20 seconds.
pitfalls: Listing technologies without a result or a reason for choosing them.
A number you cannot explain, or one that mixes your work with other changes.
Saying only "we", so your own contribution is invisible.
A five-minute opening answer that leaves no room for questions.
Describing a project with no failure or trade-off; it sounds unreal and gives the interviewer nothing to probe.

interview.q: Walk me through a project on your resume.
interview.a: Start with the problem and why it mattered, then your role and the team size, the key decision and the alternative I rejected (and why), the result with a number, and what I would change. About 90 seconds, then I stop and let them ask. I choose a project where I can go deep on any detail.

interview.q: How do you describe your own contribution on a team project?
interview.a: I say "we" for the team result and "I" for what I decided, built or fixed, with specifics: "I designed the cache layer and wrote the migration". I am honest about parts others owned, and I can still explain how those parts worked.

interview.q: How did you measure the improvement you list on your resume?
interview.a: I name the source (a dashboard, a load test, a before and after in production), the period and the conditions, and what else changed in that time. If the number was an estimate I say so. Being exact about measurement matters more than a big number.

interview.q: What would you do differently in that project?
interview.a: A specific, honest change: for example, load test earlier, write the runbook before launch, or choose a simpler design. It shows reflection. I avoid a disguised strength such as "I worked too hard".

interview.q: Tell me about a technical decision you made and the alternatives.
interview.a: I describe the options considered, the criteria (latency, cost, complexity, team skills), what I chose and why, how I validated the choice and whether it held up. A decision with trade-offs and a clear reason is a better answer than a perfect story.

title: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and 0-1 BFS
tagline: Pick the right shortest-path algorithm in 30 seconds, and code Dijkstra with a heap without bugs.
explain: Shortest-path questions appear as maps and routes, network delays, cheapest flights, and grids with different costs per cell. The skill is choosing the algorithm from the properties of the edges, then coding it cleanly. This lesson gives the decision rule and the standard implementation.
## Choose the algorithm from the weights

- All edges cost the same (or you count edges): BFS, O(V + E).
- Edge weights are 0 or 1: 0-1 BFS with a deque; push 0-weight neighbours on the front and 1-weight neighbours on the back.
- Non-negative weights: Dijkstra with a min-heap, O((V + E) log V).
- Negative weights, or a limit on the number of edges: Bellman-Ford, O(V * E).
- All pairs on a small graph: Floyd-Warshall, O(V^3).
- A directed acyclic graph: process in topological order and relax each edge once, O(V + E).
## Dijkstra step by step

Keep dist[v], the best known cost from the source. Start with dist[source] = 0 and a min-heap holding (0, source). Repeatedly pop the entry with the smallest distance. If it is older than the best known distance for that node, skip it (a stale entry). Otherwise that distance is final, so relax each outgoing edge: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push (dist[v], v).

The heap stores a node several times, once for each improvement. This lazy deletion avoids the decrease-priority operation that Python's heapq lacks. With a binary heap the cost is O((V + E) log V). Wikipedia notes the original array-based version is Theta(V^2) and a Fibonacci heap gives Theta(E + V log V), but the binary heap is what you code in an interview.
## Why it needs non-negative weights

When the node with the smallest distance is popped, any other route to it must start with an edge from an unfinished node, which already costs at least as much. This breaks when an edge is negative: a later negative edge could make the route through an unfinished node cheaper. The usual fix is Bellman-Ford, which repeats relaxation over all edges V - 1 times and can detect a negative cycle on one more round.
## Variants that come up

- Network delay time: the answer is the largest of the shortest distances; if some node is unreachable, return -1.
- Path with the minimum effort or the minimum of the maximum edge: use a heap, but the relaxation uses max instead of a sum.
- Cheapest flight with at most K stops: Bellman-Ford limited to K + 1 rounds, using a copy of the distances for each round.
- A grid with costs per cell: treat each cell as a node with four edges and use Dijkstra.
- Return the path itself: keep prev[v] and walk back from the target.
## What to say in the interview

Ask about weights and whether a path or only a cost is needed. State the algorithm choice and why, give the complexity in terms of V and E, mention lazy deletion, and name the failure case: negative edges. Test on a graph where the fewest-edges path is not the cheapest.
keyPoints: Equal weights: BFS. Weights 0 or 1: 0-1 BFS. Non-negative: Dijkstra. Negative or limited edges: Bellman-Ford.
Dijkstra pops the smallest tentative distance, which is final, then relaxes its outgoing edges.
Use a heap with lazy deletion: skip a popped entry if its distance is greater than the best known.
Cost with a binary heap is O((V + E) log V).
Negative edges break the "popped means final" argument; ask about weights first.

sql.title: Dijkstra with a heap, path recovery and network delay time

exercise: Solve from scratch: network-delay-time, path-with-minimum-effort (grid, max of differences) and cheapest-flights-within-k-stops. For each, write which algorithm you choose and why in one sentence, then code it. Then take the example graph from the lesson, run Dijkstra by hand on paper with a heap table (pop, relax, push), and explain what changes if the edge B-A becomes -2.
pitfalls: Using BFS on a weighted graph and returning the fewest hops.
Marking a node visited when it is pushed instead of when it is popped, so a cheaper route to it is ignored.
Forgetting the stale-entry check, so each node is processed several times.
Using Dijkstra when weights may be negative, without asking.
Returning the maximum distance for network delay without checking that every node was reached.

interview.q: How does Dijkstra's algorithm work and what is its complexity?
interview.a: Keep a min-heap of (distance, node). Pop the smallest; if it is stale skip it, otherwise its distance is final. Relax each outgoing edge: if dist[u] + w beats dist[v], update and push. With a binary heap the cost is O((V + E) log V). It finds the cheapest path from one source to all nodes.

interview.q: Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edge weights?
interview.a: It relies on the smallest popped distance being final, since any other path would have to pass through nodes at least as far away. A negative edge can later make a path through an unfinished node cheaper, so a finalized distance may be wrong. Use Bellman-Ford instead, which also detects negative cycles.

interview.q: How do you choose between BFS, Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford?
interview.a: Equal weights or counting edges: BFS. Non-negative weights: Dijkstra. Negative weights or a limit on the number of edges: Bellman-Ford. Weights of only 0 and 1: 0-1 BFS with a deque. For a DAG, relax in topological order in O(V + E).

interview.q: What is lazy deletion in a Dijkstra implementation?
interview.a: Python's heapq has no decrease-key. Instead, when a distance improves I push a new (distance, node) entry and leave the old one. When an entry is popped with a distance larger than the best known, it is stale and I skip it. The heap can hold up to E entries, which keeps the cost at O((V + E) log V).

interview.q: How do you find the cheapest flight with at most K stops?
interview.a: Run Bellman-Ford for K + 1 rounds. In each round relax all edges using the distances from the previous round (a copy), so a path never uses more edges than the round number. Return the distance to the destination, or -1 if it is infinite.

The Bellman-Ford, 0-1 BFS and Floyd-Warshall points, the lazy-deletion pattern and the choice rule are standard textbook material that I selected and ordered, so the selection is my judgment. Amazon's topic page (read) lists algorithms as tested. Python code runs and carries asserts. Priorities and hours are my judgment; the roadmap raises the priority for roles that need it.

scenes.title: Dijkstra from S on a weighted graph

steps.title: The prompt: cheapest route, not fewest hops
body: Edges now have weights (time, cost, distance). BFS finds the path with the fewest edges, which is not the cheapest: S to A is one edge of weight 4, but S, B, A costs 1 + 2 = 3.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest path from one source to every node, as long as no edge weight is negative.

card.title: Idea
lines: repeat: take the unfinished node with the smallest dist
relax each outgoing edge: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w)

steps.title: Start: S is 0, everything else is unknown
body: Keep a min-heap of (distance, node). Push (0, S). All other distances start at infinity because no path is known yet.

card.title: Python
lines: if d > dist.get(u, inf): continue   # stale entry

steps.title: Pop S (0): relax A and B
body: S is the closest unfinished node, so its distance 0 is final. Relax its edges: A = 0 + 4 = 4 and B = 0 + 1 = 1. Push both on the heap.

steps.title: Pop B (1): a better route to A appears
body: B is now the smallest. Its distance 1 is final, because every other route starts with an edge of weight at least 4. Relax B's edges: A through B is 1 + 2 = 3, which beats 4, so update it. C = 1 + 5 = 6.
The old entry (4, A) is still in the heap. It is skipped later with the check d > dist[u]: this is "lazy deletion", a way to avoid a decrease-key operation.

predict.question: B (distance 1) is popped and the edge B-A has weight 2. What is the new distance to A?
predict.why: 1 + 2 = 3 is smaller than the current 4, so A improves to 3. This improvement of a distance is called relaxing an edge.

steps.title: Pop A (3): C improves to 4
body: A is final at 3. Relax A-C: 3 + 1 = 4, better than 6, so C becomes 4.

steps.title: Pop C (4): D is reached
body: C is final at 4. Relax C-D: 4 + 3 = 7. The stale heap entries are skipped when they are popped.

steps.title: Pop D (7): finished
body: Every node is final: A 3, B 1, C 4, D 7. To recover the route, store the previous node whenever you improve a distance (prev[v] = u) and walk back from D: D, C, A, B, S.
Cost: every edge relaxes at most once successfully per heap push, so O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap. Use it for road routing, network delay and cheapest-cost problems.

steps.title: When Dijkstra is wrong
body: The argument "the smallest distance is final" holds only if no later edge can make a path shorter, which needs non-negative weights. With a negative edge a node you finished could still improve.

Use Bellman-Ford for negative edges (V - 1 rounds over all edges, O(V * E)), or limit the number of edges, as in "cheapest flight with at most K stops". For unit weights, plain BFS is simpler; for weights 0 or 1, a deque works (0-1 BFS).

callout.text: Always ask: are weights non-negative? If you do not ask, you may use the wrong algorithm.

title: Binary Search Patterns: Bounds and Search on the Answer
tagline: One template, three uses: find a value, find a boundary, and find the smallest answer that works.
explain: Binary search is easy to describe and easy to get wrong. Interviewers use it to see whether you can keep an invariant. One reliable template, used for every variation, removes almost all off-by-one errors.
## The template: lower bound on a half-open range

Use the range [lo, hi) with lo = 0 and hi = n. While lo < hi, take mid = (lo + hi) // 2. If the value at mid is too small, the answer must be to the right, so lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid may be the answer, so keep it: hi = mid. When the loop ends lo == hi, and that index is the first position that is not too small. If lo == n, no such value exists. The invariant is "the answer, if it exists, is in [lo, hi]".

The cost is O(log n). In Python the standard library does this for you: bisect_left returns the first index whose value is not less than the target, and bisect_right returns the first index whose value is greater than the target.
## Variations built from the template

- Exact search: find lower_bound(x) and check that it is in range and equal to x.
- First and last position of x: lower_bound(x) and upper_bound(x) - 1; the count is the difference.
- Insert position: lower_bound.
- Rotated sorted array: at each step one half is sorted; test whether the target is in that half.
- Minimum of a rotated array: compare mid with the right end.
- Peak element: move toward the larger neighbour.
## Binary search on the answer

Many problems do not give a sorted array, but the answer lies in a numeric range and a yes or no check is monotonic: once a guess works, every larger guess works too (or the reverse). Then search for the first value for which feasible(x) is true. The cost is the number of guesses, log of the range, times the cost of one check.

- Koko eating bananas: the smallest speed finishing in h hours.
- Capacity to ship packages within D days: the smallest capacity.
- Split array largest sum: minimize the largest part.
- Integer square root: the largest x with x * x <= n.
- The smallest divisor so that the sum of ceilings is within a threshold.
## Pitfalls that cost marks

Mixing the two range styles (closed [lo, hi] with half-open updates) causes infinite loops and skipped answers. Writing hi = mid - 1 in a lower-bound search can discard the answer. A feasibility check that is not monotonic makes the search meaningless, so state why it is. In languages with fixed-size integers compute lo + (hi - lo) // 2 to avoid overflow; in Python integers do not overflow.
## How to explain it

Say what the range is, what the invariant is, why each update keeps it, and why the loop ends (the range shrinks every time). Then give the cost. Run the template on a tiny example, including the cases where the target is smaller than all values and larger than all values.
keyPoints: Template: lo, hi = 0, n; while lo < hi: mid; if too small lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid; the answer is lo.
Keep mid when it might be the answer (hi = mid); skip it only when it is definitely too small.
bisect_left and bisect_right are the lower and upper bound.
Binary search on the answer needs a monotonic yes or no check: state why it is monotonic.
Cost is log(range) times the cost of one check.

sql.title: Lower bound, upper bound and first or last position
Binary search on the answer

exercise: Write lower_bound from memory without looking, then use it to solve search-insert-position, first-last-position (both in the problem bank), and find-minimum-in-rotated-array. Then solve min-eating-speed and ship-packages with the first_true helper. For each one write the range, the feasibility function and one sentence on why it is monotonic. Finally run your lower bound by hand on [1, 3, 5] with targets 0, 4 and 6.
pitfalls: Mixing closed and half-open range styles, which causes an infinite loop or a skipped answer.
Using hi = mid - 1 in a lower-bound search, which can discard the answer.
A feasibility check that is not monotonic, so binary search gives nonsense.
Forgetting that lo can equal n, meaning there is no such value.
Using binary search on unsorted data without saying that sorting comes first.

interview.q: How do you avoid off-by-one errors in binary search?
interview.a: I fix one range style, usually the half-open [lo, hi), and one invariant: the answer, if it exists, is in the range. If mid is too small I do lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid. The loop runs while lo < hi and ends with lo == hi. I check on a one-element, empty and all-smaller or all-larger example.

interview.q: What is the difference between bisect_left and bisect_right?
interview.a: bisect_left returns the first index whose value is not less than the target (lower bound); bisect_right returns the first index whose value is greater than the target (upper bound). For a value present several times, the two differ by its count. Together they give first position, last position and count.

interview.q: What does binary search on the answer mean?
interview.a: When a problem asks for the minimum or maximum value of something and a yes or no check of "is x enough" is monotonic, I binary search over the range of x instead of over an array. The cost is log of the range times the cost of one check. Examples: shipping capacity, eating speed, splitting an array.

interview.q: How do you search a rotated sorted array in O(log n)?
interview.a: At every step one half around mid is sorted. Compare the target with that half's ends: if it lies inside, search that half, otherwise search the other. To find the minimum, compare a[mid] with the last element: if larger, the minimum is to the right, otherwise keep mid.

interview.q: Why must the check be monotonic for binary search on the answer?
interview.a: Binary search throws away half of the range by assuming that a failed guess means everything on one side also fails. That holds only if feasibility changes from False to True once and never goes back. If it does not, the discarded half may contain the answer.

scenes.title: Lower bound: first value >= 8

steps.title: The prompt: where does 8 belong?
body: In the sorted list [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13], find the first index whose value is at least 8. This "lower bound" is the building block for insert position, first occurrence and counting.
Use a half-open range [lo, hi): the answer is always inside it, and hi = n means "no such value". The loop runs while lo < hi.

steps.title: mid = 3 (value 7): too small
body: 7 is below 8, so the answer is to the right of mid. Set lo = mid + 1 = 4. The left half is gone for good.

steps.title: mid = 5 (value 11): possible answer
body: 11 is at least 8, so mid may be the answer or the answer may be to its left. Keep it in the range: hi = mid = 5. Never write hi = mid - 1 here, or you could throw away the answer.

predict.question: The value at mid is 11 and the target is 8. Which update is correct for a lower bound?
predict.why: mid might be the first value that is >= 8, so it must stay inside the range: hi = mid. Only a value that is too small can be skipped with lo = mid + 1.

steps.title: mid = 4 (value 9): still possible
body: 9 is at least 8, so hi = 4. The range is [4, 5).

steps.title: lo = hi = 4: the answer
body: The range is empty, and lo is the first index whose value is at least 8: index 4, value 9. If lo were 7 (equal to n), no value would be large enough.
Upper bound (first value > target) is the same with <= in the comparison. First and last occurrence of x: lower_bound(x) and upper_bound(x) - 1. Python's bisect_left and bisect_right do exactly this.

scenes.title: Binary search on the answer: slowest eating speed

steps.title: The prompt: eat all piles within h hours
body: Piles of bananas [2, 3, 5, 7] must be eaten in h = 6 hours. Each hour you pick one pile and eat up to k bananas from it. Find the smallest speed k that finishes in time.
You cannot search the piles, but you can search the answer: speeds 1 to 7 form a sorted range, and for a guess k it is easy to check whether it is fast enough.

card.title: Check a speed k
lines: hours = sum(ceil(p / k) for p in piles)

steps.title: Guess k = 4: 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 hours
body: The check costs O(n). 6 hours is within the limit, so 4 works. Could something smaller work? Keep 4 inside the range: hi = 4.

steps.title: Guess k = 2: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 hours
body: Too slow. The condition is monotonic: if a speed is too slow, every smaller speed is too slow as well, and if a speed works, every larger one works. That property is what makes binary search valid.
So the answer is above 2: lo = 3.

predict.question: Speed 2 is too slow. What can you conclude?
predict.why: The check is monotonic: a slower speed can only take more hours. So everything at or below 2 is out, and the answer is above 2.

steps.title: Guess k = 3: 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7 hours
body: Still too slow. lo = 4.

steps.title: lo = hi = 4: the smallest speed that works
body: The loop ends when lo equals hi. The answer is 4. Total cost: O(n log max_pile) because each of the log(range) guesses takes an O(n) check.
The same pattern solves: capacity to ship packages in D days, split array to minimize the largest sum, the smallest divisor under a threshold, integer square root and koko-style rate problems.

steps.title: The recipe for any "minimum such that" problem
body: 1. Say what the answer is and its range (lo and hi). 2. Write a function feasible(x) that is False, False, ..., True, True. 3. Binary search for the first True: if feasible(mid) then hi = mid else lo = mid + 1.
If a question says "minimize the maximum" or "maximize the minimum", think binary search on the answer.

callout.text: Say out loud why feasible is monotonic. That sentence is the proof that binary search is allowed.

everyday.plain: Binary search finds things by repeatedly cutting the possible places in half.
everyday.story: You guess a number between 1 and 100 and are told only higher or lower. You say 50, hear lower, say 25, hear higher, and keep halving. In about seven guesses you find it. The trick works because every answer rules out half the numbers.
maps: Choosing lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid
words: Finding a value in sorted data by repeatedly looking at the middle and discarding half.
The first position whose value is not smaller than the target.
Changing in only one direction: here, false for a while and then true forever.
A statement that stays true at every step of the loop.

title: Python Classes and the Data Model: Dunder Methods, MRO and Dataclasses
tagline: What Python calls behind the scenes (repr, eq, hash, iter, with) and how inheritance and dataclasses behave.
explain: Python interviews go beyond syntax: "what is a dunder method", "what happens if you override __eq__", "how does multiple inheritance resolve methods", "when would you use a dataclass". These questions test whether you know how the language works behind the scenes. They are also easy to practice.
## The data model: special methods

Python calls specially named methods (with double underscores, "dunder") when you use syntax or built-in functions. You do not call them yourself; you implement them so that your objects fit the language.

- Representation: __repr__ is the unambiguous form for developers and logs; __str__ is the readable form and falls back to __repr__. Always write __repr__.
- Equality and hashing: __eq__ defines ==. A class that defines __eq__ without __hash__ becomes unhashable, so it cannot be a dict key or a set member. Objects that compare equal must have the same hash, and the hash must not change while the object is in a set.
- Ordering: __lt__ and the other comparisons; functools.total_ordering fills in the rest. Return NotImplemented when you cannot compare with the other type.
- Containers: __len__, __getitem__, __contains__, __iter__.
- Iteration protocol: __iter__ returns an iterator and __next__ returns the next item or raises StopIteration. A generator function builds such an iterator for you.
- Context managers: __enter__ and __exit__ make a class work with the with statement.
- Truthiness: __bool__, or __len__ if there is no __bool__.
## Inheritance and the MRO

A class's method resolution order is the list of classes searched for an attribute. Python computes it with C3 linearization: the class itself, then a merge of the parents' own lists and the list of the parents, taking the first candidate that is not in the tail of another list. For a diamond D(B, C) with B(A) and C(A) the order is D, B, C, A. Each parent comes before the shared base, and the written order of bases is respected. Conflicting orders raise a TypeError, and ClassName.__mro__ shows the result.

super() returns a proxy that continues the search after the current class in the MRO of the instance's type, so it is not always the direct parent. In a diamond, cooperative classes that all call super().__init__() initialize each class once.
## Dataclasses

The @dataclass decorator generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated fields. Options: order=True adds the ordering methods, frozen=True makes instances immutable (assignment raises FrozenInstanceError) and, together with eq, generates __hash__, slots=True saves memory. A mutable default such as a list must use field(default_factory=list); a plain list default raises ValueError. With eq=True and frozen=False the dataclass sets __hash__ to None, so such instances are unhashable. __post_init__ is the hook for validation or derived fields, because the generated __init__ does not call a base class __init__.
## Properties, __slots__ and other details

- A property gives attribute syntax with validation, so you can add logic later without changing callers.
- __slots__ replaces the per-instance dict with fixed attributes, saving memory and preventing typos, at the cost of flexibility.
- A class attribute that is a list is shared by all instances; create per-instance state in __init__.
- Composition ("has a") is usually simpler than inheritance ("is a"); use inheritance for a real substitutable relationship.
## How to answer in the interview

Give a one-sentence definition, a tiny example, and one trap. For __eq__: "it defines ==, and if I override it I must also define __hash__ consistent with it, or the class becomes unhashable". For the MRO: "C3 order, parents before the shared base, super follows it".
keyPoints: Dunder methods let objects work with syntax and built-ins: repr, eq, hash, iter, len, with.
Overriding __eq__ without __hash__ makes a class unhashable; equal objects must have equal hashes.
The MRO is a C3 linearization: D(B, C) with a shared base A gives D, B, C, A. Check it with __mro__.
super() goes to the next class in the MRO of the instance, not simply to the parent.
Dataclasses generate init, repr and eq; use default_factory for mutable defaults and frozen=True for hashable, immutable values.

sql.title: MRO, cooperative super() and the eq and hash contract
Dataclasses, the iterator protocol and a context manager

exercise: Without running code, predict D.__mro__ for three class layouts (a diamond, a chain, and one that raises a TypeError), then check with the interpreter. Write a Money class with __repr__, __eq__, __hash__, __lt__ (with total_ordering) and __add__; then rewrite it as a frozen dataclass and compare the two. Make a Range-like class that can be iterated several times and works with len() and "in". Finally explain in two sentences why a dataclass with eq=True and frozen=False cannot be used as a dict key.
pitfalls: Overriding __eq__ and forgetting __hash__, then being surprised that the object cannot go in a set.
Using a mutable default (a list or dict) as a dataclass field or as a function default.
Assuming super() always means the direct parent class.
Putting mutable state in a class attribute, so every instance shares it.
Writing __str__ but no __repr__, so logs and the debugger show unhelpful text.

interview.q: What are dunder methods and why do they exist?
interview.a: They are specially named methods that Python calls for built-in syntax and functions: __repr__ for repr(), __eq__ for ==, __len__ for len(), __iter__ for loops, __enter__ and __exit__ for with, and so on. Implementing them lets your own classes behave like built-in types.

interview.q: What happens if you define __eq__ but not __hash__?
interview.a: Python sets __hash__ to None, so instances become unhashable and cannot be put in a set or used as dict keys. If equal objects should be usable as keys, define __hash__ from the same fields used in __eq__, and keep those fields immutable.

interview.q: What is the MRO and how does Python compute it?
interview.a: The method resolution order is the list of classes searched for an attribute. Python uses C3 linearization: the class, then a merge of the parents' linearizations and the list of bases, taking the first head that is not in the tail of another list. For a diamond D(B, C) the order is D, B, C, A, and conflicting base orders raise a TypeError.

interview.q: What does super() do?
interview.a: It returns a proxy that looks up the next class after the current one in the MRO of the instance's type. In a plain class that is the parent, but in multiple inheritance it can be a sibling. Cooperative classes all call super() so each initialiser or method runs once.

interview.q: When would you use a dataclass, and what are its traps?
interview.a: For classes that mainly hold data: it generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated fields. Traps: a mutable default needs field(default_factory=...); with eq=True and frozen=False the instance is unhashable; frozen=True makes it immutable and hashable; validation belongs in __post_init__.

references.title: The Python 2.3 Method Resolution Order (Python docs)

basis: Sources: the Python dataclasses documentation (read in full: defaults, order, frozen, the eq and hash rules, default_factory, ValueError for unhashable defaults, __post_init__) and the Python HOWTO on the method resolution order (read in full: the C3 merge rule, the diamond result D A B C, monotonicity, conflict errors, duplicate bases). The data model reference page was only partly read verbatim (the sections on objects and types); the details of special method names, such as __eq__ and __hash__, come from a summary of that page and from my own knowledge of Python, and the samples check each of them by running. The HOWTO does not cover super(), so the super() explanation is general knowledge that I verified by the asserts. The interview framing and the order of topics are my judgment. Priorities and hours are my judgment; the roadmap raises the priority for roles that need it.

scenes.title: Method resolution order in a diamond

steps.title: The prompt: which greet() runs?
body: Class D inherits from B and C, and both inherit from A. If A, B and C each define greet(), and D does not, which one does d.greet() call? With several parents, Python needs a clear, repeatable order.
The answer is the method resolution order (MRO), the linearized list of a class and its ancestors. You can print it: D.__mro__.

steps.title: Each class has its own linearization
body: The linearization of A is just [A]. For B(A) it is [B, A], and for C(A) it is [C, A]: a class comes first, then its parents in order.

steps.title: Merge them: D, B, C, A
body: L[D] = D + merge([B, A], [C, A], [B, C]). The rule: take the first head that does not appear in the tail of any other list. B qualifies, so take B. Next, A is in the tail of [C, A], so skip it and take C. Now A is free, so take A.
Result: D, B, C, A. Parents are searched before the shared grandparent, and the order of the base classes (B before C) is respected.

predict.question: For class D(B, C) with B(A) and C(A), what is D.__mro__ (names only)?
predict.why: C3 linearization puts D first, then B and C in the written order, and A only after both of its subclasses: D, B, C, A. A depth-first search would wrongly give D, B, A, C.

steps.title: Attribute lookup walks the MRO
body: d.greet() looks in D, then B, then C, then A, and uses the first class that defines greet. The same order applies to every attribute, not only to methods.

steps.title: super() follows the MRO, not "the parent"
body: super() means "the next class after this one in the MRO of the instance's class". Inside B, super() is C when the object is a D, but A when the object is a plain B. That is why cooperative methods, where each class calls super().__init__(), run every class exactly once.
Rule of thumb: if you use multiple inheritance, call super() in every class and accept **kwargs, so the chain is never broken. Prefer composition or small mixins to deep hierarchies.

card.title: Python
lines: return "B " + super().greet()   # next in MRO of type(self)

steps.title: When the order is inconsistent
body: Python refuses a class whose base order cannot be linearized: class X(A, B) together with class Y(B, A) cannot be combined into Z(X, Y), and raises TypeError (older versions say "MRO conflict"). Listing the same base twice is also an error.
The linearization is monotonic: if one class comes before another in a base class's order, it does in every subclass too.

callout.text: A TypeError from conflicting bases means two of your classes disagree about the order of their parents. Reorder the bases.

everyday.plain: Python classes can plug into the language itself: printing, comparing, looping and the with statement all call special methods you can write.
everyday.story: A family recipe says "ask Grandma if you are stuck". If a recipe has two grandmothers, there must be a fixed order for who you ask first. Python does the same for classes with several parents: it makes one ordered list and asks each in turn.
maps: The fixed order of who to ask
Asking the next person in the list
A diamond in the class tree
words: A method with double underscores, such as __len__, that Python calls for you.
The order in which Python searches the classes of an object for a method.
A class whose basic methods are generated from its annotated fields.
Safe to use as a dict key or set member because its hash never changes.

title: SQL Interview Patterns: Nth Highest, Top N per Group, Duplicates and NULL Traps
tagline: The ten query shapes that appear again and again, and the ties-and-NULL traps that fail answers.
explain: SQL screens for analyst, data and backend roles reuse a small set of query shapes. If you know the shapes and the traps, most questions become a matter of choosing the right one. This lesson lists them with the reasoning, and the code samples run against an in-memory SQLite database, so you can check each answer.
## Ranking: Nth highest and top N per group

Window functions number or compare rows without collapsing them. A window function is written with an OVER clause, and its PARTITION BY splits the rows into groups. Three ranking functions behave differently on ties: row_number gives unique numbers (1, 2, 3, 4), rank gives equal rows the same number and then skips (1, 1, 3, 4), and dense_rank does not skip (1, 1, 2, 3). SQLite's documentation describes exactly this, including that rank returns the row_number of the first peer.

- Nth highest distinct salary: dense_rank over salary descending, filter on N, select DISTINCT.
- Top N per group: row_number with PARTITION BY the group and ORDER BY the measure, then filter in an outer query or CTE. Add a tiebreaker for repeatability.
- A window function cannot be used in WHERE, so wrap the query.
## Finding duplicates and counting

Duplicates: GROUP BY the columns that define "the same" and keep groups with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. To delete duplicates and keep one row, keep the minimum id per group. Remember that WHERE filters rows before grouping and HAVING filters groups after aggregation. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts distinct values.
## Missing rows: anti-joins and the NULL trap

To list customers who have no orders, use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN with a check that the right-hand key IS NULL. Avoid NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL: x NOT IN (1, NULL) is unknown, never true, so the whole query returns no rows. Related trap: a WHERE filter on the right table of a LEFT JOIN removes the NULL rows, turning it into an inner join. Put the filter in the ON clause.
## Running totals, changes and consecutive rows

Running total: SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY date). Change from the previous period: x - LAG(x) OVER (ORDER BY date); the first row gets NULL. The default window frame with an ORDER BY runs from the start to the current row, including peers with the same value, so use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW if equal values must not be added together. For consecutive sequences ("three days in a row"), subtract a row number from the date to build a group key.
## Joins and shape questions

Know INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins, and be able to say how many rows come out: a join on a non-unique key multiplies rows. Self-joins find pairs or an employee's manager. A CASE expression inside an aggregate pivots rows into columns (SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)).
## How to answer

Restate the question, ask about ties, NULLs and empty groups, write the smallest query that could work, test it mentally on a three-row table, and then say how an index would help (filters and join keys, not the ranking itself). Mention the SQL dialect if a feature, such as DISTINCT ON or QUALIFY, is not everywhere.
keyPoints: row_number is unique, rank leaves gaps after ties, dense_rank does not: pick by how ties should behave.
Top N per group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY measure DESC), then filter in an outer query.
Duplicates: GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.
NOT IN returns nothing when the subquery has a NULL: use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL.
LAG and SUM OVER give period changes and running totals; the first row's LAG is NULL.

sql.title: Nth highest, top N per group and duplicates, checked on SQLite
sql.code:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INT, email TEXT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES
 (1, 'Ana', 'eng', 90, 'a@x.io'), (2, 'Bo', 'eng', 90, 'b@x.io'), (3, 'Cy', 'eng', 80, 'c@x.io'),
 (4, 'Di', 'ops', 70, 'd@x.io'), (5, 'Ed', 'ops', 60, 'e@x.io'), (6, 'Flo', 'ops', 60, 'b@x.io');
""")

def q(sql, *args):
    return db.execute(sql, args).fetchall()

# ranking functions on ties
rows = q("""SELECT name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, id),
                   RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC), DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)
            FROM emp WHERE dept = 'eng' ORDER BY id""")
assert rows == [("Ana", 1, 1, 1), ("Bo", 2, 1, 1), ("Cy", 3, 3, 2)]

# second highest distinct salary
assert q("""SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM (
              SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM emp) WHERE r = 2""") == [(80,)]

# a salary that does not exist returns no rows (the caller can map this to NULL)
assert q("""SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM (
              SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM emp) WHERE r = 9""") == []

# top 2 per department, with a tiebreaker
top2 = q("""WITH r AS (SELECT name, dept, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn FROM emp)
            SELECT dept, name FROM r WHERE rn <= 2 ORDER BY dept, rn""")
assert top2 == [("eng", "Ana"), ("eng", "Bo"), ("ops", "Di"), ("ops", "Ed")]

# duplicate emails
assert q("SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1") == [("b@x.io", 2)]

# delete duplicates, keep the lowest id
db.execute("DELETE FROM emp WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM emp GROUP BY email)")
assert q("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp") == [(5,)]

sql.title: Anti-joins, the NOT IN NULL trap, LAG and running totals
sql.code:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'ann'), (2, 'bob'), (3, 'cat');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, NULL);
CREATE TABLE sales(month TEXT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('2026-01', 100), ('2026-02', 150), ('2026-03', 120);
""")

def q(sql):
    return db.execute(sql).fetchall()

# who never ordered? correct forms
left = q("""SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
            WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.name""")
exists = q("""SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS
              (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY name""")
assert left == exists == [("bob",), ("cat",)]

# the trap: one NULL in the subquery makes NOT IN return nothing
assert q("SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)") == []

# filter in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join; in ON it keeps unmatched rows
in_where = q("""SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
                WHERE o.id > 1 GROUP BY c.id""")
in_on = q("""SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.id > 1
             GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id""")
assert in_where == [("ann", 1)]
assert in_on == [("ann", 1), ("bob", 0), ("cat", 0)]

# running total and change from the previous month
rows = q("""SELECT month, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month),
                   amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month) FROM sales ORDER BY month""")
assert rows == [("2026-01", 100, None), ("2026-02", 250, 50), ("2026-03", 370, -30)]

# conditional aggregation pivots rows into columns
assert q("""SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN amount >= 120 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), SUM(CASE WHEN amount < 120 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
            FROM sales""") == [(2, 1)]

exercise: Create the two tables from the samples in SQLite (or Postgres) and, without looking, write: the third highest distinct salary, the top 3 per department, all duplicate emails, customers with no orders (in two different ways), a running total and month-over-month change, and the number of orders per customer including customers with zero. For each, write one line about what happens with ties and with NULL. Then break the NOT IN query on purpose by inserting a NULL and watch the result change.
pitfalls: Using rank or row_number when the question means "the Nth distinct value".
Filtering on a window function in WHERE, which is not allowed: wrap the query.
NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL, which returns no rows.
A WHERE condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN, which silently makes it an inner join.
Counting with COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN, which counts the unmatched row as 1; count a column of the right table instead.

interview.q: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK?
interview.a: All number rows in an ordering. row_number is unique even for ties (1, 2, 3, 4); rank gives ties the same number and skips the next ones (1, 1, 3, 4); dense_rank gives ties the same number without gaps (1, 1, 2, 3). For the Nth highest distinct value use dense_rank.

interview.q: How do you get the top 3 salaries in each department?
interview.a: Number the rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) in a CTE or subquery and select rows with the number at most 3. If ties must all be included, use DENSE_RANK or RANK instead. Window functions cannot be filtered in the same SELECT.

interview.q: Why can NOT IN return no rows, and what do you use instead?
interview.a: If the subquery returns even one NULL, then x NOT IN (...) evaluates to unknown for every row, so nothing passes the filter. Use NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery, or a LEFT JOIN and filter for the right-hand key being NULL.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.a: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can use COUNT, SUM and so on. Use WHERE first to reduce the rows, HAVING only for conditions on aggregates.

interview.q: How would you calculate month-over-month change?
interview.a: Aggregate to one row per month, then use LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month) to get the previous month and subtract: amount - LAG(amount) ... The first month has no previous row, so the result is NULL, and I would say how to treat that. Percentage change divides by the previous value, guarding against zero.

basis: Sources: the SQLite window-functions page (read: an OVER clause identifies a window function, row_number, rank and dense_rank and how rank relates to row_number, lag and lead returning NULL when there is no row, the default frame, PARTITION BY; the sections on frames and the version history were partly from a summary, so the SQLite 3.25 start of window-function support is not independently confirmed). The NOT IN NULL behavior, the LEFT JOIN filter trap and the query shapes are standard SQL that I chose from experience with typical screening questions, which is my own judgment, not a published list. Every query in the samples runs on SQLite with asserts, though dialects differ (for example, Postgres has DISTINCT ON and some engines have QUALIFY). Priorities and hours are my judgment; the roadmap raises the priority for roles that need it.

scenes.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK on tied salaries

steps.title: The prompt: the second highest salary
body: Salaries: Ana 90, Bo 90, Cy 80, Di 70. "Second highest" is ambiguous when there are ties. Most interviewers mean the second highest distinct value: 80.
Ranking functions give each row a number inside an ordering, and they treat ties differently. Choosing the wrong one is the classic mistake. Ask: what should happen with ties?

steps.title: ROW_NUMBER: always unique
body: row_number() numbers the rows 1, 2, 3, 4, even for equal salaries (the tie is broken arbitrarily unless you add a tiebreaker). The row numbered 2 is Bo with 90, the same as the top salary, which is wrong for "second highest distinct".

card.title: SQL
lines: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn

steps.title: RANK: ties share a number and leave a gap
body: rank() gives equal rows the same number and then skips: 1, 1, 3, 4. There is no rank 2 at all, so "WHERE rank = 2" returns nothing.

predict.question: With salaries 90, 90, 80, 70, what does RANK() give the row with 80?
predict.why: Two rows share rank 1, so the next rank is 3 (rank skips numbers after a tie). DENSE_RANK would give 2.

steps.title: DENSE_RANK: no gaps
body: dense_rank() gives 1, 1, 2, 3. The row with rank 2 is Cy, 80: the answer. Use DISTINCT or LIMIT 1 because several rows can share the rank.
Quick rule: row_number for "exactly N rows", rank for competition ranking with gaps, dense_rank for "the Nth distinct value".

card.title: SQL
lines: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r

steps.title: Top N per group: PARTITION BY
body: "Top 2 earners in each department": number the rows inside each department with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id), then filter on that number in an outer query. You cannot filter on a window function in the same SELECT, so wrap it in a subquery or a CTE.
Add a tiebreaker (such as id) to the ORDER BY so the result is deterministic.

card.title: SQL
lines: PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn

steps.title: Traps: NOT IN with NULL, HAVING, and joins
body: NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery contains a NULL, because x NOT IN (1, NULL) is unknown. Prefer NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL for "customers with no orders".

title: Design a Distributed Cache
tagline: Partition, evict, replicate and protect the database: the full design behind "add Redis" in an interview answer.
explain: Almost every system design answer says "add a cache", and a good interviewer then asks you to design it. The cache is a small distributed system of its own: it must partition data, survive failures, decide what to evict, and avoid harming the database it protects. This lesson gives the design in the order to present it.
## Requirements and numbers

Ask about read and write rates, the size of the working set, the acceptable staleness, and whether data loss is allowed (usually yes, because the cache can be rebuilt). From the hit rate you can compute the load on the database: at 100,000 reads a second and a 90% hit rate, 10,000 reads a second still reach it, so a few points of hit rate matter a lot. The numbers in this lesson are assumptions to practice with.
## Partitioning: consistent hashing

The first idea, node = hash(key) % N, moves most keys when N changes, which makes the cache cold exactly when you scale or recover. Consistent hashing places node points on a ring and assigns each key to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. Virtual nodes even out the load. Redis Cluster uses a related approach with 16,384 hash slots that are assigned to nodes, and the Dynamo paper describes consistent hashing with replication.
## Read and write paths

Cache-aside is the default: the application reads the cache, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache with a TTL. On a write, update the database first and then delete the cached key (deleting is safer than updating because it avoids storing a stale value). Write-through and write-back exist, with different trade-offs in consistency and durability. Routing can live in a client library (one fewer hop) or in a proxy tier (simpler clients).
## Eviction and expiry

Memory is finite. LRU evicts the least recently used key and is a sound default; LFU keeps frequently used keys. Redis documents policies such as noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-lru and volatile-ttl, where the volatile policies only consider keys with an expiry. TTLs bound staleness; add random jitter so keys do not all expire at the same time.
## The hard problems

- Hot keys: balanced keys do not mean balanced traffic. Use a short-lived local cache in each app server, or replicate the hot key under several names.
- Stampede: when a popular key expires, many requests miss together. Allow one rebuild per key (singleflight or a lock), refresh early, and serve stale data while refreshing.
- Staleness: delete after the database commit and keep a TTL; know that a race can reintroduce an old value briefly.
- Failure: a lost node means misses, so rate-limit and break the circuit to protect the database, and replace nodes gradually.
- Replication: a replica per shard keeps most data through a failover; asynchronous replication is normally acceptable.
## How to present it

Requirements and numbers, then API and data placement, then the read and write paths, then eviction, then replicas, then the failure cases (hot key, stampede, node loss), and finish with what you would monitor: hit rate, evictions, latency percentiles and memory. Naming the failure modes is what separates a diagram from a design.
keyPoints: hash(key) % N moves most keys when N changes; consistent hashing moves only about 1/N.
Cache-aside: read the cache, on a miss read the database and fill with a TTL; on a write, commit then delete the key.
LRU is a good default; LFU keeps popular keys; TTL with jitter bounds staleness and avoids synchronized expiry.
Hot keys need a local cache or replication; stampedes need one rebuild per key.
Protect the database: rate limits, circuit breaker, warm up new nodes gradually; the database is the source of truth.

sql.title: A consistent hash ring with virtual nodes: how many keys move?
An LRU cache with TTL, using a fake clock
sql.code:
from collections import OrderedDict

class TTLCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity, clock):
        self.capacity, self.clock = capacity, clock
        self.data = OrderedDict()                    # key -> (value, expires_at); order = recency

    def get(self, key):
        item = self.data.get(key)
        if item is None:
            return None
        value, expires = item
        if self.clock() >= expires:                  # expired: behave as a miss
            del self.data[key]
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)                   # mark as recently used
        return value

    def set(self, key, value, ttl):
        self.data[key] = (value, self.clock() + ttl)
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        while len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)            # evict the least recently used

now = [0]
cache = TTLCache(2, lambda: now[0])
cache.set("a", 1, ttl=10)
cache.set("b", 2, ttl=10)
assert cache.get("a") == 1                           # a is now the most recent
cache.set("c", 3, ttl=10)                            # evicts b, the least recently used
assert cache.get("b") is None and cache.get("a") == 1 and cache.get("c") == 3
now[0] = 11
assert cache.get("a") is None                        # expired by TTL

def get_or_load(cache, key, loader, ttl, calls):
    """Cache-aside; a real system also needs one rebuild per key (singleflight)."""
    value = cache.get(key)
    if value is None:
        calls.append(key)
        value = loader(key)
        cache.set(key, value, ttl)
    return value

calls = []
assert get_or_load(cache, "x", lambda k: k.upper(), 10, calls) == "X"
assert get_or_load(cache, "x", lambda k: k.upper(), 10, calls) == "X"
assert calls == ["x"]                                # the second read was a hit

Then run the Ring sample, change the number of virtual nodes from 100 to 1, and explain what happens to the balance.
pitfalls: Placing keys with hash % N and not noticing that scaling empties the cache.
Updating the cached value on a write instead of deleting it, which can store stale data.
Ignoring hot keys: balanced keys do not mean balanced traffic.
No plan for a stampede, so one expiry sends thousands of queries to the database.
Treating the cache as the source of truth.

interview.q: How do you partition keys across cache nodes, and why not hash(key) % N?
interview.a: With consistent hashing: nodes (with virtual points) sit on a ring and a key goes to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. With modulo, changing N remaps most keys, so the cache becomes cold and the database is flooded.

interview.q: What is cache-aside and how do you keep it consistent with the database?
interview.a: The application reads the cache; on a miss it reads the database and fills the cache with a TTL. On a write it updates the database, then deletes the key. A short TTL is the safety net for the race where a slow reader refills an old value, so staleness is bounded but not zero.

interview.q: How do you handle a hot key?
interview.a: Add a small short-TTL cache in each application server, replicate the key under several names (key#0 to key#N) and read a random one, and detect hot keys from access counts. Consistent hashing balances keys, not traffic, so a single popular key can overload one node.

interview.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: When a popular key expires, many requests miss at once and all query the database. Prevent it by allowing one request to rebuild the key (singleflight or a lock) while others wait or use the stale value, by refreshing before expiry, and by adding jitter to TTLs.

interview.q: Which eviction policy would you choose?
interview.a: LRU is a good default because recently used data is likely to be used again. LFU suits stable popularity. In Redis, allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu treat every key as a candidate, while volatile policies only consider keys with a TTL. I would measure hit rate and evictions before changing the policy.

steps.title: Which node owns a key? hash(key) % N
body: The simplest rule: node = hash(key) % N. It spreads keys evenly, but when N changes from 3 to 4, almost every key maps to a different node. The cache is suddenly cold, and the database takes all the traffic.
On average only 1 in N keys keeps its node after resizing with the modulo rule: about 25% stay when going from 3 to 4 nodes.

steps.title: Consistent hashing: only about 1/N of the keys move
body: Place nodes (many virtual points per node) on a hash ring and give each key to the next node clockwise. Adding node 4 takes over only the arcs next to its points, so about a quarter of the keys move, and they come from all the other nodes evenly. Removing a node sends only its keys to the next nodes.
Virtual nodes smooth out the load, and let a bigger machine own more points. Dynamo and Redis Cluster use related ideas: Redis Cluster uses 16,384 fixed hash slots instead of a ring.

steps.title: The read path: cache-aside
body: The client library computes the owner and asks that node. On a hit it returns the value in about a millisecond. On a miss the application reads the database and writes the value to the cache with a TTL. Putting the routing in the client library avoids an extra network hop; a proxy tier is the alternative, easier to change but one more hop.
The cache stores only what can be recomputed. The database stays the source of truth.

steps.title: Replication and availability
body: If a cache node dies, its keys become misses and the database takes the extra load. For a large cache, keep a replica of each node (a primary and a replica per shard) so a failover keeps most of the data, or accept the cold start and protect the database with limits.
A cache is allowed to lose data, so asynchronous replication is normally enough.

steps.title: Eviction and TTL: memory is finite
body: When memory is full the node evicts keys. LRU (least recently used) is the common policy; LFU (least frequently used) keeps popular keys longer. Redis offers policies such as noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-lru and volatile-ttl; the volatile ones consider only keys that have an expiry.
TTLs bound staleness and clean up old data. Add random jitter to TTLs so keys do not all expire together.

card.title: Policies
lines: allkeys-lru    evict least recently used, any key
volatile-ttl   evict keys closest to expiry

steps.title: A hot key overloads one node
body: Consistent hashing balances keys, not traffic. One celebrity product page can send most requests to the single node that owns its key.

Fixes: a small in-process cache in each app server with a short TTL, replicating the hot key over several nodes by adding a random suffix (key#0 to key#9) when reading, and detecting hot keys from access counts.

hud.v: one node takes all the reads

steps.title: Stampedes and stale data
body: When a popular key expires, many requests miss at once and all go to the database: a stampede. Let one request rebuild the value (a lock or request coalescing, called singleflight) while the others wait or use the stale copy, and refresh early or with jitter.

Staleness: on a write, delete the cached key after the database commit, and keep a TTL as a safety net. A race where a slow reader refills the cache with an old value just after the delete is possible, so short TTLs matter.

steps.title: When a node fails, and the summary
body: A failed node loses its share of the keys. Reads fall through to the database, so protect it: rate limits, a circuit breaker, and a fallback to slightly stale data. Add a new node and let it warm up gradually.

Summary: partition with consistent hashing, cache-aside reads, replicas for availability, LRU or LFU with TTL and jitter, local caches for hot keys, singleflight for stampedes, and the database as the source of truth.

title: Design a Metrics and Alerting System
tagline: What to measure, how to collect and store it, and how to alert without waking people for nothing.
explain: Monitoring is a common system design question for backend, SRE and platform roles, and it is also what experienced interviewers ask about your own projects: "how did you know it was broken?". The design covers measurement, collection, storage, queries and alerting. This lesson follows the order of a good answer.
## Start with what to measure

Google's SRE book recommends four golden signals for any user-facing service: latency (distinguish slow successes from fast errors), traffic (demand on the system), errors (the rate of failing requests) and saturation (how full the service is). If you can only measure four things, measure these. Then add a few metrics about the user's experience and business, such as the success rate of checkout.
## Metrics, logs and traces

Metrics are numbers over time: small, cheap and ideal for dashboards and alerts. Logs record events with detail. Traces follow one request through several services. A typical debugging path moves from a metric alert, to a trace of a slow request, to the logs of the failing component.
## Collection: pull or push

In a pull model, a collector scrapes an HTTP endpoint of each service on a schedule. The Prometheus overview describes collection as a pull model over HTTP, with targets from service discovery or static configuration, and a push gateway for short-lived jobs. Pull makes a dead target visible as a failed scrape, and gives the collector control of the load. Push suits batch jobs, firewalled clients and very large fleets, but silence becomes ambiguous.
## The data model and cardinality

A series is a metric name plus labels, for example http_requests_total{service="api", status="500"}, and each sample is a timestamp and value. Every distinct combination of label values is a new series. High-cardinality labels such as user id or a raw URL create millions of series and are the most common cause of monitoring outages. Keep labels bounded.
## Storage and queries

A time-series database exploits the pattern: samples arrive in time order and are rarely modified. It writes append-only blocks, compresses timestamps and values, indexes labels, keeps recent data on fast storage, and downsamples or expires old data. Counters are shown as rates (increase per second over a window); latency is stored as a histogram so percentiles can be estimated, since averages hide slow requests and percentiles cannot be averaged across servers.
## Alerting

An alert rule is a query evaluated on a schedule, with a duration that must hold before it fires. An alert manager groups, de-duplicates, silences and routes alerts. Alert on symptoms that users feel and tie them to service level objectives; every page should require a human action. Alert fatigue is a design failure, not a people problem.
## Scale and reliability

Shard collection by service or region, run redundant collectors, keep a long-term downsampled store for history and global queries, and monitor the monitoring system itself (a "dead man's switch" alert that fires if the system goes quiet). Be ready to explain what you drop first when overloaded.
keyPoints: Measure the four golden signals first: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
Metrics say what and how much, traces say where, logs say why.
Pull makes a dead target visible as a failed scrape; push suits short-lived jobs and firewalled clients.
Each label combination is a series: keep labels bounded and never use ids such as user_id.
Alert on user-visible symptoms with a duration, group and route alerts, and monitor the monitor.

sql.title: Counter rates with resets, and percentiles from histogram buckets
sql.code:
def rate(samples):
    """samples: list of (timestamp_seconds, counter_value). Per-second increase, treating a drop as a counter reset."""
    increase = 0.0
    for (t0, v0), (t1, v1) in zip(samples, samples[1:]):
        increase += (v1 - v0) if v1 >= v0 else v1       # after a reset the counter restarted from zero
    return increase / (samples[-1][0] - samples[0][0])

assert rate([(0, 0), (15, 30), (30, 60)]) == 2.0
assert rate([(0, 100), (15, 130), (30, 10)]) == (30 + 10) / 30       # the process restarted between samples

def percentile_from_buckets(buckets, q):
    """buckets: list of (upper_bound, cumulative_count) sorted by bound. Linear interpolation inside the bucket."""
    total = buckets[-1][1]
    target = q * total
    lower_bound, lower_count = 0.0, 0
    for upper, count in buckets:
        if count >= target:
            span = count - lower_count
            frac = (target - lower_count) / span if span else 0
            return lower_bound + (upper - lower_bound) * frac
        lower_bound, lower_count = upper, count
    return buckets[-1][0]

# latency in seconds: 50 requests <= 0.1, 90 <= 0.25, 99 <= 0.5, 100 <= 1.0
hist = [(0.1, 50), (0.25, 90), (0.5, 99), (1.0, 100)]
assert abs(percentile_from_buckets(hist, 0.5) - 0.1) < 1e-9
assert 0.25 < percentile_from_buckets(hist, 0.95) < 0.5
assert percentile_from_buckets(hist, 1.0) == 1.0

Then answer: how do you find out that the monitoring system itself has failed?
pitfalls: Using high-cardinality labels (user id, request id, raw URL) and creating millions of series.
Alerting on averages, which hide slow requests, instead of percentiles or error ratios.
Alerts without a duration, so every blip pages someone.
Alerting on causes (CPU is high) instead of symptoms users feel (errors and latency).
No alert for "the collector stopped scraping", so a dead monitor looks like a quiet system.

interview.q: What would you monitor for a new service?
interview.a: The four golden signals: latency (split successes and errors), traffic, error rate and saturation (CPU, memory, queue depth, connection pools), plus one metric that reflects the user's experience, such as checkout success. I alert on user-visible symptoms and keep the cause metrics on dashboards for investigation.

interview.q: Pull or push for collecting metrics?
interview.a: Pull (as in Prometheus) lets the collector control the load and treats a failed scrape as a signal that the target is down. Push is better for short-lived batch jobs, which cannot be scraped (Prometheus provides a push gateway for them), and for clients behind firewalls. I would use pull by default and push for batch jobs.

interview.q: What is cardinality and why does it matter in monitoring?
interview.a: Each unique combination of label values is a separate time series. A label with unbounded values, such as user_id, multiplies the series count into the millions, which exhausts memory and makes queries slow. I keep labels to small bounded sets and put high-cardinality detail in logs or traces.

interview.q: Why use percentiles and histograms instead of averages?
interview.a: An average hides slow requests: 1% of users could wait many seconds while the mean looks fine. Recording latency as histogram buckets lets you estimate p95 and p99. Percentiles cannot be averaged across servers, but histogram buckets can be summed and the percentile computed afterwards.

interview.q: How do you design alerts that do not cause alert fatigue?
interview.a: Alert on symptoms tied to service level objectives (error ratio, latency), with a duration so blips do not fire, and group and de-duplicate in an alert manager. Every page must need a human action; low urgency items go to a ticket or chat. I review noisy alerts regularly and delete or tune them.

steps.title: Collecting: pull or push

steps.title: The data model: name, labels and cardinality
body: A time series is identified by a metric name and key-value labels, for example http_requests_total{service="api", status="500"}. Each sample is a timestamp and a value. Labels make slicing easy.

steps.title: Storage: a time-series database
body: Samples arrive in time order and are rarely changed, so a time-series database writes them in append-only blocks, compresses neighbouring timestamps and values well (timestamps are regular, values change slowly), and keeps a label index to find the series for a query.

Recent data stays on fast local storage. Old data is downsampled (for example, one point per five minutes) and expires after a retention period. Each Prometheus server is standalone and does not depend on distributed storage, which keeps it simple and reliable.

steps.title: Queries: rates and percentiles
body: Counters only go up, so charts show a rate: the increase per second over a window. A query language such as PromQL does this over stored series.

steps.title: Alerting that people can trust
body: An alert rule is a query evaluated regularly: for example, error ratio above 5% for 5 minutes. The "for" duration avoids waking someone for a blip. A separate alert manager groups related alerts, removes duplicates, silences planned work and routes by severity to a pager or chat.

steps.title: Scale, high availability and the summary
body: One server cannot hold 10 million series forever. Split scraping by service or region across several collectors, run two identical collectors for availability, and send downsampled data to a long-term store for months of history and a global view across regions.

Summary: golden signals, pull-based collection with labels of bounded cardinality, an append-only time-series store with retention and downsampling, rate and histogram queries, and alerts on user impact. Monitor the monitor: an alert for "the collector stopped scraping".
